Resolved the Python 3.11 google-api-core (versions 2.28.0 to 2.43.0) performance degradation issue for new environments and image updates:

  • Images released on or after November 6, 2026 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.6, composer-3-airflow-3.2.2-build.10, composer-3-airflow-2.11.1-build.23, and composer-2.17.17-airflow-2.11.1) preinstall google-api-core 2.43.1.
  • Base container images for earlier affected Managed Airflow (Gen 3) and Managed Airflow (Gen 2) builds have been patched across all regions. Newly created environments aren't affected, even when created with an earlier build.

Existing environments continue running cached container images until updated through scheduled maintenance or a manual environment update (such as upgrading the image version, updating a PyPI package, or restarting Airflow workloads in eligible Gen 3 regions). For step-by-step mitigation instructions, see the known issue for Managed Airflow (Gen 3) or Managed Airflow (Gen 2).

Model Armor

Feature

Filter version v4 under the Latest alias includes an updated prompt injection and jailbreak detection filter with the following improvements:

  • Higher recall for indirect prompt injection (IPI) and tool calls.
  • Higher recall for conversational inputs at a lower false positive rate.
  • Higher recall for jailbreak attacks.

For more information, see Filter version history.

Policy Controller

Deprecated

Policy Controller is deprecated as of November 12, 2026, and reaches end of support on December 31, 2027. Starting January 31, 2027, you can't enable Policy Controller in fleet host projects that don't already have Policy Controller enabled. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blocks upgrades to version 1.39 and later for clusters that have Policy Controller installed. Clusters that run GKE version 1.39 and later don't support Policy Controller. On December 31, 2027, technical support, security patching on GKE version 1.38 and earlier, and the Google Cloud console dashboard for Policy Controller end.

Migrate your admission policies to Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicies, Pod Security Admission, or self-managed Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper. For more information, see Migrate from Policy Controller.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

You can deploy Secure Web Proxy as an Agent Gateway to centrally secure, govern, and monitor outbound traffic from AI agents that run on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and Cloud Run. Use this feature to control how your agents interact with large language models (LLMs), Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, remote agents, and external APIs in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. For more information, see Deploy Secure Web Proxy as an Agent Gateway.

This feature is available in Preview.

title: Agent Distraction
description: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
description: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.

title: AI Takeover: Is the Software Engineering Industry Preparing to Replace Developers?
description:
Let's stop pretending this is just another technology trend.

Something fundamental is changing in software development.

AI can write React components, generate APIs, debug applications, create tests, refactor codebases, and even build entire products from natural language instructions.

A few years ago, these capabilities sounded like science fiction.

Today, they're becoming part of everyday development.

And this raises an uncomfortable question:

Are we witnessing the beginning of an AI Takeover of the software engineering industry?

Not in some distant future.

Right now.

1. The AI Takeover Has Already Started

Remember when knowing how to write code was a competitive advantage?

It still matters, but the value of simply producing code is changing.

Consider what a developer can do today with AI tools:

  • Generate a complete React application.
  • Build reusable components from a design.
  • Create backend endpoints.
  • Write database queries.
  • Generate unit and integration tests.
  • Analyze errors and suggest fixes.
  • Refactor existing code.
  • Explain unfamiliar codebases.

Tasks that once required hours of work can sometimes be completed in minutes.

This is the first major part of the AI Takeover.

AI isn't necessarily replacing software engineers directly.

It's changing how much engineering work can be completed by one person.

And companies are paying attention.

2. The Real Threat Isn't AI. It's Developers Who Know How to Use It Better.

Here's where things get interesting.

Imagine two developers.

Developer A:

  • Writes everything manually.
  • Spends hours searching documentation.
  • Implements repetitive code.
  • Avoids AI tools because they believe traditional coding is better.

Developer B:

  • Understands programming fundamentals.
  • Uses AI to explore solutions.
  • Automates repetitive tasks.
  • Reviews generated code carefully.
  • Focuses on architecture and engineering decisions.

Both developers might have similar technical knowledge.

But their productivity can be dramatically different.

The AI Takeover doesn't necessarily mean that AI will replace every developer.

It may mean that developers who effectively use AI will outperform those who refuse to adapt.

And eventually, companies may need fewer people to accomplish the same amount of work.

That's a much more immediate concern.

3. Junior Developers Could Be the First to Feel the Impact

This is probably one of the most uncomfortable consequences of the AI Takeover.

Historically, junior developers learned by working on relatively simple tasks:

  • Fixing small bugs.
  • Building basic components.
  • Writing straightforward API integrations.
  • Creating forms.
  • Updating existing features.
  • Writing simple tests.

These tasks were opportunities to gain experience.

But many of them can now be handled by AI-assisted workflows.

So what happens to developers who are just entering the industry?

If companies automate more entry-level tasks, the traditional path from junior to senior developer could become harder.

And there's another problem.

If AI handles all the simple tasks, where will junior developers get the experience they need to become senior engineers?

This is a question the industry hasn't fully answered.

4. The AI Takeover Is Changing What It Means to Be a Developer

For years, developers were evaluated largely by their ability to write code.

But writing code is only one part of software engineering.

Consider these responsibilities:

Understanding requirements

AI can generate an implementation, but understanding what a business actually needs is a different challenge.

System architecture

Choosing how different parts of an application communicate requires understanding trade-offs, constraints, and long-term consequences.

Debugging complex systems

A generated solution might work in isolation but fail under real-world conditions.

Security and reliability

Someone must understand the consequences of shipping insecure or unreliable software.

Technical decision-making

Choosing the right solution is often more important than implementing it quickly.

This is why I believe the AI Takeover will change the definition of a valuable developer.

The most valuable engineers may not be those who write the most code.

They may be those who make the best decisions about what code should exist in the first place.

5. What Happens to Frontend Developers?

Let's look specifically at frontend development.

AI tools are already capable of generating:

  • React components.
  • Tailwind CSS layouts.
  • Responsive interfaces.
  • Form validation.
  • Custom hooks.
  • API integrations.
  • Basic application architecture.

You can describe a dashboard and receive a working implementation surprisingly quickly.

So is frontend development becoming less valuable?

I don't think the answer is that simple.

Building a visually acceptable interface is becoming easier.

Building a reliable, accessible, maintainable, and genuinely useful product is still difficult.

There is a significant difference between generating a React component and understanding:

  • React rendering behavior.
  • State management.
  • Component composition.
  • Performance bottlenecks.
  • Accessibility.
  • Browser behavior.
  • Design systems.
  • Complex application architecture.

The AI Takeover might reduce the value of repetitive frontend implementation.

But it could increase the importance of deeper frontend engineering knowledge.

6. The Dangerous Illusion of Productivity

Here's something I find particularly concerning.

AI can generate code that looks professional.

It can produce clean formatting, TypeScript interfaces, reusable components, and even tests.

But looking correct doesn't mean being correct.

Imagine a developer generating an entire feature using AI.

The feature works.

The tests pass.

The application runs.

But the developer cannot explain:

  • Why a particular state management approach was chosen.
  • Whether an effect is necessary.
  • How asynchronous operations are handled.
  • What happens when a component unmounts.
  • Whether the implementation introduces performance problems.

Are we actually improving software engineering?

Or are we creating a generation of developers who can operate AI tools without understanding the systems they build?

The AI Takeover could create an interesting paradox:

Developers might become faster at producing software while becoming less capable of maintaining it.

That isn't inevitable, but it's a real risk.

7. Will AI Replace Software Engineers?

Let's be realistic.

Predicting exactly how many software engineering jobs AI will eliminate is difficult.

There are several possible outcomes.

Scenario A: AI replaces a significant portion of development work.

Companies use increasingly capable AI systems to automate implementation, testing, maintenance, and other engineering tasks.

Smaller teams deliver products that previously required much larger teams.

Scenario B: AI increases software production.

As development becomes cheaper, more companies build software.

New products, integrations, and internal tools create additional demand for engineering work.

Scenario C: The profession changes.

Developers spend less time writing repetitive code and more time on architecture, verification, product decisions, security, and AI-assisted development.

My guess?

We'll see elements of all three.

The AI Takeover probably won't happen as one dramatic event.

It will happen through thousands of smaller changes in how companies build software, hire developers, and organize engineering teams.

8. How Should Developers Prepare for the AI Takeover?

I don't think abandoning programming fundamentals is the answer.

Quite the opposite.

Here are the areas I would prioritize.

1. Understand the fundamentals

Learn JavaScript, TypeScript, React, browser APIs, asynchronous programming, networking, and data structures.

You need to understand the code AI generates.

2. Become comfortable with AI-assisted development

Learn how to use tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

But don't just learn how to generate code.

Learn how to review, test, debug, and improve it.

3. Develop architectural thinking

Understand how applications are structured, how systems communicate, and how technical decisions affect maintainability.

4. Learn to solve problems independently

AI should accelerate your thinking, not replace it.

Try solving problems yourself before asking AI for an implementation.

5. Build real products

A portfolio of functioning applications demonstrates more than a collection of generated code snippets.

Build things, deploy them, maintain them, and learn from the problems that appear.

6. Contribute to open source

Working with established codebases teaches you things that isolated AI-generated projects often cannot.

You learn how real engineering teams review code, manage complexity, discuss trade-offs, and maintain software over time.

9. The Biggest Winners of the AI Takeover Might Not Be the Best Coders

This is probably my most controversial point.

The next generation of successful software engineers might not be the people who can type code the fastest.

They might be the people who can:

  • Understand problems deeply.
  • Communicate technical requirements.
  • Evaluate AI-generated solutions.
  • Design reliable systems.
  • Work across different technologies.
  • Make good engineering decisions.
  • Take responsibility for the software they ship.

AI makes implementation increasingly accessible.

But engineering judgment is a different skill.

And that distinction could become extremely important.

Final Thoughts: Adapt or Become Irrelevant?

I don't believe software engineering is disappearing.

But I do believe the profession is entering one of its biggest transformations.

The AI Takeover is forcing developers to reconsider what makes them valuable.

Knowing React, TypeScript, or Python is still useful.

Knowing how to build software is still important.

But simply knowing how to translate requirements into code may no longer be enough to stand out.

The developers who thrive will likely be those who combine strong fundamentals, engineering judgment, product thinking, and effective use of AI.

Don't compete with AI at generating code.

Learn to build better software with it.

And I'd genuinely like to hear your opinion:

If AI can build 80% of a modern application, will companies still need the same number of software engineers in five years?

Is the AI Takeover an opportunity for developers, a serious threat to the profession, or both?

Let's discuss.

title: How to cut token costs without dropping Claude 3.7
description:
API bills eat up project budgets. Processing text through Claude 3.7 Sonnet at $3 per million input tokens or renting AWS H100 instances directly at $6.88 per hour makes mass generation unprofitable. Rewriting production from the familiar PyTorch and CUDA stack to JAX just to save money takes too long. Free engineering hands for such massive tasks are usually unavailable.

We will break down the pricing mechanics in the hardware market and set up hybrid routing through a single gateway to redirect routine tasks to cheap TPU chips.

Where the graphics card shortage came from and the 108 billion dollars behind it

The market long believed in a natural shortage of computing power. A Wall Street Journal investigation showed the hidden mechanics of price formation. Nvidia management forced circular financing deals with cloud providers and AI startups in the second half of 2026 under the leadership of former CEO Jensen Huang. The scheme worked directly. The chipmaker gave startups loans or invested money in them on the condition of buying Nvidia equipment. The company actively absorbed the excess of semiconductor wafers from TSMC. This helped artificially keep graphics processor prices at a consistently high level. Startups received hardware while Nvidia showed record revenue.

Sharp conflicts began inside the company around the scale of guaranteed deals. Jensen Huang criticized CFO Colette Kress after her appointment as interim CEO. She demanded a sharp reduction in financial obligations and the termination of the agreement with OpenAI. The contract included guarantees of 250 billion dollars to build the largest data center.

Nvidia's official financial report for the quarter ending July 26, 2026, recorded a maximum volume of credit and lease guarantees to customers totaling 108.5 billion dollars. Out of this amount, 105 billion dollars went to support the OpenAI data center campus in Ohio. Such financial injections created the illusion of endless demand for equipment. Legal consequences have not yet arrived. The US Department of Justice and the SEC have not officially charged Nvidia with cartel collusion or stock market manipulation. Inside the company, such deals are classified as standard vendor project financing.

Redirecting TSMC silicon wafers and memory chips toward data center AI accelerators caused an instant spike in consumer prices. Memory manufacturers switched their assembly lines to produce HBM chips for servers. Regular DDR5 RAM went up in price right after graphics cards. GeForce graphics cards exceeded 160 percent of the recommended retail price. The flagship RTX 5090 model became practically unavailable for open purchase. Gamers and independent researchers lost the ability to build local workstations at a reasonable price.

Market rates for renting graphics chips were artificially inflated. The annual lease of an H100 accelerator rose from $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026. The median on-demand price reached $2.70 by June 2026. Rates for the Blackwell B200 generation fluctuate from $5.30 to $7.05 per hour of chip operation. On the AWS platform, renting an H100 instance reaches $6.88 per hour. A typical AI startup stack generating a million tokens a day became 40 percent more expensive in just one year.

How much a million tokens cost across different vendors

The difference in hardware costs directly reflects on API prices. We collected current rates for November 2026 for popular text generation models. Vendors factor the cost of equipment depreciation into every generated token.

Model name Price per 1M input tokens Price per 1M output tokens
Claude 3.7 Sonnet $3.00 $15.00
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2.00 $10.00
GPT-4o-mini $0.15 $0.60
Claude Haiku 5.5 $0.10 $0.50
Gemini 2.0 Flash $0.10 $0.40

The Gemini 2.0 Flash model is 30 times cheaper than Claude 3.7 Sonnet on input tokens. The price gap on output tokens between these same models reaches 37.5 times. Calls to the lightweight OpenAI GPT-4o-mini model cost $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output. Cached context for GPT-4o-mini costs developers $0.075.

The flagship reasoning model Claude 3.7 Sonnet in the Anthropic API costs $3.00 per million input tokens and $15.00 per million output tokens. This amount includes the mandatory generation of thinking tokens. Hitting the cache lowers the input cost to $0.30. The Claude Haiku 5.5 model is priced at $0.10 per million input and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.

The blended rate for Gemini 2.0 Flash is $0.50 per million input and million output tokens combined. This is 33 percent cheaper than the previous Gemini 1.5 Flash generation. The difference in rates is explained by data center architecture and the cost of the chips used.

The exact internal margin per token remains unknown. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic publicly disclose their profit and loss regarding the cost price of each specific token. You cannot say exactly what share of the $15 per million Sonnet tokens goes to amortizing Nvidia clusters and what covers research or electricity bills. Cartel markup estimates are calculated by analysts through the hourly chip rental cost and throughput.

Why TPU inference costs less

Chip economics rely on power consumption and production costs. The sixth-generation TPU Trillium consumes 300W TDP. The Nvidia H100 accelerator requires 700W TDP, while the power consumption of the Blackwell B200 generation reaches 1200W. The difference provides 2.3 times higher energy efficiency per watt during continuous inference. A cluster of tens of thousands of chips saves megawatts of electricity every hour. Lower heat output reduces the cost of liquid cooling systems in data centers. Cooling infrastructure takes up to a third of the budget when building a server farm based on Blackwell.

The hourly rental of a TPU v5e in Google Cloud is $1.20 per chip on demand and $0.54 with a three-year contract. Renting a TPU v6e Trillium will cost $2.70 on demand and $1.22 with long-term reservation. Renting an AWS H100 instance costs about $6.88 per hour. Thanks to full hardware stack optimization on their own TPU accelerators, Google's unit cost for Gemini model inference dropped by 78 percent in 2025.

The full cost price of Google TPU chips for third parties is also unpublished. Google sells Gemini API tokens with a subsidized margin inside its ecosystem. The exact production cost of TPUs at TSMC factories and Google's net savings per generated token remain a commercial secret of Alphabet.

Where specialized chips lose to graphics processors

Inference on specialized ASIC chips does not automatically win in speed on every request. With single interactive queries featuring low parallelism and a batch size of 1 to 4, modern Nvidia graphics processors deliver comparable or lower time to first token. The massive TensorRT and vLLM ecosystem perfectly optimizes single calls. GPU architecture with high memory bandwidth is ideal for an instant response to a single user. Graphics processors load model weights into memory faster during frequent context switching.

TPUs provide a 50 to 70 percent price advantage only on large batches starting from 32 requests. This requires high cluster utilization and a constant stream of tokens. With a three-year reservation of TPU Trillium capacity, the cost of generating a million tokens using dense 70B models drops to $0.42. The same task on AWS H100 instances on demand costs $0.91 or $0.94. Developers of low-load chatbots might not notice the speed difference, but they will see a difference in their bills.

The creators of Claude are also moving away from the CUDA monopoly

Dependence on graphics cards hits the profit margins of AI developers themselves. There is a widespread belief that advanced labs depend exclusively on the CUDA stack. In practice, the situation is changing very quickly.

Anthropic historically trained its models on Nvidia clusters. In November 2025, the company signed the largest deal in Google Cloud history. The developers of Claude reserved hundreds of thousands of TPU Trillium chips for 2026. The agreement includes scaling capacity to a million chips by 2027.

Anthropic uses this capacity to reduce infrastructure dependence on Nvidia GPUs during inference. Scaling a commercial API solely on graphics cards proved unprofitable even for market leaders. Switching to other chips became a matter of business survival.

Hybrid routing through a single API replaces rewriting code

Moving from PyTorch and CUDA to JAX and XLA on your own requires hundreds of engineering hours. For a single company, such a step is often economically pointless. Using different SDKs for different vendors is also inconvenient. Developers have to maintain several data contracts and handle different error formats.

The problem of library zoos is solved by model routing at the level of a single API gateway like AltRouter. The application sends standard JSON requests, and the router directs large contexts to the ultra-cheap Gemini Flash. Expensive GPU models are kept only for critical final output.

We can send a 50,000-token text to the Gemini 2.5 Flash model to extract facts. We pass the filtered data of 2,000 tokens to Claude Sonnet 5.5 for final formatting. Without a single gateway, a developer has to write integration with two different libraries. The code grows with extra type checks and network failure handlers for each vendor separately. Maintaining such a zoo of dependencies takes time away from the product team. In code, a manual cascade looks like a sequential call to two different APIs.

from google import genai
import anthropic

gemini_client = genai.Client(api_key="YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY")
claude_client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

raw_documents = "Very long text from the knowledge base spanning 50,000 tokens..."

# Step 1: Draft processing on a cheap model
draft_response = gemini_client.models.generate_content(
    model='gemini-2.5-flash',
    contents=f"Extract only key facts and numbers:\n{raw_documents}"
)
extracted_facts = draft_response.text

# Step 2: Final output on a smart model
final_response = claude_client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5.5",
    max_tokens=1000,
    system="Write an analytical report based on the facts.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": extracted_facts}
    ]
)

print(final_response.content[0].text)

Looking at the price list, sending 50,000 tokens directly to Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $0.10. Processing 50,000 tokens through Gemini 2.5 Flash costs $0.0135 at the rate of $0.27 per million. The subsequent sending of the compressed 2,000 tokens to Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs another $0.004. Total expenses amount to $0.0175.

Using Gemini 2.5 Flash for draft fact extraction lowers the cost of processing long context by 82.5 percent compared to sending it directly to Claude Sonnet 5.5. With a volume of ten thousand requests a day, the savings reach 825 dollars. The difference covers the salary of several developers for a month.

How to split traffic in a production application

Model selection depends on context size and latency requirements. Routing rules in the code help avoid overpaying for routine tasks.

Use case Batch size Recommended model
Interactive chat with a user 1 to 4 Claude 3.7 Sonnet
Mass background log parsing 32+ Gemini 2.0 Flash
Complex agents with function calling 1 to 4 Claude Sonnet 5.5
Context filtering for RAG 32+ Claude Haiku 5.5

Mass background log parsing requires processing millions of lines. Sending such a volume to Claude 3.7 Sonnet will bankrupt a project in a couple of days. Gemini 2.0 Flash handles the task for pennies. Complex agents with function calling require strict logic. Here Claude Sonnet 5.5 pays off its price through a minimal hallucination rate.

Background tasks and large texts go to models with a low input token price. Flagship solutions remain for tasks with a high cost of error. Splitting the streams cuts token costs without losing the quality of the final response. Set up cascade processing once to permanently untie your project budget from the cost of renting graphics cards.

title: Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 Review: i.MX8M Plus 2.3 TOPS Gateway
description:
The Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 is a fanless NXP i.MX8M Plus industrial gateway built for isolated fieldbus aggregation and 2.3 TOPS edge inference within a 2.5W to 8W power envelope, though deployments are constrained by shared RS485/CAN-FD pinouts and ETH0-only PoE input.

How Does the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 Balance Thermal Constraints and Edge Compute in Sealed Enclosures?

The Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 pairs a heterogeneous NXP i.MX8M Plus SoC (quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 up to 1.8GHz plus a real-time Cortex-M7 core) with a 2.3 TOPS NPU, capping whole-system power consumption between 2.5W and 8W for passive thermal management.

In industrial cabinet deployments, scaling compute usually drives up thermal flux density, causing x86 box PCs or high-wattage edge nodes to throttle inside unventilated NEMA/IP-rated enclosures. Compared to discrete "MCU control board + edge AI box" architectures, the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 consolidates real-time deterministic control and neural inference onto a single silicon die to eliminate inter-board harness complexity and DIN-rail footprint, though this imposes a hard 2.3 TOPS ceiling that restricts workloads to single-stream vision analytics (backed by the GC7000UL GPU and 1080p60 HEVC/H.265 and AVC/H.264 hardware codecs) or high-frequency vibration anomaly detection rather than multi-camera large vision models.

Maintaining a 2.5W to 8W thermal envelope is what allows the 105 x 80 x 30 mm (550g) aluminum chassis to operate passively across the full industrial temperature range of -40°C to 80°C. For high-vibration environments, soldered 2GB to 8GB LPDDR4 memory and 16GB to 128GB eMMC primary storage eliminate the mechanical fretting and contact failures common to SODIMM and microSD sockets. Engineers logging high-throughput time-series data or buffering video streams locally can specify an optional 256GB M.2 NVMe module, though running both the NPU and NVMe at sustained load near the 80°C ambient limit requires adequate DIN-rail clearance to maintain natural convection across the chassis.

i.MX8M Plus block diagram

Subsystem Core Specifications Engineering & Integration Notes
Processor (SoC) NXP i.MX8M Plus Quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 (up to 1.8GHz) + real-time Cortex-M7 co-processor
AI & Multimedia 2.3 TOPS NPU + GC7000UL GPU 1080p60 H.265/H.264 HW encode/decode; 1x mini-HDMI / DVI-D output
Memory & Storage 2GB - 8GB LPDDR4 Soldered 16GB - 128GB eMMC; optional 256GB M.2 NVMe SSD
Wired & RF Connectivity 2x 1000Mbps RJ45 ETH0 supports IEEE 802.3af PoE; optional Intel AX210 (Wi-Fi 6 + BT 5.3), Telit LE910 (LTE Cat-4 + GPS), Nordic nRF52840 (Mesh/Thread/Zigbee)
Isolated Industrial I/O 2x RS485 (Half-Duplex) / CAN-FD Terminal block, per-port configurable; 4x isolated DIO (24V, EN 61131-2 compliant)
Power & Environmental 12V-24V DC (±20%) or PoE 2.5W - 8W power draw; Commercial 0–60°C / Industrial -40–80°C; MTTF greater than 200,000 hours
BSP & Hardware Security Debian Linux / Yocto BSP i.MX8M Plus HAB secure boot + Infineon SLB9673 TPM 2.0; Docker, Mender OTA, BalenaOS

IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2

How Does the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 Mitigate Fieldbus Pin Contention and Electrical Noise?

The Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 integrates two isolated serial channels individually configurable for half-duplex RS485 or CAN-FD alongside four EN 61131-2 compliant 24V isolated digital I/O channels, addressing ground-loop isolation and multi-protocol aggregation directly at the terminal block.

At the fieldbus interface layer, pin multiplexing constraints and transient immunity often dictate board selection. Compared to generic gateways relying on unisolated USB-to-serial dongles, the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 integrates galvanic isolation directly onto the terminal block (certified to EMC EN 55032/5, EN 61000-6-2, and EN 61000-6-3) to prevent ground potential differences from damaging the SoC, though this introduces a strict I/O multiplexing trade-off: the two industrial serial ports share physical transceiver routing, meaning each port can only operate as either half-duplex RS485 or CAN-FD.

If a deployment requires two Modbus RTU trunks and a CANopen motion bus simultaneously, the native terminal block falls short by one channel, forcing engineers to consume the external 1x USB 3.0 Type-A or 1x USB 2.0 Type-A ports for expansion. Furthermore, because the RS485 implementation is strictly half-duplex, 4-wire full-duplex RS422 legacy equipment is not natively supported.

For wireless backhaul and local sensor networking, the hardware decouples short-range mesh protocols from wide-area uplinks via dedicated radio modules:

  • Short-Range Sensor Mesh: An optional Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 module handles Bluetooth Mesh, Thread, and Zigbee traffic independently, allowing the gateway to act as a local coordinator without bogging down the primary Wi-Fi radio.
  • WLAN & Cellular Backhaul: High-bandwidth local wireless is handled by an Intel AX210 card (802.11ax Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3 with dual-band 2.4G/5G whip antennas), while remote field deployments can populate a global-band Telit LE910 Cat-4 LTE modem with integrated GNSS/GPS.
  • Dual-NIC Segmentation & Power Routing: Two independent Gigabit Ethernet ports (2x 1000Mbps RJ45 ) allow physical air-gapping between southbound OT PLC networks and northbound IT/cloud traffic. Power can be fed via the reverse-polarity-protected 12V-24V DC (±20%) terminal or via Power over Ethernet, though IEEE 802.3af PoE PD circuitry is wired exclusively to ETH0. Field technicians must ensure PoE switches are patched specifically to ETH0 during installation.

compulab iot gate imx8pv2 front panel

How Does the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 Streamline BSP Bring-Up and Fleet Maintenance?

The Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 ships with production-ready Debian Linux images and a Yocto Project BSP, backed by i.MX8M Plus High Assurance Boot (HAB) and a discrete Infineon SLB9673 TPM 2.0 chip to shorten firmware bring-up and security hardening cycles.

In industrial Linux deployments, non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs frequently balloon during board bring-up, root-of-trust provisioning, and remote OTA infrastructure setup. Rather than burying UART headers inside the enclosure, the chassis exposes a dedicated 1x micro-USB serial console and a separate 1x micro-USB programming interface directly on the exterior panel. Firmware engineers can halt U-Boot, inspect kernel boot logs, or flash eMMC images via NXP's UUU tool without disassembling the unit or fabricating custom debug harnesses.

Full pinout tables, device tree mappings, and mechanical CAD files are publicly accessible via the IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 Reference Guide (PDF), Getting Started Wiki, Software Resources Wiki, and 3D STEP model archive.

At the application and fleet management layer, the software stack supports containerized workloads via Docker, low-code protocol wiring through Node-RED, native Modbus RTU/TCP and MQTT stacks, and turnkey cloud ingestion for Microsoft Azure IoT and BalenaOS. Compared to custom-scripted partition update mechanisms, integrating native Mender OTA support alongside a hardware watchdog and battery-backed RTC prevents bricked field units during power brownouts, while the onboard Infineon SLB9673 TPM 2.0 provides hardware-backed key storage to help OEMs meet emerging industrial cybersecurity mandates without external cryptographic dongles.

IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 IO terminal block pinout

Engineering Selection Boundaries: Target Use Cases vs. Hardware Constraints

  • Recommended Deployments (Green Light):
    • Sealed cabinet or harsh outdoor installations requiring fanless operation across -40°C to 80°C and a 15-year product availability lifecycle.
    • Brownfield PLC/sensor retrofits requiring isolated 24V digital I/O (EN 61131-2) and up to two isolated RS485 or CAN-FD trunks bridged to MQTT/Azure IoT.
    • Single-stream 1080p60 vision inspection or high-frequency sensor anomaly detection fitting within a 2.3 TOPS NPU budget.
    • Multi-radio edge aggregation combining wired Ethernet, Wi-Fi 6, LTE Cat-4, and 802.15.4 Mesh (Thread/Zigbee/BLE Mesh) in a single enclosure.
  • Hardware Constraints & Dealbreakers (Red Light):
    • High-Channel-Count Serial/CAN Hubs: The optional SIO add-on provides only two physical isolated ports shared between half-duplex RS485 and CAN-FD; simultaneous 3+ bus topologies require external expanders.
    • 4-Wire RS422 Legacy Networks: Serial ports are strictly half-duplex RS485 and cannot interface natively with full-duplex RS422 transceivers.
    • Dual-Port PoE Daisy-Chaining or Redundancy: Only ETH0 includes an 802.3af PoE PD controller; ETH1 is data-only, and the unit cannot act as a PoE PSE source for downstream IP cameras.
    • 4K Display or Multi-Stream Heavy AI: Display output caps at 1080p60 over mini-HDMI/DVI-D, and the 2.3 TOPS NPU is not sized for multi-stream high-resolution object detection.

Engineering FAQ

*Q: Can the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 run two RS485 buses and one CAN-FD bus simultaneously?*

A: No. The optional industrial I/O module provides two isolated ports total, each individually configurable for either half-duplex RS485 or CAN-FD, allowing a maximum combination of two buses.

*Q: Which ports support power input on the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2?*

A: The gateway accepts 12V–24V DC (±20%) with reverse-polarity protection via the terminal block, or IEEE 802.3af PoE exclusively through the primary ETH0 Gigabit Ethernet port.

*Q: How are custom ordering configurations structured for the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2?*

A: Configurations follow the SKU schema IOTG-IMX8PV2-DxNx-[NB256]-[WB]-[JT910G]-[SIO]-[FWMN]-[Xx]-[Tx], allowing modular selection of DRAM/eMMC density, 256GB NVMe, Wi-Fi 6, LTE, isolated I/O, nRF52840 Mesh, and temperature grade.

Availability and Ordering Information

The Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 is backed by a five-year warranty and a 15-year product availability commitment, with certified compliance across FCC, CE RED, EMC (EN 55032/5, EN 61000-6-2, EN 61000-6-3), and safety standard EN/UL/IEC 62368-1. Official pricing has not been publicly disclosed; full SKU customization, DIN-rail/wall-mount bracket accessories, and direct volume quotes are available on the Compulab IOT-GATE-IMX8PV2 product page.

Originally published on EmbedSBC — embedded systems, SBC and edge-AI hardware analysis.

title: I built an AI agent that turns scattered recipes into a print-ready cookbook
description:
Every family has one: a drawer of handwritten recipe cards, a Word doc from years ago, a few PDFs, and a camera roll full of dishes. Turning that into a real book usually means weeks of retyping and fighting with layout tools.

I built Cookbook AI so that takes minutes instead.

How it works

  1. Drop in your recipes. Paste text or upload PDFs, Word docs, or photos. The agent reads them first and drafts a page-by-page outline. Your recipes go in as-is; it doesn't rewrite them.
  2. Confirm the outline and pick a style. Review the plan, choose a look, and watch each page get designed and illustrated live. You can also just tell it what you want in chat — it asks questions, then designs the pages.
  3. Refine, then print or share. Edit any page, then export a print-ready A4 PDF or send a share link.

A few details I cared about:

  • Clean recipe layout — ingredients, steps and servings laid out clearly on every page, no manual formatting.
  • No bare pages — if a dish has no photo, the agent generates or finds an image for it.
  • Print that actually fits — every page fits A4 without overflow, so it's easy to print and bind at home.

Why an agent instead of a template

Templates still leave you with the tedious middle step: copying text into boxes and deciding what goes where. The agent takes over that part — reading unstructured input, planning the book, and laying out every page — so you only make the decisions that matter: which recipes, and which look.

Who's using it

  • Families turning grandma's cards into a keepsake recipe book
  • Private chefs and small kitchens making a recipe book or menu
  • Health and food creators turning a meal plan into a downloadable cookbook

Try it

It's free to start at cookbookai.io. I'd love feedback from other builders — what would you want an AI agent to handle when turning your own notes into a book?

title: copilot-setup-steps.yml: the rules, runners and limits
description:
copilot-setup-steps.yml is a workflow at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml with one job, named copilot-setup-steps, whose steps GitHub runs before Copilot cloud agent starts work, so the agent begins with your toolchain and dependencies installed. It applies only to sessions that run on GitHub Actions, and GitHub honors only six keys of that job.


What happens between assigning a task and Copilot's first edit. The setup job only exists on the Actions path.

GitHub's documentation now calls the Copilot coding agent Copilot cloud agent, and the setup steps file is now one of three places a session can get its environment from. That is the first thing to check when setup steps seem to be ignored: the file can be fine while the session never ran on Actions.

Where Copilot fits beside other agents is on CI for Cursor and Copilot coding agents. Here it is only the file: what GitHub runs, in what order, on which runners, with which secrets, and what it ignores.

First, check the session runs on Actions

GitHub now runs a Copilot session in one of two hosted environments. Cloud is a sandbox GitHub hosts; Actions is a GitHub Actions job on a GitHub-hosted runner or one you configure. Where a client lets you choose, Cloud is the default, the choice is made when the session starts and cannot be changed afterwards, and a different environment means a new session.

Setup steps, larger runners, self-hosted runners and the Windows environment all exist only on the Actions path. So do Agents variables: in a cloud sandbox only Agents secrets are available. If your repository depends on any of these, choose Actions when you delegate the task, or the agent starts in a sandbox that never read your file. A third option, a custom environment, registers a Linux machine or codespace you manage yourself.

The rules for the file

The path is fixed and the job name is the mechanism: GitHub's own example carries the comment that the job MUST be called copilot-setup-steps or it will not be picked up. The file also has to be on the default branch before it triggers at all, so a branch that adds it changes nothing until it merges.

Only six job keys count: steps, permissions, runs-on, services, snapshot and timeout-minutes, the last capped at 59. Anything else is ignored rather than rejected. A fetch-depth on actions/checkout is overridden so the agent can roll back commits, and if you do not check out the code at all, Copilot clones it after your steps finish. Give the job contents: read only if a step clones; Copilot gets its own token for its own work.

The push and pull_request path filters are what make the file testable: a pull request that edits it runs it as an ordinary check, and once merged you can run it from the Actions tab.

name: Copilot Setup Steps
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
jobs:
  # The job MUST be called `copilot-setup-steps` or it will not be picked up by Copilot.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    permissions:
      contents: read
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
