      - run: npm ci

What happens when a step fails

This is the behavior that surprises people most, because nothing goes red. GitHub documents that if any setup step returns a non-zero exit code, Copilot skips the remaining setup steps and begins working with the environment in whatever state it reached. The session continues; the agent just has less than you meant to give it, and it falls back to discovering dependencies by trial and error, which GitHub's own documentation calls slow and unreliable.

Two habits follow. Order the steps so the one that matters most, usually the dependency install, comes first after checkout and toolchain setup, rather than after an optional cache warm-up. And treat the file's own pull_request run as its test: a failure there is visible as a check, whereas a failure inside a session only shows up in the session logs.

Secrets are Agents secrets, not Actions secrets

Copilot cloud agent does not receive Actions, Codespaces or Dependabot secrets. It has its own type, Agents secrets and variables, set at repository or organization level under Settings, Secrets and variables, Agents. On the Actions path they are exposed as environment variables, including to the steps in copilot-setup-steps.yml; names prefixed COPILOT_MCP_ go only to MCP servers. Secrets you once put in a repository's copilot environment were migrated to the repository-level Agents type automatically.

Because they arrive as environment variables, a private registry needs no secrets. expression in the workflow. An .npmrc that reads the token from the environment is enough for npm ci in the setup steps and for every install the agent runs afterwards.

# .npmrc, committed; NPM_TOKEN is an Agents secret
@your-org:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}

Runners: larger, self-hosted and Windows

runs-on moves the agent off the default ubuntu-latest, and each destination comes with conditions. Copilot cloud agent is only compatible with Ubuntu x64 and Windows 64-bit runners; macOS is not supported anywhere. Organization owners can also set a default runner type and switch off repository overrides, in which case your runs-on has no effect.

Runner What GitHub requires Example runs-on
Larger GitHub-hosted Larger runners set up for the organization; with Azure private networking, outbound access to the Copilot hosts ubuntu-4-core
Self-hosted Ephemeral single-use runners recommended (ARC or the Runner Scale Set Client); integrated firewall disabled, or the agent is blocked; your own network controls your ARC scale set name
Windows Self-hosted or larger runners; the integrated firewall is not compatible with Windows your Windows runner label

The hosts a self-hosted or privately networked runner must reach, besides the standard Actions hosts, are uploads.github.com, user-images.githubusercontent.com, and whichever of api.individual.githubcopilot.com, api.business.githubcopilot.com and api.enterprise.githubcopilot.com match the Copilot plans in use, per the GitHub Docs page read on 2026-11-12.

services and snapshot

services works as it does in any job, which is the cleanest way to give the agent a real database or cache to run integration tests against instead of letting it mock one. snapshot is the less obvious key: in workflow syntax it generates a custom image, with each successful run of a job carrying it producing a new image version. It belongs to GitHub's custom images feature for larger runners, so read that documentation before relying on it here.

The same file also configures Copilot code review's environment, which reuses copilot-setup-steps.yml unless you add a separate copilot-code-review.yml. Split them when review needs less than the agent does.

```.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, a larger runner with Git LFS
jobs:
copilot-setup-steps:
runs-on: ubuntu-4-core
timeout-minutes: 45
permissions:
contents: read
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
with:
lfs: true




## Where these rules come from

GitHub's Copilot documentation, read on 2026-11-12, and nothing else: the environment pages, the secrets and variables page, the organization runner page and the workflow syntax reference listed below. No recorded run backs this page, and neither evidence file in this repository has an entry for it. A session's setup log belongs to one repository and one Copilot plan, so the rules are quoted from the pages that define them rather than inferred from a log.

## FAQ

### Why is my copilot-setup-steps.yml not being used?

Three causes cover nearly every case. The file is not on the default branch yet, the job is not named exactly `copilot-setup-steps`, or the session ran in a cloud sandbox, where setup steps do not apply. Check the session logs: when the setup job runs, its steps appear there.

### Can Copilot coding agent use self-hosted runners?

Yes, through `runs-on` in the setup steps file, on Ubuntu x64 or Windows 64-bit runners. GitHub recommends ephemeral single-use runners, requires you to disable the integrated firewall for self-hosted use, and asks you to allow the Copilot API hosts through your own network controls.

### How do I give Copilot coding agent access to secrets?

Add them as Agents secrets, at repository or organization level. They reach the agent as environment variables, including inside `copilot-setup-steps.yml`, while names starting with `COPILOT_MCP_` are passed only to MCP servers. Actions secrets are not passed to the agent.

### What is the maximum timeout for copilot-setup-steps?

59 minutes. `timeout-minutes` is one of the six keys GitHub honors on the `copilot-setup-steps` job, and the documentation gives 59 as its maximum value.

## References

- [GitHub Docs: configure the development environment for agents on GitHub Actions (read 2026-11-12)](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment)
- [GitHub Docs: about cloud sandboxes, choosing where Copilot runs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/about-cloud-sandboxes)
- [GitHub Docs: configure secrets and variables for Copilot cloud agent](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/configure-secrets-and-variables)
- [GitHub Docs: configuring runners for Copilot cloud agent in your organization](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-for-organization/configure-runner-for-coding-agent)
- [GitHub Docs: workflow syntax, jobs.<job_id>.snapshot](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax)

title: When a Python List Copy Is Only Half a Copy
description:
When a Python List Copy Is Only Half a Copy

You used .copy(), but changing your copied data still affected the original.

Did the copy fail?

The answer depends on what is inside your list. A shallow copy creates a new outer list, while its elements still refer to the same objects.

Let’s explore this through a weekly schedule.

1. Adding a day keeps the original unchanged 

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised.append(["Wednesday", "Git"])

print(len(schedule))
print(len(revised))

Output:

2
3

Calling .copy() created a separate outer list.

Appending a new entry changes only revised. So far, the copy behaves exactly as you might expect.

2. Editing an existing day affects both lists

Now start again and update Monday’s subject:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'JavaScript']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

The outer lists are separate, but their first elements refer to the same inner list.

This expression:

revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

accesses that shared inner list and replaces one of its elements.

You can inspect the relationship directly:

print(schedule is revised)
print(schedule[0] is revised[0])

Output:

False
True

3. Replacing a whole entry behaves differently

Compare the previous example with this one:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised[0] = ["Monday", "JavaScript"]

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'Python']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

Here, we create a new inner list and place it into the separate outer list revised.

The original Monday entry remains unchanged.

The difference is the level at which the assignment happens:

Statement What changes?
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript" An element inside the shared inner list
revised[0] = ["Monday", "JavaScript"] An element inside the separate outer list

4. Copying each row can provide enough independence

For this schedule, we can copy both the outer list and each row:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = [row.copy() for row in schedule]
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'Python']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

The list comprehension builds a new outer list. Each row.copy() also creates a new row.

This works for our schedule because each row contains strings. It does not recursively copy every possible level of nested data.

5. Another nesting level introduces sharing again

Suppose each day contains a list of subjects:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", ["Python", "SQL"]],
    ["Tuesday", ["Git"]],
]

revised = [row.copy() for row in schedule]
revised[0][1].append("Testing")

print(schedule[0][1])
print(revised[0][1])

Output:

['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']
['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']

We copied the outer list and each row, but the subject lists inside those rows remain shared.

When this nested data needs to be independent, use deepcopy():

from copy import deepcopy

schedule = [
    ["Monday", ["Python", "SQL"]],
    ["Tuesday", ["Git"]],
]

revised = deepcopy(schedule)
revised[0][1].append("Testing")

print(schedule[0][1])
print(revised[0][1])

Output:

['Python', 'SQL']
['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']

For this structure, the nested subject lists are now independent.

Choose the copy that matches your change

Before copying a list, consider what you intend to modify.

  • Adding or removing outer entries: a shallow copy may be enough.
  • Editing individual rows: copying each row may be enough for simple data.
  • Changing mutable objects deeper inside the structure: consider a deep copy.

The useful question is: Which objects will my next operation modify, and are those objects still shared?

For further reading, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Free PCEP practice test

Preparing for PCEP? Explore my AM Academy free practice test here: https://www.udemy.com/course/python-pcep-30-03-certification-practice-tests-2026/?couponCode=FREE-COURSE-PCEP. I’m the creator of this independent preparation resource; it is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Python Institute.

title: Cutover Needs a No-Go: Microsoft, Workday, the FAA, and Starship Flight 15
description:
These four events landed in the same mid-November 2026 window. Nothing public connects them, and I am not suggesting a link.

What they share is a lesson about gates, verification and change discipline. Things fail at cutovers, at tests that touch production, and in old infrastructure that is finally being changed. One of the four shows the opposite pattern: an automated no-go that refused to proceed.

I build MigrateForge in Coimbatore: a system that moves PHP applications to Java 21 / Spring Boot and keeps cutover blocked until recorded user journeys match on both sides. That is not a claim that it would have prevented any of these incidents. It is about applying the same discipline to a software cutover.

Microsoft 365: the checker was in the failure path

Starting shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, 12 November, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint Online and Copilot were disrupted for a large part of a day, with knock-on effects for organisations that depend on them. CNBC reported that engineers were still restoring service nearly 24 hours later, and that Microsoft said on Saturday, 14 November, that it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining affected customers and regions.

Microsoft's first public account was not a traffic surge. A portion of its infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions because servers had become unexpectedly unavailable. As Ars Technica quoted from Microsoft's status updates, the company pointed to "a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable," which then strained the machines that remained. Recovery was slow in part because early fixes did not hold: some servers brought back online became unresponsive again once they received traffic.

Microsoft later said the disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." CNBC reported that the company had not detected malicious activity and would issue a full report once its assessment was complete. Until that post-incident report is published, the upgrade wording is Microsoft's stated cause, not a finished root-cause analysis.

Two points matter for anyone planning a cutover.

First, a health check is a gate. If the gate fails in a way that removes healthy capacity, the rest of the system inherits the error. "The dashboard is green" is not evidence if you have not tested the checker.

Second, a workflow that lives inside someone else's cloud inherits that cloud's outages. MigrateForge is local-first: source code stays on the client's machines, and only AI requests leave. When an AI provider is down, translation runs end PAUSED or ENVIRONMENT_INVALID and resume later with nothing lost. Capture, replay, parity verification, security sweeps and evidence reports need no AI call. Several recent nights spent $0 while still producing verified waves.

Workday: a disaster-recovery test reached production

On the evening of Friday, 13 November, Workday placed all WD1 production tenants into maintenance. The company's Community Status Page notice, quoted in full by Washington University IT, said:

While validating the weekly Maintenance Window for Disaster Recovery tenants, we have identified that tenanted services within the DR Site unexpectedly connected to Production databases. As a result, this has left data in an inconsistent state that can cause errors accessing tenants or jobs/integrations/tasks to fail with missing transaction error messages.

Florida Atlantic University's IT status page reported the same pattern that night: an issue involving the disaster-recovery environment had left production data inconsistent, and production was taken offline as a precaution. FAU said users could not access the system or complete normal business activities; Washington University had to collect time by hand for staff who could not clock in. FAU said production was available again at 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, 14 November; Washington University marked the unplanned outage resolved later that afternoon, with some updates between systems still delayed. Restoration times varied by tenant. Workday has not, in public, said how many customers were affected, and a detailed root-cause report is still outstanding.

A disaster-recovery test is supposed to prove you can survive a failure. Here the test became the failure, because the recovery copy was not isolated from live databases. For a migration, the analogue is direct. If your verification environment can write to production, or if a rehearsal shares state with the live system, you are not testing. You are touching the data you are trying to protect.

The FAA: a copper-to-fiber cutover flooded the network

On Friday, 13 November, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after communication issues hit multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The Verge reported that the stop went out at 3:44 p.m. ET and was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET, a little over four hours later.

The next day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the Department's account. At a remote FAA site, contractor L3Harris was replacing discontinued copper telecommunications lines with fiber, moving from TDM to IP. A router involved in that work "started flooding other routers": more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. That disrupted communications with aircraft and radar feeds. Controllers and pilots then grounded more than 3,500 flights. Once the stop lifted, more than 8,000 flight operations resumed that night.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have described the underlying telecom as a 1980s-era TDM network. Officials said they do not believe the event was a cyber attack. They have not yet determined whether the fault was installer error or a faulty router.

The airspace shutdown was itself a gate: when the data going to controllers was inconsistent, traffic stopped. The expensive part was that the inconsistency showed up in operation, during a change that was supposed to be routine, rather than in a rehearsal that could refuse to proceed.

Starship Flight 15: the no-go fired

The contrast is Starship Flight 15.

On Friday, 13 November, Super Heavy lifted off from Starbase, Texas. SpaceX's flight recap says the booster's boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass, with the root cause of that early cutoff still under investigation. During coast, the booster's guidance, navigation and control system triggered an automated abort, diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf of Mexico, hovered, cut its engines, and the flight termination system triggered.

About 22.5 hours after liftoff, on Saturday, 14 November, the ship returned to the same pad and was caught by the tower for the first time.

SpaceX commentator Dan Huot corrected an earlier remark on the Saturday webcast: "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do." It had detected that the booster "was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch."

The catch is the new part. The gate is old. A no-go that fires automatically, against a written criterion, is how you keep a bad state from becoming a worse one. Most software migrations have no such gate. A rewrite looks done, someone switches traffic, and production is where you find out.

What a migration gate has to do

If you are moving a business-critical PHP application to Java 21 and Spring Boot, the question is the same one that GNC answered: are we where we need to be to proceed?

MigrateForge's answer is behavioural, not ceremonial:

  1. Record real user journeys on the existing PHP system.
  2. Replay them against both the legacy PHP and the new Spring Boot application.
  3. Compare HTTP responses, database writes and outgoing API calls.
  4. Keep cutover blocked until they match.

The output is standard Spring Boot. Every wave ships an evidence report. The work is local-first, as above: code stays on the client's machines.

This is the product today for plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3. Laravel is next.

What the benchmarks actually show

These are benchmarks, not client projects.

  • WA Blast Pro, my own production multi-tenant WhatsApp SaaS (plain PHP): waves 1–2, 572 fixtures, all matching.
  • InvoicePlane v1.7.2 (open-source, CodeIgniter 3.4): waves 1–2, 286 fixtures, all matching.

In total: 4 waves, 858 fixtures, 100% parity, 0 write-effect diffs and 0 HIGH findings.

First-pass parity, before hand fixes, was 82%, with 9.7 hand fixes per 1,000 PHP lines. The gate held until the rest was closed.

We also test the checker, by planting known bugs. The self-test catch rate was 57.14% on WA Blast Pro wave 1 and 35.89% on InvoicePlane wave 1. That is not 100%, and it is why we publish it next to the parity numbers. A checker you have not tested is the Microsoft lesson in miniature.

Before release, verification caught a delete that would also have removed a client's invoices and payments, a page missing its login check, data visible across tenants, and a skipped cashback payout. It also found defects in the original PHP applications.

Full evidence is at migrateforge.com/proof.

A starting point

If you run a PHP estate and a Java cutover is on the horizon, the free migration report is ₹0: size, risks, an indicative wave plan and a price range, with no source code required. It is on migrateforge.com.

For a comparison of manual rewrites, AI coding agents and parity-gated replay, see the earlier piece: PHP to Java 21 Migration in 2026: Manual Rewrite vs AI Coding Agents vs Parity-Gated Replay.

title: Cursor's breach chain started in plain-text agent traces: 23,276 public repos carry the same leak
description:
Cursor published its final incident report on November 13, two weeks after a malicious copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension appeared in its VS Code extension marketplace. I read the whole thing. The interesting part is not the extension. It is the first link in the chain.

The chain, in five steps

The report reconstructs the attack like this:

  1. An attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, an inference provider. The key was exposed on Fireworks' side.
  2. With that key, the attacker copied data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share training data with Fireworks. The bucket held coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode.
  3. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted. Cursor says less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed this way.
  4. Starting from those credentials, the attacker reached SaaS tools Cursor uses internally, then archived source repositories, support data, email conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the support team.
  5. On October 29, using a stolen credential from that data, the attacker placed malicious builds of the Claude Code extension directly on the cache that served the marketplace. Open VSX never carried them, and Anthropic published nothing. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions could have received the bad build, which lived for about 11 hours. BleepingComputer reported the payload installed persistent SSH backdoors.

Read step 3 again. The breach did not start with a zero-day. It started with working credentials sitting in plain text inside stored agent transcripts. Everything after that was climbing. If you run sessions outside Privacy Mode, or you paste a token into a command to unblock an agent at 6pm, you are producing the same artifact class that made step 3 possible.

Two numbers worth sitting with

Cursor says traces were exposed for fewer than 0.05% of users, and API credentials for less than 0.01% of customers. Small percentages, and they still yielded enough working credentials to reach internal systems and poison a marketplace cache.

That is the arithmetic of stored secrets. An attacker does not need a large share of users leaking credentials. One valid key with the right scope is enough. Cursor's own response reads like agreement: the team rotated every credential in use across internal systems, not just the exposed ones, moved all inference traffic off the vendor, and added secret scanning across internal data sources.

The same leak, sitting on your disk

Two weeks later, on the file side of the same problem, GitGuardian published a count that dwarfs the numbers Cursor had to contain. Per CSO Online's report of the research: 31,088 distinct secrets in .claude/settings.local.json files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories, with 5,343 of them still valid when detected. Of the occurrences GitGuardian could check, 67% were working credentials.

I wrote about the mechanism when Apiiro's smaller count came out: approving a command with "Yes, and don't ask again" saves the exact command string, secret included, into a project-level file. That article covered 1,379 distinct secrets in 1,122 files. Apiiro counted default branches. GitGuardian crawled every public commit back to January 2025 and found twenty times more.

The pattern holds everywhere agent tooling writes down what happened:

  • The shared team file, .claude/settings.json, carried another 8,271 secrets, 1,283 of them valid, in GitGuardian's tally relayed by Ground Truth.
  • Public Docker Hub images held 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files across 543 image repositories, because a Dockerfile COPY . . ignores your .gitignore. One valid Cloudflare token appeared across 559 image tags.

Why your scanner misses one in five

Apiiro ran gitleaks and TruffleHog, the two most used open-source secret scanners, over all 104,185 public copies of the file. Of the 1,122 files holding a real secret, 215 were flagged by neither, close to one in five. The reason is structural. Scanners look for provider formats, a prefix followed by high-entropy string. A password after PGPASSWORD=, or inside an sshpass command, is just a word on a command line. Agent artifacts record what ran, not what was sensitive, so the exact place agents write secrets is the place format-based detection covers worst.

A rotation order that matches the chain

Order your cleanup by how the attacker actually used the data, not by how easy each step is.

First, rotate anything you ever pasted into a vendor support chat or ran through a session whose logs you do not control. Cursor's report lists "some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team" among the exposed data. That class of credential outlives your account with the vendor.

Second, rotate credentials that reached a committed file, then clean the file. Rotation first, always, because git history and forks keep old copies. Check whether the file was ever committed on any branch:

git log --all --full-history --oneline -- .claude/settings.local.json

Third, rotate anything baked into a published image. Deleting the file from the repo does not recall published tags; one database password in GitGuardian's data sits in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Five places credentials sit in plain text

Run this audit across all five, in one pass:

  1. Agent traces and transcripts, local session logs included. You are checking for commands that carried a token or password inline.
  2. .claude/settings.local.json, the file behind the 23,276 repos.
  3. .claude/settings.json, committed on purpose by teams, so it spreads by design.
  4. Container images, via a COPY . . that had no .dockerignore to stop it.
  5. Support conversations and shared debugging threads.

A quick pattern probe for the config side:

grep -rnE "(PGPASSWORD=|sshpass|Bearer |AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH) PRIVATE KEY)" \
  .claude ~/.claude/settings.json 2>/dev/null

It will not catch everything, that is the one-in-five lesson, but it catches the shapes scanners skip.

Rules that shrink the vault

Four habits remove most of this surface:

  • Never approve a secret-bearing command with "don't ask again". Write the allow rule as a pattern without the secret, and pass the secret as an environment variable.
  • Add .claude/ and .env* to .dockerignore in every image that builds from a repo where agents run: 
.claude/
**/.claude/
.env*
**/.env*
  • Treat agent config files as secret-bearing in CI, with pattern checks for command-line secret shapes, not just key-format detectors. I keep a 22-rule scanner for exactly this class of file.
  • Decide about traces the way you decide about screen recordings. If a command would be dangerous to replay in public, it does not belong in any session that logs it.

Per Ground Truth's coverage of CSO's reporting, Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code, said the tool has not done secrets scrubbing and that built-in secret scanning and an auto mode are being explored. Until something ships there, the file-level discipline is on you.

What I took from the report

The extension malware was the loud part, and I covered the config-boundary questions when it dropped. The quiet part is that a bucket of 2025 transcripts contained working credentials at all. Your exposure is probably not a marketplace cache. It is the artifacts your own tooling writes on every machine you own, and the copies of those artifacts you never audited. Rotate first, then audit, then write the rules that keep the vault empty.

If you want the incident timeline and the indicators of compromise, the primary sources are Cursor's report and their October 30 security notice. My earlier piece on what agent configs can and cannot contain covers the extension side of this event.

title: Docker layer caching not working: read the CACHED count first
description:
When Docker layer caching GitHub Actions not working is the complaint, the clock is a bad witness and the build log is a good one: a build that reuses nothing and a build that reuses everything can be seconds apart, and the number that separates them is how many steps printed CACHED. On a runner we measured, the same image came back with 5 cached steps when the cache was wired correctly and 0 in every one of the four ways it can quietly fail.


One image, one runner, a freshly created builder before every build. Cached step counts and seconds from job-m.sh on a latchkey-small runner, 2026-09-20.

A layer cache that is configured and not working produces a build that looks entirely normal. Nothing fails, the workflow is green, and the only evidence is that every step ran again. So this is diagnosed by counting rather than by feel.

So the method below is one reading followed by five causes. Four of them we reproduced on a runner; the third is the branch rule, which is GitHub's and not Docker's, and is quoted from documentation rather than measured. Every build here ran on a builder created fresh immediately before it, so the declared cache was the only cache in play.

The reading: count the CACHED steps

Build with plain progress output and count the steps that printed CACHED. That is the whole diagnostic, and it takes one run. A working cache on our three-stage image printed 5; every broken configuration printed 0, including ones that finished barely a second slower than the working build.

The other line worth finding is the import. When a backend is reachable, BuildKit prints that it is importing a cache manifest before it starts. If that line is missing, nothing was read, and no amount of cache-to will change it.

- run: docker buildx build --progress=plain . 2>&1 | grep -E "CACHED|importing cache"

Our own working build printed importing cache manifest as its fourth step and CACHED on the install step. A failing build printed neither and looked otherwise identical.

What the numbers looked like

Here is the same image, built nine times on one runner, with the eight builds worth comparing in the table. Read the cached column first and the seconds second, because the seconds are close together and the step counts are not. The working cache saved 1.43 seconds off a 10.56 second cold build, which is a smaller gap than most people expect and still the difference between reusing the install and repeating it.

The row that matters most is the second: writing a cache on every run while reading none costs time rather than saving it. That build took 13.43 seconds, nearly three seconds longer than doing nothing at all, because exporting is work.

Build, on a freshly created builder Cached steps Seconds
Cold, no cache backend declared 0 10.56 s
cache-to only, no cache-from 0 13.43 s
cache-from an empty local cache 0 10.62 s
cache-from a registry ref that does not exist 0 10.35 s
Warm cache, base image changed 0 10.52 s
Warm cache, lockfile changed 1 10.86 s
Warm cache, source changed 5 9.13 s
Warm cache, source changed, second pass 5 9.28 s

Measured by job-m.sh, under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-not-working/, on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20: 2 vCPU, 7,734 MB RAM, Docker 29.7.2, buildx 0.36.1, a three-stage Node image with 414 packages in its lockfile. Every row created its builder immediately before the build, so no in-builder state carried between rows, and the exported cache was 94 MB. One pass per row except the last pair, which is the same configuration twice.

Cause 1: the cache is written and never read

Both halves are required and they are separate settings, so it is easy to end up with one. cache-to writes; cache-from reads. A workflow with only the first writes a fresh cache every run, reads none of it, and pays the export cost forever: 13.43 seconds against 10.56 for no cache at all.

The signature is a build with 0 cached steps that is slower than a plain build, and a cache store that keeps growing. Add the other half, pointed at the same place.

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Cause 2: it is reading a scope nothing wrote

A cache-from that points somewhere empty does not fail. We pointed one at an empty local directory and the build ran to completion with 0 cached steps and not one line about the cache in its output, among plenty of unrelated warnings from npm and from buildx. We pointed another at a registry reference that does not exist, and that one did print an error, "failed to configure registry cache importer", and then built successfully anyway. Neither turned the workflow red.

On type=gha the same mistake wears a different hat. Docker documents the scope as a key that "By default, it is set to buildkit", and where several builds share a scope "each build will overwrite the cache of the previous, leaving only the final cache". Two images built in one workflow with the default scope take turns destroying each other, and both of them look like a cache that stopped working.

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha,scope=api
    cache-to: type=gha,scope=api,mode=max

Give every image its own scope. A build that cannot reach its cache is not an error condition to BuildKit, so the only place this shows up is the step count.

Cause 3: the branch cannot see the cache, per the docs

This is the one cause here we did not reproduce, and it is not a Docker setting: it applies only to type=gha, which stores its blobs in the Actions cache and inherits its rules. A run can restore caches from its own branch and from the default branch, and a pull request can also reach the base branch, but never a sibling or a child branch.

So the first build on a new feature branch is cold unless the default branch has written a cache it can inherit. That is documented behavior, not a fault. Export on pushes to the default branch and let pull requests read what those runs wrote.

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]      # writes the cache every other run inherits
  pull_request:           # reads it

Cause 4: mode=min kept the part you needed

On a multi-stage build, mode=min exports only the layers that reached the final image, and the installing stages are usually not among them. The cache looks present, the step count is above zero, and the expensive stage rebuilds anyway.

We measured that pair separately on a four-stage version of the same image: mode=max restored in 9.7 seconds and stored 98 MB, mode=min restored in 11.3 and stored 70. Writing 28 MB less bought a slower build. If your Dockerfile has more than one stage, you want mode=max.

The mode comparison is from job-b.sh, under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-in-github-actions/, on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20, and not from this page's script. That script ran twice: its first attempt aborted at a docker buildx rm under set -e, and the committed version differs from it by one added line.

Cause 5: the base image moved under you

BuildKit checks the base image first and compares each later instruction against the cached layers, so a different FROM invalidates the entire build. We changed one digit, node:20-slim to node:22-slim, with a warm cache in place, and the count went from 5 cached steps to 0 and the build back to 10.52 seconds, which is cold.

A floating tag does this without a commit. node:20-slim is rebuilt upstream regularly, and the day it moves every job rebuilds from scratch with nothing changed in your repository. Pin the digest if cold builds are expensive enough to care about, and accept that you now own the upgrade.

# a tag that moves when upstream rebuilds
FROM node:20-slim

# a base that cannot move without a commit
FROM node:20-slim@sha256:<digest>

What we ran, so you can disagree with it

One script, job-m.sh, run once on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 20 September 2026, committed under content/repro/timings/docker-layer-caching-not-working/ with its unedited job-m.log and a status file naming the job id, the runner size and the exit code. The log carries the plain progress output of every build, including the CACHED lines counted here.

What it does not cover. type=gha was never exercised: the log records ACTIONS_CACHE_URL unset outside a GitHub-hosted job, so the scope and branch rules here are quoted from documentation read the same day. The backend used was type=local, with no network between builder and store, so the seconds are a floor. One pass per row means they carry noise: the step counts are the finding, not the tenths.

FAQ

How do I check whether buildx is reading my cache?

Build with --progress=plain, count the steps that printed CACHED, and look for the line where BuildKit says it is importing a cache manifest. On our runner a working cache printed 5 cached steps and that import line; every broken configuration printed 0 and no import, while finishing within about a second of a plain build.

Why does my build still take the same time with cache-from set?

Most often because nothing was ever written where it is reading, or because only cache-to was configured somewhere else and the two point at different scopes. A cache-from that finds nothing is not an error: our build against an empty cache directory ran to completion without one line about the cache in its output, and the one against a missing registry printed an importer error and then succeeded anyway.

Does a new base image rebuild every layer below it?

Yes. BuildKit checks the base image first and invalidates everything after a layer that does not match, so a different FROM rebuilds the lot. We changed node:20-slim to node:22-slim with a warm cache and went from 5 cached steps to 0. A floating tag can do this with no commit of yours.

What does "failed to compute cache key" mean?

It is a different problem from a cache miss: BuildKit could not resolve an input it needs to hash, almost always a COPY or ADD of a path that does not exist in the build context. Check the path against your .dockerignore and against the context directory you actually passed, because a file excluded from the context is missing as far as the builder is concerned.

References

  • Docker Docs: cache invalidation rules (verified 2026-09-20)
  • Docker Docs: GitHub Actions cache backend and scope (verified 2026-09-20)
  • Docker Docs: cache storage backends (verified 2026-09-20)
  • GitHub Docs: cache scope and branch restrictions (verified 2026-09-20)

title: Recording screen, system audio and mic to MP4 in the browser (WebCodecs + mp4-muxer)
description:
I built a small meeting recorder that runs as a PWA in Edge. It records the screen, the other people's voices (system audio) and my own microphone into one MP4. This post is about how it works, including the parts that took me a while to get right.

What I wanted:

  • one MP4 with screen + system audio + mic
  • hours of recording without holding the file in memory
  • files that seek properly in any player

Setup: Windows 11, Microsoft Edge (Chrome behaves the same). APIs: getDisplayMedia, Web Audio, MediaStreamTrackProcessor, WebCodecs, File System Access API. MP4 muxing is done by mp4-muxer (MIT).

Why not MediaRecorder

MediaRecorder is the easy option, but I wanted control over a few things:

  • Seeking. WebM files from MediaRecorder have no duration or cues, so some players can't seek in them.
  • Frame rate and keyframes. Meeting screens barely move, so I record at 8 fps to keep files small, but still want a keyframe every 5 seconds so seeking is quick and accurate.
  • Pause. Paused time should be cut out, not left as a gap.

WebCodecs gives you all of that. The price is that you manage timestamps yourself.

1. Screen and system audio 

const displayStream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia({
  video: { frameRate: { ideal: 8, max: 8 }, height: { max: 1080 }, displaySurface: 'monitor' },
  audio: { suppressLocalAudioPlayback: false, echoCancellation: false, noiseSuppression: false, autoGainControl: false },
  systemAudio: 'include',
  selfBrowserSurface: 'exclude',
  monitorTypeSurfaces: 'include',
});
displayStream.getVideoTracks()[0].contentHint = 'text';
  • On Windows, you only get system audio if the user picks Entire screen and ticks Also share system audio in the share dialog. Sharing a single window gives you no audio. Users won't guess this, so the app says it in one line under the button.
  • Echo cancellation and friends are for microphones. They do nothing useful on system audio, so they're off.
  • contentHint = 'text' tells the encoder to favor sharp detail over smooth motion. Slide text stays readable.

2. Mixing in the microphone

Two separate audio tracks in one MP4 confuse some players (they play only the first). I mix them into one with Web Audio:

const audioCtx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 48000 }); // create inside the click handler
const dest = audioCtx.createMediaStreamDestination();
dest.channelCount = 2;

const sys = displayStream.getAudioTracks();
if (sys.length) audioCtx.createMediaStreamSource(new MediaStream(sys)).connect(dest);

const mic = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: { echoCancellation: true, noiseSuppression: true } });
audioCtx.createMediaStreamSource(mic).connect(dest);

const mixedTrack = dest.stream.getAudioTracks()[0];

Create the AudioContext in the click handler. If you create it on page load it can start suspended, and you get a silent file.

3. Encoding video yourself

MediaStreamTrackProcessor hands you frames one by one, which you feed to a VideoEncoder:

const reader = new MediaStreamTrackProcessor({ track: videoTrack }).readable.getReader();
const first = (await reader.read()).value;
const w = even(first.displayWidth), h = even(first.displayHeight); // H.264 needs even sizes

// try H.264 profiles from best to most compatible
const common = { width: w, height: h, bitrate: 500_000, bitrateMode: 'variable', framerate: 8, latencyMode: 'realtime', avc: { format: 'avc' } };
let cfg = null;
for (const codec of ['avc1.640033', 'avc1.4d0033', 'avc1.42e033', 'avc1.640028']) {
  if ((await VideoEncoder.isConfigSupported({ ...common, codec })).supported) { cfg = { ...common, codec }; break; }
}

const venc = new VideoEncoder({
  output: (chunk, meta) => muxer.addVideoChunk(chunk, meta),
  error: e => console.error(e),
});
venc.configure(cfg);

The loop does three things:

const FRAME_US = 1e6 / 8, KEYFRAME_US = 5_000_000;
const base = first.timestamp;  // recording start
let lastTs = -1, lastKeyTs = -Infinity;

for (let frame = first; frame; ) {
  const ts = Math.max(frame.timestamp - base, lastTs + 1);           // 1. keep timestamps increasing
  if (lastTs < 0 || (ts - lastTs >= FRAME_US * 0.75 && venc.encodeQueueSize < 4)) { // 2. drop extras
    const out = new VideoFrame(frame, { timestamp: ts, duration: FRAME_US });
    const key = ts - lastKeyTs >= KEYFRAME_US;                       // 3. keyframe every 5 s
    if (key) lastKeyTs = ts;
    venc.encode(out, { keyFrame: key });
    out.close();
    lastTs = ts;
  }
  frame.close();
  const r = await reader.read();
  frame = r.done ? null : r.value;
}
  1. Timestamps. When nothing on screen changes, frames stop coming for a while. I take each frame's own timestamp minus the start time, and force it to be strictly increasing.
  2. Dropping frames. max: 8 is a hint, not a promise. Frames that arrive too soon, or while the encoder is backed up (encodeQueueSize), get dropped.
  3. Keyframes. Without regular keyframes, seeking is slow and lands in the wrong place.

And close every frame. Forget frame.close() and you run out of memory within seconds.

4. Audio timestamps from the sample count

For audio, I compute the timestamp from how many samples I've written. Paused time simply never gets counted.

let samples = 0;
// inside the loop (ad is an AudioData)
const n = ad.numberOfFrames, ch = ad.numberOfChannels;
const buf = new Float32Array(n * ch);
for (let c = 0; c < ch; c++) ad.copyTo(buf.subarray(c * n, (c + 1) * n), { planeIndex: c, format: 'f32-planar' });
const out = new AudioData({
  format: 'f32-planar', sampleRate: ad.sampleRate, numberOfFrames: n, numberOfChannels: ch,
  timestamp: Math.round(samples / ad.sampleRate * 1e6), data: buf,
});
samples += n;
aenc.encode(out);
out.close(); ad.close();

While paused, incoming AudioData is just thrown away. On resume, the video side recalculates its base time. The result is a file with the paused section cut out.

The audio encoder tries AAC (mp4a.40.2) first and falls back to Opus.

5. Writing to disk as you go

This made the biggest difference. mp4-muxer has FileSystemWritableFileStreamTarget, which writes straight into a File System Access stream:

// ask for a folder once; keep the handle in IndexedDB for next time
const dir = await showDirectoryPicker({ id: 'rec', mode: 'readwrite', startIn: 'videos' });
const file = await dir.getFileHandle('recording.mp4', { create: true });
const writable = await file.createWritable();

const muxer = new Mp4Muxer.Muxer({
  target: new Mp4Muxer.FileSystemWritableFileStreamTarget(writable),
  fastStart: false,               // streaming, so the moov box goes at the end
  firstTimestampBehavior: 'offset',
  video: { codec: 'avc', width: w, height: h },
  audio: { codec: 'aac', numberOfChannels: 2, sampleRate: 48000 },
});

// on stop
await venc.flush(); await aenc.flush();
muxer.finalize();
await writable.close();

With ArrayBufferTarget, the whole recording sits in memory until you stop. A long meeting in high quality can run out of memory and lose everything. I started that way and switched to streaming. In an automated test that records and saves 100 times in a row, memory doesn't grow (renderer process went from 86 MB to 57 MB).

A FileSystemDirectoryHandle can be stored in IndexedDB as-is. Next time you only check queryPermission / requestPermission and reuse the same folder.

6. Smaller gotchas

  • Static screen = short video. If the last frame came long before you pressed stop, the video track ends early. On stop, I encode the last frame once more with the stop time as its timestamp.
  • Double-clicking Start. Users can click again while the share dialog is open. A simple flag prevents two recordings at once.
  • Folder picker uses up the click. showDirectoryPicker consumes the user activation, so calling getDisplayMedia right after it fails. The app asks the user to click once more.

7. Shipping it to the Microsoft Store

PWABuilder turns the URL into a .msixbundle you can submit. The package is just a shell that opens the site, so code updates are a web deploy with no Store re-review (remember to bump the service worker cache name).

A side effect I didn't plan for: because it installs from the Store like any standard app, with no drivers or virtual audio devices, it also works on locked-down work PCs where you can't install regular desktop software. (Some companies block the Store itself, and please follow your company's policy and tell people when you record.)

The app is called LiteRec, and I'm the developer. 10 recordings are free, then it's $0.99/month.
https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9ntvppczz2gf

Happy to answer questions about any of the WebCodecs bits in the comments.

title: Pruebas de API con Newman: de 0 a 121 aserciones en un pipeline que despliega en Vercel
description:
Actividad Grupal 2: API Testing: Calidad y Pruebas de Software (SI-784), Universidad Privada de Tacna.
Autores: Milton H. Flores Chino y Manuel Andre Dongo Palza.

Repositorio: https://github.com/miltom123/si784-grupal2-api-testing
API en producción: https://si784-api-envios.vercel.app

El problema

Probar una API "a mano" con Postman sirve el primer día. Al tercer cambio ya nadie repite los 20 clics, y los errores llegan a producción. Para este trabajo nos pusimos una regla simple: ningún cambio llega a producción si no pasan las pruebas, y las mismas pruebas se repiten contra la URL pública después de desplegar.

Para eso construimos una API pequeña y la probamos con dos herramientas:

  • Newman, la versión de línea de comandos de Postman. Cubre las pruebas funcionales y de contrato, y es el tema de este artículo.
  • k6 para las pruebas de carga. Mi compañero Manuel lo explica en su artículo.

La API bajo prueba

Es una API REST sin estado que cotiza envíos entre departamentos del Perú. Está hecha con Node.js 20 y Hono.

Método Ruta Qué hace
GET /v1/health Estado y versión
GET /v1/departamentos?zona= 25 departamentos con su zona
GET /v1/departamentos/{codigo} Un departamento (404 si no existe)
POST /v1/cotizaciones Calcula el precio del envío
GET /v1/openapi.json Contrato OpenAPI 3

Las reglas de negocio tienen suficientes detalles para que valga la pena probarlas:

  • Tarifa base de S/ 8 en la misma zona y S/ 12 entre zonas.
  • S/ 2.50 por cada 0.5 kg iniciado.
  • Recargo de selva, servicio express ×1.6 y seguro del 1 %.
  • IGV del 18 %.

Los errores siempre tienen la misma forma:

{ "error": { "code": "VALIDACION", "message": "...", "campo": "pesoKg" } }

Pruébala tú mismo:

curl -X POST https://si784-api-envios.vercel.app/v1/cotizaciones \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"origen":"TAC","destino":"ARE","pesoKg":2.3}'

Por qué Newman

  • La colección es un archivo JSON versionado en el repositorio, junto al código que prueba.
  • Corre en cualquier CI con npx newman run, sin abrir Postman.
  • Tiene reporteros de consola, JUnit y HTML (newman-reporter-htmlextra), así los resultados quedan como artefactos del pipeline.
  • La misma colección se ejecuta contra localhost y contra producción. Solo cambia la variable baseUrl.

Diseño de la colección: 22 peticiones en 4 carpetas

En vez de editar a mano un JSON de 1000 líneas, la colección se genera con un script (generar-coleccion.mjs) a partir de una lista legible de casos. Las aserciones que se repiten se escriben una sola vez:

const cotizacionValida = [
  status(200),
  `pm.test('cumple el esquema de cotización', () => pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(${s(esquemaCotizacion)}));`,
  `pm.test('IGV es el 18 % del subtotal', () => { const d = pm.response.json().desglose; pm.expect(d.igv).to.be.closeTo(d.subtotal * 0.18, 0.011); });`,
  `pm.test('total = subtotal + IGV', () => { const r = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(r.total).to.be.closeTo(r.desglose.subtotal + r.desglose.igv, 0.011); });`
];

Las cuatro carpetas siguen técnicas clásicas de diseño de casos:

  1. Salud y catálogo. Health check, listado, filtro por zona en minúsculas, zona inválida (400) y departamento inexistente (404).
  2. Cotizaciones válidas (partición de equivalencia). Misma zona, distinta zona con express, y selva con valor declarado. Cada caso verifica montos exactos: por ejemplo, Tacna → Arequipa con 2.3 kg debe costar S/ 16.82.
  3. Valores límite. 0.1 kg y 50 kg se aceptan; 0.09 kg, 50.01 kg y un valor declarado de 10 001 devuelven 422.
  4. Errores y robustez. Campos faltantes, tipo incorrecto ("2" en lugar de 2), JSON mal formado (400), Content-Type: text/plain (415) y ruta inexistente (404).

Tres trucos que valen la pena

1. Validar el contrato con JSON Schema, no solo el status:

pm.test('el error sigue el contrato', () => pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(esquemaError));
pm.test('señala el campo pesoKg', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().error.campo).to.eql('pesoKg'));

2. Aserciones a nivel de colección, que se ejecutan después de cada petición:

pm.test('responde en menos de 3 s', () => pm.expect(pm.response.responseTime).to.be.below(3000));
pm.test('responde JSON', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Content-Type')).to.include('application/json'));

3. Comparar dos respuestas con pm.sendRequest. Probamos una propiedad del negocio, "express siempre cuesta más que estándar", lanzando una segunda petición desde el script de pruebas:

pm.sendRequest({ url: pm.environment.get('baseUrl') + '/v1/cotizaciones', method: 'POST', /* ... servicio: 'express' */ },
  (err, res) => pm.test('express > estándar', () => {
    pm.expect(res.json().total).to.be.above(pm.response.json().total);
  }));

Ejecutarla en local 

npm install
npm start          # API en http://localhost:3000
npm run test:api   # newman + reportes HTML y JUnit en reports/

│              requests │   22 │   0 │
│            assertions │  121 │   0 │

El pipeline: probar → desplegar → volver a probar

El workflow de GitHub Actions (ci-cd.yml) tiene tres jobs encadenados:

git push a main
   └─▶ Job 1: unitarias + Newman + k6 smoke (contra localhost)
         └─▶ Job 2: vercel deploy --prod
               └─▶ Job 3: Newman + k6 (contra la URL pública)
  1. Pruebas locales. Levanta la API dentro del runner y corre las pruebas unitarias (node:test), Newman y un smoke de k6.
  2. Despliegue. Usa la CLI de Vercel con el secreto VERCEL_TOKEN. El job obtiene el dominio de producción desde la API de Vercel y lo expone como output.
  3. Pruebas contra producción. Recibe esa URL y ejecuta la misma colección: 
- name: Pruebas funcionales con Newman (producción)
  run: |
    npx newman run tests/postman/envios.postman_collection.json \
      --env-var baseUrl="$BASE_URL" \
      --reporters cli,htmlextra,junit,json \
      --reporter-htmlextra-export reports/newman-produccion.html

Con jq, el resultado JSON de Newman se convierte en una tabla del resumen de la ejecución. Así se ve sin descargar nada. Los reportes HTML quedan como artefactos.

Resultados en producción

Ejecutadas Fallidas
Peticiones 23 (22 + 1 sendRequest) 0
Aserciones 121 0

Mientras desarrollábamos, la propia corrida de Newman detectó una aserción de Content-Type que se serializaba mal al generar la colección. Por eso las aserciones exactas sobre montos usan valores redondeados a centavos y closeTo donde hay cálculos con decimales.

Lecciones

  • Genera la colección desde código. Los cambios se revisan en un diff legible y nadie edita a mano el JSON exportado.
  • Prueba el contrato, no solo el status. Un 200 con un campo de menos también es un bug.
  • Repite las pruebas después de desplegar. Lo que pasa en localhost puede fallar en la plataforma, por enrutamiento, cabeceras o variables de entorno.
  • Valores límite y errores fueron la mitad de los casos y donde aparecieron más sorpresas.

¿Y el rendimiento? Eso lo cubre k6. Lo explica mi compañero Manuel en su artículo; mientras tanto, el script está en tests/k6/carga.js.

title: Scanning 3.8B Lines of Code Across 7,135 GitHub Repos: Measuring Cognitive Ownership & PR Review Risk
description:
AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect. Most high-performing engineering teams use coding assistants every day for boilerplate, migrations, and test scaffolding.

For CTOs, CISOs, and Staff Reviewers, the real systems problem is review velocity versus generation throughput: when diff volume scales faster than human review bandwidth, teams risk losing cognitive ownership, missing unverified third-party dependencies, and merging over-engineered abstractions.

To move this conversation away from guesswork and noisy probabilistic "AI detectors," we have been tracking deterministic static-analysis heuristics across 7,135 open-source GitHub repositories (~3.8 billion lines of code and 16.0 million pattern hits) on SlopCodeMonitor.

4 Governance Vectors Across 7,133 Repositories

Rather than guessing who or what wrote a function, the benchmark maps static findings into four operational review indices (0–100):

  • PR Review Velocity Impact (Mean: 22.28 / 100): Structural complexity, oversized functions, and branching density that slow down human pull-request triage.
  • Cognitive Ownership Risk (Mean: 13.93 / 100): Silent broad exception handling, opaque control-flow nesting, and patterns that obscure runtime failure modes.
  • Agent Over-Engineering Ratio (Mean: 12.5 / 100): Unnecessary wrapper layers, boilerplate proliferation, and premature abstraction.
  • Hallucinated Dependency & Supply-Chain Risk (Mean: 4.73 / 100): Unverified package surfaces and dependency hygiene signals relevant to AppSec and slopsquatting defense.

Important caveat: these scores are heuristic engineering prompts for human review, not proof of AI authorship or confirmed security vulnerabilities.

Language-Level Benchmarks

Structural review signals vary significantly across ecosystems depending on type systems, standard library breadth, and packaging conventions. You can explore the per-language distributions directly:

  • Python Benchmark
  • TypeScript Benchmark
  • Rust Benchmark
  • Go Benchmark

Live Examples & Static README Badges for Maintainers

Widely battle-tested infrastructure codebases maintain remarkably low pattern-signal density despite massive scale:

  • kubernetes/kubernetes:
