If your open-source repository is among the 7,135 scanned projects, you can look it up on slopcodemonitor.ai and grab a zero-backend static SVG badge (or Shields.io endpoint) for your README.md, or suggest a repository for the next scan cycle.

Curious what static signals or diff-size guardrails your engineering org relies on to keep PR reviews sustainable—feedback on the methodology and edge cases is very welcome.

title: "Same access as last year's locum": a four-block brief that keeps the exclusions
description:
"Same access as last year's locum, but this one also needs the X-ray archive, and can they have the on-call rota?"

That is a complete-sounding request. It is not a complete instruction. The dangerous part is the word same: it hides the exclusions that were the whole point of last year's setup, and it treats a new permission as a small add-on.

Say you're the one-person office-systems helper at a small veterinary practice — this is a labelled hypothetical, not a client story. Twice a year a locum covers holidays. I build Maildoer, and follow-up emails like this one are why I care about the brief below. The brief itself is useful even if you never touch the tool: it is the page I would fill in by hand before cloning anyone's account.

Why "same as last year" is an incomplete instruction

Last year's locum note, if you still have it, usually contains three different kinds of fact:

  1. Standing exclusions — things no locum should get, such as the payroll folder, or full after-hours alarm rights.
  2. Last time's exceptions — a one-off that applied to that person only (a shared inbox for a particular consultant, a temporary ultrasound login).
  3. This year's additions — the X-ray archive, the on-call rota, a new lab portal.

If you copy last year's account and then add the new items, you may also copy a one-off that should have died with last year's locum. If you build a fresh account from the new email alone, you will drop the exclusions, because the new email never mentions them.

There is often a fourth problem: the new ask conflicts with a standing rule. "Can they have the on-call rota?" sounds reasonable until you look back and see that locums only receive the rota after their first day, once a named vet has walked them through the out-of-hours list.

The four-block locum access brief

Keep one short page per locum visit. Four blocks only:

LOCUM ACCESS BRIEF
Practice: [name]
Cover dates: [start] – [end]
Person: [locum name]

1. STANDING EXCLUSIONS (do not copy these away)
   - Payroll / accounts folder: no
   - Full alarm set/unset rights: no (day-one set only, if needed)
   - Owner WhatsApp group: no

2. THIS LOCUM'S EXTRAS (new this visit, not assumed)
   - X-ray archive: requested
   - On-call rota: requested — see open question
   - Lab portal: not requested

3. SYSTEMS AND INBOXES IN SCOPE
   - Clinical system: yes, standard locum role
   - Shared "nurses" inbox: yes
   - Shared "accounts" inbox: no (see exclusions)
   - Last year's one-off: consultant inbox for Dr X — expired, do not recreate

4. OPEN QUESTION
   - On-call rota: last year's rule was "after day one, once a named vet has walked through the list." Grant now, or keep that rule?

The brief has one job: make "same" explicit before anyone presses Duplicate User.

A two-email walkthrough

Email 1, last summer (kept as the access note, not as a ticket comment that later gets buried):

Locum cover 4–15 August. Standard clinical login and the nurses inbox. No payroll folder. No full alarm rights — reception will set the alarm on day one if they stay late. No owner WhatsApp group. Do not give the on-call rota until a named vet has walked them through it on day one. They will not need the consultant inbox for Dr X after this fortnight.

Email 2, this autumn:

Same access as last year's locum, but this one also needs the X-ray archive, and can they have the on-call rota?

Email 2 is only safe if Email 1 is still in front of you. The exclusions and the expired consultant inbox live only in the first message. The rota question is not a yes; it is a conflict with a rule already written down.

Before any account is copied, the confirmation back to the practice manager should restate all of that, not just the new extras:

I'll set this up as last August: clinical login, nurses inbox, no payroll folder, no full alarm rights, no owner WhatsApp group, and I won't recreate the Dr X consultant inbox. New this time: X-ray archive. One question before I go further: last year the on-call rota was held back until day one, after a named vet had walked through the list. Do we keep that rule, or grant the rota from the first morning?

Do not grant the extras until the open question is answered. Adding the X-ray archive and the rota in the same step as cloning the account is how an exclusion disappears without anyone noticing.

Pitfalls I would watch for

  • Treating the newest email as the whole spec. "Also the X-ray archive" is an addition, not a replacement for the earlier note.
  • Cloning last year's account as a shortcut. You will revive expired one-offs (the consultant inbox) along with the useful access.
  • Silent yeses. "Can they have the on-call rota?" may already have a written answer from last year. Surface the conflict; don't resolve it quietly.
  • Leaving the brief in your head. If you are off, the next person will only see Email 2, and the exclusions will vanish.
  • Offboarding that only disables the login. When the locum leaves, tick the brief: extras revoked, shared-inbox membership removed, any temporary password notes destroyed. The brief is also the leaving checklist.

What I'd do differently next time

I would date every line in the exclusions block, so a two-year-old "no" can be reviewed rather than treated as law. I would also keep this brief as a living file in the same place as the earlier email, not as a comment on a closed ticket. And I would never use "Duplicate User" as the first action; I would fill the four blocks first, even if that feels slower than copying a known-good account.

Where a later email fits

The habit above stands on its own. Where Maildoer comes in: a later email from the same person is read together with their earlier ones, not as if it were the first. "Same access as last year's locum, but…" can be checked against the August exclusions and the rota rule, instead of starting from a blank account. They can also reply to a result and adjust it without restating the whole history. I don't claim it holds every message forever — only that a follow-up is not handled in isolation.

Want to test the brief above? Send the two emails (or a close stand-in) to do@maildoer.com. 100 credits come with your first email.

When you set up a temporary account, do you keep a written list of what last year's person was not allowed to see, or only a list of what they could do?

title: Docker push manifest invalid from a registry
description:
A docker push manifest invalid failure is the registry refusing the document that describes your image, not the layers, and the reason sits in a detail field that no Docker client prints. Fetch the response body yourself, or change the media types buildx writes, because those are the only two moves that touch the actual disagreement.


The registry answers 400 with code "MANIFEST_INVALID" and a detail naming the media type. Neither client prints the detail, which is why the log looks empty of reasons.

What this error means

Layers upload normally, sometimes all of them, and the step dies on the last request of the push. The wording depends on which client pushed. BuildKit and buildx surface the transport failure and the status code. The classic Docker daemon surfaces the registry error code instead, which renders as the word "manifest invalid" printed twice, because the code and its default message are the same phrase. Neither one prints the sentence that says which media type was refused. We have not recorded a run for this page, and the block below is assembled from the strings each component formats rather than captured from a job.

```Constructed from the strings each component formats, not a recorded run

14 exporting manifest list sha256:c3b9d1a2

14 ERROR: failed to push acme/api:1.4.2: unexpected status from PUT request to https://registry.example.internal/v2/acme/api/manifests/1.4.2: 400 Bad Request

--- the body that came with that 400, fetched separately with curl
{"errors":[{"code":"MANIFEST_INVALID","message":"manifest invalid","detail":"unsupported manifest media type and no default available: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json"}]}




## Common causes

### The registry does not map the OCI media type you pushed

The registry looks the request `Content-Type` up in a table of unmarshal functions, and a registry old enough to predate OCI image indexes has no entry for one. There is no fallback unless a default is registered, which is exactly what the detail sentence says when it ends "and no default available". In our experience this is the common shape behind a 400 on the last request of a push.

### Attestations pulled the whole export into OCI types

Provenance and SBOM attestations cannot be described in the Docker manifest format, so an export that carries them uses OCI media types regardless of what you would otherwise have got. A workflow that turned on provenance for supply-chain reasons can start failing against a registry that was fine the week before, with no change to the Dockerfile.

### A BuildKit upgrade changed the default

BuildKit pins media-type behavior to a compatibility version. On the current path as of 2026-09-20, an image export that does not set `oci-mediatypes` defaults to OCI media types. On the historical path that covers v0.15.0 through v0.31.x, an export without attestations defaulted to Docker media types instead. Upgrading the builder therefore changes what you push without changing your workflow.

### The manifest is schema 1 and something in the chain refuses it

This is the other direction and it is usually a pull rather than a push. A base image published years ago can still be served as `application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws`, which modern clients decline. The wording overlaps with the push case enough to be confusing, and the fix has nothing to do with your exporter.

## How to fix it

### Write Docker media types from the image exporter

The exporter takes `oci-mediatypes` as a boolean option. Setting it false makes buildx write the classic manifest and manifest list formats, which is what a registry that refused the OCI index is asking for. Set it on the output rather than globally, so a second push to a modern registry is unaffected.



```Terminal
docker buildx build \
  --output type=image,name=registry.example.internal/acme/api:1.4.2,oci-mediatypes=false,push=true \
  .

Turn off the attestations that force OCI

  1. Add --provenance=false and --sbom=false to the build that pushes to the strict registry.
  2. Keep them on for the registry that accepts them, if you publish to both.
  3. Treat this as a concession, not a cleanup: you are giving up supply-chain metadata to satisfy a registry. 
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
  with:
    push: true
    provenance: false
    sbom: false
    tags: registry.example.internal/acme/api:1.4.2
    outputs: type=image,oci-mediatypes=false

Pin the exporter behavior across a BuildKit upgrade

The compatibility-version exporter option pins the digest-affecting image assembly behavior, which includes the media-type default. Pinning it makes the upgrade that changes the default a deliberate step rather than something you find out about from a registry.

--output type=image,name=acme/api:1.4.2,push=true,compatibility-version=20

For the schema 1 direction, replace the image

If the type in the detail ends manifest.v1+prettyjws, nothing about your exporter is involved. The image on the other end is in a format current clients removed support for. Repoint the reference at a maintained tag, or mirror the old image through a registry that converts it, and leave your push settings alone.

docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw quay.io/coreos/etcd:v3.3.10 | head -5

How to prevent it

  • Pin compatibility-version on any push that goes to a registry you do not control.
  • Push a throwaway tag from a new builder version before you move the real pipeline to it.
  • Keep one curl step in the workflow that prints the registry response body on failure.
  • Record which of your registries accept OCI indexes, because the log will not tell you later.

The useful sentence is in the body, and the client throws it away

A registry built on the distribution project answers a manifest upload it cannot parse with HTTP 400 and the error code MANIFEST_INVALID. The code carries a default message that happens to read "manifest invalid", and the specific reason goes in a separate detail field.

Then the client drops it. In the distribution client library an error renders as its code followed by its message, and the Detail property is not part of that rendering at all, so a structured error whose detail names the exact media type prints as "manifest invalid: manifest invalid". The containerd path does not do better: its unexpected-status error stores the response body on the struct and formats only the method, the URL and the status. So the answer is on the wire and not in your log.

Where the string is formed What reaches the Actions log
Registry, PutManifest in the distribution handlers HTTP 400, code MANIFEST_INVALID, message "manifest invalid", detail naming the type
Registry, UnmarshalManifest in distribution "unsupported manifest media type and no default available: " and the type, as the detail
Distribution client, its error rendering The code and the message only, so "manifest invalid: manifest invalid"
containerd remotes, its unexpected-status error Method, URL and status only, so "400 Bad Request" with no reason

Read in distribution/distribution on 2026-09-20: the handler that returns the code, the function that formats the detail, and the error type that renders code and message and not detail.

Get the detail out of the registry yourself

Because no client prints it, the fastest diagnosis is to make the same request by hand and read the body. A HEAD against the tag is enough to see the negotiation, and a PUT replay is rarely necessary once you know which types the registry advertises it will accept.

Do this from the job that failed rather than from your laptop, because the token, the registry host and the proxy are all part of what you are testing.

- name: Ask the registry what it says
  run: |
    TOKEN=$(echo "${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}")
    curl -sS -i -X HEAD \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
      -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
      "https://registry.example.internal/v2/acme/api/manifests/1.4.2"

What "unsupported media type" does and does not point at

Two strings in this area are about the old schema 1 format, not about OCI, and reading them backwards sends you to the wrong fix. The distribution sentence "unsupported manifest media type and no default available" appears with application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v1+prettyjws in m3db/m3#4396, where a modern daemon refuses to pull a 2018-era image. The go-containerregistry library has its own "unsupported MediaType" error, and in that library it is raised only for schema 1 manifests, with a link to the issue explaining that the project will not support them.

So when you find either phrase while searching, check the direction before you act. Pulling an ancient image is a schema 1 problem and the fix is a newer image. Pushing a fresh buildx image to a registry that will not take it is an OCI problem, and the fix is on the exporter.

The builder version decides the default, so pin it

BuildKit pins the behavior that affects an image digest, media types included, to a compatibility version you can set as an exporter option. Three values exist at the time of writing and only the newest one defaults an unset oci-mediatypes to OCI, which is why a builder upgrade is a plausible answer to "nothing changed and it broke".

Set it on the push that goes to the strict registry. You are not freezing the builder, only the part of its output that the registry has an opinion about.

BuildKit compatibility version Default when oci-mediatypes is unset
30, the current path as of 2026-09-20 OCI media types
20, the v0.15.0 through v0.31.x path Docker media types, unless the export carries attestations
10, the v0.13.0 and v0.14.0 path Differs from 20 on git source file modes and on zstd, not on media types

Values and wording read in the BuildKit repository on 2026-09-20. An export that carries attestations uses OCI media types on every one of these, because attestations require them.

Why no recorded run backs this page

This failure needs a registry that refuses a format, and every registry the reproduction harness can reach accepts both OCI and Docker manifests. Recording a run would mean standing up a deliberately old registry build, pushing to it, and then presenting the result as though it were a registry you might actually use. That would record our configuration and teach nothing about yours.

The parts that are checkable without a run are checked: the code that returns the status, the function that writes the detail, and the two error types that decline to print it. What a run would add is a screenshot of a log we can already tell you is missing the important line.

FAQ

Why does the log say manifest invalid twice?

Because the error code and its default message are the same words. The distribution client renders an error as its code, lowercased with underscores turned into spaces, followed by the message. MANIFEST_INVALID becomes "manifest invalid" and its default message is also "manifest invalid", so you get both halves. The part that differs between cases is the detail, which that rendering leaves out.

Does oci-mediatypes=false lose anything?

It gives up the formats that attestations need, so an export carrying provenance or an SBOM cannot use it. It also writes the older manifest and manifest list types, which every registry understands, so nothing else about the image changes. Treat it as a compatibility setting for one destination rather than a default you apply everywhere.

How do I see the detail field the client hides?

Repeat the request with curl from the same job and read the response body. The registry returns a JSON object with an errors array, and each entry carries code, message and detail. The detail is the sentence naming the media type. Registry access logs show the status but usually not the body, so the client-side repeat is the quicker route.

Is a 400 on a push ever worth retrying?

No. A 400 from the manifest endpoint means the registry parsed your request and declined its content, which will be identical on the next attempt. Retries are the right answer for the 5xx range, where the registry did not get far enough to judge the request. Spending runner minutes on a retry here buys the same 400 twice.

References

  • distribution: the manifest handlers that return MANIFEST_INVALID
  • distribution: UnmarshalManifest, where the media type detail is written
  • BuildKit: compatibility-version and the media type defaults
  • Docker docs: the image exporter and its options
  • m3db/m3#4396: a schema 1 image refused with the same media type sentence

title: Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
description:
During a routine review on a client's Laravel and Vue project, one pull request added a Composer package with a perfectly reasonable name for parsing VAT numbers. The code looked fine and the tests passed locally for the author, because he had copied a helper from an assistant's answer and installed the package by hand. The CI build failed with "package not found". The package had never existed. The assistant had invented a plausible name. That time the failure was harmless. The worrying part is that anyone can register a missing name on a public registry, and attackers do watch for names that assistants tend to invent.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command against Composer 2.8, npm 10 and pnpm 9. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and through Loop Origin I maintain production SaaS codebases where a growing share of code is AI-assisted.

📚 Series Navigation — Maintaining AI-Written Code in Production

  • Part 1: Reviewing AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist That Catches Real Bugs
  • Part 2: Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code
  • Part 3 (This Post): Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
  • Part 4: Static Analysis Gates: PHPStan, TypeScript Strict & Coverage in CI
  • Part 5: Decision Records So AI Context Doesn't Rot
  • Part 6: Measuring AI Coding Impact With DORA Metrics, Not Vibes

Related earlier posts: Subresource Integrity & CDN Script Pinning · Cron Jobs That Never Ran: Heartbeats & Dead-Man Switches

How do you stop AI coding assistants from adding fake or risky dependencies?

Direct answer: Treat every new dependency in an AI-assisted PR as a review item. Verify the package exists on the official registry, check its age, maintainers and downloads, require lockfile changes to be reviewed, block unapproved packages with an allowlist in CI, run composer audit and npm audit, and pin versions so drift only happens through deliberate update PRs.

Two different problems

It helps to separate them because the fixes differ.

Hallucinated packages are names that do not exist, or did not exist when the model was trained. Researchers have measured this: a 2024 study of code-generating models ("We Have a Package for You!", Spracklen et al.) found a meaningful share of suggested packages did not exist, and many invented names repeated across prompts. Repeated names are what make "slopsquatting" possible: someone registers the invented name and waits.

Dependency drift is quieter. The assistant suggests "^2.0" where you had "2.4.1", adds a second HTTP client because it did not notice the one you already use, or pulls an old major version from its training data. Nothing breaks today. Six months later you have three date libraries and a security advisory on one of them.

Risk signals compared

Signal Hallucinated / typo package Legit but risky Healthy dependency
Exists on Packagist / npm No, or created very recently Yes Yes
Age of first release Days or weeks Years, but last release long ago Years, steady releases
Maintainers One new account One inactive maintainer Several, known org
Weekly downloads Near zero Declining Stable or growing
Install scripts (postinstall) Often present Sometimes Rare, documented
Source repo link Missing or mismatched Archived Active, matches package

No single row decides it. A brand-new package with one maintainer, an install script and no repository link should stop the PR until someone checks it by hand.

Step 1: make dependency changes visible in review

Most teams collapse composer.lock and package-lock.json in the diff view, which is exactly where surprises hide. I add a small CI step that prints a readable summary of what changed:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/dependency-diff.sh — summarise added/removed packages vs main
set -euo pipefail
git fetch origin main --depth=1

echo "== Composer packages added =="
diff <(git show origin/main:composer.lock | jq -r '.packages[].name' | sort) \
     <(jq -r '.packages[].name' composer.lock | sort) | grep '^>' || echo "none"

echo "== npm packages added (top level) =="
diff <(git show origin/main:package.json | jq -r '.dependencies + .devDependencies | keys[]' | sort) \
     <(jq -r '.dependencies + .devDependencies | keys[]' package.json | sort) | grep '^>' || echo "none"

Post that output as a PR comment and reviewers see "added: acme/vat-parser" in plain text instead of a 3,000-line lockfile.

Step 2: verify each new package exists and looks healthy

For Composer, the Packagist API gives you creation date and download counts:

pkg="acme/vat-parser"
curl -sf "https://repo.packagist.org/p2/${pkg}.json" > /dev/null \
  || { echo "BLOCK: ${pkg} not found on Packagist"; exit 1; }
curl -s "https://packagist.org/packages/${pkg}/stats.json" | jq '.downloads.total'

For npm:

npm view some-package time.created maintainers repository.url --json
npm view some-package scripts.postinstall

I fail the build when a package is missing, and flag for manual review when it is younger than 90 days or has fewer than a few thousand total downloads.

Step 3: an allowlist for production dependencies

For client projects with strict needs, an explicit allowlist works well. It is just a file in the repo:

{
  "composer": ["laravel/framework", "guzzlehttp/guzzle", "spatie/laravel-permission"],
  "npm": ["vue", "axios", "pinia", "dayjs"]
}

CI compares top-level dependencies against it. Adding a package means a one-line change to the allowlist that a senior reviewer approves, which forces the conversation "do we need this, and do we already have something that does it?". That question alone has removed duplicate HTTP and date libraries from several projects we maintain.

Step 4: pin versions and control drift 

// composer.json — prefer exact or tight ranges for production apps
"require": {
  "php": "^8.3",
  "laravel/framework": "11.31.*",
  "guzzlehttp/guzzle": "7.9.2"
}

# .npmrc
save-exact=true
ignore-scripts=true   # enable per-package only when needed

Then let a bot (Renovate or Dependabot) open grouped update PRs on a schedule. Updates become deliberate and reviewable, not a side effect of someone pasting an assistant's snippet. ignore-scripts=true blocks install scripts by default, which removes one of the most common ways a malicious package runs code on a developer laptop or CI runner.

Step 5: audit continuously 

composer audit --locked --format=summary
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high

Run both on every PR and nightly on main. Nightly matters because advisories are published after you merge.

Teaching the assistant your stack

Prevention is cheaper than detection. In the repo's assistant instructions file (whatever your tool reads, such as a rules or AGENTS.md file) list the approved libraries for common jobs: "HTTP: Guzzle. Dates: Carbon. Validation: Laravel validator. Never add a new dependency without saying so explicitly." In our experience this cuts surprise packages sharply, though it never replaces the CI checks.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] CI prints added/removed packages as a readable PR comment.
  • [ ] Builds fail when a new package does not exist on the official registry.
  • [ ] Packages younger than 90 days or with very low downloads need manual approval.
  • [ ] Production dependencies are on an allowlist with senior approval for changes.
  • [ ] Versions are pinned (save-exact, tight Composer constraints) and updated via bot PRs.
  • [ ] Install scripts are disabled by default.
  • [ ] composer audit and npm audit run on every PR and nightly.
  • [ ] Assistant instruction files list approved libraries for common tasks.

FAQ

How common are hallucinated packages really?

Common enough to plan for. Published research found that a noticeable percentage of package names suggested by code models did not exist, with open models doing worse than commercial ones. Even a small rate matters when a team merges hundreds of suggestions a month.

Isn't npm audit enough?

No. Audit tools only know about published advisories. A freshly registered malicious package has no advisory yet, which is why existence, age and allowlist checks come first.

Should we ban AI assistants from adding dependencies?

Banning tends to fail quietly. Requiring dependency changes to be explicit, summarised and approved works better and still lets the assistant save time.

What about private registries?

A private mirror (Private Packagist, Verdaccio, Artifactory) that only proxies approved packages is the strongest control. Make sure scoped names cannot fall through to the public registry, or you invite dependency confusion.

How do we clean up existing drift?

Start with composer show --direct and npm ls --depth=0, find duplicates doing the same job, pick one, and migrate in small PRs with characterization tests from Part 2 guarding behaviour.

Can Loop Origin help set this up?

Yes. We add these gates as part of our custom web application and maintenance work, usually in a day or two for a typical Laravel and Vue codebase.

Next in this series, Part 4 covers static analysis gates: PHPStan, TypeScript strict mode and coverage in CI.

title: Sizing a market in Africa with public data: a worked example and a free dataset of the 54 countries
description:
Market sizing is one of the most common exercises in consulting case interviews, and in real projects too. When the market is in Africa, many candidates freeze: they do not know the orders of magnitude, or they quote figures without a year or a source. This post shows a simple method with real World Bank figures, and shares a clean dataset of 13 key indicators for all 54 African countries that you can reuse.

The dataset

The dataset gives, for each African country, the latest World Bank value of 13 indicators (growth, inflation, GDP, GDP per capita in current and PPP dollars, population, life expectancy, access to electricity, internet use, drinking water, forest area, unemployment and poverty), each with its year and its World Bank code. Country names are in English and French. It is a snapshot of 14 November 2026, under CC BY 4.0.

  • Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/omaribanbdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures
  • Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/omaribnabdillah/africa-key-economic-figures-54-countries
  • GitHub: https://github.com/omaribnabdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures 
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("hf://datasets/omaribanbdillah/africa-54-countries-key-figures/africa-54-countries-key-figures-wide.csv")
df[["country_en", "population", "internet", "internet_year", "gdpPerCapita"]].head()

A worked example: how many people could use a mobile service?

Say a client wants to launch a paid mobile learning service in West and East Africa, and asks how many potential users each country has. A first, top-down estimate takes three steps.

1. Start from the population. Senegal had about 18.9 million people in 2025, Côte d'Ivoire 32.7 million, Kenya 57.5 million and Nigeria 237.5 million.

2. Keep only the people who use the internet. The share of internet users was 60.1% in Senegal, 41.4% in Côte d'Ivoire, 35.0% in Kenya and 41.2% in Nigeria (2024 values). This gives about 11.4 million internet users in Senegal, 13.6 million in Côte d'Ivoire, 20.1 million in Kenya and 97.9 million in Nigeria.

Note that the population is a 2025 figure and the internet share a 2024 figure. That is normal with public data, but say it out loud in an interview: "I am combining the 2025 population with the 2024 internet share, so this is an order of magnitude."

3. Narrow down to people who can pay. Here the choice of measure matters. GDP per capita in current US dollars was about 1,224 dollars in Nigeria and 3,050 dollars in Côte d'Ivoire in 2025. In purchasing power parity (PPP), the order flips: about 9,532 international dollars in Nigeria against 8,209 in Côte d'Ivoire. Current dollars tell you what a price in dollars means for a household. PPP tells you what people can buy at local prices. For a service priced in local currency, PPP is often the better guide. For a service priced in dollars, look at current dollars.

From there, you apply assumptions that you state clearly: the share of the target age group, the share that would pay, the price. The data gives you a solid base. Your judgment does the rest.

Sanity checks that impress interviewers

  • Access to electricity. A phone needs to be charged. Access to electricity was 82.9% in Senegal and 62.5% in Nigeria in 2024, but as low as 5.4% in South Sudan and 13.4% in Chad. A service that assumes daily use will not reach the same share everywhere.
  • Totals. The 54 countries have about 1.5 billion people. If your country estimate is a large share of that, check your logic.
  • Year and source. Always say where a number comes from and how old it is. "About 11 million internet users in Senegal, from World Bank data for 2024 and 2025" sounds far more credible than a bare number.
  • Modeled figures. Unemployment in this table is a modeled estimate by the International Labour Organization, not a survey count. Use it for orders of magnitude, not for precise comparisons.

Common mistakes

  1. Mixing current dollars and PPP dollars in the same calculation.
  2. Using a figure without its year, when some values are two or three years older than others.
  3. Treating a regional average as if it applied to every country. Africa has 54 very different economies: South Africa's GDP was about 427 billion dollars in 2025, that of the Comoros about 1.8 billion.

Practice

The best way to get comfortable is to repeat the exercise with different countries and products until the method becomes automatic. Pick a country, write down three figures with their year, and build a quick estimate in under five minutes.

Disclosure: I am the founder of Invea, the company behind Consulting 360, a mobile app to prepare consulting case and fit interviews, with sourced profiles of the 54 African countries. It is free to download on iPhone (App Store) and Android (Google Play): https://consulting360.app/. The dataset above comes from the same country data, and it is free to reuse with credit.

Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators, CC BY 4.0.

title: My AI Agent Works for Me Every Day. Here's How I Make It Prove Everything.
description:
An entry for the zkVerify Agent Games — Creator Track. #AgentGames

I don't run demos. My AI agent — it goes by アカメ — works for me every day: it farms testnets, plays strategy ladders, enters agent competitions, hunts for security bugs, and manages paper-trading positions. I am not a developer babysitting a chatbot. I give orders in chat, and the agent does the work while I do other things.

That arrangement only works because of one rule I enforce on everything it does:

If it can't be verified, it didn't happen.

The problem with trusting an agent

An AI agent will happily tell you a task is done. It will report numbers it never measured, describe transactions it never sent, and summarise results it never checked. I learned this the expensive way: reports that sounded precise and were simply wrong — a leaderboard rank quoted from a stale page, a "successful" edit that never reached the file on disk, a balance copied from a worker's summary instead of the chain.

So we rebuilt the working relationship around proof. Not vibes, not confidence — artefacts a third party can check.

What proof looks like in practice

On-chain receipts for anything that moves value. Every mint, claim or trade the agent executes comes back with a transaction hash and the resulting balance, read from the chain — not from the tool that sent it. When it reports a free mint, I can open the receipt myself: contract, token id, value 0, gas paid. When a swap has no safe route, the rule is to stop and say so, not improvise.

Signed, inspectable work for competitions. In the agent competitions we enter, every submission carries the full transcript of the session that built it, checked by a gate: did an agent session actually write this code? Was it revised at least once? Do the timestamps fall inside the competition window? Entries that can't prove their own authorship are rejected before judging. That's the right default — and it's exactly the pattern Agent Games pushes further with zero-knowledge proofs of an agent's decisions.

Live sources over summaries. Any number the agent passes to me — a rank, a price, a score — has to be re-read from its source first: the API, the chain, the log. Anything it could not verify gets labelled unverified, in those words. That one habit killed an entire category of confident nonsense.

A paper trail I can audit. Standing orders live in files I can read: what the agent may do on its own, what needs my approval first, what is stopped entirely. When it oversteps, I correct the file, not just the conversation — so the correction survives.

Why Agent Games gets it right

Most agent competitions judge outputs. Agent Games judges evidence: a gatekeeper agent doesn't just decide whether a payment passes — it proves the decision was made correctly, against a verification key it doesn't control. A trading agent doesn't just claim it followed its strategy — every move carries a proof the platform checks against the committed policy.

That is the same lesson my daily work taught me, formalised: a proof can verify perfectly and still authorise the wrong action — so you verify the decision, not just the signature. The agents that will deserve real responsibility are the ones whose work product ships with its own evidence.

The receipts

This isn't theory. In the last month my agent has, among other things:

  • Executed dozens of on-chain mints and claims, every one reported back with its transaction hash and post-transaction balance.
  • Run a daily testnet trading farm under a written mandate (buy/sell rules fixed in advance, deviations reported the same day).
  • Competed in agent strategy ladders and build competitions where every entry is signed and transcript-gated.
  • Filed security reports only where a finding could be reproduced end-to-end — no proof-of-concept, no report.

Each of those leaves a public or inspectable record. That's the standard I hold it to, and the standard this tournament is built around.

Agents are going to be given real work and real assets. The question isn't whether they'll act — it's whether anyone can check what they did. Build agents that can prove it.

— upss, competing in the zkVerify Agent Games, Season 01. #AgentGames

title: Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
description:
A SaaS team I worked with rolled out passkeys last spring and celebrated a big drop in password-reset tickets. Three months later, a review of their support logs showed something uncomfortable. Their "lost my passkey" flow sent a magic link to the account email, the link stayed valid for seven days, it could be reused, and changing the email address did not require any re-authentication. Sign-in had become very strong. Recovery was still the weakest version of their old password reset. Attackers rarely break the front door when there is an unlocked side door right next to it.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every snippet against current OWASP Forgot Password and Authentication guidance, NIST SP 800-63B, Laravel 11 and Node 22. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and I build the free developer tools at PixelValut. Everything here is about hardening recovery in an app you own.

📚 Series Navigation — Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps

  • Part 1: Rolling Out Passkeys Without Locking Users Out
  • Part 2: Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation
  • Part 3: CSRF in 2026: SameSite, Fetch Metadata & Origin Checks
  • Part 4 (This Post): Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
  • Part 5: Protecting Login Endpoints: Credential-Stuffing Signals & Adaptive Rate Limits
  • Part 6: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions

Related earlier posts: Browser Secrets That Leak: Token Storage, Quotas & Outbound Controls · OAuth 2.1, OIDC ID Tokens & PKCE Forensics

How do you secure account recovery when users sign in with passkeys?

Direct answer: Treat recovery as a sign-in method with the same strength as your weakest factor. Use single-use, high-entropy tokens stored only as hashes, expire them in 15–30 minutes, give the same response whether or not the account exists, rate-limit per account and IP, notify every existing channel, revoke sessions after recovery, and add a cooldown before sensitive changes.

Why recovery is the real security boundary

Your account is only as strong as the easiest path into it. With passwords, that path was usually phishing. With passkeys, phishing gets much harder, so the easiest path moves to recovery: email links, SMS codes, support desk overrides and "change email" forms. If any of those accepts less proof than a passkey, that is now your effective security level.

The goal is not to make recovery impossible. Users do lose phones. The goal is to make recovery slower, louder and more auditable than normal sign-in, so a real owner gets back in and an impostor gets noticed.

Recovery methods compared

Recovery method Strength Main risk User friction When I use it
Second registered passkey (another device) High User never registers one Low Always prompt after first passkey
Single-use recovery codes (printed/stored) High Lost or stored in plain notes Medium Offer at enrolment, require confirmation
Email magic link Medium Mailbox compromise, long-lived links Low With short expiry + notifications + cooldown
SMS code Low–medium SIM swap, interception Low Avoid as sole factor; secondary signal only
Support desk / ID check Varies Social engineering of agents High Last resort, with scripted verification

The single most effective change is getting users to register a second passkey or save recovery codes at enrolment. Every account that has one rarely needs the weaker paths at all.

Building a safe recovery token

Most recovery bugs I find are in token handling. The token should be random, single-use, short-lived and never stored in plain text.

Node (Express) example:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const TOKEN_TTL_MS = 20 * 60 * 1000; // 20 minutes

export async function issueRecoveryToken(db, userId) {
  const raw = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); // 256 bits
  const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest('hex');

  // Invalidate any earlier unused tokens for this user
  await db.query('UPDATE recovery_tokens SET used_at = now() WHERE user_id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL', [userId]);
  await db.query(
    'INSERT INTO recovery_tokens (user_id, token_hash, expires_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)',
    [userId, hash, new Date(Date.now() + TOKEN_TTL_MS)]
  );
  return raw; // only ever sent in the email, never logged
}

export async function consumeRecoveryToken(db, raw) {
  const hash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest('hex');
  const { rows } = await db.query(
    `UPDATE recovery_tokens SET used_at = now()
     WHERE token_hash = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
     RETURNING user_id`,
    [hash]
  );
  return rows[0]?.user_id ?? null; // atomic: second use returns null
}

The UPDATE ... RETURNING makes consumption atomic, so two requests racing with the same link cannot both succeed. Storing only the SHA-256 hash means a database leak does not hand out working links. You can sanity-check your hashing output with a hash generator while debugging, using test values only.

Laravel: the built-in password broker already hashes tokens and expires them. Tighten the defaults in config/auth.php:

'passwords' => [
    'users' => [
        'provider' => 'users',
        'table' => 'password_reset_tokens',
        'expire' => 20,   // minutes, default is 60
        'throttle' => 120, // seconds between requests per user
    ],
],

For a passkey "add a new device" recovery flow, reuse the same broker pattern rather than inventing a second token system.

Same response, every time

The recovery form should never tell a stranger whether an account exists:

app.post('/recover', recoverLimiter, async (req, res) => {
  const user = await findUserByEmail(req.body.email);
  if (user) {
    const token = await issueRecoveryToken(db, user.id);
    await sendRecoveryEmail(user, token);
  }
  // Identical body, status and similar timing either way
  res.status(202).json({ message: 'If that account exists, we sent a link.' });
});

Send the email from a queue job so response time does not reveal whether a message was actually sent.

After recovery: limit the blast radius

Getting back in should not immediately unlock everything. After a successful recovery I apply four rules:

  1. Revoke all other sessions and refresh tokens. Part 2 of this series covers server-side revocation.
  2. Notify every channel on file, including the old email if it was changed, with a clear "this wasn't me" link.
  3. Start a cooldown (for example 24–72 hours) before changing email, adding payout details, exporting data or removing other passkeys.
  4. Log the event with timestamp, IP range and user agent so support can review it later.

When checking cooldown windows and token expiry in logs, a Unix timestamp converter saves a lot of mental arithmetic.

The support desk is part of your auth system

Many real account takeovers go through a helpful support agent. Give agents a script: verify through existing channels, never change the email and the recovery method in the same ticket, and require a second agent for overrides on high-value accounts. Record every manual override as an auth event, not just a ticket note.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every user is prompted to add a second passkey or save recovery codes at enrolment.
  • [ ] Recovery tokens are at least 128 bits of randomness, single-use and stored as hashes.
  • [ ] Tokens expire in 30 minutes or less and earlier tokens are invalidated on reissue.
  • [ ] The recovery endpoint returns the same response whether or not the account exists.
  • [ ] Recovery is rate-limited per account and per IP.
  • [ ] All sessions are revoked after recovery and every channel is notified.
  • [ ] Sensitive changes have a cooldown after recovery.
  • [ ] Support overrides are scripted, logged and reviewed.

FAQ

If users have passkeys, why keep email recovery at all?

Because people lose devices and not everyone syncs passkeys. Removing email recovery entirely tends to push users to support, which is often weaker. Keep it, but make it short-lived, noisy and followed by a cooldown.

Are SMS codes acceptable for recovery?

As a secondary signal, sometimes. As the only factor, I avoid them because of SIM-swap risk. NIST classes SMS as a restricted authenticator for this reason.

How long should a recovery link last?

I use 15–30 minutes. Long enough to switch to an email app, short enough that an old email in a compromised mailbox is useless.

Should recovery codes be hashed too?

Yes. Store them like passwords, using a slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2, and mark each one used after a single redemption.

Does a cooldown annoy legitimate users?

Slightly, and that is the trade-off. Explain it clearly in the UI ("For your safety, email changes are paused for 48 hours after recovery"). Most users accept it when they understand why.

What should I monitor?

Spikes in recovery requests, recoveries followed quickly by email or payout changes, and many recovery requests from one IP range. Those patterns usually show an attack before customers report it.

Next in this series, Part 5 covers protecting login endpoints with credential-stuffing signals and adaptive rate limits.

  • TikTok: PixelValut (@pixelvalut007)

title: A prompt-injected model cannot skip your approval step
description:
A human-in-the-loop design usually has the same shape: the model proposes an action, the graph stops at an approval step, a person says yes or no, and only then does the tool run. The guarantee you want is that the model has no way to reach the tool without passing the stop.

That guarantee holds only if every path around the stop is closed, including the paths a model can influence by text alone. A model that has read a hostile web page or a poisoned document can be steered into producing unusual output: a tool name you did not expect, a routing hint, a message that looks like a human answer. This post lists the places where 10xGraph decides on the graph's side instead of trusting that output, and what you still have to do yourself. It describes behaviour and design, not ways to attack a particular app.

10xGraph is open-source, self-hosted infrastructure for AI applications. You write the agents, tools and tasks; 10xGraph runs them behind an API server with authentication, role-based access, tenant isolation, durable state in Postgres and Redis, background jobs, metrics and tracing, and generates Docker and Kubernetes deploy files. MIT licensed, by 10xScale. Formerly Agentflow.

The reference pages are Interrupts and the security model.

Handoffs only go where a handoff tool says

Handoff is how one agent passes the conversation to another, through a tool made with create_handoff_tool. If any tool call named transfer_to_<X> moved the run to node <X>, a steered model could name a node that your edges never lead to, and that includes a node behind an approval step.

So a handoff is honoured only when the ToolNode holds a tool of that name created by create_handoff_tool. Any other transfer_to_* call is an ordinary tool call, and if no such tool exists it gets the usual "Tool not found" result.

The same rule covers Command(goto=...) returned from your own code. A target that is neither a node in the graph nor END raises GraphError with code GRAPH_007, naming the node it came from and the unknown target.

Starting a run at a chosen node with current_node is a separate, intended feature (a frontend can send the agent the user picked). If a node needs an entry guard, enforce it inside the graph. The change above is about what the model can do, not what your caller can do.

Tools hidden by tools_tags cannot be called

An Agent can advertise only the tools that match tools_tags. Showing the model only the tagged tools is not enough on its own, because the ToolNode could still run any registered name the model happened to guess.

So the Agent records the names it advertised on the assistant message (metadata["allowed_tools"]), and the dispatch step refuses a call to anything outside that list with the same "Tool not found" error. If you use tags to keep a destructive tool away from a low-trust agent, the tag holds at run time and not just in the prompt.

A tool name cannot be claimed twice

When a ToolNode also connects to an MCP server, a remote tool could otherwise take over the name of a local tool, so calls meant for your function would go to the server. A collision between an MCP tool and a local or remote tool on the same ToolNode raises ValueError ("Rename one of them"), and the check runs outside the code that swallows connection errors, so it cannot be hidden by a failed server ping.

Forged tool results are refused

Remote tools run on the client, and the client sends the result back to resume the run. That is the one case where the API accepts a message with the tool role, and it is narrow.

  • Client messages may only have the user role. The assistant and system roles are refused, and so is a tool message that carries anything other than tool results.
  • A tool result is accepted only for a remote tool call that is waiting for one on that thread. A result for a call the model never made, a second result for the same call, or a result for a server tool is refused.
  • A client tool can never carry the name of a server tool. Otherwise a client could declare a tool with the name of the one paused for approval and post a "result" for it.

The effect is that the approval path cannot be satisfied by pretending to be the model or the tool.

A resume answers one specific question

A resume carries a value, and the value can be bound to the prompt it answers:

  • The client can send interrupt_id with the resume on invoke, stream and WebSocket. If the thread is not paused, or is paused at another interrupt (a stale tab, a retried request after the first answer was consumed), the API answers 409 and records nothing. This is how a late "yes" fails to approve a different request.
  • The core checks the id again and, when the interrupt declared a response_schema (a JSON Schema), validates the value against it. A mismatch raises InterruptMismatchError (INTERRUPT_001), and a value that does not satisfy the schema raises ResumeValidationError (INTERRUPT_002). Nothing is recorded in either case.

The API checks the id first and answers 409 before a stream starts. It also passes the id to the core, which enforces it again.

from tenxgraph.utils import interrupt

async def refund(amount: float) -> str:
    decision = interrupt(
        {"amount": amount},
        message=f"Refund ${amount}?",
        reason="tool_approval",
        response_schema={
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"approved": {"type": "boolean"}},
            "required": ["approved"],
        },
    )
    if not decision or not decision.get("approved"):
        return "Refund declined"
    return issue_refund(amount)

Without interrupt_id, a resume answers whatever the thread is paused at, as before. Send the id from any client where a person can have two tabs open.

What you still own

  • None of this makes a model trustworthy. It removes shortcuts around your graph.
  • Authentication, role-based access and ownership are separate layers, covered in the security model. Another user's thread answers 404. Permissions apply per route; there are no per-tool permissions, so decide inside the tool who may do what.
  • A tool that must be safe against a steered model should still validate its own arguments and use idempotency keys. See Interrupts for how to place the stop before the tool, not after it.

Frequently asked questions

Does this stop prompt injection?

No. Nothing stops a model from being steered by text it reads. These controls limit what a steered model can do to the parts of the graph you did not give it: the route it takes, the tools it can call and the approval a human gives.

Can a client approve an interrupt by sending a tool result?

No. The API accepts a tool result only as the answer to a remote tool call that is waiting for one. A result for a server tool, for a call the model never made, or a second result for the same call is refused.

What does interrupt_id add to a resume?

It ties the answer to the exact prompt the human saw. If the thread is paused at a different interrupt, or not paused at all, the API answers 409 and nothing is recorded.

Originally published on the 10xGraph blog.

title: 87% of Wall Street fears AI as biggest financial risk, Fed survey says
description:
Artificial intelligence has emerged as the biggest risk to the financial system according to the Federal Reserve's contacts. 87% of respondents in the latest Fed survey cited AI as a significant risk, up from 50% in spring 2026, driven by elevated stock market valuations, cyberattacks, and the complex financing of AI infrastructure.

The dramatic increase reflects growing concern among bankers, investors and regulators about how the accelerated adoption of generative AI could destabilize financial markets, from algorithmic trading to credit assessment and fraud detection.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's survey, released this week, shows that AI-linked risks already outweigh traditional concerns such as inflation, geopolitics and standalone cyberattacks.

For Nvidia and other AI companies, the message is clear: Regulatory scrutiny isn't going to wane. The Fed and IMF are already monitoring the circular financing loop that links chipmakers to data centers and neoclouds.

title: Depot vs WarpBuild for GitHub Actions runners
description:
Depot vs WarpBuild used to be a tie on price and is not one today: Depot lists a 2 vCPU Linux runner at $0.006 a minute, which is GitHub-hosted list price to the cent, and WarpBuild lists the same shape at $0.004. WarpBuild is a third cheaper at every Linux size both sell, so the case for Depot now has to be made on what the extra money buys.


10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, at rates read 20 September 2026. The macOS halves are identical, so the Linux rate is the whole difference; the dashed band is the Latchkey plan the compute bars exclude.

Depot sells ephemeral EC2 runners with a RAM disk in front of the root disk, 2 GB at 2 vCPU rising to 32 GB at 64 vCPU, and a cache its documentation describes at up to 1,000 MiB/s. Usage is tracked by the second with no one-minute minimum, and minutes come bundled into a plan, $20 a month with 2,000 or $200 with 20,000, rather than a standing free tier.

WarpBuild sells three things from one account: managed cloud runners at $0.004 a Linux minute, remote Docker builders priced separately from $0.06 a minute, and a bring-your-own-cloud mode at $0.002 a minute where runners execute inside your own AWS, GCP or Azure account and the compute lands on your cloud bill. Billing is per minute, and cache is a line item rather than an allowance.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

Depot WarpBuild Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk, 2 GB RAM disk) $0.004 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 130 GB disk, 4 GB RAM disk) $0.008 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier None standalone: 2,000 minutes with the $20/month Developer plan, 20,000 with the $200/month Startup plan Not published. Sign-up needs no card until you reach a usage or credit limit 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Per-second usage tracking, with whole minutes billed at the end of the month and no one-minute minimum Per minute, in its own words: "CI runners are billed on a per-minute basis" Per minute
Runner sizes and OS 2 to 64 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64 (Graviton4); Windows Server 2022 and 2025 from 2 vCPU, with no Hyper-V; macOS at 8 vCPU 2 to 32 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64; Windows from 4 vCPU; macOS M4 Pro at 6 and 12 vCPU; Linux on Apple silicon at 6 and 12 vCPU 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence Depot Cache, 25 GB included on Developer and 250 GB on Startup, then $0.20/GB/month; not isolated by branch Cache storage $0.20 per GB-month plus $0.0001 per write or restore; snapshot restore $0.04 per job and $0.025 per hour of snapshot storage Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration A RAM disk on every runner, plus remote container builds as a separate product Remote Docker builders billed separately, 16 vCPU at $0.06/min up to 192 vCPU at $0.88/min, driven by Warpbuilds/build-push-action@v7; cache TTL 10 days latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits Not published Advertised as unlimited job concurrency, with an explicit no-queue guarantee only on Enterprise Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run Ephemeral EC2 instances in Depot's AWS account, or in your own account on Depot Managed WarpBuild's own cloud, or your AWS, GCP or Azure account under BYOC at $0.002/min Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries Not offered Not offered Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required Change the runs-on label. The repository must be owned by a GitHub organization Sign up, install the WarpBuild bot from its dashboard rather than the GitHub marketplace, then change the runs-on label to a runner ID A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

The rate cards, size by size

This is the table the two vendor sites no longer agree on, and it is the reason this page needed rewriting. WarpBuild doubles its rate with every vCPU step from $0.004, and so does Depot from $0.006, so the gap stays at a third all the way up.

Linux x64 Depot WarpBuild GitHub-hosted Latchkey
2 vCPU $0.006 $0.004 $0.006 $0.0025
4 vCPU $0.012 $0.008 $0.012 $0.005
8 vCPU $0.024 $0.016 $0.022 $0.01
16 vCPU $0.048 $0.032 $0.042 $0.02
32 vCPU $0.096 $0.064 $0.082 Not offered
2 vCPU arm64 $0.006 $0.003 $0.005 Not offered

Two things fall out of that table that neither vendor page says out loud. The first is that Depot matches GitHub-hosted list price at 2 and 4 vCPU and then passes it: at 8 vCPU it is $0.024 against GitHub's $0.022, and at 32 vCPU $0.096 against $0.082, because GitHub's ladder flattens as it climbs and Depot's does not. The second is arm64, where WarpBuild charges $0.003 and Depot charges its x64 rate of $0.006, so the architecture that is usually the cheap one costs twice as much on Depot.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, priced three ways

The usual workload: 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, on a private repository, at the rates above.

10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
Depot $60 at $0.006/min $160 at $0.08/min $220 before plan fees
WarpBuild $40 at $0.004/min $160 at $0.08/min on a 6 vCPU M4 Pro $200
Latchkey $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

The macOS half is identical, which is why the Linux rate decides it: $20 a month on this mix, and $200 a year at three times the volume. Depot also starts from a plan fee of at least $20, where WarpBuild publishes no monthly fee at all, so the gap on a small account is wider than the table shows. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

BYOC is the line that makes WarpBuild structurally different rather than just cheaper. At $0.002 a minute, the same 10,000 Linux minutes cost $20 in WarpBuild fees, and then your own cloud account pays for the instances, which is a number WarpBuild cannot publish because it is yours. That is the right buy if you hold committed spend or need jobs inside your VPC, and the wrong one if nobody on the team wants another AWS footprint to own.

Then the cache meters, which are easy to miss on both. WarpBuild charges $0.20 per GB-month of cache storage plus $0.0001 for every write or restore, so a 50 GB cache is $10 a month plus roughly $1 per 10,000 operations, and a snapshot restore is $0.04 a job on top. Depot includes 25 GB on the Developer plan and charges $0.20 per GB-month after that, so the same 50 GB is $20 of plan plus $5 of storage. Cheap either way at this size, and worth checking before a monorepo pushes it to 500 GB.

Reliability

An Actions SLA appears on these pages only as something you buy: WarpBuild lists a contractual 99.9% uptime SLA and unlimited concurrency under Enterprise, and Depot publishes no figure on its pricing page. Depot does publish one honest constraint worth repeating, which is that Apple licensing makes its macOS capacity inelastic, so macOS jobs can queue at busy times.

On both, a job that fails for a reason unrelated to your code fails, bills the minutes it burned, and waits for a person. That is the whole category of work these rate cards do not price, and it is measurable in your own history: count the runs that passed on the second attempt with no code change between them. Exit code 137 and npm network errors in CI are the two that most often look like a runner problem and are not.

When to choose Depot

  • Your jobs are short and numerous, so per-second tracking with no one-minute minimum beats a lower per-minute rate on a wide matrix.
  • Your jobs are disk-bound: 100 GB at 2 vCPU with a RAM disk in front of it is more machine than the rate suggests.
  • You need 64 vCPU Linux, or Windows at 2 vCPU, neither of which WarpBuild publishes.
  • You want container builds and runner minutes from one vendor, with a cache the docs rate at up to 1,000 MiB/s.

When to choose WarpBuild

  • Your bill is mostly Linux minutes. A third off at every size is the plainest saving on this page.
  • You build on arm64: $0.003 against Depot's $0.006 at 2 vCPU is half price, and below GitHub's own arm64 rate of $0.005.
  • You want runners inside your own cloud account. BYOC at $0.002 a minute plus your compute is a different cost structure, not a discount.
  • Your Docker builds want a dedicated remote builder you size yourself, from 16 vCPU at $0.06 a minute up to 192 vCPU at $0.88.
  • One caveat: Windows starts at 4 vCPU on WarpBuild, and at 4 vCPU the two vendors are level at $0.016 a minute.

Switching: the exact diff

Both are a label change on top of one account step: Depot needs the repository to be owned by a GitHub organization, and WarpBuild needs its bot installed from the WarpBuild dashboard rather than the GitHub marketplace. Nothing else in the workflow moves, and because runner selection is per job you can run this exact diff on two jobs in the same file and compare a fortnight of real runs.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: warp-ubuntu-latest-x64-4x

   build-arm:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
+    runs-on: warp-ubuntu-latest-arm64-4x

The verdict

On published rates this is now WarpBuild's comparison to lose: a third off Depot at every Linux size, half price on arm64, no plan fee to clear first, and a BYOC mode that changes the cost structure rather than the discount. Depot is not overpriced so much as differently priced, and the two things it sells that WarpBuild does not publish are per-second metering and a genuinely large disk under every runner, both of which matter more than the rate if your matrix is wide or your jobs thrash the filesystem. Price them against your own billed-to-elapsed ratio rather than against each other. Neither of them does anything about the run that failed on a registry timeout at 2am, which is the line item that never appears on a rate card.

FAQ

Is WarpBuild cheaper than Depot?

On Linux, yes, and by a consistent third: $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU, $0.008 against $0.012 at 4, and $0.064 against $0.096 at 32, read 20 September 2026. On arm64 it is half: $0.003 against $0.006. macOS is level at $0.08 a minute, and Windows is level at $0.016 for 4 vCPU. Depot can still win on a matrix of very short jobs, because it tracks usage by the second and WarpBuild bills per minute.

Are Depot runners 3x faster than GitHub-hosted?

That is Depot's own claim, published as "up to 3x faster than a GitHub-hosted runner", and it is not a benchmark you can reproduce from the page: it names no workload. What is checkable is the hardware behind it, which is a larger disk, a RAM-disk accelerator and a cache Depot rates at up to 1,000 MiB/s. We have not run our own comparison yet, so we are not repeating a multiplier as though it were measured.

What is WarpBuild BYOC and what does it actually cost?

BYOC runs the runners inside your own AWS, GCP or Azure account while WarpBuild keeps the control plane. The published fee is $0.002 a minute for Linux and for Windows on AWS and Azure, with add-ons free, and the instances themselves appear on your cloud bill at whatever you pay for them. For 10,000 Linux minutes that is $20 in WarpBuild fees plus your own compute, against $40 on its managed runners and $60 on Depot.

Do Depot and WarpBuild support arm64 runners?

Both do, at very different prices. WarpBuild publishes arm64 from $0.003 a minute at 2 vCPU up to $0.048 at 32 vCPU, a 25% discount against its own x64 rate. Depot runs arm64 on Graviton4 and charges the same as x64, $0.006 at 2 vCPU. GitHub-hosted arm64 sits between them at $0.005. Latchkey has no arm64 runner at all, which is a real gap on this page and not one worth papering over.

References

  • Depot GitHub Actions runner types and per-minute prices
  • Depot pricing and plan inclusions
  • WarpBuild pricing: runners, Docker builders, BYOC and add-ons
  • WarpBuild cloud runner IDs and shapes
  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates by runner

title: Sketching Method Estimates Token Attribution With Far Fewer Evaluations
description:
Researchers propose algorithm estimating leave-one-out attribution for all n prompt tokens using O(sqrt(log(1/epsilon))/epsilon) model evaluations, rather than n, under stability assumption. They also prove matching lower bound, showing method is asymptotically optimal.

Why it matters

Cheaper attribution could make it practical to identify which prompt parts drive outputs, aiding debugging, auditing and prompt design.

Analysis

The paper addresses leave-one-out attribution, normally requiring one evaluation per token. Its sketching algorithm needs far fewer calls when outputs are stable, and the matching lower bound suggests the rate cannot be substantially improved. The main uncertainty is whether the stability assumption holds reliably for large models and realistic prompts.

Source: arXiv

title: Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results
description:
Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results

Imagine copying a player’s inventory before updating it. You add a new item to the copy, then discover that the original inventory has changed too.

Python is behaving consistently—but understanding that behaviour requires knowing which objects your variables refer to.

Let’s explore list references and copying through a different set of examples.

1. Two names can share one inventory 

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['map']

The assignment saved_items = player_items gives the existing list another name. It does not save an independent snapshot.

Both names refer to the same list, so removing an item through player_items also affects what you see through saved_items.

Create a separate outer list when you need a snapshot:

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items.copy()

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['torch', 'map']

For this list of strings, a shallow copy provides the separation we need.

2. += and + can behave differently

These two operations look similar, but their effect on a list’s aliases differs.

Using += 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks += ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read', 'practise']

For a built-in list, += extends the existing list. Since shared_tasks refers to that list too, it sees the change.

Using + 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks = tasks + ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read']

Here, + creates a new list. The assignment then makes tasks refer to it.

shared_tasks still refers to the original list.

Remember: For built-in lists, += modifies the existing object, while + produces a new one.

3. A function can modify the caller’s list

Consider a function that adds a participant:

def register(names):
    names.append("Maya")

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
register(participants)

print(participants)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

During the call, the parameter names refers to the same list as participants. The function modifies that shared list.

However, reassigning the parameter behaves differently:

def register(names):
    names = names + ["Maya"]
    return names

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
updated = register(participants)

print(participants)
print(updated)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah']
['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

The expression names + ["Maya"] creates a new list. Reassigning the local name names does not reassign participants.

The function returns the new list so the caller can use it.

4. Equal lists are not necessarily the same list

Python provides two comparisons that answer different questions:

first = [4, 8]
second = first.copy()
third = first

print(first == second)
print(first is second)
print(first is third)

Output:

True
False
True

Here is what each comparison checks:

Expression Question
first == second Do these lists contain equal values?
first is second Are these references to the same object?
first is third Are these references to the same object?

Use == to compare list contents. Use is when you specifically need to check object identity.

5. A copied list can still share dictionaries

Nested data does not have to contain inner lists. The same issue arises with dictionaries inside a list.

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = products.copy()
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

0
0

The outer list was copied, but the dictionaries inside it remain shared.

For this data, a deep copy creates independent dictionaries too:

from copy import deepcopy

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = deepcopy(products)
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

12
0

Choose the copy depth based on which mutable objects need to be independent. Deep copying can do unnecessary work when sharing nested objects is intentional.

How to reason through these examples

Before predicting the output, identify:

  1. Which lines create new lists.
  2. Which names refer to the same list.
  3. Which operations modify existing objects.
  4. Whether a copy still contains shared mutable objects.

This approach helps you explain the behaviour instead of memorising individual examples.

For more detail, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Free PCEP practice test

Preparing for PCEP? I create Python learning resources through AM Academy, and you can access my free practice test here: https://www.udemy.com/course/python-pcep-30-03-certification-practice-tests-2026/?couponCode=FREE-COURSE-PCEP. title: Stripe webhook mistakes that lose or repeat payments
description:
A Stripe webhook endpoint is a public URL that moves money and access. Five coding mistakes let a forged request or a plain retry do the wrong thing.

A Stripe webhook endpoint is an ordinary web address that Stripe calls when something happens in your account: a payment succeeds, a subscription renews, a dispute opens. Whatever your handler does next, such as shipping a product, switching on a plan or crediting a balance, is real. That makes the endpoint a target for two kinds of trouble. Someone outside Stripe can post a made-up event to it, and Stripe itself can legitimately deliver the same event more than once. Many webhook bugs that cost money come from five habits in the handler code: parsing the body too early, skipping the signature check, turning off the age check, ignoring event ids, and doing slow work before answering. This…
