title: Rust 1.100 Is Out. I Installed It This Morning and Tried the Three Things That Actually Matter
description:
Rust 1.100.0 landed on Thursday, November 12. Three days later I upgraded my own machine from 1.99.1 and spent the morning putting the headline features through their paces: the never type, custom allocators, and Cargo's two new supply-chain features. Everything below ran on my machine, and the numbers are the ones I actually saw.

The upgrade itself

One command, about ninety seconds, and rustc --version went from 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13) to 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09). Nothing broke on the way up. That matters, because this release does carry one change the release notes flag as potentially breaking, and I'll get to it.

The never type, ten years later

The headline is !, the never type. It's the type of an expression that never produces a value. A panic!(), an endless loop, a function that exits the process. People have been able to use it for years. But naming it anywhere a type goes, writing Result<u32, !> for a result that can never fail, took ten years and five failed stabilization attempts to land.

The first thing I tried was the obvious one:

let ok: Result<u32, !> = Ok(42);

It compiles, and it reads the way you'd hope. This result has no error case, and the type system now says so out loud. Infallible is now just an alias for !, which tidies up a decade of Result<T, Infallible> signatures.

The part worth paying attention to is the fallback change, because it's the one that can bite existing code. When the compiler can't work out what type a ! expression should be, it used to fall back to (). On 1.100 it falls back to ! instead, on every edition, not just 2024. I checked this directly with a snippet where the type is genuinely unconstrained: a closure that never runs, collecting into a Vec of unknown element type:

let v: Vec<_> = (0..0).map(|_| panic!()).collect();
println!("element type: {}", std::any::type_name_of_val(&v));

On 1.99.1 that prints alloc::vec::Vec<()>. On 1.100.0 it prints alloc::vec::Vec<!>. Same code, different inferred type. Most code will never notice. The fallback only matters where a type was left completely unspecified. But if your build breaks after this upgrade and the error mentions ! where you expected (), this is the change to look at. The other two things the release notes flag for the same reason: closures now capture variables used in if let more precisely, and some Box implementations were generalised to arbitrary allocators, which can surface as new inference errors.

Custom allocators: Vec in my own arena

The second big item is the core of the allocator API, first proposed years ago and unstable until now. Vec and Box can live in an allocator you define, instead of the global one. I wrote a tiny bump allocator: a fixed 64 KiB buffer, a cursor, nothing else. Then I put a Vec inside it:

let bump = Bump::new();
let mut v: Vec<u32, &Bump> = Vec::new_in(&bump);
for i in 0..1000 {
    v.push(i * i);
}

It ran first try. The output:

Vec in bump arena: len=1000, sum=332833500, arena used=8176 bytes
Box in bump arena: 0xdeadbeef, arena used=8184 bytes

A thousand squares, 8,176 bytes of arena used. The Vec's four allocations (it grows 4, 8, 16… up to 4,096 bytes, plus alignment padding) land exactly where you'd expect, and a Box::new_in next to it takes 8 more bytes. The sum checks out against the closed form (999 × 1000 × 1999 / 6 = 332,833,500), so the Vec really holds what I think it holds.

Who is this for? Not most of us, honestly. If you're writing a game engine, an embedded runtime, or anything where allocation patterns are part of the design, this is the release you've been waiting for. Vec::new_in, Vec::with_capacity_in and Box::new_in are the whole story. If you're writing a web service, you'll probably never touch it, and that's fine. It's a foundation, not a feature you have to use.

Two smaller additions from the same release that I will use: bool::toggle() (finally, no more flag = !flag) and core::mem::DropGuard, which runs a closure when it drops while keeping the value usable in the meantime. Both worked exactly as documented.

Cargo's two supply-chain features

Cargo gets the most practical upgrade in this release, and both parts are about the same worry: the dependencies you pull in.

Unused dependency warnings. Cargo now tells you when a dependency in your manifest is never used, through the new cargo::unused_dependencies lint. I added itoa to a test project and used nothing from it:

warning: unused dependency `itoa`
  --> Cargo.toml:10:1
   |
10 | itoa = "1"
   | ^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `itoa`

Warn by default, and it becomes a hard error if you set it to deny in [lints.cargo]. I tried both, and the deny version fails the build with the same message as an error. This is the kind of lint that pays for itself the first time it catches a dependency someone added "just in case" three years ago.

Dependency cooldowns. Set registry.global-min-publish-age and the resolver skips crate versions published more recently than that age, unless they're already in your lockfile. The idea is simple. Most malicious crate versions get caught within days of publication, so waiting a week before adopting anything new closes that window. One gotcha I hit while setting it up: "7d" is rejected. The value has to read like "7 days":

error: invalid value for `registry.global-min-publish-age`:
expected a value of the form "N seconds/minutes/hours/days/weeks/months",
got: "7d"

With "7 days" in place, the build passed with the locked versions untouched. I should be honest about the limit of what I tested here: the protection only bites on a fresh resolve, when the resolver is choosing versions. My test project already had a lockfile, so I watched the config get accepted, not the resolver refuse a version. The next fresh project I start will be the real test.

Did anything get faster?

I timed clean release builds of a small project (serde, serde_json, clap) on both toolchains, twice each:

Toolchain Run 1 Run 2
1.99.1 29.1s 29.4s
1.100.0 31.1s 29.9s

No measurable difference. The 1.100 numbers sit inside the same noise band as 1.99.1, and a two-second spread on a 30-second build of a small project is not a finding. It's the machine breathing. Nobody should upgrade for compile speed. (The release does stabilise -Cprofile-sample-use, sample-based PGO, which is a real performance lever for production binaries. But that's a profiling setup, not something a clean-build timer would show.)

Should you upgrade?

Yes, and the checklist is short. Run your test suite on 1.100 before you commit to it. The fallback change is narrow but real, and it's exactly the kind of thing that shows up in one weird corner of a big codebase rather than everywhere at once. If you maintain a library, the Box generalisation is the other one to watch for. Everything else in this release is additive: the never type, the allocator API, the Cargo lints and the cooldowns are all things you can adopt when they fit, not things you have to deal with on upgrade day.

The round number is a coincidence, mostly. Rust 1.100 is not a new era and not a rewrite. It's a solid release with one ten-year-old feature finally landing, one genuinely useful Cargo upgrade, and a small breaking change hiding in the compatibility notes. Read those notes, run your tests, then upgrade. That's the whole plan.

Sources

  • Rust 1.100.0 release notes: dev-doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html (Version 1.100.0, 2026-11-12)
  • Never type, custom allocators, Cargo lints and cooldowns, compatibility notes: same page, sections Language / Libraries / Stabilized APIs / Cargo / Compatibility Notes
  • Every number in this article comes from runs on my own machine on 2026-11-15: rustc 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09), upgraded from rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: GitHub Actions arm64 runners pricing, size by size
description:
GitHub Actions arm64 runners pricing is a discount that grows with the machine: 16.7 percent below x64 on the standard 2-core Linux runner, and 39.5 percent below it at 64 cores, read from GitHub's runner pricing reference on 21 September 2026. The standard Windows runner is the exception that catches people out, because arm64 and x64 are both $0.010 a minute there, so switching a small Windows job to arm64 saves nothing at all.


The arm64 discount at each Linux size, computed from the per-minute rates published on docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing and read on 21 September 2026.

There is one arithmetic question on this page and everything else serves it: how much slower is your job allowed to be on arm64 before the cheaper minute stops being cheaper? The answer is the ratio of the two rates, it is different at every size, and at the standard size it is tighter than most people expect.

The rates below are GitHub's published ones. They changed from a multiplier model to flat per-minute rates, so nothing here needs a conversion step, and since 28 October 2026 the included allowance is a dollar amount spent at each runner's rate, so an arm64 minute spends less of it than an x64 one.

Every arm64 rate, against the x64 rate beside it

Standard Linux arm64 is $0.005 a minute against $0.006 for standard Linux x64. That is the rate most workflows would move to, and it is the smallest discount on the page: one tenth of a cent a minute, or $10 a month on ten thousand minutes.

The larger runners are where the money is. Linux arm64 at 4 cores is $0.008 against $0.012, at 8 cores $0.014 against $0.022, at 16 cores $0.026 against $0.042, at 32 cores $0.050 against $0.082, and at 64 cores $0.098 against $0.162. The discount widens monotonically from a third to just under 40 percent, and there is no arm64 runner at 96 cores, so the top of the x64 ladder has no cheaper twin.

Windows behaves differently at both ends. The standard Windows runner is $0.010 a minute on arm64 and $0.010 on x64, an identical rate, so the arm64 discount does not exist at standard size. On the larger Windows runners it reappears and is the largest on the rate card: $0.014 against $0.022 at 4 cores, rising to $0.194 against $0.322 at 64. There is also a 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner at $0.008 with no x64 counterpart at that size.

Machine arm64 rate x64 rate arm64 discount Slower it may run and still pay
Linux 2-core, standard $0.005 $0.006 16.7% 20%
Linux 4-core, larger $0.008 $0.012 33.3% 50%
Linux 16-core, larger $0.026 $0.042 38.1% 61%
Linux 64-core, larger $0.098 $0.162 39.5% 65%
Windows 2-core, standard $0.010 $0.010 none not at all
Windows 16-core, larger $0.050 $0.082 39.0% 64%

Rates from Actions runner pricing, read 21 September 2026. The break-even column is the x64 rate divided by the arm64 rate, rounded down to a whole percent.

What the break-even column actually means

Read the last column as a permission rather than a promise. On the standard Linux runner, arm64 costs five sixths of x64, so an arm64 job may take up to 20 percent longer and cost exactly what the x64 job cost. Beyond that the cheaper minute buys you a more expensive job, and you have also made every pipeline slower.

Twenty percent is not a lot of headroom. It is comfortably inside the range an interpreted test suite moves by between two architectures, and it is well inside what an emulated container costs, so on the standard runner the switch has to be measured rather than assumed. On a 16-core larger runner the same job is allowed to be 61 percent slower before it stops paying, which is enough headroom that the decision usually goes the other way.

Rounding shortens the odds again at the small end, because GitHub "rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute". A 65-second job bills two minutes on either architecture, so the whole saving on that job is $0.002, and a matrix of twenty short jobs saves four cents a run. The arm64 discount is a large-job and large-machine instrument.

Where the saving lands on a real month

Take ten thousand Linux minutes a month in private repositories. On the standard x64 runner that is $60 and on standard arm64 it is $50: a real ten dollars, and not a number anyone will notice on an invoice. Put the same work on a 4-core larger runner and it is $120 against $80, which is a $40 difference on the same ten thousand minutes, and on a 16-core runner it is $420 against $260.

Two rules move that number more than the architecture does. Larger runners draw on the included allowance at their own rate on Team and Enterprise Cloud, so an $18 Team allowance covers 2,250 minutes of a 4-core arm64 runner at $0.008 before every minute bills, and larger runners are not free on public repositories while standard runners are. An open source project running on ubuntu-24.04-arm pays nothing; the moment it switches to a larger arm64 runner for speed, it starts paying for every minute.

None of this is a rate you can improve by moving vendor on the arm64 line specifically, and it would be dishonest of us to imply otherwise: Latchkey sells Linux x64 managed runners at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU with 8 GB and does not sell arm64 at all. Ubicloud does, publishing $0.00125 a minute for a 2 vCPU arm64 runner on its own pricing page read the same day, which is below every rate on this page. What Ubicloud CI is works through what that rate comes with.

Before you move the label

The labels are ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and ubuntu-26.04-arm on Linux, and windows-11-arm on Windows. In a private repository they give you 2 vCPU with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD, the same shape as the x64 standard runner; in a public repository the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB.

The cost of getting this wrong is not a failed build, it is a slow one that still bills. Anything that pulls a container image without an arm64 variant will either fail to pull or quietly run under emulation, and an emulated job is several times slower, which turns a 16.7 percent discount into a large net loss. The compatibility work is the subject of running GitHub Actions on ARM; this page is only the rate card behind it.

Measure one workflow at both labels for a week before you move the rest, and compare billed minutes rather than wall clock, because rounding is what you are actually charged on. For the model behind the whole rate card, see how GitHub Actions pricing works, and for the larger-runner ladder in full, GitHub Actions larger runners pricing.

# x64 today
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

# arm64, same 2 vCPU and 8 GB in a private repo, $0.005 against $0.006
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm

# both, for one week, so you can compare billed minutes rather than guess
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        runner: [ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}

FAQ

How much cheaper are GitHub arm64 runners than x64?

It depends entirely on the size. Standard Linux arm64 is $0.005 against $0.006, a 16.7 percent discount. Larger Linux runners run from 33.3 percent cheaper at 4 cores to 39.5 percent at 64. Standard Windows arm64 is the same $0.010 as x64, so there is no discount there at all.

How much slower can an arm64 job be before it costs more?

Divide the x64 rate by the arm64 rate. On the standard Linux runner that is 1.2, so a 20 percent slowdown is break-even. On a 4-core larger runner it is 1.5, and at 64 cores it is about 1.65. The bigger the machine, the more slowdown the discount absorbs.

Are arm64 runners free on public repositories?

The standard arm64 runners are, because the use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited on public repositories, and ubuntu-24.04-arm is a standard runner. Larger runners of any architecture are billed even on public repositories, so switching a public project to a larger arm64 runner starts a bill that did not exist before.

Is there a 96-core arm64 runner?

No. The published arm64 Linux ladder stops at 64 cores and $0.098 a minute, while x64 continues to 96 cores at $0.252. If a job genuinely needs 96 cores there is no cheaper architecture available for it, and the question becomes whether the job parallelises well enough to justify the top of the x64 ladder at all.

Which arm64 runner labels does GitHub publish?

On Linux, ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and ubuntu-26.04-arm; on Windows, windows-11-arm and windows-11-vs2026-arm. In private repositories they are 2 vCPU with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD, and in public repositories the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB.

References

  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every arm64 and x64 per-minute rate (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: hosted runner specifications and the arm64 workflow labels (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, included compute usage and the larger-runner rules (verified 2026-11-12)
  • Ubicloud pricing: a second published arm64 runner rate card (verified 2026-09-21)

title: Why Enterprise CTOs Won't Deploy AI-Migrated Code (And How We Built 3-Way Shadow Testing in Go)
description:
Why Enterprise CTOs Won't Deploy AI-Migrated Code (And How We Built 3-Way Shadow Testing in Go)

By Vishal Raj • Live Cloud Demo: https://shadowdiff-demo.fly.dev/ • Open Source: https://github.com/vishalrajofficial/ShadowDiff

Every engineering leader running legacy systems has had the exact same thought over the past twelve months:

"We have a 12-year-old Java 7 Spring monolith / Python 2 Django app that everyone is terrified to touch. Why don't we feed it into Claude 3.7 / GPT-4 / Gemini, rewrite it in Go or FastAPI, and deploy it to Kubernetes next quarter?"

Teams try it. And initially, the results look miraculous. In a few afternoons, an AI coding assistant refactors thousands of lines of archaic boilerplate into idiomatic Go code. Unit test suites are generated. The code compiles. Staging health checks return 200 OK.

Then the engineering team approaches the VP of Engineering or CTO to cut over production traffic.

And the cutover is rejected.

Why? Because in enterprise finance, logistics, e-commerce, and healthcare backends, AI gets 95% of the refactoring right, but the remaining 5% of invisible contract deviations can cause catastrophic outages or silent data corruption.

Here is what that 5% looks like, why traditional testing cannot catch it, and how we built ShadowDiff—an open-source 3-way differential shadow testing engine with database side-effect diffing and automated regression test synthesis in Go.

1. The Anatomy of the 5% Failure Rate

When refactoring code manually, human engineers write integration tests for known assumptions. But AI-migrated code fails in ways humans never think to test for:

Case 1: Serialization Asymmetry

In Java, Jackson may omit null fields or serialize empty collections as {}. In Go, encoding/json serializes nil slices as null or omits them entirely with omitempty. If downstream client apps (mobile SDKs, legacy partner microservices) expect "items": [] and receive "items": null, client parsers crash.

Case 2: Numeric Float Precision Drift

A legacy Java service calculates billing discounts using BigDecimal with half-up rounding. The refactored Go service computes float64 discounts, creating subtle discrepancies (e.g. 14.50 vs 14.500000000000002). Both return HTTP 200, but downstream billing reconciliation triggers financial drift.

Case 3: Silent Database Mutation Corruption

The HTTP response body is identical: {"status": "success", "order_id": "ORD-1092"}. But under the hood, the legacy service wrapped writes inside BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT and wrote an entry to audit_logs, while the refactored service used an ORM with default autocommit and omitted the audit_logs insert. In a partial network partition, data is half-committed, and compliance auditability is broken.

Case 4: The ORM N+1 Query Loop Explosion

The legacy service used an optimized, hand-tuned raw SQL JOIN. The AI converted it to idiomatic ORM struct methods that loop over orders and query the user table one query per row. In staging with 10 records, latency is 4ms. In production with 100,000 orders, database connection pools exhaust in 20 seconds.

2. Why Traditional Shadow Testing Fails: The Noise Catastrophe

To catch these issues, teams attempt traffic shadowing (mirroring real production traffic to the refactored service in parallel).

However, traditional 2-way diffing immediately hits a brick wall: Alert Fatigue.

Every modern API returns non-deterministic fields: timestamps, ephemeral trace IDs, dynamic nonces, CSRF tokens, cache headers, and execution timestamps. When you diff the legacy service against the refactored service, 99% of requests differ purely because of runtime noise. Engineers spend entire weeks writing brittle regex ignore-lists, only to miss true bugs.

3. The Solution: Mathematical 3-Way Differential Noise Cancellation

To solve this, ShadowDiff implements the Diffy Model using twin baseline replicas:

  1. Baseline Runtime Noise: N = P1 (xor) P2. Any difference between two identical instances running the exact same legacy code (P1 and P2) is guaranteed to be non-deterministic noise.
  2. Raw Candidate Divergence: R = P1 (xor) S.
  3. Pure Semantic Regression: D = R \ N.

By mathematically subtracting the noise set N from candidate drifts R, ShadowDiff guarantees zero false alarms. If a timestamp diverges between P1 and P2, it is automatically suppressed when comparing P1 and S. Only genuine contract bugs reach developer triage.

4. Database Side-Effect & Mutation Interception

Responses returning 200 OK do not mean database integrity is preserved. ShadowDiff injects an immutable trace header (X-ShadowDiff-Trace-ID) across both mirrored requests and correlates executed SQL statements:

  • Missing Mutations: Flags when legacy writes to tables (e.g. audit_logs, ledger_entries) that the refactored code forgot to touch.
  • Transaction Boundary Leaks: Detects when legacy code operated inside atomic BEGIN...COMMIT blocks, but refactored code ran autocommit statements vulnerable to partial failures.
  • N+1 Query Explosions: Flags when refactored ORMs query relational tables in loops instead of batch joined queries.

5. Safe Mutating Traffic: Ephemeral Copy-on-Write (CoW) Sandboxing

How do you safely shadow mutating traffic (POST, PUT, DELETE) without charging customer credit cards twice or polluting the database?

ShadowDiff supports Ephemeral Copy-on-Write Database Sandboxing:

  1. Transactional Savepoint Rollbacks: Injects boundary headers ensuring shadow mutations execute within a transactional savepoint that automatically rolls back when the shadow request completes.
  2. Ephemeral Per-Run Schema: Clones table definitions into a disposable schema and drops it immediately upon request completion.
  3. Serverless Cloud CoW Branching: Coordinates via API with Neon / Supabase serverless PostgreSQL to provision zero-storage copy-on-write database branches on demand.

6. Closing the Loop: Autonomous GitHub PR Bot & CI/CD Gating CLI

When a genuine bug is isolated, ShadowDiff automates the fix lifecycle:

  • Autonomous GitHub PR Bot: Prompts Google Gemini (gemini-2.0-flash) with the raw requests, side-by-side JSON contract drifts, and SQL execution watermarks. Gemini synthesizes a turnkey Go integration test reproducing the exact edge case. The GitHub Bot creates a branch, commits the test file, and automatically opens a rich Pull Request with visual diff tables and local verification commands.
  • CI/CD Shadow Gating CLI (shadowdiff gate): Teams can block deployments in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI before promoting AI-refactored code if parity drops below 100%, or an N+1 query loop or missing SQL write is detected.

7. Try the Live Cloud Demo

You can interact with ShadowDiff right now in your browser without installing anything:

  • Live Cloud Sandbox: https://shadowdiff-demo.fly.dev/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/vishalrajofficial/ShadowDiff

8. Summary: How to Safely Modernize Legacy Backends

AI is the most powerful code translation tool in history. But code conversion without runtime contract verification is reckless. By combining Envoy wire-speed traffic mirroring, mathematical 3-way differential noise cancellation, SQL side-effect mutation diffing, ephemeral Copy-on-Write database sandboxing, and autonomous AI regression test synthesis, engineering teams can finally give CTOs the mathematical certainty they need to deploy AI-refactored backends into production with confidence.

title: Empresia Scraper in Python: Company Reports and Daily New Incorporations from the BORME
description:
Empresia.es is a free Spanish company directory built on the Commercial Registry. Every company has a report with its CIF, CNAE activity code, share capital, sales band, employees, address, phones, board, officers and the announcements it published in the BORME (Spain's Official Gazette of the Commercial Registry). It also lists, day by day and province by province, every company that was incorporated, dissolved or changed its capital. For lead generation, KYC or market research, that is a clean B2B dataset. Here is how to pull it into Python, and what to watch out for.

Why not plain requests 

import requests

r = requests.get("https://www.empresia.es/empresa/mercadona/")
print(r.status_code)  # 200, for now

Empresia renders everything on the server, so a single request works. The problem starts at volume: the site sits behind Cloudflare, and a crawl of thousands of company pages from one IP is exactly what gets throttled. Sending each request through Scrape.do rotates the IP on every call and retries failures. A plain request is enough, no extra parameters: 1 credit per page, about 2 seconds.

TOKEN = "<your_token>"

def fetch(url):
    r = requests.get("https://api.scrape.do/", params={"token": TOKEN, "url": url}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text

Where the data is on a company page

There is no JSON-LD and no API behind the page. The data sits in a few predictable blocks:

  1. div.datos-ident: name, phones, fax, address, websites and e-mail, then label/value pairs (span.list-group-item-heading followed by p.list-group-item-text) for CIF, incorporation date, share capital, sales band, registry, last filed accounts, employees, governing body and auditor.
  2. #organigrama: the board, one li per person with the role after the link.
  3. #ListaRelaciones: officers with appointment and removal dates.
  4. #ListaEventos: the BORME timeline (changes of address, appointments, capital increases), each with a link to the official PDF.

Two details catch people out. The e-mail is not in the HTML as text: Cloudflare replaces it with [email protected] and a data-cfemail attribute, a hex string whose first byte is the XOR key for the rest. And the sales figure is a band ("Superior a 2.500.000 euros"), kept in the title of a tooltip, not in the visible text.

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def decode_cfemail(hex_str):
    data = bytes.fromhex(hex_str)
    return bytes(b ^ data[0] for b in data[1:]).decode()


def company(slug):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(f"https://www.empresia.es/empresa/{slug}/"), "html.parser")
    box = soup.select_one("div.datos-ident")
    fields = {}
    for label in box.select("span.list-group-item-heading"):
        value = label.find_next_sibling("p", class_="list-group-item-text")
        if value:
            fields[label.get_text(strip=True)] = value
    purpose, _, cnae = fields["Objeto social"].get_text("\n", strip=True).partition("\nCNAE ")
    sales = fields["Ventas"].select_one("[title]")
    email = box.select_one("[data-cfemail]")
    return {
        "name": box.select_one("span.bolder").get_text(strip=True),
        "cif": fields["CIF"].get_text(strip=True),
        "cnae": cnae,
        "purpose": purpose,
        "capital": fields["Capital social"].get_text(strip=True),
        "sales_band": sales["title"] if sales else "",
        "employees": fields["Número empleados"].get_text(strip=True),
        "registry": fields["Registro"].get_text(strip=True),
        "email": decode_cfemail(email["data-cfemail"]) if email else "",
        "board": [(a.get_text(strip=True), a.find_next_sibling(string=True).strip())
                  for a in soup.select("#organigrama li a")],
    }

In a live run on Mercadona this returned the CIF, CNAE 4711, the sales band, 108,742 employees, the registry (Valencia), the decoded e-mail and 13 board members, from one request. Values Empresia shows as - (Mercadona's share capital, for example) come back as -, so clean them before loading the data anywhere.

Every new company, every day

The most useful part of Empresia for lead generation is the BORME by day. Each weekday the gazette publishes every incorporation, and Empresia lists them by act and province:

/borme/fecha/2026-11-13/acto/constitucion/provincia/barcelona/

Change constitucion to disolucion, ampliacion-de-capital, cambio-de-domicilio-social or nombramientos for other acts. On 13 November 2026 there were 41 act types across 34 provinces, and Barcelona alone had 71 new companies. Each row links to the announcement, which has a small table with the registry, start date, share capital, corporate purpose and registered address:

import csv

BASE = "https://www.empresia.es"


def new_companies(date, province):
    url = f"{BASE}/borme/fecha/{date}/acto/constitucion/provincia/{province}/"
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    for row in soup.select("#contenido table tbody tr"):
        name = row.select_one("a.lk")
        event = row.select_one('a[href*="/evento/"]')
        yield name.get_text(strip=True), BASE + event["href"]


def announcement(url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    cells = [td.get_text(" ", strip=True) for td in soup.select("div.eventonly table td")]
    return dict(zip(cells[::2], cells[1::2]))


with open("new_companies.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["company", "registry", "start", "capital", "purpose", "address"])
    for name, link in new_companies("2026-11-13", "barcelona"):
        d = announcement(link)
        writer.writerow([name, d.get("Registro"), d.get("Fecha inicio"), d.get("Capital"),
                         d.get("Objeto social"), d.get("Domicilio")])

That is one request for the list plus one per company: 72 credits for a full day of Barcelona incorporations. Run it on a schedule and you have a daily feed of companies that did not exist last week.

Search, and its ceiling

Search is /busqueda/?q=<text>&pagina=<n>. Results mix companies (EMPRESA), officers (DIRECTIVO) and trademarks (DISTINTIVO), and Empresia stops at 100 results: past the last page it quietly sends page 1 again, so compare the "Mostrando del X al Y" counter before trusting a page. For anything broader than a name, the BORME lists by province are the better entry point.

Skip the code

The same scraper is an open-source package with a CLI:

pip install empresia-scraper
export SCRAPEDO_TOKEN=<your_token>
empresia-scraper telefonica mercadona -f csv -o companies.csv
empresia-scraper --borme 2026-11-13 --province madrid --details -o new_companies.json

Source and tests: github.com/bugrahansss/empresia-scraper

Use the data responsibly

The data comes from public registers, but officers are real people and their names are personal data under the GDPR. Use it for legitimate purposes such as B2B research or KYC, keep only what you need, honour objection requests and respect Empresia's terms.

Run it at scale with Scrape.do

Every page is one plain Scrape.do call with a rotating IP: no proxy pool, no Cloudflare handling, no headless browser. 1,000 company reports cost 1,000 credits. Get 1000 free credits and start scraping with Scrape.do.

title: Fixing a Concurrency Bug an Architect Caught in My Flink-Qdrant Connector
description:
The connector nobody had built yet

Apache Flink didn't have an official SQL connector for Qdrant, the vector database. I use both — Flink for streaming pipelines, Qdrant for the embedding store downstream — so I built flink-connector-qdrant to close that gap: a Flink SQL sink that upserts points into Qdrant directly from a streaming job, no glue code in between.

It shipped, people started using it, and then an architect reviewing it on LinkedIn pointed out something I'd missed.

The bug

My upsert path stored a version number per point so that if the same ID arrived twice, the connector could tell which write was newer and keep that one. Straightforward, except for one thing: storing a version number alone doesn't guarantee atomic ordering under concurrent writers.

Picture two parallel sink tasks racing on the same point ID. Writer A has version 5, writer B has version 6. There's no guarantee B's write lands after A's just because its version number is higher — depending on timing, A can still land last and silently overwrite the newer data. A bare version field tells you which value should win; it doesn't make the database enforce that when two writes are in flight at the same time.

That's a real data-correctness bug, not a style nit. In a streaming sink, "newer data wins" is the whole point of upserts.

The fix

I added an opt-in version-field option: when configured, the connector deduplicates by highest version within a batch before the Qdrant write goes out, instead of trusting Qdrant to sort it out writer by writer. Same version field the architect was looking at, but the ordering guarantee now lives on my side of the wire, where I actually control it.

I shipped it as three separate commits — a fix for the dedup logic, a feat for the opt-in config surface, and a docs commit explaining when to turn it on — instead of squashing it into one. Reviewing a bug fix is easier when you're not also reviewing a new feature flag in the same diff, and it meant the person who raised the issue could actually see the fix land commit by commit rather than taking my word for it.

The other repo

Same week, I pushed multi-cluster support into apache-flink-mcp-server — it lets AI assistants talk to a Flink cluster over MCP (Model Context Protocol), but until now it only knew about one cluster at a time, which doesn't match how anyone actually runs Flink. It also picked up its listing on the Glama MCP directory.

Neither of these projects is glamorous. They're the kind of infrastructure that's only interesting when it's wrong. But getting real review from someone who actually reads the code, and being able to turn that into a fix the same week, is the part of open source that's worth writing about.

If you're running vector search behind a Flink pipeline, or you want an AI assistant that can actually see what's happening in your Flink cluster, both repos are open for issues and PRs.

title: Why Did My Python List Change? Understanding References and Copies
description:
Why Did My Python List Change? Understanding References and Copies

You create a list, assign it to another variable, and change one item. Then you discover that your original list has changed too.

If that has surprised you, the key is understanding what assignment does in Python.

Let’s work through a few examples, starting with a simple shopping list.

1. Assignment does not create a copy 

shopping = ["milk", "bread", "eggs"]
backup = shopping

backup.append("coffee")

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread', 'eggs', 'coffee']
['milk', 'bread', 'eggs', 'coffee']

Despite its name, backup is not a separate list.

This statement:

backup = shopping

binds another name to the same list. Calling append() through either name changes that shared object.

You can check whether two names refer to the same object using is:

print(shopping is backup)

Output:

True

The lesson: Giving a list another name does not duplicate it.

2. Changing a list differs from reassigning a variable

Now consider this example:

shopping = ["milk", "bread"]
backup = shopping

backup = ["coffee"]

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread']
['coffee']

Why did shopping stay unchanged this time?

The statement:

backup = ["coffee"]

creates a new list and makes backup refer to it. It does not modify the original list.

Compare these two operations:

Operation Effect
backup.append("coffee") Changes the list that backup refers to
backup = ["coffee"] Makes backup refer to a different list

When tracing Python code, ask: Does this line change an existing object, or change which object a name refers to?

3. Use a copy when you need a separate list

For a flat list of strings, the copy() method provides the separation we wanted:

shopping = ["milk", "bread"]
backup = shopping.copy()

backup.append("coffee")

print(shopping)
print(backup)

Output:

['milk', 'bread']
['milk', 'bread', 'coffee']

You can also create a shallow copy of a list using a full slice:

backup = shopping[:]

Both approaches create a new outer list. But “shallow” matters when the list contains other lists.

4. A shallow copy can still share nested lists

Suppose you keep scores in a nested list:

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = scores.copy()

backup[0][0] = 99

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[99, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

The outer lists are separate, but they contain references to the same inner lists.

We can check both levels:

print(scores is backup)
print(scores[0] is backup[0])

Output:

False
True

Changing an element inside a shared inner list affects what both outer lists display.

However, replacing an entire item in the copied outer list behaves differently:

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = scores.copy()

backup[0] = [99, 20]

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[10, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

Here, we replaced a reference in backup. We did not modify the shared inner list.

5. Copy nested data when independence is required

For this nested-list example, deepcopy() also copies the inner lists:

from copy import deepcopy

scores = [[10, 20], [30, 40]]
backup = deepcopy(scores)

backup[0][0] = 99

print(scores)
print(backup)

Output:

[[10, 20], [30, 40]]
[[99, 20], [30, 40]]

Use deep copying when the nested mutable data needs to be independent. It is not necessary for every list: a shallow copy may provide exactly the behaviour you need.

6. Watch out for repeated nested lists

The same reference issue appears when building a grid:

grid = [[0, 0]] * 3

grid[0][0] = 1

print(grid)

Output:

[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]

The multiplication repeats references to one inner list. It does not create three independent rows.

Create each row separately instead:

grid = [[0, 0] for _ in range(3)]

grid[0][0] = 1

print(grid)

Output:

[[1, 0], [0, 0], [0, 0]]

The list comprehension creates a new inner list on each iteration.

A useful habit when reading Python code

Whenever a question involves lists, pause at assignments and modifications:

  • Does another variable refer to the same list?
  • Was a shallow copy created?
  • Are any inner lists still shared?
  • Is the code modifying an object or reassigning a name?

Predict the output first, then run the example. Explaining why the result occurs is more useful than memorising it.

For further reading, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Free PCEP practice test

Preparing for PCEP? I create Python learning resources through AM Academy, and you can access my free practice test here: https://www.udemy.com/course/python-pcep-30-03-certification-practice-tests-2026/?couponCode=FREE-COURSE-PCEP. This is an independently created preparation resource, not an official Python Institute exam.

title: Namespace vs Blacksmith for GitHub Actions runners
description:
Namespace vs Blacksmith looks like a price win for Namespace at $0.002 a minute against $0.004, until you notice that Namespace's 2 vCPU shape carries 4 GB of RAM and Blacksmith's carries 8 GB. Match the memory and they are level at $0.004 prepaid, so the real decision is prepaid commitment and cache volumes against a standing free tier and a simpler bill.


Published Linux rates lined up by memory rather than core count, read 20 September 2026. Namespace pairs 2 GB per vCPU, Blacksmith pairs 4 GB.

Namespace sells compute across devboxes, builds and GitHub Actions runners, with a label grammar rather than a fixed size list: nscloud-{os}-{arch}-{shape}, with suffixes that attach a cache volume or extra features. Rates come in two columns, a prepaid rate inside your plan and a higher overage rate outside it, which rewards teams that can forecast their usage.

Blacksmith sells one thing, managed GitHub Actions runners on its own bare metal, at a single published rate per platform with 3,000 free minutes a month and no plan to pick. It is the simpler purchase, and the simplicity is most of what you are buying.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

Namespace Blacksmith Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.002 prepaid, $0.003 overage (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM) $0.004 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk) $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.004 prepaid, $0.006 overage (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) $0.008 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 80 GB disk) $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier A 30-day trial on the pay-as-you-go Developer plan; no standing monthly free minutes 3,000 free minutes a month, printed on every runner card 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity A one-minute minimum, then each following 15 seconds rounded down Not published Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Shapes 2x4 through 32x64 on amd64 and arm64; Windows Server 2022 on amd64; macOS arm64 images from Sonoma to Tahoe; disk not published 2 to 32 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64; Windows Server 2025 at 2 to 32 vCPU in public beta; macOS M4 at 6 and 12 vCPU 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence Tagged cache volumes attached with a label suffix; 20 GB by default, up to 50 GB on Team and 100 GB on Business; snapshots at $0.002/GB-hr with 5,000 GB-hr free on Team Colocated cache intercepts actions/cache, 25 GB free per repo per week; sticky disks are ext4 volumes, 5 per job, evicted after 7 days idle, $0.50/GB/month Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration Remote builders are on by default; the docs tell you to remove docker/setup-buildx-action so it does not override them useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder@v2 and useblacksmith/build-push-action@v2, with layers on a persistent sticky disk latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits Published per plan, and counted in vCPU: 32 on Developer, 64 on Team, 160 on Business for Linux; 12, 24 and 48 for macOS. A single job is capped at 3 hours on Developer and 5 on Team None imposed, per the runner docs Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run Namespace Compute, on AMD EPYC for amd64 and AmpereOne or Apple silicon for arm64 Blacksmith's own regions: Ashburn, Phoenix, Amsterdam and Frankfurt Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries Not offered Not offered Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required Change the runs-on label, and append -with-cache plus a cache tag label to attach a cache volume Install the GitHub App, then change the runs-on label A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

Match the memory before you compare the rate

Namespace prices by machine shape, and its shapes pair 2 GB of RAM with each vCPU. Blacksmith pairs 4 GB with each vCPU on x64. That means the two rate cards are not describing the same machine at the same row, and a straight 2 vCPU comparison flatters Namespace by exactly the amount of memory it left out.

Lined up by memory instead of by core count, the published Linux rates read like this: 8 GB costs $0.004 prepaid or $0.006 overage on Namespace (a 4x8 shape), $0.004 on Blacksmith (a 2 vCPU runner) and $0.0025 on Latchkey. 16 GB costs $0.008 prepaid on Namespace, $0.008 on Blacksmith and $0.005 on Latchkey. Namespace and Blacksmith are level at matched memory, and Namespace gives you twice the cores for the same money at that point, which is a real advantage on parallel work and no advantage at all on a single-threaded build.

Which framing is right depends on your jobs. If your test suite is memory-hungry and single-threaded, buy memory and Blacksmith is straightforwardly cheaper per gigabyte. If it shards cleanly, buy cores and Namespace is ahead.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

What you will find elsewhere is each vendor's own figure, measured on a workload the vendor chose. Those numbers are not wrong, but they are not comparable to each other, and none of them is your repository. The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week: runner selection is per job, so three jobs in the same workflow file can run on three providers, and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, priced three ways

The usual month, 10,000 Linux minutes and 2,000 macOS minutes. Namespace is shown on a 2 vCPU 4 GB shape, which is its best case, and then again at 8 GB so the machines match.

10,000 Linux minutes 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
Namespace, 2 vCPU 4 GB 10,000 min at multiplier 2 = 20,000 unit minutes 2,000 min at multiplier 60 = 120,000 unit minutes $160: the $100 Team plan covers 100,000 of the 140,000, and the 40,000 over it bill at $0.0015
Namespace, 4 vCPU 8 GB 10,000 min at multiplier 4 = 40,000 unit minutes 2,000 min at multiplier 60 = 120,000 unit minutes $190: 160,000 unit minutes, so 60,000 over the plan at $0.0015 is $90 on top of the $100
Blacksmith, 2 vCPU 8 GB $28 after 3,000 free minutes $160 at $0.08/min $188
Latchkey, 2 vCPU 8 GB $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

Namespace does not bill minutes, it bills unit minutes, which are wall-clock minutes multiplied by the shape: a 2 vCPU Linux runner counts 2, a 4 vCPU one counts 4, and the 6 vCPU macOS runner counts 60, because macOS carries a 10x platform multiplier on top of its cores. The $100 Team plan is not a fee on top of the rate, it buys 100,000 of those unit minutes, and anything past them is $0.0015 each. That is why the two Namespace rows land at $160 and $190 rather than at the arithmetic you would do for a flat-rate vendor: the plan and the minutes are one purchase, not two. Below 100,000 unit minutes a month the Team plan is the whole bill, which makes Namespace cheapest here by a wide margin; past it the effective rate creeps back toward the $0.0015 overage.

Namespace is also the only vendor here that is cheaper per macOS minute than GitHub-hosted, at $0.06 prepaid against $0.062. If your bill is mostly macOS, that is worth more than any Linux rate on this page. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

Reliability

Neither publishes a runner SLA on the pages read here, but both publish a concurrency position and the two are opposites. Blacksmith states it imposes no limit at all on simultaneous jobs or vCPUs. Namespace caps it by plan and counts it in vCPU rather than jobs: 32 vCPU of Linux concurrency on Developer, 64 on Team, 160 on Business, with macOS on its own ladder of 12, 24 and 48.

A cap denominated in vCPU is easy to misread, and it is the number to check before you widen a matrix. Namespace's 64 vCPU on Team is thirty-two 2 vCPU jobs at once, or eight 8 vCPU ones, so making runners bigger and making the matrix wider draw on the same budget. Namespace also caps a single job at 3 hours on Developer and 5 on Team, against GitHub's 6, which matters for long integration suites.

Both are silent on failure handling, which is the honest answer for both: a job that dies on a registry timeout or an out-of-memory kill fails, bills, and waits. The one operational difference worth knowing is Blacksmith's capacity model, where runners are provisioned for repositories that have the GitHub App installed, so a repository using blacksmith-* labels without the app can quietly starve the pool for everyone else.

When to choose Namespace

  • You can forecast usage and commit to a plan, so the prepaid rate is the rate you actually pay rather than the one on the marketing page.
  • Your jobs parallelise. At matched memory you get twice the cores for the same money.
  • Your bill is macOS-heavy: $0.06 prepaid per macOS minute is the lowest on this page and below GitHub-hosted.
  • You want cache volumes you control by tag and size, up to 100 GB on Business, rather than a fixed per-repo allowance.
  • You are buying more than runners. Devboxes, container builds and Bazel remote caching come off the same plan and the same balance.

When to choose Blacksmith

  • You want one rate, no plan decision and no commitment: $0.004 a Linux minute with 3,000 free minutes a month, and an overage rate that does not exist because there is no plan to exceed.
  • Your jobs need memory more than cores. 8 GB at 2 vCPU against Namespace's 4 GB is the difference between a build that completes and one that gets killed by the kernel.
  • You want arm64 at $0.0025/min, which is the lowest published arm64 rate in this comparison.
  • Your cache story is actions/cache and you want it transparently faster with no workflow edits, rather than a volume you attach and size yourself.

Switching: the exact diff

Both are label changes. Namespace encodes the shape in the label and needs an extra suffix before a cache volume is attached, so the diff is slightly wordier; Blacksmith needs the GitHub App installed on each repository that uses its labels.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-4x8-with-cache

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404

The verdict

The headline rate says Namespace is half the price and the machine specification says they are level, so the tiebreak is what kind of buyer you are. If you can commit to a plan, want cores rather than memory, and are willing to learn a label grammar and a cache-volume model, Namespace is genuinely cheaper and sells you macOS below GitHub-hosted price, which nobody else here does. If you want a rate you can quote without a footnote, 3,000 free minutes to start on, and 8 GB of RAM at the smallest size, Blacksmith is the easier purchase and the better memory-per-dollar. Neither of them repairs a failed job, and at these rates the re-runs you are already paying for are a bigger number than the gap between the two.

FAQ

Is Namespace cheaper than Blacksmith?

Per vCPU, yes; per gigabyte of RAM, no. Namespace lists $0.002/min prepaid for a 2 vCPU 4 GB shape and Blacksmith lists $0.004/min for a 2 vCPU 8 GB runner. At matched 8 GB the Namespace shape is 4x8 at $0.004 prepaid, which is level with Blacksmith and twice the cores. Namespace's prepaid rate also assumes a plan; its overage rate is 50% higher.

Which GitHub Actions services let you run jobs on faster hardware without self-hosting?

Namespace, Blacksmith, Depot, RunsOn, WarpBuild, Ubicloud and Latchkey all sell managed runners you adopt with a runs-on change, and GitHub sells larger runners up to 96 vCPU. All of them exist because the standard private-repo Linux runner is 2 vCPU with 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of disk, and plenty of builds outgrew that years ago.

How do Namespace cache volumes differ from Blacksmith sticky disks?

Namespace cache volumes are attached by adding a suffix and a tag to the runner label, default to 20 GB, and cap at 50 GB on Team or 100 GB on Business, with snapshot storage billed per GB-hour. Blacksmith sticky disks are ext4 volumes mounted by an action, up to 5 per job, billed at $0.50/GB/month and evicted after 7 days without use. Blacksmith also transparently redirects actions/cache to a colocated cache with 25 GB free per repo per week, which needs no workflow change at all.

Does either of them retry a job that failed for a transient reason?

Neither publishes automatic detection and repair of transient failures. Both will run your job on faster hardware, and both will bill you for the run that died on a DNS blip and again for the re-run. That is the gap Latchkey is built around, and it is a different axis from speed or price.

References

  • Namespace pricing, prepaid and overage rates by shape
  • Namespace runner labels, shapes and cache volumes
  • Blacksmith pricing
  • Blacksmith runner instance types
  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates and minute multipliers

title: GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute
description:
GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute is $0.010 for the standard 2-core machine, against $0.006 for the equivalent Linux runner, read from GitHub's runner pricing reference on 21 September 2026. That is a 1.67 times premium rather than the tenfold one macOS carries, which is why Windows rarely dominates a bill on its own and almost always shows up as a matrix leg that nobody has questioned since it was added.


The same 8,000 minutes of runner time priced on each operating system at the standard per-minute rates published on docs.github.com and read on 21 September 2026.

A Windows minute is not expensive enough to be obvious and not cheap enough to ignore. It is the runner type most often bought by default, through an operating system matrix copied from a template, and the cost of that default is small per run and durable across years.

This page states every published Windows rate, prices a worked month against the same work on Linux, and then does the part that actually saves money: separating the jobs that genuinely need Windows from the ones sitting on it out of habit.

The Windows rates, stated exactly

The standard Windows runner, which is what windows-latest gives you, is $0.010 a minute on x64 and also $0.010 on arm64. In a private repository it is a 2 vCPU machine with 8 GB of memory and 14 GB of SSD; in a public repository the standard runners are 4 vCPU with 16 GB and cost nothing.

The larger Windows runners start at 4 cores and $0.022 a minute, then $0.042 at 8, $0.082 at 16, $0.162 at 32, $0.322 at 64 and $0.552 at 96. That top rate is the most expensive minute GitHub sells outside its GPU tier, more than double the 96-core Linux rate of $0.252, and the gap between the two ladders widens at every step.

There is one rate on the Windows card that looks like a mistake and is not. The 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner is $0.008 a minute, which is less than the $0.010 standard Windows runner. It is still a larger runner, so it is billed on public repositories, where the standard runner is free, and it needs an organization on Team or Enterprise Cloud. On a private repository on those plans it draws on the included allowance like any other runner, so there it is simply the cheapest Windows minute on the card.

Windows runner Rate per minute 8,000 minutes a month The same work on Linux
Standard 2-core, x64 or arm64 $0.010 $80 $48 at $0.006
Larger 4-core, x64 $0.022 $176 $96 at $0.012
Larger 8-core, x64 $0.042 $336 $176 at $0.022
Larger 16-core, arm64 $0.050 $400 $208 at $0.026
Larger 96-core, x64 $0.552 $4,416 $2,016 at $0.252

Rates from Actions runner pricing, read 21 September 2026. The Linux column is the same core count on the Linux ladder, for the same 8,000 minutes.

What the included allowance is worth on Windows

Since 28 October 2026 the allowance is a dollar amount, not a minute count, and GitHub deducts each minute at its runner's rate. A GitHub Team plan includes $18 a month: that is 3,000 standard Linux minutes, 1,800 standard Windows minutes, or about 290 macOS minutes.

That removes the old trick of steering the allowance toward the most expensive runner. In dollars, $18 is $18 whichever job draws it, and GitHub states that "No eligible usage type has priority over another". What still matters is that Windows minutes empty it 1.67 times faster than the same minutes on Linux.

The second rule is the one that surprises people on the first invoice after a speed push. Larger runners now draw on the allowance on Team and Enterprise Cloud, but at their own rate: moving a Windows job from windows-latest to a 4-core larger runner at $0.022 spends the allowance 2.2 times as fast, so $18 covers about 818 minutes instead of 1,800, and the marginal change on a small account is larger than the rate table suggests.

Rounding, and why a Windows matrix leg costs more than it runs

GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute. Windows jobs pay for that more than Linux ones, because the same rounding is applied to a more expensive minute and because Windows runners tend to spend longer in setup before any of your own work starts.

Put numbers on it. A matrix of six Windows jobs that each take 80 seconds uses eight minutes of machine time and bills twelve, because every leg rounds to two. At $0.010 that is $0.12 a run rather than $0.08, half as much again, repeated on every push for as long as the matrix exists. Consolidating those six legs into two longer jobs recovers most of the difference without changing what is tested.

The same arithmetic is why splitting a Windows suite into more shards for speed can cost more than it saves. Each new shard is a new job and a new rounding boundary, so past a certain point you are buying wall clock with billed minutes. Sharding tests across runners has the point where that trade turns.

What actually needs Windows

A short list: .NET Framework, which never left Windows; anything calling Win32 or COM directly; MSI packaging and Authenticode signing; Windows GUI and installer tests; and drivers or services that only exist on the platform. If your product ships a Windows binary that customers run, you need at least one job here and there is no argument to have.

A much longer list does not. Modern .NET builds and tests cross-platform, so a library targeting net8.0 or later is usually verified adequately on Linux with one Windows leg on the default branch rather than on every pull request. JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust test suites that touch no platform API are on Windows because a template put them there. Linting, formatting, dependency audits and documentation builds never need it.

The change is a trigger, not a rewrite: run the full operating system matrix on the default branch and on a schedule, and run Linux alone on pull requests. On the worked month above, moving three quarters of 8,000 Windows minutes to Linux turns $80 into $20 plus $24, which is $36 saved a month for a coverage difference most teams find acceptable. How to reduce GitHub Actions costs prices six more changes on the same basis, and how GitHub Actions pricing works has the model behind the rates.

# before: every push fans out to three operating systems
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

# after: pull requests get Linux, the full matrix runs where it earns its keep
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && fromJSON('["ubuntu-latest"]') || fromJSON('["ubuntu-latest","windows-latest","macos-latest"]') }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 30

Where a cheaper runner helps, and where it does not

Be precise about the limit. Latchkey publishes Linux runners only, at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU with 8 GB, so nothing we sell makes a Windows job cheaper. What a cheaper Linux rate changes is the price of everything you move off Windows, which on the worked month above is the larger half of the saving rather than the smaller one.

If Windows itself is the line you need to cut, the market does sell it and we do not, so price the vendors that publish a Windows rate against your own billed minutes rather than against a headline. The honest summary of this page is that Windows is rarely the problem on a GitHub Actions invoice and is frequently a third of it on a matrix nobody has reviewed since it was written.

Start by measuring rather than moving. Identifying high cost GitHub Actions workflows shows how to get minutes broken down by workflow and runner type, which is the only view that separates the Windows lines from the rest.

FAQ

How much does a GitHub Actions Windows runner cost per minute?

The standard Windows runner is $0.010 a minute on both x64 and arm64, against $0.006 for the standard Linux runner. Larger Windows runners start at $0.022 a minute for 4 cores and reach $0.552 for 96. Standard runners of every type are free and unlimited on public repositories.

Are Windows minutes billed with a multiplier?

Not any more. GitHub publishes a flat per-minute rate for each runner, so a Windows minute is billed at its own rate rather than as a multiple of a Linux one. Since 28 October 2026 the allowance is counted the same way, in dollars at each runner's rate, so a Team plan's $18 covers 1,800 Windows minutes against 3,000 Linux ones.

Why is the 2-core Windows arm64 larger runner cheaper than the standard one?

Its rate is lower: $0.008 a minute against $0.010. It is still a larger runner, so it is billed even on public repositories, where the standard Windows runner is free, and it needs an organization on Team or Enterprise Cloud. On a private repository on those plans it draws on the included allowance like any other runner and is the cheapest Windows minute available.

Do I need a Windows runner for a .NET project?

Only for .NET Framework, Win32 or COM interop, MSI packaging, Authenticode signing, and anything that ships a Windows-only binary. Modern cross-platform .NET builds and tests fine on Linux, so a common arrangement is Linux on every pull request and the full matrix on the default branch and on a schedule.

References

  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every Windows per-minute rate (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: hosted runner specifications for Windows images and labels (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, included compute usage and larger-runner rules (verified 2026-11-12)

title: Your Database Isn't Slow, It's Waiting: 5 Counter-Intuitive Truths About PostgreSQL Lock Contention
description:
Your Database Isn't Slow, It's Waiting: 5 Counter-Intuitive Truths About PostgreSQL Lock Contention

When database latency spikes suddenly, backend engineers routinely jump to standard performance troubleshooting: analyzing execution plans, looking for missing indexes, or trying to refactor seemingly expensive queries. However, this reflex often misdiagnoses the true underlying bottleneck.

The core reality of database performance is that a struggling database often isn't performing complex, CPU-intensive calculations at all—it is simply waiting on a locked resource. Relational databases rely on locks to maintain data consistency during concurrent updates. When these locks are held longer than expected, incoming queries stall, creating a perception of poor execution performance.

Understanding the mechanics of PostgreSQL lock contention, distinguishing waiting states from active execution, and knowing how to diagnose lock dependencies are essential skills for maintaining scalable systems. This article explores five counter-intuitive truths about PostgreSQL lock contention, common diagnostic traps, and operational strategies for prevention.

Takeaway 1: Your "Slow Query" Might Not Be Doing Any Work At All

When a transaction updates a record in PostgreSQL, it acquires a row-level lock to prevent concurrent modifications from corrupting data. As long as that initial transaction remains open, the lock stays active.

There is a fundamental difference between slow query execution and lock contention:

  • Slow Query Execution: The database engine is actively using system resources (CPU, I/O) to process work, such as scanning large tables or performing complex joins.
  • Lock Contention: The query has been sent to the database, but execution cannot proceed because it is waiting for a conflicting lock held by another transaction to be released.

When Transaction A updates a customer record and holds the row lock, subsequent requests—such as Transaction B and Transaction C attempting to update or execute conflicting operations on that same record—are forced to queue up. This creates a cascading backlog of stalled requests.

Crucially, lock contention does not mean that every query touching the table—or even the specific row—will block. PostgreSQL's Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) architecture ensures that standard read operations (SELECT) do not block on row update locks, and write operations do not block non-conflicting reads. Contention arises strictly when concurrent operations request incompatible lock modes on the same database target—such as multiple concurrent UPDATE or DELETE statements targeting the same tuple, or explicit row-locking clauses like SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

"A slow query is not always doing expensive work. Sometimes it is simply waiting for someone else's transaction to finish."

Developers frequently misdiagnose lock contention because traditional latency metrics measure elapsed execution time from request start to completion. Because a waiting query remains open while stalled, execution time metrics register it as "slow," masking the reality that the query spent its entire lifespan dormant, waiting for an upstream lock release rather than executing database operations.

Takeaway 2: The Silent Killer Called "Idle in Transaction"

One of the most dangerous states for a PostgreSQL session to enter is state = 'idle in transaction'.

In PostgreSQL, idle in transaction means a backend process has executed a BEGIN statement and potentially run one or more queries, but it is currently waiting for the application client to send the next command. No active SQL queries are being processed on the database server during this pause.

Consider a common production incident sequence:

  1. Transaction A opens a database transaction (BEGIN) and executes an UPDATE on a row, successfully acquiring a row-level lock.
  2. Before sending a COMMIT or ROLLBACK, the application logic performs non-database work—such as executing an external API call, running complex application code, or hitting an unhandled error/pause.
  3. While the application is paused or stalled, the database connection sits in an idle in transaction state. Even though the database session is executing zero queries and consuming virtually no CPU, it continues to hold all acquired row-level locks. Subsequent transactions (Transaction B, Transaction C) attempting to modify the same resource immediately stall, building up latency across the application stack.

Takeaway 3: Increasing Connection Pools Can Make the Incident Worse

When latency rises and requests begin timing out, a common operational impulse is to scale up the application's database connection pool to handle the backlog. During a lock contention incident, this reaction is a trap that often exacerbates the failure.

It is vital to distinguish between these two failure modes:

  • Connection Pool Exhaustion: The application runs out of available database client connections because all pool connections are actively serving legitimate traffic.
  • Lock Contention: Database connections are stalled behind a single blocking transaction that holds a required lock.

When lock contention is the root cause, adding more connections to the pool does not speed up processing. Instead, it simply opens more pathways for incoming application requests to enter the database, attempt the conflicting operation, and join the waiting queue behind the primary blocking process.

Rather than resolving the issue, expanding the pool causes:

  • Rapid occupation of newly added connections.
  • Compounded latency as more application worker threads stall.
  • Cascading application-level timeouts across dependent services.

Takeaway 4: PostgreSQL Has Built-In Detectives for Unmasking Blockers

PostgreSQL provides system views and diagnostic functions to inspect active session states and expose lock contention: pg_stat_activity and pg_locks.

High-Level Inspection with pg_stat_activity

The pg_stat_activity system view offers real-time insight into process states across backend engines. Key fields include:

  • pid: The process ID of the backend session.
  • state: The current status of the session (e.g., active, idle in transaction).
  • query_start: The timestamp when the currently executing query began.
  • xact_start: The timestamp when the current transaction started.
  • wait_event_type & wait_event: Indicates if and why a backend is waiting (e.g., wait_event_type = 'Lock').
  • query: The text of the most recent or currently active query.

Deep Lock Inspection with pg_locks

While pg_stat_activity shows session status, pg_locks exposes the exact lock hierarchy and resource targets. pg_locks details every lock held or awaited by active processes, categorized by locktype (such as relation, tuple, or transactionid), lock modes (e.g., RowExclusiveLock acquired during updates versus AccessExclusiveLock acquired during schema migrations), and the Boolean status granted.

When diagnosing complex lock trees, joining pg_locks with pg_stat_activity allows database architects to map explicit target dependencies. By filtering for records where granted = false, engineers can identify blocked processes, trace their required target resource (relation or tuple), and match it to the session where granted = true for that exact resource and conflicting lock mode.

Query 1: Identifying Blocking and Blocked Sessions 

SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Query 2: Tracking Idle Transactions Holding Locks 

SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now() - xact_start AS transaction_duration, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

Takeaway 5: Session Termination Is a Last Resort, Not a Solution

When a blocking process brings down database throughput, forcefully terminating the backend session (e.g., via pg_terminate_backend) is often attempted. However, session termination carries distinct architectural risks and must not be treated as a default operational fix.

Risks of Terminating Sessions

  • Transaction Rollbacks: Terminating a session forces an immediate rollback of the active transaction, which can leave application workflows in inconsistent or uncoordinated states.
  • Application-Side Consequences: The client application communicating over that connection receives sudden connection errors, potentially leading to unhandled retries or broken state machines.

Prevention Strategies and Operational Safeguards

Rather than relying on manual intervention during outages, production environments should enforce operational safeguards:

  • Keep Transactions Short: Scope transactions strictly to essential database operations to minimize lock hold duration.
  • Remove External Logic from Transactions: Avoid making external API calls or executing non-database application logic inside open database transactions.
  • Explicit Transaction Termination: Ensure client application code paths guaranteed execution of explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK commands under all conditions, including error states.
  • Configure Transaction Timeouts: Use built-in database timeouts to automatically mitigate abandoned transactions. Specifically, configure idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to automatically terminate sessions that remain idle within an open transaction beyond a specified threshold.
  • Proactive Monitoring: Instrument continuous monitoring for transaction age, lock wait counts, and blocking sessions before they escalate into outages.
  • Establish Operational Protocols: Create strict, documented procedures before manually terminating any database backend process.

Conclusion: The Mental Shift Every Engineer Needs

Managing relational database performance effectively requires a fundamental distinction between query execution efficiency and concurrency management. Adding indexes and rewriting SQL queries will not resolve system slowdowns if the database spends its time waiting on concurrent lock holders.

Before writing a new index or refactoring query logic during a latency incident, engineers should adopt a simple diagnostic step:

Before optimizing a slow query, check whether it's actually waiting for a lock.

Originally published on gokairo.dev.
