title: I got tired of Redis and Kafka eating my RAM, so I rebuilt them in Rust hitting 1.6M RPS (as a student)
description:
Hey everyone, I’m Yasir. I’m an 18-year-old software engineering student from Pakistan, and for the last few months, I’ve been going down a very deep, very complex rabbit hole: Systems Programming in Rust.
When I started learning about distributed systems, I noticed a recurring theme: tools like Apache Kafka and Redis are absolute industry standards, but they come with a catch. Kafka relies heavily on the JVM (hello, GC pauses and massive memory footprints), and standard in-memory stores often hit bottlenecks when scaling across modern multi-core CPUs due to OS-level thread contention and locks.
I didn't have the budget to run massive AWS clusters for my personal projects. I needed something that could run on a potato but still handle enterprise-level throughput.
So, I decided to build my own.
Enter Velocity-Suite (Velocity-MQ & VelocityDB)
I built two core **infrastructure pieces entirely from scratch in Rust:
Velocity-MQ: A zero-GC, lock-free message queue (Kafka alternative).
**VelocityDB: A thread-per-core, lock-free in-memory store (Redis alternative).
My goal wasn't just to write another wrapper. I wanted to bypass traditional OS bottlenecks entirely. Here is the architecture that made it happen:
1_. Bypassing the Kernel with io_uring
Traditional synchronous I/O or even epoll wasn't cutting it for the persistent disk I/O I wanted. I integrated Linux io_uring for asynchronous I/O. By using O_DIRECT, the system completely bypasses the OS page cache. This means zero-copy transfers straight from the disk to the application memory, resulting in microsecond latencies._
2. Thread-per-Core Architecture
Instead of having multiple threads fighting over a shared state (and melting the CPU with context switches), I used a thread-per-core model. Each thread owns its data. No locks, no mutexes blocking the hot path.
3. Lock-Free Concurrency
To allow threads to communicate without slowing down, I heavily utilized lock-free data structures (like ring buffers) and atomic pointers. Fighting the Rust borrow checker while dealing with std::sync::atomic memory ordering (Acquire/Release semantics) was probably the hardest thing I’ve ever done, but the performance payoff was insane.
The Benchmarks 🚀
After weeks of debugging segmentation faults and memory ordering bugs, I finally ran the benchmarks on my local machine:
VelocityDB: **Reached **1.6M+ Requests Per Second (RPS). Click this : https://github.com/developer-yasir/velocitydb .
Velocity-MQ: Pushed 600k+ ops/sec with virtually zero garbage collection overhead. https://github.com/developer-yasir/Velocity-MQ
Running this on minimal RAM felt like a superpower.
Why I am sharing this (I need your help!)
I am incredibly proud of what I've built, but I am also just a 1st-semester CS student. I know for a fact that my code isn't perfect. Systems programming is brutal, and edge cases around memory barriers and crash recovery are terrifying.
I am putting this out here because I want to learn from the best.
If you are a senior Rustacean, a systems engineer, or just someone who loves high-performance backends, I would be honored if you could look at my code.
Roast my architecture.
Tell me where my memory ordering is flawed.
Open an issue if you see a bug.
You can check out the code here:
🔗 https://github.com/developer-yasir/

If you find this project interesting or helpful, dropping a ⭐ on the repo would mean the world to me and keep me motivated to keep building!
Let me know your thoughts in the comments. Let's talk about io_uring and Rust!

title: Build a WooCommerce to Shopify redirect map with 40 lines of Python
description:
When a WooCommerce store moves to Shopify, nearly every URL changes. WooCommerce lets you shape permalinks; Shopify doesn't. Products always live under /products/, collections under /collections/, pages under /pages/ and posts under /blogs/<blog-name>/. Shopify treats those prefixes as fixed.

That means the SEO side of a migration comes down to one file: a list of every old URL that gets traffic or has links, each pointing at its new Shopify address with a 301. Shopify's URL redirect import takes a CSV with two columns, Redirect from and Redirect to, so the job is to produce that file and check it before launch.

Here is the small script we use as a starting point, and the checks we run around it.

Step 1: collect the old URLs

Don't rely only on the sitemap. Combine three sources:

  • The WordPress sitemap (Yoast, Rank Math or core wp-sitemap.xml).
  • Search Console: Performance → Pages, last 16 months, exported to CSV. These are the URLs Google actually shows.
  • Your backlink tool or Search Console's Links report: pages other sites link to.

Put them all in one text file, one URL per line, and de-duplicate.

Step 2: map them by pattern

WooCommerce's default bases are /product/ and /product-category/. Check Settings → Permalinks in WordPress first, because many stores change them (/shop/, /item/, /category/), and adjust the patterns below.

import csv, re, sys
from urllib.parse import urlparse

RULES = [
    (r"^/product/([^/]+)/?$",                lambda m: f"/products/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/product-category/(?:.+/)?([^/]+)/?$", lambda m: f"/collections/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/product-tag/([^/]+)/?$",            lambda m: f"/collections/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/shop/?$",                           lambda m: "/collections/all"),
    (r"^/\d{4}/\d{2}/([^/]+)/?$",             lambda m: f"/blogs/news/{m[1]}"),
    (r"^/(about-us|contact|shipping|returns)/?$", lambda m: f"/pages/{m[1]}"),
]

def map_path(path):
    for pattern, target in RULES:
        m = re.match(pattern, path)
        if m:
            return target(m)
    return None

def main(infile, outfile):
    unmapped = []
    with open(outfile, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["Redirect from", "Redirect to"])
        for line in open(infile):
            path = urlparse(line.strip()).path or "/"
            if path == "/":
                continue
            new = map_path(path)
            if new:
                w.writerow([path.rstrip("/") or "/", new])
            else:
                unmapped.append(path)
    print(f"{len(unmapped)} URLs need a manual decision:")
    print("\n".join(unmapped))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

Run it with python map_redirects.py old-urls.txt redirects.csv. Everything it can't match is printed so a person decides where it goes. That list is usually short but important: landing pages, old campaign URLs and posts without a date in the path.

A few notes on the patterns:

  • Nested categories flatten. /product-category/clothing/hoodies/ becomes /collections/hoodies, because Shopify has no nested collection paths. If two child categories share a slug under different parents, the script will map them to the same collection: check for duplicates.
  • Tags only map if you actually build matching collections. Otherwise send them to the nearest real collection.
  • Blog posts land under /blogs/news/ because Shopify's default blog is called News. Change it if you create a different blog.
  • Keep slugs identical where you can. If blue-hoodie stays blue-hoodie, the map is easy to read and easy to audit.

Step 3: check the targets exist

A redirect to a 404 is worse than no redirect. Before importing, request every target on the Shopify development store (with the storefront password, or from an admin session) and flag anything that isn't a 200. If you used Shopify's Store Migration app or a CSV import, remember imported products start as drafts, so publish them on the dev store before testing.

Step 4: import, then re-test on launch day

Import redirects.csv under Online Store → Navigation → URL Redirects → Import. On launch day, after DNS points at Shopify, request each old URL and confirm it returns a single 301 to the expected path, not a chain. Then watch Search Console's Pages report for new 404s for the next few weeks and add redirects as they appear.

What the script doesn't cover

Redirects keep link equity flowing, but rankings also depend on the content that loads at the new address. Carry over titles and meta descriptions from Yoast or Rank Math, image alt text and product descriptions. Customer passwords can't move at all, so plan the customer communication too. If you'd rather hand the whole move to a team, Dzimark runs WooCommerce to Shopify migration projects for stores in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.

FAQ

Does Shopify let me keep /product/ URLs?
No. Product URLs always start with /products/, which is why every product needs a redirect.

Do I need an app for redirects?
No. Shopify's built-in URL Redirects page imports a CSV. Apps help mainly with bulk editing and monitoring 404s after launch.

Should I redirect URLs that get no traffic?
Redirect anything with traffic, links or that appears in Search Console. Thin, empty archives can go to the closest collection.

Can I import historical orders at the same time?
Not with a CSV. Shopify points to apps such as Matrixify or LitExtension for order history.

Further reading: the full WooCommerce to Shopify migration guide on the Dzimark blog.

title: Databricks AI Tools: The SQL Commands Your Coding Agent Should Use
description:
What databricks experimental aitools is, the five commands that matter, why it changes how coding agents and scripts talk to Databricks SQL, and the sharp edges I found while testing it.

Suppose you ask your coding agent a simple question: "Which pickup zip codes have the most taxi trips?"

The data is in a Databricks table, the agent has the Databricks CLI, it should take one command... right?

Without help, it takes many!

The agent lists the SQL warehouses to find an ID, it writes a JSON body for the Statement Execution API and it sends it with databricks api post.

It polls until the state is SUCCEEDED, then it parses result chunks or it skips all of that and writes a Python script with a SQL connector.

Each step is a place to make a mistake, and each mistake costs tokens and time.

The Databricks CLI now has a command group built for exactly this job. It is called aitools.

We run every important command against a real workspace, we look at the sharp edges, and then I explain why I think you should pay attention to it.

Databricks AI Tools in one minute

The Databricks CLI is the command-line tool for Databricks.

You install it on your laptop or in continuous integration (CI), and you sign in with a profile from ~/.databrickscfg.

Data engineers use it to deploy Declarative Automation Bundles, run Lakeflow Jobs, and call the Databricks REST APIs.

aitools is two command groups inside the Databricks CLI:

Command group What it does Who uses it
databricks aitools Installs Databricks skills and plugins into coding agents You, once per machine or project
databricks experimental aitools tools Runs SQL and reads table metadata, with output that an agent can parse Your coding agent, your scripts, and you

A coding agent is an AI assistant that runs commands in your terminal, such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex CLI.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions that tells the agent how to do a task. The Databricks skills come from the databricks-agent-skills repository.

A SQL warehouse is the Databricks compute that runs SQL and every tools command below needs one.

The Statement Execution API is the Databricks REST API that runs SQL on a SQL warehouse and the databricks api post is the Databricks CLI command that sends a raw POST request to a REST API, these two are the manual path from the story above.

The second group sits under experimental, and the Databricks CLI is honest about it:

CLI tools to be used by AI agents. These tools are optimized for AI coding agents
like Claude Code and Cursor. The tools can change at any time. There are no
stability guarantees for these tools.

Keep that warning in mind. We come back to it in the negatives.

Our example

Everything in this guide uses one workspace profile and one public table:

Profile:   aws-workspace
Table:     samples.nyctaxi.trips
CLI:       Databricks CLI v1.26.0

samples is a catalog that Databricks ships with every Unity Catalog workspace, so you can run every command here without creating data.

To keep the commands short, I define a small shell function first:

# ~/.zshrc (or paste into your terminal)
ait() { databricks experimental aitools tools "$@"; }

From now on, ait query ... means databricks experimental aitools tools query ....

Add -p <profile> if your profile is not the default.

Command 1: get-default-warehouse

Every tools command needs a SQL warehouse, if you do not give one, the Databricks CLI picks one for you.

To see which one it picks:

ait get-default-warehouse --output json

{
  "id": "9810e746a2babb0b",
  "name": "Serverless Starter Warehouse",
  "state": "RUNNING"
}

That is all it does, and that is the point!

The agent does not need to list SQL warehouses and guess.

If you want every command to use a specific SQL warehouse, set an environment variable:

export DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID=9810e746a2babb0b

Or pass --warehouse <id> on each query and statement submit command.

Command 2: query

This is the main command, it runs SQL, waits for the result, and prints it.

ait query "
  SELECT pickup_zip, count(*) AS trips, round(avg(fare_amount), 2) AS avg_fare
  FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 3"

When an agent runs it (a non-interactive terminal), the output is JSON:

[
  { "avg_fare": "10.62", "pickup_zip": "10001", "trips": "1227" },
  { "avg_fare": "10.98", "pickup_zip": "10003", "trips": "1181" },
  { "avg_fare": "10.91", "pickup_zip": "10011", "trips": "1129" }
]

The help text says that in an interactive terminal it renders a table, and large results open an interactive table browser.

I only ran it non-interactively, so I have not seen the browser.

Look at the values again: "1227" is a string, not a number, every value comes back as a string.

That is fine for an agent that reads the text, but a script that sums the column must cast it first.

Many ways to send SQL

query accepts SQL from four places:

ait query "SELECT 1"                    # positional argument
ait query --file report.sql             # a file (-f)
ait query report.sql                    # a positional argument that ends in .sql and exists
echo "SELECT 1" | ait query             # stdin

Parameters, not string building

This is the feature I like most!

Use :name markers in the SQL and bind values with --param:

ait query --output csv \
  --param zip:INT=10001 \
  --param since:DATE=2016-02-14 \
  "SELECT tpep_pickup_datetime, fare_amount
   FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
   WHERE pickup_zip = :zip AND tpep_pickup_datetime >= :since
   ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 3"

tpep_pickup_datetime,fare_amount
2016-02-14T00:10:08.000Z,7.5
2016-02-14T00:17:38.000Z,23.0
2016-02-14T00:23:36.000Z,30.0

name=value binds a string, name:TYPE=value binds a typed value, such as DATE or INT.

The Databricks CLI sends an empty value as NULL, it does not support positional ? markers.

Why does this matter? An agent that builds SQL by gluing strings together can, one day, glue in a quote character from your data.

Parameters remove that whole class of bug.

--output csv is useful on its own, you can export a result to a file without a notebook:

ait query --output csv "SELECT * FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips LIMIT 1000" > trips.csv

Many queries in parallel

Pass more than one SQL statement and the Databricks CLI runs them at the same time, up to --concurrency statements (default 8).

I passed two queries, the second one has a typo on purpose:

ait query \
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips" \
  "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips"

Error: multiple queries require --output json (got "text"); pass --output json to
receive a JSON array of per-statement results

The help text says "Multi-query output is always JSON".

In v1.26.0, it is not always JSON: you must ask for it, so add --output json:

ait query --output json \
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips" \
  "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips"
echo "exit=$?"

[
  {
    "sql": "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips",
    "statement_id": "01f1e012-704d-163a-b2d2-17ed3cd4c4f2",
    "state": "SUCCEEDED",
    "elapsed_ms": 1348,
    "columns": ["n"],
    "rows": [["21932"]]
  },
  {
    "sql": "SELECT nope FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips",
    "statement_id": "01f1e012-7052-197a-a61c-dedd88e64047",
    "state": "FAILED",
    "elapsed_ms": 1276,
    "error": {
      "message": "[UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function parameter with name `nope` cannot be resolved. Did you mean one of the following? [`dropoff_zip`, `pickup_zip`, `fare_amount`, `trip_distance`, `tpep_dropoff_datetime`]. SQLSTATE: 42703; line 1 pos 7",
      "error_code": "BAD_REQUEST"
    }
  }
]
exit=1

Three things to notice:

  1. The good query still returns its result: One failure does not hide the other answers.
  2. The error carries the suggestion: An agent reads "Did you mean pickup_zip" and fixes its own SQL on the next try.
  3. The exit code is 1: Any failed query makes the whole command fail, so CI checks and scripts can trust it.

Also, notice the shape changed!

A single query returns a list of objects ({"trips": "1227"}), a batch returns columns and rows as arrays.

If you parse the output in a script, you must handle both shapes.

Command 3: discover-schema

Before an agent writes SQL against a table, it needs to know the columns.

Without this command, it runs DESCRIBE, then a sample SELECT, then maybe a null check... that's three round trips per table!

discover-schema does all of it in one command:

ait discover-schema samples.nyctaxi.trips

COLUMNS:
  tpep_pickup_datetime: timestamp
  tpep_dropoff_datetime: timestamp
  trip_distance: double
  fare_amount: double
  pickup_zip: int
  dropoff_zip: int

SAMPLE DATA:
  Row 1:
    tpep_pickup_datetime: 2016-02-13T21:47:53.000Z
    tpep_dropoff_datetime: 2016-02-13T21:57:15.000Z
    trip_distance: 1.4
    fare_amount: 8.0
    pickup_zip: 10103
    dropoff_zip: 10110
  ...

NULL COUNTS:
  total_rows: 21932
  tpep_pickup_datetime_nulls: 0
  ...

For each table you get the column names and types, five sample rows, the null count per column, and the total row count.

Pass many tables in one call, use the full CATALOG.SCHEMA.TABLE name:

ait discover-schema samples.tpch.orders samples.tpch.customer samples.tpch.lineitem

All the probes share one budget of --concurrency statements (default 8), however many tables you pass.

The help text says that Ctrl+C cancels the running statements on the server.

A small warning: the sample rows are real data. If a table holds personal data, the agent now has five rows of it in its context. Point the agent at tables it is allowed to see.

Command 4: statement submit, status, get, cancel

query waits for the result, that is what you want most of the time.

Sometimes you do not want to wait, a large OPTIMIZE, a long backfill, or a heavy report can run for minutes.

An agent that blocks on it cannot do anything else.

The statement commands split the work into steps:

Command What it does Blocks?
statement submit Sends the SQL and returns a statement_id at once No
statement status <id> Reads the current state one time No
statement get <id> Waits until the statement finishes, then prints the result Yes
statement cancel <id> Asks the server to stop the statement No

Here is the full cycle:

ait statement submit "
  SELECT pickup_zip, sum(fare_amount) AS total
  FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 2"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "PENDING",
  "warehouse_id": "9810e746a2babb0b"
}

STATEMENT_ID=01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2

ait statement status "$STATEMENT_ID"
ait statement get "$STATEMENT_ID"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "SUCCEEDED"
}
{
  "statement_id": "01f1e012-7467-1656-b3f5-73910324e0d2",
  "state": "SUCCEEDED",
  "columns": ["pickup_zip", "total"],
  "rows": [["11422", "19209.5"], ["11371", "14798.84"]]
}

To stop a statement, use cancel, I submitted a slow self-join on the same table, then cancelled it at once:

ait statement cancel "$STATEMENT_ID"
ait statement status "$STATEMENT_ID"

{
  "statement_id": "01f1e01e-4981-1152-92c5-79b495d9e88a",
  "state": "CANCELED"
}
{
  "statement_id": "01f1e01e-4981-1152-92c5-79b495d9e88a",
  "state": "CANCELED",
  "error": {
    "message": "statement reached terminal state CANCELED"
  }
}

The first CANCELED is optimistic, the API returns no body on cancel, so the Databricks CLI assumes it worked. The second one comes from the server.

If you need to be sure, always run status after cancel, a statement get on a cancelled statement prints the same error and exits with code 1.

One difference is easy to miss: The help text says that Ctrl+C on query cancels the statement on the server, but Ctrl+C on statement get only stops waiting. The statement keeps running, and the SQL warehouse keeps working.

If an agent stops waiting, it must also run statement cancel.

Command 5: aitools install

The tools commands are useful, but the agent must know they exist, that is the job of the other command group.

I noticed this the first time I listed my profiles, the Databricks CLI printed a hint before the list:

Databricks skills are not installed. To work with Databricks reliably, first run: databricks aitools install

databricks aitools install finds the coding agents on your machine and installs the Databricks skills for them.

For Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot, it installs a plugin through the agent's own CLI, for the others (Cursor, OpenCode, Antigravity, Pi, Gemini CLI, Goose, Kiro), it writes raw skill files.

To install for one agent, in the current project only:

databricks aitools install --agents claude-code --scope project

Useful flags:

Flag What it does
--agents claude-code,cursor Act only on the named agents
--scope project or global Install for this repository, or for your user
--skills name1,name2 Install only the named skills (with --skills-only or --path)
--experimental Include experimental skills
--path <dir> Write the skill files to a folder, so you can read them first

The group also has list, update, uninstall, and version.

I did not run install for this article, if you want to know what the skills tell your agent before you trust them, use --path and read the files.

The sharp edges

So far so good... right?

Mostly... here is what can hurt you.

It runs any SQL, not only SELECT, the same command that reads a table can drop a catalog:

ait query 'DROP CATALOG IF EXISTS `my_catalog` CASCADE'

The Databricks CLI does not ask "are you sure?". The only guard is the permissions of the identity behind the profile.

If an agent uses your admin profile, the agent has admin rights.

So give the agent its own identity, such as a service principal (an identity for automation, not for a person), and its own profile.

Grant it only what it needs to read:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO `agent-readonly`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA main.reporting TO `agent-readonly`;

It also needs CAN USE on one SQL warehouse, with these grants, a DROP fails on the server, however the agent writes it. Then keep the agent's own approval rules for anything that is not a read.

Quote carefully in zsh and bash: Backticks inside double quotes run a shell command. Use single quotes around SQL that has backtick identifiers, as above.

It can start a SQL warehouse: If the default SQL warehouse is stopped, the first query starts it. That costs money. Pin a small SQL warehouse with DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID for agent work.

Values are strings in JSON: Cast before you do maths in a script.

Batches need --output json: At least in v1.26.0.

It is experimental: Flags, output shapes, and command names can change in any Databricks CLI release. Do not build a production pipeline on the exact JSON shape.

Why you should pay attention

I see three reasons.

  1. Databricks now treats coding agents as real users of the Databricks CLI: Databricks wrote these commands for agents, said so in the help text, and ships the skills that teach agents to use them. I read that as a signal about where the tooling is going. That part is my opinion, not a fact from the docs.
  2. One command replaces a fragile chain: Find a SQL warehouse, submit, poll, parse, handle errors: query does all of it. Fewer steps means fewer wrong guesses and fewer wasted tokens.
  3. It is useful without an agent. Parameter binding, CSV export, parallel batches with a correct exit code, and asynchronous statements are good tools for shell scripts and CI checks too.

Positives

  • One command for "run this SQL and give me the result", with structured output.
  • Named, typed parameters instead of string building.
  • discover-schema gives columns, samples, and nulls for many tables in one call.
  • Parallel batches return per-query results and a non-zero exit code on any failure.
  • Asynchronous statement commands for long work.
  • aitools install puts the instructions where the agent can find them.

Negatives

  • Experimental, no stability guarantee, and I already found one gap between the help text and the behaviour.
  • Two output shapes, and every value is a string.
  • No built-in guard against destructive SQL, safety depends on your identity and agent permissions.
  • Auto-detection can pick, and start, a SQL warehouse you did not expect.
  • Sample rows from discover-schema put real data into the agent's context.

My default recommendation: install the skills in one project, pin a small SQL warehouse, give the agent a read-only profile, and let it use query and discover-schema for a week.

Wrapping up

If your coding agent talks to Databricks SQL through databricks api post or a one-off Python script, it is working too hard.

databricks experimental aitools tools gives it one command to run SQL, one to understand tables, and a small set to handle long work.

databricks aitools install tells the agent those commands exist.

Treat it as experimental, because it is, give it a narrow identity, because it can run any SQL.

If you already use it in CI or with a coding agent, please tell me in the comments what worked and what broke.

Then try one command today:

databricks experimental aitools tools discover-schema samples.nyctaxi.trips

title: PageSpeed mobile: como levei um site HTML estático de 64 para 97
description:
Não sou programador. Sou corretor de planos de saúde e sócio de uma corretora, e cuido pessoalmente dos nossos sites. Nesta semana passei alguns dias mexendo na performance de quatro sites em HTML estático, e o resultado me surpreendeu: o pior deles saiu de 64 para 97 no PageSpeed Insights mobile.

Vou contar o que fiz, na ordem, com os números reais. Se você tem um site feito a partir de um template pronto (desses com Bootstrap, jQuery e uma dúzia de plugins), é bem provável que o seu tenha os mesmos problemas.

Transparência: fiz esse trabalho com ajuda de IA (Claude), que escreveu os scripts e conferiu cada etapa comigo. As decisões, os testes e os números são dos meus sites.

O incômodo: o WordPress estava mais rápido que o HTML puro

Nosso site principal, de planos da Amil Saúde, roda em WordPress com plugin de cache e marca 94 no mobile. Já os sites menores, feitos em HTML estático, que em teoria deveriam voar, estavam entre 63 e 79.

Não fazia sentido, não é mesmo? HTML puro não tem banco de dados, não tem PHP, não tem nada. O problema não era o tipo de site. Era tudo o que o template carregava sem usar.

O caso deste artigo é um site sobre a linha Amil Black (a linha topo da operadora, que substituiu o antigo Amil One em março de 2026). Ele estava assim no PageSpeed mobile:

  • Desempenho: 64
  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): 7,4 s

Sete segundos para o maior elemento aparecer na tela de um celular. Muita gente desiste antes disso.

Passo 1: descobrir o que o template carregava de graça

Abri o <head> e o fim do <body> da home. Esta era a lista de scripts, carregada em todas as páginas:

<script src="plugins/jQuery/jquery.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/magnific-popup/jquery.magnific.popup.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/slick/slick.min.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/filterizr/jquery.filterizr.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/js?key=..."></script>
<script src="plugins/google-map/gmap.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/syotimer/jquery.syotimer.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/aos/aos.js"></script>
<script src="plugins/swiper/swiper.min.js"></script>
<script src="js/script.js"></script>
<script src="js/menu-black.js"></script>

O site não tem mapa, não tem carrossel, não tem contador regressivo, não tem galeria com filtro. O único script que realmente fazia alguma coisa era o último, menu-black.js, que é o menu.

No CSS, a mesma história: Bootstrap completo, Slick, Slick Theme, Themify Icons e Font Awesome 4.5 vindo de uma CDN.

Uma curiosidade: em outro dos sites, o script.js do template tinha um trecho de CSS colado no final do arquivo. Isso é erro de sintaxe, então o script nunca executou, provavelmente durante anos, e ninguém percebeu. Era peso puro.

Como tirar sem quebrar nada

Antes de apagar qualquer coisa, tirei print de página inteira de todas as páginas, no desktop (1280 px) e no celular (390 px), com o Playwright. Depois de cada mudança, tirei os prints de novo e comparei pixel a pixel.

Para comparar, usei uma tolerância pequena (diferença maior que 24 em algum canal de cor), porque gradientes de fundo às vezes variam um pouco entre uma renderização e outra e geram "diferença" que o olho não vê.

Também conferi três coisas que print não mostra:

  1. Erros de JavaScript no console (pageerror no Playwright).
  2. O menu: o mega menu no hover do desktop e o hambúrguer no celular.
  3. O botão "voltar ao topo".

Esse terceiro item me pegou. O botão dependia do script.js antigo, que era jQuery. Tirei o jQuery e precisei de um substituto. Foram seis linhas de JavaScript puro, no arquivo do menu que já existia:

document.addEventListener('click', function (e) {
    var b = e.target.closest ? e.target.closest('.back-to-top') : null;
    if (!b) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' });
});

Resultado: 11 scripts a menos por página, além dos CSS de Slick, Slick Theme e Font Awesome.

Passo 2: PurgeCSS no Bootstrap

Mesmo sem os plugins, o bootstrap.min.css tinha 141 KB, e o site usa uma fração disso: o grid, alguns utilitários e o collapse do menu.

Usei o PurgeCSS, passando como conteúdo todos os HTML e os JS que sobraram:

import { PurgeCSS } from 'purgecss';
import fs from 'fs';

const result = await new PurgeCSS().purge({
  content: ['site/*.html', 'site/js/*.js'],
  css: ['site/plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.css'],
  safelist: {
    standard: ['show', 'collapse', 'collapsing', 'fade', 'active', 'open'],
    greedy: [/^modal/, /^dropdown/, /^navbar/, /^nav-/]
  }
});

fs.writeFileSync('site/plugins/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.css', result[0].css);

A safelist é a parte importante. Classes que o JavaScript adiciona na hora (como show no menu aberto) não aparecem no HTML, e o PurgeCSS apagaria essas classes se você não avisar.

  • Bootstrap: 141 KB → ~26 KB
  • Themify Icons: 18,6 KB → ~1 KB (o site usa meia dúzia de ícones)

💡 Dica: depois de purgar, coloque um ?v=4 (ou qualquer número novo) no link do CSS. Sem isso, quem já visitou o site continua com o arquivo antigo em cache e você fica achando que algo deu errado.

Passo 3: a imagem do LCP (aqui estava o 7,4 s)

O maior elemento da primeira tela era a imagem principal da home: um PNG de 399 KB.

Convertida para WebP, com uma versão menor para o celular:

  • amil-black-hero.webp (700 px): 24,9 KB
  • amil-black-hero-400.webp (400 px): 11,6 KB 
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="images/amil-black-hero.webp"
      imagesrcset="images/amil-black-hero-400.webp 400w, images/amil-black-hero.webp 700w"
      imagesizes="(max-width: 575px) 88vw, 532px" fetchpriority="high">

<img src="images/amil-black-hero.webp"
     srcset="images/amil-black-hero-400.webp 400w, images/amil-black-hero.webp 700w"
     sizes="(max-width: 575px) 88vw, 532px"
     width="700" height="525" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"
     alt="Mulher sorrindo segurando o cartão do plano Amil Black">

O width e o height evitam que a página "pule" quando a imagem chega (é o CLS). O sizes diz ao navegador que, no celular, a imagem ocupa 88% da largura da tela, então ele baixa a versão de 400 px.

E aqui encontrei o erro mais curioso de todos. Outra imagem, uma foto que fica no meio da página, estava marcada com fetchpriority="high":

<img src="images/amil-black/amil-black.jpg" alt="..." fetchpriority="high">

Ou seja: o navegador baixava com prioridade máxima uma foto que o visitante só vê depois de rolar a tela, competindo com a imagem que realmente importava. Troquei por loading="lazy" e converti essa foto também para WebP, em três tamanhos.

💡 Dica: procure fetchpriority="high" no seu site inteiro. Deve existir no máximo um por página, e só na imagem do LCP.

Aproveitei para reescrever os alt das imagens. Se a imagem tem texto escrito nela (banner, chamada), o alt deve dizer o que está escrito, não só descrever a cena.

Passo 4: as fontes do Google sem travar a página

O style.css do template começava a carregar as fontes assim:

@import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Open+Sans:400,600,700|Poppins:300,400,500,600,700|Work+Sans:400,500,600|Roboto:100,200,300,400,500,600,700,800,900");

Isso é ruim por dois motivos:

  1. @import dentro do CSS é uma cadeia: o navegador baixa o style.css, só então descobre o @import, só então vai ao Google. Tudo isso antes de pintar o texto.
  2. Quatro famílias e 20 pesos. O site usa duas famílias e três pesos.

Tirei o @import e coloquei no <head> de cada página:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="stylesheet"
      href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Open+Sans:wght@400;600;700&family=Poppins:wght@400;600;700&display=swap"
      media="print" onload="this.media='all'">
<noscript>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Open+Sans:wght@400;600;700&family=Poppins:wght@400;600;700&display=swap">
</noscript>

O truque do media="print" faz o navegador baixar a fonte sem bloquear a renderização. Quando termina, o onload aplica a fonte na tela. O display=swap mostra o texto com a fonte do sistema enquanto isso.

Passo 5: gzip e cache no .htaccess

O servidor é Apache (hospedagem compartilhada comum). Sem nenhuma configuração, ele não comprimia nada e não dizia ao navegador por quanto tempo guardar os arquivos.

<IfModule mod_deflate.c>
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE text/html text/css text/plain text/xml
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE application/javascript application/json
  AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE application/xml image/svg+xml font/woff2
</IfModule>

<IfModule mod_expires.c>
  ExpiresActive On
  ExpiresByType image/webp "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType image/png  "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType font/woff2 "access plus 1 year"
  ExpiresByType text/css   "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 month"
  ExpiresByType text/html  "access plus 0 seconds"
</IfModule>

Tudo dentro de <IfModule>: se o módulo não existir no servidor, o bloco é ignorado e o site não cai com erro 500.

HTML com cache zero é de propósito: assim, quando eu atualizo uma página, o visitante vê a versão nova na hora. Imagens e fontes quase nunca mudam e podem ficar um ano em cache. CSS e JS têm o ?v= para forçar a atualização quando eu mexo neles.

No site de Brasília, só esse passo levou a nota de 78 para 89. Foi o ajuste com melhor custo-benefício de todos.

O resultado

Métrica (mobile) Antes Depois
Desempenho 64 97
First Contentful Paint — 1,1 s
Largest Contentful Paint 7,4 s 2,6 s
Total Blocking Time — 0 ms
Cumulative Layout Shift — 0,001
Speed Index — 2,7 s
SEO — 100

Não anotei todas as métricas do "antes", só a nota e o LCP. Fica a lição: tire print completo do PageSpeed antes de começar.

Fiz o mesmo processo nos outros três sites:

O que ainda falta

  • LCP de 2,6 s: está um pouco acima do verde, que vai até 2,5 s. No print do PageSpeed, o banner de cookies cobre boa parte da tela do celular, e desconfio que ele esteja sendo contado como o maior elemento. É o próximo teste.
  • Acessibilidade em 85: provavelmente é o contraste do texto dourado sobre o fundo preto e a ordem dos títulos. Ajuste fino, mas importa.

Checklist para o seu site

  • Liste os scripts e CSS de cada página: para cada um, pergunte "o que quebra se eu tirar?". Em template pronto, a resposta costuma ser "nada".
  • Tire prints antes e depois: de todas as páginas, desktop e celular. Compare automaticamente.
  • Purgue o Bootstrap: com uma safelist para as classes que o JavaScript adiciona.
  • Ataque a imagem do LCP: WebP, srcset, preload e fetchpriority="high" só nela.
  • Procure fetchpriority errado: um por página, no máximo.
  • Tire o @import de fontes do CSS: carregue só as famílias e os pesos que você usa, sem bloquear.
  • Configure gzip e cache: sempre dentro de <IfModule>.
  • Coloque ?v= nos arquivos alterados: para o cache não esconder a sua mudança.

Se você tem um site parado em 60 e poucos no mobile, comece pela imagem do LCP e pelo .htaccess. São os dois passos que mais mexeram na nota aqui.

Ficou alguma dúvida, ou você já passou por algo parecido com template pronto? Me conta nos comentários.

title: How I made refunds automatic in a pay-per-use SMS code service
description:
I built Simuno, a service that sells temporary phone numbers for receiving SMS verification codes. This post is about the one part I found hardest: making the refund automatic, so a customer never has to ask for their money back.

The problem

Codes don't always arrive. The number may already be used on that app, or the app may refuse that number range. On most services like this you then argue with support. I wanted the opposite: if the number expires with no code, the full amount returns to the wallet by itself.

That sounds simple. It isn't, because three things can try to settle the same order at the same moment: a background worker that expires orders, a webhook from the supplier, and the user pressing cancel.

Decision 1: a ledger, not a balance

Every balance change is an entry in an append-only ledger. The cached balance on the user is updated in the same database transaction as the entry and the order status change. That needs MongoDB to run as a replica set, even on one node, because transactions are not available on a standalone server.

Decision 2: one refund per order, enforced by the database

Each refund entry carries a unique key built from the order id. If the worker, the webhook and the cancel button all fire together, only one insert succeeds. The others see a duplicate key error and stop. The order status change is also a compare-and-set, so an order that is already refunded cannot move again.

Decision 3: ask the supplier before you refund

A code can arrive in the last seconds. Before cancelling or refunding, the system asks the supplier for the latest state once more. If a code just arrived, the number is kept and the code is shown, instead of refunded and lost. This was a bug in my first version: a late code could be lost because the refund won the race.

Decision 4: fall through suppliers at the same price limit

Numbers come from more than one upstream supplier. If the first one has no stock or rejects the price, the order tries the next with the same maximum price, so the customer never pays more because of a fallback.

What I would do again

  • Write the refund path before the happy path. It touches the wallet, the order state machine and the supplier calls, so it shapes everything.
  • Make the failure case a test: duplicate refunds, a code arriving during cancel, a supplier timeout.
  • Keep the ledger append-only. Debugging money is much easier when nothing is ever edited.

Stack: Next.js, MongoDB (replica set), Redis, a Node worker for polling and expiry, and a Telegram bot and Mini App on the same backend.

If you have run a similar system, I would like to hear how you handle the race between a late success and an expiry.

title: How I Built an Autonomous AI News Digest Agent in 48 Hours (Node.js, OpenRouter & Nodemailer)
description:
We live in an era of unprecedented information overload. Every morning, millions of professionals wake up, open dozens of browser tabs, scroll through chaotic social media feeds, and attempt to filter through mountains of noise just to stay informed on the topics that actually matter to their industry. Traditional RSS readers require manual curation, and modern news aggregators are flooded with clickbait, algorithmic bias, and distracting ads.

As a backend developer, I realized I didn't need another third-party SaaS subscription or bloated browser extension to solve this problem. I needed a custom-built, proactive intelligence system that could do the heavy lifting for me.

Over a fast-paced 48-hour build sprint, I engineered a fully autonomous, cron-driven backend agent from first principles. Without relying on heavy frameworks or black-box wrappers, this agent wakes up on a strict schedule, fetches breaking metadata from external news sources, scrapes and sanitizes raw web payloads, passes the content through an advanced Large Language Model for high-signal summarization, and dispatches a beautifully formatted HTML newsletter straight to my inbox.

Here is the complete architectural deep dive into how I designed, built, and shipped this autonomous system.

The Philosophy: Shifting from Reactive CRUD to Proactive Agents
Most junior and mid-level backend portfolios look identical: a standard Express server hooked up to a database handling CRUD operations waiting for a frontend client to make an HTTP request. While essential, these systems are entirely reactive. They sit idle until a human interacts with them.

Autonomous agents represent a fundamental shift in systems architecture. They are proactive. They operate independently in the background, orchestrated by time-based triggers or event streams, executing complex workflows without human intervention.

Building this news agent taught me how to think in terms of asynchronous pipelines. Instead of managing synchronous request-response lifecycles, I had to design a decoupled workflow where data flows seamlessly across distinct domain services—from ingestion and scraping to AI transformation and final delivery.

Architectural Blueprint: The 4-Stage Pipeline
To ensure the system remained modular, maintainable, and easy to debug, I decoupled the architecture into distinct, single-responsibility modules:

The Ingestion Layer: Responsible for querying external news providers (such as The Guardian Content API) using secure, environment-scoped credentials to harvest fresh breaking article metadata and target URLs.

The Scraping and Filtering Layer: Takes the raw article URLs, pulls the core Document Object Model (DOM) content, strips away irrelevant boilerplate, and filters out low-signal entries.

The AI Summarization Layer: Passes the sanitized text payload to an LLM via the OpenRouter SDK. Instead of forcing me to read dense, 2,000-word articles, the model extracts core themes, key takeaways, and executive summaries.

The Dispatch Layer: Transforms the summarized text strings into a responsive, beautifully styled HTML card and pushes it out via an automated SMTP email service using Nodemailer.

The Orchestration Layer: Powered by a background cron scheduler that manages exact execution times, ensuring the pipeline fires reliably without manual triggers.

Deep Dive into Core Pipeline Execution

  1. Managing Asynchronous Data Flow The backbone of the entire application is an isolated asynchronous pipeline function. Rather than cluttering the global scope with mutable state arrays, each execution cycle initializes a clean execution scope.

The pipeline begins by calling the ingestion module to fetch article metadata. Once URLs are retrieved, the scraper module extracts the underlying text content. After passing the payload through a strict filter to discard empty or malformed items, the data is handed off to the LLM summarizer. Finally, the enriched object is pushed to the email dispatch service. Wrapping this entire sequence in robust try-catch blocks ensures that if an external API times out or throws an error, the system logs the failure gracefully without crashing the entire Node process or leaving background workers hanging.

  1. Crafting Responsive HTML Newsletters Delivering text via plain, unstyled emails looks unprofessional and degrades readability. To solve this, I designed a custom email delivery module that constructs a clean newsletter card.

Because major email clients (like Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail) notoriously strip out external stylesheets and complex CSS layout rules, I utilized robust inline styling techniques. The module takes the raw string output from the LLM summarizer, splits the text paragraphs cleanly, and wraps them in structured paragraph tags with explicit margins and line heights. These paragraphs are then injected into a centered, max-width container featuring a dark navy header banner and a soft, neutral background. This guarantees crisp, consistent rendering across both desktop and mobile email clients. Furthermore, authentication is handled securely through Google's App Passwords, allowing the application to authenticate via SMTP without exposing primary account credentials in plaintext config files.

  1. Background Orchestration with Cron An autonomous agent is only as good as its scheduling reliability. To automate the pipeline, I integrated a background cron manager.

One of the most valuable lessons I learned during this build was the importance of cron expression syntax. Standard cron schedulers utilize a 5-field format representing minutes, hours, day of the month, month, and day of the week. Initially, misconfiguring second-level parameters led to aggressive loop behaviors. Sticking strictly to standard 5-field syntax resolved execution timing completely, allowing me to configure precise daily triggers (such as running at 7:00 AM and 3:00 PM) while binding the runtime environment to a local timezone to prevent UTC offset discrepancies. Additionally, keeping an Express server running alongside the scheduler allowed me to expose a manual webhook endpoint, making local debugging and testing effortless via curl commands.

Engineering Challenges and Hard-Won Lessons
Every rapid development sprint comes with unexpected hurdles. Building this agent over two days surfaced two notable engineering challenges:

SMTP Authentication Barriers: When first wiring up Nodemailer with a personal Gmail account, I ran into strict authentication blocks due to Two-Step Verification policies. Learning how to navigate Google's security architecture to generate dedicated App Passwords reinforced the importance of secure secret management and zero-trust configuration practices.

Cron Granularity and Overlapping Runs: During early testing, setting cron intervals too aggressively caused overlapping pipeline executions when an external scraping or LLM request took slightly longer than expected. This highlighted the necessity of building idempotent background tasks and adding locking mechanisms or database state checks.

What Comes Next?
Building a fully functional autonomous news digest agent in 48 hours proved how powerful lightweight Node.js backends can be when combining external APIs, local scraping engines, and generative AI models.

The immediate next phase of development involves integrating MongoDB persistence. By storing the unique hashes or URLs of articles that have already been emailed, the agent will be able to perform deduplication checks. If the underlying news source has not published a fresh top story between cron intervals, the agent will intelligently skip execution rather than dispatching redundant updates.

If you are an engineer looking to sharpen your backend skills, step away from standard frontend CRUD apps for a weekend. Build something that runs in the background, talks to multiple APIs, reasons over data using an LLM, and delivers value autonomously. The architectural insights you gain will completely transform how you approach software design.

title: Why "it works on my machine" isn't enough for open-source QA
description:
When you build an open-source testing framework, you reach a point where the code is done, the tests are passing, and the features are implemented.

For a lot of developers, that's the end of the line. "It works on my machine. I'm done."

But for a framework to be truly valuable to a client, that is only the halfway point. The code existing is not the same thing as the code being reliable.

I've been building Praman, an open-source QA engine in Python. The test suite just crossed 910 passing tests. The API automation, browser sessions, configuration, and reporting are all implemented. But as I look at my roadmap, I realize the hardest work is still ahead: proving it actually works in the real world.

Here is why building a framework for real clients requires a different mindset.

When you build a feature, it's easy to mark it as "done" in your head. But a QA framework requires independent validation.

If I build a wheel and test it locally, that proves the wheel builds. It doesn't prove that a developer in a different environment can install it, import it, and run a test without it breaking. To prove that, I have to build the wheel, spin up a completely isolated Python 3.12 environment, install the wheel from scratch, and run an external client smoke test.

Only then is the packaging "done."

Phase 5 of my roadmap is AI-assisted testing. It's the most exciting part. I want to build LLM integration, failure analysis, and suggested fixes.

But I am deliberately not starting it yet.

If I introduce an AI agent that analyzes failures, but my JSON failure reports are inconsistent, the AI will give me bad analysis. If I add LLM code generation, but my isolated installation tests aren't passing, the AI will generate tests that don't run.

You cannot build advanced AI features on top of a shaky foundation. The execution, reporting, and evidence systems have to be bulletproof first.

I created a "Foundation Release Candidate" checklist for the next milestone. It doesn't just ask "does the code exist?" It asks:

  • Does the latest wheel build and install independently?
  • Do the external client tests pass?
  • Are failure screenshots and redaction verified?
  • Does the latest hosted GitHub Actions run succeed?

If any of these are false, the foundation isn't ready.

A passing test suite is a great milestone. It means you have 910 examples of your code doing the right thing. But a reliable framework is not just about the tests you write. It's about isolated client installation, clean CI pipelines, and documenting exactly what has been verified.

If you are building a tool for other developers, don't just ask if it works on your machine. Ask if it works on theirs.

You can see the current progress and the roadmap on the repository: https://github.com/pranromumu/praman

title: Identify high cost GitHub Actions workflows
description:
To identify high cost GitHub Actions workflows you need three numbers that the billing dashboard does not give you: minutes by workflow, minutes by job inside the worst workflow, and the share of your runs that are retries of a previous attempt. All three come from the REST API and the usage report, and the third one is the one almost nobody measures and frequently the largest.


The three measurements and where each one comes from. Endpoint paths from the GitHub REST API reference for Actions workflow runs, read on 21 September 2026.

The billing page shows a total. A total tells you that CI costs money and nothing about where it goes, and optimisation aimed at the wrong job is the most common way a team spends a sprint and saves nothing.

Everything below is read-only and takes under an hour on a repository you already have a token for. Do it before you change a single workflow file, and rank what you find by money rather than by minutes, because a Linux job and a macOS job of the same length are not the same line on the invoice.

One: minutes by workflow

The workflow timing endpoint returns billable milliseconds per operating system for a single workflow, which is exactly the breakdown the billing dashboard will not give you. Loop it over the workflow list and you have a ranked table in a few seconds.

Read the result as a ranking rather than as an invoice. The figure is machine time in milliseconds, and the bill rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute, so a workflow made of many short jobs will cost more than this endpoint suggests and a workflow made of a few long ones will cost about what it says.

There is one answer that looks like a broken script and is not. On a public repository the billable object comes back empty, because the use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited there. If you get nothing back from a public repository, nothing is wrong: there is nothing to bill. Larger runners are the exception and are charged on public repositories too.

# per-workflow billable time, ranked
gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows --paginate \
  --jq '.workflows[] | "\(.id)\t\(.name)"' |
while IFS=$'\t' read -r id name; do
  ms=$(gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/$id/timing" \
        --jq '[.billable[]?.total_ms] | add // 0')
  printf "%8.1f min  %s\n" "$(echo "$ms/60000" | bc -l)" "$name"
done | sort -rn

Run this first. It almost always shows one or two workflows dominating, which turns an open-ended optimisation project into a specific one.

Two: where the minutes go inside that workflow

Once you know which workflow is expensive, the question is which job inside it. The run timing endpoint gives billable milliseconds per operating system for a single run along with the total run duration, and the jobs endpoint gives you the start and completion timestamps of every job in that run.

Average across the last fifty runs rather than reading one. A single run tells you about one moment of registry weather; fifty tell you which job is structurally slow. The pattern that comes back most often is that dependency installation, not compilation and not the tests, is the largest single block of time in the pipeline.

Keep the two operating systems separate while you do it. A five-minute macOS job and a five-minute Linux job are $0.31 and $0.03 respectively, so a ranking by duration puts them side by side and a ranking by cost puts them ten rows apart. Sort by minutes multiplied by that runner type's published rate, never by minutes alone.

# average per-job duration across the last 50 runs of one workflow
gh run list --workflow=ci.yml --limit 50 --json databaseId --jq '.[].databaseId' |
while read -r id; do
  gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/$id/jobs" \
    --jq '.jobs[] | [.name, (((.completed_at|fromdate) - (.started_at|fromdate))/60)] | @tsv'
done | awk -F'\t' '{s[$1]+=$2; n[$1]++} END {for (k in s) printf "%8.1f min avg  %4d runs  %s\n", s[k]/n[k], n[k], k}' | sort -rn

Three: the number nobody measures

Every workflow run carries a run_attempt field, and it is 1 on a first attempt. Count how many of your recent runs are at attempt 2 or higher and you have the share of your bill that bought the same work twice.

This is the measurement that changes what you do next, because no per-minute discount touches it. A pipeline that re-runs a meaningful share of its jobs is paying for the failure, paying again for the retry, and paying a third time in the hour between the failure and somebody noticing. If that share is more than a few percent, reliability is your cost problem and the rate is a distraction.

Look at what the retries are for while you are there. Retries of registry timeouts, DNS failures and runner losses are a different problem from retries of a genuinely flaky test, and they are the ones with nothing to do with your code at all.

# what fraction of recent runs are attempt 2 or later?
gh run list --limit 200 --json databaseId --jq '.[].databaseId' |
while read -r id; do
  gh api "/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/$id" --jq '.run_attempt'
done | awk '{t++; if ($1>1) r++} END {printf "re-runs: %d of %d (%.1f%%)\n", r, t, 100*r/t}'

The one report the API cannot replace

The API is per repository. The usage report is per account, and it is the only surface that attributes spend to a workflow file across an organisation. GitHub offers a summarized report covering up to a year and a detailed report covering up to 31 days, and the detailed one adds two fields that matter here: username and workflow_path.

Read discount_amount before you read anything else. That field carries the usage that was discounted, including your included allowance and the discounts for standard runners in public repositories and for self-hosted runners. Reading gross_amount without it is how a team concludes that its open source project costs thousands of dollars a month.

The reports are delivered by email to the address on the account and you can only request one at a time, so start the request before you begin the API work rather than after. Group the result by sku first: that single grouping usually answers the question, because the expensive SKU is rarely the one people name when you ask them to guess.

Question Where the answer is What that source cannot tell you
Which workflow costs most? Workflow timing endpoint, per repository Anything about rounding, or about other repositories
Which job inside it? Run timing and jobs endpoints Money, until you multiply by the runner rate yourself
How much is re-runs? run_attempt on recent runs Why they were re-run
Who and what across the org? Detailed usage report, 31 days Anything older than 31 days
Is storage the problem? Usage report, grouped by SKU Which artifact or cache is responsible

Report types and field names from GitHub billing reports, read 21 September 2026.

Turn the measurement into a decision

Five findings, five different next moves. If installation dominates, cache the dependency directory and key it to the lockfile hash. If a wide matrix of short jobs dominates, the rounding is the cost and consolidation is the fix. If one long job dominates, shard it or size it up, and check the break-even first. If re-runs dominate, nothing about runner choice helps you. If macOS dominates, move everything that does not need Xcode, because that minute is more than ten times a Linux one.

Only after that is the rate worth touching. A cheaper runner multiplies whatever is left, so it is the last change rather than the first, and it is worth the most to the team that has already removed the work it was never going to need. How to reduce GitHub Actions costs prices seven changes against one worked month, and the cost calculator prices your own month at two rates.

If the numbers came back surprising rather than clarifying, why is my CI so expensive works through what each shape of invoice usually means.

FAQ

How do I see GitHub Actions minutes by workflow?

Call the workflow timing endpoint for each workflow id, which returns billable milliseconds broken down by operating system, and sort the result. The billing dashboard does not provide this breakdown. Treat the numbers as a ranking, because the invoice rounds every job up to a whole minute and this endpoint does not.

Why does the timing endpoint return nothing for my repository?

Almost certainly because the repository is public. Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited on public repositories, so there are no billable milliseconds to report. Larger runners are billed even on public repositories, so a public repository using those will still return figures.

What is the biggest hidden GitHub Actions cost?

Re-runs. A retry buys the same work a second time, and the failure is often unrelated to the code that triggered it. Measure the share of runs with a run_attempt above 1 before optimising your per-minute rate; above a few percent it dominates any rate difference on the market.

What is the difference between the summarized and detailed usage reports?

The summarized report covers up to a year and sums usage by date, SKU, repository and cost centre. The detailed report covers a maximum of 31 days and adds username and workflow_path, which is what lets you attribute spend to a specific workflow file. Both arrive by email and you can only request one at a time.

References

  • GitHub REST API: Actions workflow runs, timing and jobs endpoints (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub billing reports: usage report types and every field (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, the rates to multiply minutes by (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: Actions billing, rounding, allowances and public repositories (verified 2026-09-21)

title: I tested whether a 4B model could replace a 12B one in a tool-using agent. My first test was wrong.
description:
Two pre-registered runs on local models, a reader's correction between them, and the one place the small model still breaks.

I wanted to know whether a 4B local model could replace a 12B one in a small tool-using agent. I ran it as an experiment, with the prediction written down before each run. Both models ran on Ollama on one laptop, at temperature 0.7, with no API.

The set-up

  • 24 order-desk tasks: refund an order, refund and add a note, check stock and add a note.
  • Each task ran clean and under three injected tool faults: a timeout, a one-off error, an empty result. That makes 96 task-and-fault combinations per round.
  • Baseline: gemma4 12B. Candidate: qwen3.5 4B. Same prompt, same tools, same retry settings.
  • The rule for the verdict was fixed before the run: is the 4B within 10 points of the 12B?

Run 1: my prediction lost

I predicted the 4B would be close enough. It was not. The 12B passed 96 of 96. The 4B passed 70 of 96, and the run stopped after one round with a verdict of BLOCK.

Most of the failures were one behaviour. In 21 of the 26, the 4B was asked to check stock for an order and its only call was to the stock tool, with the order id as the product code. It never looked the order up.

A reader caught a flaw in the test

In my set-up that wrong call raised an exception and ended the trial. The model never saw "unknown SKU". So I had measured "makes a wrong first call, where a wrong call is fatal". I had not measured "cannot do the task". I published a correction and ran it again.

Run 2: the error goes back to the model

One change, the same for both models: a tool's error is returned to the model as a message. My prediction, written first: inconclusive.

  • 12B: 480 of 480.
  • 4B: 428 of 480 (89%).
  • The 4B made the wrong first call about as often as before: in 21 of 32 stock-note trials in run 1, and in 108 of 160 in run 2.
  • Shown the error, it looked the order up next in 106 of those 108, and 68 of the 108 passed.
  • Only 2 of 480 trials never did the lookup at all.

The test could not decide whether the 4B is within 10 points of the 12B. The gap landed at 10.8 points. So the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE: the run crossed neither the PASS nor the BLOCK threshold.

Where it still breaks

Two things going wrong in one trial. When the 4B made the wrong first call and then the lookup came back empty (the injected fault), it passed 0 of 26. In 21 of the 26 it read the error, looked the order up once, got nothing back, and stopped. The 12B retried the empty lookup every time, 120 of 120.

Where the wrong first call was the only lasting problem (no injected fault, or a timeout that a retry clears), the 4B went on to pass 52 of 58.

What I took from it

  • Know whether your tools raise their errors or return them. Here it changed what the test measured: in run 2, 77 of the 4B's 428 passes came after a tool error that would have ended the trial under run 1's set-up.
  • In this suite, looking at one problem at a time flattered the 4B. Half of its 52 failures in run 2 (26) were the compound case above.
  • I did not see any of this by reading sample outputs. I saw it by counting what each trial did with its tools.

Limits

One suite, one prompt, two models, one machine. The two runs used different seeds, so 73% against 89% is two observations, not a measured effect of returning errors. The breakdowns were chosen after seeing the data. None of this says anything about these models in general.

Check it yourself

The harness is my own open-source tool, ARCI. It runs a baseline and a candidate on the same tasks with injected tool faults and gives PASS, BLOCK or INCONCLUSIVE with a stated error bound.

  • Both runs, both pre-registrations and the correction
  • The raw records of every trial, with the command that re-derives both verdicts
  • The same comparison on your own two models
  • Repository

If you have measured this on other small models, I would like to know: does returning tool errors close most of the gap, or is that specific to this pair?

The numbers were recounted from the stored trial records before publishing, and those records are public at the links above. First published on my blog, Real or Noise.
