title: Why Ctrl+P Truncates ChatGPT & Claude Threads — Purifying SPA DOMs into Crisp Vector PDFs
description:
Try opening a 20-turn architecture or debugging conversation in ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or DeepSeek right now and pressing Cmd+P (Ctrl+P) to save a PDF reference for your team wiki or tablet.

Three things almost always go catastrophically wrong:

  1. Only Page 1 Prints (The 100vh Flex Scroll Trap): Everything above or below the current viewport disappears because modern single-page chat apps lock html, body to height: 100vh; overflow: hidden and scroll an inner flex: 1; overflow-y: auto container. Browser print engines paginate the root document viewport—not nested scrollboxes!
  2. Code Blocks & Tables Get Sliced Horizontally: <pre><code> blocks styled with overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre clip the right 40% of your SQL queries or TypeScript types, and page breaks slice single lines of code vertically in half.
  3. Dark Mode Torches Printer Toner: Terminal dark slate backgrounds (#0f172a), sticky composer drawers, sidebar thread histories, and low-contrast #94a3b8 text produce muddy, ink-soaked pages.

Many existing "ChatGPT to PDF" tools work around this by rasterizing the DOM onto an HTML5 <canvas> (html2canvas) and wrapping giant PNG screenshots inside a PDF container—resulting in 25 MB files where you cannot Cmd+F search or copy-paste a single line of code, or worse, requiring terrifying <all_urls> "Read and change all your data on all websites" permissions.

We built and open-sourced CleanPrint & AI-Chat to PDF Studio (live on Mozilla Firefox Add-ons and unpacked for Chrome/Edge/Brave) to produce true 80 KB selectable vector PDFs in <50ms locally. Here is how the DOM purification and @media print architecture works under the hood.

1. Escaping the 100vh Scroll Container Trap Non-Destructively

If you try to mutate ChatGPT or Claude's live React/Next.js Fiber tree in-place—stripping overflow: hidden and deleting sidebar nodes—two bad things happen: CSS specificity wars with Tailwind utility classes break layout unpredictably, and the moment React reconciles state, your mutated DOM crashes with hydration/removeChild errors when the user returns to their chat.

Instead, CleanPrint treats the live SPA DOM as read-only input, extracts a clean semantic AST, mounts an isolated sibling root (#cleanprint-studio-root) directly under document.body, and hides sibling app shells purely via a reversible root class:

html.cleanprint-studio-active,
html.cleanprint-studio-active body {
  background: #e2e8f0 !important;
  height: auto !important;
  overflow: visible !important;
  margin: 0 !important;
  padding: 0 !important;
}

html.cleanprint-studio-active body > *:not(#cleanprint-studio-root) {
  display: none !important;
}

Why is body > *:not(#cleanprint-studio-root) { display: none !important; } so effective?

  • Every nested 100vh React wrapper (#__next, main, sticky navbars, composer inputs) stays completely intact in memory—preserving scroll position, React event listeners, and streaming state.
  • #cleanprint-studio-root sits in normal document block flow with height: auto, allowing Blink, Gecko, and WebKit's native print pagination engine to lay out 1 to 100+ vector pages effortlessly.
  • Clicking Restore Original Web View simply removes html.cleanprint-studio-active and unmounts #cleanprint-studio-root, restoring window.scrollTo(0, savedScrollY) with zero page reload.

2. Multi-Platform AI Turn Extraction + Density Fallback

Different LLM interfaces mark up conversation turns differently, and those selectors evolve. In src/purifier.js, our parser cascades through three tiers before falling back to an article link-density scorer (for GitHub READMEs, MDN docs, and engineering blogs):

// Tier 1: OpenAI / ChatGPT semantic author role attributes
var roleNodes = doc.querySelectorAll('[data-message-author-role]');

// Tier 2: Claude, Copilot & Gemini custom elements / test IDs
var combinedTurnNodes = doc.querySelectorAll(
  '[data-testid="user-message"], .font-claude-message, ' +
  '[data-content="user-message"], [data-content="ai-message"], ' +
  'user-query, model-response, .copilot-chat-message'
);

// Tier 3: Generic turn wrappers & link-density article root fallback

Inside each turn, a recursive walker normalizes headings (h1–h6), inline formatting runs (code, strong, em, resolved a[href]), Markdown tables, blockquotes, lists, and fenced <pre><code> blocks—automatically detecting the programming language either from language-* classes or adjacent header pills (sql, python, typescript) while ignoring UI buttons like "Copy" or "Edit".

3. Passing Mozilla AMO Security Review: Zero innerHTML & Least-Privilege MV3

If you have ever submitted an extension to Mozilla Add-ons (AMO), you know their automated linter and human security reviewers strictly flag any assignment to .innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, or outerHTML inside privileged scripts due to DOM XSS risks when parsing untrusted web pages.

CleanPrint contains zero .innerHTML calls across the entire codebase (enforced automatically by our build script before running syntax checks in JavaScriptCore). Every purified card, table cell, inline code badge, and multi-tab Table of Contents entry is constructed through a tiny 25-line hyperscript helper using document.createElement and textContent:

function el(tag, attrs, children) {
  var node = document.createElement(tag);
  if (attrs) {
    Object.keys(attrs).forEach(function (k) {
      if (k === 'className') node.className = attrs[k];
      else if (k === 'textContent') node.textContent = attrs[k];
      else if (k.indexOf('on') === 0 && typeof attrs[k] === 'function') {
        node.addEventListener(k.slice(2).toLowerCase(), attrs[k]);
      } else if (attrs[k] != null) {
        node.setAttribute(k, String(attrs[k]));
      }
    });
  }
  (children || []).forEach(function (ch) {
    if (ch == null) return;
    node.appendChild(typeof ch === 'string' ? document.createTextNode(ch) : ch);
  });
  return node;
}

Equally important is Manifest V3 permission hygiene. CleanPrint requests strictly:

"permissions": ["activeTab", "scripting", "storage"]

No <all_urls>. No persistent content scripts slowing down every page load. purifier.js is injected strictly on-demand via scripting.executeScript when—and only when—you click the toolbar icon. For cross-browser compatibility between Chromium (service_worker) and Firefox MV3 (background.scripts + browser_specific_settings.gecko with data_collection_permissions.required: ["none"]), we maintain clean target manifests sharing 100% of the runtime JS.

4. Print-Media CSS That Never Cuts Off Code Blocks or Wastes Toner

To ensure exported PDFs read like typeset technical handouts rather than broken web dumps, our print stylesheet combines four rules:

/* 1. Wrap long code lines cleanly instead of clipping horizontally */
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-pre {
  white-space: pre-wrap;
  word-break: break-word;
  overflow-x: visible;
  line-height: 1.5;
}

/* 2. Keep code blocks, tables, figures & headings anchored across page breaks */
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-heading,
#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-qa-header {
  break-after: avoid;
  page-break-after: avoid;
}

#cleanprint-studio-root .cp-avoid-break,
#cleanprint-studio-root pre,
#cleanprint-studio-root table {
  break-inside: avoid;
  page-break-inside: avoid;
}

/* 3. Eco Low-Ink Mode: strip dark terminal fills into crisp monochrome hairlines */
#cleanprint-studio-root.cp-low-ink .cp-code-block {
  background: #ffffff !important;
  color: #0f172a !important;
  border: 1.25px solid #334155 !important;
}

Toggling Eco Low-Ink Mode replaces solid #1e293b code backgrounds and tinted prompt cards with pure #ffffff paper fills and sharp #334155 borders—cutting black toner/ink usage by roughly 65%–75% on code-heavy LLM threads while boosting laser-print legibility.

Install or Inspect the Source (MIT Licensed)

  • 🦊 Firefox Official Add-on (1-Click Install): CleanPrint & AI-Chat to PDF Studio on Mozilla Add-ons
  • 📦 Chrome / Edge / Brave Release .zip & MIT Source: github.com/963239327/cleanprint-ai-chat-to-pdf
  • 👀 Interactive Web Preview: Try CleanPrint Formatting in Browser
  • 📚 CleanPrint Pro ($5.99 Lifetime Offline Key): Unlocks our Multi-Tab Print Queue Binder (combine 10+ ChatGPT threads & docs into one research PDF with an auto-generated Table of Contents), Academic Serif / 2-Column Study / 2-Up Booklet themes, and marginless URL header removal via Gumroad.

Happy printing—and may your <pre><code> blocks never get chopped at column 80 again!

title: PostgreSQL and pgvector: When Should AI Applications Use a Separate Vector Database?
description:
An AI application can keep business records, embeddings and searchable documents in PostgreSQL, or introduce a dedicated vector system. The right decision depends on retrieval quality, access controls, scaling requirements and the cost of keeping multiple data stores synchronized.

An organization building an AI knowledge assistant may already store its documents, users and permissions in PostgreSQL. To make those documents searchable by meaning, the application needs embeddings. These are numerical representations of content that allow software to find semantically related passages.

One option is to store embeddings alongside application data using the pgvector extension. Another is to maintain a separate vector-search system. Both architectures can support retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

The question is whether a separate database solves a measurable problem or introduces complexity that the application does not yet need.

What pgvector adds to PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL already provides relational storage, transactions, joins, indexing and full-text search. pgvector adds vector data types, similarity operators and approximate nearest-neighbor indexes, which find close matches quickly without checking every vector.

An application can store document chunks, their embeddings and associated metadata in PostgreSQL. When a user asks a question, the application creates an embedding of that question and searches for similar document embeddings. The retrieved passages can then provide context to a language model generating an answer.

pgvector does not generate embeddings, enforce the correctness of model-generated answers or automatically determine whether a document is safe for a particular user to read. Those remain responsibilities of the application and its security architecture.

Importantly, pgvector is an extension, not a PostgreSQL 19 feature. Its existing capabilities work across supported PostgreSQL versions, and the pgvector README lists support for PostgreSQL 13 and later, so check which versions your release supports. For what changes in PostgreSQL itself, see our article on PostgreSQL 19 and its release candidate.

Source: pgvector official documentation.

How an enterprise RAG application retrieves documents

Consider a hypothetical internal knowledge assistant used by Finance and Human Resources employees. The organization stores documents and access metadata in PostgreSQL. Each document is divided into searchable passages, with an embedding associated with each passage.

A typical retrieval operation has several stages.

1. Authenticate the user. The application establishes the user’s identity and authorized organizational context.

2. Determine the permitted document scope. The server identifies which documents the user is entitled to access, using trusted authorization data rather than user-supplied instructions.

3. Generate the question embedding. An embedding model converts the user’s question into the same compatible vector representation used for the stored passages.

4. Retrieve matching passages. PostgreSQL searches for semantically similar content while applying the appropriate document-access conditions.

5. Enforce the access boundary. The application verifies that only permitted content can be passed to the model. Database-side row-level security can provide another enforcement layer where correctly configured.

6. Generate the response. The language model uses authorized passages as supporting context. The application can retain source references for traceability.

Interactive figure: view it in the original article

Suppose a Finance employee asks about an expense-approval policy. A Human Resources document might be semantically similar, but similarity does not make that document authorized. The database query and surrounding application controls must prevent restricted material from entering the model’s context.

PostgreSQL row-level security

PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) can restrict which records a database role may read or modify. It can help enforce tenant or document boundaries independently of ordinary application filtering.

However, enabling RLS does not automatically make every connection safe. Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS bypass policies. Table owners normally bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is configured. Applications also need to establish authorization context safely, especially when connections are pooled or reused.

RLS should be tested with realistic user roles, including negative tests proving that unauthorized documents cannot be retrieved. An ordinary WHERE tenant_id = ... clause is useful for query filtering, but should not be treated as a complete security boundary when the calling application can alter or omit it.

Source: PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies.

Exact search and approximate indexes solve different problems

By default, pgvector performs exact nearest-neighbor search. This finds the nearest matching vectors under the selected distance measure, providing a useful baseline against which approximate results can be evaluated. As vector collections and request volumes grow, exact search may become more expensive.

pgvector supports two principal approximate indexing methods.

Index How it works Important trade-off
HNSW Organizes vectors into a navigable graph Strong speed and recall characteristics for many workloads, with additional build time and memory requirements
IVFFlat Groups vectors into lists and searches selected lists Requires suitable training data and tuning of search breadth

Approximate indexes can return different results from exact search. That is why latency alone is an insufficient performance measure. Teams should also measure recall, which indicates how many expected nearest-neighbor results were retrieved compared with an exact-search baseline.

For an AI assistant, a faster result may be less useful if an important document is consistently omitted.

Source: pgvector, Indexing.

Filtering can affect retrieval quality

Enterprise searches rarely depend on vector similarity alone. Results may also be filtered by organization, document type, project or access scope. With approximate indexes, PostgreSQL can apply filtering after the index scan has selected candidates, and this can return fewer results than requested.

For example, if a search examines 40 candidates and only 10% satisfy a category filter, approximately four may remain on average. That is an illustration of selectivity, not a guaranteed outcome for every search.

pgvector introduced iterative index scans in version 0.8.0 on October 30, 2024. Iterative scans can continue examining more index candidates when filtering removes too many results, subject to configured resource and scan limits. Other approaches include ordinary PostgreSQL indexes, partial vector indexes and table partitioning, depending on query patterns. These mechanisms should be selected through measurement.

Tenants that share one approximate index can also affect each other. The pgvector documentation says vectors from one tenant can change recall and speed for other tenants, and recommends list partitioning or separate tables for tenant isolation.

A correctly enforced authorization filter must never be weakened merely to increase the number of search results. A retrieval system returning fewer authorized passages may produce a less complete answer. Returning unauthorized passages is a different and more serious failure.

Sources: pgvector changelog, pgvector filtering guidance and pgvector multitenancy.

Hybrid search combines different forms of relevance

Semantic similarity is useful when users describe a concept without using the exact wording found in a document. Keyword search remains important for identifiers, product names, policy numbers and technical terms.

PostgreSQL supports full-text search through facilities such as tsvector and tsquery. Applications can combine those results with pgvector similarity search. For example, a knowledge assistant searching for a specific incident number may benefit from exact text matching, while a broader troubleshooting question may benefit from semantic retrieval.

Ranked results can be combined using techniques such as reciprocal rank fusion, which merges two ranked lists by position, then optionally reranked using another relevance model. However, hybrid search does not guarantee better retrieval in every application. Teams should evaluate representative questions, expected documents and final ranking quality.

Sources: PostgreSQL full-text search and pgvector hybrid search.

When does a separate vector database become useful?

A dedicated vector system may become worthwhile when an application’s retrieval requirements exceed what its existing PostgreSQL environment can support effectively. Examples include independently scaling vector-search traffic, specialized distributed indexing, very large search collections or retrieval features that are unavailable in the chosen PostgreSQL deployment.

But moving embeddings to another system creates additional responsibilities.

Consider a document update. The application changes the source document in PostgreSQL. It must also regenerate affected embeddings and update the vector index. Until synchronization finishes, searches may retrieve outdated content.

Deletion creates a related problem. Removing a document from the transactional database must also remove or invalidate its vector representations.

Permission changes are particularly important. If a user’s access is revoked, stale access metadata in another search system must not allow restricted content to reach the model.

An architecture with two data stores therefore needs a reliable way to propagate changes, handle failures, retry safely and determine when search data is current. Change-data capture, which streams changes out of the database, transactional outbox patterns, which record the change event in the same transaction as the data, and event processing can help, but each requires implementation and operational ownership. The authoritative permission check should remain enforceable even when the search index is delayed.

These synchronization boundaries are part of the cost of adopting a separate vector system.

Embedding models introduce another migration boundary

An embedding is generated using a particular model and representation. Changing the embedding model may change vector dimensions, distributions and similarity behavior. Embeddings produced by incompatible models should not be combined as though their distances were directly comparable.

Organizations should record embedding-model identifiers, versions and relevant generation settings. A model migration may require generating new embeddings, rebuilding indexes and evaluating retrieval quality before switching production queries. During a transition, old and new representations may need to coexist.

pgvector also has indexing limits that depend on the representation. Its documented HNSW support includes vector values up to 2,000 dimensions and halfvec values up to 4,000 dimensions. These limits concern the relevant index representation, not a universal restriction on every possible storage or search strategy. The application’s embedding-model choice therefore affects index design.

Source: pgvector, Vector Types and Indexing Limits.

How should a team choose?

A useful evaluation compares the existing PostgreSQL approach with a separate vector system using the same representative workload.

Evaluation area Question to answer
Retrieval quality Are expected relevant passages consistently found?
Authorization Can unauthorized documents ever reach the model context?
Performance Does search latency meet the target under realistic concurrency?
Filtering Do selective tenant and metadata conditions preserve acceptable recall?
Updates and deletions How quickly does the search index reflect source changes?
Operations What are the indexing, backup, monitoring and recovery requirements?
Scaling Can retrieval demand grow without harming transactional workloads?
Cost What is the combined infrastructure and maintenance expense?

The comparison should not assume that the most specialized technology is automatically the most suitable. A small or moderately sized application may find that PostgreSQL with pgvector meets its needs with fewer systems to manage. A larger application may justify an independent search tier when workload isolation, specialized features or independent scaling delivers measurable benefits. Those outcomes are workload-dependent and should be established through tests, not generic database-size thresholds.

Operations also include keeping the extension patched. The pgvector changelog records fixes for possible index corruption during HNSW vacuuming in version 0.8.3 on June 17, 2026, and for buffer overflows during IVFFlat index builds in versions 0.8.6 on July 29 (on 32-bit systems) and 0.8.7 on October 1, 2026. Teams should run a current patch release and test index maintenance, such as vacuuming and rebuilds, before relying on an index in production.

Source: pgvector, Changelog.

What the architecture decision comes down to

PostgreSQL and pgvector allow application records, embeddings, metadata and text search to remain within one database environment. This can simplify AI applications that already depend heavily on relational data. A separate vector system may provide valuable capabilities, but requires attention to synchronization, deletions, authorization and operational ownership.

Neither architecture automatically guarantees search relevance or secure retrieval.

Start with verified retrieval and access-control requirements. Use PostgreSQL with pgvector when it meets them effectively, and introduce a separate vector system when measurements justify the additional complexity.

References and further reading

  1. pgvector, Official Repository. Supported vector types, similarity search, indexing, filtering and multitenancy.
  2. pgvector, Changelog. Version history, iterative index scans and patch releases.
  3. PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies. Database authorization behavior and bypass conditions.
  4. PostgreSQL, Full Text Search. Keyword retrieval and ranking.
  5. PostgreSQL, Full Text Search Introduction. The tsvector and tsquery types.
  6. PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN. Execution-plan inspection and performance evaluation.
  7. pgvector, Release and Security History. Extension releases and maintenance updates.

Sources verified November 6, 2026. pgvector releases often, and the 0.8.7 release on October 1, 2026 fixed an IVFFlat index build bug and is not presented as introducing the architectural capabilities discussed here, so check the sources above before you act. Performance and architecture guidance are analytical recommendations, not independent TechiesJournal benchmark results.

title: Building a Production-Grade Streaming AI-Agent Chat Workspace with Shadcn UI & React
description:
Most AI chat tutorials stop at a basic <input> box and a unstyled <div> list. When you ship a real AI-Agent Workspace to production, users immediately expect multi-thread conversation history, smart auto-scrolling that doesn't hijack manual reading, syntax-highlighted markdown blocks with one-click copy hooks, and clean attachment trays.

Here is the core frontend architecture pattern to keep a React + TypeScript + Shadcn UI streaming chat interface responsive at 60fps.

1. Non-Intrusive Auto-Scroll During Token Streaming

When an LLM streams tokens rapidly, forcing scrollIntoView() on every chunk locks the user out of scrolling up to read earlier paragraphs. Track whether the user is near the bottom before auto-scrolling:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

export function useSmartChatScroll(dependency: unknown) {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const [shouldAutoScroll, setShouldAutoScroll] = useState(true);

  const handleScroll = () => {
    const el = containerRef.current;
    if (!el) return;
    const distanceFromBottom = el.scrollHeight - el.scrollTop - el.clientHeight;
    setShouldAutoScroll(distanceFromBottom < 80);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    if (shouldAutoScroll && containerRef.current) {
      containerRef.current.scrollTop = containerRef.current.scrollHeight;
    }
  }, [dependency, shouldAutoScroll]);

  return { containerRef, handleScroll };
}

2. Memoizing Message Bubbles to Prevent Re-Render Lag

During active streaming, only the last message in the array changes on each token. Wrap completed message components in React.memo so React doesn't re-parse heavy markdown syntax across 50 historical messages every 20 milliseconds.

3. Collapsible Multi-Thread Sidebar & Dark-Mode Tokens

Using Shadcn UI CSS variables (--background, --card, --muted, --border) paired with a collapsible drawer keeps desktop workspaces spacious while adapting cleanly to mobile viewports without layout shift.

⚡ Skip the UI Boilerplate

title: Measuring PR Cognitive Load with Deterministic Python AST Heuristics
description:
AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect—most engineering teams rely on coding assistants daily to accelerate boilerplate, test scaffolding, and migrations.

The real architectural bottleneck is review throughput versus generation velocity. When pull requests grow from 150 lines to 1,200+ lines, human reviewers hit cognitive fatigue. Two failure modes tend to slip past fatigued code reviews:

  1. Loss of Cognitive Ownership: Deeply nested control flow, redundant defensive wrappers, or silent exception swallowing (except Exception: pass) that compile cleanly and pass happy-path tests while obscuring failure states.
  2. Unverified Dependency Surface: Unfamiliar or hallucinated package imports introduced during rapid iteration without supply-chain verification.

Rather than relying on probabilistic "AI text detectors" (which are noisy and largely irrelevant to production reliability), teams get far higher signal from deterministic AST heuristics wired directly into PR triage.

Minimal AST Heuristics in Pure Python (stdlib)

Using Python's built-in ast module, we can flag review-friction hotspots in milliseconds before a human reviewer even opens the diff:

import ast

class ReviewFrictionVisitor(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.max_depth = 0
        self._depth = 0
        self.silent_broad_excepts = 0

    def _enter_branch(self, node):
        self._depth += 1
        self.max_depth = max(self.max_depth, self._depth)
        self.generic_visit(node)
        self._depth -= 1

    visit_If = visit_For = visit_While = _enter_branch
    visit_Try = _enter_branch

    def visit_ExceptHandler(self, node):
        is_broad = node.type is None or (
            isinstance(node.type, ast.Name) and node.type.id == "Exception"
        )
        if is_broad and len(node.body) == 1 and isinstance(node.body[0], ast.Pass):
            self.silent_broad_excepts += 1
        self.generic_visit(node)

Why Deterministic Structural Signals Beat Authorship Guessing

For Engineering Leads, CISOs, and Staff Reviewers, who (or what) typed a function matters much less than how expensive it will be to debug at 3 AM:

  • Control-flow nesting depth > 5 correlates strongly with missed edge cases during code review.
  • Silent broad except blocks mask upstream timeouts and schema drift.
  • Dependency delta gates force explicit justification whenever a PR adds a package outside the organization's verified lockfile baseline.

I put together a small zero-dependency reference snippet here if you want to experiment with custom AST checks in CI: evan-mercer-dev/ast-review-signals.

How is your team adapting PR review gates as commit volume scales up? Curious what deterministic checks have given you the highest signal-to-noise ratio.

title: Namespace vs GitHub hosted runners, and the unit minute
description:
Namespace vs GitHub hosted runners is awkward to compare because Namespace does not sell runner minutes: it sells unit minutes, where one unit is 1 vCPU with 2 GB of RAM for a minute, times a platform multiplier. Convert it and a 2 vCPU Linux runner is $0.002 a minute prepaid against GitHub's $0.006, on 4 GB of RAM rather than 8, which is the caveat that decides most of this page.


10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month, at rates read 20 September 2026. On the shape that matches GitHub on memory the month is 160,000 unit minutes and $190; on the 4 GB shape it is 140,000 and $160.

GitHub-hosted runners need no explanation and no account: an included allowance of $12 to $300 of compute a month by plan (2,000 to 50,000 standard Linux minutes), a standard private-repo Linux runner of 2 vCPU, 8 GB and 14 GB of disk, every platform GitHub sells, and free unlimited use on public repositories at 4 vCPU and 16 GB.

Namespace sells compute across devboxes, Docker builds and GitHub Actions runners from one meter. You pick a shape through a label such as nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16, and the bill is vCPU count times minutes times a platform multiplier of 1 for Linux, 2 for Windows, 10 for macOS and 7 for Linux on Apple silicon. Rates come in two columns, prepaid inside a plan and about 50% higher as overage outside it.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

GitHub-hosted Namespace Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD on a private repo; free on public repos) $0.002 prepaid, $0.003 overage (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM). The 2 vCPU with 8 GB shape is $0.004 prepaid $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner with 16 GB $0.004 prepaid at 4 vCPU and 8 GB; $0.008 prepaid at 4 vCPU and 16 GB $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier $12 of compute a month on Free, $18 on Pro and Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), private repos only A 30-day trial of the pay-as-you-go Developer plan; no standing monthly allowance 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute A one-minute minimum, then the following 15-second steps rounded down: its docs say 70 seconds bills as one minute Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on Apple silicon and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU Shapes from 1 vCPU up to 64 vCPU and 512 GB on amd64 and arm64; Windows; macOS on Apple silicon; Linux on Apple silicon in early access 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch Cache volumes attached by label, snapshots at $0.002/GB-hour with 5,000 GB-hours free on Team and 15,000 on Business, storage at $0.0048/GB-day Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store Docker builds are a separate meter: 1,000 included on Team and 2,500 on Business, $0.05 per build on Developer, $10 per 1,000 after that, with cross-invocation caching latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Denominated in vCPU, not jobs: 32 vCPU on Developer, 64 on Team, 160 on Business. macOS is 12, 24 and 48 vCPU Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Namespace Compute: AMD EPYC for amd64, AmpereOne or Apple silicon for arm64, M5 Max and M4 Pro for macOS Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself Not offered Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required None; this is the default Change runs-on to one nscloud label, plus companion labels for a cache volume A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

How to compute a Namespace bill

The formula Namespace publishes is vCPU count times minutes times the platform multiplier, and its own worked example is 4 vCPU for 5 minutes on Linux, which is 20 unit minutes. Shapes that are not the standard 1 vCPU to 2 GB ratio are charged on whichever is larger, cores or half the memory, so a 2 vCPU shape with 8 GB counts as 4 units rather than 2. That rule is the whole trick: memory is priced, it is just priced as cores.

Shape Unit minutes per minute Prepaid Overage GitHub-hosted equivalent
Linux 2 vCPU, 4 GB 2 $0.002 $0.003 $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB
Linux 2 vCPU, 8 GB 4 $0.004 $0.006 $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB
Linux 4 vCPU, 16 GB 8 $0.008 $0.012 $0.012 at 4 vCPU and 16 GB
Linux 8 vCPU, 32 GB 16 $0.016 $0.024 $0.022 at 8 vCPU and 32 GB
Windows 4 vCPU, 16 GB 16 (2x multiplier) $0.016 $0.024 $0.022 at 4 cores
macOS 6 vCPU, 14 GB 60 (10x multiplier) $0.06 $0.09 $0.062 on a 3 or 4 core runner

Line the shapes up by memory and the picture is less dramatic than the headline rate but still one-sided: at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, the machine GitHub actually gives you, Namespace prepaid is $0.004 against $0.006, a third cheaper rather than two thirds. At 4 vCPU and 16 GB it is $0.008 against $0.012, the same third. The two-thirds saving only exists if your jobs are genuinely happy on 4 GB of RAM, and a Java, Gradle or large Node build usually is not.

The other end of the table is where the multipliers bite. macOS costs 10 unit minutes per vCPU-minute, so a 6 vCPU macOS runner is $0.06 prepaid and $0.09 as overage against GitHub's $0.062, which means Namespace is cheaper on macOS only while you stay inside a plan. Windows doubles the same way. The cheap Linux rate tells you nothing about either.

The rounding difference nobody prices

GitHub rounds every job up to the nearest whole minute. Namespace applies a one-minute minimum and then rounds the following 15-second steps down, and its documentation gives the example that 70 seconds of usage is one billable minute. On a single job that is noise; on a matrix it is not.

Take 40 jobs that each finish in 70 seconds, which is 46.7 minutes of real work. GitHub bills 80 minutes, because every job rounds from 1 minute 10 seconds to 2, and at $0.006 that is $0.48. Namespace bills 40 minutes, one per job, and a 2 vCPU 4 GB shape is 2 unit minutes each, so 80 unit minutes at $0.001 prepaid is $0.08. Most of that $0.40 gap is the rate: billing the same 80 minutes at $0.002 would be $0.16. The remaining $0.08, a fifth of the gap, is rounding, and rounding is the part you cannot optimize away by buying a smaller runner.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, priced three ways

The usual workload, 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month on a private repository. For Namespace the arithmetic runs in unit minutes, and the shape decides it: matched to the machine GitHub gives you, a 2 vCPU runner with 8 GB is 4 units a minute and the Linux half is 40,000 unit minutes; the 4 GB shape is 2 units a minute and 20,000. The macOS half is 2,000 times 60 units either way, and the $100 Team plan covers the first 100,000 unit minutes.

10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
GitHub-hosted $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min $184
Namespace on Team, 2 vCPU and 8 GB 40,000 unit minutes 120,000 unit minutes $190: the $100 plan plus 60,000 overage unit minutes at $0.0015
Namespace on Team, 2 vCPU and 4 GB 20,000 unit minutes 120,000 unit minutes $160: the $100 plan plus 40,000 overage unit minutes at $0.0015
Latchkey $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

On the machine that matches GitHub's, Namespace is $190 against $184, so on this particular mix it is six dollars dearer rather than cheaper, and the cheaper row underneath it buys half the memory. What moves the total is macOS: 120,000 of those unit minutes are 2,000 macOS minutes at a 10x multiplier, which swamps a Linux rate that is a third lower. Note also what the $100 buys. It is not a fee on top of the compute, it is the compute, so the comparison holds only if you would actually use 100,000 unit minutes; a team that burns 30,000 pays $100 for 30,000. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

What GitHub-hosted still wins on

  • Public repositories, where standard runners are free and unlimited on a 4 vCPU and 16 GB machine.
  • An included allowance with no plan decision: $12 of compute on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), and no commitment to reach the best rate.
  • Memory per core. GitHub pairs 4 GB with each vCPU on its standard Linux runner; Namespace standard shapes pair 2 GB, and you buy cores to get memory.
  • A concurrency limit you can reason about. GitHub counts jobs, 20 to 500 by plan; Namespace counts vCPU, 32 on Developer and 64 on Team, so one 32 vCPU job can consume the whole Developer allowance.
  • Job duration. GitHub allows 6 hours per job; Namespace publishes a maximum instance duration of 3 hours on Developer and 5 on Team, rising to 24 on Business.
  • One vendor, one bill, one status page, and the reference images every action in the marketplace is tested against.

Switching: the exact diff

Namespace is a label change like everything else in this category, with one rule to remember: only one nscloud label is allowed in runs-on, and cache volumes arrive as companion labels rather than as inputs on a step. That makes the diff slightly longer than the usual one-liner and still nothing like a migration.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-4x8

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on:
+      - nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16-with-cache
+      - nscloud-cache-tag-my-repository
+      - nscloud-cache-size-50gb

The verdict

Namespace is genuinely cheaper than GitHub-hosted on private-repo Linux, by a third at matched memory and by two thirds if your jobs fit in 4 GB, and its billing rounds in your favor where GitHub rounds against you. A cheap Linux rate is not the same as a cheap month, though: the worked example above, on the matched 8 GB shape, lands at $190 against GitHub's $184, because 2,000 macOS minutes at a 10x multiplier are most of the bill. The price of that is a model you have to do arithmetic in, a plan you have to commit to for the prepaid rate, and two ceilings that GitHub states differently: concurrency measured in vCPU rather than jobs, and a maximum instance duration of 3 hours on the entry plan against GitHub's 6. On public repositories the comparison does not start, because free and unlimited on a bigger machine beats every rate on this page. Neither vendor does anything about a job that fails for a mechanical reason, which is the line item both rate cards leave out.

FAQ

How much does Namespace cost per minute?

There is no single per-minute price, because Namespace bills unit minutes: one unit is 1 vCPU plus 2 GB of RAM for a minute, at $0.001 prepaid or $0.0015 as overage on Linux. A 2 vCPU shape with 4 GB is therefore $0.002 a minute prepaid, a 2 vCPU shape with 8 GB is $0.004, and a 4 vCPU shape with 16 GB is $0.008. Windows consumes units at 2x and macOS at 10x.

Is Namespace cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners?

On private repositories, yes, at every Linux shape: $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, $0.008 against $0.012 at 4 vCPU and 16 GB, and $0.016 against $0.022 at 8 vCPU. On public repositories no, because standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited there. On macOS it depends on the plan: $0.06 prepaid beats GitHub's $0.062, and the $0.09 overage rate does not.

What is a unit minute?

One unit is 1 vCPU and 2 GB of RAM running for one minute, multiplied by a platform factor of 1 for Linux, 2 for Windows, 10 for macOS and 7 for Linux on Apple silicon. Shapes with more memory than the standard ratio are charged on half their memory instead of their cores, so 8 vCPU with 32 GB counts as 16 units a minute rather than 8. Namespace's own example is 4 vCPU for 5 minutes on Linux, which is 20 unit minutes.

What are the Namespace runner labels?

The machine label is nscloud-{os}-{arch}-{shape}, for example nscloud-ubuntu-24.04-amd64-8x16 for 8 vCPU and 16 GB, and only one nscloud label is allowed in runs-on. Cache volumes are added with a -with-cache suffix plus companion labels naming the cache tag and its size in gigabytes, which is also how you keep two repositories from sharing one volume by accident.

References

  • Namespace pricing: unit minutes, shapes, plans and concurrency
  • Namespace runner labels, shapes and cache volumes
  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates by runner
  • GitHub-hosted runner specifications
  • GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency

title: Making a browser game for kids? The five things a parent checks in the first minute
description:
For developers of small web games aimed at children: what a parent looks for before letting a child play, and what that means for how you build and list your game.

Short answer: Parents searching "free online games for kids no download" have already solved the download part. What they check next is whether the game has chat, asks for an account, shows ads, has an in-game shop, and whether it is the right kind of game at all. If your game answers those five questions on its own page, in plain words, it is much easier to say yes to.

This comes from writing a parents' guide for SlowDen, a free browser-game site. Its Kids Games shelf holds the 16 games (counted 15 November 2026) whose own studios tagged them for children, with Horror and Shooting left out. SlowDen did not make those games, and it does not age-rate games. Below is what writing that guide taught me about the developer side.

1. Is there chat?

This is the first question, and usually the deciding one. If your game has no chat, say so on the page. If it has online multiplayer, say whether players can message each other, and how.

Every game I picked for the guide is single-player or pass-and-play on one device, like Ludo Legend (pass one device between turns). Games on the same kids shelf with online battles were left out, not because they are bad, but because a parent cannot tell from the listing what happens in them.

2. Does it ask for an account?

A browser game that opens without a sign-up passes this instantly. If you need saves, consider local storage first. If you do ask for a login, explain why on the page before the form appears.

3. Are there ads, and who chooses them?

Free web games are usually paid for by ads, and parents know it. What worries them is not knowing what the ad will be. On SlowDen, partner games run inside Playgama's player and Playgama serves its own ads there, which SlowDen does not choose; the Safety page says exactly that. If you control your own ads, say what you allow.

4. Is there a shop, and is it real money?

In-game coins, shops and daily rewards are common even in calm games. Burger Restaurant Simulator 3D has a shop key and a daily-reward key in its own controls list, and Obby: Climb and Slide lets you spend coins on floaties and pets. That is fine, as long as the listing says whether the currency can be bought with real money.

5. Is it the right kind of game?

This is where tags matter. A kids shelf built from studio tags is only as good as the tags. A game tagged "kids" whose description talks about weapons and explosives gets filtered out by a careful human, and a parent who finds it the hard way will not come back.

The games that were easiest to recommend described themselves plainly:

  • My Town Home: Family Playhouse calls itself a dollhouse you play rather than a game you win, and lists both mouse and finger controls.
  • TB World says nothing is timed or scored.
  • Animal Hair Salon explains its whole loop in one sentence: pick an animal, pick a tool, click the hair.

What should a developer put on the listing?

Question One line that answers it
Chat? "No chat or messaging." / "Online play, no text chat."
Account? "No sign-up. Progress is saved in your browser."
Ads? "Ads appear between levels."
Shop? "Coins are earned in play and cannot be bought."
Controls? "Mouse, or tap on a phone or tablet."

Five lines (examples, adjust them to what your game really does). They cost nothing and they answer the exact questions a parent is asking.

Common questions

Do I need an age rating for a browser game? SlowDen does not issue or require one. Describing your content honestly does more for parents than a badge they cannot check.

Should I tag my game "kids" if adults play it too? Only if it suits children. Tags decide which shelf a game lands on, so a wrong tag puts it in front of the wrong audience.

Where can I submit a browser game for kids? SlowDen accepts finished browser games for review on its submit page, free. Being listed is not a guarantee of traffic.

From the SlowDen blog. SlowDen (slowden.com) is a free browser-game site; the games mentioned are made by the studios named on their pages, not by SlowDen.

title: The Security Bugs That Look Fine in Code Review
description:
I recently finished 41 secure-coding labs across TypeScript, Java and C#. The biggest lesson was not about exotic exploits. The bugs that cause real damage usually look like perfectly reasonable code, and they pass review because every line makes sense on its own.
Here are five patterns that stood out, each with the one-line habit that prevents it. The examples use TypeScript and NestJS, but the ideas apply everywhere.

  1. Checking who you are, but not whose data it is Authentication answers "who is this?" Authorization answers "can they touch this object?" Many APIs do the first and forget the second. This is the classic broken object-level authorization (IDOR) bug. // Looks fine, but any logged-in user can read any invoice return this.invoices.findOne({ where: { id } });

// Scope the query to the owner
return this.invoices.findOne({ where: { id, ownerId: user.id } });
Habit: every query that loads something by ID should also be scoped to the caller, or go through an explicit permission check.

  1. Trusting a token because it "verifies" A token that passes signature verification is not automatically a token you should accept. Pin the algorithm, the issuer and the audience, and check expiry. jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', audience: 'my-api', }); The same applies to identity headers set by a gateway. If your service trusts x-user-id, make sure nothing outside the gateway can set it. Habit: decide exactly what a valid token must contain, and reject everything else.
  2. Race conditions in business logic Imagine a voucher with a quota of one. Two requests arrive at the same moment, both read remaining = 1, and both succeed. Nothing was "hacked"; the logic simply was not atomic. // Read, check, then write: two requests can both pass the check const v = await repo.findOne({ where: { id } }); if (v.remaining > 0) { v.remaining--; await repo.save(v); }

// Let the database do the check and the write in one statement
const res = await db.query(
'UPDATE vouchers SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND remaining > 0',
[id],
);
if (res.rowCount === 0) throw new ConflictException('Quota exhausted');
Habit: anything involving money, quotas or inventory needs an atomic update or a transaction with the right isolation.

  1. Webhooks that can be replayed Verifying a webhook signature proves it came from the sender. It does not prove it is new. An attacker who captures one valid request can send it again. Check the signature, check the timestamp is recent, and store event IDs so each one is processed once. Habit: signature plus timestamp plus idempotency key. All three.
  2. Letting clients decide which fields to set Mass assignment happens when you pass a request body straight into your model and a client adds "role": "admin". In NestJS you can reject unknown fields globally: app.useGlobalPipes( new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }), ); Habit: define the fields a client may send, and drop or reject everything else. A small checklist Before I open a pull request now, I ask: • Is this query scoped to the caller? • Is every token or header I trust actually verified, and only for what it should prove? • Can two requests at once break this rule? • Could a captured request be replayed? • Can a client set a field it should not? Over to you Which of these have you seen in a real codebase? And what is the one security habit you wish you had learned earlier? I would love to hear it in the comments. I am a software engineer working with NestJS, TypeScript, Python and Soroban. You can find my work on GitHub at github.com/OthmanImam.

title: Replication Lag Is a Network Decision: Keeping Cross-Cloud Databases Honest
description:
Replication Lag Is a Network Decision: Keeping Cross-Cloud Databases Honest

A database replica in another cloud can report healthy while falling steadily behind. The link is up, bandwidth looks ample, no packet loss alarms are firing, and yet the lag counter climbs from two seconds to twenty to two hundred. When a failover is needed, that replica is not a copy. It is an older version of the truth, and the gap was created as much by network choices as by the database itself.

Replication across clouds rewards teams that design for lag explicitly, in seconds and in business terms, rather than treating it as a database setting that will look after itself.

1. Define lag in time and in consequences, not in bytes

Bytes behind is a misleading number. A megabyte of small updates can take longer to apply than a gigabyte of bulk inserts, depending on indexes, constraints, and row by row work on the replica. What matters to the application is time: how old is the newest transaction visible on the replica, and what breaks if that age grows?

Set three thresholds before any link is ordered. A normal threshold, where replica reads are safe. A degraded threshold, where replica reads are stopped or labelled stale and writes on the primary are watched closely. And a failover threshold, beyond which promoting the replica means accepting named data loss, and a named person must approve it. Writing those thresholds down while everyone is calm prevents the worst conversation in incident response: discovering during a failure that nobody agreed what lag was acceptable.

Measure lag at the replica, from the replica point of view, and graph it continuously. Averages hide the problem. The 95th percentile and the maximum in each hour are where the risk lives.

2. Bandwidth is rarely the bottleneck people expect

Teams often size a cross-cloud link by total replication volume per day, then discover peak behaviour is different. Replication is bursty. A batch job, a backfill, a checkpoint, or a deployment that touches many rows can send an hour of changes in five minutes. If the link, a VPN gateway, or a firewall in the path is sized for the average, the burst queues, latency rises, and the queue itself becomes lag that drains slowly long after the burst ends.

Size for the burst you cannot reschedule, and measure the whole path, not just the circuit. Gateways, stateful firewalls, and NAT devices in the path each have throughput and session limits that behave like bandwidth when they saturate. A link diagram that stops at the circuit edge misses the devices that actually throttle replication in production.

Latency matters in a quieter way. Synchronous or semi synchronous replication pays the round trip on every commit. Moving a primary and its replica further apart can add milliseconds that look trivial in a network report and are decisive for transaction throughput. For asynchronous replication, latency still sets how quickly a problem is even visible on the other side.

3. Give replication its own path, or at least its own protection

Replication traffic sharing a path with backups, analytics exports, and general internet egress will lose at the worst moment, because those other workloads are also bursty and often larger. Where a dedicated path is not justified, give replication explicit protection: a reserved share of bandwidth, a separate queue, or a traffic class that is not starved when bulk transfers run.

Separation also helps diagnosis. If replication, backup, and user traffic share one counter, a lag spike has three possible causes and no quick answer. Separate counters per traffic class turn an argument into a reading. The same applies to routing: know exactly which gateways and firewalls replication traverses, keep that list short, and alert when the path changes. A silent reroute through a smaller gateway can halve throughput without any device reporting down.

4. Match the write pattern to the link you actually have

Some lag is created on the primary. Long transactions hold changes invisible to replication until they commit, then release them all at once. Frequent small checkpoints, large unindexed updates on the replica side, and schema changes applied without a replication plan all show up first as network shaped symptoms.

Practical steps that help without heroics: keep long running transactions visible with an age alert, not just a count. Apply schema changes in a tested order that replication can follow. Pause or throttle known bulk jobs when lag crosses the degraded threshold, automatically if possible, rather than hoping the replica catches up while the job continues. And test the replica apply rate separately from the link rate. If the replica can only apply changes at half the speed the primary generates them at peak, no network upgrade will close the gap.

5. Decide in advance what the system does when lag grows

A replica falling behind should trigger behaviour, not just a notification. Useful responses, in order of increasing cost, include stopping stale reads, shedding non essential writes, throttling batch work, and preparing users for a possible failover with data loss. Each response should be tied to the thresholds from the first section, with an owner and a way to reverse it when lag recovers.

Recovery needs design too. When a link returns after an outage, the replica will try to catch up at full speed. That catch up burst can saturate the same path production traffic needs, and can overload the replica disk. Rate limit catch up where the database allows it, watch primary retention carefully, and make sure transaction logs cannot expire before the replica has consumed them. The most expensive version of this failure is a replica that fell so far behind during an outage that it must be rebuilt from scratch, extending the window with no usable copy at all.

6. Test lag under fault, not just under load

Load tests show whether replication keeps up on a good day. Fault tests show whether it degrades predictably: add latency, drop the primary path and force the backup, pause the link for thirty minutes, then restore it and time the catch up. Record three numbers from each test: peak lag, time to return below the normal threshold, and whether any automatic protection actually fired.

Those numbers belong in the failover runbook, next to the thresholds. A team that knows catch up after a thirty minute outage takes two hours can make an honest decision at minute ten. A team guessing will either wait too long or promote a stale replica too early.

Teams that run private multi-cloud connectivity as a managed estate tend to treat replication paths, thresholds, and catch up behaviour as part of the network design itself, not as an afterthought left to the database team alone. That is the approach taken by CloudVerg, where VergMesh handles multi-cloud networking and VergForge helps keep the surrounding platform consistent, so database copies in different clouds stay copies in practice, not just in the architecture diagram.

title: Why is my CI so expensive? A diagnostic
description:
Why is my CI so expensive is almost never a mystery once you know which of two meters moved: the rate you are paying per minute, or the number of minutes you are buying. This page names six shapes of GitHub Actions invoice, says what each one usually is, and gives the one check that confirms or clears it before you change any workflow.


The six causes sorted under the two meters they move. Rates and storage prices from docs.github.com, read on 21 September 2026.

A CI bill has exactly two inputs, and every cause below is one of them wearing a different hat. Either the work got more expensive per minute, which is a runner type or a runner size, or there is more work, which is triggers, retries or storage.

Work down the list in order. It is ordered by how much money each cause typically accounts for, not by how likely it is, and the first two together explain most invoices that doubled without anyone deploying anything unusual.

Start by asking which meter moved

Pull the usage report and group it by SKU. If one SKU grew, the rate moved: somebody added a macOS or Windows leg, or switched a job to a larger runner. If every SKU grew together, the volume moved: more triggers, more retries, or more branches. That single grouping saves an afternoon of guessing, and it is the only view that separates the two.

Then check the date the growth started against your own history. A bill that stepped on a specific day is a change somebody made; a bill that has been climbing for six months is your repository growing. The first has a commit behind it and the second does not, and they need entirely different answers.

What the invoice looks like What it usually is The check that settles it
Roughly ten times a Linux baseline macOS minutes Group the usage report by SKU and look for the macOS line
Stepped up on one specific day A larger runner was switched on Search the workflows for a size label, and check how fast it now spends the allowance
Climbs with the size of the team More pushes, no caching, no filters Count runs per week against merged pull requests per week
Minutes high, wall clock low A matrix of short jobs and per-minute rounding Compare billed minutes against summed job durations
A sizeable share of runs are retries Flaky or transient failures Count runs with run_attempt above 1
Grew without any minutes changing Artifact and cache storage Look for the storage SKUs rather than the Actions minutes SKU

SKU names and report fields from GitHub billing reports, read 21 September 2026.

Cause one: the machine, not the workload

A macOS minute is $0.062 and a standard Linux minute is $0.006, so one iOS job is worth ten of anything else on the invoice. Windows is $0.010, a gentler premium that is nonetheless two thirds more than Linux for work that frequently did not need Windows in the first place. If the macOS or Windows line is the tall one, the answer is not to make those jobs faster, it is to run fewer of them.

Larger runners are the version of this that appears overnight. They cost roughly double per doubling of cores, they spend a Team or Enterprise Cloud allowance at that higher rate, and they are billed on public repositories where standard runners are free. A single pull request that changed runs-on to a 16-core label can produce a step change in the bill with no other visible cause, and the allowance running out sooner at the same time makes the step look larger than the rate difference alone.

Confirm by reading the label, not by reading the workflow name. GitHub Actions larger runners pricing has every size and rate, and Windows runner cost prices the matrix leg most teams have forgotten they added.

Cause two: work you did not need to start

Workflows are triggered by pushes, not by relevance. A pull request that edits a README starts the same build as one rewriting the networking layer, and it bills the same. Push twice within five minutes and the first run keeps going, obsolete and fully charged, unless something cancels it.

These are volume causes, so they scale with the team rather than with the product, which is why they show up as a bill that climbs steadily rather than one that steps. The shape to look for is runs per week growing faster than merged pull requests per week.

The fixes are three lines of YAML and they are priced, against one worked month, in how to reduce GitHub Actions costs. This page deliberately does not repeat them, because a tactic list and a diagnostic are different documents and splitting one answer across two pages helps nobody.

Cause three: the same work, billed twice

A retry buys the same minutes again. If a meaningful share of your runs are second attempts, that share of the bill produced no additional information about your code, and it is the one cause on this page that no per-minute discount touches: a 30 percent cheaper runner applied to a pipeline that re-runs 15 percent of its jobs saves less than fixing the flakiness would.

Separate the two kinds before you act. A test that fails on real non-determinism is your code and needs a fix in the test. A job that failed on a registry timeout, a DNS failure or a lost runner is not your code at all, and those minutes are pure waste in both directions: you pay for the failure, you pay for the retry, and the pipeline sits red until a human presses a button.

Count it rather than estimating it. The command is in identifying high cost GitHub Actions workflows, and it is three lines.

Cause four: rounding, and cause five: storage

GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute. A twelve-leg matrix of 40-second jobs uses eight minutes of machine time and bills twelve, and the gap is invisible in every dashboard that reports duration. If your billed minutes are well above the sum of your job durations, rounding is the difference and the fix is fewer, longer jobs.

Storage is the cause that produces a bill with no minutes behind it at all. Artifacts and packages share an allowance and cost $0.25 per GB-month beyond it; Actions cache has its own 10 GB per repository and costs $0.07 per GB-month above that. Both accrue hourly, which is the part that catches people: deleting an artifact stops future charges and does not refund the hours already recorded.

A retention policy is usually the whole fix, and the default is generous: artifacts and logs are retained for 90 days unless you say otherwise. Cache and artifact storage cost works through the arithmetic and the retention change that lands on 1 October 2026.

Cause six: nothing changed, and that is the answer

Sometimes the bill is correct and the expectation was wrong. Included usage resets monthly, and since 28 October 2026 it is a dollar amount spent at each runner's rate rather than a minute count: $18 on Team buys 3,000 Linux minutes but only about 290 macOS minutes, so how far it goes depends on which runners spent it. A plan change, a new organisation, a change in how the allowance is counted, or a repository moving from public to private will all produce a step with no workflow change behind it.

Private is the big one. Standard runners are free and unlimited on public repositories, so a repository that goes private starts paying full rate for work that was genuinely free the week before, and nothing in the workflow files will show you why.

Once you know which of the six it is, the order of operations is the same every time: stop the work you did not need, then move the work that is on the wrong machine, then and only then argue about the rate. Running out of minutes covers what happens when the allowance goes rather than when the invoice grows.

FAQ

Why did my GitHub Actions bill suddenly double?

A step on a specific date is nearly always a runner change: a macOS or Windows leg added to a matrix, or a job moved to a larger runner. Larger runners double roughly per doubling of cores and spend the included allowance at that higher rate, so it runs out sooner and the step is bigger than the rate difference alone would suggest.

Why is my CI expensive when the jobs are short?

Per-minute rounding. Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute, so a wide matrix of 40-second jobs bills roughly a minute and a half for every minute it actually runs. Compare your billed minutes against the sum of your job durations; if there is a large gap, consolidating legs recovers most of it.

Can a cheaper runner fix an expensive CI bill?

It multiplies whatever is left after the other five causes, which makes it the last change rather than the first. It does nothing at all about re-runs, storage, or jobs that should never have started, and those three account for most invoices that surprised somebody.

My repository is public. Why am I being charged for Actions at all?

Standard runners are free on public repositories, but larger runners are always charged there, at their per-minute rate. Storage is the other possibility: artifacts and caches are billed by the GB-month regardless of what kind of repository produced them.

References

  • GitHub: Actions billing, allowances, rounding and storage accrual (verified 2026-11-12)
  • GitHub: Actions runner pricing, every per-minute rate by runner (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub billing reports: grouping usage by SKU, repository and workflow (verified 2026-09-21)
  • GitHub: dependency caching limits and the 7-day eviction policy (verified 2026-09-21)

title: Are You a CSS Developer or a CSS Expert? 9 Tests I Failed Styling a 12,400-Line Photo Editor
description:
Most developers can make a button blue, centre a div and copy a flexbox cheat sheet.

CSS experts know what happens when the browser disagrees with you: when the page flashes white before it turns dark, when a phone's address bar eats the bottom of your layout, when a "simple" gradient border refuses to follow rounded corners, and when your grey text looks elegant on your monitor and invisible in sunlight.

I found out which one I was while styling APIC, a free photo editor that runs entirely in your browser: edit, convert, compress, resize and remove backgrounds, with no sign-up. It is one HTML file of about 12,400 lines, and its whole look lives in just ~1,100 lines of CSS inside it. This post is about those 1,100 lines (and the HTML around them).

Every test below is a real decision or a real bug from that file. The code is trimmed for reading, but the ideas are exactly what ships. 👇

New here? Good. This post is written for you too. Every test has a plain English part first, then the code, then the "what is really going on" part. If you only read the plain English parts, you will still learn something true. If you are an expert, skip straight to the code and the last line of each test.

🧰 Five words you will see (read this once)

Word What it means, no jargon
Custom property (--bg) A variable for CSS. Define a colour once, use it everywhere with var(--bg).
Pseudo-element (::before) A free extra box the browser lets you attach to any element, with no extra HTML.
Stacking context A "layer fence". Things inside it can be ordered among themselves, but cannot escape it.
Viewport The part of the page you can currently see on screen.
Paint The moment the browser actually draws pixels on your screen.

📊 APIC's CSS by the numbers

These are counted straight from the file:

  • ~1,100 lines of CSS
  • 666 uses of var(--...): the whole design runs on variables
  • 33 @media queries
  • 20 uses of color-mix()
  • 12 @keyframes animations
  • 18 :focus-visible rules (keyboard users get a visible outline)
  • 8 prefers-reduced-motion: reduce guards (people who get dizzy from animation get less of it)
  • 20 <details> elements (accordions with no JavaScript)

Now the tests. Score yourself honestly.

Test 1: Does your dark site flash white before it turns dark?

In plain English. You choose "light mode", you reload the page, and for a split second the screen is dark before it switches. That flash is the browser drawing the page with the wrong colours, then fixing them. It looks cheap, and it hurts if you are in a dark room.

Why it happens. The browser paints as soon as it has your HTML and CSS. If the code that picks your theme runs after that, the first frame is already wrong.

The fix. Pick the theme in a tiny script in the <head>, so it runs before the first paint:

<head>
<script>
  // Runs before anything is drawn
  (function () {
    var mode = 'system';
    try {
      var m = localStorage.getItem('apic_theme');
      if (m === 'light' || m === 'dark' || m === 'system') mode = m;
    } catch (e) {}                       // storage can be blocked, so never trust it

    var t = mode === 'system'
      ? (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: light)').matches ? 'light' : 'dark')
      : mode;

    document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', t);
  })();
</script>

And the CSS only has to change a handful of variables:

:root {                                   /* dark is the default */
  --bg: #07070a;   --bg-2: #0d0d13;   --bg-3: #14141c;
  --line: rgba(150, 255, 210, .14);
  --text: #eef1f6; --text-muted: #8b8fa3;
}
html[data-theme="light"] {                /* light only overrides the values */
  --bg: #f2f3ee;   --bg-2: #e8e9e1;   --bg-3: #dcded2;
  --line: rgba(10, 40, 25, .14);
  --text: #0c0e0a; --text-muted: #5b5f52;
}
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }

APIC's light theme overrides 8 variables. The other 600+ places that use colours never needed to know a second theme exists.

Three small details separate "it works" from "it works every time":

  1. try/catch around localStorage. Private modes and strict settings can make it throw. A theme script that crashes leaves you with no theme at all.
  2. Three modes, not two: light, dark and system. "Follow my device" is a real choice, so it gets stored as one.
  3. The script is inline and in the head. A script loaded from a file, or placed at the bottom, runs too late. Being render-blocking is exactly what you want here.

Developer: toggles a class after the page loads.
Expert: decides the theme before the first pixel exists.

Test 2: Can one line make a see-through header that works in both themes?

In plain English. A sticky header that is slightly see-through, so content blurs underneath it as you scroll, looks premium. The trap: "slightly see-through" needs a colour with transparency, and you have two themes with two different background colours.

The old way: write rgba(7, 7, 10, .82) for dark, then write a second rgba(...) for light. Now you have two numbers to keep in sync forever.

The expert way: color-mix() takes the colour from your variable and mixes it with "nothing":

header.top {
  position: sticky; top: 0;
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--bg) 82%, transparent);  /* 82% bg, 18% see-through */
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);                                  /* blur what's behind it */
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line);
}

/* when you scroll, the border quietly turns slightly green */
header.top.scrolled {
  border-bottom-color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--green) 22%, var(--line));
}

Switch the theme and --bg changes, so the header changes with it. No second rule. APIC uses this trick 20 times: hover glows, drag-and-drop highlights, active buttons, the lot.

rgba() cannot do this, because it wants raw numbers, not "whatever --bg currently is". color-mix() works in all current major browsers.

Developer: copies a colour and lowers its alpha, twice.
Expert: derives colours from the tokens, so there is only one source of truth.

Test 3: Why does my glow lag, or vanish behind the wrong thing?

In plain English. APIC's main card has a soft rainbow glow behind it. When you open a photo, the glow fades out so the picture is easy to see. Simple idea. Two things can go wrong: the glow ends up in the wrong layer, and the animation stutters on cheap phones.

.studio {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;                    /* 1. build a layer fence around this card */
}
.studio::before {                        /* the glow is a free extra box */
  content: "";
  position: absolute; inset: -1px;
  z-index: -1;                           /* behind the card's content... */
  border-radius: inherit;
  background: var(--grad-brand);         /* green → cyan → pink */
  opacity: .28;
  filter: blur(18px);
  will-change: opacity, transform;
  transition: opacity .9s var(--ease-out), transform 1.1s var(--ease-out);
}
.studio.has-image::before {              /* JS adds .has-image; CSS does the animation */
  opacity: 0;
  transform: scale(.94);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .studio::before { transition: none; }  /* 3. respect people who opt out of motion */
}

1. isolation: isolate creates a stacking context, the "layer fence" from the glossary. Without it, z-index: -1 means "go behind whatever the page decides", and that can change when some ancestor gets a transform or opacity later. With the fence, it means "behind this card's content", always.

2. Only cheap properties animate. Fading (opacity) and moving or scaling (transform) are the two things browsers can usually animate on the GPU without re-measuring the page. The expensive part is the blur, and the blur never changes, so it is drawn once and then just faded. Animating box-shadow, width or filter itself would redo that work on every frame.

3. Reduced motion. Some people get dizzy or distracted by animation, and their system tells your site so. One @media line is the whole accommodation.

Notice who does what: JavaScript only flips a class (has-image). CSS owns every pixel of the animation. That split keeps both sides small.

Developer: animates box-shadow and wonders why it is janky.
Expert: animates only opacity and transform, and builds a fence first.

Test 4: Can you put a gradient on a rounded border?

In plain English. You want a thin rainbow outline around a rounded floating bar. Sounds like one line: border: 1px solid <gradient>. It is not. A border can only be a flat colour, and the tool made for fancy borders, border-image, ignores border-radius. Your corners come out square.

The trick: don't use a border at all. Draw a gradient box, then cut a hole in the middle, so only a 1px ring is left:

#apicDock::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute; inset: -1px;
  border-radius: inherit;               /* the ring follows the rounded corners */
  padding: 1px;                         /* 1px = the thickness of the ring */
  background: var(--grad-brand);
  opacity: .55;
  pointer-events: none;                 /* never block clicks on the real bar */

  -webkit-mask: linear-gradient(#000 0 0) content-box, linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
  -webkit-mask-composite: xor;          /* older browsers */
  mask: linear-gradient(#000 0 0) content-box exclude, linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
  mask-composite: exclude;              /* standard */
}

How to read it. A mask says "show the element only where the mask is solid". Here are two solid masks:

  • one covers the content box (the middle),
  • one covers the whole box.

exclude means "show where they don't overlap". The only place the two masks differ is the thin padding strip around the edge. That strip is your ring, and because the element itself has rounded corners, so does the ring.

APIC ships both the -webkit- version and the standard one, because older browsers only know the prefixed one.

Developer: gives up and uses a wrapper <div> with a gradient background and a smaller <div> on top.
Expert: subtracts one shape from another with a mask.

Test 5: How do you animate something to "gone", when display: none can't be animated?

In plain English. When you open a photo, APIC's tagline fades and slides up, and its space collapses so the editor moves up smoothly. When you close the photo, it comes back. You cannot animate display, and you cannot animate height: auto. So how?

.eyebrow {                                /* visible state */
  max-height: 40px;  overflow: hidden;
  opacity: 1;        transform: none;
  visibility: visible;
  transition: max-height .5s var(--ease-out),
              opacity .35s ease,
              transform .5s var(--ease-out),
              visibility 0s linear 0s;    /* flip to visible immediately */
}

body.studio-active .eyebrow {             /* hidden state */
  max-height: 0;
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(-12px);
  visibility: hidden;
  pointer-events: none;
  transition: max-height .5s var(--ease-out),
              opacity .35s ease,
              transform .5s var(--ease-out),
              visibility 0s linear .5s;   /* ...but wait .5s before hiding */
}

Two ideas hold this up:

  • max-height instead of height. Browsers can animate between two numbers (40px → 0px) but not between a number and auto. Pick a ceiling that is safely bigger than the content, and animate to it.
  • The delayed visibility flip. That last line is the expert part. visibility: hidden makes an element unclickable, unfocusable and invisible to screen readers, which is what you want eventually. But if it flipped instantly, the fade would never be seen. So when hiding, it waits .5s (the length of the animation) and then flips. When showing, it flips right away so the fade-in can be seen.

Without this, you get one of two bad endings: an invisible tagline that keyboard users can still tab into, or a tagline that vanishes with no animation at all.

Developer: display: none and a jump.
Expert: fades first, then removes it from the page's reach.

Test 6: Why does 100vh hide the bottom of my layout on a phone?
