In plain English. On a phone, the browser's address bar slides away as you scroll. 100vh means "the screen height with the bar hidden", so when the bar is showing, the bottom 60 or so pixels of your layout are tucked underneath it. Buttons you can't tap. That is not your imagination.

Modern CSS has three honest heights:

Unit Meaning
lvh the large viewport: bars hidden
svh the small viewport: bars showing, so it always fits
dvh the dynamic viewport: follows the bars live

APIC uses them on purpose. The photo area must never push the tools off screen, so it uses svh:

:root {
  --apic-header: 66px;
  /* Old browsers: vh. Photo is never smaller than 260px, never taller than 60% of the screen,
     and always leaves 330px for the title bar, tabs and first controls. */
  --apic-img-max: max(260px, min(60vh, calc(100vh - 330px - (var(--apic-header) - 62px))));
}
@supports (height: 100svh) {              /* Browsers that understand svh override it */
  :root {
    --apic-img-max: max(260px, min(60svh, calc(100svh - 330px - (var(--apic-header) - 62px))));
  }
}

body.studio-active .studio-wrap {
  min-height: calc(100vh  - var(--apic-header));   /* fallback */
  min-height: calc(100svh - var(--apic-header));   /* wins if understood */
}

Read max(260px, min(60svh, …)) as a sandwich: "at least 260px, at most 60% of the screen, and never so tall that the controls fall off." APIC's full-screen design studio (a position: fixed; inset: 0 overlay) is different: it should fill the screen exactly, and keep doing so as the bar slides in and out, so it uses dvh: #dsApp { height: 100vh; height: 100dvh; }.

The pattern is also worth stealing: write the old value first, then the new one on the next line. A browser that doesn't understand the second line ignores it. No JavaScript, no feature detection.

Developer: height: 100vh, tests on desktop, ships.
Expert: knows which of three heights each element actually means.

Test 7: Is a small screen the same thing as a finger?

In plain English. No. A small laptop window is small but has a precise mouse. An iPad is big but has a thumb. If your "mobile layout" is triggered by width, both get the wrong thing.

CSS can ask about the pointer instead:

@media (pointer: coarse) {                       /* "the main input is a finger" */
  html { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%; }
  .btn, .tool-btn, .quick-btn { min-height: 44px; }          /* finger-sized targets */
  select, input[type=number], input[type=text], textarea {
    font-size: 16px;                                         /* stops the iPhone zoom-in */
    min-height: 44px;
  }
  input[type=range] { min-height: 32px; }
}

/* the area you draw on with a finger or mouse */
#overlay.active {
  cursor: crosshair;
  touch-action: none;                  /* drawing must not scroll or zoom the page */
  -webkit-touch-callout: none;
  user-select: none;
}

Three small rules, three real problems:

  • 44px is the size Apple's guidelines recommend for a tappable thing. Smaller, and people hit the wrong button.
  • 16px inputs. On iPhone Safari, tapping a text field with a font smaller than 16px makes the whole page zoom in. Annoying, and it does not zoom back out on its own.
  • touch-action: none on the drawing layer. Without it, dragging your finger across a photo to erase a background scrolls the page instead. The browser has to be told "this area is mine".

Developer: @media (max-width: 600px) and hope.
Expert: designs for the input device, not the screen size.

Test 8: Is your "stylish" grey text actually readable?

In plain English. Dark themes love soft grey text. It looks calm in a design tool. Then someone opens your site outdoors, or is tired, or is 55, and the secondary text turns into fog.

You do not have to guess. Readability has a number: the contrast ratio. WCAG, the accessibility standard, asks for 4.5 or more for normal text (level AA), and 7 or more is the gold level (AAA). Here is the whole calculation, in 5 lines of JavaScript:

const lin = c => (c /= 255) <= 0.03928 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4;
const lum = hex => {
  const [r, g, b] = [1, 3, 5].map(i => lin(parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16)));
  return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b;      // how bright the eye sees it
};
const ratio = (a, b) => { const [x, y] = [lum(a), lum(b)].sort((p, q) => q - p); return (x + .05) / (y + .05); };

ratio('#8b8fa3', '#07070a');   // 6.28
ratio('#a3a9bd', '#07070a');   // 8.59

APIC's first dark theme used #8b8fa3 for muted text. That is already a pass. But a late "dark-mode legibility pass" lifted it anyway, and it started with one line of variables:

html:not([data-theme="light"]) {
  --text-muted: #a3a9bd;                 /* was #8b8fa3 */
  --line: rgba(160, 255, 220, .20);      /* was .14: borders you can actually see */
  --btn-text: #d9deec;
}
Muted text on Before After
page background #07070a 6.28 8.59
card #0d0d13 6.05 8.27
raised panel #14141c 5.72 7.82

That moves every one of them from "passes" to "gold level", with three variable changes, not 200 selector edits. This is the quiet payoff of Test 1: when your colours live in variables, an accessibility fix is a small diff.

(The bright green of the main buttons is easy: #39ff9d against the page is 15.3.)

Developer: "it looks fine on my monitor."
Expert: measures it, and fixes it where the colour is defined.

Test 9: How much can your HTML do before you write any JavaScript?

In plain English. CSS gets the glory, but a lot of "interactive" features are already built into HTML. Using them means fewer bugs, less code, and a page that works for people using keyboards and screen readers.

1. An accordion in four lines. APIC's FAQ and its advanced tool sections are 20 <details> elements:

<details class="faq-item">
  <summary>Is APIC really free?</summary>
  <p>Yes. APIC is a free online photo editor that runs in your browser…</p>
</details>

.faq-item summary:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--cyan); outline-offset: 2px; }

You get open and close, keyboard support (Tab, Enter, Space) and screen readers announcing "expanded" or "collapsed", for free. CSS only adds a focus outline so keyboard users can see where they are. That is the whole component.

2. Landmarks. The page uses <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section> ×7 and <footer> instead of a pile of <div>s. Screen reader users can jump straight to "main content". Search engines also understand the page's shape.

3. One honest security line. In the <head>:

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'">

It does two small things: no old-style plugins (object-src 'none'), and nobody can sneak in a <base> tag that redirects your relative links elsewhere (base-uri 'self'). It is a small policy and I will not pretend it is a full shield. Honest, narrow rules are better than a big one nobody maintains.

4. A page that explains itself to machines. A short block of JSON-LD in the head tells crawlers "this is a free photo-editing app, here is its feature list, here are the questions people ask". Plus Open Graph tags so a pasted link shows a proper preview card instead of a bare URL.

Developer: builds an accordion with divs, an onclick and an isOpen variable.
Expert: uses the element that already exists.

🎁 Bonus: a checkerboard with zero image files

When you open a transparent PNG in an image editor, you see the grey checkerboard behind it. APIC draws it with one declaration:

.has-alpha {
  background-image: repeating-conic-gradient(#8a8a8a 0% 25%, #5c5c5c 0% 50%);
  background-size: 18px 18px;
}

A conic gradient sweeps around a centre point like a clock hand. This one says "grey A for the first quarter turn, grey B for the second quarter, then repeat". Each stop starts at 0%, which is earlier than where the previous one ended, so the browser snaps it up to the previous stop, which gives hard edges instead of a blend. Four quarters make two light squares and two dark ones. Shrink it to an 18px tile, repeat it, and you have a checkerboard.

No PNG to download, no extra request, and it stays sharp on any screen.

😬 Two tests I still fail in APIC's own code

A post called "tests I failed" would be dishonest if it only covered the ones I fixed. I audited the shipping file for this article and found two:

Fail 1: smooth scrolling ignores reduced motion. The file has html { scroll-behavior: smooth; } and no matching opt-out. So someone who asked their device to minimise motion still gets animated scrolling on anchor links. The fix is to only turn it on for people who haven't asked otherwise:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  html { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
}

Fail 2: safe-area insets that do nothing. APIC writes bottom: calc(18px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)) for its back-to-top button, so it should clear the iPhone's home bar. But env(safe-area-inset-*) only returns real values if the page asks to draw edge to edge:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, viewport-fit=cover">

The file's viewport tag doesn't have viewport-fit=cover, so in that file those env() lines quietly resolve to their 0px fallback. The CSS half was written; the HTML half was missing. The lesson fits this whole series: a line of code that never errors can still never run.

🔍 Check my work in 60 seconds

Don't trust me, trust DevTools. Open APIC, press F12, then:

  1. Elements → <html>. Watch data-theme flip when you change the theme (Test 1).
  2. Styles panel → search isolation, mask-composite, color-mix. Every technique above is in there (Tests 2 to 4).
  3. Toolbar → device icon. Pick a phone, then look at the layout with the address bar showing (Test 6).
  4. Rendering tab → "Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion". Watch the glow animation switch off (Test 3).
  5. Pick any grey text → click the colour swatch. DevTools shows the contrast ratio for you (Test 8).

🏆 Your score

Tests you already knew You are…
0–3 A CSS developer. You build things that work. Pick one test above and recreate it from scratch. That is how this stuff sticks.
4–6 Solid. You have shipped real interfaces and met real browsers.
7–9 A CSS expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

And the part nobody puts in a score table: the experts in this post aren't people who memorised more properties. They're people who stopped asking "what does this line do?" and started asking "what will the browser do before, after and instead?"

Which test did you fail first? Mine is in the "Two tests I still fail" section, so you already know. Tell me yours below 👇 (and if you spot a mistake in my code, say so. That's the point of this series.)

Try APIC, and break it

Open APIC is free, runs in your browser, and (per its own description) processes images on your device rather than uploading them. Try the background remover, drag in a transparent PNG for the checkerboard, switch themes for Test 1, then open DevTools and hunt for every technique above.

Not just try it: break it too. I want feedback, because feedback is what makes the next version better.
Desktop version:
[APIC DESKTOP]🖥️💻
-----> https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/APIC/releases/download/APIC/APIC.zip

📢 remove.bg is shutting down on December 1. Here is a free alternative

If you use remove.bg, you have a deadline. The service has announced that its standalone website and self-serve API close on 1 December 2026 at 9:00 am CET. Background removal is moving into Canva, the developer API is moving to Leonardo.Ai, and unused pay-as-you-go credits expire the same day. (Always check remove.bg's own notice for the latest details.)

If what you actually need is "drop in a photo, get a transparent PNG", APIC does that for free, and everything you just read about is how it is built:

  • 🔒 Runs in your browser. The AI model runs on your own device using WebAssembly. Per APIC's own description, your photos are not uploaded to a server.
  • ⚡ Three model sizes. Lite (about 5 MB), Fast (about 44 MB) and Maximum (about 176 MB). The model downloads once, is cached on your device, and later runs start much faster.
  • 🆓 No paid tiers and no credits. There is nothing to run out of on December 1. You can edit without an account, and the site signs you in with Google only when you export.
  • 🧰 More than a remover. Resize, compress to a target file size, convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO and PDF, remove objects, social media size presets, and a batch studio for many images at once.

What APIC is not: it is a web tool, not an API and not a Photoshop plugin. If a script or a plugin depends on remove.bg, you need a developer replacement (remove.bg points API users to Leonardo.Ai). And no tool is perfect on every photo, so try your hardest images (hair, glass, fine edges) before you switch a real workflow.

Do these before December 1, whatever you choose:

  1. Use up any remove.bg credits. They do not roll over.
  2. Download your invoices and usage reports while the account still exists.
  3. Test APIC on 5 of your real photos. It takes two minutes: apic-online.vercel.app

title: Accept crypto payments in Python
description:
A minimal Moonvex integration in Python with Flask and requests: create a checkout, send the customer to the Moonvex page where they pick the coin and network, receive the webhook and verify its HMAC-SHA256 signature with the standard library. Works for any WSGI app.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET.

pip install flask requests

# environment variables on the server
export MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
export MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...

2. Create a checkout

POST /v1/payments with requests: Authorization: Bearer and Idempotency-Key in the headers; orderId, amount as a string and currency (USD, EUR, UAH, RUB or a coin) in the body. Without network the API creates a checkout and the customer picks the coin and network on the Moonvex page. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl (https only) is where the Back buttons lead. A 201 response returns an object with object: "checkout", id (inv_…) and paymentUrl.

# app.py
import os
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

import requests
from flask import Flask, abort, redirect

app = Flask(__name__)
API = "https://api.moonvex.org"


def db() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    conn = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn


def create_checkout(order_id: int, amount: str, attempt: int = 1) -> dict:
    r = requests.post(
        API + "/v1/payments",
        headers={
            "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY"],
            # a retry with the same key never creates a second checkout
            "Idempotency-Key": f"order-{order_id}-{attempt}",
        },
        json={
            "orderId": str(order_id),
            "amount": amount,
            "currency": "USD",  # no network: the customer picks the coin on the checkout page
            "description": f"Order #{order_id}",  # shown as “You are paying for”
            "returnUrl": f"https://shop.example.com/orders/{order_id}",  # the Back buttons
        },
        timeout=15,
    )
    checkout = r.json()
    if r.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(checkout["error"]["code"] + ": " + checkout["error"]["message"])
    return checkout  # {"object": "checkout", "id": "inv_…", "paymentUrl": …}


@app.post("/orders/<int:order_id>/pay")
def pay(order_id: int):
    with closing(db()) as conn:
        order = conn.execute("SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE id = ?", (order_id,)).fetchone()
    if order is None:
        abort(404)
    # total is stored as TEXT "25.00", so the amount is sent as a string
    checkout = create_checkout(order["id"], str(order["total"]))
    return redirect(checkout["paymentUrl"], code=303)

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook. In Flask: redirect(payment["paymentUrl"], code=303).

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. In Flask the raw body is request.get_data(), and hmac.compare_digest compares signatures in constant time.

# moonvex_signature.py
import hashlib
import hmac
import time


def verify_moonvex(raw: bytes, header: str, secret: str, tolerance: int = 300) -> bool:
    """Checks Moonvex-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, t + "." + raw)>"""
    parts = [p.split("=", 1) for p in (header or "").split(",") if "=" in p]
    t = next((v for k, v in parts if k == "t"), None)
    if t is None or not t.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(t)) > tolerance:
        return False
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), t.encode() + b"." + raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    # compare_digest is constant-time; during a secret rotation there are two v1 values
    return any(hmac.compare_digest(expected, v) for k, v in parts if k == "v1")

# app.py (continued)
import json

from flask import request

from moonvex_signature import verify_moonvex


@app.post("/moonvex/webhook")
def moonvex_webhook():
    raw = request.get_data()  # raw bytes, before JSON parsing
    if not verify_moonvex(raw, request.headers.get("Moonvex-Signature", ""), os.environ["MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]):
        return "bad signature", 400
    event = json.loads(raw)
    if event["type"] in ("payment.confirmed", "payment.overpaid"):
        mark_paid_once(event["id"], event["data"]["orderId"])
    # payment.cancelled also arrives when the customer switches coins: do not cancel the order on it
    return "", 200

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open. In SQLite that is INSERT OR IGNORE plus a cursor.rowcount check in one transaction.

# app.py (continued)
# CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);


def mark_paid_once(event_id: str, order_id: str) -> None:
    # the second "conn" is a transaction: commit on success, rollback on error
    with closing(db()) as conn, conn:
        cur = conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?)", (event_id,))
        if cur.rowcount == 1:  # first delivery of the event
            conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = ? AND status <> 'paid'", (int(order_id),))

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • Use request.get_data(), not request.json: the signature covers the original bytes and re-serialising changes them.
  • Keep amounts as Decimal or strings. 0.1 + 0.2 in float is not 0.3, and in payments that is an error in cents.
  • Always pass a timeout to requests.post; without it a hung request holds the worker forever.
  • verify_moonvex accepts every v1 value in the header, so a secret rotation causes no downtime.
  • Need one fixed coin instead of the customer's choice? Add network (and asset when currency is USD) to the same request, for example "network": "TRON", "asset": "USDT": that is the classic payment in one coin. The checkout above is the recommended flow.

FAQ

Is there an official Python SDK?

The official SDK is for Node.js (@moonvex/node). In Python requests or httpx is enough: the API is plain HTTPS with JSON, and signature verification is the dozen lines shown in this guide.

What if the customer does not pay in time?

The checkout is valid until expiresAt; the window is set with expiresInMinutes, 5 to 1440 minutes, 30 by default. If the customer started a payment and did not pay it in time, it moves to EXPIRED and you receive payment.expired. To let them try again, create a new checkout with a new Idempotency-Key (for example, bump the attempt number at the end of the key); if the API answers DUPLICATE_ORDER, that order number is closed, so use a new orderId such as 1001-2.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/python

title: Sephora API Example: A Price and Stock Check Tool for an AI Agent
description:
Ask an AI agent what Rare Beauty's Soft Pinch Liquid Blush costs at Sephora, and the first thing it sees is the search result: "listPrice": "$16.00 - $25.00". Which number goes in the answer? The $16 is a 3.2 mL mini. The $25 is the 7.5 mL full size. Per millilitre, the mini costs 50% more.

That is not a rare case. I asked the Sephora API 15 shopping questions, typed the way a shopper types them, and 11 of the 15 products came back with a range instead of a price. Search itself did well: the first result matched the product named in 15 of 15 questions. The trouble starts after that, when the agent has to pick a size, a shade and a store.

What I asked, and how

The questions were the plain kind: "dior lip glow oil", "tatcha water cream", "ysl libre perfume", "dyson airwrap", "olaplex no 3", and ten more across makeup, skincare, hair and fragrance. For each one I ran what an agent connected to the Sephora API would run, on 4 November 2026:

  1. /search-by-keyword with the question, 10 results.
  2. /product-details for the product the shopper meant, which lists every size and shade as a SKU.
  3. /product-availability for that product's default SKU, within 10 miles of one of five US cities (New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Houston, Seattle).

Over MCP, these are three tools: RapidAPI's gateway turns every endpoint of the API into one (how to connect it). So the raw responses below are exactly what a model would read. In all that was 116 search rows, 15 product records with 140 SKUs, and 204 store rows.

The search price is usually a range

Product Search says Default SKU Best value Smallest size pays
Rare Beauty Soft Pinch Blush $16.00 - $25.00 7.5 mL, $25 7.5 mL, $3.33/mL +50%
Drunk Elephant Protini $24.00 - $99.00 50 mL, $72 100 mL, $0.99/mL +62%
Glow Recipe Dew Drops $20.00 - $49.00 40 mL, $36 80 mL, $0.61/mL +118%
The Ordinary Niacinamide $6.00 - $10.80 30 mL, $6 60 mL, $0.18/mL +11%
Sol de Janeiro Bum Bum Cream $24.00 - $48.00 240 mL, $48 240 mL at $44, $0.18/mL +75%
Olaplex No.3PLUS $34.00 - $68.00 100 mL, $34 250 mL, $0.27/mL +25%
Tatcha The Water Cream $25.00 - $93.00 50 mL, $74 75 mL, $1.24/mL +34%
YSL Libre Eau de Parfum $38.00 - $225.00 90 mL, $185 100 mL, $1.40/mL +171%
Huda Beauty Easy Bake $24.00 - $42.00 2 x 6.5 g, $42 20 g, $2.00/g +100%

In 9 of the 11 ranges, the low end is the price of the smallest size. An agent that reports "from $24" for Drunk Elephant's Protini is quoting a 15 mL jar of a cream most people buy at 50 mL. An agent that reports the high end is often quoting the biggest bottle. Neither is what the shopper meant by "how much is it".

The product record does not settle it either. Each product has a default SKU (the currentSku in /product-details, the same SKU the search row points to for 13 of the 15), and it is often neither the cheapest nor the most common size. For YSL Libre it is the 90 mL bottle at $185. For Glow Recipe it is the 40 mL at $36, a size the search range never mentions.

Per millilitre or gram, the smallest size cost more in all 9 products with a real choice of sizes, a median of 62% more than the best-value size. YSL Libre is the extreme: the 10 mL spray works out at $3.80/mL, the best value is $1.40/mL. And that best value is not the biggest bottle. The 100 mL at $140 costs less than the 90 mL at $185, and it is the one SKU with isOnlineOnly: true. An agent comparing sizes by eye would miss it. An agent that computes price per mL finds it at once.

Shades and models have prices too

11 of the 15 products carried more than one list price across their SKUs. Sizes explain most of it, but not all. Laneige's Lip Sleeping Mask costs $24 in most flavours and $25 in three, two of them limited editions. Charlotte Tilbury's Matte Revolution costs $37, except in two shades at $39. So "how much is the Pillow Talk lipstick" has a right answer only after the agent resolves the shade to a SKU.

Dyson is the other kind of ambiguity. The search for "dyson airwrap" returned 7 different multi-stylers in the top 10, at $649, $699 and $749, plus attachments. The first one, the agent's natural pick, had isOutOfStock: true on its only SKU, and none of the 6 stores near Houston had it. A good answer there is a question back to the user: which Airwrap?

Store stock: read the units, not the label

Across the 204 store rows, 160 said "In Stock", 18 "Limited Stock" and 26 "Out of Stock". 14 of the 15 products were on a shelf somewhere near their city. Three details matter for an agent:

The label is not a unit count. 4 store rows said "In Stock" with exactly 1 unit on hand. 4 said "Limited Stock" with 5 or more, up to 21 for The Ordinary's serum in Houston. If the user is about to drive somewhere, inStoreAvailability is the number to pass on.

Some stores are inside Kohl's. 24 of the 204 rows were Sephora counters inside Kohl's stores (storeType is not SEPHORA), and 15 of them had the item. That is worth saying in the answer, because a shopper heading to "the Sephora in Jersey City" will not find a standalone store.

The search row's pickup flag says nothing about stores. pickupEligible was false on all 116 search rows, including the 14 products that were in stock nearby. It describes the search context, not shelves. Only /product-availability answers "can I pick it up today?"

The tool

None of this needs a model to reason about it. It needs a tool that does the arithmetic and hands the model a short answer: every size once with its price per mL or gram, the SKU for the shade the user named, and the nearest stores with units. Here is that tool, runnable as printed with a RapidAPI key:

"""A price and stock check tool for an AI agent, over the Sephora API on RapidAPI.

Three calls (search, product record, store stock) in, one small answer out: every size with
its price per mL or gram, the shade or size the shopper asked for, and the nearest stores
that have it.

    RAPIDAPI_KEY=... python3 sephora_price_check.py "rare beauty soft pinch liquid blush" Happy 40.758 -73.9855
"""
import json
import os
import re
import sys

import requests

HOST = "real-time-sephora-api.p.rapidapi.com"
BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST)


def headers():
    if "API_BASE" in os.environ:
        return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}"))
    return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def dollars(text):
    m = re.search(r"\$([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)", text or "")
    return float(m.group(1).replace(",", "")) if m else None


def amount(size):
    """'0.25 oz/ 7.5 mL' -> (7.5, 'mL'), '0.21 oz/6 g' -> (6.0, 'g'). None if neither is given."""
    m = re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*ml", size or "", re.I) or re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*g\b", size or "", re.I)
    if not m:
        return None
    return float(m.group(1)), "mL" if "ml" in m.group(0).lower() else "g"


def sku_row(k):
    price = dollars(k.get("salePrice")) or dollars(k.get("listPrice"))
    a = amount(k.get("size"))
    return {
        "sku": k["skuId"],
        "option": k.get("variationValue"),
        "size": (k.get("size") or "").strip() or None,
        "price_usd": price,
        "was_usd": dollars(k.get("listPrice")) if k.get("salePrice") else None,
        "per_unit": "%.2f/%s" % (price / a[0], a[1]) if a and price else None,
        "online_only": k.get("isOnlineOnly"),
        "sold_out_online": k.get("isOutOfStock"),
    }


def check_price(query, option=None, lat=None, lon=None):
    rows = get("/search-by-keyword", keyword=query, pageSize=10)
    full_size = [r for r in rows if not r["displayName"].lower().startswith("mini ")]
    if not full_size:
        return {"error": "no product found for %r" % query}
    product = full_size[0]
    details = get("/product-details", productId=product["productId"])

    skus, seen = [], set()
    for k in [details["currentSku"]] + details.get("regularChildSkus", []):
        if k["skuId"] not in seen:
            seen.add(k["skuId"])
            skus.append(sku_row(k))
    chosen = skus[0]  # the product's default SKU
    if option:
        chosen = next((s for s in skus if option.lower() in (s["option"] or "").lower()), chosen)

    # Many shades share a size and a price, spelled several ways: list each size and price once
    sizes = {}
    for s in skus:
        key = (amount(s["size"]) or s["size"], s["price_usd"])
        sizes.setdefault(key, dict(s, options=0))["options"] += 1
    answer = {
        "product": "%s %s" % (product["brandName"], product["displayName"]),
        "url": details.get("fullSiteProductUrl"),
        "chosen": chosen,
        "sizes": [{"size": v["size"], "price_usd": v["price_usd"], "per_unit": v["per_unit"],
                   "online_only": v["online_only"], "options": v["options"]} for v in sizes.values()],
    }
    if lat is not None:
        stock = get("/product-availability", skuId=chosen["sku"], latitude=lat, longitude=lon, radius=10)
        stores = stock["data"]["stores"]
        answer["stores"] = [{"store": x["displayName"], "miles": x["distance"], "units": x["inStoreAvailability"],
                             "status": x["availabilityStatus"], "inside_kohls": x["storeType"] != "SEPHORA"}
                            for x in stores if x["inStoreAvailability"] > 0][:5]
        answer["stores_checked"] = len(stores)
    return answer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    q = sys.argv[1]
    opt = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
    lat, lon = (float(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4])) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else (None, None)
    result = check_price(q, opt, lat, lon)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=1))
    print("answer: %d characters" % len(json.dumps(result, separators=(",", ":"))))

For the blush in the shade Happy, near Times Square, it chose SKU 2362085 (7.5 mL, $25, $3.33/mL), listed the two sizes once each (14 shades of the full size, 8 of the mini at $5.00/mL), and returned the five nearest stores with units, Times Square first with 97. The whole answer was 1,007 characters. The three raw responses behind it run to about 199,000 characters in my test calls (13,228 for the search, 129,780 for the product record, about 55,700 for the stores), roughly 49,700 tokens at four characters a token. That is an estimate, since every model's tokenizer differs, but the gap is the point.

To give it to Claude or another agent, wrap check_price as one tool with three inputs (query, option, and a location), in whatever framework you use, or as a tool of your own MCP server next to the gateway's endpoint tools.

Pitfalls in the data

Size strings are free text. Fenty's Gloss Bomb has 10 SKUs and 7 spellings of its size, among them 0.3 oz/ 9 mL, 0.30 oz, 0.3 oz/9 oz and 0.30 oz/9 g. Huda Beauty's powder has 7. Parse the mL or gram figure, and treat a size with neither as unknown. Four SKUs had no size at all.

Same size, different price. Sol de Janeiro's Bum Bum Cream has two 240 mL SKUs, at $48 and $44, and nothing in the size field says how they differ. Tatcha and Drunk Elephant list refills of the 50 mL at $68 and $63 next to the jars at $74 and $72; there the size says "Refill". Show the user both.

Minis live in two places. A mini is often both a SKU of the main product and a separate "Mini ..." product in search. 39 of the 116 search rows were minis or sets. The tool skips the "Mini" products in search and gets the mini sizes from the main record, so each size appears once.

Sales are rare and live in salePrice. Only 1 of the 116 search rows was on sale (a Charlotte Tilbury mini lipstick set, $26 down to $18.20). When salePrice is set, it is the price, and listPrice is the was-price.

The range and the record can disagree. For 14 of the 15 products, the search range matched the lowest and highest SKU prices exactly. For Laneige's mask, the range started at $23 while every SKU in the product record cost $24 or $25. Quote the record.

What I would do next

Add a size preference to the tool ("the usual size", "the best value", "travel size") so the agent can answer the question the user asked without asking back, and cache product records for a day, since prices change less often than stock.

The Sephora API is on RapidAPI with a free plan for testing. More examples are in the Sephora API repo on GitHub, and the Sephora API overview on LinkedIn covers what the data includes. Building a shopping agent on beauty data, or need the catalog as a dataset? Get in touch.

title: Why Is Your Encrypted RDS Instance Refusing Connection Requests?
description:
Why this matters: When you enable encryption at rest for Amazon RDS or Aurora using AWS KMS, the database instance relies on the KMS service to decrypt its storage volumes on the fly. If the IAM identity or the RDS service-linked role loses its cryptographic permissions, the database may enter an inaccessible state or fail to perform essential operations like snapshots or cross-region replication, leading to silent production failures.

Consider a hypothetical pipeline that utilizes an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. You have enforced encryption at rest using a Customer Managed Key (CMK). The infrastructure is deployed via Terraform, and you have strictly scoped IAM roles for the application services connecting to the database. Everything passes CI, but once deployed, the application encounters persistent "Access Denied" errors, and the database instance frequently reports performance degradation during automated snapshot intervals.

Symptoms

You observe the following in your monitoring tools:

  • Application logs report connection timed out or authentication failed errors, even though credentials are correct.
  • The RDS console displays a status of "Available," but attempts to create a manual snapshot fail with an AccessDeniedException.
  • CloudWatch Metrics show a spike in KMSKeyError or similar diagnostic events.

The false lead here is to assume a network or VPC security group issue. You might spend hours checking Security Groups or NACLs, only to find that the network path is perfectly clear. The culprit is almost always a mismatch between the KMS Key Policy and the IAM role permissions required to perform the kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey operations.


Photo by Victor Barrios on Unsplash

1. The KMS Key Policy is Too Restrictive

The most common failure pattern occurs when the KMS Key Policy does not explicitly grant the RDS service-linked role (or the specific IAM role interacting with the database) the necessary permissions to perform cryptographic operations.

How to confirm:
Check the Key Policy in the AWS KMS console or via the CLI:

aws kms get-key-policy \
    --key-id <your-kms-key-id> \
    --policy-name default

How to fix:
Ensure your Key Policy allows the RDS service to use the key. A standard policy block should look like this:

{
  "Sid": "AllowRDSUse",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "Service": "rds.amazonaws.com"
  },
  "Action": [
    "kms:Encrypt",
    "kms:Decrypt",
    "kms:ReEncrypt*",
    "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
    "kms:DescribeKey"
  ],
  "Resource": "*"
}

2. Missing Permissions for the IAM User/Role

Even if the Key Policy is open, your application or the user attempting to access the database must have an IAM policy that allows them to use the key.

How to confirm:
Check the IAM policy attached to the principal executing the connection:

aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
    --policy-source-arn <your-iam-role-arn> \
    --action-names kms:Decrypt kms:GenerateDataKey \
    --resource-arns <your-kms-key-arn>

How to fix:
Attach an inline or managed policy to the IAM role that allows the kms:Decrypt action for your specific key ARN. Avoid using Resource: "*".

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt",
        "kms:GenerateDataKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "<your-kms-key-arn>"
    }
  ]
}

3. KMS Key Scheduled for Deletion

If you recently performed a cleanup of "unused" keys, you might have inadvertently scheduled the key used by your RDS instance for deletion.

How to confirm:
Check the key status:

aws kms describe-key --key-id <your-kms-key-id>

Look for the KeyState field. If it is PendingDeletion, the database will lose access to the key material required to decrypt its storage.

How to fix:
Cancel the deletion immediately if the waiting period has not expired:

aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id <your-kms-key-id>

4. Cross-Account KMS Access Failures

In complex architectures, the RDS instance might reside in one account while the KMS key resides in a centralized security account. This requires a two-way trust: the KMS key policy must trust the RDS account, and the RDS account's IAM role must have permission to use the key.

How to confirm:
Check if the Key Policy allows access from the external account ID:

{
  "Sid": "AllowExternalAccountAccess",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::<external-account-id>:root"
  },
  "Action": "kms:*",
  "Resource": "*"
}

How to fix:
Update the Key Policy to include the ARN of the IAM role in the remote account, or the root user of that account, then ensure the remote IAM role has the corresponding policy described in point #2.


Photo by Shubham Dhage on Unsplash

Preventing it

  • Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Validation: Use tflint or checkov to scan your Terraform templates for overly permissive or missing KMS key policies before deployment.
  • Service-Linked Roles: Never attempt to manually modify or delete the AWSServiceRoleForRDS service-linked role. It is managed by AWS and required for RDS to interact with KMS.
  • CloudTrail Auditing: Set up an EventBridge rule to alert you whenever a kms:DisableKey or kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion event occurs.
  • IAM Access Analyzer: Enable IAM Access Analyzer to identify if your KMS key policies allow access from outside your account, which helps in identifying accidental misconfigurations in multi-account environments.

Clean up

If you created resources for testing, ensure you clean them up to avoid ongoing costs:

  1. Delete the RDS/Aurora instance: aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier <your-instance-id> --skip-final-snapshot (Use --final-db-snapshot-identifier if you wish to retain data).
  2. Disable/Delete the KMS Key: If the key is no longer needed, schedule its deletion: aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id <your-kms-key-id> --pending-window-in-days 7.
  3. Remove IAM Policies: Delete any temporary IAM roles or policies created for testing the access scenarios.

Cover photo by Kedibone Isaac Makhumisane on Unsplash.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and is intended for technical review and fact-checking before publication.

title: GitHub-hosted vs self-hosted vs managed runners
description:
The github hosted vs self hosted runners question has a third answer that did not exist when the question was first asked, and for most teams it is the right one: managed runners. Stay GitHub-hosted while your minutes fit the included allowance or your repositories are public, go self-hosted when you need hardware, network position or persistent state that nobody rents, and take managed runners for everything in between, which is most CI.


The same job under three models, with the published rates read 20 September 2026. The self-hosted column has no per-minute rate because GitHub charges nothing for it.

Every GitHub Actions job runs on a runner, and there are exactly three places that runner can come from: GitHub, you, or a vendor who operates it for you. That choice is the largest single lever on what CI costs and how much of your week it takes.

They are not a ladder you climb but three trades: GitHub-hosted trades money for zero setup, self-hosted trades your time for control, and managed runners trade a vendor relationship for most of the self-hosted economics without the pager. Plenty of mature teams run all three at once, because runner selection is per job.

Every rate and limit below was read from docs.github.com or the named vendor's own page on 20 September 2026, and GitHub's included allowance, now a dollar amount, was read again on 12 November 2026. The self-hosted column has no published per-minute rate, and says so rather than carrying a made-up figure.

Comparison

GitHub-hosted Self-hosted Managed (Latchkey shown)
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 on a private repo (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD); free and unlimited on public repos Not published, because GitHub does not charge for it: its billing page states Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners. You pay your cloud bill, including the idle minutes between jobs $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner; the free public-repo standard runner is already 4 vCPU and 16 GB Your instance rate. A 4 vCPU cloud VM is cheap per hour and expensive per idle hour, which is the whole economic argument $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier $12 of included compute a month on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006), private repos only; on Team and Enterprise Cloud larger runners can draw on it, and they are billed on public repos Unlimited from GitHub. Your cloud provider has opinions 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute Your cloud provider's, which is usually per second with a minimum, applied to instance uptime rather than job time Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on M-series and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU x64 and 64 vCPU arm64 Anything you can boot and install the runner agent on, including hardware nobody rents: GPUs, bare metal, an on-premises box next to the license dongle Varies by vendor. Latchkey is 2 to 16 vCPU on Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 only; Blacksmith and Depot add arm64, Windows and macOS
Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch actions/cache still goes to GitHub and keeps the same 10 GB limit, unless you run your own cache server. What you do get free is a warm local disk between jobs Vendor-provided and usually larger: Latchkey publishes no size and keeps entries 14 days, 25 GB per repo per week on Blacksmith, metered storage on Depot and Namespace
Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store Whatever you build. A persistent BuildKit cache on a long-lived host is the single best reason to self-host, and it is also the thing that fills the disk Vendor actions with a managed layer cache: latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, or Blacksmith's builder on a sticky disk
Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Your fleet size, and your autoscaler's reaction time. Unlimited in theory, queued in practice Not published by most vendors; Blacksmith states it imposes none. Latchkey sets 20, 40 or 80 busy runners per workspace by plan
Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Your infrastructure, your VPC, your network position. This is the reason most regulated teams are here The vendor's cloud, or your own account on the vendors that offer a bring-your-own-cloud mode
Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself None, and the runner host is now also yours to fix when it wedges, fills up or goes offline mid-job Latchkey diagnoses and retries transient failures inside the run; most managed vendors do not offer this
Setup change required None; this is the default Runner agents, an autoscaler, images, patching, secrets rotation, disk cleanup, plus a runs-on label A runs-on label change, and for some vendors a GitHub App install

GitHub-hosted: the default, and why it stops being free

The standard runner is the whole story. On a private repository it is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD; on a public repository the same ubuntu-latest label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. That asymmetry is why a workflow gets slower the week a repository is made private.

The bill arrives from two directions. Minutes are rounded up per job, so a matrix of forty 70-second jobs bills as 80 minutes rather than 46.7. And the included allowance is a dollar amount, deducted at each runner's per-minute rate, so a Team plan's $18 covers 3,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006 but only about 290 macOS minutes at $0.062.

The ceilings are the other half: 14 GB of disk is why no space left on device is so common, and 8 GB of RAM is why exit code 137 turns up on builds that were fine last quarter.

Self-hosted: cheap compute, expensive attention

GitHub charges nothing for self-hosted Actions usage; its billing page says so in as many words. What you pay instead is your cloud bill plus the part nobody costs in advance: the autoscaler that has to be right, the images that drift, the disk that fills because a persistent BuildKit cache is why you self-hosted, and the runner that goes offline halfway through a release.

The economics only work at high utilisation. A fleet sized for your worst hour is mostly idle for the other twenty-three, and idle bills. Ephemeral autoscaled runners fix that and reintroduce the cold start you were avoiding, in exchange for the strongest security posture of the three models, because nothing survives between jobs.

None of this argues against self-hosting. It argues for being honest about why. There are four good reasons: hardware nobody rents, a network position you need, a compliance answer that requires jobs inside your own account, and volume large enough that a flat cloud commitment beats any metered rate. "It is cheaper" is not one of them on its own, because it is only cheaper once you refuse to count your own time.

Managed runners: the model that did not exist for the original question

A managed runner vendor operates the fleet and sells you the minutes. To the workflow it is indistinguishable from GitHub-hosted: same actions, same secrets, same matrix, one different label. To the invoice it is closer to self-hosted, because you pay compute rates rather than platform rates.

The category is crowded enough to have shape. Blacksmith and Depot sell runners on their own hardware with arm64, Windows and macOS. Namespace sells shapes and cache volumes on a prepaid plan. RunsOn and the bring-your-own-cloud modes run the fleet inside your AWS account, a hybrid of this model and the last. Latchkey sells Linux x64 only and adds what none of the others do: diagnosing a transient failure and retrying it inside the run.

The honest cost of this model is vendor risk, and it is not theoretical: BuildJet shut down in March 2026 and Cirrus CI followed in June. The mitigation is the thing that makes adoption cheap. Because it is a label, leaving is a label.

Cost: the same month under all three models

Ten thousand Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus two thousand macOS minutes a month, on a private repository. The self-hosted row is the only one where the published price is not the price.

Linux compute macOS compute What else you pay Monthly total
GitHub-hosted $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min Nothing $184
Self-hosted Your instance rate for the hours the fleet is up, not the minutes jobs run Apple hardware or a licensed Mac cloud; the most expensive thing to self-host Autoscaler, images, patching, disk cleanup, and the pager Not publishable: it is your cloud bill plus your time
Managed (Latchkey) $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $5 to $49 a month for the plan, plus seats past the plan's own at $5 $149 plus the plan

The row that will not resolve to a number is the point of the table, not a gap in it. Self-hosted cost is dominated by utilisation and by engineering hours, and both of those are yours. Measure it rather than guess: the hours your fleet was up last month times your instance rate, plus the hours your team spent on it. Teams that do this honestly find the compute was the small half. Two things make self-hosting look better than that sounds: GitHub charges nothing for the Actions usage itself, and a warm disk with a persistent build cache is worth real minutes on a Docker-heavy pipeline. The managed row is gross too: its plan fee is separate from the compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off.

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. There is no honest ranking without running the same workload on all three, and the number everyone quotes is a vendor multiple measured on a workload the vendor chose.

What the published specifications do say: a standard private-repo GitHub-hosted runner is the smallest machine of the three at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, a self-hosted runner is as fast as whatever you buy and starts warm if it is long-lived, and managed vendors sell larger sizes at lower rates than GitHub's larger runners.

Reliability

Each model fails differently, and that is more useful than any uptime number. GitHub-hosted fails as an opaque platform incident you wait out. Self-hosted fails as your infrastructure: a full disk, a wedged agent, a runner that lost communication mid-job and took the run with it. Managed runners fail as a vendor incident, plus the risk the vendor leaves the market.

All three behave the same on a bad job: a registry timeout or an out-of-memory kill bills, and the re-run bills again. Self-hosting makes this worse rather than better, because host state joins your failure surface. To size that line item before you pick a model, count the runs in your Actions history that passed on a second attempt with no code change in between.

When to choose each

  • GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, when your minutes fit the included allowance, when your bill is mostly macOS (it is the cheapest macOS of the three), or when adding a vendor would mean redoing a compliance answer.
  • Self-hosted when you need hardware nobody rents, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs inside your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Budget the fleet as infrastructure, because that is what it is.
  • Managed when the answer to "why are we self-hosting" is only ever cost, when your Linux bill has outgrown the included allowance, or when you want larger machines without operating them. Check the vendor's OS coverage first: Latchkey is Linux x64 only, so a macOS or Windows job stays where it is.

Switching: the exact diff

Moving between GitHub-hosted and managed is one line per job. Moving to self-hosted is one line per job plus a fleet, which is the asymmetry the table cannot show.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: latchkey-medium      # managed: label only

   gpu-eval:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu]   # plus an agent, an image and an autoscaler

   ios:
     runs-on: macos-latest        # left alone: cheapest macOS of the three

The verdict

Stay on GitHub-hosted if your repositories are public or your minutes fit the allowance, because nothing paid competes with free and the default costs you no decision. Self-host when you have a reason that is not cost, which means hardware, network position, compliance or a persistent cache, and budget it as infrastructure with a person attached rather than as a saving. For everyone else, and that is most teams, managed runners are the model the original question did not have: self-hosted economics, no fleet, and a runs-on line you can revert in a minute if it disappoints. The caveats are real and worth saying out loud. Managed vendors leave the market, most of them cover only some operating systems, and none of the three models, on its own, does anything about the job that failed at 2am for a reason that had nothing to do with your code.

FAQ

When should you use self-hosted runners vs GitHub-hosted runners?

Self-host when you need something GitHub does not rent: GPUs or other specific hardware, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs in your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Stay GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, your minutes fit the allowance, or your bill is mostly macOS. Choosing self-hosted purely to save money usually means the ops time has not been counted.

Per minute charges for self hosted runners?

GitHub's billing page states that Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners, as read on 20 September 2026. What you pay is your cloud provider's instance rate for the whole time the fleet is up, not just the minutes jobs run, which is why utilisation rather than rate decides whether self-hosting is cheaper.

Which GitHub Actions services let you run jobs on faster hardware without self-hosting?

Managed runner vendors: Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, WarpBuild, Ubicloud, RunsOn and Latchkey, plus GitHub's own larger runners, which go to 96 vCPU on x64. All of them are adopted with a runs-on label change, and the vendors are typically cheaper per minute than GitHub's larger runners at the same size.

What hardware do GitHub-hosted runners actually give you?

On a private repository the standard Linux runner is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD. On a public repository the same label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. Windows matches Linux, and macOS on Apple silicon is 3 vCPU with 7 GB. The 14 GB of disk is the same on all of them, which is why disk-full failures appear on jobs with plenty of memory.

References

  • GitHub Actions billing, including self-hosted runners and cache allowance
  • GitHub Actions runner pricing: per-minute rates
  • GitHub-hosted runner specifications
  • GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency
  • Latchkey runner sizes and rates

title: Google pairs confidential TPU 8tx with AMD EPYC hosts instead of Axion
description:
Originally published on The Daily Flare.

Google announced on November 9 that its new TPU 8tx confidential-AI system will pair its accelerator with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host CPUs, rather than its Axion processor.

The announcement came six days before TechRadar published its analysis on November 15. The TPU 8tx uses the same accelerator silicon as Google’s TPU 8t, which is designed for training, but changes the host processor and network configuration for confidential workloads.

Google introduced the eighth-generation TPU 8t and TPU 8i in April 2026. The 8t targets large-scale model training, while the 8i is intended for inference, sampling and reasoning. Both systems use Google’s Arm-based Axion CPU as their host. The new 8tx configuration is designed for confidential inference and small-scale training, including work for regulated businesses and government customers.

Taiwanese outlet INSIDE reported that the 8tx retains the TPU 8t’s 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of high-bandwidth memory, while adopting the Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google says the revised system can deliver up to twice the 8t’s latency performance with a near-zero performance penalty. Those figures describe Google’s claims, not independently reported test results.

AMD says its EPYC processors coordinate workloads, prepare data and provide high-throughput communication with the TPU accelerators. They do not replace the TPUs’ AI processing role. The host-and-accelerator arrangement is central to the system’s confidential-computing design: AMD says its Secure Encrypted Virtualization technology works with the TPU environment to extend protections to connected accelerators.

In AMD’s description, the system checks an accelerator’s identity and security configuration before granting it direct access to protected memory. AMD says prompts, model weights and intermediate data remain encrypted in host memory and while moving between the host and accelerators, with hardware isolation during accelerator execution. Google described the system as “keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use.”

TechRadar pointed to Google’s existing confidential-computing support as a likely explanation for using EPYC rather than Axion. Google’s documentation lists Confidential VM configurations based on AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization and Intel Trust Domain Extensions. It does not list Axion-based C4A or N4A instances among those configurations, and states that TPUs cannot currently be attached to Confidential VMs.

That evidence suggests Google’s established confidential-computing trust chain is currently built around x86 processors. Axion, which Google unveiled in 2024 as its first data-center processor, is based on Arm’s Neoverse V2. Qualifying a separate Axion-based security stack would require establishing and reviewing that chain for a product whose purpose is to protect sensitive data in use. Google has not confirmed that this is why it chose EPYC, so the explanation remains an inference from its documented support.

AMD said Google security specialists have conducted deep reviews of its security-processor firmware. The company also said SEV already supports Google services including Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow. That existing use gives EPYC a role in extending Google’s confidential-computing offering to TPU workloads.

Google Cloud infrastructure chief Mark Lohmeyer told reporters that selected customers would be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers. The system is therefore intended to protect workloads not only in Google-operated facilities but also when customers run it in third-party locations. Hardware attestation, which checks a system’s identity and security state, is part of the mechanism for allowing model owners to place sensitive data and model weights on hardware operated elsewhere.

The host choice is also tied to the accelerator’s interface, according to ServeTheHome. It reported that Google selected AMD’s Turin-generation EPYC processors to match the TPU 8t’s PCIe Gen5 x16 connection; a newer PCIe Gen6 host would not provide additional bandwidth to the accelerator. The outlet also connected that choice to Google’s 2027 qualification schedule.

AMD cautions that its Infinity Guard security features vary by EPYC generation and processor series, and require enablement by a server manufacturer or cloud provider. The protections available in a particular 8tx deployment therefore depend on the configuration enabled by its provider.

title: Property Webhook Recovery with Queue Retries, Exponential Backoff, and Delayed Redrive
description:
Short answer: make recovery the design constraint: keep one delivery ID across every attempt, classify failures before retrying, use capped exponential backoff with jitter, and send exhausted work to a dead-letter queue that operators can inspect and redrive safely.

Consider a property-management SaaS sending a lease.payment_recorded webhook to an accounting integration. The useful data flow is event store to queue to delivery worker to recipient, with a delivery ledger recording each transition. A timeout leaves the sender with an uncomfortable fact: the recipient may have applied the payment even though the worker never saw the response. A queue retry policy controls when another request runs. It cannot, by itself, prevent that request from repeating the business effect.

That distinction drives the whole design.

What should a simple queue retry policy preserve for SaaS background jobs?

Start with the recovery record, not the delay formula. For each delivery, preserve the immutable event ID, tenant and property scope, destination, payload version, attempt number, first enqueue time, next eligible time, and final disposition. Keep credentials and sensitive request headers out of this record. The goal is to answer three operational questions without piecing together scattered logs: what should have happened, why did automated delivery stop, and can an operator replay it without creating a second payment entry?

The delivery ID is the anchor. Generate it once and send the same value as an idempotency key on every attempt, including manual redrive. For property prop_204, lease lease_881, and payment pay_7319, delivery whd_01JQ7K6N9M2A remains whd_01JQ7K6N9M2A on attempt two and on a later DLQ replay. Don't replace it with a new job ID when moving between queues. A new audit ID for the replay action is useful, but it is a different identifier with a different job.

There is a hard limit here. If the recipient neither honors an idempotency key nor provides a way to query whether it applied an event, the sender cannot guarantee one business effect after an ambiguous timeout. Local deduplication can stop the queue from processing the same completed delivery twice, but it cannot reverse an unknown remote side effect. In that situation, stick with documented at-least-once delivery and require the recipient to deduplicate by immutable event ID. This pattern is not suitable when the business operation must be exactly-once but the receiving contract offers no deduplication mechanism.

How should the worker choose between retrying and dead-lettering?

Recovery needs an explicit classification before it needs exponential backoff. A retryable result says another attempt may succeed later. A permanent result says more attempts will waste capacity or repeat an invalid request. Delivered means the recipient acknowledged the request according to the integration contract. Keep that protocol-specific mapping in the HTTP adapter rather than spreading status checks through queue code, because authentication rejection, payload rejection, rate limiting, and an ambiguous network outcome have different operational meanings.

Worker result Queue transition Operator meaning
Delivered Record delivery, then acknowledge No redrive is needed for this delivery ID
Retryable with budget remaining Record the next attempt, then schedule it Automated recovery is still active
Permanent or attempts exhausted Record the failure, then dead-letter Human review is required before redrive

This ordering prevents a poison message from spending the retry budget while healthy lease events wait behind it. It also makes the DLQ meaningful: entries arrive because automation made an explicit terminal decision, not because every error followed the same timer until a counter happened to expire.

Implementation starts with an auditable delayed-message state machine

Use a deliberately small policy first: seven total attempts, a one-second base delay, a 15-minute cap, and full jitter. These numbers are operating choices for the example, not universal defaults. A rent-accounting update that remains useful for an hour has a different retry horizon from a door-access event. I'm not sure a fixed schedule can fit every recipient; observed recovery time and delivery age should decide later tuning.

The queue interface below exposes business transitions rather than a particular library. That keeps the worker testable and makes transport changes less invasive. More important, it forces retryAt and deadLetter to carry the original delivery record instead of creating an unrelated message.

type WebhookJob = {
  deliveryId: string;
  propertyId: string;
  destination: string;
  eventType: "lease.payment_recorded";
  payload: { leaseId: string; paymentId: string; amountCents: number };
  attempt: number;
  firstQueuedAt: string;
};

type SendResult =
  | { kind: "delivered" }
  | { kind: "retryable"; reason: string }
  | { kind: "permanent"; reason: string };

interface QueuePort {
  acknowledge(deliveryId: string): Promise<void>;
  retryAt(job: WebhookJob, availableAt: Date): Promise<void>;
  deadLetter(job: WebhookJob, reason: string): Promise<void>;
}

interface DeliveryLedger {
  wasDelivered(deliveryId: string): Promise<boolean>;
  markDelivered(deliveryId: string, deliveredAt: Date): Promise<void>;
  recordRetry(
    deliveryId: string,
    attempt: number,
    availableAt: Date,
  ): Promise<void>;
  recordDeadLetter(
    deliveryId: string,
    reason: string,
    failedAt: Date,
  ): Promise<void>;
}

const policy = {
  maxAttempts: 7,
  baseDelayMs: 1_000,
  maxDelayMs: 15 * 60_000,
};

function nextDelayMs(attempt: number, random: () => number): number {
  const exponential = policy.baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1);
  const cap = Math.min(exponential, policy.maxDelayMs);
  return Math.floor(random() * cap);
}

async function processWebhook(
  job: WebhookJob,
  queue: QueuePort,
  ledger: DeliveryLedger,
  send: (job: WebhookJob) => Promise<SendResult>,
  now: () => Date = () => new Date(),
  random: () => number = Math.random,
): Promise<void> {
  if (await ledger.wasDelivered(job.deliveryId)) {
    await queue.acknowledge(job.deliveryId);
    return;
  }

  const result = await send(job);

  if (result.kind === "delivered") {
    await ledger.markDelivered(job.deliveryId, now());
    await queue.acknowledge(job.deliveryId);
    return;
  }

  if (result.kind === "permanent" || job.attempt >= policy.maxAttempts) {
    const reason =
      result.kind === "permanent" ? result.reason : "attempts_exhausted";
    await ledger.recordDeadLetter(job.deliveryId, reason, now());
    await queue.deadLetter(job, reason);
    return;
  }

  const availableAt = new Date(
    now().getTime() + nextDelayMs(job.attempt, random),
  );
  const nextJob = { ...job, attempt: job.attempt + 1 };
  await ledger.recordRetry(job.deliveryId, nextJob.attempt, availableAt);
  await queue.retryAt(nextJob, availableAt);
}

Full jitter selects a delay from zero to the current capped exponential value. Injecting the random function and clock is not ceremony — it makes the schedule deterministic under test. With random fixed at 0.5, the first delay is 500 ms and the second is 1,000 ms. Also test the attempt-seven boundary, a permanent rejection that schedules no retry, and the ambiguous outcome where the recipient applies the payment but the sender does not observe the response. Every execution must retain the same delivery ID.

One ordering detail deserves scrutiny: recording delivery and acknowledging the queue are separate operations. If the worker stops between them, the message can appear again, which is why wasDelivered runs before the send. If it stops after the remote side effect but before markDelivered, only recipient-side idempotency can close the gap. Exactly-once language tends to hide this boundary. Don't use it unless the entire end-to-end contract earns it.

Governance turns dead-letter redrive into a controlled production change

A DLQ is an isolation boundary, not permanent event history. AWS documents that dead-letter queues hold messages that were not successfully consumed, that their retention needs deliberate configuration, and that a redrive policy can restrict which source queues may use them. The portable lesson is to separate environments and event families whenever shared dead-letter storage would blur authorization, retention, or ownership.

Redrive should preserve evidence. Leave the failed delivery record intact, write a separate audit entry for who initiated replay and which selection criteria they used, then enqueue the original delivery identity. Before release, show a dry count grouped by destination and failure reason. Apply a destination rate limit and provide a stop control. Otherwise a recovery action can recreate the pressure that caused the backlog — only faster.

Be conservative.

For the property webhook, an operator might select exhausted deliveries for one accounting destination after its credentials were corrected. The tool should report how many lease.payment_recorded events match, reject a mixed-tenant selection unless authorization permits it, and redrive at a bounded rate. It should not edit the payload, reset the immutable event ID, or erase the old attempts. If the payload itself needs correction, create a new business event through the normal application path; replay is not a hidden data editor.

Dead-letter storage is also the wrong place for compliance history or long-term tenant support records. Keep the authoritative business event and delivery audit in durable application storage when those requirements outlive queue retention. The catch is extra state and another consistency boundary. For very low-volume, noncritical jobs where duplicates have no business impact, a ledger may cost more operational effort than it returns; a basic retry counter and failure log can be the better choice. Property payment webhooks do have a duplicate side effect, so the ledger earns its keep here.

Migration tests belong in the operational recovery rehearsal

Exponential backoff spaces attempts, but many workers can still contend for the same unhealthy recipient. Set a per-destination concurrency budget so one accounting endpoint cannot occupy the whole worker pool, then put a separate limit on global concurrency. Keep queue polling independent from outbound request timeouts. Delay is not recipient protection.

Measure outcomes rather than queue depth alone. Split delivered, retry-scheduled, permanently rejected, and dead-lettered work by destination. Track the age of the oldest eligible message and oldest dead-letter entry, because a stable total depth can conceal one tenant that is no longer making progress. Alerts should point to an operator action such as pausing one destination or reviewing one failure class; a generic “queue high” page creates noise but gives no recovery decision. Deployment belongs in the same runbook. Delayed messages may be decoded by a newer worker, so version the envelope and retain compatible decoders for the maximum delivery window, or explicitly migrate queued records. During rollback, verify that both worker versions derive the same delivery identity, since one small difference in that calculation defeats deduplication even if the backoff math is perfect. Before launch, run one complete recovery rehearsal: enqueue a payment webhook, produce a retryable result, verify a delayed copy with the unchanged ID, exhaust the attempt budget, inspect the dead-letter record, correct the destination configuration, redrive at a limited rate, and confirm one recipient-side effect. Repeat with a permanent rejection and confirm that it never returns to the active queue. Check that logs omit secrets, dashboards expose property and destination scope, and an operator can halt redrive without stopping unrelated tenants. This is the acceptance test for operational recovery; a unit test of nextDelayMs cannot replace it.

The final choice is modest: use the simplest queue in your environment that provides delayed availability, explicit acknowledgement, dead-letter isolation, and controlled redrive. A library-backed queue can fit a team already operating its data store and wanting retry controls in application code. A managed queue can fit a team that would rather hand off queue operations. Neither option supplies idempotency or a recovery contract for you. Keep correctness in delivery identity, keep evidence in the ledger, and tune backoff only after actual destination behavior gives you a reason.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/delayed

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: Get South Korea's CPI, unemployment, base rate and KRW/USD in English with Python
description:
If you model Asian economies, build a macro dashboard, or give an AI assistant a "what's inflation in Korea?" tool,
you eventually need South Korea's official numbers. They live in two places:

  • KOSIS — Statistics Korea's portal (CPI, employment, population, births…)
  • ECOS — the Bank of Korea's database (base rate, exchange rates, money supply, GDP…)

Both have free official APIs. In practice two things slow people down: you register for a key on each portal, and
KOSIS returns table, item and category names in Korean, so you end up building your own translation and parsing
layer before you can plot anything.

This post shows a shortcut: two small Apify actors that call those official APIs for you and return clean,
English-labelled time series — no Korean account or API key on your side.

What you get back

One row per observation, with English labels, a numeric value, the unit and the source:

table period item value unit
KOSIS DT_1J22003 2026-10 CPI, whole country 120.73 2020=100
KOSIS DT_1DA7001S 2026-10 Unemployment rate, total 2.0 %
ECOS 722Y001 2026-10 Bank of Korea base rate 3.0 % per annum
ECOS 731Y001 2026-11-13 KRW per USD 1332.4 Won

A small sanity check I like: CPI comes from Statistics Korea in KOSIS and is mirrored by the Bank of Korea in ECOS.
Pulled independently, both returned 120.05 / 120.43 / 120.73 for Aug–Oct 2026.

Every row also carries an attribution block (source, table, the official table URL, retrieval date), so a chart
or an AI answer can cite where the number came from.

1. Python: several KOSIS tables in one call 

# pip install apify-client pandas
from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats").call(run_input={
    # ORGID/TBLID from the kosis.kr table URL; up to 20 tables per run
    "tables": ["101/DT_1J22003", "101/DT_1DA7001S"],
    "periodType": "M",
    "startPeriod": "202401",
    "endPeriod": "202610",
})
df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

cpi = df[(df.table_id == "DT_1J22003") & (df.item_id == "T") & (df.category_code == "T10")]
unemp = df[(df.table_id == "DT_1DA7001S") & (df.item_id == "T80") & (df.category_code == "0")]
print(cpi[["period", "value"]].tail(3))
print(unemp[["period", "value"]].tail(3))

Note on size: this pulls every item and category of both tables — 1,634 rows for this period (about $3.27).
To fetch only what you need, run one table at a time with "itemId" and "classL1" set (CPI total:
"itemId": "T", "classL1": "T10"; unemployment rate total: "itemId": "T80", "classL1": "0") — 34 rows each.

Any table you can open on kosis.kr works — the address bar shows orgId=…&tblId=…. You don't need to know how many
classification levels a table has; the actor detects that. If one table id is wrong, the other tables still return
and the bad one is named in the run log (a failed table produces no rows, so it isn't charged).

2. Python: Bank of Korea rates and FX 

run = client.actor("kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats").call(run_input={
    # STATCODE or STATCODE/ITEMCODE1 — item codes differ per table
    "statCodes": ["722Y001/0101000", "901Y009/0"],   # base rate, CPI
    "frequency": "M",
    "startPeriod": "202401",
    "endPeriod": "202610",
})
rates = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
print(rates.pivot(index="period", columns="stat_code", values="value").tail(3))

For daily KRW/USD use "statCodes": ["731Y001/0000001"], "frequency": "D". All tables in one run share the
frequency. Not sure about codes? Run the actor with "mode": "items" and a table code to list its items.

3. From an AI assistant (MCP)

Apify's MCP server (https://mcp.apify.com) exposes public actors as tools for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor,
VS Code and other MCP clients. After adding it, a prompt like this works:

Use the Apify actor kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats to get South Korea's monthly CPI and unemployment rate
(tables 101/DT_1J22003 and 101/DT_1DA7001S) from 2024-01 to 2026-10 and chart them.

Because rows are already in English with units and a source URL, the assistant can answer and cite in one step.

Ready-made examples (one click)

  • Korea CPI, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats/examples/korea-cpi-monthly
  • Korea unemployment rate, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/kosis-korea-stats/examples/korea-unemployment-rate-monthly
  • Bank of Korea base rate, monthly — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats/examples/korea-base-rate-monthly
  • KRW/USD, daily — https://apify.com/kdata-hub/ecos-korea-stats/examples/krw-usd-exchange-rate-daily

Cost and limits

  • Pay per result: $2 per 1,000 rows. A 34-month CPI series filtered to the headline index is 34 rows (about $0.07); a whole multi-item table costs more, so filter items when you can.
  • Up to 20 tables per run; maxRecords caps rows per table and the run reports truncation.
  • The numbers are the official KOSIS / ECOS values, not estimates; if the official source has a gap, the row says so (value_status) instead of inventing a value.

When not to use this

If you only need one or two headline series and are happy with a monthly lag, a free aggregator may be enough.
This is for when you want any Korean table, in English, with sources, from code or an AI tool — without
setting up Korean accounts and translation yourself.

Data: Statistics Korea (KOSIS) and Bank of Korea (ECOS). The actors are independent tools that call the official
open APIs; they are not affiliated with or endorsed by those institutions.
