title: A small test for the denominator in a research results table
description:
A table says a study enrolled 120 participants and reports 24 events. The numerator is easy to spot. The tricky part is whether those 24 events were measured among all enrollees or among the 96 participants with observed outcomes.

In this synthetic example, 24 of the 96 participants with observed outcomes had an event. The observed-case percentage is 25%. If you use 120 as the denominator and report 20%, readers can wrongly infer that the other 24 participants had no event.

Put the population in the table

Quantity Count
Enrolled 120
Outcome observed 96
Outcome missing 24
Events among participants with an observed outcome 24

A regression fixture can catch the accidental denominator swap before an export:

def observed_rate(enrolled, observed, events):
    if not 0 <= events <= observed <= enrolled:
        raise ValueError("Counts must reconcile")
    return events / observed if observed else None

assert observed_rate(120, 96, 24) == 0.25
assert observed_rate(120, 0, 0) is None

Keep the source column and time point next to each of the three counts. This check catches inconsistent bookkeeping. It leaves open how to handle missing outcomes for the actual study: decide that separately using the protocol and the assumptions that fit the data.

For reporting an observational study, consult the STROBE checklists, including the items on participants and missing data. RigorMed can organize a protocol, a results table, and the manuscript draft in one research project for review. The numbers above are for teaching and came from no participant records.

Disclosure: This article was generated with AI and checked for the numbers, code, and example boundaries.

title: How to Scrape Workday Job Postings from any myworkdayjobs.com Site
description:
How to Scrape Workday Job Postings from any myworkdayjobs.com Site

A surprising number of large employers — from NVIDIA and Adobe to retailers and banks — host careers on Workday. The public site lives under a myworkdayjobs.com URL. If you recruit against those companies, or you want their openings in a spreadsheet, clicking through the career portal does not scale. This guide shows how to scrape Workday job postings from any public myworkdayjobs.com site.

You will use the Workday Jobs Scraper on Apify. Paste one or more career-site URLs and get titles, locations, country, remote flag, time type, posting date, job ID and the full description. Keyword, location, remote and recency filters are built in.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need

  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

You do not need a Workday employee login or an internal tenant ID. The public career site URL is enough.

How to run it in the Apify Console

Step 1: Open the Actor

Go to https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs and click Try for free.

Step 2: Paste the career site URL

Example: https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite. You can add several employers in one run.

Step 3: Filter and cap

Use search text, location, remote-only or posted within N days if you only want fresh roles. Set max jobs per site low for a first run. Leave details on to get full descriptions.

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. Job IDs plus posting dates make incremental watches easy.

The same company can have more than one Workday site (for example a student site and a professional site). Add each URL you care about. You pay for saved jobs.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs").call(run_input={
    "careerSites": [
        "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite"
    ],
    "maxJobsPerSite": 50,
    "includeDetails": True
})

# Write every dataset item, then export from the Console or keep going in code.
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item)

The JavaScript client (apify-client on npm) uses the same Actor id and the same input object. You can also start the run with a plain HTTP POST to the Apify API if you prefer.

Sample output

Here is a shortened example of one dataset record (field values are illustrative of the schema, taken from a real sample run shape):

{
  "company": "nvidia",
  "careerSite": "NVIDIAExternalCareerSite",
  "jobId": "JR2026556",
  "title": "Firmware Engineer",
  "url": "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite/job/Israel-Tel-Aviv/Firmware-Engineer_JR2026556",
  "location": "Israel, Tel Aviv",
  "postedOn": "Posted Today",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-12",
  "allLocations": [
    "Israel, Tel Aviv",
    "Israel, Beer Sheva"
  ],
  "country": "Israel",
  "countryCode": "IL",
  "remote": false,
  "remoteType": null,
  "timeType": "Full time",
  "validThrough": null,
  "hiringOrganization": "IL00 Mellanox Technologies, Ltd.",
  "applyUrl": "https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite/job/Israel-Tel-Aviv/Firmware-Engineer_JR2026556",
  "descriptionText": "NVIDIA is seeking a dedicated Firmware Engineer to join our NIC Firmware Core team in Beer-Sheva/Tel-Aviv. You will contribute to the development of brand-new networking adapter te…",
  "descriptionHtml": "<p>NVIDIA is seeking a dedicated Firmware Engineer to join our NIC Firmware Core team in Beer-Sheva/Tel-Aviv. You will contribute to the development of brand-new networking adapter…",
  "scrapedAt": "2026-11-12T22:14:14.812Z"
}

Once the run has finished, open the dataset in the Console and use Export > CSV if a spreadsheet is your destination. JSON is usually better for code and for language models.

What to use the data for

Agency recruiters watch a roster of enterprise clients. In-house talent teams benchmark how competitors write similar roles. Researchers study location and remote patterns at large employers. A scheduled daily run with posted within 1 day is a simple new-jobs alert.

Pricing

Pay-per-result pricing starts at $1.50 per 1,000 saved jobs on the Apify Free plan, with lower unit prices on paid Apify plans, plus a small per-run start fee. Always check the live pricing on the Actor page, because plans and unit prices can change. For a first test, keep the input tiny so you can inspect the schema before you scale up.

Scheduling and automations

In the Apify Console you can schedule the Actor (daily or hourly) and leave the same input in place. For incremental jobs, prefer a "since" or "posted after" style filter when the Actor offers one, so you are not paying to re-collect old rows. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-workday-jobs through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

Job descriptions belong to the employer. Use them for search, analysis or applications, not to clone a careers site. Follow the employer's terms. The Actor is not affiliated with Workday or any employer mentioned as an example.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

Next step

Open the Actor and run a small job: Workday Jobs Scraper: Any myworkdayjobs.com Career Site.

If you later want this on a schedule, save the input that worked, add a date filter where it applies, and export CSV automatically from the dataset or from the API snippet above.

title: Semantic Retrieval Evaluation Sets for Internal Engineering Docs in Node.js (5 Tests)
description:
Short answer: build a small, versioned evaluation set from real documentation questions, score retrieval with recall@k and ranking quality, then choose the fastest index that clears your relevance threshold. For a logistics team watching a carrier web page, keep latency as a constraint, not as a substitute for finding the paragraph that explains the change.

Retrieval approach Pick it when Watch for
Lexical search (BM25) Error codes, route names, and exact terms dominate Synonyms and paraphrases can be missed
Vector search Engineers ask concept-shaped questions across varied wording Similar-sounding passages can outrank the answer
Hybrid search Queries mix identifiers with natural language Two scores need a repeatable fusion rule

The evaluation set is the control surface. Without it, a new embedding model or chunk size is only a feeling in a dashboard. Store the query, the expected document or passage, and the acceptable rank in a file that can be reviewed like code.

Measure it twice.

What should a semantic retrieval evaluation set contain for internal engineering documentation?

Start with the question types your on-call team actually asks. A logistics example might be: “What changed in the carrier cutoff page after the 02:00 crawl?” The answer is a dated diff record, while the supporting context may be the parser runbook and the alert policy. Label both the primary passage and acceptable secondary passages; otherwise a useful runbook hit looks like a false negative.

I initially treated every query as a single-answer lookup. That made the score look precise and the review painful. Some questions have several valid passages, and a page-change alert often needs the newest version, not merely a semantically similar older one.

Use five small slices: exact identifier, paraphrase, multi-hop procedure, negative query, and freshness-sensitive query. Give each slice its own count. A 50-query set with 10 items per slice is easier to inspect than one opaque score, and it exposes a regression such as “good prose, bad error-code matching.” Keep a stable query_id; append new cases instead of rewriting old labels. For each case, retain the source URL, repository path, revision, and the human explanation for why a passage is acceptable. That extra context turns a score review into an engineering conversation: the person changing chunking can see whether a miss came from tokenization, metadata filtering, or an outdated label, then update one fixture and rerun the same slice instead of arguing from a dashboard aggregate.

Here is the kind of failure worth preserving. Query carrier-cutoff-02 retrieves the current alert policy at rank 1, an old carrier page at rank 2, and the parser runbook at rank 3. A naive evaluator marks that as a pass because the right topic appeared. A production reviewer marks it as a freshness failure because the alert must cite the current page revision. Keep the case, add the revision constraint to its label, and make the next index run prove that the old page no longer wins. That single example tests chunk metadata, ranking, and the alert contract together; it is more informative than another dozen easy paraphrases.

A negative query matters. “Which carrier page is covered by this alert?” should return no confident match when that carrier is outside the monitored set. Treating the top vector as an answer creates a plausible citation for an absent fact.

How do you measure retrieval quality and latency without fooling yourself?

For each query, record the ranked IDs returned by the retriever and a timestamp for the request. Recall@k asks whether any acceptable passage appears in the first k results. Mean reciprocal rank rewards putting the first acceptable passage near the top. Neither metric says the text is current, so add a freshness check for documents with revisions or crawl timestamps.

Here is a compact TypeScript scorer. It assumes labels are passage IDs, not generated answers. That distinction keeps retrieval evaluation separate from generation quality.

type Case = {
  queryId: string;
  relevant: Set<string>;
  expectedMaxAgeHours?: number;
};

type Result = { id: string; ageHours?: number };

export function score(cases: Case[], ranked: Map<string, Result[]>, k: number) {
  let recalled = 0;
  let reciprocalRank = 0;

  for (const item of cases) {
    const results = ranked.get(item.queryId) ?? [];
    const top = results.slice(0, k);
    const hit = top.findIndex((r) => item.relevant.has(r.id));
    if (hit >= 0) {
      recalled += 1;
      reciprocalRank += 1 / (hit + 1);
    }
  }

  return {
    recallAtK: cases.length === 0 ? 0 : recalled / cases.length,
    meanReciprocalRank: cases.length === 0 ? 0 : reciprocalRank / cases.length,
  };
}

Run the same cases against lexical, vector, and hybrid candidates. Capture p50 and p95 latency beside the quality scores. A p95 spike is operationally different from a small mean change: page-change alerts arrive in bursts, so tail latency can delay a notification even when average retrieval looks fine.

The practical gate is two-dimensional. Set a minimum recall for each slice, then set a p95 budget for the alert path. If hybrid search raises recall for error-code queries but breaks the budget, route only those queries to hybrid or reduce the candidate set. Your mileage may vary; the right threshold depends on how costly a missed change is.

Which indexing and chunking choices survive real documentation churn?

Chunk by meaning before tuning vector dimensions. Keep a heading with the procedure it governs, preserve code blocks as intact units, and attach metadata such as repository, path, revision, and crawl time. For a changed carrier page, store the old and new fingerprints so the evaluator can ask for the current passage explicitly.

Elasticsearch supports BM25 and vector fields in one search system; PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps embeddings beside relational metadata; Vespa offers ranking expressions for combining signals. These are different operational shapes, not a leaderboard. Pick the system your team can back up, inspect, and reindex predictably. A hybrid design still needs one canonical document ID so score comparisons remain meaningful.

The failure mode I watch is stale truth. A semantically perfect match to last month’s cutoff is wrong for today’s alert. Add a freshness feature or a hard filter, and put at least one intentionally stale case in every evaluation run.

When a case fails, save the query, top five IDs, scores, document revisions, and latency. A reviewer should be able to explain the failure without rerunning production traffic. Group failures by cause: bad label, missing chunk, synonym gap, stale metadata, or ranking tie.

Keep a tiny change log next to the set. Record why a label changed and which parser or index version caused it. A 202 response from an indexing job is not evidence that the passage is searchable; verify visibility in the same environment used by the alert worker.

One short rule: never optimize an aggregate while a slice is red.

Limits and trade-offs

Evaluation sets do not remove judgment. Labels can encode one team’s vocabulary, and a five-slice set can underrepresent rare incidents. Expand it from reviewed misses, but freeze a regression subset so improvements cannot erase old failures.

Vector retrieval is not suitable when exact identifiers are the whole query; stick with lexical or hybrid search then. A large hybrid stack is also a poor fit for a small documentation corpus that changes weekly, where a simpler index is easier to reindex and audit. The catch is maintenance: every new chunking rule, embedding model, and freshness policy changes the behavior you must measure.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/rrf.html
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://docs.vespa.ai/en/reference/rank-features.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance_API

title: A CSS Grid Column Set to 1fr Still Overflows? The Minimum Is Not Zero
description:
We built a simple two-column page. The side menu had a fixed width. The main column was 1fr, which we read as "take whatever width is left." Then we put a long, unwrapped line of code in the main column. The page grew a horizontal scrollbar. The main column was wider than the leftover space. The 1fr did not shrink.

This is a CSS Grid issue. It is close in spirit to a flex item's automatic minimum, but the property that surprises people here is the track size itself.

The layout 

<div class="page">
  <nav class="side">Menu</nav>
  <main class="main">
    <pre>npm install some-long-package-name-and-then-another-one</pre>
  </main>
</div>

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr;
  width: 400px;
}

.main pre {
  margin: 0;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

The page is 400 pixels wide. The menu is 120 pixels. You would expect the main column to be the rest, about 280 pixels. You would also expect the long line to sit inside it, or to scroll inside it. That is not what happens.

What we measured

We pasted this layout into Chrome and measured the boxes on November 13, 2026, in Chrome 156.

The long line in this snippet measured about 430 pixels. The main column grew to that same width, about 430 pixels. The 400-pixel page then overflowed. The 1fr track did not stay in the leftover space.

Why a bare 1fr has a content minimum

fr means a fraction of leftover space. MDN's page on grid-template-columns adds a key detail. When fr is used on its own, not inside minmax(), it implies an automatic minimum. MDN writes this as minmax(auto, <flex>). So 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr).

The 1fr is only the maximum. The minimum is auto. For a grid item, that automatic minimum is based on its content when the item is not a scroll container. The CSS Grid specification covers this in section 6.6. A single long line that cannot wrap sets a floor for the track: the track will not get narrower than that line.

So the track will not go below that line's width, even when the line is wider than the leftover space. The page overflows.

Two direct fixes

The first fix is to set the minimum to zero in the track list:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 120px minmax(0, 1fr);
  width: 400px;
}

In the same Chrome test, the main column shrank to the leftover space: 280 pixels, after the 120-pixel menu. The long line no longer forced the column open.

The second fix leaves 1fr as it is and puts min-width: 0 on the grid item in that column:

.main {
  min-width: 0;
}

That also gave a 280-pixel main column in our test.

If you want the long line to scroll inside the main column, add overflow: auto on .main as well. In a third test, overflow: hidden on .main also let the column shrink to 280 pixels. It clipped the leftover content, so the page itself no longer overflowed. We prefer minmax(0, 1fr) or min-width: 0, and overflow: auto when the content should scroll inside the column.

Equal columns have the same trap

grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr looks like two equal halves. It is two tracks that each have a content minimum. In our 400-pixel page, we put the same long line in the left column and a short word in the right. The left column grew to the full width of the line. The right column was only 37 pixels wide. They were not equal.

grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 1fr) made both columns 200 pixels, which is half of the 400-pixel page.

If you want equal, shrinking columns, write the zero minimum on each track.

A short checklist

  • A bare 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr). The auto is a content minimum.
  • Long unwrapped text, a wide table, or a large image can hold that track open.
  • Use minmax(0, 1fr) on the track, or min-width: 0 on the item.
  • Do this for every 1fr track that should be allowed to shrink.
  • If the content is still wider than the column, set overflow on the item so the extra scrolls or clips inside it.

Browser support is broad. On MDN, grid-template-columns and minmax() are marked Baseline widely available from October 2017.

Sources

  • MDN, grid-template-columns: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/grid-template-columns
  • MDN, minmax(): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/minmax
  • W3C CSS Grid Layout Module Level 1, section 6.6 (automatic minimum size) and section 7.2.4 (fr unit): https://www.w3.org/TR/css-grid-1/#min-size-auto

PIXEL RECRUITING LLC looks for frontend and UI engineers who can explain why a grid track will not shrink, not only paste a fix. We are a direct staffing partner for Mastercard in O'Fallon, MO. You can see how we work at pixelrecruiting.com.

title: What Is a Bounding Box (BBOX) in GIS? A Practical Guide to Faster Geospatial Queries
description:
If you have ever worked with interactive maps, GIS applications, or location-based services, you have probably encountered the term Bounding Box (BBOX).

Bounding boxes are one of the simplest yet most powerful concepts in geospatial development. They help applications retrieve only the geographical data needed for a particular map view instead of loading an entire dataset.

Whether you are building a real estate application, a digital land mapping platform, a delivery tracking system, or a GIS dashboard, understanding BBOX queries can significantly improve performance.

In this article, we'll explore how bounding boxes work and how to implement them using JavaScript, PostgreSQL, and PostGIS.

1. What Is a Bounding Box?

A Bounding Box is a rectangular geographical area defined by its minimum and maximum coordinates.

It is commonly represented using four values:

  • Minimum Longitude (MinX)
  • Minimum Latitude (MinY)
  • Maximum Longitude (MaxX)
  • Maximum Latitude (MaxY)

The standard BBOX representation is:

BBOX = minX, minY, maxX, maxY

For example:

83.50, 26.70, 83.60, 26.80

This defines a rectangular geographical region.

Instead of searching an entire country or district, an application can use this rectangle to retrieve only geographical objects that intersect the visible area.

2. Why Are Bounding Boxes Important?

Imagine building a digital map containing 10 million land parcels.

A simple API that returns every parcel would create several problems:

  • Large API responses
  • High database load
  • Increased network usage
  • Slow map rendering
  • Poor mobile performance

Now imagine a user opens the map and views only a small village.

Does the browser really need all 10 million polygons?

Obviously not.

This is where Bounding Box filtering becomes useful.

When a user moves or zooms the map, the application calculates the visible geographical boundaries and sends them to the backend.

The backend queries only the relevant geographical records.

This technique is commonly known as viewport-based data loading.

3. How BBOX Works in a Map Application

The overall workflow is straightforward:

  1. A user opens an interactive map.
  2. The map library calculates the current visible geographical boundaries.
  3. The frontend extracts minimum and maximum coordinates.
  4. These coordinates are sent to a backend API.
  5. The backend performs a spatial database query.
  6. Only matching geographical features are returned.
  7. The frontend renders those features on the map.

This process repeats when the user moves or zooms the map.

4. Getting BBOX Coordinates Using Leaflet

Leaflet provides a simple API to retrieve the visible map boundaries.

const bounds = map.getBounds();

const bbox = [
    bounds.getWest(),
    bounds.getSouth(),
    bounds.getEast(),
    bounds.getNorth()
].join(',');

console.log(bbox);

Example output:

83.50,26.70,83.60,26.80

You can use these coordinates to request geographical data from your backend.

async function loadParcels(map) {
    const bounds = map.getBounds();

    const bbox = [
        bounds.getWest(),
        bounds.getSouth(),
        bounds.getEast(),
        bounds.getNorth()
    ].join(',');

    const response = await fetch(
        `/api/parcels?bbox=${encodeURIComponent(bbox)}`
    );

    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error('Failed to load parcels');
    }

    return response.json();
}

You can call this function when the map finishes moving:

map.on('moveend', () => {
    loadParcels(map);
});

For production applications, consider debouncing requests, cancelling outdated requests, and avoiding unnecessary queries at low zoom levels.

5. Implementing BBOX Queries with PostgreSQL and PostGIS

PostGIS provides powerful spatial functions for working with geographical data.

Assume you have a table containing land parcels:

CREATE TABLE land_parcels (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    village_id BIGINT,
    khasra_number VARCHAR(50),
    boundary GEOMETRY(MultiPolygon, 4326)
);

First, create a spatial index:

CREATE INDEX land_parcels_geom_idx
ON land_parcels
USING GIST (boundary);

Now you can retrieve parcels intersecting a given bounding box.

SELECT
    id,
    khasra_number,
    ST_AsGeoJSON(boundary)::json AS geometry
FROM land_parcels
WHERE ST_Intersects(
    boundary,
    ST_MakeEnvelope(
        83.50,
        26.70,
        83.60,
        26.80,
        4326
    )
);

Here is what happens:

  • ST_MakeEnvelope() creates a rectangular geometry.
  • ST_Intersects() checks whether a parcel intersects that rectangle.
  • ST_AsGeoJSON() converts geographical geometry into GeoJSON.

The spatial index helps PostgreSQL narrow down candidate geometries before performing the exact spatial intersection test.

6. ST_Intersects vs ST_Within vs ST_Contains

PostGIS provides several spatial functions. Choosing the correct one depends on your application requirements.

Function Purpose
ST_Intersects Returns geometries that share any portion of space
ST_Within Checks whether one geometry is completely inside another
ST_Contains Checks whether one geometry completely contains another
ST_Envelope Returns the rectangular bounding box of a geometry
ST_MakeEnvelope Creates a rectangle from four coordinates

For viewport-based map loading, ST_Intersects() is generally a good choice because it includes polygons that partially overlap the visible map.

7. Building a BBOX API Endpoint

You can expose this functionality through a REST API.

For example:

GET /api/parcels?bbox=83.50,26.70,83.60,26.80

A simplified Go handler might look like this:

func GetParcels(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    bbox := strings.Split(r.URL.Query().Get("bbox"), ",")

    if len(bbox) != 4 {
        http.Error(w, "Invalid bbox", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    // Parse and validate coordinates.
    // Execute a parameterized PostGIS query.
    // Return matching features as GeoJSON.
}

In production, always validate coordinate ranges, reject non-finite values, enforce a maximum bounding-box area, and use parameterized SQL queries.

You should also consider limiting the number of returned features.

8. Performance Optimization Techniques

BBOX filtering is useful, but a few additional techniques can make a geospatial application significantly faster.

Use Spatial Indexes

Always consider a GiST spatial index for frequently queried geometry columns.

Without an appropriate index, spatial queries may require scanning a large number of records.

Implement Zoom-Based Filtering

At a low zoom level, displaying individual land parcels may be unnecessary.

For example:

  • Zoom 5: Display state boundaries.
  • Zoom 8: Display district boundaries.
  • Zoom 11: Display village boundaries.
  • Zoom 15: Display individual land parcels.

These are illustrative thresholds; actual zoom levels depend on your map and data.

Use Vector Tiles

For very large datasets, vector tiles can be more efficient than returning complete GeoJSON responses.

Technologies such as MapLibre GL JS and Martin can help build vector-tile-based mapping systems.

Cache Frequently Requested Regions

Village-level maps are often requested repeatedly.

Caching frequently accessed geographical data can reduce database load and improve response times.

Avoid Excessive API Requests

Do not send a new request for every small movement of the map.

Use debouncing, request cancellation, and appropriate caching strategies.

9. Real-World Example: Digital Land Mapping

Consider a platform that allows users to explore village-level land maps.

A single village might contain thousands of land parcels.

Loading every parcel for an entire district would be inefficient.

Instead, the application can:

  1. Load administrative boundaries first.
  2. Allow users to navigate to a particular village.
  3. Retrieve land parcels based on the visible map boundaries.
  4. Display individual plot polygons.
  5. Fetch additional information when a user selects a plot.

This approach reduces unnecessary data transfer and makes interactive land maps more responsive.

For a practical example of the land-information domain, explore BhuKhoj, an independent platform focused on helping users discover village land maps and plot-related information.

You can explore the platform here:

BhuKhoj – Explore Village Land Maps and Plot Information

10. Common BBOX Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can encounter problems when implementing spatial queries.

Incorrect Coordinate Order

GeoJSON and PostGIS geographic coordinates generally use longitude first, followed by latitude.

Ignoring Coordinate Reference Systems

A BBOX expressed in EPSG:4326 cannot be directly compared with geometries stored in a different coordinate reference system without appropriate transformation.

Not Validating Coordinates

Always validate minimum and maximum coordinates before executing database queries.

Returning Too Much Data

A bounding box can still cover a very large geographical area. Use zoom-level restrictions, result limits, and vector tiles where appropriate.

Ignoring Antimeridian Crossing

A bounding box that crosses the international date line needs special handling because its minimum longitude may be greater than its maximum longitude.

Conclusion

Bounding Box queries are an essential technique for building scalable geospatial applications.

By combining viewport-based loading, PostGIS spatial indexes, and efficient frontend map libraries, developers can build applications that handle large geographical datasets without overwhelming the browser or database.

If you are building GIS dashboards, land mapping applications, or location-based services, understanding BBOX filtering is a valuable addition to your engineering toolkit.

Useful Resources

  • PostGIS Documentation
  • Leaflet Documentation
  • GeoJSON Specification
  • MapLibre GL JS
  • OpenStreetMap

BhuKhoj is an independent land-information platform and is not affiliated with any government department. Always verify important land-related information through official government records.

title: When 75% Is Not the Whole Score: Auditing Predictions by Denominator
description:
A 75% score over four rows

Put one number on the table and break it open. Suppose an eight-row inventory and its predictions show 75% correct. That fraction covers four records: id0, id1, id4, and id6. id2 abstains, id3 has no prediction line, id5 is invalid because of conflicting duplicates, and id7 has null gold. None enters the A/C=3/4 numerator or denominator, but the inventory still has eight rows. The number itself does not say which rows left, so the per-row filters belong next to it.

prediction-metric-desk is a local audit desk that compares an inventory with saved predictions and counts them. It trains nothing, infers nothing, and does not rewrite invalid rows. The eight-row fixture is a fixed fault set included in the package. The inventory has N=8 records, with K=7 known gold and null gold for id7. The predictions file has 11 physical lines, including one broken JSON line, one extra ID, and duplicate id5 lines. These rows stay in the report.

The screenshot comes from the standalone App page and is uncropped. The App renders NLL as ∞ and notes zero true-class probability. The exported JSON writes the same condition as value:null and infinite:true, two representations with no change to the metric definition.

Record-level map

One clarification first: labels are ["a","b","missing"], and "missing" is a legitimate taxonomy string, not a missing value. id4 has gold label "missing" and predicted label "missing", so this line counts as correct. That is separate from id3's missing state, which means there is no prediction line at all.

id gold prediction line C D E
0 a predicted a, probabilities [0.8,0.1,0.1] yes yes yes
1 a predicted b, probabilities [0,1,0] yes yes yes
2 b predicted null, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] no yes no
3 b no prediction line no no no
4 "missing" predicted "missing", no probabilities yes no yes
5 "missing" two lines: a and typo, invalid no no no
6 a predicted a, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] yes yes yes
7 null predicted b, probabilities [0.1,0.8,0.1] unscored no yes

From the table: C contains id0, id1, id4, and id6; three of them are correct, so A=3, C=4, and A/C=75%. id2 has probabilities but a null predicted_label, so it is abstained and enters D but not C or E. id4 has a decision and no probabilities, so it enters C/E and not D. id5 has two conflicting physical lines, so the record is invalid and stays out of C/D/E; both original lines remain visible in prediction_lines, while line_accounting carries counts such as invalid_lines and not the raw rows themselves. id7 has null gold, is not scored, and enters E only. The extra ID is separate from inventory cases.

C and D both equal 4 in this fixture by coincidence, but their members differ: id2 is in D and not C, id4 is in C and not D. Reading 4 as the same filter misses that difference.

Coverage needs three rates

E counts a single valid prediction line with a non-null predicted_label, regardless of gold, so id7 qualifies and E=5. C counts decided rows among known gold, so C=4. C/K=4/7 asks what share of known-gold rows decided; E/N=5/8 asks what share of inventory emitted a label; A/C=3/4 asks what share of those decisions were correct. Treating A/C as overall accuracy drops the first two denominators.

U=K-C=3. If I force all three undecided rows to answer, completed accuracy runs from A/K=3/7 to (A+K-C)/K=6/7. The range assumes all three are wrong or all three are right. It is not a confidence interval and not a promise. It shows how sensitive the current 0.75 is to those rows.

Probability support and decision labels

D counts known-gold rows with one valid prediction line and a non-null probabilities vector, four in this fixture. Label order is a, b, "missing"; id1 has true class a and vector [0,1,0], whose first term for a is zero. Mean NLL is therefore infinite. The exported report writes value:null, infinite:true, zero_probability_rows:1, and support:4; the page renders ∞. I do not clip the value, renormalize the vector, or fabricate a one-hot output. predicted_label may also differ from probabilities argmax: id6 has predicted_label a while its argmax is b. The report records that mismatch and does not override the policy label.

Reproduce the fixture with one command

From the package root, with Node 22 or newer and no existing output file:

node audit_cli.mjs data/fault-inventory.json data/fault-predictions.jsonl my-audit.json

stdout is JSON. This block is an excerpt of key fields, not the full stdout; the full report is written to my-audit.json with cases as record-level status, prediction_lines as original physical lines with line errors, and line_accounting as a physical-line summary.

{
  "denominators": {"N": 8, "K": 7, "E": 5, "C": 4, "A": 3, "U": 3, "D": 4},
  "metrics": {
    "coverage": 0.625,
    "known_gold_coverage": 0.5714285714285714,
    "conditional_accuracy": 0.75,
    "completion_bounds": [0.42857142857142855, 0.8571428571428571],
    "nll": {"value": null, "infinite": true, "zero_probability_rows": 1, "support": 4}
  }
}

That command verifies the table without recomputing the 3080-row result. Entry points and fixed version:

  • Standalone App page
  • HF Space
  • Fixed source commit cb003655f55c5a9153bceaa7fde897ec598d7011

I still recommend the standalone App page as the stable entry point. The inline Hub view appeared blank in a minimized Edge environment on 2026-11-13, and that cause remains unproven. On 2026-11-14, a signed-out inline browser environment previewed and applied the fault fixture and showed N=8, C=4, A=3, D=4, conditional accuracy 3/4, known-gold coverage 4/7, and infinite NLL. That success is limited to the new signed-out context; it does not show the original Edge issue is fixed, the root cause is known, or every browser and entry point works.

What the report carries

Active audit work and newly imported inputs live in browser memory and clear on refresh. There is no autosave and no crash checkpoint. A downloaded JSON report itself remains on disk, but it cannot be reimported as a checkpoint, and refreshing does not reload it automatically. The exported report contains full original inventory and predictions, so I check what is inside before sharing. SHA256 proves byte consistency, not provenance, authorization, or gold-label reliability.

The 3080-row BANKING77 predictions were generated from saved int8 logits and frozen temperature 0.75 by the earlier work; prediction-metric-desk audits that saved result. It gives 2779 correct and 301 incorrect while retaining the original seven normalized train/test overlaps. The tool does not regenerate logits, fit a temperature, or perform new calibration. That is not new training, inference, blind evaluation, or generalization evidence. The implementation and synthetic fixture are Apache 2.0. The BANKING77 source data and derived outputs stay CC BY 4.0 with attribution to PolyAI and Casanueva et al. 2020.

By Renchao Wu.

English original.

title: CSS Grid Explained with Simple Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

CSS Grid is a layout system built into CSS that lets you place items in rows and columns at the same time. You turn a parent element into a grid container with display: grid, define the columns and rows, add spacing with gap, and the browser lines everything up for you. In this guide you will learn the core ideas step by step, build a complete card gallery you can copy, and see when Grid beats Flexbox.

What Is a Grid Container?

Every grid starts with a container. Pick the element that wraps your items, a div, a section or a main element, and set display: grid on it. That one line changes how its direct children behave. The children become grid items, and the container controls where they sit.

Think of it like a spreadsheet. Columns run down, rows run across, and each item sits in a cell where a row and a column meet. Lines are the borders between cells, and tracks are the rows and columns themselves. You describe the spreadsheet, and the browser builds it.

If you are still sorting out which language does what on a page, our guide to the difference between HTML, CSS and JavaScript is a friendly place to start. HTML gives the structure, CSS, including Grid, gives the layout.

The MDN guide to the basic concepts of grid layout explains containers, items, lines and tracks in detail, and it is worth bookmarking as you practise.

Step 1: Create Your First Grid

Start with simple HTML and one CSS rule:

<div class="box">
  <div>One</div>
  <div>Two</div>
  <div>Three</div>
</div>

.box {
  display: grid;
}

That is a real grid already. With no columns defined, Grid creates one column and stacks the three items in three rows. The magic starts when you describe the columns and rows yourself.

Step 2: Define Columns and Rows

Two properties do most of the work. grid-template-columns sets how many columns there are and how wide each one is. grid-template-rows does the same job for rows.

.box {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 200px 200px;
  grid-template-rows: 100px 100px;
}

This says: make three columns, each 200 pixels wide, and two rows, each 100 pixels tall. Six items fill it perfectly. A seventh item creates a new row automatically, which is handy and also a common surprise.

Fixed sizes are clear, but they do not adapt to different screens. That is why Grid has a unit made just for this job.

Step 3: Meet the fr Unit

The fr unit means one fraction of the free space. It is Grid only, and it makes columns share space fairly without any maths from you.

grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;

Here the free space is split into three equal parts. Change it to 2fr 1fr and the first column gets twice the share of the second. It is like slicing a cake where one guest politely, and correctly, gets a bigger slice.

Writing the same value again and again gets dull, so use repeat():

grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);

That line means the same as 1fr 1fr 1fr, but it is shorter and easier to change. The full MDN CSS grid layout reference lists every Grid property you will meet as you grow.

Step 4: Add Space with gap

Items that touch each other look cramped. The gap property adds space between rows and columns, and only between them, never around the outside edge.

.box {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 16px;
}

One value sets both gaps. Two values set them separately: gap: 24px 16px means 24 pixels between rows and 16 between columns. Before gap, developers used margins and fixed the extra edge space by hand. Grid skips that headache.

Terminal style code listing for this article: the gallery CSS rules, the verified check on the test file, and the layout measurements for a 900 pixel container.

Step 5: Place Items with grid-column

By default, each item takes one cell and they flow in order. Sometimes one item deserves more room, like a featured card at the top of a gallery. Use grid-column on that item:

.featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

span 2 means this item stretches across two columns. You can also name exact lines: grid-column: 1 / 3 means start at line 1 and end at line 3, the same width. Beginners usually find span easier, so start there. The row version is grid-row.

Good structure helps Grid too. Using meaningful elements for your sections and cards, as covered in our guide to HTML semantic tags explained with examples, keeps your markup clear while Grid handles the visual placement.

Step 6: A Complete Card Gallery You Can Copy

Now put it all together. This is the exact example tested for this article. It builds a gallery with a wide featured card and four normal cards:

<div class="gallery">
  <article class="card featured">
    <h2>Featured</h2><p>Wide card.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 2</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 3</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 4</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Card 5</h2><p>Normal card.</p></article>
</div>

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 16px;
  max-width: 900px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}
.card {
  background: #eef6ff;
  padding: 20px;
  border-radius: 8px;
}
.featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

Here is what happens. The gallery has three equal columns. In a 900 pixel container, each column is 289.33 pixels wide, because the two 16 pixel gaps use 32 pixels first: (900 minus 32) divided by 3. The featured card spans two columns, so it is 594.67 pixels wide. Row one holds the featured card and Card 2. Row two holds Cards 3, 4 and 5. No floats and no extra wrapper divs.

We verified this example in a standalone HTML file: the CSS braces were balanced, all the Grid properties were present, and the five article elements were correctly opened and closed. Try changing repeat(3, 1fr) to repeat(2, 1fr) and watch the gallery rebuild into two columns.

Grid vs Flexbox: Which One Should You Use?

Grid and Flexbox are friends, not rivals. Flexbox lays items out in one direction, a row or a column. Grid works in two directions at once. If you know the shape of the whole page, Grid usually wins. For a line of items that should wrap and centre, Flexbox is often simpler. Our companion guide to CSS Flexbox explained with simple examples covers that case in the same style.

Question CSS Grid Flexbox
Main job Page layouts in rows and columns Items in a single row or column
Directions Two: rows and columns together One at a time
Best for Galleries, dashboards, whole pages Menus, toolbars, centring items
Item placement You can place items in exact cells Items flow and size by content
Typical start grid-template-columns justify-content and align-items

A common pattern is Grid for the page and Flexbox inside each card.

Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting

Putting display: grid on the wrong element. Grid only controls direct children. If your cards are wrapped in extra divs, the wrapper becomes the item, not the card. Check your HTML nesting first.

Expecting gap around the outside. gap adds space only between tracks. If you want space around the whole grid, add padding to the container.

Confusing columns and rows. grid-template-columns controls widths as you read across. If your layout looks rotated, you probably swapped the two template properties.

Fixed sizes that overflow small screens. Three 200 pixel columns need at least 600 pixels plus gaps. On a phone that overflows. Prefer fr units for flexible columns, and test at a narrow width.

Forgetting that extra items create new rows. Grid adds rows for items you did not plan for. Check your item count when a layout looks taller than expected.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is CSS Grid hard for beginners?

No. Start with display: grid, grid-template-columns and gap. Those three alone build most beginner layouts, and the rest can wait.

What does 1fr mean in Grid?

It means one fraction of the free space left after fixed sizes and gaps are taken away. Three columns of 1fr share that space equally.

Should I learn Grid or Flexbox first?

Learn Flexbox basics first if you mainly centre items and build menus, then learn Grid for full page layouts. In practice you will use both together.

Does Grid work in all modern browsers?

Yes. Grid is supported in all modern browsers, including Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, so the examples in this article are safe to use today.

How do I make a grid item span two rows?

Use grid-row: span 2 on that item, in the same way grid-column: span 2 spans two columns.

Conclusion

Grid stops being scary once you see it as a described spreadsheet: a container, columns and rows you define, fr units that share space fairly, gap for breathing room, and grid-column when one item needs more space. Copy the gallery, change the numbers, and break it on purpose.

title: Catching PostgreSQL Double-Spends in 60ms on the Wire Protocol (Without Touching App Code)
description:
Imagine a classic wallet withdrawal endpoint in Go, Python, Node, or Rust. Everything is wrapped inside a database transaction:

tx, _ := pool.Begin(ctx)
defer tx.Rollback(ctx)

var balance int64
_ = tx.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = $1", walletID).Scan(&balance)
if balance < amount {
    return ErrInsufficientFunds
}

_, _ = tx.Exec(ctx, "UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2", amount, walletID)
_ = tx.Commit(ctx)

Your unit tests pass. Your sequential integration tests pass. Code review looks clean.

Then in production, a mobile client retries on a flaky network or a webhook fires twice in the same millisecond. Wallet 1 starts with balance = 100. Both POST /withdraw requests for 100 return 200 OK. The database now says balance = -100.

Why? Because PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED, where each statement sees a snapshot of data committed before that statement began. Most critical concurrency bugs in backend systems aren't memory data races inside one process. They are interleavings of SQL transactions across the network:

  • Check-then-act double spends
  • Lost updates (SET balance = $computed overwriting a concurrent write)
  • Write skew across multiple rows or aggregate checks (SELECT COUNT(*))
  • Phantom inserts before uniqueness or quota checks
  • Lock-order deadlocks when two endpoints touch rows in opposite order

Load tests (k6, wrk) only hit that microsecond race window by luck and give you no deterministic way to replay the failure. Thread model checkers like tokio-rs/loom only see threads and atomics inside a single Rust binary, stopping at the socket boundary.

So I built PgLoom, an open-source (Apache-2.0) deterministic race-condition model checker written in Rust that operates directly on the PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol.

Voskan / pgloom

Deterministic race-condition testing for PostgreSQL-backed services. A wire-protocol proxy explores how transactions interleave and finds double spends, lost updates and deadlocks, with exact replay. No code changes, any language.

PgLoom

Deterministic race-condition testing for anything that talks to PostgreSQL.

PgLoom is a model checker that sits between your service and PostgreSQL as a wire-protocol proxy. It fires concurrent requests at your service, holds every database round trip at a gate, and systematically explores how the transactions can interleave. When an interleaving breaks an invariant (a double spend, a lost update, a negative balance, a deadlock), it prints the exact schedule, explains the root cause, and writes a file that replays the bug deterministically in milliseconds.

No SDK, no code changes, no sleeps: point the service's DATABASE_URL at the proxy. It works the same for Go, Rust, Python, TypeScript, Java or anything else that speaks the PostgreSQL v3 protocol.

$ pgloom demo

Plain-text transcript 
✗ RACE CONDITION DETECTED  [demo-wallet-withdraw]
  Explored 3/50 schedules in 66ms (1-preemption trace)
  Violated Invariants:
    • no_negative_balance: Wallet balance must never drop below zero
      Observed DB state:
…
View on GitHub

How PgLoom Works Without SDKs or Code Changes

Every database-backed service already funnels its state transitions through one narrow choke point: DATABASE_URL.

Instead of instrumenting your application code, PgLoom sits as a stateful TCP proxy between your unmodified service and a real PostgreSQL instance (tested across PostgreSQL 12 through 17):

  1. Wire-Turn Gating (pgloom-wire): PgLoom speaks the PostgreSQL v3 frontend/backend protocol, parsing Simple Query, Extended Query pipelines (Parse, Bind, Describe, Execute, Flush, Sync), and COPY streams. Whenever a worker completes a protocol round trip, PgLoom holds that turn at a gate before forwarding it upstream. Because it works at the wire level, it doesn't care whether your app is written in Go (pgx), Python (psycopg / asyncpg), TypeScript (pg / Prisma), Java (JDBC / Hibernate), or Rust (sqlx / tokio-postgres).
  2. Source-DPOR Schedule Exploration (pgloom-engine): Blindly permuting every query across workers blows up factorially. PgLoom extracts read/write footprints from SQL statements, enriches them with pg_catalog metadata (foreign keys and triggers), and uses Source-DPOR (dynamic partial-order reduction with sleep sets) to skip Mazurkiewicz-equivalent schedules that are guaranteed to produce the exact same database state.
  3. Parking Row-Lock Waiters via pg_blocking_pids() (pgloom-pgctrl): What happens when Worker B executes UPDATE (or SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE) on a row already locked by Worker A? Postgres blocks Worker B inside the lock manager, so ReadyForQuery won't come back until Worker A finishes. A naive proxy would hang. PgLoom polls pg_blocking_pids(), recognizes that Worker B is blocked by Worker A, parks Worker B, hands control back to Worker A, and flags true lock cycles as deadlocks.
  4. Real COMMITs + Sub-Millisecond Resets: A tempting shortcut in test harnesses is wrapping each run in BEGIN / SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK. Unfortunately, faking commits with savepoints silently changes READ COMMITTED visibility semantics and hides real bugs. PgLoom executes genuine COMMITs against PostgreSQL on every schedule and restores dirty tables in <1ms from an UNLOGGED snapshot schema.

What a Scenario Looks Like

Pointing PgLoom at an existing service takes a single pgloom.yaml file. Here is a complete double-spend scenario against an HTTP wallet service:

version: 1
name: "wallet-withdraw-double-spend"

database:
  upstream: "postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres"
  proxy_listen: "127.0.0.1:15432"
  setup_sql: |
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS wallets (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, balance BIGINT NOT NULL);
    TRUNCATE wallets;
    INSERT INTO wallets (id, balance) VALUES (1, 100);

target:
  command: "go run ."
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:15432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
    LISTEN_ADDR: "127.0.0.1:18080"
  ready_http: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/healthz"

workers:
  - id: "req_a"
    http:
      method: "POST"
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/withdraw"
      headers: { Content-Type: "application/json" }
      body: '{"wallet_id": 1, "amount": 100}'
  - id: "req_b"
    http:
      method: "POST"
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:18080/withdraw"
      headers: { Content-Type: "application/json" }
      body: '{"wallet_id": 1, "amount": 100}'

invariants:
  sql:
    - name: "no_negative_balance"
      description: "Wallet balance must never drop below zero"
      assert_true: "SELECT COALESCE(MIN(balance), 0) >= 0 FROM wallets"
      diagnostic_query: "SELECT id, balance FROM wallets"
  responses:
    - name: "at_most_one_successful_withdrawal"
      max_2xx_count: 1

Running pgloom run explores the interleavings in ~60ms, prints the exact step-by-step execution trace, runs the built-in SQL Fix Advisor, and writes .pgloom-repro.json so anyone on your team (or CI) can replay that exact schedule deterministically via pgloom replay:

[FAIL] RACE CONDITION DETECTED  [wallet-withdraw-double-spend]
Explored 3/50 schedules in 66ms (1-preemption trace)
Observed DB state: id=1, balance=-100 (req_a=200, req_b=200)

+------+------------------------+------------------------+
| Step | Worker req_a (pid 205) | Worker req_b (pid 204) |
+------+------------------------+------------------------+
|  t3  | SELECT balance -> 100  |                        |
|  t4  | UPDATE balance - 100   |                        |
|  >>  |       --- context switch (preempt) ---->        |
|  t5  | [paused before COMMIT] | SELECT balance -> 100  |
|  t6  |                        | UPDATE balance - 100   |
|      |                        | [blocked by req_a]     |
|  t7  | COMMIT -> HTTP 200 OK  |                        |
|  t9  |                        | lock granted -> UPD 1  |
| t10  |                        | COMMIT -> HTTP 200 OK  |
+------+------------------------+------------------------+

Fix Option A (Pessimistic Lock):
  SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
Fix Option B (Atomic Guarded Update):
  UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1;

"Why Not Just Set SERIALIZABLE Everywhere?"

Whenever transaction anomalies come up, someone reasonably asks: why not turn on SERIALIZABLE (Postgres SSI) globally?

If you have low write contention and clean transaction-retry boundaries from day one, SSI is awesome. In practice, two things push most high-throughput production backends back toward READ COMMITTED with targeted locking or atomic predicates:

  1. Hot-row 40001 retry storms: On hot merchant accounts, fee pools, or shared inventory counters, SERIALIZABLE aborts concurrent writers with SQLSTATE 40001 instead of queuing them cleanly in Postgres's lock manager. Under load bursts, that turns into retry loops and p99 tail-latency spikes, whereas FOR NO KEY UPDATE or a guarded UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= $1 serializes just that row in one pass.
  2. Legacy codebases & side-effect hazards: Most existing services and ORMs aren't structured around pure, side-effect-free retry closures. Forgetting a 40001 retry handler leaks HTTP 500s under contention; retrying naively when the handler also touches Redis, logs an audit event, or calls a payment gateway risks duplicate side effects.

And if you do run SERIALIZABLE, PgLoom is complementary: it deterministically forces 40001 serialization conflicts in CI so you can prove your retry loop actually converges and preserves both DB and HTTP invariants.

Try It Locally in 10 Seconds

PgLoom ships with a self-contained pgloom demo command that spins up an in-process vulnerable wallet handler, catches the double-spend, patches the query with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, and re-verifies every interleaving (using your local Postgres or spinning up a throwaway postgres:17-alpine container):

# Via Cargo (Rust 1.89+):
cargo install pgloom --locked
pgloom demo

# Or grab a prebuilt static binary (Linux x86_64/arm64 & macOS Apple Silicon/Intel):
curl -sSfL https://github.com/Voskan/pgloom/releases/latest/download/pgloom-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz | tar -xz
./pgloom-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/pgloom demo

title: Playwright Email Fixtures Need Better Failure Evidence
description:
Email tests rarely fail because an email is completely absent. More often, the test sees the wrong message, reads the inbox too early, or loses the evidence that would explain what happened. A temp mail generator can provide a useful isolated fixture, but isolation alone does not make an end-to-end test diagnosable.

This is the workflow I use when a Playwright email test is flaky: define the expected states, capture the first useful evidence, and make every retry explain what changed. The goal is not to add more waits. It is to make the failure tell us which boundary broke.

The failure is often a missing state, not a missing email

Consider a signup test that requests a verification code. The test opens an inbox and waits for a message with the subject “Verify your account.” It passes locally, then fails in CI with “message not found.”

That message hides several different failures:

  • The signup request never completed.
  • The message was sent to a previous fixture address.
  • The inbox API returned an older message first.
  • The email arrived after the polling deadline.
  • The code was present, but the selector matched the wrong element.
  • The test found the message but failed while parsing its body.

Each case needs a different fix. A longer timeout only makes some of them slower. The first diagnostic step is to record the boundary events: fixture created, address submitted, request accepted, message observed, code extracted, and verification completed.

Model the fixture as a state ledger

I prefer a small state ledger over a single waitForEmail() helper. The ledger gives each transition a timestamp and a compact detail value without storing the whole mailbox contents in every log line.

type EmailState =
  | "fixture-created"
  | "address-submitted"
  | "message-observed"
  | "code-extracted"
  | "verified"
  | "expired";

const states: Array<{ name: EmailState; at: string; detail?: string }> = [];

function mark(name: EmailState, detail?: string) {
  states.push({ name, at: new Date().toISOString(), detail });
}

The ledger should be attached to the test result when a step fails. Do not log the verification code itself; record its source message ID, subject, and age instead. This keeps the artifact useful without turning a CI report into a copy of the inbox.

A state ledger also catches an easy-to-miss problem: the first clue are often in the order of events. If message-observed occurs before address-submitted, the test may be reading a stale message or sharing a fixture across workers.

Build a diagnostic Playwright helper

The helper should poll for a message using a stable identity, not a broad text match. A good identity usually combines the fixture address, a test-run token, and a bounded age. Subject text can be part of the check, but it should not be the only check.

async function waitForVerification(page: Page, token: string) {
  const deadline = Date.now() + 30_000;

  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    const message = await readLatestMessage();
    if (message && message.runToken === token) {
      mark("message-observed", message.id);
      const code = extractCode(message.text);
      if (!code) throw new Error(`Message ${message.id} has no code`);
      mark("code-extracted", message.id);
      return code;
    }

    await page.waitForTimeout(1_000);
  }

  mark("expired", `token=${token}`);
  throw new Error("Verification message did not arrive before the deadline");
}

In the real helper, keep the polling interval and deadline configurable. Capture one sanitized response summary on timeout: message count, newest message timestamp, and the requested token. That is usually enough to tell whether delivery or matching failed.

If a selector is involved, prefer a role or a data attribute that the application owns. Avoid a selector such as text=123456; another message can contain the same number. Playwright is very good at reporting selector failures, but only when the test gives it a stable target.

Keep the mailbox boundary explicit

The mailbox is an external dependency even when it is created by a test service. Give each worker a unique address or run token, and clean it up after the test. Also separate the browser timeout from the email delivery timeout. They measure different things and should produce different errors.

When documenting fixtures, search terms can be messy. Someone may write tepm mail com or temp gamil com in a failure ticket. Keep those phrases in troubleshooting notes if they help search older incidents, but do not turn them into selectors or production validation rules. The phrase temp mail mail can likewise appear in an imported test description without being a reliable fixture identifier.

For privacy-sensitive flows, review what the fixture service retains and who can access it. These privacy notes for email checks are a useful reminder that test data still deserves a boundary and a deletion policy.

A repeatable CI failure checklist

When the test fails, check the evidence in this order:

  1. Identity: Was the same address or run token used from setup through message lookup?
  2. Application event: Did the signup request return the expected status before polling began?
  3. Delivery: Did any message arrive within the deadline, even if it had an unexpected subject?
  4. Matching: Did the message contain the current token, or was it stale?
  5. Parsing: Was the message body format different from the local fixture?
  6. Browser state: Did the page navigate, reload, or lose the verification form while waiting?
  7. Artifact quality: Can another engineer replay the relevant inputs from the CI artifact?

If the failure is intermittent, save a small replay pack with the state ledger, sanitized message metadata, request correlation ID, and the final page screenshot. An approach based on replay packs for easier debugging works well because it preserves the facts without asking a developer to guess which retry was meaningful.

Questions that help classify the failure

Should I increase the email timeout first?

No. First determine whether the message arrived late, arrived under a different identity, or was never requested. Increase the deadline only when delivery latency is the known cause, and keep the failure artifact so the new budget remains visible.

Is a temp mail generator suitable for every test?

It is useful for isolated signup and verification scenarios, especially when each run gets a unique fixture. It is less suitable for tests that need long-term mailbox history, guaranteed retention, or sensitive production-like data. In those cases, a controlled fake mail adapter may be more predictable.

What makes an email test reliable?

Reliable tests have unique identity, explicit states, bounded polling, stable selectors, sanitized evidence, and cleanup. They also fail at the first broken boundary. That last part matters most: a test that says “verification failed” is hard to repair, while one that says “message arrived for the previous run token” points directly to fixture isolation.

The practical rule is simple: treat email as a sequence of observable states, not a single asynchronous event. Once Playwright records that sequence, flaky failures become smaller QA problems with evidence instead of mysterious red builds.
