title: UPI MDR Is Back: What NPCI's Supreme Court Defence of the 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate Means for Payment Engineers
description:
For six years I never had to build a fee line for UPI. Every card integration I have shipped carries a fee column in its ledger; every UPI one carried a zero, and most teams eventually dropped the column to tidy the schema. If the reporting is accurate, that tidy-up is about to cost somebody a bad month-end.

I will say my position up front. Most merchants will never compute this fee, because their gateway deducts it. The teams that must build real fee logic are PSPs, aggregators and platforms that settle to sub-merchants. Everyone else needs a place to store the fee and a reconciliation check that understands it. I would not build a full engine unless I sit on the settling side of the flow.

The first sections explain the concept; the later ones cover the design and code. Payment engineers can jump to Part 4.

What I am relying on, and what I have not seen

My inputs are press coverage of NPCI's 3 November 2026 submission to the Supreme Court and the RBI's 5 November 2026 cyber-resilience Master Directions for non-bank payment system operators. The affidavit itself I have not read. The Rs 2,000 threshold and the 0.4% ceiling are the reported numbers; confirm slabs and the effective date against primary documents before shipping. Coverage of the Vyapaar Saksham incentive scheme contradicted itself, so it stays out of every calculation below. It is also the reason the code keeps each number in configuration rather than constants.

Part 1: The plain-language version

UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is India's instant bank-to-bank payment system, used through QR scans or phone-number handles. NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) is the non-profit entity that operates it.

MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) is the cut a merchant gives up on each electronic payment. Cards make the idea familiar: pay Rs 1,000 by card and the shop may receive about Rs 980, the remainder being split between the card network and the two banks. Cards have typically sat around 1.8-2%, depending on category and card type, which is why the proposed ceiling of 0.4% is a fifth of that.

UPI has charged merchants nothing since 2020. Small shops had no reason to refuse it, which is a big part of why it spread so fast. The running cost did not vanish, though; banks and the operator carried servers, fraud tooling and support, partly offset by government incentives.

As reported, NPCI told the court a revised MDR framework is needed for the system to stay financially sustainable. The proposal is narrow:

  • It applies only to P2M payments, i.e. person-to-merchant.
  • P2P, person-to-person, stays free.
  • It applies only above Rs 2,000 per transaction.
  • It is capped at up to 0.4%.
  • Merchants cannot pass it on to customers.

A Rs 1,500 grocery bill is untouched. A Rs 10,000 electronics bill at the full 0.4% costs the merchant Rs 40, and the customer still pays Rs 10,000.

Scale is what makes it matter: UPI has been running at well over 20 billion transactions a month, so even a fraction of them above the threshold adds up to a real revenue line. This would be the first time the rail has carried an explicit price.

Part 2: Why this is hard even though the rule sounds simple

The rule fits in five bullets, but each one conceals an engineering choice.

"Only person-to-merchant." The UPI protocol carries merchant category information, but not every payment arrives labelled cleanly. A neighbourhood tea stall may collect on a personal QR code. A freelancer may use a personal handle for business. Whether a payment is P2M depends on how the receiver is registered in your system, and you may have to treat the registration as the source of truth instead of the payer's app.

"Above Rs 2,000." Is that strictly above, or at or above? Is it measured on the transaction amount or on the order total when an order is split across payments? Does the fee apply to the entire amount or only to the portion above Rs 2,000? Reporting so far does not settle these questions, so I model them as policy options. Card pricing is the closest precedent: interchange is applied to the whole transaction amount, not an excess over a slab, and slab edges are defined per category in the network's own rules. My bet is the same here: full amount, strictly above the threshold, measured per transaction rather than per order. I would still keep the other combinations switchable, since a split cart paying Rs 1,200 twice is exactly the case someone will try to game.

"Up to 0.4%." The words "up to" mean the effective rate may vary by merchant category or by agreement. Your engine needs a rate lookup, not a global constant.

"Cannot be passed on." This is a checkout rule. If your platform has ever offered a "convenience fee" line for certain payment methods, that logic now becomes a compliance risk for UPI. You need a technical guard, not just a policy document.

Refunds and reversals. This is the case I would settle before any other, because it is where fee logic goes wrong most often. If a Rs 10,000 payment is refunded, is the Rs 40 returned to the merchant? Card networks usually return interchange on a full reversal, but nothing I have read says what UPI will do. Model it as a policy flag, and post the fee reversal as its own ledger line linked to the original, so a partial refund can prorate it. Dispute outcomes through NPCI's UDIR process need the same treatment.

On a payment integration I worked on earlier, fee rules ended up in three places: a spreadsheet finance maintained, a controller constant and a database trigger. Nobody planned that; each was a quick fix at the time. Within a few months they disagreed on edge cases, and we spent a painful stretch working out which of the three the bank's numbers actually matched. That is why I now insist on one fee engine, one source of truth and one audit trail. My wider background is in the experience section.

Part 3: The money flow, step by step

Follow a UPI merchant payment and note where the fee enters.

  1. The customer approves the payment in their UPI app. The customer's bank debits the full amount, with no deduction.
  2. NPCI routes the instruction and the merchant's acquiring side receives a credit notification. The acquirer is the bank or provider that onboards the merchant.
  3. Your payment backend, whether you are a PSP (payment service provider) or a merchant platform, records a successful collection for the gross amount.
  4. At settlement time, the money that reaches the merchant is the gross amount minus the MDR, and possibly minus tax on that fee. Taxes on fees are another reason to keep the fee as its own record.
  5. Reconciliation compares what your ledger expects against what the bank statement and the NPCI settlement file actually show.

Step 1 is identical to today: the customer sees the same debit. Everything new sits on the merchant side, in steps 3 to 5, so this is back-office work rather than anything a user would notice. Note too who does the deducting. If you collect through a payment aggregator or gateway, it takes the MDR before paying you out, and your system only needs to mirror what it was told. Settlement cycles are typically T+1 or similar, and the aggregator's settlement report, not your own estimate, is the authority on what was deducted. Only if you are the settling party do you compute the fee yourself.

A ledger entry for a Rs 10,000 payment should end up as three lines instead of one:

Account Debit Credit
Customer collection (gross) 10,000.00
Merchant payable 9,960.00
MDR income / expense 40.00

A single net number is not enough. If you store only Rs 9,960, you cannot later prove to the merchant or an auditor why it was not Rs 10,000.

Part 4: Architecture of a fee engine

For anyone who does settle, this is the design I would use: four small components, deliberately kept apart.

Classifier. Takes the payment event and decides P2M or P2P, with a reason string. The reason matters when a merchant disputes a charge six months later.

Policy resolver. Given the merchant, category and date, returns the active fee policy: threshold, rate, whether the fee applies to the full amount or the excess, rounding mode, and an effective-from date. Policies are versioned, never edited in place.

Calculator. A pure function. Amount plus policy in, fee out. No database calls, no clock reads. Pure functions are cheap to test with thousands of edge cases.

Ledger writer. Writes the gross, fee and net lines atomically with the policy version that produced them.

The pure calculator is what lets me sleep. In the market-data systems I run, I use the same discipline to make results replayable, which I wrote about in deterministic market data replay. For fees the payoff is the same: given the same inputs and the same policy version, you get the same paise every time, even years later.

Money rules I do not bend

  • Use BigDecimal, or integer paise. Never double.
  • Pick one rounding mode, record it in the policy, and apply it once per transaction.
  • Store the fee at the time of the transaction. Do not recompute it later from the current policy, or old data will change when rates change.
  • Make the write idempotent. UPI callbacks get retried, and a duplicate callback must not charge a duplicate fee. The pattern I use is the one in my post on the transactional outbox and idempotent consumers.

Part 5: A Spring Boot sketch of the fee engine

Treat this as a sketch to adapt, not a drop-in. Every threshold, rate and mode comes from a policy record, because the final slabs and effective date are not mine to hard-code.

public enum PayeeType { P2P, P2M }

public enum FeeBasis { FULL_AMOUNT, EXCESS_OVER_THRESHOLD }

public record FeePolicy(
        String version,
        BigDecimal threshold,        // e.g. 2000.00, from config
        boolean thresholdInclusive,  // is exactly 2000.00 charged?
        BigDecimal rate,             // e.g. 0.004 for 0.4%, or lower per category
        FeeBasis basis,
        RoundingMode rounding,
        LocalDate effectiveFrom) {}

public record FeeResult(BigDecimal fee, String policyVersion, String reason) {}

public final class MdrCalculator {

    public FeeResult compute(PayeeType type, BigDecimal amount, FeePolicy p) {
        if (type == PayeeType.P2P) {
            return new FeeResult(BigDecimal.ZERO.setScale(2), p.version(), "P2P_EXEMPT");
        }
        int cmp = amount.compareTo(p.threshold());
        boolean charged = p.thresholdInclusive() ? cmp >= 0 : cmp > 0;
        if (!charged) {
            return new FeeResult(BigDecimal.ZERO.setScale(2), p.version(), "BELOW_THRESHOLD");
        }
        BigDecimal base = p.basis() == FeeBasis.FULL_AMOUNT
                ? amount
                : amount.subtract(p.threshold());
        BigDecimal fee = base.multiply(p.rate()).setScale(2, p.rounding());
        return new FeeResult(fee, p.version(), "P2M_ABOVE_THRESHOLD");
    }
}

The service around it loads the policy that was active on the transaction date, not today's, and posts the ledger lines in one database transaction:

@Service
class SettlementPostingService {

    private final PolicyRepository policies;
    private final LedgerRepository ledger;
    private final MdrCalculator calculator = new MdrCalculator();

    SettlementPostingService(PolicyRepository policies, LedgerRepository ledger) {
        this.policies = policies;
        this.ledger = ledger;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void post(UpiCollection c) {
        if (ledger.existsByUpiRef(c.upiRef())) {
            return; // retried callback, already posted
        }
        FeePolicy policy = policies.activeOn(c.merchantCategory(), c.txnDate());
        FeeResult fee = calculator.compute(c.payeeType(), c.amount(), policy);

        BigDecimal net = c.amount().subtract(fee.fee());
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.collection(c.upiRef(), c.amount()));
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.mdr(c.upiRef(), fee.fee(), fee.policyVersion(), fee.reason()));
        ledger.save(LedgerEntry.merchantPayable(c.upiRef(), net));
    }
}

The unique constraint on upiRef in the database is the real idempotency guard. The existsBy check is a cheap shortcut, and the constraint catches the race when two callbacks arrive at once.

Blocking surcharges at checkout

The no-pass-through rule needs a guard at the point where the cart total is built. I prefer to make it structurally impossible instead of relying on code review:

public CheckoutQuote quote(Cart cart, PaymentMethod method) {
    BigDecimal base = cart.total();
    BigDecimal methodFee = feeSchedule.customerFeeFor(method, base);

    if (method == PaymentMethod.UPI && methodFee.signum() != 0) {
        // The merchant bears MDR. A customer-facing fee on UPI must never exist.
        audit.record("UPI_SURCHARGE_BLOCKED", cart.id(), methodFee);
        methodFee = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    }
    return new CheckoutQuote(base, methodFee, base.add(methodFee));
}

Silently zeroing the fee is a choice. In a stricter setup, I would throw and fail the quote so the misconfiguration is noticed in testing rather than papered over in production. Either way, the audit event is the part a regulator will ask for.

Part 6: Reconciliation, where fee bugs actually show up

Calculating the fee correctly is half the job. The other half is proving that what you calculated matches what actually arrived. A reconciliation check compares three sources: your ledger, the acquirer's settlement file, and the bank credit.

The check I would run nightly, per merchant per settlement cycle:

public ReconReport reconcile(String merchantId, LocalDate cycle, SettlementFile file) {
    BigDecimal expectedGross = ledger.sumCollections(merchantId, cycle);
    BigDecimal expectedFee   = ledger.sumMdr(merchantId, cycle);
    BigDecimal expectedNet   = expectedGross.subtract(expectedFee);

    BigDecimal reportedFee = file.totalFee(merchantId);
    BigDecimal reportedNet = file.totalNet(merchantId);

    List<Break> breaks = new ArrayList<>();
    if (expectedFee.compareTo(reportedFee) != 0) {
        breaks.add(Break.feeMismatch(expectedFee, reportedFee));
    }
    if (expectedNet.compareTo(reportedNet) != 0) {
        breaks.add(Break.netMismatch(expectedNet, reportedNet));
    }
    // Transaction-level diff only when totals disagree, to keep the job cheap
    if (!breaks.isEmpty()) {
        breaks.addAll(txnLevelDiff(merchantId, cycle, file));
    }
    return new ReconReport(merchantId, cycle, breaks);
}

Raw settlement data from NPCI and the acquirer arrives as files, and the column layout differs by bank, so write one adapter per source that maps into a common SettlementFile shape rather than scattering parsing through the job. Two practical points from experience. First, compare fee totals separately from net totals. If only the net differs, you cannot tell whether the cause is a wrong fee, a missing transaction or a timing cut-off. Splitting them narrows the search immediately. Second, a difference of a few paise across thousands of rows is almost always rounding. If the acquirer rounds per transaction and you round per batch, you will drift. Match their rule exactly and record it in the policy.

The threshold boundary deserves its own test. I would add test cases at 1,999.99, 2,000.00 and 2,000.01, with both inclusive and exclusive settings. That is where an off-by-one in a comparison quietly turns into a recurring mismatch on exactly the payments people round to, like a Rs 2,000 bill.

If you want to see how I approach large volumes with predictable behaviour, the projects section and my write-up on high-throughput Java under virtual threads cover the throughput side of reconciliation jobs.

Part 7: The second half of the news, RBI's cyber-resilience Master Directions

The same week brought a second development that affects the same operators. On 5 November 2026 the RBI issued cyber-resilience Master Directions for non-bank payment system operators, often shortened to PSOs. These are the non-bank companies that run wallets, payment gateways and similar services under RBI authorisation.

I have not memorised every clause, and you should read the text itself, but the direction of travel matches what I have seen in other regulated sectors: stronger security controls, incident reporting, and evidence that you can prove what happened. For a fee engine this matters in concrete ways:

  • Audit trails. Every fee decision should be reconstructible: which policy version, which inputs, which result. The reason and policyVersion fields above exist for this purpose.
  • Change control. A rate change is a financial change and a security-relevant one. Policies should be versioned, approved by two people and logged.
  • Access control. Who can edit fee policies, and who can view merchant settlement data? Keep those roles separate.
  • Resilience. If the fee engine is down, do you fail closed and hold settlement, or fail open and post later? Decide deliberately and document it.

I wrote about producing this kind of evidence automatically in DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code. The regulators differ, but the engineering habit is shared: make compliance a by-product of how the system runs, not a quarterly scramble.

What I would do this week

Rules like these tend to arrive with short notice and a long tail of clarifications. Rather than wait for every detail, I would prepare the parts that will not change:

  1. Put a fee field in your ledger. Gross, fee and net as separate lines, even if the fee is zero today.
  2. Tag every payee as P2P or P2M with a stored reason, and decide who owns corrections when the tag is wrong.
  3. Move all thresholds, rates and rounding rules into versioned policy records. No constants in code.
  4. Add the surcharge guard to checkout and alert on any attempt.
  5. Add the fee-versus-net split to nightly reconciliation.
  6. Read the primary texts. Confirm the slabs, the basis of calculation, the effective date and any carve-outs against the NPCI affidavit and the RBI Master Directions, and treat unconfirmed items such as the Vyapaar Saksham scheme as unknown until a primary source says otherwise.

My honest view is that the 0.4% itself is the least interesting number. What matters is that India's flagship public digital rail now has a price signal in it, and every system that touched it assumed that price was zero. Systems built on a hidden assumption break in surprising places, usually in a reconciliation report at month end.

If you are planning this change and want a second pair of eyes on a fee engine, ledger design or reconciliation job, reach me through the contact section. Before that, open your current UPI ledger schema today and check whether it has a place to store a fee next to the gross amount. If it does not, that is your first ticket.

Related Articles

  • Transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for Spring Boot payment systems
  • ASEAN cross-border QR payments: an EMVCo router in Spring Boot

title: Turning a Past Coding-Agent Run into an Evaluation Case
description:
I want to know whether a change to my coding-agent setup actually helps. But in everyday development, each issue is different. Completion times and successful runs alone tell me little about whether a new model, harness, or set of instructions is better.

I tried turning one past development task into an evaluation case: give a fresh agent session the original requirements and starting source, then check the implementation it produces.

The useful discovery was how much of that starting point I already had. My saved job contained the initial requirements and starting commit SHA. I could extract the task and retrieve the source from Git without building an agent to reconstruct missing files.

This article is adapted from my Japanese article on Zenn.

What I borrowed from Trace2Eval

The experiment was inspired by Trace2Eval, a paper about constructing coding-agent evaluations from real user interactions.

Its reconstruction process recovers three inputs: the user's task, the workspace before the interaction, and the initial execution environment. A candidate agent receives that context and produces an artifact for evaluation.

For files, the process uses content observed in the trace and infers or retrieves what is missing. It excludes artifacts created during the session and distinguishes dependencies that existed initially from those installed during execution.

I borrowed the idea of preparing those three inputs, but adapted the method to my own records:

Input What I used
Requirements The initial job saved by my development system
Starting source The Git tree at the job's recorded starting SHA
Execution environment A runnable approximation based on observed versions and the lockfile

This is an independent implementation inspired by the paper, rather than a reproduction of its full pipeline. I did not refer to the authors' implementation code.

I also simplified two substantial parts. I omitted the loop that replays original tool calls, compares their results, and repairs the recovered environment. For scoring, I implemented task-specific behavioral checks instead of adopting the paper's rubric and LLM-judge approach.

The code is in spike-trace2eval.

The task I chose

My development system, coding-worker, retains requirements, starting commits, tool events, patches, and verification output.

I selected a run that implemented yuurei issue #195. yuurei is my tool for running and recording coding-agent experiments.

The task was to support a task body supplied as a string:

  • Execute it without creating a task file inside the project.
  • Produce the same task digest for identical content, whether supplied through a file or as a string.

The requirements came from the issue body, acceptance criteria, and constraints saved at the start of the original run.

I deliberately chose a tractable case. It had retained initial requirements and a starting SHA, limited external-service dependencies, and behavior I could check by executing the CLI.

“Solving it again” meant implementing those requirements in a fresh session from the original source. The new patch did not have to match the old one.

The input was more than a chat log

I used the saved records for one execution:

Record Purpose
Initial job Recover the issue body, acceptance criteria, constraints, check commands, budget, and starting SHA
Event log Inspect the initial prompt, tool operations, and environment observations
Manifest Cross-check the run identity and starting SHA
Checksum list Check consistency of the saved evidence files
Original patch and verification output Evaluator-side references, excluded from the new agent's input

The event log contained 6,588 events and 85 distinct tool operations from one session. I also used the target repository's Git data.

That distinction matters: the log did not contain a complete source snapshot. The starting SHA let me retrieve that snapshot from Git.

The raw trace, full initial prompt, and patches are private. The public repository contains the recovery and evaluation code, synthetic tests, and reports with limited evidence detail.

Building the evaluation inputs

The following describes the current implementation, including safeguards added after the first real run. I separate those later changes from the historical result below.

Extract the initial task

The pipeline cross-checks the run identity and starting SHA across the job, manifest, and event log. It also checks event sequences, tool-call/result pairing, and evidence checksums.

Requirements are extracted mechanically from the initial job, with a source reference for each field. The issue body, for example, comes from job.issue.body.

I also regenerated the initial prompt from the saved job and the historical template, then checked that it matched the prompt recorded in the event log.

I chose not to summarize the full trace into a new task description. The trace also contains investigation, failed attempts, edits, and the final answer. Rewriting the task from all of that could introduce hints unavailable at the start.

Here, the original requirements were already present. Extracting them directly made their provenance easier to inspect.

Retrieve the starting source

The pipeline retrieves only the recorded starting commit into a new directory. It checks that HEAD matches the pinned SHA, history contains one commit, there are no remotes, and the working tree is clean.

The current implementation also removes and checks Git metadata that could retain the operator's local paths.

This recovers the Git-tracked source. It cannot recover unrecorded local files.

Prepare an approximate environment

The original log showed Node 26.8.2 and pnpm 11.6.0, while the starting repository configuration declared Node 24.

I selected the observed versions: Node 26.8.2 and pnpm 11.6.0. The environment record keeps observations, selected values, unknowns, and deviations separate.

Dependencies are installed from the starting commit's lockfile. Generated dependencies such as node_modules are kept distinct from the starting source. Setup and existing checks run in a separate working copy to confirm that the selected environment is usable.

The exact original OS version, full PATH and environment variables, internal harness instructions, and automatically injected context were unavailable. I treated the result as a documented approximation.

The environment documentation records the selection.

Limit the agent's input package

The package has four entries:

Input Contents
task.md Requirements and execution conditions derived from the initial job
source/ Source at the starting commit
environment.json Environment observations and deviations
setup.sh Dependency setup procedure

The original trace, patch, final answer, and evaluator stay on the evaluation side. Checks inspect file inventories, hashes, provenance, escaping symlinks, and Git history.

The pipeline uses Python's standard library and separates extraction, source preparation, environment preparation, input inspection, controls, execution, scoring, and reporting. Each stage leaves a record, and the next stage requires valid preceding records.

The evaluator was specific to this task

Preparing the inputs was only part of constructing an evaluation case. I still needed a way to decide whether the new implementation satisfied the task.

The starting commit already passed all five existing repository checks. Passing those checks again would not demonstrate that the new feature worked.

I therefore implemented behavioral checks derived from the requirements. The evaluator runs the modified yuurei CLI and checks:

Check What it establishes
File input Existing file-based task execution still works
String input A supported inline form, such as stdin, executes
Body integrity The supplied body reaches the runtime unchanged
Digest correctness Both input forms produce the body's SHA-256
Digest equality Identical bodies have identical digests across input forms
Different content Changing the body produces the expected different digest
Input provenance Files retain their actual path; inline input has an identifier such as stdin
File creation No new project files appear outside evaluator-managed locations

A dummy runtime records the body it receives. This checks that the content reached the runtime, beyond whether the command exited successfully. These behavioral checks require no model inference.

The evaluator also runs the existing tests, build, lint, format, and knip checks. A result is satisfied only if all required behavioral and repository checks pass. Missing verification does not count as success.

I tested the evaluator with two controls:

  • The unchanged starting source must fail.
  • The source with the original implementation patch applied must pass.

The original patch is used only by the evaluator for that control. It is excluded from the new agent's inputs.

These controls establish that the evaluator can distinguish those two states. They do not prove that it rejects every possible incorrect implementation.

The task inputs came from saved records, but the task-specific evaluator was implemented as part of this proof of concept. It was not generated automatically.

One fresh attempt

I gave the prepared inputs to OpenCode with opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash and ran one new session.

Item Result
Termination completed
Elapsed time 521.5 seconds, about 8 minutes 42 seconds
Generated patch 8 files, 13,084 bytes
Behavioral checks All passed
Five existing repository checks All passed
Verdict satisfied

See the run report.

The result means that a fresh implementation, starting from the same source and requirements in an approximate environment, passed the checks I prepared.

The original execution used the same model through an OpenCode-based setup. This was a fresh attempt, not a comparison between models. The original run went through coding-worker's adapter; the new run invoked the harness directly.

Later safeguards do not change the original result

Review after the run found input-separation problems.

Git's FETCH_HEAD and reflog still contained the operator's local path and Git identity. Environment-variable inheritance also used a blocklist, so most operator environment-variable names were passed through.

I subsequently added Git metadata cleanup and inspection, and changed environment-variable inheritance to an allowlist. I did not rerun the original experiment under those revised conditions.

The inspected tool trace showed no reads of that metadata or the original host-side source. But an absence of recorded reads does not establish that access was technically impossible.

Network and access outside the working directory were not fully isolated at the OS level. The original solution was also public, so I cannot establish that it was absent from the model's training data.

The successful outcome belongs to that one run, under those historical conditions. Because the original evidence and generated patch are private, public materials alone cannot support a complete independent recheck of the run.

What I want to preserve from future runs

The most useful lesson was about the records to retain.

The initial job supplied the requirements. Git supplied the starting source. The event log supported prompt consistency checks and environment observations.

A long execution log and a recoverable starting point are different things.

Saving initial requirements and a starting SHA is a practice I can carry into other tasks. The task-specific evaluator remains additional work when adding cases.

Without changing coding-worker, I connected existing records to case construction, fresh implementation, and scoring. This experiment did not cover requirements added during a conversation or reconstruction from incomplete traces.

Next, I want to freeze the inputs and scoring conditions, run a new experiment with the current safeguards, and try another case with a reconstruction difficulty absent from this one.

If I can preserve past work as tasks that remain runnable after model and harness changes, I can gradually build an evaluation set closer to my own development work.

References

  • Trace2Eval paper — reconstruction procedure in §3.2 and Appendix A.2
  • PoC plan — selected case and simplifications
  • Evaluation design — input boundaries, behavioral checks, and controls
  • Assessment of the first run — assessment at a specific revision of PR #5, excluding subsequent fixes

title: Jira said Done. It wasn't, and the bug showed up later. So I made Jira check first.
description:
Picture this. The ticket moved to Done on Friday. The pull request was merged, CI was green, everyone moved on.

On Monday the checkout total was wrong.

The test that should have caught it was still there. It just didn't check anything anymore. In the last commit, labelled "fix flaky test", one line had changed:

- expect(total(cart)).toBe(90);
+ expect(total(cart)).toBeDefined();

The old line checked that the total is exactly 90. The new one only checks that there is some total. 0 passes. 900 passes. So CI went green, and Jira said Done.

Nobody lied. A developer in a hurry, or an AI agent told to "make the tests pass", took the shortest road to green. In a code review it looks like a one-line tidy-up, so nobody stops it.

The same trick, again and again

I first noticed this while building proof-of-done, a small tool that stops an AI agent from saying "done" before the tests really pass. The quickest way to a green CI was rarely fixing the code. It was one of these:

  • Skipping a test: it.skip(...), @pytest.mark.skip, @Disabled
  • Deleting a test and not replacing it
  • Loosening a check: toBe(90) becomes toBeDefined(), assert.equal(a, b) becomes assert.ok(a)

CI can't see any of this. A skipped test doesn't fail. A deleted test doesn't fail. A loosened check passes even more easily. All three make CI more green.

So I asked one question: before a ticket moves to Done, do its tests still prove what they proved before?

So I made Jira check first

Proof of Done for Jira is a free, open-source Jira app. When someone moves a work item to Done, it reads the pull requests behind it (on GitHub or Bitbucket) and checks four things:

  1. every pull request is merged
  2. CI ran and passed
  3. code changes came with test changes
  4. no test was skipped, deleted or loosened to get green

If something is wrong, Done is blocked, and it shows exactly why: the file, the line, and the test before and after.

It also shows the commit history, and marks the exact commit where CI turned green right after a test was changed:

▶ Watch the 4-minute demo on YouTube

How it knows a test got weaker

It reads the pull request diff line by line. The main rule is simple: a loose check is a problem only when it replaces an exact check about the same thing.

  • expect(user).toBeDefined() in a brand-new test: fine.
  • expect(total(cart)).toBe(90) removed and expect(total(cart)).toBeDefined() added in its place: caught.

It also knows the honest changes that look similar, so it doesn't block good work:

  • tests moved to a new file (the same test names show up again)
  • an expected value changed, like 200 to 201 (still an exact check)
  • a test renamed, or a check made stronger

It works for JavaScript, Python, Java and Go tests. I tested it on 113 small examples: it caught all 66 shortcuts and blocked none of the 47 honest changes. On 100 real merged pull requests from three of my own repositories, it blocked none. The benchmark is in the repo, so anyone can run it with npm run benchmark.

What else you get

  • Create a task to fix this: one click turns the block into a sub-task, with the file, the line and the pull request already written in.
  • A dashboard for team leads: what's ready, what's blocked, and every catch in the project.
  • Override with a reason: if a block is wrong, a project admin can let it through, and the reason stays on the ticket.
  • A receipt on Done: a comment with exactly what was checked, for anyone who asks later.

Try it in 5 minutes

You need a Jira site where you are an admin. Nothing to download.

  1. Install Proof of Done for Jira.
  2. Create a Jira project with the key DEMO and four work items: DEMO-1 to DEMO-4. It reads a ready-made demo repository, so you don't connect anything.
  3. Open Jira settings → Apps → Proof of Done settings, pick DEMO under Turn it on for a project, and press Apply.
  4. Move each work item to Done.

All four demo pull requests are merged with green CI. Only DEMO-1 is really done. The other three get blocked, each with its reason.

Use it on your own project

  1. In the same settings page, add a line like SHOP=your-name/your-repo (or SHOP=bitbucket:workspace/repo for Bitbucket). SHOP is your Jira project key, the letters before the number in SHOP-12.
  2. For a private repository, paste a read-only token. It is stored encrypted.
  3. Turn it on for your project and press Apply.
  4. Put the ticket key in the pull request title or branch name, like SHOP-12: fix checkout total.

Work with no code, like a design or a meeting, just gets the label no-code and goes to Done.

Ask it in Rovo

Rovo is Atlassian's AI chat inside Jira. The app adds its own Rovo agent, called Proof of Done, so anyone on the team can just ask whether a ticket is really done.

Setup: nothing extra. Once the app is installed and turned on for a project (the steps above), the agent is there. You need a Jira site with Rovo, which comes with the Standard, Premium and Enterprise plans. If the agent doesn't show up right after installing, give it a few minutes.

How to use it:

  1. In Jira, click Ask Rovo at the top right. The chat opens on the side.
  2. Type @Proof and pick Proof of Done from the list of agents.
  3. Ask in plain words:
    • "Is DEMO-2 really done?" → "DEMO-2 is not done yet", with the file, the line, the test before and after, and what to fix.
    • "Is DEMO-1 really done?" → yes: the pull request is merged, CI passed and the tests were kept.
    • "Which commit turned CI green for DEMO-4?" → commit a03b524, right after the test was loosened.
    • "What is blocking this from Done?" while you are on any ticket.

It answers only about tickets the person asking can see in Jira.

Ask it from your own AI agent (MCP)

The same check works from Claude Code or any other MCP client:

  1. A Jira admin turns it on once: Atlassian Administration → your site → Connected apps → Proof of Done for Jira → Tools → Enable tools.
  2. Add it to your agent. In Claude Code: 
claude mcp add --transport http proof-of-done https://mcp.atlassian.com/forge/487a9b05-d2bc-4e8f-98ce-2c533e95676f
  1. Sign in with your Atlassian account when asked, then ask your agent "Is SHOP-12 really done?".

Check before merge on Bitbucket

A second small app runs the same check on the Bitbucket pull request itself, before anyone presses Merge:

  1. Install it from the Bitbucket install link.
  2. In Bitbucket: Workspace settings → Custom merge checks, turn them on.
  3. In your repository: Repository settings → Custom merge checks → Add → Proof of Done.

On Bitbucket Premium the check can be made required, so Merge stays locked until it passes.

The full setup guide for all of this is in the README.

Links

  • Demo video: youtu.be/1SK-aSDd0xo
  • Code: github.com/WST2002/proof-of-done-jira
  • Demo repository: github.com/WST2002/proof-of-done-demo
  • The tool it started from: proof-of-done and its 36-second demo
  • More demos on my YouTube channel
  • My entry for Atlassian Codegeist 2026: Devpost page

Your turn

Have you seen a test quietly get weaker just to make CI green? What did the change look like? I'd love to add real examples to the benchmark.

title: Grade once, prove it forever: 46,756 settled calls and the case for an append-only grading ledger
description:
Every prediction system eventually makes a promise like this: "our hit rate is 57%." That is a claim about the past, and it is only meaningful if the past cannot be edited. In almost every system I have audited, the grade is a mutable boolean on the same row as the prediction, updated by whatever job ran last. The row is not a record. It is a cache of the most recent writer's opinion.

The case study: a production system with 46,969 prediction rows, 46,756 of them settled. All figures come from the live database.

What a grade actually contains

A grade is not a boolean. It is a tuple: the frozen inputs, the outcome source, the rule version that mapped outcome to verdict, and the instant the verdict was written. Change any one of the four and you have a different claim wearing the same primary key.

The failure is structural, not a bug. UPDATE ai_predictions SET hit = ... has no memory. When the outcome feed corrects a score ninety minutes after full time, the settle job overwrites the verdict and the previous one ceases to exist. Nobody can prove afterwards whether the row was graded once or nine times.

The evidence: a row that keeps changing

The schema has both settled_at and updated_at. The gap between them is a lower bound on row mutation after grading — not proof of re-grading, because any column write touches updated_at, but it is enough to show the row is not frozen.

SELECT
  count(*)                                                              AS settled,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '1 minute')  AS late_1m,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '1 day')     AS late_1d,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE updated_at > settled_at + interval '7 day')     AS late_7d,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE settled_at > updated_at)                        AS impossible,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NULL)                                    AS settled_no_grade,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE settled_at IS NULL)                             AS settled_no_ts
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled;

 settled | late_1m | late_1d | late_7d | impossible | settled_no_grade | settled_no_ts
---------+---------+---------+---------+------------+------------------+---------------
   46756 |   35414 |   26831 |   21145 |         93 |              120 |           329

75.7% of settled rows were written more than a minute after their own settlement timestamp. 57.4% more than a day later. 45.2% more than a week later. And 93 rows carry a settlement timestamp that is later than their last write — an ordering that cannot happen if settlement is a single atomic act.

The trend shows a process problem being fixed by accident:

Cohort (by created_at) settled written >1d after settlement share
2026-06 2,735 2,735 100.0%
2026-07 2,637 2,636 100.0%
2026-08 164 164 100.0%
2026-09 9,752 8,808 90.3%
2026-10 21,865 11,117 50.8%
2026-11 9,603 1,371 14.3%

Older cohorts were re-touched by every downstream backfill: calibration columns, visibility flags, learning timestamps. Each write was legitimate; collectively they destroyed the only audit trail we had.

A 25-row ledger for 35,414 mutations

One table records a re-grade: r132_settle_reverify_log, 25 rows, spanning 2026-09-22 to 2026-11-09. Of those, 8 changed the recorded outcome and 4 flipped the verdict.

Read that ratio again: when a re-grade was logged, 32% of the time the answer changed. That is the real value of an audit trail — it tells you the base rate of your own corrections. And 25 logged events cannot explain 35,414 mutated rows.

There is a quieter signal. The table has two boolean grade columns, hit and hit_1x2, and they disagree on 391 of 46,636 rows. Two fields meant to say the same thing, disagreeing on 0.84% of the corpus, with no documented rule about which wins. When a consumer asks "what is the hit rate", the honest answer is "of which column".

The 342 rows a guard was designed not to see

The system does recompute grades to check itself. A guard compares stored hit against a recomputation from actual_result and prediction_direction: 1,428 runs recorded, 343 flagged abnormal, most recent run 2026-11-15 12:21.

Latest reading: hit_vs_recalc = 0.74%, mismatch = 342 of n = 46,427, against a 2.0% threshold. The guard is green, and stays green while up to ~928 rows are wrong. A percentage threshold turns an integrity question into a tolerance question, and tolerance always wins — nobody wants a red dashboard.

Here is the query that produces the 342, split by whether the call had one label or two:

SELECT
  prediction_direction LIKE '%/%' AS multi_label,
  count(*)                                                              AS n,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)                                            AS graded_true,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit = (actual_result = split_part(prediction_direction,'/',1)))
                                                                        AS fits_primary_only,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit = (actual_result = ANY(string_to_array(prediction_direction,'/'))))
                                                                        AS fits_any_of_pair
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled AND hit IS NOT NULL AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1;

 multi_label |    n  | graded_true | fits_primary_only | fits_any_of_pair
-------------+-------+-------------+-------------------+------------------
 f           | 29389 |       17319 |             29364 |            29364
 t           | 17039 |        9282 |             12171 |            16722

Single-label rows are clean: 29,364 of 29,389 agree with strict equality, a 0.09% residual. Two-label rows are not. The production rule is clearly "hit if the outcome is either label" — that explains 16,722 of 17,039. But 317 rows fit neither reading. They were graded under a rule that no longer exists, or by a code path since rewritten, and the row cannot tell you which.

That is the concrete cost: not that 317 rows move the headline number (0.68% of 46,756), but that you cannot distinguish "wrong" from "graded under an older rule" and therefore cannot fix either. You can only overwrite, which is how you got here.

The hash column that cannot identify a row

odds_snapshot_hash is the right instinct and the wrong implementation. 2,039 rows have it NULL. Among non-null values, 2,511 groups share a value, and the largest single value is shared by 357 rows, because the hash covers the market-price snapshot rather than the row. Coverage also arrived late: 31.9% of June rows, 96.0% of July, 99.9%+ from September. The field cannot answer "which inputs produced this verdict", only "which snapshot was current" — a weaker claim.

The fix: two pieces, both small

Piece one is an append-only grade ledger with a hash chain. Each entry commits to the previous entry's digest, so the history is verifiable by walking it. The canonical serialization matters more than the hash function — if two processes serialize the same grade differently, the chain reports tampering that did not happen.

import hashlib, json

FIELDS = ("prediction_id", "model_id", "direction", "prob_hash",
          "home_score", "away_score", "outcome", "verdict",
          "rule_version", "graded_at")

def canonical(payload: dict) -> bytes:
    body = {k: payload[k] for k in FIELDS}
    # sort_keys + no whitespace + explicit separators = one byte string per grade
    return json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()

def link(payload: dict, prev_digest: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(prev_digest.encode() + b"|" + canonical(payload)).hexdigest()
    return digest, prev_digest

def verify(entries: list[dict]) -> dict:
    prev = "0" * 64
    bad = []
    for e in entries:
        if e["prev_digest"] != prev:
            bad.append((e["prediction_id"], "broken_link"))
        expect, _ = link(e, prev)
        if expect != e["digest"]:
            bad.append((e["prediction_id"], "payload_changed"))
        prev = e["digest"]
    return {"entries": len(entries), "violations": bad, "head": prev}

Piece two is a database-level refusal. A trigger that rejects any change to the grading columns once a final entry exists turns "we promise to grade once" into "the database will not let us do otherwise". Corrections then go through a new ledger entry with a reason code, not an UPDATE.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION reject_regrade() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.hit IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.hit
     OR OLD.actual_result IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.actual_result
     OR OLD.match_home_score IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.match_home_score
     OR OLD.match_away_score IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.match_away_score
     OR OLD.settled_at IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.settled_at THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'grade is immutable; append a correction entry instead (id=%)', OLD.id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER ai_predictions_grade_frozen
BEFORE UPDATE ON ai_predictions
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION reject_regrade();

Rollout order matters

Do not turn the trigger on first. Freeze what you have, label it, then close it.

  1. Backfill one ledger entry per settled row, marked origin = 'backfill'. This deliberately blesses today's values, including the 342 mismatches.
  2. Quarantine the 342 into a disputed column rather than overwriting. A human adjudicates them exactly once.
  3. Resolve hit vs hit_1x2: one canonical, the other derived in a view. Two writable booleans for one fact is a bug on a schedule.
  4. Then enable the trigger, routing every correction through an append-only entry with rule_version and reason.
  5. Run verify() hourly and alarm on any violation, not on a percentage. A chain either verifies or it does not.

The payoff is not tidiness. With a chain you can answer what is currently unanswerable: the published hit rate on 1 October, recomputed from entries that existed on 1 October; how many verdicts changed after the fact; whether a model improved from better calls or from a re-grade. Without it, every historical number is a claim about the current contents of a mutable table — and that claim quietly improves whenever someone cleans the data.

One more reason: this corpus feeds a public leaderboard. One match carries 358 graded calls from 358 model variants, three more carry 120 or more. A single rule change applied to that cluster moves a ranking without any model having changed. Sorting by a number whose rows can be rewritten is not measurement; it is a snapshot of whoever ran last.
Grade once. Keep the receipt. Make the receipt impossible to edit.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。
