title: Refactoring in Java 21+: Records and Pattern Matching for Readable Code
description:
Introduction to Legacy Code in Java

For years, Java developers have relied on extensive class hierarchies, multiple type checks using the instanceof operator, and explicit type casting to model data and handle complex conditional structures. This traditional approach not only increases the volume of source code but also introduces latent runtime risks, such as ClassCastException, while severely hindering long-term software maintainability.

With the release of Java 21, the language has matured significantly thanks to stable, high-impact features such as Records and Pattern Matching for switch. These modern tools allow architects and developers to write highly expressive, safe code aligned with Google Java Style standards. Below, we will analyze a real refactoring case from a legacy design to a modern, self-documenting design.

The Problem: Legacy Code with Verbose Checks

Let's consider a typical enterprise application processing network or database operation responses using abstract classes and multiple subclasses along with chained if-else blocks to determine the received response type:

// BEFORE: Verbose and error-prone legacy code
public abstract class Response {
}

public class SuccessResponse extends Response {
    private final String data;
    public SuccessResponse(String data) { this.data = data; }
    public String getData() { return data; }
}

public class ErrorResponse extends Response {
    private final String errorCode;
    public ErrorResponse(String errorCode) { this.errorCode = errorCode; }
    public String getErrorCode() { return errorCode; }
}

public class ResponseProcessor {
    public static String process(Response response) {
        if (response instanceof SuccessResponse) {
            SuccessResponse success = (SuccessResponse) response;
            return "OK: " + success.getData();
        } else if (response instanceof ErrorResponse) {
            ErrorResponse error = (ErrorResponse) response;
            return "FAIL: " + error.getErrorCode();
        } else {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown response type");
        }
    }
}

This traditional pattern presents several drawbacks: it requires writing manual constructors, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString methods, while duplicating unnecessary casting logic inside conditional structures.

The Solution: Records and Pattern Matching in Java 21

We can radically refactor this design using sealed interfaces, Records to model immutable data concisely, and Pattern Matching applied to the switch statement. This combination completely eliminates explicit casting and ensures exhaustiveness of analyzed cases.

// AFTER: Clean, modern, and safe code in Java 21
public sealed interface Response permits Response.Success, Response.Error {
    record Success(String data) implements Response {}
    record Error(String errorCode) implements Response {}

    /**
     * Processes the response safely using pattern matching.
     *
     * @param response the response received from the server
     * @return a formatted string with the processing result
     */
    static String process(Response response) {
        return switch (response) {
            case Success(var data) -> "OK: " + data;
            case Error(var code) -> "FAIL: " + code;
        };
    }
}

Architectural Advantages and Maintainability

  1. Boilerplate Reduction: Records automatically generate the canonical constructor, accessors, string representations, and equality contracts.
  2. Type Safety (Exhaustiveness): The Java compiler validates that all subtypes of a sealed interface are covered in the switch, preventing runtime errors from forgotten branches.
  3. Extreme Readability: Deconstruction patterns allow direct access to internal record components inside the pattern itself.

Auto-Documentation with Artificial Intelligence (Auto-Doc AI)

Using modern standards like Java 21 drastically facilitates the task of Auto-Doc AI tools. Thanks to the clear semantics of sealed interfaces and records, automated documentation generators can infer precise contracts without requiring redundant annotations. By integrating automatic formatters under the Google Java Style standard, we guarantee that code structure remains uniform across the entire development team, reducing friction in code reviews and elevating the overall quality of the corporate repository.

Try it interactively: Format, validate, and auto-document your java directly in JW Solutions Code Formatter & Auto-Doc AI.
Originally published at jw-solutions.com.

title: Circular Dependencies Between Modules in a Database: A Real Dependency, or One Table in the Wrong Module?
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: A cycle between modules is counted from two things: the foreign keys, and the list that says which table belongs to which module. On a 34-table PostgreSQL store split into seven modules, ten cycles fell to three when addresses moved to the accounts module and to zero when stock_levels moved to shipping, with no constraint changed. A cycle is a real dependency when every table already sits with the module that writes it; then one foreign key has to go, or the two modules are one.

A circular dependency between two modules is not only a fact about your foreign keys. It is a fact about your foreign keys and about the list that says which table belongs to which module, and changing that list can remove the cycle without touching the database. So before you break a dependency, check whether one table is filed in the wrong module.

I measured it on a 34-table PostgreSQL 18.3 store with 43 foreign keys, split into seven modules. That split gave ten cycles between modules. Moving addresses from shipping to accounts left three. Moving stock_levels from catalog to shipping left none. Not one constraint changed. This post shows the query that counts the cycles, how to tell which tables are worth moving, and what a cycle looks like when no move can remove it.

Why does a cycle between modules depend on where the boundaries are?

Because module A depends on module B as soon as one table in A references one table in B, so moving a single table can add or remove a whole dependency.

Tools that check module structure treat a cycle as an error. Spring Modulith's verification requires that "the dependencies between modules have to form a directed acyclic graph", and the acyclic dependencies principle says the same about packages. Those checks read the code. The database has the same graph, drawn by foreign keys, and those checks never read it.

Here is the part of the store that matters. A user has addresses, a user has a default address, and a warehouse has an address:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id                  BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email               TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    default_address_id  BIGINT
);

CREATE TABLE addresses (
    id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    line1    TEXT NOT NULL
);

ALTER TABLE users
    ADD CONSTRAINT users_default_address_id_fkey
    FOREIGN KEY (default_address_id) REFERENCES addresses (id);

CREATE TABLE warehouses (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    address_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES addresses (id)
);

I had filed addresses under shipping, next to warehouses, carriers and shipments. That one choice makes accounts depend on shipping (users.default_address_id) and shipping depend on accounts (addresses.user_id). File addresses under accounts and both of those keys stay inside one module. The keys are the same; the cycle is gone.

How do you list the cycles between modules from the database?

Write the module of each table into a small table, join it to pg_constraint twice, and walk the result with a recursive query.

The mapping is the part no catalog can give you, so it is a table you fill in:

CREATE TABLE table_domains (
    table_name  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    domain      TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO table_domains (table_name, domain) VALUES
    ('users', 'accounts'), ('roles', 'accounts'), ('user_roles', 'accounts'),
    ('sessions', 'accounts'), ('password_resets', 'accounts'),
    ('addresses', 'shipping'), ('carriers', 'shipping'), ('warehouses', 'shipping'),
    ('shipments', 'shipping'), ('shipment_items', 'shipping'),
    ('brands', 'catalog'), ('categories', 'catalog'), ('products', 'catalog'),
    ('product_variants', 'catalog'), ('product_images', 'catalog'),
    ('stock_levels', 'catalog'), ('reviews', 'catalog'),
    ('campaigns', 'marketing'), ('coupons', 'marketing'),
    ('newsletter_subscriptions', 'marketing'), ('wishlists', 'marketing'),
    ('carts', 'orders'), ('cart_items', 'orders'), ('orders', 'orders'),
    ('order_items', 'orders'), ('order_status_history', 'orders'),
    ('payment_methods', 'billing'), ('invoices', 'billing'),
    ('payments', 'billing'), ('refunds', 'billing'),
    ('tickets', 'support'), ('ticket_messages', 'support'),
    ('ticket_attachments', 'support'), ('return_requests', 'support');

The first query lists every dependency between two modules, with the tables that cause it:

SELECT c.domain AS from_domain, p.domain AS to_domain,
       count(*) AS foreign_keys,
       string_agg(k.conrelid::regclass::text, ', '
                  ORDER BY k.conrelid::regclass::text) AS from_tables
FROM pg_constraint k
JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
GROUP BY c.domain, p.domain
ORDER BY 1, 2;

On the store it returns 14 rows. Three of them point out of shipping and three point into it, which is where every cycle will turn out to run:

from_domain to_domain foreign_keys from_tables
accounts shipping 1 users
catalog shipping 1 stock_levels
orders shipping 1 orders
shipping accounts 1 addresses
shipping catalog 1 shipment_items
shipping orders 1 shipments

The second query walks those dependencies and prints each cycle once, starting from its alphabetically first module:

WITH RECURSIVE edges AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT c.domain AS src, p.domain AS dst
    FROM pg_constraint k
    JOIN table_domains c ON c.table_name = k.conrelid::regclass::text
    JOIN table_domains p ON p.table_name = k.confrelid::regclass::text
    WHERE k.contype = 'f' AND c.domain <> p.domain
),
walk AS (
    SELECT src AS start, dst AS at, ARRAY[src] AS path
    FROM edges
    UNION ALL
    SELECT w.start, e.dst, w.path || e.src
    FROM walk w
    JOIN edges e ON e.src = w.at
    WHERE w.at <> w.start
      AND w.at > w.start
      AND NOT w.at = ANY (w.path)
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' > ') AS cycle
FROM walk
WHERE at = start
ORDER BY cardinality(path), cycle;

It returns seven:

accounts > shipping
catalog > shipping
orders > shipping
accounts > shipping > catalog
accounts > shipping > orders
catalog > shipping > orders
accounts > shipping > orders > catalog

The query reads declared foreign keys only. This store also has three columns the application treats as references with no constraint behind them: orders.coupon_id, tickets.order_id and return_requests.shipment_id. The first one adds a dependency from orders to marketing, and with it three more cycles the catalog cannot see. Counting those three columns, there are ten.

Now move the table. One UPDATE each, and the cycle query again:

UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'accounts' WHERE table_name = 'addresses';
UPDATE table_domains SET domain = 'shipping' WHERE table_name = 'stock_levels';

After the first UPDATE the query returns two cycles, catalog > shipping and catalog > shipping > orders. After the second it returns no rows.

Two limits before you trust it on your own database. The join is an inner join, so a table missing from table_domains drops out of the count without an error, and conrelid::regclass::text writes a table outside the search_path as shop.addresses and a mixed-case or reserved name in double quotes, so the mapping has to spell names the same way. This lists every table the mapping misses (it will name table_domains itself, which is fine):

SELECT c.oid::regclass AS unmapped_table
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p')
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND c.oid::regclass::text NOT IN (SELECT table_name FROM table_domains);

Which tables are worth trying in another module?

The tables that hold a foreign key into another module, and of those, the ones whose rows the other module writes.

Counting is a poor guide, and I checked that by brute force. With 34 tables and seven modules there are 204 ways to move one table to another module. A script tried all of them against the ten cycles:

Result of moving one table Moves Example
Fewer cycles 38 addresses to accounts: 3
Same count 77 sessions to billing: 10
More cycles 89 warehouses to support: 25

More than twice as many moves make it worse as make it better, and the second best move by the numbers is nonsense: putting users in the catalog module leaves four cycles. A low count proves nothing about whether the table belongs there.

So ask who owns the rows, and use the count only to confirm. Two questions settle most tables:

  • Which module writes it? An address row is created when a user fills in a form, and addresses.user_id is NOT NULL with ON DELETE CASCADE: the row cannot exist without its user and dies with it. That is accounts. Shipping reads addresses; it does not own them.
  • If more than one module writes it, whose fact is it? stock_levels has a composite primary key of variant_id and warehouse_id and one quantity column. It is contested: receiving and dispatch change it, and an order flow that reserves stock would too. What tips it is the key. A row is a quantity at a warehouse, and warehouses belong to shipping, while the catalog describes what a product is, not how many are on a shelf. A team that runs stock as its own inventory module would file it there, with warehouses, and get the same zero.

A third option is to give the contested table a module of its own. That does not help when two tables reference each other. I put addresses alone in a new locations module and got four cycles, one of them accounts > locations, because users and addresses point at each other. Two tables that reference each other form a cycle wherever you draw the line between them; they can only share a module, or lose one of the two keys.

Is a circular dependency between modules real, or is one table in the wrong module?

It is real when every table already sits with the module that writes it and the cycle is still there.

To see one, I added a column that many order tables grow sooner or later, on top of the cycle-free split:

ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN latest_shipment_id BIGINT REFERENCES shipments (id);

The cycle query returns one row, orders > shipping: shipments.order_id points one way and the new column points back. Both tables are where their writers are: the order flow writes orders, dispatch writes shipments.

The move test agrees. I ran the 204 single moves again and exactly one clears the cycle: moving orders into the shipping module, which leaves an orders module without its orders table. Moving two tables together, shipments and shipment_items into orders, clears it as well, and that is not a table changing module. It is shipping losing its shipments, which is merging the two modules under another name.

Boundary cycle Real cycle
What clears it Moving one table to the module that writes it Only moving tables away from the module that writes them, or merging two modules
Schema change needed None One foreign key dropped or turned around
On the store addresses and stock_levels: ten cycles to zero orders.latest_shipment_id
Who decides Whoever owns the module list Whoever owns the two modules' code

For a real cycle one direction has to go. Here the back reference is the weak one: the latest shipment of an order is the row in shipments with the highest id for that order_id, so a query can derive it and the column can be dropped. Dropping only the constraint and keeping the column does not count: the reference is still there, the catalog query just stops seeing it, as it already fails to see orders.coupon_id. When neither direction can go, merging the two modules is the honest answer: they were one module all along.

How does Schemity show which cycles come from the boundaries?

It counts the cycles from the diagram's context views, so trying a table in another module is a drag, one button and a new count.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. To understand your schema at the module level it has two pieces. A context view is a saved, focused view of the schema that shows only a subset of entities and the relationships between them. The Context Map draws each context view as one node and derives the arrows between them from the foreign keys in the diagram.

I connected the store, grouped its tables into seven legends, and made a context view per legend with Sync from legends. The map showed 17 dependencies and its Cycles list showed ten cycles, not seven, because the diagram also counts the three undeclared columns as inferred relations. Clicking an arrow lists the keys behind it, which is the list you need for the ownership questions above.

Moving a table is dragging it into the other legend and pressing Sync from legends again, which adds it to one context view and removes it from the other. After addresses moved, the map showed 15 dependencies and three cycles. After stock_levels moved, 14 dependencies and none.

An AI agent can do the same reading over the local MCP server. get_context_views returns the dependencies, the keys behind each and the cycles. The built-in prompt Organize a diagram by domain groups the tables from your codebase, puts a table several domains use with the domain that writes it, and ends by asking the agent to say, for each cycle, whether one table looks like it belongs in another domain or the dependency is real.

Schemity does not make that call itself. It lists every cycle the same way and does not mark one as a boundary cycle and another as real. The count is computed; the ownership decision is yours.

What to do with a cycle between modules

Check the module list before you change the schema.

A cycle that one sensible table move removes was never a dependency between the modules. List the foreign keys behind both directions. If one of them sits in a table the other module writes, move the table and count again. If every table is where it belongs, drop or turn around one key, and say in the review which one and why.

The same picture, drawn from a live database, is in how a DDD context map is already in your foreign keys. Once the cycles are gone, the remaining arrows are the keys that cross a boundary, and whether to keep foreign keys between modules is the next decision. If the database has no module names at all, start with grouping a legacy database by domain. And when two tables reference each other with NOT NULL columns, the problem is older than modules: the first row cannot be inserted.

title: Stop the jump when a web font loads, measured with three Google fonts
description:
With font-display: swap, the browser shows text in a fallback font first and swaps in the web font when it arrives. If the two fonts take up different space, the text reflows and everything below it moves. CSS has four descriptors to make a local fallback font take up the same space: size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override.

I wanted to know how big the jump really is for the fonts I use on demo sites, and whether the fix works, so I measured it.

The setup

One paragraph of 250 characters at 17px, set in three Google fonts: Hanken Grotesk, Manrope and Space Grotesk. The fallback is Arial. I ran this in headless Chromium on Linux, where Arial isn't installed, so I used Liberation Sans, which was made to have the same metrics as Arial.

Two column widths: 343px (a phone with 16px margins) and 560px. Two line heights: 1.6 and normal.

How far the text moves with a plain fallback

Paragraph height, real font vs. plain fallback:

Font 343px, line-height: 1.6 343px, normal 560px, 1.6 560px, normal
Hanken Grotesk 163.1 vs 163.1 132 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 80
Manrope 163.1 vs 163.1 138 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 92 vs 80
Space Grotesk 190.3 vs 163.1 154 vs 120 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 80

Two different things are going on.

With line-height: normal, every font shifts, even when the line breaks are identical. "Normal" means "use the font's own ascent, descent and line gap", and those differ: Manrope's ascent and descent add up to 1.37 times the font size; Arial's ascent and descent are 1.12, about 1.15 with its line gap. So every line grows when Manrope arrives. Here that's 12 to 18px for one paragraph, more on a page of them.

With a fixed line-height: 1.6, only the line count matters. Each line is 27.2px whatever the font, so Hanken and Manrope don't move the paragraph at all. Space Grotesk does: it's about 8% wider than Arial, so at 343px the text needs 7 lines instead of 6 and the paragraph grows by one line, 27.2px.

So the first fix is free: set a unitless line height on body text. That removes the line-box part of the shift for every font; what's left comes from line breaks.

Writing the fallback @font-face

For the width, size-adjust scales the fallback's glyphs. For the line box, the three overrides set the ascent, descent and line gap the fallback should report. Both can be measured in the console once the web font has loaded:

async function fallbackFor(family, localName = 'Arial') {
  await document.fonts.load(`100px "${family}"`);
  const sample = 'Small-batch beans roasted every Tuesday in our Portland shop, shipped the same week so they reach you while the flavor is still bright.';
  const ctx = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d');
  const measure = (font) => { ctx.font = `100px ${font}`; return ctx.measureText(sample); };
  const web = measure(`"${family}"`);
  const local = measure(`"${localName}"`);
  const sizeAdjust = web.width / local.width;
  const pct = (n) => (n * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
  return `@font-face {
  font-family: "${family} Fallback";
  src: local("${localName}");
  size-adjust: ${pct(sizeAdjust)};
  ascent-override: ${pct(web.fontBoundingBoxAscent / 100 / sizeAdjust)};
  descent-override: ${pct(web.fontBoundingBoxDescent / 100 / sizeAdjust)};
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}`;
}

Two details:

  • The overrides are divided by sizeAdjust. They're percentages of the font size, and the font size of the fallback is already scaled by size-adjust, so without the division the line box comes out too tall by the same factor.
  • The width ratio comes from a real sentence, not the alphabet. Letter frequency matters: a font with a wide "m" and narrow "i" averages differently on prose than on "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz".

What it printed (with 'Liberation Sans' as the local name):

Font size-adjust ascent-override descent-override
Hanken Grotesk 100.8% 99.2% 29.7%
Manrope 102.4% 104.5% 29.3%
Space Grotesk 109.3% 89.6% 26.5%

Then use the fallback right after the web font:

body {
  font-family: "Space Grotesk", "Space Grotesk Fallback", sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

After

Same paragraph, real font vs. adjusted fallback:

Font 343px, 1.6 343px, normal 560px, 1.6 560px, normal
Hanken Grotesk 163.1 vs 163.1 132 vs 132 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 88
Manrope 163.1 vs 163.1 138 vs 138 108.8 vs 108.8 92 vs 92
Space Grotesk 190.3 vs 190.3 154 vs 154 108.8 vs 108.8 88 vs 88

Every height matches, including line-height: normal, and Space Grotesk's fallback now wraps to 7 lines like the real font.

What it doesn't fix

Widths only match on average. At 100px, the adjusted fallback for Space Grotesk set my test paragraph on one line within 0.5% of the real font's width (12213px vs 12157px). At 17px, on this Linux machine, it came out 6% wider (2163px vs 2038px on one line), while the plain fallback was 7% narrower. I suspect font hinting rounding each glyph's width to whole pixels at small sizes, but I didn't dig into it. Line breaks matched for my paragraph; a different paragraph can still break on a different word. The fix makes a reflow much smaller and much rarer, not impossible.

The local font has to exist. local("Arial") matches nothing on a machine without Arial; then the fallback face is skipped and the next font in the stack is used, unadjusted. Mac and Windows ship Arial. Many Linux systems don't, but often have Liberation Sans, so src: local("Arial"), local("Liberation Sans"); covers both with the same numbers. A system with only DejaVu Sans would need its own fallback face.

Headings need their own check. A display serif against Georgia or Times needs a separate fallback face and separate numbers.

Short version

  1. Use a unitless line height for body text. That alone removed the vertical shift for two of the three fonts.
  2. For the rest, generate a fallback @font-face with size-adjust and the three overrides, measured on real text, with the overrides divided by size-adjust.
  3. Measure the result: paragraph heights at a phone width and a desktop width, real font vs. fallback.

If you're doing this for a site you didn't build, you first need to know which fonts it renders and which weights. I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that lists every font a page actually renders, with its role, weights and where it loads from; there's a guide here: what font is this website using. DevTools' Rendered Fonts gives you the same for one element at a time.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every number comes from running the snippet and layout tests described above in headless Chromium.

title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen in a React chat: the migration details that actually matter
description:
Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen) on November 12, 2026. It's the fast, cheaper model in the Gemini 4 family, sitting below Carbon and Argon. It's on the free and paid tiers of the Gemini API and AI Studio, and the paid price is flat across the whole context window: $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens (thinking tokens count as output).

Google's launch post says that compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash it finishes tasks 2.5x faster at its default setting and more than triples Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%). Those are Google's numbers. I haven't benchmarked them myself.

What I did test is the boring part: wiring Hydrogen into a streaming React chat with the Vercel AI SDK, and checking what actually goes over the wire. A few details in the migration guide are easy to miss.

What changed for developers

From the official "What's new in Gemini 4 Hydrogen" guide:

  • Four thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default) and a new xhigh. minimal is rejected with an error.
  • One unified window: input, thinking and output share 1,048,576 tokens. A single request still caps at 65,536 output tokens, streaming or not. To go longer you use background execution or client-side continuation.
  • Sampling params are gone: remove temperature, top_p and top_k. In-range values are ignored, and out-of-range values return a 400.
  • No explicit caching: cachedContents / caches.create aren't supported. Implicit caching runs automatically on prompts of at least 4,096 tokens and discounts cached input by 95%.
  • Thought signatures matter: if you manage history yourself with generateContent, send prior model turns and thought signatures back unchanged.

The guide also suggests running your evals at all four levels and picking the lowest level that meets your quality bar. That's good advice for a chat UI, where latency is most of the user experience.

SDK support

@ai-sdk/google 4.0.119 added the gemini-4-hydrogen model ID and the xhigh thinking level (see the package changelog). I used ai@7.0.173 with @ai-sdk/google@4.0.121.

The route handler 

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages, type UIMessage } from 'ai';
import { google } from '@ai-sdk/google';

export const maxDuration = 60;

type Level = 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh';

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages, level = 'medium' }: { messages: UIMessage[]; level?: Level } =
    await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: google('gemini-4-hydrogen'),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    // No temperature/topP: Hydrogen ignores them (out-of-range values return a 400).
    providerOptions: {
      google: { thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel: level, includeThoughts: true } },
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({ sendReasoning: true });
}

I default to medium because Google's own table recommends it for responsive chat and interactive coding. high is the API default, though, so if you omit the level you pay for more thinking than a chat turn usually needs.

The client

A plain useChat component that shows reasoning in a collapsible block and lets the user pick the thinking level for each message:

'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';
import { useChat } from '@ai-sdk/react';

export function Chat() {
  const [input, setInput] = useState('');
  const [level, setLevel] = useState<'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh'>('medium');
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, stop } = useChat();

  return (
    <div className="mx-auto flex max-w-2xl flex-col gap-4 p-4">
      {messages.map((m) => (
        <div key={m.id} className={m.role === 'user' ? 'self-end' : 'self-start'}>
          {m.parts.map((part, i) =>
            part.type === 'reasoning' ? (
              <details key={i} className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">
                <summary>Thinking</summary>
                <p className="whitespace-pre-wrap">{part.text}</p>
              </details>
            ) : part.type === 'text' ? (
              <p key={i} className="whitespace-pre-wrap">{part.text}</p>
            ) : null,
          )}
        </div>
      ))}
      <form
        className="flex gap-2"
        onSubmit={(e) => {
          e.preventDefault();
          if (!input.trim()) return;
          sendMessage({ text: input }, { body: { level } });
          setInput('');
        }}
      >
        <select value={level} onChange={(e) => setLevel(e.target.value as typeof level)}>
          <option value="low">low</option>
          <option value="medium">medium</option>
          <option value="high">high</option>
          <option value="xhigh">xhigh</option>
        </select>
        <input className="flex-1 border px-2" value={input} onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)} />
        {status === 'streaming' ? (
          <button type="button" onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
        ) : (
          <button type="submit" disabled={status === 'submitted'}>Send</button>
        )}
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}

Swap the raw elements for shadcn Button, Select and Collapsible if that's your stack. The data flow stays the same.

How I tested it (and what I didn't)

To be upfront: I didn't call the live API for this post. I ran the code above on Node 24 with a custom fetch that records the outgoing request and replies with a fake SSE stream. That checks the wiring, not the model's quality or speed. Here's what it showed:

  1. The request is right. It hits models/gemini-4-hydrogen:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse with thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel, includeThoughts: true }. The UI stream comes back as reasoning-start / reasoning-delta / reasoning-end followed by text-* parts, which is exactly what the details block renders.
  2. temperature is still forwarded, with no warning. Passing temperature: 0.2 put "temperature": 0.2 in generationConfig, and result.warnings was empty. Per Google's guide the server ignores in-range values, so this won't break anything. But if your shared config sets something out of range, you'll get a 400 and the SDK won't have warned you. I'd strip sampling params for Hydrogen.
  3. thinkingLevel: 'minimal' passes through unchanged. The provider's types still allow it for older models, so a config copied from a Gemini 3 app will type-check and then fail at the API. Search your code for minimal.
  4. The portable reasoning option maps correctly. reasoning: 'xhigh' became thinkingLevel: 'xhigh' on Hydrogen. On gemini-4-argon, the SDK downgraded it to high and raised a compatibility warning, which matches the changelog note that xhigh maps only for Hydrogen.

Honest limits

  • The speed and benchmark figures above are Google's, not mine.
  • xhigh costs more and responds more slowly, and Google warns it can overthink simple prompts. Don't make it the default in a chat box.
  • Thinking tokens are billed as output at $7.50/1M, so includeThoughts plus high on every turn adds up. Log usage.outputTokenDetails.reasoningTokens, which the SDK exposes, and watch it.
  • If you rely on explicit context caching for a big system prompt, that path is gone. Check whether implicit caching (prompts of 4,096+ tokens) covers your case.

Sources

  • Google: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen (Nov 12, 2026)
  • Google AI Studio docs: What's new in Gemini 4 Hydrogen
  • Vercel AI SDK: @ai-sdk/google changelog (4.0.119)

If you'd rather not hand-roll the reasoning, tool-call and message components, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style ones built for this kind of stream.

title: Node.js Image Thumbnail Processing Times Out Before Object Storage Upload
description:
Thumbnail upload timeouts are usually diagnosed at the wrong boundary. The object store gets blamed, while the request is still decoding an oversized source image, allocating memory for a resize, or waiting for a slow encoder. Split the work into three measured stages: decode and resize, encode, then upload. Keep the upload out of the application response path, and use a direct multipart or presigned transfer for large originals.

The practical rule is simple: resize before the network, but do not make the web request own the whole resize-and-upload job. A queue worker can produce a 320px thumbnail, record each stage's duration, and upload the result with a bounded retry policy. That gives you a useful failure signal instead of one 30-second timeout.

Why does processing image thumbnails time out before upload?

Start with timestamps, not a new storage vendor. Log the source byte count, pixel dimensions, output byte count, decoder time, encoder time, and upload time. A 12 MB JPEG and a 12,000 by 8,000 JPEG are different problems. The latter can consume far more memory even when its compressed file is modest.

I use separate timers because one total duration hides the decision. If decode and resize consume 2.8 seconds but upload consumes 180 ms, changing buckets is busywork. If encoding dominates, try a faster library or a less expensive output format. If upload dominates, inspect transfer size, connection reuse, part size, and whether the app is proxying bytes that could move directly to object storage.

Here is the shape of a worker. It uses sharp for the CPU-heavy step and a direct object write for the small derivative. The important part is the boundary around each timer, not the particular bucket provider.

import sharp from "sharp";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const sourcePath = process.argv[2];
const bucket = process.env.THUMBNAIL_BUCKET;
const key = process.env.THUMBNAIL_KEY;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!sourcePath || !bucket || !key || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("Usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=... THUMBNAIL_BUCKET=... THUMBNAIL_KEY=... tsx worker.ts input.jpg");
}

const input = await readFile(sourcePath);
const resizeStarted = performance.now();
const output = await sharp(input)
  .rotate()
  .resize({ width: 320, withoutEnlargement: true })
  .webp({ quality: 82 })
  .toBuffer();
const resizeMs = Math.round(performance.now() - resizeStarted);

const uploadStarted = performance.now();
const host = ["api", "infrai", "cc"].join(".");
const route = ["v1", "storage", "object", "put", encodeURIComponent(bucket), encodeURIComponent(key)].join("/");
const url = `https://${host}/${route}`;
let response: Response | undefined;
for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
  response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "image/webp",
      "Idempotency-Key": `thumbnail:${key}`,
    },
    body: output,
  });
  if (response.status !== 429) break;
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.min(retryAfter, 30) * 1000 * 2 ** attempt));
}
if (!response || !response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Thumbnail upload failed: ${response?.status ?? "no response"} ${await response?.text()}`);
}
const uploadMs = Math.round(performance.now() - uploadStarted);

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  inputBytes: input.byteLength,
  outputBytes: output.byteLength,
  resizeMs,
  uploadMs,
}));

This deliberately uploads the small derivative, not the original. For the original, give the browser a short-lived presigned destination or use multipart upload. The application should authorize the key and content constraints; it should not stream every image through its own memory and connection pool.

The retry is bounded. A retry without an idempotency key is how a harmless timeout becomes a duplicate write.

Which storage choice fits the access-control problem?

The hard choice is not “which object store is fastest?” It is access control versus delivery simplicity. A public object URL is convenient for a product gallery, but public-read access is a poor default for private catalog assets, user uploads, and unlisted media.

Option Good fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Mature presigned uploads, multipart workflows, and detailed storage controls More provider-specific configuration and policy surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object operations when the delivery path already lives near Cloudflare Check which S3 features and edge delivery controls your workflow needs
Alibaba Cloud OSS Teams already operating in Alibaba Cloud regions or using its object-storage ecosystem Portability and feature parity need an explicit test, not an assumption
A unified REST storage layer A small team that wants one contract while changing the backing vendor Verify concurrency, recovery, CORS, and retention requirements first

S3 is the conservative baseline. R2 and OSS can be reasonable when geography, existing accounts, or delivery architecture decides the result. Infrai is a reasonable choice for this private-thumbnail workflow when one REST contract and one credential surface matter more than provider-specific storage semantics. It offers one plain REST API, so a worker does not need another provider SDK just to write a derivative. Its self-describing discovery surface is available without a key, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that reduces the glue around a worker written in a less common runtime. The object-write contract stays stable if the backend vendor changes. That is useful only if the layer exposes the controls your application actually needs.

For the stated thumbnail job, a storage API with a single object-write contract is a strong fit when the worker owns authorization and the objects remain private. It is a weak fit for a public image host: there is no public or public-read ACL and no permanent public URL. It also lacks object versioning, object lock, and an If-Match conditional write. Those are not cosmetic omissions. They affect recovery, compliance, and concurrent publishing.

What would I change at scale?

At low volume, the worker above is enough to expose the bottleneck.

At scale, I would put originals and derivatives on separate keys, make the derivative key deterministic, and let a queue own retries. A retry must not create a second logical asset. Keep the source object until the derivative has been verified, then apply retention deliberately; lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum in the unified storage option described here, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. I would also keep a small sample of stage timings for every deployment, because a faster encoder can move the bottleneck to the network and make an old timeout threshold look mysteriously random across image sizes, regions, and worker concurrency.

I would also cap image dimensions before decoding. That is a memory limit, not merely an optimization. Reject malformed or absurd dimensions early, and record request IDs alongside stage timings so an individual slow job can be traced across the worker and storage service.

Browser-direct upload needs another check. The bucket model has a cors_rules field, but there is no independent CORS configuration route exposed for self-service. If the browser must upload directly, configure that requirement through a provider that supports it or place a controlled upload service in front. Do not discover this after shipping the client flow.

The trade-off is clear. S3 gives the broadest familiar toolbox. R2 and OSS may fit an existing regional or edge strategy. A unified API reduces integration surface and lets the worker keep its contract while the backend changes, but it cannot erase missing storage semantics. Pick the smallest system whose access-control and recovery model matches the images you are storing.

Infrai's unified API layer also changes the developer workflow in a concrete way. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. A thumbnail worker can inspect the storage contract before wiring its queue, then call it over plain HTTP without adding a provider SDK. The wider surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so adding queue or observability calls later does not require another client library and another vendor-specific integration.

Further reading

  • Sharp documentation
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation
  • Amazon S3 pricing

title: Our Chrome extension sat untouched for four months. Review took one day.
description:
MapWit was written over five days in April. It could read a Google Maps search, score every business in it, and export the lot to Excel, and it did — the first exports are dated 21 April. Then nobody touched it for four months.

When we came back to it, the build still worked. It had no tests. It shipped its own source code to anyone who opened DevTools. On the Indian Google domain, where most of its users would land, it installed and did nothing at all — and the change that fixed that introduced a bug that got the most important fact about every business wrong.

It went live on the Chrome Web Store on 14 September, one day after submission and on the first review round. Most of the work between those two states was not adding things. It was finding out what the extension actually did, and removing the parts a reviewer would reasonably object to — including a feature that worked.

This is the full account: how a lead gets from a Maps result to a row in a spreadsheet, what we measured, where it broke the first time it met live Google Maps, and what we cut.

TL;DR

  • The most useful signal was the one we were getting wrong. A business with no website is the best lead MapWit can find, and on google.co.in every business looked like it had one — the extension was reading the listing's own Maps link as the business's site. Those leads lost 5 points out of 10. Seven test cases now fail if it comes back.
  • One of thirty hostile URLs got past our private-address guard. The browser's URL parser rewrites ::ffff:127.0.0.1 into hex before our code sees it, so a dotted-quad check never matches. A throwaway harness found it in minutes; reading the code had not.
  • We went from 0 tests to 171 in one day, and the tests found real bugs. Bulk review analysis lost every business but the first in a batch. A missing setting clamped to 1 instead of the default of 8. Neither would have shown up in a demo.
  • Review passed first time because the review had already happened. We cut outreach drafting to satisfy the single-purpose rule, made website access optional, stopped shipping 2.1 MB of sourcemaps, bundled the fonts, and wrote a packaging script that refuses to zip a build that breaks any of six rules.
  • The first live run of the rebuilt extension found three bugs that 166 tests had not. A year glued to a star rating became a phone number: Est. 2005 next to 4.5(177) read as 20054.5(177.

MapWit, in one paragraph

MapWit is a Chrome side panel for people who sell to local businesses — web studios, agencies, freelancers. You search Google Maps the way you already would ("dentists in Pune"), and the businesses appear in the panel as you scroll. A Deep scan opens each listing to collect its website, phone, address and recent reviews. Enrich visits each business's own website for email addresses, social profiles and a site-quality check. Every lead gets a score from 1 to 10, you can filter to the ones with no website at all, and Analyse reviews writes a one-sentence summary of what customers complain about. Then you export to Excel, written in the browser with SheetJS. There is no server, no account and no subscription; leads live in your browser's storage, and the one AI feature runs on your own OpenRouter key.

The premise is in the product page's first line: a bought lead list is rows somebody has already sold twice. The businesses worth calling are the ones already visible on Maps with no website or a bad one, and the fastest way to find them is to qualify a search you were going to run anyway.

Diagram: Everything above the line happens in the browser. Two things cross it, and both are opt-in: Enrich fetches a business's own website only after you allow website access, and review text goes to OpenRouter only when you click Analyse with your own key. The README used to say nothing leaves the machine. That was never true, and it now says what does. See it in the original post.

How to generate leads from Google Maps with MapWit

The practical version first, in the order the extension's own tour walks through it.

  1. Install it and open the side panel. Add MapWit from the Chrome Web Store (Chrome 114 or later) and click its toolbar icon. The panel opens beside the page and stays open while you use the map.
  2. Search Google Maps the way you would anyway. A category and a place works best: dentists in Pune, interior designers in Indiranagar. Scroll the results and each business appears in the panel as it renders. Load more scrolls the list to the end of the search for you; Google Maps shows about 120 results per search.
  3. Deep scan. It opens each listing and collects the website, phone, address and recent reviews. It is the slow step on purpose, because it paces itself, so start it and let it run.
  4. Enrich (optional). It visits each business's own website for email addresses, social profiles and a site-quality check. Chrome asks once for website access the first time you use it.
  5. Analyse reviews (optional). With your own OpenRouter key, it writes one sentence on what customers praise and complain about, which is often the opening line of a call.
  6. Find the best leads. Sort by lead score, switch on No website only, or search by name or category. The score is built from these signals:
Signal Points What it usually means for a pitch
No website +4 A website build, and the strongest single reason to call
Own website scores 3 or less out of 10 +2 A redesign: no HTTPS, no mobile layout, slow, or visibly stale
Phone number +2 You can call today
Email address +2 You can write first
50+ reviews and no website +1 An established business with an obvious gap, not a new one
Rating between 3.5 and 4.2 +1 Real customers, and room to improve
Missing 4 or more of 7 social platforms +1 A thin presence generally
  1. Export. Choose Excel, sorted by score, with 19 columns including the AI review insight, or JSON for a CRM import.

That is the whole workflow, and it takes one search to see whether the list is worth calling. What you do with the list afterwards is your responsibility. Google's Maps terms and India's data protection law both apply to it; the section near the end says how.

The rest of this post is how each of those steps works, and what it took to ship it.

How MapWit captures leads from Google Maps

There is no Maps API underneath this. MapWit reads the page you are already looking at.

A content script runs on four Maps origins — www.google.com/maps, maps.google.com, and their .co.in equivalents — and watches the results feed as it renders. Each card is a link with a stable place identifier in its URL, which becomes the lead's primary key, plus a few lines of text that hold the name, rating, review count, category and, sometimes, a phone number and an outbound link. Load more scrolls the feed for you to the end of the search. Google Maps shows about 120 results per search; on the live test it reached 106 and stopped where the list stopped.

Deep scan is the slower half. For each captured lead it opens the listing's detail panel and reads the fields Maps exposes there with stable data attributes — website, address, phone — plus up to 15 recent reviews, each cut to 400 characters. Only a panel that has actually finished loading, with a heading that matches the listing that was clicked, counts as scanned. An earlier version marked a lead done as soon as it had clicked it, which meant a slow load produced a lead with nothing in it and no way to tell.

The side panel is a real Chrome side panel, not a popup, which is why the manifest sets minimum_chrome_version to 114: below that the API does not exist, and the toolbar button installs and silently does nothing. A popup would have been simpler and would have closed every time you clicked the map.

The fragile part is worth saying plainly. The result cards use obfuscated class names that Google can change on any deploy, and several of the patterns that pull a rating or an "Open now" out of card text match English interface strings. On a Maps interface set to another language MapWit captures less. The detail panel is sturdier, because the website, address and phone rows carry data-item-id attributes that have been stable for years — which is also why Deep scan is the reliable path and card capture is the fast one.

How MapWit scores a Google Maps lead

A score only earns its place if it sorts the list the way the person calling would. The whole point table is in step 6 above; it is small enough to show in full, and it has no hidden terms. The total is clamped to 1–10, and 8 or above is labelled hot, 5 or above warm. It is a pure function shared by the service worker and the side panel so the two can never disagree about a number.

The site-quality score out of 10 is equally blunt, and deliberately so. It checks five things on the business's home page: served over HTTPS (2), a mobile viewport tag (2), a response under three seconds (2, or 1 under six), a copyright year from this year or last (2), and a mailto: or tel: link somewhere on the page (2). None of that is a design judgement, and all of it is something a salesperson can say out loud on a call: your site doesn't load on a phone.

Two classification rules matter more than the weights. A listing whose only outbound link is a booking platform — Booksy, Fresha, Setmore and twelve others on the list — has no website of its own. That is a pitch, not a site to crawl. And a link back into Google itself is not a website at all, which is the rule the extension broke on google.co.in (below).

Enrichment, and the one address the guard missed

Enrich visits the business's own site to find what Maps does not show: email addresses, social profiles, and the quality signals above. It tries up to six paths — /, /contact, /contact-us, /contactus, /about, /about-us — with an eight-second timeout and a 512 KB cap per page, and stops early once it has two likely email addresses, keeping the best three with contact@ ranked above support@ above info@.

That is the only feature that needs to fetch arbitrary websites, so it is the only one behind the broad website permission — and that permission is optional. The extension installs without it. The first time you click Enrich, Chrome asks. Settings can revoke it, and revoking it mid-run stops enrichment with the leads left pending rather than failed.

Fetching arbitrary URLs has a sharper problem than permissions. The URL comes from a Maps listing, which is data we do not control. A listing whose website field says http://192.168.1.1/ would be fetched from the user's own machine, inside their own network — their router, their NAS, their office intranet. That is server-side request forgery with a browser as the server, and it is exactly the kind of thing a reviewer probes on an extension that can reach any host.

So before any fetch, a guard refuses non-HTTP schemes, ports other than 80 and 443, embedded credentials, single-label names like router or nas, private suffixes like .local and .internal, and every private, loopback, link-local and shared address range, including 169.254.169.254, where cloud providers serve instance credentials. The list follows the OWASP SSRF guidance and the RFC 1918 and RFC 6598 ranges.

Rather than trust the list, we wrote a throwaway harness with thirty hostile inputs and ran the guard against it. Twenty-nine were refused. One got through.

http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/     allowed   ← loopback, written as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address

The guard checked IPv6 hosts for a dotted IPv4 address inside the mapped prefix. It never saw one, because the browser's URL parser had already rewritten the host before our code read it. The WHATWG URL Standard serialises every IPv6 address as hexadecimal pieces, so [::ffff:127.0.0.1] arrives as [::ffff:7f00:1] — the same address, spelled so that a dotted-quad regex cannot match it. (IPv4-mapped addresses are defined in RFC 4291.) The fix decodes both spellings:

// IPv4-mapped addresses. The WHATWG parser rewrites `::ffff:127.0.0.1` to its
// hex form `::ffff:7f00:1`, so both spellings have to be decoded — checking
// only the dotted form lets ::ffff:127.0.0.1 straight through.
const hex = h.match(/^::(?:ffff:)?([0-9a-f]{1,4}):([0-9a-f]{1,4})$/);
if (hex) {
  const hi = parseInt(hex[1], 16);
  const lo = parseInt(hex[2], 16);
  return isPrivateIpv4(`${hi >> 8}.${hi & 0xff}.${lo >> 8}.${lo & 0xff}`);
}

The same parser is also why three other inputs needed no special code at all. http://2130706433/, http://0x7f000001/ and http://0177.0.0.1/ — loopback in decimal, hex and octal — are all normalised to 127.0.0.1 before the guard looks. The parser that caused the bug fixed three others for free. It is the same lesson as the time six of our agent's seventeen tools turned out never to have run: the code you have read is not the code that runs, and the only way to find the difference is to execute it against something hostile.

There is one residual risk, and it is written down rather than hidden. The fetch follows redirects, so a public site can answer with a redirect to a private address. In a Manifest V3 service worker, redirect: 'manual' returns an opaque response, so the hops cannot be inspected one at a time; instead the final URL is re-checked. That means the request to the internal host is still sent. What the guard prevents is its content reaching the extension — the step that turns a forged request into a leak.

Deduplication, and the write that lost leads

The same business turns up more than once: in two searches, or in a search and then a Deep scan of the same listing. Leads are merged on the Maps place ID first and a normalised phone number second, and a merge only ever fills empty fields. A value we already captured is never overwritten by a later, possibly worse, read of the same page. The score is recomputed after every merge, because a Deep scan can make a lead newly eligible for "50+ reviews and no website".

Merging on phone number has a known cost: two branches of a chain that share one number collapse into a single lead. For the people using this — who call a business, not a branch — that is usually what they want, and it is recorded as a known limit rather than a bug.

The dedup logic was fine. The bug was around it. Every writer to the lead store went through a single write queue, except the enrichment worker, which wrote directly. A lead captured by the content script while enrichment was patching another one could be overwritten by enrichment's stale copy of the list. Nothing crashed; a lead just disappeared. The fix moved the queue into the store module so there is no other way to write — the kind of bug that only exists because two parts of the code were each correct on their own.

Storage had a quieter version of the same problem. chrome.storage.local defaults to 10 MB, which is roughly 1,500 to 3,000 deep-scanned leads with their review text, and quota errors were being swallowed. The extension now holds unlimitedStorage, and a full store is an error you can see.

The AI runs on your key, not ours

The one AI feature reads a business's recent reviews and writes one sentence about them: what customers praise, and what they complain about, which is usually the opening line of a sales call. It shipped in April calling Google's Gemini API directly, with the model name hard-coded:

export const GEMINI_MODEL = 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview';

A pre-submission audit flagged it. Nobody had checked that slug still existed; the file had already churned once from a different preview model, and its own error strings said "not available on this API key". The question "does this model still exist?" had no durable answer — any answer would rot the next time Google renamed a preview.

So we removed the question rather than answering it. The direct Gemini integration was deleted. MapWit now talks to OpenRouter, which puts hundreds of models behind one endpoint whose format is very similar to OpenAI's Chat API, and the model is a setting. On the day we switched, the catalogue listed 418. The default is a ~latest alias that always resolves to the newest Gemini Flash, and a stale model is now an error on the Settings page with a named cause instead of every AI feature failing silently.

Bring-your-own-key is also what makes "no server" true. If the requests went through us, we would hold review text for businesses we had never heard of and an API bill tied to a free product. With the user's key, the text goes from their browser to OpenRouter and back, and Settings has a section headed What leaves your browser.

Letting users pick any model found the next bug. One model spent its entire output budget of 1,024 tokens on internal reasoning and returned no answer at all. OpenRouter's reasoning controls fixed most of it — reasoning tokens count against the output budget on most providers, so a model left to think freely can spend all of it: the call now asks for low reasoning effort with 2,048 tokens, and if a model still returns only reasoning, it retries once with four times the room before giving up with a message that suggests a non-reasoning model.

Bulk analysis is where the design had to be deliberate. Analysing one business at a time would mean a hundred requests for a hundred leads, and OpenRouter rate-limits free models to 20 requests a minute. So requests are batched — up to eight businesses, or 24,000 characters of review text, whichever fills first — and paced, one in flight, at least 3.1 seconds apart. A hundred leads is about thirteen requests; twenty is three. If a rate-limit response arrives anyway, the run pauses for as long as OpenRouter says to and retries the same batch, rather than stopping.

Two things about that took tests to find. The first is Manifest V3's service worker lifecycle: Chrome stops an idle extension worker after thirty seconds, and a rate-limit pause can be two minutes of silence. The run makes a cheap extension API call every twenty seconds, which resets the timer. The second was a plain parsing bug. Some models return a batch answer as a bare JSON array instead of an object, and the shared helper that stripped code fences from model output extracted only the first object it found — so every business but the first in a batch silently lost its insight. It passed every manual check, because a manual check is one business.

Being polite to Google Maps

Deep scan opens listings one after another, and Google Maps notices when a session does that quickly. It does not return an error. It slows down: the detail panel keeps spinning, and a naive scanner either records an empty lead or, as ours used to, resets the page and loses its place.

We researched how Maps behaves under load before changing anything, and the conclusion was not to go faster. MapWit now paces itself, rests, and backs off further every time Maps stops answering. It pauses while its tab is hidden, since Chrome throttles background tabs and Maps stalls with them. It keeps its progress in session storage, so a reload picks up with the listings it had not reached. And if Google shows a captcha, it stops and waits for you — it does not try to solve it, and it never will.

That is a product decision as much as an engineering one. MapWit reads the search you ran, in your own signed-in session, at a pace a person clicking through the same results could plausibly keep. It is not a crawler, and the day it needs to behave like one is the day it should not exist.

One piece is still unfinished. Maps' loading spinner in the results feed carries no role="progressbar" and no aria-busy, so Load more cannot yet tell "still loading" from "finished". It stops correctly at the end of a list today, but it cannot wait politely in the middle of one. That is the first item for 1.0.1.

What we deleted to pass review

Chrome Web Store review is a person reading your listing, your permissions and your code. The documented rules are public, and nearly every rejection story we could find was a known rule broken knowingly. So we reviewed MapWit against them before submitting it, and removed what failed.

A working feature. MapWit used to draft cold outreach — an email and a WhatsApp message tailored to each lead. It worked, and it was arguably the most impressive thing in the extension. It was also a second purpose. The store's quality guidelines require an extension to have a single purpose that is narrow and easy to understand, and "scores leads, and also writes sales emails" is two. We first removed the UI, then found the service worker still answered the outreach messages — so a reviewer reading the bundle would still find cold-email generation in a lead-scoring extension. The handlers went too: 237 lines, their prompts, three settings and three spreadsheet columns. The source is kept under a git tag for a later version, where it may be its own product.

The broad permission, as a requirement. Website access became optional, as above. The tabs permission was removed entirely — querying tabs by URL works with host permissions alone, and the only behaviour that changed is one the code already wanted.

2.1 MB of source code. The build shipped sourcemaps, which embed the full original source, comments included. Two of them were web-accessible to google.com pages. They are off.

Anything that loads from somewhere else. Manifest V3 forbids remotely hosted code, and a stylesheet from Google Fonts is not code, but it is a request we did not need to explain. The fonts are bundled, which is why fonts are 62% of the 1.6 MB build: 66 files, about 1 MB. We would rather ship weight than a network dependency on the one page that has to work offline.

A hand-written User-Agent, left over from April, that dressed enrichment requests up as Chrome/latest. The browser sends its own; the invented one only added a question a reviewer would ask. And a button labelled "Scrape more", which is now "Load more" — words in a listing are read as intent.

Then we made the rules executable. npm run package type-checks, runs the tests, builds, and refuses to produce a zip if the build contains any sourcemap, requires a broad host permission, contains any outreach string, uses eval( or new Function(, references Google Fonts, or has a manifest version that disagrees with package.json. Every one of those six has been true of this repository at some point. Its first run failed: two preconnect tags to Google Fonts were still in the HTML after the stylesheet import had gone.

The listing copy got the same treatment. The store description says qualify and capture, never "scrape" or "harvest", carries a line saying MapWit is not affiliated with Google, and answers the privacy questions field by field. The privacy policy and terms went live on this site before submission, not after.

Submitted on 13 September; published on the 14th. No rejection, no resubmission. Google's review documentation says most reviews finish within a few days and that broad host permissions, or a lot of hard-to-review code, can make one take longer. We had neither left.

Where it broke

Every test in the repository runs against pure modules or a mocked Maps page. On 12 September, with 166 tests passing, we ran the rebuilt extension against live Google Maps. It found three bugs.

Signed-out sessions get a limited view. Maps serves a reduced interface to a signed-out browser — "You're seeing a limited view of Google Maps" — and the new throttling code read that banner as a block and refused to scan. Deep scan did nothing at all. It is now a notice in the panel, and the scan runs.

Promo cards moved the end of the list. Maps now places promotional cards after its "You've reached the end of the list." text, so the end-of-list check, which read the last item, never fired. It reads the last five now.

A year became a phone number. A salon card read Est. 2005 followed immediately by its rating, 4.5(177). In the card's flattened text those run together, and the phone pattern matched 20054.5(177. Ratings are stripped before phone matching now, and a candidate with a decimal point between digits is rejected. The regression test uses the real card text.

After those three: Deep scan saved 5 of 5 listings on a live search, and Load more ran to 106 results and stopped where the list ended.

The worst bug, though, was older and quieter, and no live run on google.com would have found it. When we added the Indian Maps domains in August, nobody updated the classifier that decides whether a link is the business's own website or a link back into Google. It only knew google.com. On google.co.in, the card's own /maps/place/ link was taken as the business website, so "No website" never appeared — on exactly the domain an Indian user types — and every one of those leads lost the 4 points for no website and the 1 for "50+ reviews and no website". The product's best signal was silently off for the market it was built in. Any Google country domain now classifies as Google, and seven test cases fail if the old pattern returns.

The two surfaces no automation could reach — Enrich's permission prompt, and Analyse reviews with a real OpenRouter key — were run by hand in real Chrome. Both work.

What 171 tests bought

The test suite did not exist on the morning of 12 September. By the evening it had 171 cases across 16 files, and it had found:

  • the batch parser that dropped every business but the first;
  • a missing "reviews per business" setting clamping to 1 instead of the default of 8, because Number(null) is 0;
  • concurrent writes to the token ledger dropping entries, and an AI cache hit that never wrote its result back to the lead;
  • email parsing that discarded real hello@, hi@ and admin@ inboxes, and a "prefer contact emails" sort that ran after the list had already been cut to three.

None of those would have shown up in a demo. All of them would have shown up in the first week of someone actually using it. The pattern is the same one we hit when our agent passed every red-team probe: a green result from the check you already had tells you very little, and the useful tests are the ones written to try to break a specific claim.

What the suite does not do is also worth stating. It covers pure modules and a mocked Maps page, and the Chrome APIs are faked. There is no CI; the tests run on a laptop and inside the packaging script. The mocked Maps page is our description of Google's markup, which is exactly the thing that changes without notice, and the only real check of that is a person running a search.

What is still true

MapWit is free. The AI feature costs whatever your OpenRouter model costs, and nothing to us. There is no paywall and no telemetry, so the honest answer to "how many people use it" is that we see the store's own counters and nothing else, and they are not yet worth quoting.

It also carries a risk we would rather name than have someone discover. Google's end-user Maps terms say you may not copy Maps content, "mass download or create bulk feeds of the content", or use it to build "a business listings database, mailing list, or telemarketing list" for a service that substitutes for Google Maps. A lead list sits uncomfortably close to that sentence, and the store that lists MapWit belongs to Google. We have built it to be as conservative as we know how — it reads only the search you ran, in your own session, at a human pace, stops at a captcha, and says plainly that it is not affiliated with Google — but that is a posture, not a licence. A product that depends on another company's page, and sits this close to its terms, can be removed by that company. We decided to ship knowing that, rather than not ship.

The same reasoning applies to what you do with the export. Business phone numbers and emails are often a person's details — a sole proprietor's mobile is their mobile — and in India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act applies to how you store and use them. MapWit keeps the data on your machine; what happens after you click Export is on you, and the terms on this site say so.

And the extension is 9,748 lines of TypeScript, a 1.2 MB zip, and five months old, with work on six days of it: three in April, one in August, two in September. That ratio is the most instructive number in this post. The April version did almost everything the published one does. What it lacked was evidence: that it worked on the domain its users would use, that it could not be pointed at a user's own network, that its batch parser did not lose data, that nothing in the bundle contradicted the listing. None of that is a feature, and all of it is why review took a day.

Verdict

A Chrome extension is easy to build and slow to trust. The five April days produced a tool that worked on the machine it was written on. The September days produced one we could describe accurately to a stranger — in a store listing, a privacy policy, a permission prompt and a reviewer's queue — and every one of those descriptions forced a change in the code before it could be true.

If there is one practice to take from this, it is the packaging gate. Every rule a reviewer might apply, and every mistake you have already made once, should be a line in a script that refuses to produce the zip. We wrote it on the last day. It should have been the first.

MapWit is free, and it will tell you which dentists in Pune do not have a website. It is off the Chrome Web Store for now: on 23 October 2026 Google took version 1.2.0 down, citing its branding guidelines, and a fixed version is under appeal. The product page will say when it is back.

Every figure here is first-party, taken from the MapWit repository and its build between 21 April and 14 September 2026 across 16 commits, 11 of them on 12 September. Test counts are vitest runs on the published commit (171 passing, 16 files). Sizes are the store zip (1,259,577 bytes) and the built dist/ directory (1,648,035 bytes). Live-Maps results are from one search session on 12 September and are a smoke test, not a benchmark. Chrome and OpenRouter behaviour is quoted from their documentation as of September 2026. This is one extension, one codebase, one author.

FAQ

What does MapWit do?

MapWit is a free Chrome extension that captures the businesses in a Google Maps search into a side panel, scores each one from 1 to 10 as a sales lead, and exports them to Excel or JSON. It can open each listing for its website, phone, address and reviews, visit the business's own website for email addresses and a site-quality check, and summarise its reviews with AI using your own OpenRouter key. It is built for web studios, agencies and freelancers who sell to local businesses.

How do you generate leads from Google Maps?

Search Google Maps for a business category in a place, such as "dentists in Pune", then qualify the results rather than calling all of them. The strongest signals are a business with no website, a poor website, or a phone number and email you can reach. MapWit does this inside Chrome: it captures the search results into a side panel, scores each business from 1 to 10, filters to the ones with no website, and exports the list to Excel.

Is MapWit free?

Yes. MapWit has no subscription, no account and no paywall. The optional review-analysis feature uses your own OpenRouter API key, so you pay OpenRouter directly for whatever model you choose — and nothing if you never use that feature.

Does MapWit send my data to a server?

No, MapWit has no server. Leads are stored in your browser's own extension storage. Two things leave your browser, and both are opt-in: Enrich fetches a business's own public website after you grant the optional website permission, and Analyse reviews sends review text to OpenRouter using your key. Settings lists both under "What leaves your browser".

How does MapWit score a lead?

MapWit adds points for signals a salesperson cares about: 4 for no website, 2 each for a phone number and an email address, 2 if the business's own site scores 3 or less out of 10 for quality, 1 for a rating between 3.5 and 4.2, 1 for 50 or more reviews with no website, and 1 for missing four or more of seven social platforms. The total is clamped to 1–10; 8 and above is hot.

Why does MapWit need permission to access all websites?

Only the Enrich feature needs it, because it visits each business's own website to look for email addresses and check site quality — and those websites could be anywhere. MapWit installs without that permission and asks for it the first time you click Enrich. It refuses to fetch private, local or internal network addresses even when it has the permission.

Is it legal to extract business leads from Google Maps?

It depends on how you do it and what you do with the data, and this is not legal advice. Google's end-user Maps terms prohibit copying Maps content and mass downloading or creating bulk feeds of it, and business contact details can be personal data under India's DPDP Act. MapWit reads only the search you run in your own session, at a human pace, and stops at a captcha rather than solving it — but responsibility for how an exported list is used stays with the person using it.

Does MapWit work on google.co.in?

Yes. MapWit runs on www.google.com/maps, maps.google.com, www.google.co.in/maps and maps.google.co.in. The Indian domains were added because most users in India land there, and an early version misread every business on google.co.in as having a website — fixed before launch and covered by tests.

Which browsers does MapWit support?

MapWit needs Chrome 114 or later, because it runs in Chrome's side panel, which does not exist in earlier versions. It is published on the Chrome Web Store. An Edge Add-ons submission has not been made yet.

title: Backorders and Partial Shipments: Modelling Order Splits in a Supply Chain Database Without Losing the Original Order
description:
A customer places an order for 500 units, but the warehouse has only 320 available. The business ships the available quantity immediately and sends the remaining 180 units when replenishment arrives.

Operationally, this is a routine supply chain scenario. From a database perspective, however, it creates several questions. Should the original order quantity be changed? How should multiple shipments reference the same order? What happens when one shipment is cancelled or only partially delivered? And how can the application prevent the remaining quantity from being allocated twice?

A reliable supply chain system must preserve the original customer commitment while tracking every fulfilment event separately. This requires a clear distinction between an order, its fulfilment allocations, shipment records, and backorder quantities.

Why Order Splitting Needs a Separate Data Model

A common but fragile implementation stores a single shipped_quantity field on the order and updates it whenever a shipment leaves the warehouse.

This can work for simple transactions, but it becomes difficult to maintain when orders are split across multiple warehouses, carriers, delivery dates, or fulfilment methods.

For example:

  • Original order: 500 units
  • First shipment: 200 units
  • Second shipment: 120 units
  • Remaining backorder: 180 units

If the system stores only the current shipped quantity, it may show that 320 units have shipped. But it does not necessarily explain which shipment carried each quantity, when it left, which warehouse fulfilled it, or whether the customer received it.

The database should retain the original order and represent each fulfilment movement independently.

Separate Customer Orders From Fulfilment Records

A practical relational model can use the following entities:

Table Purpose
sales_orders Stores the original customer order
sales_order_lines Stores ordered products and quantities
fulfillment_orders Represents fulfilment work created from an order
fulfillment_order_lines Records allocated quantities
shipments Stores individual dispatch records
shipment_lines Connects shipped quantities to order lines
backorder_lines Tracks quantities awaiting fulfilment
inventory_reservations Records stock reserved for specific demand

The original sales_order_lines record should retain the ordered quantity. Shipment activity should not overwrite that value.

A simplified order-line record might contain:

order_line_id: 701
order_id: 9001
product_id: 450
ordered_quantity: 500
unit_price: 120.00
status: partially_fulfilled

Each shipment line then references the original order line:

shipment_line_id: 801
shipment_id: 3001
order_line_id: 701
shipped_quantity: 200

A second shipment can reference the same order line with another quantity. The relationship preserves the original customer commitment while creating a traceable fulfilment history.

Calculating the Remaining Backorder Quantity

The outstanding quantity should be derived from the original ordered quantity and the quantities that count as fulfilled under the business's fulfilment policy.

A basic calculation is:

Remaining Quantity = Ordered Quantity - Net Fulfilled Quantity

For example:
