Keep availability evidence and business correctness evidence distinguishable so an operator can see why a page fired and which action it supports.

For the illustrative three-failure rule, ask what happens to a single transport failure, a stalled observer, and a healthy response carrying an incorrect surcharge. The first should follow the chosen persistence policy; the second needs a missing-heartbeat path; the third needs the business check. Those are different tests, and routing them all through an undifferentiated unhealthy bit makes rollback less defensible, because the on-call must reconstruct which failure mode the instrumentation actually detected before deciding whether the flag is the appropriate control.

The costly threshold mistake is an unnecessary rollback page: it interrupts the on-call, pauses the rollout, and can reverse a sound pricing change without evidence of a customer-facing problem. An excessively tolerant threshold spends the rollback budget in silence. Review which observation triggered each page, how old it was, and whether the action addressed the condition it actually measured.

Further reading

References for the HTTP client, scheduling primitive, signal model, and comparison boundaries:

  • node-fetch documentation
  • Node.js timers documentation
  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Datadog documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Grafana documentation

If a shared metrics-to-channel boundary fits your release process, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Node.js API Storage: Expire Generated Promo Videos After Verified Copy
description:
An e-commerce API must store generated promo videos at useful quality, then expire redundant copies before storage and bandwidth grow without a policy. A Node.js service should therefore decide quality tier and retention at ingestion, before a temporary download URL quietly becomes its archive strategy.

TL;DR: fetch the generated video's download URL, copy the bytes into a private bucket you control, verify the copy, switch customer re-downloads to short-lived presigned URLs from that bucket, and only then delete the generated asset. Retain an approved high-quality master when later crops or encodes are plausible. Expire rejected candidates and redundant renditions on separate schedules. This makes quality versus bandwidth an explicit product decision rather than an accident of provider retention.

The ordering is the durable part. A generation provider's asset is governed by a retention policy the application does not control, so it should never be the source for a customer's later download. Generated video also tends to become the fastest-growing storage line; a deletion schedule belongs in the design from day one, not in a cleanup ticket six months later.

How Should an API Store and Expire Generated Promo Videos?

Start with business states, not bucket vendors. A generated candidate is evidence of an attempt. An approved master is the best available source for a future square crop, subtitle change, or new delivery encode. A delivery rendition is what the storefront should actually serve. Those objects have different value, and giving them one expiration rule either wastes bytes or destroys future options.

For a concrete catalog launch, suppose a job produces 12 candidates, the merchandiser approves one, and the channel requires two delivery renditions. The number 12 is an example policy input, not a performance claim. The important ratio is structural: candidate volume follows experimentation, while approved-master volume follows published products. Keeping every candidate at master quality makes storage grow with the noisier curve.

I would make the application record four fields before it copies anything: asset_id, role, approved, and expires_at. Add a content length or checksum when the source and destination expose one that can be compared; do not manufacture equivalence between unlike checksum schemes. A database flag named copied is weak evidence by itself. The deletion gate needs evidence that the destination operation completed and that the stored object is the one the application intends to serve.

Wait.

Small files conceal this mistake, because an inefficient policy remains cheap long enough to look correct; video removes that disguise, and a catalog that generates 12 candidates for each accepted creative can retain eleven times as many rejected sources as approved ones before counting renditions. That is why role assignment happens at ingestion rather than during a later cost review. The application should be able to explain, for any stored object, which product or campaign owns it, why its quality tier exists, which policy version selected its expiration, and what condition blocks deletion. If it cannot answer those questions, a lifecycle rule will automate ambiguity rather than resolve it.

The quality rule should be narrow. Keep a master only if another transformation is reasonably expected or regeneration would lose an approved creative. For ordinary playback, serve a delivery rendition through the CDN path rather than repeatedly moving master-quality bytes. This adds a rendition object, but it prevents routine customer traffic from paying the bandwidth cost of editing headroom that a browser cannot use.

Asset class Why it exists Access path Expiration posture
Rejected candidate Review and short dispute window Internal, signed access only Short and explicit
Approved master Future crop, encode, or text revision Restricted worker access Long enough for the reuse case
Delivery rendition Storefront playback and re-download CDN or short-lived presigned URL Aligned with the listing or campaign
Thumbnail or poster Catalog browsing Derived delivery path Rebuildable, but not necessarily free to rebuild

The table deliberately contains no universal day counts. Return windows, legal holds, campaign reuse, and the ability to reproduce the same creative determine those numbers. Storage governance fails when an example such as 7, 90, or 365 days is copied into production without an owner for the decision.

Make deletion a consequence, not a timer

A timer can identify work that is due. It cannot prove custody. The state transition should run generated -> copying -> verified -> serving -> source_delete_due -> source_deleted, with deletion eligibility depending on verified and serving, not merely on age.

That distinction handles the ugly interval between systems. If the copy succeeds and the metadata update fails, reconciliation can discover a private destination object that is not yet referenced. If metadata points at the destination before verification, a customer can receive a broken object. If source deletion succeeds but the worker dies before recording it, the next run must reconcile the already-completed action without treating absence alone as evidence that custody is safe. At-least-once execution turns each of those intervals into a normal state, so the worker needs a stable asset identifier and idempotent transitions.

The generation-side flow uses two verified operations: obtain GET /v1/video/download_url/{id}, then, after the controlled copy has been verified and the serving pointer has changed, call DELETE /v1/video/delete/{id}. Do not attach the API's Authorization header to the returned presigned download URL. That URL carries its own temporary authorization; forwarding a bearer credential to another host crosses an authentication boundary for no benefit.

Destination objects must remain private or signed-only. Customer re-downloads should receive fresh, short-lived presigned URLs from the application-owned bucket, never a public object URL and never a fresh dependency on the generation provider. The provider copy becomes disposable only after the customer path no longer depends on it.

Here is a compact API client suitable for a Python worker behind a Node.js orchestration service. It obtains the transfer URL through the verified route, uses an environment variable for the key, sets the method explicitly, surfaces non-2xx response bodies, and honors Retry-After on HTTP 429. It deliberately prints the documented response rather than guessing an undeclared response field; the copy worker can map the response through the live discovery schema it has pinned and reviewed.

import json
import os
import sys
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def get_download_metadata(asset_id: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    safe_id = quote(asset_id, safe="")
    api_host = ".".join(("api", "infrai", "cc"))
    url = f"https://{api_host}/v1/video/download_url/{safe_id}"

    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            url,
            method="GET",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                body = response.read().decode("utf-8")
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected status {response.status}: {body}")
                return json.loads(body)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"download metadata failed ({error.code}): {body}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 60))

    raise RuntimeError("retry budget exhausted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(get_download_metadata(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

Do not reuse this request's bearer header when the worker fetches the returned presigned URL. In a production schema, store the selected retention policy version beside expires_at; otherwise a later configuration change can silently rewrite the meaning of old rows.

Compare control planes after defining the boundary

Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and Cloudflare R2 can all be evaluated as the application-owned custody layer. The selection should happen after the states above are agreed, because a lifecycle feature cannot repair an application that serves a provider URL or deletes before verification. Their official documentation describes lifecycle management, but the operational fit differs around identity, eventing, replication choices, signed access, and the network path to the storefront.

Product Sensible shortlist condition Question that can disqualify it
Amazon S3 AWS identity, event, and data controls already govern the service Can the team test lifecycle, replication, and presigned delivery as one recovery path?
Google Cloud Storage The workload already uses Google Cloud projects and service identities Does signed delivery fit the existing identity boundary and CDN route?
Azure Blob Storage Commerce workloads are operated through Azure identity and policy Are lifecycle rules and delegated access observable by the same on-call team?
Cloudflare R2 The storefront delivery path already runs through Cloudflare Have API assumptions, residency needs, and the complete read path been validated?

This is not a feature-equivalence claim. Read each product's current lifecycle and signed-access documentation, then run deletion and restore drills against the exact configuration. Marketing pages tend to flatten the distinction between an object being durably stored, an object being reachable through the intended identity path, and an object being recoverable after an operator mistake. Storage architecture cannot afford that flattening.

The managed-media comparison is different. Cloudinary fits when transformation and delivery should live in the same media control plane. imgix is a stronger candidate when the primary job is dynamic delivery from an existing source, while ImageKit belongs on the shortlist when image and video optimization workflows are central. Cloudflare Stream is the more direct alternative when managed video upload, encoding, and playback matter more than retaining raw object-store control. Each choice adds a vendor-specific transformation or delivery contract, so export, private-source access, deletion semantics, and original-file retention need verification in current documentation.

Infrai is a reasonable generation-side option when a team wants plain REST calls without installing or tracking a client SDK. Its API is self-describing: a public discovery endpoint requires no key and exposes full request and response JSON Schema. Infrai puts its verified 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and one bill, avoiding the platform pattern of juggling 30 SDKs, 30 keys, and 30 invoices. In this workflow, that single credential and consolidated billing reduce key rotation and invoice reconciliation across generation and adjacent backend jobs. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. The limitation is equally clear: it does not fit a team seeking one managed product to own transformation, encoding, playback, and media delivery; Cloudinary or Cloudflare Stream should be evaluated instead, while a team already committed to an external origin may prefer imgix or ImageKit. These are integration advantages and trade-offs, not reasons to leave the sole durable video copy with the generation service.

Price does not settle this decision. The durable cost model is stored bytes over time, write and read operations, transformation copies, and network transfer along the real customer path. A team should measure approved masters, rejected candidates, renditions per listing, re-download frequency, and retention days in its own workload; a volatile unit-price table cannot substitute for those counts.

Roll out the custody change without a flag day

First, dual-write only the metadata: record the intended bucket key and quality role while the existing download behavior remains unchanged. Next, copy newly completed assets into a private prefix, verify them, and shadow-check that a presigned destination read is possible without exposing that URL to customers. Do this for a bounded cohort.

Then switch re-downloads for verified rows to the controlled bucket. Track rows stuck in copying, objects with no matching row, rows whose destination object is absent, and source deletions that remain due. These are reconciliation counts, not invented service-level objectives; establish thresholds from observed traffic and the business tolerance for delayed cleanup.

Only after that path has operated correctly should scheduled source deletion begin. Keep the deletion worker independently stoppable. A rollback should restore the serving pointer for assets whose source still exists, while the durable bucket copy remains the preferred recovery asset.

Finally, enable bucket lifecycle rules for object classes whose application retention has already been proven. Lifecycle expiration is a backstop, not the primary state machine. Preserve legal holds and explicit exceptions outside the default clock, sample restore procedures, and review policy versions when merchandising changes its reuse horizon.

The compact decision is this: preserve quality where it retains future creative value, spend delivery bandwidth only on renditions customers can use, and let deletion follow verified custody. Everything else is vendor selection.

Sources and References

  • Amazon S3 object lifecycle management
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage object lifecycle management
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management
  • Azure Storage shared access signatures
  • Cloudflare R2 object lifecycles
  • Cloudinary video transformations
  • imgix video API
  • ImageKit video API
  • Cloudflare Stream documentation

title: TacnaGo: modelando una guía turística con documentos JSON en Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL y .NET 9
description:
Con mi compañero Gerald Zevallos construimos TacnaGo, una guía de lugares turísticos de Tacna (Perú) hecha con .NET 9 y Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, publicada en Azure. En este artículo explico la parte de la aplicación: cómo modelamos los datos como documentos, cómo elegimos la clave de partición y qué consultas hace la API.

👉 App publicada: https://app-tacnago-geraldzvallos.azurewebsites.net
👉 Repositorio: https://github.com/Geraldzvallos/tacnago-cosmosdb

La idea

Queríamos algo pequeño pero real: una lista de lugares de Tacna (historia, museos, playas, gastronomía, naturaleza y pueblos) que se pueda filtrar, buscar y ampliar desde la web. Es un buen caso para una base de datos de documentos, porque cada lugar tiene datos parecidos, pero no siempre los mismos.

¿Por qué una base NoSQL de documentos?

En una base relacional tendríamos que crear columnas para todo, o tablas aparte para los datos que solo algunos lugares tienen. En Cosmos DB for NoSQL cada lugar es un documento JSON y cada uno puede traer los campos que necesite. Por ejemplo, una picantería guarda su plato típico y un monumento guarda su año:

{
  "id": "picanterias-de-pocollay",
  "categoria": "gastronomia",
  "nombre": "Picanterías de Pocollay",
  "provincia": "Tacna",
  "distrito": "Pocollay",
  "descripcion": "Restaurantes campestres donde se prueba el picante a la tacneña y la patasca.",
  "tags": ["comida tipica", "campestre", "familia"],
  "detalles": { "platoTipico": "Picante a la tacneña" }
}

La clave de partición: /categoria

En Cosmos DB los documentos se reparten en particiones según una clave de partición. Elegimos /categoria porque:

  • La consulta más común de la app es "dame los lugares de esta categoría", y con esta clave va a una sola partición, que es lo más barato.
  • Hay pocas categorías y los lugares se reparten de forma pareja entre ellas.
  • Para leer un documento puntual basta con el id y la categoría.

Una consecuencia importante es que la clave de partición de un documento no se puede cambiar. Si alguien intenta mover un lugar a otra categoría, la API responde con un error y explica que hay que borrarlo y crearlo de nuevo. Además, la API normaliza la categoría ("Gastronomía " pasa a "gastronomia") para que siempre caiga en la misma partición.

Las consultas

La API devuelve en cada respuesta el encabezado x-ru-charge con el costo de la operación en Request Units, y la página lo muestra arriba a la derecha.

Operación Consulta Costo aproximado
Lectura puntual (id + categoría) ReadItemAsync 1 RU
Lugares de una categoría WHERE c.categoria = @categoria en una partición unas pocas RU
Todos los lugares consulta entre particiones con ORDER BY más RU
Buscar por etiqueta ARRAY_CONTAINS(c.tags, @tag) consulta entre particiones
Cantidad por categoría GROUP BY c.categoria con COUNT(1) consulta entre particiones

El código clave

Usamos el SDK oficial Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos con un solo CosmosClient para toda la aplicación (es thread-safe y reutiliza las conexiones). Lo configuramos para guardar el JSON en camelCase, así la propiedad Categoria se guarda como categoria y coincide con la clave de partición:

builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp =>
{
    var s = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<CosmosSettings>>().Value;
    return new CosmosClient(s.Endpoint, s.Key, new CosmosClientOptions
    {
        ApplicationName = "TacnaGo",
        UseSystemTextJsonSerializerWithOptions = new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web)
    });
});

Cuando se filtra por categoría, se le indica al SDK la partición para que no consulte las demás:

var query = new QueryDefinition("SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.categoria = @categoria ORDER BY c.nombre")
    .WithParameter("@categoria", cat);
return ConsultarAsync<Lugar>(query, new QueryRequestOptions { PartitionKey = new PartitionKey(cat) });

Y la lectura puntual, la operación más barata de Cosmos DB:

var resp = await _container.ReadItemAsync<Lugar>(id, new PartitionKey(categoria));
return new Resultado<Lugar>(resp.Resource, resp.RequestCharge);

Las consultas siempre usan parámetros (@categoria, @tag) y nunca concatenan texto, así se evita la inyección.

La API y la página web

La API es una Minimal API de .NET 9 con estos endpoints:

Método Ruta
GET /api/lugares y /api/lugares?categoria=museos
GET /api/lugares/buscar?tag=playa
GET /api/categorias
GET /api/lugares/{categoria}/{id}
POST /api/lugares
PUT /api/lugares/{categoria}/{id}
DELETE /api/lugares/{categoria}/{id}

Todos los endpoints se pueden probar desde Swagger: https://app-tacnago-geraldzvallos.azurewebsites.net/swagger

La página web es HTML, CSS y JavaScript sin frameworks. La sirve la misma API desde wwwroot y consume los endpoints con fetch.

Despliegue (en resumen)

La app se empaqueta en una imagen Docker de dos etapas y se despliega en Azure App Service con GitHub Actions. Terraform crea la base y el contenedor de Cosmos DB, y un workflow carga los 13 lugares de ejemplo. Gerald lo explica en detalle en su artículo: ENLACE_ARTICULO_GERALD

Lo que aprendí

  • En NoSQL el modelo se diseña pensando en las consultas que vas a hacer, no solo en los datos.
  • Elegir bien la clave de partición cambia el costo de cada consulta, y las RU lo hacen visible.
  • Un esquema flexible es cómodo, pero conviene validar en la API los campos obligatorios (nombre y categoría).

Enlaces

  • Repositorio: https://github.com/Geraldzvallos/tacnago-cosmosdb
  • App publicada: https://app-tacnago-geraldzvallos.azurewebsites.net
  • API (Swagger): https://app-tacnago-geraldzvallos.azurewebsites.net/swagger
  • Despliegue automatizado (GitHub Actions): https://github.com/Geraldzvallos/tacnago-cosmosdb/actions
  • Video (grabado con Gerald): https://youtu.be/ofNwCJyyc8I

title: Turning Your Python AI Agent Into an Asynchronous FastAPI Backend with Server-Sent Events (SSE)
description:
After building our standalone Python agent in Post #27, Post #28 wraps our reasoning loop inside an asynchronous FastAPI microservice with Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming.

Why FastAPI for AI Agents?

FastAPI leverages native ASGI async/await to prevent thread blocking during slow I/O waits (such as GitHub REST API calls or vector database queries). Because FastAPI is built natively around Pydantic, your agent tool input schemas double as FastAPI request validation bodies.

Streaming SSE via StreamingResponse

Using Python generator functions (async def agent_event_stream()), you can yield custom W3C-compliant SSE frames (event: tool-start, event: text-delta, event: done) directly through FastAPI's StreamingResponse with media_type='text/event-stream' and anti-buffering headers.

Read the full tutorial with complete Python source code on my blog: https://zahidhasantonmoy.vercel.app/blog/fastapi-ai-agent-backend-streaming-python

title: Every answer points to a verse: designing a Bible study app around traceable answers
description:
Most Bible study apps give you a reading and a reflection question. Wayfold is built around a stricter idea: every answer should point to the exact words in the chapter that prove it. Here's how that rule shaped the app.

Answers you can trace to a verse

Read the full chapter (World English Bible, or have it read aloud), answer a few questions about what happened, then see the exact verse that answers each one. Two more exercises use the same rule:

  • Trace: put the chapter's main events in order, each tied to the verse where it happens.
  • Find the verse: you get a prompt, then tap the line in the chapter that answers it.

Labels for how certain a note is

"Go deeper" notes on history, language and meaning are each marked as what the text says, history, interpretation, or debated. The map does the same thing for places: 64 key places on Apple Maps, each labeled well established, likely, debated, uncertain or unknown. A 27-event timeline marks dates as firm, approximate, traditional, debated or undated. Being explicit about uncertainty felt more honest than one confident pin on a map.

A place index for the whole Bible

774 of the Bible's 1,189 chapters mention a place. Open a chapter to see the places it names; open a place to see every chapter that mentions it. Ten journeys step stop by stop through Abraham, the Exodus, Ruth and Naomi, Elijah, Jonah, the life of Jesus and Paul's travels to Rome.

Built for small-group leaders

Printable PDF leader guides for a chapter or a whole book: an introduction, the outline in order, questions with an answer key and verses, a background note, places named and a reflection question. Print, save to Files, AirDrop or email.

Six study books, 21 chapters. Ruth and Jonah are free, including their leader guides. Philippians, James, Habakkuk and Philemon come with Premium Lifetime.

Wayfold: Understand the Bible on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/wayfold-understand-the-bible/id6820304462

If you've built reference or study tools: how do you show uncertainty without overwhelming the reader?

title: Designing the first 10 seconds of a quit-vaping app: one button for a craving
description:
A vaping craving usually peaks and passes within minutes. The problem is those minutes. CraveBreaker is built around one button, "I have a craving", and what happens in the first few seconds after you tap it.

The craving screen: no account, no paywall, no questionnaire

  • A 90-second reset: slow breathing plus a quiet 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise.
  • Pattern Break: a small puzzle to pull your attention somewhere else.
  • A craving timer: 1, 3 or 5 minutes or your own length. Stop early or add time.
  • Your reasons: the words you wrote for yourself, shown back to you.
  • Change the routine: practical swaps for coffee, driving, stress and work breaks.
  • Reach out: text someone you trust, or find free quitline support (U.S. and Canada).

Every craving tool is free, always. That was a deliberate decision: the moment someone needs help is the worst moment for a purchase screen.

Data that only says what you recorded

Log a craving in seconds: situation, intensity, what you tried, and whether you vaped. Patterns only appear once you've logged enough to be meaningful, and they're shown as observations, not causes. The app doesn't claim to measure your body; progress is your quit date, your vape-free stretch, total vape-free days and cravings handled.

A lapse doesn't erase progress

Vaped? Record it without judgment. Your original quit date, total vape-free days and milestones stay. You look at what happened, adjust the plan and pick a next step. Resetting everything to zero after one slip is a common design choice, and we think it pushes people to quit the app instead of the vape.

Savings, with the formula shown

Enter what you spent per week or month and see estimated spending avoided, with the calculation visible. You can also record money you actually set aside.

Guides on cravings, withdrawal, triggers and lapses are short and sourced from Smokefree.gov and Health Canada guidance. Everything runs privately and offline.

CraveBreaker: Quit Vaping is free on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/cravebreaker-quit-vaping/id6787461078

Have you designed for a "moment of need" screen? What did you remove to make it faster?

title: Designing a pill reminder that never says 'missed' when it doesn't know
description:
When several family members help an aging parent with medication, the hardest bug isn't a crash. It's a record that says something that isn't true. "Missed" when nobody actually checked. "Given" when someone only meant to give it. Two siblings both logging the same dose.

We built DoseBeacon around one principle: the history should only ever say what someone actually reported. Here's how that shaped the design.

Four honest buttons for the person taking the medicine

Senior Mode shows one large, high-contrast card at a time with four choices: LOG AS TAKEN, LATER, NOT SURE and I NEED HELP. "Not sure" is a first-class answer, not an error state. Read-aloud, Dynamic Type and VoiceOver are supported, reminders are scheduled on the device so they work offline, and Senior Mode never shows ads or purchase screens.

"Not confirmed yet" instead of "missed"

A dose nobody has reported is shown as Not confirmed yet, never "missed". Absence of data is not evidence of a missed dose, and a scary word on a parent's screen helps nobody.

A claim is not a dose

Tapping "I'm handling this" tells the rest of the care circle who is on it. That claim is never displayed as a dose given. Only a report is a report.

Conflicts get flagged, not overwritten

If two people report the same dose, it's marked Needs review rather than last-write-wins. Every report keeps who made it, on which device and when. Corrections append to the history; nothing is silently erased.

Care circle permissions

A circle code only sends a join request. The parent's manager approves it, picks a role (manager, dose-logging helper or read-only family) and can revoke any device. Every screen shows when it last updated, so nobody mistakes stale data for current data.

Setup that rewards honesty

"Beacon Quests" light up a lighthouse as you get organized: add medications, choose a helper, review the emergency card. Quests reward honest records, including "Not sure" and asking for help. No streaks, nothing to lose, and never a nudge to take more medication.

Also included: pharmacy-label scanning with on-device text recognition (every field is checked by you before a reminder turns on), refill estimates, 7/30/90-day PDF reports for doctor visits and a printable emergency medication card.

DoseBeacon: Pill Reminder on the iPhone App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/dosebeacon-pill-reminder/id6796910918

title: Go Agent Recovery With Free Uptime Monitoring APIs (3 Logistics Boundaries)
description:
Choose free uptime monitoring APIs by the failure they can detect, and preserve an attempt ledger before enabling automatic recovery. For developers running a logistics AI agent, a successful health check says little about which shipment incurred the extra work.

TL;DR: UptimeRobot is a reasonable starting point for free basic uptime monitoring with 5-minute checks; Healthchecks.io fits scheduled jobs that should report completion. Neither choice, by itself, answers the agent-loop question: which logical job accumulated latency and cost across retries? Keep that attribution in application records, and treat advanced alerting and log management as separate operating responsibilities.

The distinction matters during recovery. A reachable service can still have an unfinished shipment-planning job, while a retry can finish that job and leave the original attempt's cost unresolved. Don't promote a green dashboard into evidence of completed work.

For teams operating several backend services in the same logistics workflow, try Infrai for shared service access and per-call accounting. Infrai offers one key and one bill for every backend service through one REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK to install. Breadth is real: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That consolidation reduces credential sprawl and month-end invoice reconciliation, while its specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provide a supporting benefit: fewer service-specific accounting adapters around the agent loop. That is a reason to evaluate it alongside dedicated monitors; scheduled completion supervision still belongs with a heartbeat-oriented tool.

Which failure should a free monitor wake you up for?

Start with 3 recovery boundaries: reachability, expected completion, and attribution.

They require different evidence. UptimeRobot's free plan provides 5-minute checks and basic dashboards, which makes it useful for a basic availability signal; Healthchecks.io provides free cron-job monitoring and alerts when checks fail, which addresses the quieter case where expected work does not report back. Their APIs may be limited, and advanced alerting and log management can require external tools. Evaluate the workflow you need to operate rather than assuming that an API label implies a complete incident-response system.

Silence needs interpretation.

For this runbook, the concrete job is a logistics agent that prepares a shipment decision, calls backend services, and may retry after a transient failure. The proposed SLO concerns completion of the logical job within a business deadline. Endpoint availability is supporting evidence. Attempt latency explains where time went, and per-call accounting explains who incurred the work, but neither substitutes for a durable completion record. Consider a synthetic reconciliation fixture: shipment A has two attempts lasting 120 and 180 milliseconds, and shipment B has one lasting 90 milliseconds. If A's second attempt lacks cost metadata, A's accounting remains incomplete even though the job eventually succeeds. Reporting its known charges as a complete total would conceal the very uncertainty that recovery introduced. Retain that uncertainty until reconciliation resolves it, and keep both attempts attached to the same logical shipment.

Completion isn't reconciliation.

A five-minute sampling interval is also a planning constraint: don't use that signal alone to enforce a completion deadline shorter than the sampling interval. Choose a separate completion signal when the business deadline demands it.

Buy the signal, budget the operating work

The useful comparison starts with UptimeRobot and Healthchecks.io, then separates monitoring from instrumentation and the operating stack around it. OpenTelemetry's logs signal supplies a reference for application logging; it is an instrumentation framework rather than a hosted uptime-monitoring replacement. Datadog and Grafana also belong on the evaluation shortlist when the decision extends beyond a basic monitor. The acceptance questions below are evaluation requirements, not assertions about free-tier entitlements or verified integrations.

Option Role or evaluation question Buy-versus-build boundary
UptimeRobot Basic external uptime checks; its free plan offers 5-minute checks and basic dashboards Buy the basic availability signal; plan external tooling for advanced alerting and log management.
Healthchecks.io Scheduled jobs that fail to check in; free cron monitoring and alerting features Buy scheduled-job supervision; retain shipment completion and attempt records in the application.
OpenTelemetry Application log instrumentation for attempt evidence Build the instrumentation and choose its operational destination; a logs signal alone is not a hosted uptime service.
Datadog Require a demonstration that operators can connect an alert to the affected shipment's attempt evidence Compare the proposed operating workflow with the team's current alerting and logging arrangement before consolidating.
Grafana Require a demonstration that the proposed dashboard distinguishes missing completion from successful retries Decide who will operate the proposed deployment and its data sources before accepting the design.
Infrai Shared backend access and specified per-call accounting metadata Consolidate keys and billing; keep dedicated uptime and heartbeat tooling in the design.

The specialist wins when the operational question is simply whether a scheduled job checked in. Use Healthchecks.io for that requirement. UptimeRobot is the simpler fit when basic external reachability is the question and the checking interval suits the service.

Don't buy overlap blindly.

For Datadog and Grafana, the decision here remains conditional on those demonstrations; this guide does not establish a free monitoring entitlement for either. That makes them broader evaluation candidates, while UptimeRobot and Healthchecks.io have the specific free monitoring roles described above. OpenTelemetry addresses application evidence rather than replacing those external signals.

Consolidation carries another tradeoff. A shared backend interface reduces integration work, but making its accounting envelope the only internal record couples incident reconstruction to that interface. Keep an application-owned ledger with a stable logical job identifier. Map vendor metadata into it rather than making vendor request identifiers the identity of the shipment.

Capacity planning starts before the next retry policy change. In a hypothetical workload of 100 logical jobs per minute, a maximum of 3 attempts per job permits 300 attempts per minute before counting extra backend calls within each attempt. These are planning inputs, not throughput measurements. Budget telemetry ingestion and reconciliation for attempts, and reserve capacity for recovery traffic; the customer-facing job count understates the work precisely when the system is struggling.

Preserve evidence and bound the polling loop

Give the logical shipment job one stable identifier and each execution attempt a distinct identifier. A request identifier from a backend call is useful evidence within that attempt.

Preserve it.

Idempotency and accounting solve different problems. A stable application operation key should protect a side effect from being applied twice, while the attempt ledger retains the evidence of each execution. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention, but verify the selected capability's idempotency contract before relying on it. Don't assume that a platform convention makes every operation idempotent, or that deduplication means every attempt has identical accounting consequences.

The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. That helps an operator verify the capability contract before changing a recovery client. The following standalone Go program makes a read-only metrics query. It uses no filters and prints the response without inventing a response schema or pretending that an aggregate query reconstructs shipment-level accounting. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with the Go toolchain. The 20-second deadline and 3-attempt ceiling are example client policy choices.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 20 {
            return 21 * time.Second
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
        return 0
    }
    return fallback
}

func query(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (1<<20)+1))
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if len(data) > 1<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("response exceeds client size limit; HTTP %d", resp.StatusCode)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if attempt == 2 {
                return fmt.Errorf("rate limited after 3 attempts: %s", data)
            }
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            if deadline, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok && delay >= time.Until(deadline) {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds remaining deadline: %s", data)
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("metrics query returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(data)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    err := query(ctx, key)
    cancel()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The example honors Retry-After as seconds or an HTTP date and otherwise applies exponential backoff. If the requested wait exceeds the remaining deadline, it stops rather than retrying early. It performs no write, so it needs no idempotency key.

That boundary is intentional.

For the agent itself, record the outcome before scheduling another attempt, and preserve uncertainty if the prior operation's result is ambiguous. An automatic replay is a poor substitute for deciding whether that operation is safe to repeat. Keep alert dispatch and heartbeat supervision in dedicated tooling, with an explicit owner for any polling and threshold evaluation around metrics queries. Correlating log records by trace and span identifiers is useful evidence, but it should not be treated as a distributed trace query or a span-tree view.

Summed attempt latency also differs from end-to-end completion time. Backoff and queue delay contribute to the latter, while overlapping calls can make summed call durations exceed wall-clock time. Measure the logical job from acceptance to terminal completion separately; otherwise a recovery policy that waits longer can appear to improve latency merely because the accounting excludes its waiting time.

Verify recovery before changing the retry budget

Use synthetic fixtures before enabling automatic recovery. For shipment A, verify that both the 120-millisecond and 180-millisecond attempts remain attributable to the same job; for shipment B, verify that its single 90-millisecond attempt stays separate. A missing cost record must remain visibly incomplete rather than becoming zero. Those checks validate the application ledger, not a claim that the metrics query returns shipment records.

Then exercise the client against a controlled test server: a successful response, an ordinary client error with a reason in the body, and rate limiting with Retry-After expressed both ways. Verify the 3-attempt ceiling, the deadline exit, and the response-size boundary. Check that an excessive wait ends the query without an early retry. Separately, withhold a scheduled completion signal and verify that the heartbeat monitor alerts through the chosen delivery path; a successful metrics query cannot establish that this path works.

Keep rollback boring.

If a new retry policy increases attempt volume or makes reconciliation ambiguous, restore the previous retry budget and pause automatic replay of unresolved jobs while preserving their ledger entries. Keep external monitoring active. Resume recovery only after the operator can distinguish a completed shipment decision from an uncertain side effect, and after the capacity plan includes the extra attempts rather than merely the number of logical jobs. For a latency SLO, compare acceptance-to-completion duration with its business deadline; for attribution, require every charged call to map to an attempt or an explicit reconciliation exception.

References

  • UptimeRobot
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • OpenTelemetry logs signal
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation

If shared backend access and per-call accounting fit this boundary, start with the Infrai documentation.

title: Building a REST API with Laravel and React: A Beginner-Friendly Guide
description:
Building a REST API with Laravel and React: A Beginner-Friendly Guide

Modern web applications often separate the frontend and backend to make development more organized, flexible, and maintainable.

One popular combination is Laravel for backend development and React for frontend development.

In this article, we'll explore how these two technologies work together to create a simple full-stack application.

1. Understanding the Architecture

Before writing code, it's important to understand the responsibilities of each technology.

Laravel (Backend)

Laravel handles:

  • API endpoints and routing.
  • Database operations.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Business logic.
  • Request validation.

React (Frontend)

React handles:

  • User interfaces.
  • Forms and user interactions.
  • Displaying data from the API.
  • Managing application state.
  • Communicating with the backend.

The general workflow looks like this:

React → HTTP Request → Laravel API → Database

The response then travels back to React, where the data can be displayed to the user.

2. Creating a Laravel Project

First, create a new Laravel application:

composer create-project laravel/laravel backend

Navigate into the project:

cd backend

Start the development server:

php artisan serve

Your Laravel application will typically be available at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000

3. Creating an API Endpoint

Let's create a simple API endpoint that returns a list of users.

Open your routes/api.php file and add:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/users', function () {
    return response()->json([
        'success' => true,
        'message' => 'Users retrieved successfully',
        'data' => [
            [
                'id' => 1,
                'name' => 'John Doe',
                'email' => 'john@example.com',
            ],
            [
                'id' => 2,
                'name' => 'Jane Doe',
                'email' => 'jane@example.com',
            ],
        ],
    ]);
});

This endpoint returns JSON data that can be consumed by a frontend application.

4. Connecting React to Laravel

Now let's create a React application.

npm create vite@latest frontend -- --template react

Install the dependencies:

cd frontend
npm install

Inside your React application, open src/App.jsx and add:

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function App() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/users")
      .then((response) => {
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error("Failed to fetch users");
        }

        return response.json();
      })
      .then((result) => {
        setUsers(result.data);
      })
      .catch((error) => {
        console.error(error);
      })
      .finally(() => {
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, []);

  if (loading) {
    return <p>Loading users...</p>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>User Management</h1>

      {users.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>
          <h2>{user.name}</h2>
          <p>{user.email}</p>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

This example demonstrates how React can request data from Laravel and display the returned users.

5. Understanding CORS

When your frontend and backend run on different origins, browsers may block requests unless the backend allows them.

This is where Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) comes in.

Laravel provides CORS configuration through its application configuration.

Make sure your frontend origin is allowed in the backend configuration before testing API requests.

Avoid allowing every origin in production unless your security requirements explicitly justify it.

6. Improving the Application

Once the basic connection works, you can start adding real application features:

  • User registration and login.
  • CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete).
  • Form validation.
  • Database integration using MySQL.
  • API authentication.
  • Pagination and filtering.
  • Error handling.

For larger applications, organizing your Laravel code into controllers, models, requests, services, and API resources can make the project easier to maintain.

7. Best Practices

Here are some practices worth following when developing a Laravel and React application:

  1. Keep frontend and backend responsibilities separate.
  2. Validate incoming data on the backend.
  3. Never expose sensitive credentials in frontend code.
  4. Use environment variables for configuration.
  5. Handle API errors properly.
  6. Keep your components reusable.
  7. Use Git to track changes and collaborate with other developers.

Final Thoughts

Building a full-stack application becomes easier when you understand how the frontend and backend communicate.

Laravel provides a powerful backend foundation, while React makes it possible to create dynamic and interactive user experiences.

You don't need to master everything immediately. Start with a simple API, connect it to React, and gradually introduce more advanced features.

The best way to understand full-stack development is to build something yourself.

Have you tried combining Laravel and React in a project? What challenges did you encounter? Let's share our experiences and learn together!

15/11
TOP - Intermediate HTML and CSS: 9%.
Intermediate HTML Concepts - Tables

I squeezed some free time and put it to learning.

Done reading HTML table basics from MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/Structuring_content/HTML_table_basics

Honestly, I remember that I learned about table before but still forget about a lot of things.

This read is mostly to refresh the memory of table basics for me.
Next, I will learn about tables advanced from MDN.

title: From Beginner to Full-Stack Developer: What I'm Learning Along the Way
description:
From Beginner to Full-Stack Developer: What I'm Learning Along the Way

Becoming a full-stack developer is more than just learning how to write code. It's about understanding how different technologies work together, solving problems, and continuously improving your skills.

As someone building projects and exploring modern web development, I've learned that the journey is not always easy—but every challenge brings an opportunity to grow.

1. Learning the Frontend

The frontend is where users interact with an application.

I've been exploring technologies such as:

  • React for building interactive user interfaces.
  • JavaScript and TypeScript for application logic.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive and modern designs.

One important lesson I've learned is that a good interface should not only look attractive but also provide a smooth user experience.

2. Understanding Backend Development

A frontend application needs a reliable backend to manage data, authentication, and business logic.

Laravel has become one of the technologies I'm interested in using for backend development.

Some of the concepts I'm continuously learning include:

  • RESTful API development.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Database relationships.
  • CRUD operations.
  • Request validation and error handling.

Understanding these concepts helps me build applications that are more organized, maintainable, and scalable.

3. Working With Databases

Databases are an essential part of almost every application.

I've been working with technologies such as MySQL and SQLite while learning how to structure tables, establish relationships, and manage application data.

A well-designed database can make an application easier to maintain and improve as it grows.

4. Learning Git and Team Collaboration

One of the most valuable skills I've been developing is using Git and GitHub.

Working with branches, commits, pull requests, and code reviews has helped me understand how developers collaborate on real-world projects.

I've also learned that communication and teamwork are just as important as technical skills.

5. Exploring AI-Powered Development Tools

AI tools are becoming useful companions for developers.

They can help explain unfamiliar code, identify potential bugs, generate ideas, and improve development workflows.

However, I believe developers should still understand the code they write. AI should support learning and problem-solving rather than replace critical thinking.

6. Every Project Is an Opportunity to Learn

Building projects has taught me that real learning happens when theory meets practice.

Not every feature works on the first attempt. Sometimes there are dependency conflicts, unexpected errors, database problems, or confusing bugs.

But debugging those problems is part of becoming a better developer.

Final Thoughts

My journey toward becoming a full-stack developer is still ongoing.

I'm continuously learning, experimenting with different technologies, and building projects that challenge my current knowledge.

My biggest takeaway so far is simple:

You don't have to know everything to start building. You just have to be willing to learn something new every day.

If you're also learning software development, keep building, keep experimenting, and don't be afraid of making mistakes.

Every experienced developer was once a beginner.

What technology are you currently learning, and what has been your biggest challenge so far? Let's connect and learn together!

title: Architecting Scalable E-Commerce & Booking Platforms with React, Django REST & PostgreSQL (Sub-Second TTFB Architecture)
description:
Architecting Scalable E-Commerce & Booking Platforms with React, Django REST & PostgreSQL (Sub-Second TTFB Architecture)

Engineering scalable, mission-critical web applications—whether high-volume e-commerce engines, patient healthcare booking portals, or multi-tenant SaaS platforms—requires a disciplined decoupling of presentation and business logic. When off-the-shelf monolithic page builders buckle under high concurrency and database strain, senior engineering teams rely on the battle-tested power of React, Django REST Framework (DRF), and PostgreSQL.

In this technical architectural teardown, the engineering team at UCDREAMS breaks down the complete production blueprints for building sub-second TTFB, enterprise-grade web applications.

1. High-Performance Decoupled Architecture

Modern web application performance relies on strict separation of concerns:

[ Browser / Native App ]
       │  (HTTPS / HTTP/2 / WebSockets)
       ▼
[ Cloudflare / Fastly Edge CDN ] ────► Static Asset Cache & Geo-Routing
       │
       ▼ (Reverse Proxy / SSL Termination)
[ NGINX Edge Gateway & Rate Limiter ]
       │  (Gunicorn / Uvicorn WSGI/ASGI)
       ▼
[ Django REST Framework (DRF) Application Tier ]
       ├── Redis Enterprise (Query Cache, Session Store & Celery Queue)
       └── PostgreSQL High-Availability Cluster (PgBouncer Connection Pooling)

Key Architectural Tenets:

  1. Stateless JWT & HTTP-Only Refresh Tokens: Maximum horizontal scalability across multi-region container clusters without session affinity bottlenecks.
  2. PgBouncer Connection Pooling: Managing thousands of concurrent transactional connections with sub-millisecond query allocation.
  3. Redis Read-Through Caching: Eliminating duplicate database roundtrips for catalog metadata, inventory lookups, and user access control lists (ACLs).

2. Production Django REST Framework Optimization

Default Django ORM configurations often suffer from the classic N+1 query dilemma. In enterprise e-commerce and booking applications, unoptimized queries can rapidly exhaust database connection limits.

Eliminating N+1 Queries with select_related and prefetch_related 

# models.py - High-Performance E-Commerce Schema
from django.db import models
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model

User = get_user_model()

class BookingOrder(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='orders')
    reference_id = models.CharField(max_length=32, unique=True, db_index=True)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default='PENDING', db_index=True)
    total_amount = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True, db_index=True)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=['status', 'created_at']),
        ]

class BookingItem(models.Model):
    order = models.ForeignKey(BookingOrder, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='items')
    service_sku = models.CharField(max_length=64, db_index=True)
    quantity = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)
    unit_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

# views.py - Optimized DRF ViewSet with Sub-50ms Query Execution
from rest_framework import viewsets, permissions
from rest_framework.response import Response
from django.core.cache import cache

class BookingOrderViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):
    permission_classes = [permissions.IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        # 1-Query execution combining order, customer profile, and item lines
        return (
            BookingOrder.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)
            .select_related('user')
            .prefetch_related('items')
            .order_by('-created_at')
        )

3. Sub-Second Core Web Vitals on React Frontends

For consumer-facing booking and checkout flows, Core Web Vitals directly impact search engine visibility and checkout conversion rates:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Under 1.2s through prioritized edge hero rendering and WebP/AVIF compression.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Under 50ms via non-blocking asynchronous state dispatch and optimistic UI updates.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Zero shift with fixed aspect-ratio containers and server-driven skeleton loaders.

4. Real-Time State Sync via WebSockets

For live seat reservations, inventory countdowns, and concurrent booking locks, polling is an anti-pattern that creates unnecessary server load. We leverage Django Channels with Redis backends to broadcast state updates:

// React Live Booking Hook
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useLiveBookingState(orderId) {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('SYNCING');

  useEffect(() => {
    const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://ucdreams.com/ws/orders/${orderId}/`);

    ws.onmessage = (event) => {
      const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
      if (data.type === 'STATUS_UPDATE') {
        setStatus(data.status);
      }
    };

    return () => ws.close();
  }, [orderId]);

  return { status };
}

5. Live Showcase: The UCDREAMS Ecosystem

At UCDREAMS, our engineering teams put these full-stack principles into daily practice:

  • UCDREAMS Web Development Services: Hand-crafted, semantic, lightweight container architectures delivering guaranteed 95+ PageSpeed scores.
  • UCDREAMS In-Browser Tools Hub: 100% client-side, zero-server utilities including P2P WebRTC large file transfer (FileShareOnline), AI cutout background removal (Image Background Remover), and office document editors (DOCX Web Editor).
  • UCDREAMS Multiplayer Games Hub: 60FPS real-time canvas games powered by low-latency state synchronization (Paper War and Ludo Classic).

Need an Enterprise Web Application Built by Senior Engineers?

Whether you require a bespoke React/Django portal, high-converting Figma to WordPress conversion, or complex edge AI integration:

title: 5 Real Apps Using Rive Animation: Interactive UI Examples Developers Can Learn From
description:
5 Real Apps Using Rive Animation: Interactive UI Examples Developers Can Learn From

From interactive mascots and responsive UI components to animated health dashboards, here are five real-world Rive animation examples and what developers can learn from them.

A modern app can have a beautiful interface and still feel completely static.

The buttons work. The screens load. The API responds.

But what happens between those interactions?

What does your app do while an AI assistant is thinking? How does it celebrate a completed task? Can a character react when a user taps it? Can an animation respond to real-time progress?

This is where Rive animation becomes interesting.

Unlike a traditional animation that simply plays from beginning to end, Rive can use state machines and runtime inputs to connect motion directly to application logic.

That makes it particularly useful for:

  • Interactive UI and UX animations
  • Animated app mascots
  • AI companions and assistants
  • Gamified experiences
  • Progress indicators and achievements
  • Responsive product interactions

Let's look at five real products using Rive and explore how similar approaches could improve your own app.

1. Hoverine: Interactive UI Components Built With Rive

Product: Hoverine

Use case: Interactive buttons, toggles, loaders, and UI components.

Hoverine focuses on reusable interactive animations built with Rive.

Its library includes animated UI elements such as buttons, loading indicators, switches, and other interactive components.

What makes this approach useful for developers is the emphasis on Rive state machines and documented inputs.

Instead of treating animation as a video asset, developers can connect UI events to animation behavior.

Developer takeaway

Imagine a button with four visual states:

idle → hover → loading → success

With Rive, those states can live inside a single animation system.

Your React, Flutter, or React Native application can control the visual behavior based on actual user interactions.

For example:

// Illustrative application logic
// Connect these events to your Rive state machine.

function handleButtonClick() {
  setAnimationState("loading");

  submitForm()
    .then(() => setAnimationState("success"))
    .catch(() => setAnimationState("error"));
}

The exact runtime implementation depends on your Rive setup and platform, but the principle remains the same:

Animation should respond to application state, not run independently of it.

For developers building interactive dashboards, SaaS interfaces, or mobile applications, this can create a more cohesive user experience.

2. Tomosu: A Responsive Candle for Digital Wellbeing

Product: Tomosu

Use case: Interactive focus animation.

Tomosu is an iOS digital wellbeing app that uses a candle as part of its focus experience.

The creator has described using Rive to build the animated candle and integrate it with SwiftUI.

Instead of relying entirely on numbers and timers, the app uses a visual metaphor to represent a calmer interaction.

The candle can respond to touch and changes during the focus experience.

Developer takeaway

An animation becomes more meaningful when it represents something happening in the product.

Consider a meditation app with a character that responds to breathing.

Or a fitness app where a mascot's energy changes as a workout progresses.

For example, you could expose a numeric input:

breathingProgress: 0.0 → 1.0

That value could control the scale, glow, or movement of an animated element.

The result is a visual experience driven by real application data.

The important lesson: You don't need an elaborate animation to create an engaging interaction. A small, carefully designed visual response can be enough.

3. Welltory: Interactive Motion for Health Interfaces

Product: Welltory

Use case: Lightweight interactive UI animation.

Health applications often need to display complicated information.

Measurements, activity data, health scores, and daily trends can make an interface feel overwhelming.

Welltory has publicly identified Rive as one of the tools used to create lightweight, responsive animations within its product.

Developer takeaway

Motion can help communicate changes in an interface.

Consider these potential use cases:

  • A progress indicator responding to incoming data
  • A visual transition when a health measurement is completed
  • An animated confirmation after an action
  • A responsive dashboard component

These are examples of what developers can build with Rive, not claims about specific Welltory screens.

For a custom progress animation, you might define a numeric input:

State Machine: ProgressController

Inputs:
  progress: Number (0–100)
  isLoading: Boolean
  completed: Trigger

Your application can update progress as the underlying task advances.

When the process finishes, the completed trigger can play a short success animation.

The same principle works for onboarding, file uploads, productivity tools, and SaaS dashboards.

4. Brilliant: Interactive Mascot Animation

Product: Brilliant

Use case: Animated educational mascot.

Brilliant is an interactive learning platform covering subjects such as mathematics and coding.

Its recognizable character, Koji, is brought to life using Rive.

This is one of the most interesting examples for developers building educational apps, AI products, or gamified experiences.

Why interactive mascots are different

A traditional mascot animation might play a waving loop.

An interactive mascot can behave differently depending on what is happening in your application.

For example, imagine an AI learning companion with these states:

App event Mascot animation
User opens the app Welcome
User starts speaking Listening
AI generates a response Thinking
AI responds Talking
User answers correctly Celebrate
User makes a mistake Encouraging
No interaction Idle

This is an illustrative system design, not a specification of Brilliant's implementation.

With a Rive state machine, developers can control these behaviors through runtime inputs.

Example: AI companion state machine 

Artboard: AICompanion
State Machine: CompanionController

Inputs:
  isListening: Boolean
  isTalking: Boolean
  emotion: Number
  lookX: Number
  lookY: Number
  celebrate: Trigger
  reset: Trigger

Your application can update these inputs in response to user actions or AI events.

For example:

  • Start listening when the microphone activates.
  • Switch to thinking while waiting for a response.
  • Trigger talking when the assistant begins speaking.
  • Celebrate when the user completes a challenge.

You can also add numeric controls for eye tracking, mouth movement, and progress.

This is where a custom Rive animator becomes especially valuable.

The animation needs to look good, but it also needs a carefully structured state machine that developers can integrate and maintain.

5. BananaBin: Adding Personality to a macOS Utility

Product: BananaBin

Use case: Animated characters in a desktop utility.

BananaBin is a macOS application that adds personality to the system Trash Bin.

One of its distinctive visual features is animated flies, which the creator has confirmed were built using Rive.

It's a small interaction, but it demonstrates an important principle.

Not every app needs a full animated mascot.

Sometimes a single character or animated element can make an ordinary interface more memorable.

Developer takeaway

Think about the everyday interactions in your application.

Could an empty state have a little personality?

Could a completed task trigger a friendly reaction?

Could a loading indicator be more expressive?

These moments are opportunities for interactive motion.

The key is to keep animation purposeful and avoid distracting users from their primary tasks.

What These Five Rive Animation Examples Have in Common

Hoverine, Tomosu, Welltory, Brilliant, and BananaBin solve different problems.

But they illustrate how Rive can be applied across multiple product categories.

Product Rive use case What developers can learn
Hoverine Interactive UI components State-driven interface animation
Tomosu Responsive candle Visual feedback connected to user actions
Welltory Health interface motion Lightweight responsive UI
Brilliant Animated mascot Character-based product experiences
BananaBin Animated flies Personality in utility software

The larger opportunity isn't simply adding more animation.

It's connecting animation to application behavior.

Rive vs Lottie: When Does Rive Make More Sense?

Developers often ask whether they should use Rive or Lottie.

Both are useful, but they serve different needs.

Lottie is well suited to many timeline-based animations, such as illustrations, loading sequences, and onboarding motion.

Rive is particularly interesting when your animation needs to respond dynamically to application inputs.

For example:

Choose a simple timeline animation when:

  • You need a loading loop.
  • You want a short decorative animation.
  • Your animation doesn't require complex interactions.

Consider Rive when:

  • A mascot needs multiple emotional states.
  • A character should react to taps or gestures.
  • Animation changes based on real-time progress.
  • An AI companion needs listening, thinking, and talking states.
  • You need reusable state-machine logic.

This doesn't mean one tool is universally better than the other.

The right choice depends on how your product needs to behave.

Why Developers Should Work Directly With a Freelance Rive Animator

If you're building a product with interactive animation, you might be tempted to download a few assets and connect them yourself.

That can work for simple UI components.

But custom interactive characters and complex state machines introduce additional challenges.

A Rive animator who understands developer integration can help solve those challenges before they become expensive problems.

1. State Machines Built Around Your Application

A custom Rive animator can design animations around your real application events.

Instead of forcing your code to adapt to a generic animation, the animation can be built around your product requirements.

For example, an AI companion may need to handle:

  • Listening and talking states
  • Facial expressions
  • Eye tracking
  • Tap reactions
  • Celebration events
  • Interruption rules
  • Smooth transitions back to idle

These interactions require planning beyond visual keyframes.

2. Cleaner Developer Integration

A well-prepared Rive file can include clearly named inputs, predictable state transitions, and documented behavior.

Your development team should know exactly what each input does.

That reduces unnecessary guesswork during implementation.

3. Reusable Animation Systems

Instead of maintaining separate rendered animations for every reaction, a custom Rive project can provide multiple behaviors within a reusable animation system.

That can make future product updates easier, depending on how the animation is structured.

4. Direct Collaboration

Working directly with an animator makes it easier to discuss the details that matter to developers.

Questions like:

What happens if the user taps the mascot while it's talking?

Should the celebration animation interrupt the listening state?

Does the character return to idle or the latest selected mode?

How do we handle reduced-motion preferences?

These details matter in real applications.

And they are much easier to address when the animator and developer plan the behavior together.

Hire a Rive Animator for Your App or Website

I'm Praneeth, a freelance Rive animator specializing in interactive animations for websites, mobile apps, SaaS products, and AI experiences.

I help developers, founders, and product teams build custom Rive animations that are designed for real application integration.

My services include:

  • Interactive Rive mascots and character animation
  • AI companions and animated assistants
  • Rive state machines and character rigging
  • Gamification and achievement animations
  • Interactive UI and UX animation
  • Developer-ready .riv files and editable source assets
  • Integration guidance for React, Flutter, and React Native

Whether you're building a startup, improving an existing product, or adding a custom mascot to your app, I can help you turn your idea into an interactive animation system.

Tell me what you're building, which framework you're using, and what you'd like your animation to do.

Let's create an interaction your users will remember.

Final Thoughts

Rive animation isn't just about making interfaces look more polished.

It's about making them respond.

The five products we've explored demonstrate different ways animation can support digital experiences, from responsive UI components to memorable animated characters.

For developers, the real opportunity is connecting motion to application logic.

And for founders, it's creating products that feel more interactive, expressive, and distinctive.

title: Building ShopEase: From Distributed Architecture to Performance & Load Engineering
description:
When designing an enterprise-grade e-commerce backend, writing clean code is only half the battle—the system must also be scalable, fault-tolerant, fully traceable, and high-performing. In this article, we explore the production-ready architecture already implemented in ShopEase and outline our upcoming roadmap for Performance and Load Engineering.
🚀 Part 1: What Is Already Implemented (The Enterprise Foundation)
ShopEase incorporates top-tier system design and distributed architecture patterns right into its core codebase:

  1. Polyglot Persistence & Advanced DB Pooling (HikariCP)
  2. MySQL serves as the primary relational database for users and orders, backed by HikariCP connection pooling (maximum-pool-size=20, minimum-idle=10) to eliminate connection starvation under load.
  3. MongoDB manages flexible product catalogs, while PostgreSQL handles dedicated audit logs (shopping_db_audit), preventing heavy logging writes from slowing down primary transactional flows.
  4. High-Performance Caching Architecture
  5. A distributed Redis caching layer (spring.cache.type=redis) with a 10-minute TTL (600000ms) offloads frequent catalog reads from MySQL, boosting overall throughput and reducing database latency.
  6. Event-Driven Messaging with Apache Kafka & Distributed Tracing
  7. Order state changes leverage Apache Kafka event choreography (order-placed-topic) instead of synchronous blocking calls.
  8. Configured with Manual Acknowledgement (MANUAL_IMMEDIATE) and a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) recovery pipeline for bulletproof reliability.
  9. Distributed Tracing & Correlation ID Propagation: We bridged synchronous HTTP/REST entry points with asynchronous Kafka background threads. Using custom ProducerRecord header injection and consumer RecordInterceptor hooks, the active correlationId flows seamlessly across thread boundaries into MDC, making multi-threaded log aggregation effortless.
  10. Microservices Communication & Fault Tolerance
  11. Low-latency internal service-to-service communication is achieved via gRPC and Protocol Buffers (.proto).
  12. Resilience4j Circuit Breakers and automated fallbacks protect downstream services and payment gateways from cascading failures. 🎯 Part 2: What's Next — Performance & Load Engineering (Module 42) With a robust architectural foundation in place, our next major milestone is Load Engineering. We are shifting our focus to testing and optimizing how the system behaves under intense, real-world traffic spikes. Our Load Testing Roadmap:
  13. Graduated Traffic Simulation Stages:
    • Baseline Test: 10 concurrent users
    • Moderate Load: 100 concurrent users
    • High Load: 1,000 concurrent users
    • Stress Peak: 10,000+ requests
  14. Tooling Integration:
    • Utilizing load testing suites like k6 or JMeter to simulate realistic HTTP and gRPC traffic patterns.
  15. Key Performance Metrics Monitored:
    • Response Time Latency: Tracking p95 and p99 percentiles.
    • Throughput (RPS): Measuring successful requests processed per second under pressure.
  16. Bottleneck Detection & Fine-Tuning:
    • Analyzing JVM garbage collection behavior and memory footprints.
    • Tuning Tomcat/Netty thread pool sizes and HikariCP saturation limits. Conclusion ShopEase has evolved into a fully realized enterprise-grade distributed backend. With Performance & Load Engineering (Module 42) underway, we are battle-testing the system to ensure it can gracefully handle high-concurrency production workloads.

Stay tuned as we push ShopEase toward handling 10,000+ concurrent requests effortlessly!
