title: A stab at superpowers
description:
I've been using AI workflows to build applications for a little over one year now. I decided, for the first time, to use a pre-baked industry methodology: superpowers.

Superpowers caught my attention because it resembles how I currently work with AI. I plan my work and chunk it down into smaller deliverables, which I execute through tdd.

I have a few dimensions I wanna assess out of this experiment:

  • the end result feature correctness and UX;
  • the generated code;
  • cost, both time and tokens;
  • ergonomics: how I feel about this workflow;

Running the experiment

I used my agentic hobby project, conveyor, as the guinea pig for this. Conveyor is a TUI that lets me see which stage of the SDLC my iterations are: Pull Request, merge queue, merged or deployed. A feature it lacks is tabs. I wanna be able to cycle through PRs I wrote and PRs I need to review, for instance.

To keep it simple, this iteration focused on adding tabs just for the PRs column.

I gave two distinct Claude Code sessions running Sonnet 5.5 on medium the same initial prompt:

Let's plan a feature: tabs. Right now each column shows a fixed view based on its config. I would like to add the ability of having multiple configs for each column, and you'd cycle through them by pressing a key that defaults to . I'm ok breaking the current tab behaviour. I envision these tabs appearing at the top of the column. The currently selected one gets a visible highlight.

Both got the PR through the automatic review cycle without any further interaction with me, and in about 40 minutes I had two working versions of the same feature. I was excited to try them out!

Artifacts & Results

Artifact Current workflow Superpowers
Issue/plan https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/issues/79 https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/issues/80
Pull request https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/pull/82 https://github.com/piacsek/conveyor/pull/81
Screenshot
Cost Current workflow Superpowers
Build wall time 41min 42min
Token cost - main session 104.9k 196.7k
Token cost - subagents 483k 1.28M
Token cost - total 587.9k 1.477M

My thoughts

Both implementations worked first time! And both of them kept retrocompatibility with the existing configuration schema.

However, I must say that I'm intrigued. My current workflow beat superpowers in all the dimensions I was interested in analysing: it basically took the same time for almost a third of the token cost to produce an outcome I enjoyed more.

  • UI: I don't like the tab number showing up, it's confusing since it's so close to the PR count above;
  • Code: I prefer the Tab abstraction over the View one - it clicks faster in my mind;
  • Ergonomics: To my surprise, my current workflow asked me more questions than superpower's brainstorming skill: 5x1 - I felt more in the loop;

I wasn't expecting such one-sided result. If you've used superpowers, please comment how you operate it! I'm interested in experimenting more with it.

Thank you for reading, have a great day!

title: SmartInventory: Sistema de control de inventarios con Couchbase, React y tecnología NoSQL
description:
Autor: Soanny Geraldine Rivas Gutierrez, Stevie Marca Aguilar
Fecha: 10 noviembre de 2026

1. Introducción

Una adecuada administración de inventarios es fundamental para mantener el control de los productos y evitar pérdidas ocasionadas por errores en los registros.

Con este propósito desarrollamos SmartInventory, una aplicación web que permite gestionar productos, supervisar existencias y registrar movimientos de almacén de manera organizada.

El sistema utiliza Couchbase Capella como base de datos NoSQL en la nube, junto con React, Node.js y Express. También incorpora herramientas de automatización para facilitar las pruebas y el despliegue de la aplicación.

2. Objetivo del proyecto

SmartInventory busca optimizar el seguimiento de inventarios mediante una plataforma que centraliza la información de productos, proveedores y movimientos.

Entre sus principales objetivos se encuentran:

  • Administrar productos, categorías y proveedores.
  • Registrar entradas, salidas y ajustes de inventario.
  • Evitar movimientos que generen existencias negativas.
  • Identificar productos con niveles bajos de stock.
  • Consultar indicadores y reportes.
  • Mantener un historial de los movimientos realizados.

3. Herramientas y tecnologías utilizadas

Para implementar la aplicación se utilizaron las siguientes tecnologías:

Tecnología Utilidad
React 18 Interfaz de usuario
Tailwind CSS Diseño visual
Node.js y Express Desarrollo de la API REST
Couchbase Capella Base de datos NoSQL
JWT Autenticación
GitHub Actions Automatización CI/CD
Render Despliegue en la nube

La combinación de estas herramientas permite separar la interfaz, la lógica de negocio y el almacenamiento de información.

4. Funcionamiento de SmartInventory

La plataforma dispone de diferentes módulos para facilitar la gestión del almacén.

Panel principal: presenta indicadores sobre productos activos, unidades disponibles, movimientos recientes y alertas.

Productos: permite registrar, consultar, modificar y desactivar artículos.

Categorías y proveedores: facilita la organización del catálogo y la administración de los proveedores.

Movimientos: registra las entradas, salidas y ajustes, manteniendo información sobre las cantidades y los responsables.

Alertas: identifica automáticamente productos agotados o con existencias inferiores al mínimo establecido.

Reportes: permite consultar información relacionada con las existencias y los movimientos registrados.

Además, se contemplan los roles de administrador y almacenero, con permisos diferentes según sus responsabilidades.

5. Almacenamiento con Couchbase Capella

Uno de los componentes más importantes del proyecto es la implementación de Couchbase Capella, una base de datos NoSQL que almacena información mediante documentos JSON.

La estructura principal está organizada de la siguiente manera:

Couchbase Capella
│
└── Bucket: smartinventory
    │
    └── Scope: inventario
        │
        ├── usuarios
        ├── productos
        ├── categorias
        ├── proveedores
        └── movimientos

Cada producto contiene información como nombre, código, precio, cantidad disponible y stock mínimo.

Por ejemplo:

{
  "id": "PROD-001",
  "nombre": "Teclado Mecánico",
  "precioVenta": 79.90,
  "stockActual": 15,
  "stockMinimo": 5,
  "estado": "ACTIVO"
}

Couchbase también permite utilizar SQL++ para consultar y filtrar documentos JSON, facilitando la recuperación de información.

6. Control de stock y seguridad

Una característica importante de SmartInventory es la validación de los movimientos de inventario.

Cuando se registra una salida, el sistema verifica que exista suficiente cantidad disponible.

Por ejemplo, si un producto tiene 10 unidades y se solicita retirar 15, la operación se rechaza para evitar que el inventario quede en negativo.

También se utilizan transacciones ACID, que permiten actualizar las existencias y registrar el movimiento como una operación conjunta.

El proyecto incorpora mecanismos para manejar conflictos cuando varios usuarios intentan modificar simultáneamente el stock de un mismo producto.

Para la seguridad se utiliza autenticación mediante JWT, contraseñas protegidas con bcrypt y restricciones de acceso según el rol.

7. Automatización y publicación en la nube

SmartInventory integra un flujo de CI/CD mediante GitHub Actions.

Este proceso permite ejecutar pruebas automáticas y compilar el proyecto cuando se realizan cambios en el repositorio.

Si las verificaciones terminan correctamente, el flujo puede activar el despliegue en Render mediante los mecanismos configurados.

La plataforma dispone de dos servicios principales:

  • Frontend: aplicación React publicada como sitio web.
  • Backend: API REST desarrollada con Node.js y Express.

El backend se comunica con Couchbase Capella para consultar y actualizar la información del inventario.

8. Resultados y aprendizajes

El desarrollo de SmartInventory permitió aplicar conocimientos sobre bases de datos NoSQL, arquitectura web, consultas SQL++, seguridad y automatización.

Uno de los aprendizajes más importantes fue comprender cómo mantener la consistencia de las existencias cuando varios usuarios registran movimientos al mismo tiempo.

Asimismo, la integración con servicios en la nube permitió conocer el proceso de publicación de una aplicación full stack.

9. Conclusiones

SmartInventory demuestra cómo las tecnologías NoSQL pueden utilizarse para desarrollar soluciones prácticas de administración de inventarios.

El uso de Couchbase Capella facilita el almacenamiento documental, mientras que las transacciones contribuyen a mantener la integridad de las operaciones.

La implementación de React, Node.js, GitHub Actions y Render permitió integrar el desarrollo frontend, backend y despliegue dentro de un mismo proyecto.

En conjunto, SmartInventory constituye una solución funcional para gestionar productos, controlar existencias y supervisar movimientos de almacén utilizando tecnologías modernas.

10. Enlaces del proyecto

Repositorio GitHub:

https://github.com/Stevien04/SmartInventory

Aplicación desplegada:

https://smartinventory-app.onrender.com

API del sistema:

https://smartinventory-api-29jb.onrender.com/api/health

Video demostrativo:

https://youtu.be/g1ksH2ASxBw

title: From a Static Site to Multi-Region DR: 12 AWS Reference Architectures, Explained
description:
Most AWS diagrams I find online fall into one of two groups. Some are simple enough to fit on a slide but skip the details that break in production. Others are complete reference architectures with forty icons and no clear starting point.

I wanted something in between, so I built a catalog of 12 AWS reference architectures. It starts with a static site and grows one concern at a time until it reaches multi-region disaster recovery. Each diagram is a single self-contained HTML page with the services involved, the numbered information flow, comments on the parts that are easy to misread, and one practical note to consider before you build it.

  • 🌐 Live catalog: https://josesaid.github.io/aws-architecture-diagrams/
  • 💻 Source: https://github.com/josesaid/aws-architecture-diagrams

This article walks through the 12 architectures, explains why each one exists, and shows two of them as Java infrastructure code with the AWS CDK.

The problem: knowing which services go together

AWS has more than 200 services. Learning what each one does is the easy part. The hard part is knowing which services go together for a specific problem and in what order a request moves through them.

That gap shows up in familiar ways:

  • A static site ends up with a public S3 bucket because nobody explained Origin Access Control.
  • An SQS consumer processes the same message twice because the visibility timeout is shorter than the Lambda timeout.
  • A RAG assistant gives poor answers because the embeddings at query time come from a different model than the ones used during ingestion.
  • A disaster recovery plan exists on paper, but nobody defined the RTO and RPO, so nobody can say whether it is good enough.

None of these are exotic. They are what happens when you know the services but not how they fit together. Each diagram in the catalog targets one of these combinations and calls out the detail that tends to go wrong.

How each diagram is structured

Every page follows the same layout so you can compare them quickly:

  1. Summary: one paragraph describing what the architecture solves.
  2. Services: the AWS services involved, as chips.
  3. Diagram: the services, with numbered arrows for user traffic and dashed lines for configuration (for example, ACM providing a certificate to CloudFront).
  4. Comments: what the diagram simplifies and why.
  5. Information flow: the numbered steps a request follows, one service at a time.
  6. Note to consider: the operational detail that usually causes trouble.

The pages are plain HTML and CSS with no build step and no framework, so they load instantly and can be hosted anywhere. The catalog itself runs on GitHub Pages.

The 12 architectures

1. Static HTML site

Route 53 → CloudFront (ACM certificate) → private S3 bucket with OAC.

The baseline. Route 53 resolves the domain, CloudFront serves the site over HTTPS, and S3 stores the files in a bucket that only CloudFront can read. Users never reach the bucket directly.

Note to consider: if users see old content after a deploy, CloudFront is serving cached objects. Create an invalidation or wait for the TTL to expire.

2. Layered security for a static site

Diagram 1 + AWS WAF + AWS Shield + AWS KMS.

The same site with protection layers. WAF evaluates every request against managed rules (OWASP, bots, rate limits), Shield Standard mitigates DDoS attacks at no extra cost, OAC keeps the bucket private, and KMS encrypts the objects at rest.

Note to consider: WAF is billed per Web ACL, per rule and per million requests. Start with managed rules and a rate limit, and review the logs before adding custom rules.

3. Automated deployment (CI/CD)

Source bucket → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → site bucket + CloudFront invalidation.

A code change triggers the pipeline. CodeBuild installs dependencies, runs the tests and builds the site, then publishes it and invalidates the cache. Using two separate buckets, one for the source and one for the published site, prevents uncompiled code from going live.

Note to consider: if the tests fail, the previous site stays live. Turn on S3 versioning so you can roll back quickly.

4. Dynamic site with ALB, ECS and RDS

CloudFront → ALB → ECS Fargate (private subnets) → RDS, with static files from S3.

The first architecture with server-side logic. CloudFront splits the traffic: dynamic requests go to the load balancer and static assets come from S3. Only the ALB is exposed, and RDS has no public access.

Note to consider: the RDS security group should accept traffic only from the ECS security group. Multi-AZ keeps the database available when an availability zone fails.

5. Serverless site with login and API

Amplify Hosting + Cognito + API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB.

Cognito issues JWT tokens, API Gateway validates them with a Cognito authorizer, and Lambda only runs business logic on top of DynamoDB. No servers to patch.

Note to consider: define Cognito user groups from the start so you can control permissions without changing the authentication code later.

6. Asynchronous processing with SQS

API Gateway → SQS (+ dead-letter queue) → Lambda → DynamoDB, with notifications via SNS.

Requests are accepted fast and processed later. If Lambda is slow or fails, messages wait in the queue instead of being lost. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue.

Note to consider: the SQS visibility timeout must be longer than the maximum Lambda execution time. Otherwise the same message gets processed twice. The Java section below shows how to set it.

7. Events and orchestration with Step Functions

API Gateway → EventBridge → Step Functions → Lambda (validate, charge) → Aurora Serverless v2.

EventBridge decouples the producer of an event from its consumers. Step Functions stores the state of each execution and retries failed steps with backoff, so the order workflow stays easy to audit.

Note to consider: Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable processes. Express workflows cost less for high volumes of short executions, but they do not keep execution history the same way.

8. Real time with AppSync and DynamoDB Streams

AppSync (GraphQL) → DynamoDB → Streams → Lambda → AppSync subscriptions.

Changes reach every connected client without polling. AppSync manages the WebSocket subscriptions for you.

Note to consider: subscriptions are billed per connection and per message. Use subscription filters so each client receives only the events it needs.

9. Data and analytics on a data lake

Applications → Data Firehose → S3 (data lake) → Glue Catalog → Athena → QuickSight.

Firehose batches the records into S3, Glue keeps the table catalog, Athena queries the files with SQL, and QuickSight builds the dashboards. Organize the bucket in layers (raw and curated) and partition by date, because Athena charges for the data it scans.

Note to consider: validate the partitions and the Glue schema before building dashboards. A badly defined table returns wrong results without raising an error.

10. Generative AI with RAG on Amazon Bedrock

API Gateway → Lambda → OpenSearch Serverless (vector search) → Bedrock, with documents ingested from S3.

The model does not know your documents. Lambda retrieves the relevant chunks from OpenSearch and sends them to a Bedrock model together with the question. Embeddings must come from the same model during ingestion and at query time.

Note to consider: cost grows with the amount of context you send. Limit the number and size of the retrieved chunks.

11. Managed Kubernetes with EKS

Route 53 → ALB (created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller) → EKS pods → RDS/Aurora, images from ECR.

AWS manages the control plane, and the pods run on worker nodes in private subnets. An Ingress resource creates the ALB for you.

Note to consider: set CPU and memory requests and limits on every pod. Without them, the scheduler cannot spread the load well, and one pod can starve the others.

12. Multi-region and disaster recovery

Route 53 failover + health checks → ECS in us-east-1 (primary) and us-west-2 (secondary) → Aurora Global Database.

Route 53 sends traffic to the primary region while its health checks pass and fails over to the secondary when they do not. Aurora Global Database replicates the data across regions, typically with under one second of lag.

Note to consider: define your RTO and RPO before you choose a strategy. Active-active lowers RTO but roughly doubles compute cost. Pilot light or warm standby cost less but take longer to recover.

From diagram to code: two architectures in Java with the AWS CDK

A diagram is only useful if you can build it. The AWS CDK lets you define the same infrastructure in Java, so the security decisions in the diagram live in typed, reviewable code.

Diagram 1: a private bucket behind CloudFront with OAC

A common mistake is to make the bucket public and point CloudFront at the S3 website endpoint:

// ❌ Common mistake: public bucket, reachable without CloudFront
Bucket site = Bucket.Builder.create(this, "SiteBucket")
        .publicReadAccess(true)
        .blockPublicAccess(BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ACLS)
        .websiteIndexDocument("index.html")
        .build();

Anyone can then skip CloudFront, and with it your WAF rules, your HTTPS redirect and your caching. The diagram's version keeps the bucket fully private and lets only CloudFront read it through Origin Access Control:

import software.amazon.awscdk.Stack;
import software.amazon.awscdk.StackProps;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.BehaviorOptions;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.Distribution;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.ViewerProtocolPolicy;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.cloudfront.origins.S3BucketOrigin;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.BlockPublicAccess;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.Bucket;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.s3.BucketEncryption;
import software.constructs.Construct;

public class StaticSiteStack extends Stack {

    public StaticSiteStack(Construct scope, String id, StackProps props) {
        super(scope, id, props);

        // ✅ Private bucket: no public access, TLS only, versioned for rollbacks
        Bucket site = Bucket.Builder.create(this, "SiteBucket")
                .blockPublicAccess(BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ALL)
                .encryption(BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED)
                .enforceSsl(true)
                .versioned(true)
                .build();

        // CloudFront reads the bucket through Origin Access Control (OAC).
        // The CDK adds the bucket policy that allows only this distribution.
        Distribution.Builder.create(this, "SiteCdn")
                .defaultBehavior(BehaviorOptions.builder()
                        .origin(S3BucketOrigin.withOriginAccessControl(site))
                        .viewerProtocolPolicy(ViewerProtocolPolicy.REDIRECT_TO_HTTPS)
                        .build())
                .defaultRootObject("index.html")
                .build();
    }
}

Versioning on the bucket is what makes the "roll back quickly" note in diagram 3 possible.

Diagram 6: an SQS consumer that does not process messages twice

The duplicate-processing bug from diagram 6 usually looks like this:

// ❌ Common mistake: default visibility timeout (30 s) with a 60 s Lambda.
// While Lambda is still working, the message becomes visible again
// and a second invocation picks it up.
Queue orders = new Queue(this, "Orders");

The fix is to make the visibility timeout clearly longer than the function timeout (AWS recommends at least six times) and to add a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing:

import software.amazon.awscdk.Duration;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Code;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Function;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.Runtime;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.lambda.eventsources.SqsEventSource;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.sqs.DeadLetterQueue;
import software.amazon.awscdk.services.sqs.Queue;

// Messages that fail 3 times are kept here for 14 days for inspection
Queue dlq = Queue.Builder.create(this, "OrdersDlq")
        .retentionPeriod(Duration.days(14))
        .build();

Function worker = Function.Builder.create(this, "OrderWorker")
        .runtime(Runtime.JAVA_21)
        .handler("com.example.orders.OrderWorker::handleRequest")
        .code(Code.fromAsset("target/order-worker.jar"))
        .memorySize(1024)
        .timeout(Duration.seconds(30))
        .build();

// ✅ Visibility timeout = 6 x the Lambda timeout
Queue orders = Queue.Builder.create(this, "Orders")
        .visibilityTimeout(Duration.seconds(180))
        .deadLetterQueue(DeadLetterQueue.builder()
                .queue(dlq)
                .maxReceiveCount(3)
                .build())
        .build();

// Report partial batch failures so one bad message
// does not force the whole batch to be retried
worker.addEventSource(SqsEventSource.Builder.create(orders)
        .batchSize(10)
        .reportBatchItemFailures(true)
        .build());

With reportBatchItemFailures turned on, the handler returns only the IDs of the messages that failed:

public class OrderWorker implements RequestHandler<SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse> {

    @Override
    public SQSBatchResponse handleRequest(SQSEvent event, Context context) {
        List<SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure> failures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (SQSEvent.SQSMessage message : event.getRecords()) {
            try {
                process(message.getBody()); // must be idempotent: SQS is at-least-once
            } catch (Exception e) {
                failures.add(new SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure(message.getMessageId()));
            }
        }
        return new SQSBatchResponse(failures);
    }
}

Even with the right timeout, SQS standard queues deliver at least once, so process should be idempotent. For example, use the order ID as a conditional write key in DynamoDB.

Best practices across the 12 diagrams

A few rules repeat across the catalog:

  • Expose one entry point. CloudFront, the ALB or API Gateway faces the internet. Buckets, containers and databases stay private.
  • Separate intake from processing. Queues (diagram 6) and event buses (diagram 7) let you absorb spikes and retry failures without losing requests.
  • Treat configuration as part of the architecture. OAC, security groups, visibility timeouts and pod limits are not details to fix later. They decide whether the design works.
  • Know what you pay for. WAF rules, Athena scans, AppSync connections and Bedrock context all scale with usage. Each diagram's note points out the main cost driver.
  • Decide RTO and RPO before you design for resilience. Multi-AZ, multi-region and active-active are answers to different questions.

Conclusion

The catalog is meant as a map: start with the static site, add security and CI/CD, move to containers or serverless, then add asynchronous processing, events, real time, analytics, generative AI, Kubernetes and multi-region resilience as the problem requires.

Key takeaways:

  • Learn AWS services in combinations, not one by one.
  • Each architecture has one detail that usually breaks it. Learn that detail early.
  • Infrastructure as code in Java with the CDK turns those details into code you can review.

Browse the diagrams at https://josesaid.github.io/aws-architecture-diagrams/. The source is on GitHub. Which architecture would you add as number 13?

title: Private Object Storage Uploads in 2026 — Signed Document Download URLs by Deadline
description:
Short answer: retain signed customer-support documents in a private bucket, keep ownership and the deletion deadline in the application database, and issue a short-lived signed URL only after each download is authorized. Infrai is worth trying for that narrow upload-and-presign boundary when a team wants plain REST calls without installing and maintaining a storage SDK; it is not the compliance archive.

The deciding quantity is effective cost over the document's full life, not a storage unit price. Count upload and inspection calls, retained bytes, downloads and egress, the database state that makes deletion reproducible, cleanup execution, reconciliation, and the engineering burden of another client library and credential. A design that makes the initial PUT easy but leaves an operator unable to prove deletion is cheap only on the first invoice.

For a support system, the record might be a signed agreement.pdf or authorization.docx. Its object key can be users/user_4821/documents/doc_91a7/original.pdf, but the database must separately hold user_4821, doc_91a7, the content type, a digest, and delete_at. Object metadata is a display aid, not an ownership index: server-side listing can filter by key prefix, not by metadata.

What belongs in the retention cost ledger?

Start with one workload row per document class rather than one blended storage estimate. Record average object size, uploads, HEAD checks, signed downloads, average retention days, egress, replacements, and deletion attempts. Then add two labor terms that vendor calculators tend to omit: integration upkeep and reconciliation. The latter is the recurring work needed to compare database intent with stored reality, find an expired object that remains, or find an active database row whose bytes are absent.

The exercise changes the decision. Suppose support agents review some signed records repeatedly while most are never reopened. Storage duration may be a minor term; download egress and authorization traffic may dominate the active subset. I'm not sure which term will dominate in a particular queue without its access logs, so I would not rank providers from a hypothetical average. Measure the distribution, especially its long tail.

This is also where Infrai has a concrete operational argument. Its storage capability is exposed through a plain REST API, so any service able to send HTTP can use it without adopting a provider SDK or tracking a client-library release line. The supporting benefit is consolidation: one key and one billing surface can cover this storage boundary and other backend capabilities, reducing credential and invoice reconciliation work. Neither point removes object storage, egress, database, or deletion-job costs; they remove specific integration work.

No magic here.

The ledger should charge failed business operations even when every storage request behaves correctly. A support agent can authorize a download just as the retention worker begins deletion; two replacement requests can target the same logical document; a database commit can succeed before an upload is visible to the rest of the application flow. These are coordination boundaries. Treating them as a provider selection problem hides the system that must actually resolve them.

How should private object storage handle signed document download URLs?

The central invariant is: a caller receives a signed download URL only while the database says the caller may read the document and the deletion deadline has not passed. Keep the bucket private because public or public-read access is unavailable, and never persist a presigned URL as though it were the document's permanent address. It is a bearer capability with a limited life.

Three more invariants make the retention story auditable:

  1. The database, not object metadata, is authoritative for owner, logical document identity, current object key, retention state, and deletion deadline.
  2. A replacement receives a new document identity or passes through a database-serialized state transition. There is no object versioning and no If-Match conditional write protection, so concurrent overwrite is not a safe compare-and-swap mechanism.
  3. Deletion is a recorded workflow: mark the row due, attempt object deletion, verify the resulting state, append an audit event, and retry from durable state when the workflow is interrupted.

Exactly once is an accounting property here, not a promise that a network call runs once. Give each business transition a stable operation id, persist it with the document row, and make a repeated worker execution converge on the same terminal state. A 429 is routine backpressure; it should cause bounded exponential delay, honoring Retry-After, rather than a tight retry loop or a second logical operation.

Lifecycle policy can provide a backstop when deadlines are day-granular, but its minimum is one day. It cannot express an hour-level deletion obligation. Abandoned multipart fragments also lack an automatic cleanup rule, which means a workload using multipart upload must account for its own abort and reconciliation process. These details belong in the operating bill because each requires execution, observation, and an audit trail.

Which boundary should own retention and deletion?

The options are not interchangeable. This table compares the boundary that a customer-support service would actually own, rather than pretending that a common API shape makes governance features equivalent.

Option Sensible fit Hidden operating work Retention or deletion boundary
Amazon S3 directly A team that needs a specialist storage relationship and provider-native governance controls Operate its SDK or HTTP signing, credentials, policies, and separate billing reconciliation Evaluate provider-native versioning and immutable-retention controls against the compliance rule
Google Cloud Storage directly An organization committed to GCS and its surrounding cloud controls Maintain a GCS-specific integration and include its access and egress behavior in the workload model Prefer this route when GCS coverage or organization-level cloud policy is mandatory
Cloudflare R2 directly A team that wants to contract with and configure R2 without an intermediary API Own the provider integration, credentials, and migration path Validate the required retention controls directly; S3 compatibility does not itself prove governance equivalence
Infrai storage A service that values a plain REST boundary, one key, and consistent backend conventions The application still owns deadline state, reconciliation, and exact deletion scheduling Private signed access fits; object lock, versioning, cross-region automatic replication, and metadata search do not

My recommendation is deliberately conditional: try Infrai for private document transfer and signed delivery when SDK upkeep and cross-service credential reconciliation are meaningful costs, while the application is already responsible for authorization and an auditable deletion workflow. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is useful during integration because request schemas and runnable examples can be inspected without a key. The catch is that this choice is not suitable for write-once regulated records that require provider-enforced immutability, automatic cross-region replication, or recovery from accidental overwrite; use a specialist storage product with the required control instead. Stick with Google Cloud Storage when direct GCS coverage is a hard platform requirement, since GCS is not among the covered storage vendors.

Public hosting is out too. There is no public/public-read ACL, and public_url remains null, so a permanent public link, static website, or image-hosting design needs a different product. Browser-direct upload also requires a CORS decision before selection; do not assume that an S3-compatible bucket makes every browser flow portable.

Can the signed-access critical path stay small and auditable?

Yes. The following Go program requests a ten-minute download capability for an object that has already been uploaded under the owner-scoped key. The full URL and explicit POST method are intentional: they make the reviewed route visible, while url.PathEscape protects each variable path segment in a production helper. The returned signed URL must be used without the Infrai Authorization header.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    route := "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape("support-private-docs"), 1)
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{key}", url.PathEscape("users/user_4821/documents/doc_91a7/original.pdf"), 1)
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc" + route
    body := []byte(`{"expires_in":600}`)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "POST", endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "download-doc_91a7-agent_204")

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign request %s: %s", res.Status, data))
        }

        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return
    }

    panic("rate limit retries exhausted")
}

The program prints the response rather than inventing a response field that is not established here. In the service, bind the presign event to the authenticated actor, doc_91a7, the expiry request, and the storage request id in an append-only application audit record. Do not log the signed URL itself; the audit fact is that access was granted, not the reusable bearer capability.

There is a subtle cost boundary around HEAD calls. They can help reconcile the expected key before issuing access, but making every download perform redundant storage inspection increases request count and latency. If database state and the deletion worker have a strong reconciliation loop, reserve HEAD for state transitions and exception handling. If another writer can mutate the bucket outside the application, inspect more aggressively and charge those calls to the governance model. Your mileage may vary because that boundary depends on who else holds credentials.

Why reject a public bucket or overwrite-in-place design?

A public bucket fails the authorization model before cost enters the discussion. An opaque filename is not access control, a copied permanent link cannot be recalled at the support application's deadline, and public_url is unavailable in this storage surface anyway. Signed delivery keeps each grant time-limited and makes the application authorization check unavoidable.

Overwrite in place is the more tempting mistake — and the more expensive one to investigate. Without object versioning or conditional If-Match writes, two valid workers can race and leave only the last bytes at a key, while both business requests appear successful in separate logs. Assign a new docId for a replacement, store the new key beside a stable logical case id, and change the current pointer through a serialized database transaction. That adds a row and a state transition; it also preserves which PDF an agent saw, which digest was signed, and which object must be deleted on which deadline.

For immutable financial or compliance evidence, reject this application-enforced pattern. A storage system with object lock or another external WORM control is the valid choice even if its SDK, policy review, and separate invoice make the effective bill larger, because recoverability and tamper resistance are requirements rather than optional cost optimizations.

For ordinary customer-support agreements whose policy permits application-enforced deletion, close the decision record with measurable acceptance criteria: every active row resolves to one private key; every download has an authorization and audit event; every expired row reaches a verified terminal deletion state; replacement never mutates historical identity; and the monthly review accounts for retained bytes, operations, egress, integration upkeep, and reconciliation labor. If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai storage documentation and inspect the discovery schema before implementing the call.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: 5 Ways to Generate Presigned File Download URLs: Tenant Retention Rules
description:
5 Ways to Generate Presigned File Download URLs: Tenant Retention Rules

Short answer: Generate a short-lived presigned file download URL only after checking the tenant-scoped export record, and pair it with an explicit deletion schedule.

The least complicated design is a short-lived presigned download URL backed by an explicit retention record. The export service decides who may request a link, the object store decides whether the signature is valid, and a deletion worker removes the image and its export metadata on a known schedule. That division matters more than the particular S3-compatible implementation.

A logistics system usually has two different things to retain: the product image and the generated export. They should not inherit the same lifetime by accident. A product photo might support a dispute for 30 days; a CSV or ZIP assembled for a tenant might be useful for 24 hours. The download URL should live for minutes, not become a second retention policy.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workflow, storage cost is dominated by retained bytes and request activity, not by the few lines that sign a URL. A useful first estimate is:

retained gigabytes = daily uploaded image gigabytes x image retention days + daily export gigabytes x export retention days

Suppose a carrier portal receives 18 GB of product images each day, keeps source images for 30 days, and produces 6 GB of tenant exports each day. If exports stay for 24 hours, the rough retained set is 540 GB of images plus 6 GB of exports, before replicas, metadata, and incomplete multipart uploads. Letting exports sit for 30 days changes the second term to 180 GB.

That is the change I would make first: shorten export retention and record the decision, rather than weakening image quality or hiding storage behind a larger quota. The trade-off is concrete. A dispatcher who requests an old export may need to generate it again, and an incident investigator may have to rely on audit metadata instead of the original archive.

Presigned URLs do not delete objects. They grant temporary access to an object key under the permissions and signing rules of the issuer. Deletion needs its own lifecycle: an expiration timestamp, a worker or lifecycle rule, and a reconciliation path for work that stopped halfway through.

How do I generate a presigned URL for file download?

A link lifetime should be derived from the user action, not copied from object retention. For a browser download, 10 minutes is often enough to request the file, follow a redirect if the client uses one, and retry a transient network failure. A large export on a slow warehouse connection may need longer. The value belongs in configuration with an upper bound.

The request path should look roughly like this:

  1. Authenticate the operator and resolve the tenant from server-side authorization data.
  2. Load an export record whose tenant, object key, status, and expiration are all checked together.
  3. Sign a GET request for that exact key with a short lifetime.
  4. Return the URL without exposing storage credentials or allowing a caller to choose an arbitrary key.
  5. Write an audit event for the request, not the secret URL itself.

The tenant check is the important part. A URL can be cryptographically valid and still be the wrong URL for the caller if the application selected an object by an untrusted filename or guessed key. Object names are identifiers, not authorization.

Here is deliberately small Python-shaped pseudocode for the decision boundary. It shows the checks that belong before a generic S3-compatible signing call; the storage SDK call is intentionally represented by an interface so the policy does not become coupled to one library.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

MAX_LINK_AGE = timedelta(minutes=15)

def make_download_link(actor, export_id, repository, signer, now=None):
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    export = repository.find_export(export_id)

    if export is None or export.tenant_id != actor.tenant_id:
        raise PermissionError("export is not available")
    if export.status != "ready" or export.expires_at <= now:
        raise FileNotFoundError("export is not downloadable")

    lifetime = min(export.requested_link_age, MAX_LINK_AGE)
    return signer.presign_get(
        bucket=export.bucket,
        key=export.object_key,
        expires_in=int(lifetime.total_seconds()),
    )

The same boundary applies in a Node.js service: resolve the record, authorize the tenant, cap the lifetime, then call the SDK's presigning helper. The syntax changes; the security decision does not.

What can go wrong after the URL is issued?

The common failure is treating a successful signing call as a completed download. It is only a handoff. The browser may have no CORS permission to read the response, a proxy may reject a large response, or the object may be deleted while the link is still valid. A client that needs to trigger a download without reading response bytes can use a normal browser navigation; a client that reads the response from another origin needs an explicit CORS policy, including the methods and exposed headers it actually uses. The MDN CORS guidance is a good reference for the browser side, but it does not replace authorization in the export service.

A second trap is logging the full URL. Query parameters in a presigned URL are bearer credentials until they expire. Application logs, browser history, support screenshots, analytics referrers, and tracing attributes can all extend the audience beyond the original tenant user. Log the export ID, tenant ID, actor ID, and expiration time. Redact the URL.

A third trap is key reuse. If a new export overwrites an old object key, a link issued for the old export can point at new bytes. Use an immutable export identifier in the object key, or make replacement impossible. It is easier to reason about exports/{tenant_id}/{export_id}.zip than about latest.zip.

How should deletion and recovery work?

Keep three timestamps: created_at, available_until, and deleted_at. available_until is the business retention decision. The deletion process can run after that time, but the record should say when the object was actually removed. This makes a delayed worker visible without pretending that a policy clock and a storage operation are the same event.

I would use an idempotent deletion job with a small state machine: ready, delete_requested, deleted, and delete_failed. A retry must be safe. A missing object should usually converge to deleted, while an authorization or service failure should remain visible for retry and alerting. Keep the audit record after deleting the bytes; it is the evidence that the export existed and who requested it.

The job also needs a reconciliation query. It should find export rows past available_until that are not deleted, plus objects under the export prefix that have no matching row. The first set catches failed work. The second catches abandoned generation paths. Do not make reconciliation depend on a single in-memory queue.

There is a deliberate loss here. After deletion, support cannot download the old archive just because an audit event exists. That is the point of the retention decision, not a defect. If legal hold or claims handling requires preservation, represent that as an explicit hold that changes available_until; do not ask operators to copy files into an undocumented bucket.

What should the test and operations surface prove?

A useful test matrix follows the policy, not just the happy path. Test a valid tenant, a different tenant, a missing export, an expired export, a non-ready export, a link past the maximum lifetime, and a key that has already been deleted. Test the browser path separately from a programmatic cross-origin read. The MDN CORS guidance is a good reference for the browser side, but it does not replace authorization in the export service.

For operations, measure the facts that explain a bad download:

  • link requests allowed and denied, grouped by reason
  • export generation time and byte size
  • download response failures by status and tenant
  • objects past available_until
  • deletion retries and orphaned objects

Do not put signed query strings into metrics labels. High-cardinality secrets are a security problem and a noisy dashboard.
A release check should also verify that the bucket policy, CORS configuration, worker identity, and clock synchronization are consistent with the application assumptions. Signature verification is time-sensitive. A few minutes of clock drift can look like an authorization bug, while an overly broad CORS rule can turn a convenient browser download into an unintended data exposure.

The practical decision rule is compact: keep source images for the business evidence period, keep generated exports only as long as the workflow needs them, issue links for the shortest credible transfer window, and make every deletion observable. That gives a tenant-scoped download flow without allowing a temporary URL to quietly become permanent access.

Further reading

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

Orders are mutable

An order may be pending at creation and later become settled, cancelled, or otherwise updated.

Incremental fetching

Track completed file windows or batch cursors and persist progress only after successful processing.

Version-aware upserts

Compare the incoming order version with the stored version and update only when the incoming record is newer.

Operational checks

Alert on missing batches, delayed settlement, and unexpected reconciliation differences.

For a more complete implementation overview, see the FB Sports technical guide.
