title: Why Passing Tests Doesn't Mean Your Software Is Correct
description:
A Go pricing example show my green tests and high coverage can still miss a business rule defect.

Imagine a checkout service that gives customers a 10% discount on orders of $200 or more. The change has passed code review. The CI pipeline is green and the unit tests report 100% statement coverage.

Then a customer places a $150 order and recieves the discount. The service is working as written but it is not following the business rule.

How could the tests pass ?

The answer is simple

a test can run the code without checking whether the result is correct.

To understand this problem we need to seperate test execution, passing tests, code coverage, assertion quality and software correctness.

A small Go service with a real defect

Our business rule is

Apply a 10% discount only when the order subtotal is at least $200, Otherwise return the original subtotal.

The example stores money as integer cents. It assumes a non negative subtotal and rounds the discount down to a thole cent through integer division. We will focus on the discount threshold, not input validation.

Create a go module

mkdir pricing-demo && cd pricing-demo
go mod init example.com/pricing

Add pricing.go

package pricing

// FinalPrice returns the price in cents after any eligible discount.
func FinalPrice(subtotalCents int) int {
    if subtotalCents >= 10_000 { // BUG: the rule says 20_000.
        return subtotalCents - subtotalCents/10
    }
    return subtotalCents
}

The code gives the discount starting at $100 instead of $200 This matters for any subtotal from 10,000 to 19,999 cents.

For example, FinalPrice(15_000) return 13_500. The correct result is 15_000 because a $150 order should not recived a discount.

Test execution is not the same as verification

Now add pricing_test.go

package pricing

import "testing"

func TestFinalPrice_Weak(t *testing.T) {
    for _, subtotal := range []int{9_000, 20_000} {
        got := FinalPrice(subtotal)
        if got < 0 {
            t.Fatalf(
                "FinalPrice(%d) = %d, want a non-negative amount",
                subtotal, got,
            )
        }
    }
}

This test execute both path in FinalPrice one order without a discount and one with a discount. It also has an assertion, which is a check that compares an observed result with an expected condition.

But the assertion is too weak. It only checks that result is not negative. A wrong price of 13_500 would satisfy that condition, just as the correct price of 15_000 would.

Run

go test -count=1 -cover ./...

For this isolated example the test passes and Go report

coverage: 100.0% of statements

Both branches have run. Every statement in this small function has been exercised. The business rule defect is still present.

Figure 1. Passing tests confirm only the checks the suite actually makes

  1. Test Execution
    Running tests confirms that the test code was executed. However, it does not mean the tests checked important behavior.

  2. Passing Tests
    Passing tests mean all executed checks succeeded. However they do not prove that every requirement was tested.

  3. Code coverage
    Code coverage shows which parts of the source code were executed duting testing. However, high coverage does not mean the results were correct.

  4. Assertion Quality, Can the tests detect incorrect behavior ?
    Good assertions help tests catch wrong results. However strong assertions do not guarantee that every possible scenario was tested.

  5. Software Correctness, Does the software work as expected ?
    Software correctness means the system meets it requirements under relevant conditions. Passing tests provide edividence of correctness, but they cannot prove it on thier own.

Running tests, passings test and achieving high code coverage are not the same as proving software correctness. What matters is whether the tests can detect meaningful defects.

Thesese concepts support each other, but they are not interchangeable.

Go coverage tooling measures executed statement. It does not judge the quality of your expectations. The official

go.dev

explains how instrumentation redcords which parts of the source code are exercised.

Stornger tests use the business rule as expeceted result

A better test starts from the rule, not from what the implementation happens to return.

Add pricing_rule_test.go

package pricing

import "testing"

func TestFinalPrice_BusinessRule(t *testing.T) {
    tests := []struct {
        name     string
        subtotal int
        want     int
    }{
        {"ordinary order", 9_000, 9_000},
        {"below threshold", 15_000, 15_000},
        {"just below threshold", 19_999, 19_999},
        {"at threshold", 20_000, 18_000},
        {"above threshold", 25_000, 22_500},
    }

    for _, tt := range tests {
        t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            got := FinalPrice(tt.subtotal)
            if got != tt.want {
                t.Errorf(
                    "FinalPrice(%d) = %d, want %d",
                    tt.subtotal, got, tt.want,
                )
            }
        })
    }
}

This test use a test oracle, meaning a source of expected results. Here the oracle is the written business rule, expressed as exact amounts in the test cases.

go test -count=1 -cover ./...

The stronger suite fails on two cases

FinalPrice(15000) = 13500, want 15000
FinalPrice(19999) = 18000, want 19999

Notice what changed. We did not need more statement coverage to find this defect. We needed test inputs near the rule boundary and assertions that checked the actual price.

Fix the condition in pricing.go

if subtotalCents >= 20_000 {

Now both test files pass. The coverage number remaings 100% in this small example, but the tests provide stronger evidence about the discount rule.

Why 100% coverage is not 100% correctness

Figure 2. Equal statement coverage does not mean equal defect-detection ability.

Coverage answer an execution question

Which parts of this code ran while tests were running ?

it does not answer a requirements question

Did the program produce the right result ?

Coverage is useful when it points to a path that no test exercises. It is much less useful as a score for test quality. Martin Fowler makes this distinction in his article on

Test Coverage

martinfowler.com

Even 100% statement coverage leaves important gaps. A test might check only that a function returns without an error. It might use the wrong expected value. It might miss an input boundary. And a rule missing from the implementation cannot be discovered merely by measuring execution of the code that exists.

Go's coverage report is also about instrumented source statements, not a guarantee that every possible input, condition or execution order has been explored. The Go command documentation describe the available coverage options and test behavior.

Use coverage to find places that need attention. Do not treat its percentage as proof that the service meets its contract.

A pasing test it evidence, not a proof

A test has a limited claim for these inputs, in this environments, the observed result met these expectations.

That is valuable edividence, it can prevent regressions, document an example of expected behavior and detect defects early. But its strength depends on the selected cases, the correctness of the expected results and the reliability of the test environment.

A services has many more possible situations than a small test suite can usally exercise. Inputs can change dependencies can fail and concurrent requestes can arrive in difference orders. Passing tests cannot by themselves, establish that every possible behavior is correct.

This does not make testing pointless. It means we should be precise about what our tests demonstrate. Formal verification can esablish specific properties under stated assumptions, but an orinary green go test result its not that kind of mathematical proof.

How to make test result more meaningful

When reviewing a unit test, begin with the requirement. Ask what result should occur and which mistake the test should catch. In the pricing example, the key condition is the threshild at 20,000 cents, so the values just below and at that boundary are more useful than two arbitary positive amounts.

Prefer assertions about observable behavior. Checking got != want for the final amount is more informative than checking that the amount is non-negative. When a function returns an error, check both the error and relevant result, according to its contract.

Next, use coverage reports to find the code that has not been exercised. in Go, these command produce and inspect a statement coverage profile

go test -count=1 -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
go tool cover -func=coverage.out
go tool cover -html=coverage.out

The HTML view makes it easier to see which statements ran. It does not mark wak assertions or missing business requirements.

Finally review failure cases as carefully as success cases. For services, that may include invalid input dependency timeouts, retries and concurrent updates. Choose these cases based on the service's actual contract not on a target coverage percentage.

Conclusion

Passing tests are useful, but thier meaning is narrower than the green status suggests. Coverage tells us what ran Assertions tell us what was checked. Correctness depends on whether those checks reflect the real requirements.

The important question is not only whether we have tests, but whether those tests whould fail when the behavior becomes wrong. Mutation testing explores this by deliberately changing code and checking whether the tests notice.

Further reading

  • Go: Add a test, an introduction to the built-in test workflow.
  • Go: The cover story, an explanation of statement coverage and reports.
  • Go command documentation, including go test and coverage flags.
  • Martin Fowler: Test Coverage, on using coverage to find gaps rather than treating it as a quality score.

title: What stack would you choose for a matching platform?
description:
I’m working on a matching platform and considering Next.js, Tailwind CSS and Supabase/PostgreSQL. I’d like to hear from people who’ve built applications with similar technical requirements, particularly where this combination works well and where it starts to get awkward.

It’s a web-first application with a fairly complex backend. The main requirements are:

  • Reliable editing and relational data. Multi-step forms, autosave and resume across devices, with users potentially editing in multiple tabs. Some transactions affect several related records or users. Concurrent updates, retries and lost responses need to be handled without overwriting newer data or repeating an operation.

  • Matching and search. Deterministic, rules-based calculations rather than ML. Results need to track the versions of their inputs and rules, with recalculation when those change. Search includes filtering, pagination and geographical queries.

  • Authentication. Passwordless email sign-in, phone verification, account recovery and admin MFA. Verification codes need to remain single-use even when requests overlap. Revoked sessions and replaced codes must stop working.

  • Access control. Permissions depend on account status, role, the relationship between users and its current state. They can differ for each participant, resource and field, with separate rights to read history, send messages, edit data or access shared files. Changes must take effect during active sessions and govern protected responses, cached content and queued work.

  • Private media. Upload validation, image processing and asynchronous content screening. Files remain access-controlled, and a delayed processing result must not replace a newer version.

  • Messaging, jobs and integrations. Private messaging, timely updates, notifications, payment integration and scheduled work. Jobs and webhooks need to cope with duplicate or out-of-order delivery, restarts and partial failures. Time-based access rules need to stay correct across timezones and daylight-saving changes, even if a scheduled job runs late.

  • Privacy and administration. Scoped admin permissions, audit trails, aggregate reporting, retention rules, data export and deletion. Deletion and access changes also need to be accounted for in derived data, queues, external services and backup recovery.

I’d prefer managed database, authentication and storage services where possible. I also want a straightforward way to test the complete stack locally and in staging, including concurrency and failure recovery. Safe migrations, monitoring and tested backups matter, and the application needs to behave correctly with multiple instances and workers.

Would you choose Next.js and Supabase for this? Which parts would you handle within that setup, and where would you introduce a separate API, worker or service?

If you’d choose a different stack, what makes it a better technical fit? I’m particularly interested in limitations or tradeoffs you’ve encountered in production.

title: Don't File Photo-Derived Meters as a Survey
description:
I'm Tomás Herrera. Day job is backend and infrastructure at ArchyBase — mostly the path from an uploaded file to a finished artifact: validate, store, enqueue, and return a result the rest of the system is allowed to trust. This post is about a sibling product our team also builds, and specifically about a converter that turns a photo into a layout. I'm not going to talk about the vision model. That's a different layer, and a different person on the team. I'm talking about what the job is allowed to persist after a photo comes in.

The short version: a listing photo is a projection. The layout you get back is a draft estimated from what's visible in the frame. If your property record, your quote, or your inventory system files those numbers as a survey, you've promoted an estimate to a fact. I don't want that write to happen by accident.

The job is not “upload, then believe”

The product page is honest about the shape of the work, and I like that more than a magic demo. You upload a JPEG, PNG, or WebP (up to 10MB). You can add a short note about what the floor plan should look like. You pick a quality mode. You get a 2D technical plan back, as an image, and you can regenerate if the first pass misses a wall.

That last clause matters. “Regenerate if the first pass misses a wall” is not a flourish. It is an admission that a missed wall is a normal failure class, not a rare crash. A backend that treats the first successful blob as authoritative will happily store an open floor where a wall should have been.

So the durable unit of work, for me, looks closer to this than to a one-shot HTTP response:

Job {
  job_id
  input_ref          // object key for the photo
  input_kind         // room_photo | house_interior | aerial
  hint?              // optional text, not a measured brief
  quality_mode       // fast | best  (latency vs refinement; not a SLA)
  state              // queued | running | succeeded | failed
  result_ref?        // output image
  error_class?       // invalid_input | unreadable_photo | incomplete_layout | internal
  confidence_policy  // estimated_from_visible — never survey_grade
}

I made up the field names. They are not FloorAI internals. They're the checklist I want in front of any service that accepts a photo and emits a plan-shaped artifact.

Three input types are three failure classes

The page groups inputs as a room photo, a wider house interior, or an aerial / drone shot of a building. That's a product convenience. For a job queue, it's a classification problem, because the failure modes don't overlap cleanly.

A room photo usually gives you two or three walls, a floor plane, maybe a doorway, and a lot of furniture occluding the rest. The missing wall is often the one behind the camera. If you persist that result as a complete room, you've invented a fourth side from a viewpoint that never saw it.

A house interior — a wider shot, a listing gallery image, a scanned print — can show circulation and room boundaries, but only the ones in view. A corridor that turns out of frame will not appear because the model is “careful.” It will not appear because it was never in the pixels. Old or low-quality photos can still convert, which is useful for digitizing a record when no drawing exists. Useful is not the same as complete.

An aerial or drone shot is a different object. The page is explicit: you can scan a footprint when you can't walk the building room by room. A footprint is not a room schedule. If a downstream form labels the output “3-bed, 2-bath” because a listing caption said so, that's a caption write, not a measurement write. Keep those sources apart.

I would rather the API require an input_kind (or infer it and show the inference) than silently mix these into one “image-to-plan” success state. The client can then branch: a missed interior wall is “try another photo or regenerate”; an aerial result is “this is a footprint, don't ask it for closet widths.”

Reject early, estimate later

Upload validation should be boring and strict:

  • Reject empty files, wrong MIME types, and anything over the published 10MB cap before a worker starts.
  • Decode enough to know you have an actual image, not a renamed PDF.
  • Don't invent a dimension unit in preprocess just because a later renderer likes meters.

The estimate happens after that, from visible structure in the shot — walls, doorways, room boundaries the photo actually contains. The page says this directly: no tape measure is required, and dimensions are estimated from what's visible rather than from measurements you typed in. That's the product promise, and it should also be the persistence promise.

What I will not do is this:

  1. Accept a phone photo.
  2. Get a layout image with some numbers on it.
  3. OCR or hardcode those numbers into wall.length_m.
  4. Mark the unit as surveyed.

If you need a field, call it what it is: estimated_from_photo, with the source image id and the job id. A later measured drawing can replace it. A later photo can revise it. Neither should look identical to a laser-measured wall in the database.

Failures the user can act on

I care about error classes the client can branch on, not a generic “something went wrong.” A reasonable set for this product shape:

Class What happened What the user can do
invalid_input bad type, empty file, over 10MB fix the file
unreadable_photo decode failed, or the frame has no usable structure try a wider / sharper shot
incomplete_layout job succeeded, but a wall or room boundary is obviously missing regenerate, or upload a shot that includes the missing side
wrong_kind an aerial footprint was treated like an interior, or the reverse relabel the input and run again
internal worker / storage blip retry the same job or attempt

incomplete_layout is the interesting one, because it may still return an image. That's a succeeded job with a warning, or a soft failure, depending on how strict you want to be. I prefer “succeeded, with an explicit warning the first pass may have missed a wall” over a silent 200 and a floor plan that walks through a load-bearing line. The product already tells people to regenerate. The API should make that path first-class, not a folksy tip buried under a download button.

Don't auto-retry invalid_input or “I can't see a room in this picture.” That wastes worker time and trains the UI to spin. Auto-retry only the infra blips, and only with an idempotency key so you don't persist two final images for one photo.

What the output is allowed to be

The download is an image, ready to share or use as a starting reference. Starting reference is the right phrase. It is not a CAD handoff, and I have not claimed it exports a measured drawing. If someone on the team later adds a dimensioned file type, that still wouldn't make a phone photo into a survey. It would make the estimate easier to open in other tools — which is useful, and still an estimate.

The optional text field — “describe what the floor plan should look like” — is a hint, not a substitute for the hidden wall. If the photo doesn't show a second bedroom, a hint that says “two bedrooms” is a request, not evidence. I'd keep that hint on the job record so a reviewer can see what was asked, and I would not let it silently overwrite geometry that isn't in the image.

Quality modes (faster output vs more refinement) are a latency and compute trade-off. I'm not going to invent how many seconds either mode takes. The only rule I want is: both modes still write estimated_from_visible. A “best” result is not a license to drop the qualifier.

A short checklist before anyone files the result

This is the list I want next to the download button, or next to whatever internal tool first persists the artifact:

  1. Record the source photo and the job id with the layout. No orphan plans.
  2. Label the input kind: room, interior, or aerial / footprint.
  3. Treat every length as estimated from the visible frame, never as surveyed, until a real measurement replaces it.
  4. If a wall is missing, regenerate or shoot the missing side. Don't close the loop in the database by hand and call it the same job.
  5. Don't copy listing-caption room counts into the plan record just because the caption was on the same page as the photo.
  6. Let a later measured plan supersede the estimate without deleting the photo job — you want the history.

I use this converter when there is no drawing on file and a photo is all you have. That's a real situation: old units, incomplete listing packs, a job site with no blueprint in the email thread. A draft layout from a photo is much better than a blank. It is not better than a survey, and it should never be stored as if it were one.

The unpaid work, on the backend, is making that distinction boring and visible. If the only success state you have is “image arrived,” you will eventually file photo-derived meters as a survey. I'd rather fail that write on purpose.

title: Ai Can Write React Code. Can You Actually Understand It?
description:
AI Is Making React Developers Faster. But Are They Becoming Better Developers?

AI is making React developers faster. But there's a growing problem: many developers are shipping code they don't fully understand.

Let's be honest.

Writing React code has never been easier.

You can ask ChatGPT to build a dashboard, create reusable components, implement custom hooks, integrate APIs, or even refactor an entire application.

A few seconds later, you have code that looks professional.

Clean formatting. TypeScript types. Reusable components. Maybe even some optimizations.

But here's the uncomfortable question:

Do you actually understand the code you're shipping?

AI isn't necessarily making developers worse. However, using AI without understanding its output can create a dangerous illusion of productivity.

Let's look at some common examples.

1. The useEffect Addiction

One of the most common problems in AI-generated React code is unnecessary useEffect usage.

Ask an AI tool to synchronize two pieces of state, and there's a good chance it will suggest something like this:

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function UserProfile({ user }) {
  const [fullName, setFullName] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    setFullName(`${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`);
  }, [user]);

  return <h2>{fullName}</h2>;
}

Does it work?

Yes.

Is it necessary?

Not at all.

The value of fullName can be calculated directly during rendering:

function UserProfile({ user }) {
  const fullName = `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName}`;

  return <h2>{fullName}</h2>;
}

We don't need an additional state variable, an effect, or an extra render.

This is a simple example, but it highlights an important issue:

AI can generate code that works without necessarily choosing the best React approach.

2. More Components Don't Always Mean Better Architecture

AI tools often love abstraction.

Ask them to build a simple user card, and you might end up with:

  • UserCard
  • UserCardHeader
  • UserCardAvatar
  • UserCardDetails
  • UserCardActions
  • UserCardContainer

Component reuse is important in React.

But abstraction without a real purpose creates unnecessary complexity.

A good component structure should make your application easier to understand, maintain, and extend.

Not just increase the number of files in your project.

Good architecture isn't about writing more code. It's about managing complexity.

3. The TypeScript Illusion

TypeScript is supposed to help us catch mistakes before runtime.

But AI-generated TypeScript code sometimes looks strongly typed while hiding important problems.

For example:

function getUserData(data: any) {
  return data.profile.name;
}

This compiles, but what happens if profile doesn't exist?

TypeScript can't protect us from a problem we've explicitly told it to ignore.

A better approach is to define the expected data structure:

type User = {
  profile: {
    name: string;
  };
};

function getUserData(data: User) {
  return data.profile.name;
}

The problem isn't that AI uses any.

The problem is accepting weak typing without questioning it.

TypeScript should describe the actual structure of our data, not simply make compiler errors disappear.

4. Performance Optimization Without Understanding Performance

Another common AI habit is adding useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo almost everywhere.

Consider this example:

const expensiveValue = useMemo(() => {
  return items.length * 2;
}, [items]);

Is this optimization necessary?

Probably not.

The calculation is extremely cheap.

Memoization has its own costs and introduces additional complexity.

React developers should understand when optimization is actually useful instead of treating every memoization hook as a performance improvement.

Sometimes the best optimization is simply writing simpler code.

5. The Copy-Paste Developer

This is probably the biggest problem.

Imagine asking AI to implement a custom hook.

It generates 80 lines of code.

You copy it, run the application, and everything works.

But then someone asks:

  • Why did you use useRef here?
  • Why does this effect have an empty dependency array?
  • What happens if the component unmounts?
  • Why did you choose this state management approach?
  • Can you explain the data flow?

And suddenly, things get complicated.

If you cannot explain the code you're maintaining, you're not really in control of that code.

You're just depending on something you don't fully understand.

And that becomes a serious problem when your application grows.

6. AI Doesn't Know Your Entire Project

AI-generated code can look technically correct while being completely wrong for your application.

It might:

  • Introduce a dependency you don't need.
  • Ignore your existing component architecture.
  • Duplicate functionality that already exists.
  • Use outdated patterns.
  • Miss important edge cases.
  • Create security or data-handling problems.

A code snippet can be correct in isolation and still be a bad decision in your project.

This is why context matters.

Before accepting generated code, you should understand your existing architecture, conventions, and requirements.

7. So, Should React Developers Stop Using AI?

Absolutely not.

That would be the wrong conclusion.

AI is an incredibly useful development tool.

It can help with:

  • Exploring unfamiliar APIs.
  • Understanding complex concepts.
  • Generating boilerplate code.
  • Writing tests.
  • Refactoring existing components.
  • Finding potential bugs.
  • Exploring alternative implementations.

The goal isn't to write every line manually.

The goal is to remain responsible for the code you ship.

I think the best developers will be those who combine two abilities:

  1. Knowing how to use AI effectively.
  2. Knowing how to question, evaluate, and improve its output.

These skills complement each other.

But one cannot replace the other.

Final Thoughts

React development is not just about producing JSX.

It's about understanding rendering, state management, component architecture, data flow, performance, and maintainability.

AI can help you write code faster.

But it cannot automatically give you the engineering judgment needed to decide whether that code belongs in your application.

Don't measure your productivity by how much code AI generates. Measure it by how much quality software you can confidently build and maintain.

And here's a question I'd genuinely like to discuss:

If AI generates 90% of your React code, but you cannot explain how 30% of it works, are you actually becoming a better developer?

I'd love to hear different perspectives from the React community.

title: Designing a Kid-Friendly Quiz: Five UX Choices That Keep Results Lighthearted
description:
A short quiz can be a fun conversation starter for a child, but it should never feel like a test. Here are five design choices that keep a fan-made house quiz for kids simple, welcoming, and clear.

  1. Do not require background knowledge. The kids quiz uses eight simple, playful questions; children do not need to know the books to take part.
  2. Ask about approachable qualities. Its scoring looks at courage, kindness, curiosity, and ambition, giving children familiar ideas to reflect on.
  3. Make every outcome welcoming. A result should describe a quality, not rate a child or suggest one answer is better. The four house results are written warmly and positively.
  4. Explain what the result is—and is not. This is an entertainment activity, not an official sorting service or a psychological assessment.
  5. Leave room for conversation. Ask which choice felt most like the child. Remind them that traits overlap and a quiz does not define them.

Try the free Harry Potter House Quiz for Kids to see the eight-question format. It takes about three minutes, costs nothing, and requires no sign-up.

Unofficial fan-made site. Not affiliated with Warner Bros. or J.K. Rowling.

title: Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Reminder Emails Fired 8 Hours Late (Python, Node, and the Browser)
description:
Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Reminder Emails Fired 8 Hours Late (Python, Node, and the Browser)

Last month I shipped a small reminder feature: users pick a date and time, and a scheduler fires an email at that exact moment. Every reminder went out at 5:00 PM Beijing time instead of 9:00 AM. Eight hours late, every single time, no exceptions.

The user had picked "2026-11-20 09:00" in Shanghai. The database stored 1795165200. The correct value for 2026-11-20 09:00 Asia/Shanghai is 1795136400 — the gap is exactly 28,800 seconds. Somewhere between the form and the database, my code read the wall clock as if it were UTC.

Here is the annoying part: my tests passed. My laptop runs Asia/Shanghai, production runs TZ=UTC, and the bug only existed on the second machine. I'll walk through the fix in Python, the equivalent in Node, and how I check timestamps before they touch a database now.

Method 1: Python 3.11 with ZoneInfo

The original mistake was a naive datetime plus .timestamp():

# Python 3.11.1 — the buggy version
from datetime import datetime

dt = datetime(2026, 11, 20, 9, 0, 0)
print(int(dt.timestamp()))
# on my TZ=Asia/Shanghai laptop → 1795136400 (right, by accident)
# on the TZ=UTC server          → 1795165200 (wrong, +8h)

A naive datetime carries no timezone, so .timestamp() falls back to whatever the process locale says. On a UTC server, 09:00 means 09:00 UTC. On my laptop it meant 09:00 +08:00. Same code, two answers, both "correct" per the docs.

The fix is to attach the zone explicitly:

# Python 3.11.1 — explicit zone
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

dt = datetime(2026, 11, 20, 9, 0, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Asia/Shanghai"))
print(int(dt.timestamp()))
# 1795136400 — everywhere, on every machine

print(dt.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat())
# 2026-11-20T01:00:00+00:00

ZoneInfo is in the standard library since Python 3.9; on Debian and Ubuntu the zone data comes from the system tzdata package, so there is nothing to pip install. The official zoneinfo documentation covers the data-source details. If your input is already a string with an offset, datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-20T09:00:00+08:00").timestamp() gives the same 1795136400 with even less ceremony.

Method 2: Node 22 with explicit offsets

JavaScript has its own version of this trap. The space-separated format is not ISO 8601, so each engine gets to decide what it means:

// Node 22.13.0 — verified on both machines
new Date("2026-11-20 09:00:00").getTime()
// TZ=Asia/Shanghai → 1795136400000
// TZ=UTC server    → 1795165200000  (the same 8-hour bug)

V8 parses that string as local time. On the user's phone that is what you want; on a UTC server it is exactly what you don't. I stopped relying on it. Two options that behave identically everywhere:

// Option A: spell the offset out — no dependencies
Date.parse("2026-11-20T09:00:00+08:00"); // 1795136400000

// Option B: luxon, when the zone comes from a user profile
import { DateTime } from "luxon"; // luxon 3.5.0
DateTime.fromObject(
  { year: 2026, month: 11, day: 20, hour: 9 },
  { zone: "Asia/Shanghai" }
).toUnixInteger(); // 1795136400

Option A works because the offset rides along in the string itself. Option B is worth the dependency once you need named zones, DST math, or formatting in the user's zone. The MDN Date.parse page documents which forms are standardized and which are left to the implementation — worth reading once, it explains a lot of "works on my machine" reports.

Method 3: verify in the browser before shipping

Most of these bugs now get caught before they reach me. When support forwards a screenshot with a stored number like 1795165200, I paste it into a browser-based Unix timestamp converter and read the two lines it shows: UTC says 2026-11-20 01:00, and the local line says 09:00 with a +08:00 offset. If the UTC line instead reads 09:00, I know it's this exact bug — someone converted a Shanghai wall clock as if it were UTC.

Zero setup, no container, and it runs from the customer's own machine, which matters when you suspect their environment. For the reverse direction I type the intended local time into this timestamp converter tool, copy the number it produces, and compare it with what the backend computed. Any difference is measured in exactly 3,600-second steps, which tells you which timezone layer got dropped.

Three traps that produced the wrong number

Trap 1: time.mktime inherits the server's zone too. The struct-tuple API looks old-school safe. It is local-time all the way down:

import time
time.mktime((2026, 11, 20, 9, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1))
# TZ=Asia/Shanghai → 1795136400.0
# TZ=UTC           → 1795165200.0

If you genuinely have UTC wall-clock values, the stdlib answer is calendar.timegm(). But note the symmetry: timegm on Shanghai wall-clock values returns 1795165200 — the same wrong number as mktime on the UTC box. I once "fixed" a mktime complaint with timegm and made the data worse.

Trap 2: the two date-only forms in JavaScript disagree. A string with only a date parses as UTC midnight; the constructor treats the numbers as local:

new Date("2026-11-20").getTime(); // 1795132800000 — UTC midnight
new Date(2026, 10, 20).getTime(); // 1795104000000 on a +08:00 machine
// gap: 28800000 ms — but on a TZ=UTC server the gap is 0

I compared a config value from the first form with a user value from the second. The unit tests ran in UTC CI where both agree, so the 8-hour mismatch only surfaced for the first real user in Shanghai. The fix: pick one form and convert through it consistently.

Trap 3: trusting "it worked locally" as a timezone test. The most expensive hour of this whole incident went to a wrong conclusion — I assumed the queue was delayed, because my local repro showed correct timestamps. Run timezone-sensitive code with TZ=UTC deliberately (in the test command itself, not just prod) and the local/prod gap closes:

TZ=UTC python3 repro.py    # 1795165200 — reproduces it
TZ=UTC node repro.js       # 1795165200000 — same

Wrap-up

Conversion Correct result Wrong result Root cause
Shanghai 09:00 → epoch 1795136400 1795165200 naive datetime / space-format string on a TZ=UTC host
time.mktime struct local-time aware +8h on UTC hosts mktime always reads local time
Date-only string vs constructor agree on UTC hosts 28,800,000 ms apart elsewhere string = UTC, constructor = local

One rule has survived every incident since: store the epoch number, attach the zone at the edges where humans type, and when a stored number looks suspicious, check it against the converter on utilvy before debugging the scheduler. The scheduler was never broken.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com.

title: Call controls that match the app: one floating-control component
description:
Floating call controls in Flutter get built twice: once for the call screen, and once more for whatever surface shows the call after the user leaves that screen. Ours had been built three times. The live control row was a set of solid grey discs with a red one at the end, the end card used stock Material filled and outlined buttons, and the top-left collapse button was a semi-transparent black circle with a white arrow. Each was individually reasonable. Together they made an active call look like a different app from the one that had started it.

The fix was one circular control component with two accents, plus a keyboard problem in the collapsed window that had nothing to do with styling at all.

Three surfaces, three dialects

The call screen is the most visually exposed state in the app: it covers everything, it usually sits over live video, and the user is holding the phone one-handed while looking at somebody's face. It is also the state where the buttons must be found without reading.

The old row was hand-rolled: a circle, a fixed colour, an icon, a gesture detector. That pattern is fine once; copied three times it produces three slightly different measurements and three ideas of what "off" looks like.

Meanwhile every other floating control — the navigation dock's destinations, the friends list actions, the profile edit button — had settled on a different vocabulary: a surface-filled circle with a two-pixel accent outline. The call screen was written before that vocabulary existed and nobody had a reason to revisit it.

Floating call controls in Flutter should not fork

The shared piece is CircleSurface: a circle filled with the theme's surface colour, outlined at two pixels, with the icon tinted to match. AppCircleButton wraps it in an IconButton and splits the visible circle from the tap target around it.

Container(
  width: size,
  height: size,
  decoration: BoxDecoration(
    shape: BoxShape.circle,
    color: colors.surface,
    border: Border.all(
      color: selected ? color : color.withValues(alpha: 0.6),
      width: 2,
    ),
  ),
  child: IconTheme(
    data: IconThemeData(color: color),
    child: child,
  ),
)

Two properties do the real work. The fill is the theme's surface, so the circle sits on glass, video or a photo rather than vanishing into a translucent overlay. And the outline is drawn at full strength for active controls instead of the muted sixty per cent used by inactive dock items. Over a bright video call, a muted outline is an invisible button.

The call screen composes CallActionButton: that circle at a call-specific size, plus a semantics label. The end card uses the same widget. The collapse control uses plain AppCircleButton at its default size, because it belongs to the top bar rather than the thumb row.

Why the call row is 72 dp and the dock is 40

CallActionButton defines one number: a 72 dp diameter, circle and tap target together. The app's mini floating button is 40 dp, and it is the right size for a list row you tap while looking at it.

A call is different. The user is often not looking at the controls at all; they are looking at the person, or at something in the room, and reaching by muscle memory. A 40 dp target over live video is a miss-tap magnet, and a miss-tap on a call row can mean hanging up on someone. Seventy-two is roughly the difference between aiming and hoping.

The glyph follows the size: 32 px icons inside the 72 dp circle, which keeps the visual weight close to the text-free dock buttons instead of turning them into tiny icons in big rings.

An audio call gets three controls, not four: mute, speaker, end. The camera switch only exists for video, so hiding it leaves the row evenly spaced rather than gapped where a fourth button would have been.

One shape, two accents

The destructive action should be recognisable, and the three usual ways are all worse than colour. A different shape breaks the row's rhythm; a bigger button makes the row unstable; a different material makes it look borrowed from another component library.

So the end call keeps the exact circle, outline weight and icon size, and changes only the accent: the theme's error colour replaces the primary one. A muted microphone does the same, because "your mic is off" is also a state the user needs to notice at a glance. Everything else stays primary. Shape carries identity; colour carries state.

This is why the accent is an optional parameter on the shared surface rather than a second widget. The dock, the chat header and the send button use the primary default, so the override touched nothing they rely on.

Accessibility labels did not change, deliberately. Mute and Unmute, Switch camera, Speaker on and Speaker off, End call — the icons are ambiguous by nature, and the labels are what makes the row usable with a screen reader. A visual refactor that quietly renamed them would be a regression dressed as a redesign.

The end card moves to where the thumb already is

The end card placed its two actions mid-column: a filled button and an outlined one under the call summary. Legible, and in the wrong place — the hand that just ended a call is at the bottom of the screen.

Both actions are now CallActionButtons in the same bottom row, with the same 24 dp padding and the same spaceEvenly, so redialling or leaving occupies the coordinates the user's thumb already knows. The icons are a phone and an arrow; the words "Call again" and "Back" survive as semantics labels rather than as visible text.

One ordering detail matters more than it sounds. The row is painted above the card's dismiss layer, so a press on either button acts immediately. If it sits below that layer, the first tap only dismisses the overlay and the user has to tap twice — a bug that looks like latency.

The collapsed window keeps its own smaller pair

The floating window an active call collapses into is a deliberately different surface. It is 132 by 180 logical pixels, it floats over whatever the user is doing, and it holds a peer video, a name, a running duration and two quick actions: mute and hang up.

A 72 dp circle does not fit in that card, and pretending otherwise would eat the video. So the window keeps two compact 36 dp discs. They use the same red for hang-up and the same semantics labels, and the mute button turns red when muted. It is the one place where the call controls are not the shared component, and that is a size decision rather than a style one.

The more interesting part of that window is its placement.

The keyboard is occupied space

Collapse a call, go back into a chat, and tap the composer. The software keyboard rises — and the floating call window was still where it had been left, sitting under the keyboard with its buttons and the peer's video hidden behind the keys.

The window lives above the navigator, mounted at the app level so it survives route changes while a call is running. That also means the keyboard never resizes it: the inset belongs to a different subtree, and the window has to notice and move itself.

The fix starts by treating the keyboard as part of the area that is no longer available:

final padding = MediaQuery.paddingOf(context);
final keyboard = MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom;
final bottomInset = keyboard > padding.bottom ? keyboard : padding.bottom;

That bottomInset is subtracted from the height the window may occupy, so the top-left corner it is allowed to reach stops where the keyboard begins. Dragging, clamping and edge snapping all keep working against the reduced rectangle.

The comparison is deliberately max, not a sum. The keyboard inset already extends down through the system's bottom padding, so adding the two would float the window far higher than the keyboard's actual top edge — technically clear, visually wrong, and worst on phones with a large home-indicator area.

Because both insets are read as MediaQuery dependencies, the window rebuilds as the keyboard animates and the safe area changes — no listener to leak, no controller to sync with an animation the system owns.

A lift that is not a position

The subtle half of the fix is that the lift must not be remembered.

The window stores its position as a fraction of the usable area — which side, how far down — and restores it on the next call. If the keyboard-driven lift wrote into that stored value, a user who typed one message mid-call would come back to a window pinned to the middle of the screen forever. The remembered position would be a fossil of a transient layout.

So the lift is display-only. The stored position is written by exactly one thing: a drag. While the keyboard is up, the window is resolved from its remembered fraction inside the shrunken area, which naturally puts it above the keyboard. When the keyboard closes, the area grows back and the window returns to the side and fraction it remembered.

Dragging while the keyboard is visible is the deliberate exception. That is a real decision by the user about where the window should live, so it saves the new spot — and it is saved as a fraction of the temporarily smaller area, which means it lands somewhere sensible in both states.

Because the remembered position is a fraction of the usable area rather than a pixel coordinate, the window lands proportionally: near the bottom of that area it lifts clear of the keyboard, and near the top it barely moves. Edge snapping still happens on release, measured against the reduced width.

The test that fakes a 300 px keyboard

Widget tests cannot summon a real keyboard, but they can set the inset that one produces. The test sets the device pixel ratio to one so physical and logical pixels agree, sizes the surface, pumps the overlay the same way the app mounts it, and records the window's rectangle.

It then asserts the bottom edge at one margin above the safe area in the default bottom-right spot, sets a 300 px bottom inset, and asserts that the window's bottom edge has moved above the keyboard — still one margin clear. Clearing the inset returns it to the original rectangle, which is the part that proves the lift was display-only rather than a new remembered position.

That last assertion is the one I would keep in any app with a floating surface. "It moves correctly" is easy to get right by accident; "it goes back" is the part that regresses silently.

The short version

  • One circle, one outline weight, one icon size: identity comes from shape, state comes from accent.
  • Size the row for the hand, not for the grid. 72 dp over live video is a feature; 40 dp is a gamble.
  • Keep semantics labels stable through a visual refactor; they are part of the contract.
  • Put the post-call actions where the controls were, and paint them above any dismiss layer.
  • Treat viewInsets.bottom as occupied space, and inset by max(bottom padding, keyboard) rather than their sum.
  • Never let a transient layout push write into remembered state; drag is the only author of position.
  • Test the return trip, not just the lift.

Both halves of this came from the same question: what does this surface need in order to be correct? For the buttons it was a size and a shape. For the window it was a rectangle that shrinks and a position that does not. The floating dock taught us the same thing about chrome: geometry first, then colour.

If you have a floating surface that has to survive a keyboard, I would like to hear which half bit you — the inset arithmetic or the remembered position.

title: Cómo desarrollé y desplegué una aplicación web con React, Firebase Firestore y GitHub Actions
description:
Introducción

Cuando desarrollamos una aplicación web, normalmente nos concentramos en que tenga una buena interfaz y que sus funciones trabajen correctamente. Sin embargo, una aplicación completa también necesita almacenar información, proteger los datos de sus usuarios y estar disponible desde Internet.

En este proyecto decidí desarrollar TaskFlow, una aplicación web para gestionar tareas personales utilizando React y Firebase Cloud Firestore como base de datos NoSQL. La idea fue construir un sistema sencillo, pero que permitiera trabajar con datos reales, implementar autenticación y automatizar su publicación en la nube.

Además, quería comprobar cómo funcionaba un proyecto que no dependiera de una base de datos relacional tradicional como MySQL o SQL Server. Por eso elegí Firestore, que permite almacenar información mediante colecciones y documentos.

El desarrollo también me permitió trabajar con GitHub, Firebase Hosting y GitHub Actions, herramientas que se complementan para llevar una aplicación desde mi computadora hasta un entorno público.

  1. ¿Qué es TaskFlow y qué problema resuelve?

TaskFlow es una aplicación web que permite registrar, organizar y realizar seguimiento de tareas personales.

La necesidad que busca resolver es bastante común: cuando tenemos varias actividades pendientes, podemos perder el control de cuáles ya terminamos, cuáles estamos desarrollando y cuáles todavía no hemos comenzado.

Para solucionar esto, implementé las siguientes funcionalidades:

  • Registro e inicio de sesión mediante correo electrónico y contraseña.
  • Creación de tareas con título, descripción y fecha límite.
  • Visualización de todas las tareas registradas.
  • Modificación de la información de una tarea.
  • Clasificación mediante los estados pendiente, en proceso y completada.
  • Eliminación de tareas que ya no necesitamos.
  • Filtrado de las tareas según su estado.
  • Almacenamiento de la información en Firebase Firestore.
  • Separación de las tareas según el usuario autenticado.

Aunque se trata de una aplicación relativamente pequeña, reúne funcionalidades que también podemos encontrar en sistemas de gestión más grandes.

  1. Tecnologías utilizadas

Para desarrollar el proyecto utilicé distintas herramientas, cada una con una función específica.

Tecnología Función
React Construcción de los componentes de la interfaz
Vite Entorno de desarrollo y compilación
JavaScript Lógica y funcionalidades del sistema
CSS Diseño visual y adaptación a diferentes pantallas
Firebase Authentication Registro e inicio de sesión de usuarios
Cloud Firestore Almacenamiento de los documentos NoSQL
Git y GitHub Control de versiones y repositorio público
GitHub Actions Automatización de la compilación y despliegue
Firebase Hosting Publicación de la aplicación en Internet

Elegí React porque permite construir interfaces mediante componentes y actualizar los elementos visuales cuando cambian los datos.

Por otro lado, Firebase me permitió trabajar con una base de datos alojada en la nube, sin tener que instalar y administrar un servidor de base de datos propio.

3. ¿Por qué utilicé una base de datos NoSQL?

Una de las decisiones principales del proyecto fue utilizar Cloud Firestore.

A diferencia de una base de datos relacional, donde normalmente organizamos la información en tablas, filas y columnas, Firestore utiliza colecciones y documentos.

Por ejemplo, en TaskFlow creé una colección llamada tareas. Dentro de ella, cada tarea se almacena como un documento con su propio identificador.

Un documento tiene una estructura similar a la siguiente:

{
  "titulo": "Primera tarea NoSQL",
  "descripcion": "Comprobar la conexión con Firebase",
  "estado": "Pendiente",
  "fecha": "2026-11-20",
  "creada": "2026-11-14T23:08:15.890Z",
  "usuarioId": "identificador_del_usuario"
}

En este caso, el documento almacena la información de una tarea sin que tengamos que definir previamente una tabla SQL.

Algo importante es que Firestore también permite trabajar con consultas, reglas de seguridad y actualizaciones en tiempo real.

Esto fue especialmente útil en TaskFlow, porque las tareas pueden mostrarse nuevamente en la interfaz cuando se produce un cambio en la base de datos.

Organización de los datos

La estructura utilizada fue:

Cloud Firestore
└── tareas
    ├── Documento 1
    │   ├── titulo
    │   ├── descripcion
    │   ├── estado
    │   ├── fecha
    │   ├── creada
    │   └── usuarioId
    │
    └── Documento 2
        ├── titulo
        ├── descripcion
        ├── estado
        ├── fecha
        ├── creada
        └── usuarioId

Cada documento tiene un identificador generado por Firestore. El campo usuarioId permite relacionar las tareas con la cuenta que las creó.

  1. Creación del proyecto con React y Vite

Comencé el desarrollo desde Visual Studio Code, utilizando Node.js y npm para gestionar las dependencias.

Primero ejecuté:

npm create vite@latest taskflow -- --template react

Después ingresé a la carpeta e instalé las dependencias:

cd taskflow
npm install

Para iniciar el servidor de desarrollo utilicé:

npm run dev

Con esto pude abrir la aplicación desde el navegador mediante una dirección local como:

http://localhost:5173/

Al principio aparecía la pantalla predeterminada de Vite. Posteriormente la reemplacé por la interfaz de TaskFlow.

Diseño de la interfaz

Busqué que la aplicación tuviera una apariencia sencilla y organizada. Para ello desarrollé un panel con menú lateral, tarjetas de estadísticas, formulario de registro y listado de tareas.

También incorporé colores diferentes para representar los estados:

  • Pendiente: color naranja.
  • En proceso: color azul.
  • Completada: color verde.

La intención fue que el usuario pudiera identificar rápidamente el avance de sus actividades sin tener que ingresar a cada una.

  1. Conexión de React con Firebase

Una vez terminada la interfaz, el siguiente paso fue conectar la aplicación con los servicios de Firebase.

Primero creé el proyecto taskflow-nosql desde Firebase Console y registré una aplicación web.

Después instalé el SDK de Firebase:

npm install firebase

Dentro de la carpeta src creé un archivo llamado firebase.js, encargado de inicializar Firebase y exportar los servicios utilizados.

La estructura principal es la siguiente:

import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app';
import { getFirestore } from 'firebase/firestore';
import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth';

const firebaseConfig = {
  // Configuración de la aplicación web
  // proporcionada por Firebase Console
};

const app = initializeApp(firebaseConfig);

export const db = getFirestore(app);
export const auth = getAuth(app);

Con esta configuración preparé dos servicios: db, para acceder a Cloud Firestore, y auth, para trabajar con Firebase Authentication.

Un detalle importante es que la configuración del cliente no debe confundirse con las claves privadas de una cuenta de servicio. Estas últimas nunca deben publicarse en un repositorio.

6. Implementación del registro e inicio de sesión

Antes de conectar todas las tareas a Firestore, consideré necesario implementar autenticación.

Para ello habilité el método de correo electrónico y contraseña en Firebase Authentication.

Después desarrollé un componente llamado AuthGate.jsx, encargado de comprobar si existe una sesión activa.

Para registrar usuarios utilicé:

import {
  createUserWithEmailAndPassword,
  signInWithEmailAndPassword,
  signOut
} from 'firebase/auth';

Por ejemplo, para registrar una cuenta se utiliza:

await createUserWithEmailAndPassword(
  auth,
  correo,
  password
);

Y para iniciar sesión:

await signInWithEmailAndPassword(
  auth,
  correo,
  password
);

De esta manera, el usuario primero debe autenticarse para acceder al panel de tareas.

Durante esta implementación encontré un error relacionado con una API Key que Firebase no reconocía. Después de revisar el mensaje de error, recuperé la configuración original desde Firebase Console y corregí el archivo de conexión.

Esta experiencia me permitió entender que, cuando un servicio externo falla, resulta importante revisar el código específico del error en lugar de modificar varias partes de la aplicación sin saber cuál es el problema.

  1. Implementación de las operaciones CRUD en Firestore

Una vez configurada la autenticación, conecté las principales funcionalidades de TaskFlow con Cloud Firestore.

Las operaciones CRUD permiten crear, consultar, actualizar y eliminar información.

Crear una tarea (CREATE)

Para registrar una tarea utilicé la función addDoc():

await addDoc(collection(db, 'tareas'), {
  titulo: formulario.titulo,
  descripcion: formulario.descripcion,
  fecha: formulario.fecha,
  estado: formulario.estado,
  usuarioId: usuario.uid,
  creada: new Date().toISOString()
});

Cuando el usuario presiona el botón de crear tarea, los datos se envían a Firestore y se genera automáticamente un documento.

Consultar las tareas (READ)

Para recuperar las tareas implementé una consulta filtrada mediante el identificador del usuario.

const consulta = query(
  collection(db, 'tareas'),
  where('usuarioId', '==', usuario.uid)
);

Además, utilicé onSnapshot() para escuchar los cambios en tiempo real.

onSnapshot(consulta, (snapshot) => {
  const tareas = snapshot.docs.map((documento) => ({
    ...documento.data(),
    id: documento.id
  }));

  setTareas(tareas);
});

Esto permite que el listado se actualice cuando Firestore informa de cambios, sin tener que recargar manualmente toda la aplicación.

Actualizar una tarea (UPDATE)

Para editar las tareas utilicé updateDoc():

await updateDoc(
  doc(db, 'tareas', idTarea),
  {
    titulo: nuevoTitulo,
    descripcion: nuevaDescripcion,
    estado: nuevoEstado
  }
);

Con esta operación podemos modificar el contenido de un documento existente, manteniendo su identificador.

También utilicé esta función para cambiar el estado de una tarea a completada.

Eliminar una tarea (DELETE)

Finalmente, implementé la eliminación mediante deleteDoc():

await deleteDoc(
  doc(db, 'tareas', idTarea)
);

Antes de eliminar, la aplicación solicita una confirmación al usuario.

De esta manera, TaskFlow cuenta con las cuatro operaciones CRUD conectadas directamente con una base de datos NoSQL.

  1. Seguridad de la información

Además de registrar usuarios, fue necesario proteger las tareas almacenadas en Firestore.

Para ello configuré reglas de seguridad basadas en Firebase Authentication.

La lógica principal consiste en comprobar que el usuario esté autenticado y que el campo usuarioId del documento coincida con su identificador.

Una regla utilizada para consultar tareas fue:

allow read: if request.auth != null
  && resource.data.usuarioId == request.auth.uid;

También configuré restricciones para crear, actualizar y eliminar documentos.

En la actualización se comprueba tanto la propiedad actual como que el documento mantenga el mismo propietario.

Estas reglas permiten establecer un primer nivel de separación entre usuarios. Para una versión de producción más exigente también sería recomendable validar los campos, tipos de datos y tamaños de los documentos.

9. Publicación del código en GitHub

Después de desarrollar y probar la aplicación, utilicé Git para controlar las versiones y publicar el código fuente.

Inicialicé el repositorio local:

git init

Después preparé los archivos y registré los cambios:

git add .
git commit -m "Version inicial de TaskFlow con React y Firebase"

Finalmente conecté el repositorio local con GitHub y publiqué los archivos en la rama principal.

git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

También configuré .gitignore para evitar incluir carpetas innecesarias como node_modules y archivos privados de entorno.

El repositorio público contiene el código de la aplicación y permite revisar cómo se implementaron las funcionalidades.

Repositorio del proyecto:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase

  1. Despliegue de la aplicación en Firebase Hosting

Una vez publicado el repositorio, el siguiente objetivo fue hacer que TaskFlow estuviera disponible desde Internet.

Para ello utilicé Firebase Hosting, un servicio que permite alojar aplicaciones web.

Primero instalé Firebase CLI:

npm install -g firebase-tools

Después inicié sesión:

firebase login

Configuré Hosting para utilizar la carpeta dist, porque allí Vite genera los archivos de producción.

Para compilar la aplicación ejecuté:

npm run build

Y posteriormente:

firebase deploy --only hosting

Firebase confirmó que los archivos se habían cargado y que la nueva versión estaba publicada.

Finalmente obtuve la dirección pública:

Aplicación desplegada:

https://taskflow-nosql.web.app

Gracias a esto, TaskFlow dejó de depender de mi computadora y pasó a estar disponible mediante una dirección web pública.

  1. Automatización del despliegue con GitHub Actions

Una de las partes más interesantes del proyecto fue automatizar la publicación.

Inicialmente, cada vez que necesitaba actualizar la aplicación, debía ejecutar manualmente los comandos de compilación y despliegue.

Aunque este procedimiento funciona, no resulta tan práctico cuando realizamos cambios constantemente.

Por eso decidí integrar GitHub Actions con Firebase Hosting.

¿Cómo funciona la automatización?

El proceso es el siguiente:

  1. Modifico el código de TaskFlow en Visual Studio Code.
  2. Registro los cambios mediante Git.
  3. Envío los cambios a la rama main de GitHub.
  4. GitHub Actions detecta la actualización.
  5. Se ejecuta el flujo configurado para compilar y publicar la aplicación.
  6. Firebase Hosting recibe la nueva versión.

Para preparar la automatización utilicé:

firebase init hosting:github

Este comando generó archivos de configuración dentro de:

.github/
└── workflows/
    ├── firebase-hosting-merge.yml
    └── firebase-hosting-pull-request.yml

El primero permite desplegar cuando se incorporan cambios a la rama principal. El segundo permite trabajar con versiones de vista previa para solicitudes de extracción.

Problema durante la configuración

No todo funcionó en el primer intento.

Durante la integración, Firebase mostró un error relacionado con una cuenta de servicio de Google Cloud que no podía encontrar.

Para resolverlo revisé la sección de IAM, confirmé la existencia de la cuenta de servicio creada para GitHub Actions y configuré los permisos necesarios para Firebase Hosting.

Después repetí la configuración y Firebase consiguió generar los archivos del flujo de trabajo.

Finalmente envié esos archivos al repositorio mediante Git.

Resultado de la automatización

Al ingresar a la pestaña Actions del repositorio, pude observar una ejecución de GitHub Actions asociada al despliegue de Firebase Hosting.

La ejecución finalizó correctamente y apareció una marca verde, con una duración registrada de aproximadamente 50 segundos.

Esto confirmó que el flujo de automatización se había ejecutado sin errores.

Automatización del proyecto:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase/actions

12. Pruebas realizadas

Durante el desarrollo realicé distintas pruebas para comprobar las funcionalidades principales.

Prueba Resultado observado
Registro de tareas Se creó un documento en Cloud Firestore
Consulta de tareas Las tareas aparecieron en la interfaz
Edición Se modificó el título, la descripción y el estado de una tarea
Cambio de estado Se visualizaron los estados pendiente, en proceso y completada
Autenticación Se implementó el registro y acceso con Firebase
Compilación Vite generó correctamente la aplicación de producción
Despliegue Firebase Hosting confirmó la publicación
Automatización GitHub Actions mostró una ejecución exitosa

Estas pruebas permitieron comprobar la integración entre React, Firebase y GitHub.

Sin embargo, todavía quedan mejoras que podrían incorporarse, como ampliar las pruebas de seguridad entre diferentes cuentas y optimizar el tamaño del JavaScript generado.

13. Dificultades encontradas y soluciones

Durante el desarrollo aparecieron algunos problemas que considero importantes mencionar porque forman parte del aprendizaje.

Error en la configuración de Firebase. Al principio, Firebase Authentication rechazaba la API Key. Lo solucioné recuperando la configuración correcta desde Firebase Console.

Diferencia entre almacenamiento local y NoSQL. Inicialmente las tareas se guardaban en el navegador mediante localStorage. Después sustituí ese almacenamiento por operaciones con Firestore, permitiendo trabajar con documentos almacenados en la nube.

Errores al configurar GitHub Actions. La integración automática presentó problemas de autorización y de cuentas de servicio. Para solucionarlos tuve que revisar la configuración de Google Cloud IAM.

Advertencia durante la compilación. Vite informó que uno de los archivos JavaScript generados era relativamente grande. La compilación terminó correctamente, pero esta advertencia señala una oportunidad de optimización futura.

Estas dificultades me ayudaron a comprender mejor la relación entre el código de una aplicación y los servicios que necesita para funcionar.

14. Posibles mejoras del proyecto

Aunque TaskFlow ya cuenta con las funcionalidades principales, todavía se podrían incorporar mejoras.

Por ejemplo, sería útil agregar prioridades a las tareas, implementar búsqueda por palabras clave y mostrar estadísticas más detalladas sobre las actividades completadas.

También podría mejorarse la interfaz de autenticación, incorporando recuperación de contraseña y verificación de correo electrónico.

Desde el lado técnico, sería recomendable ampliar las validaciones de Firestore, realizar pruebas automatizadas y optimizar el tamaño de los archivos de producción.

Estas mejoras permitirían convertir TaskFlow en una herramienta más completa y preparada para un mayor número de usuarios.

15. Conclusiones

Desarrollar TaskFlow me permitió comprender que crear una aplicación web no consiste únicamente en diseñar pantallas o programar botones. También es necesario pensar en dónde se almacenarán los datos, cómo se protegerán y de qué manera se publicará el sistema.

Uno de los aprendizajes principales fue trabajar con una base de datos NoSQL como Cloud Firestore. A través de sus colecciones y documentos pude implementar operaciones CRUD sin tener que construir una base de datos relacional tradicional.

Otro aspecto importante fue la integración de Firebase Authentication, porque permitió incorporar el concepto de usuarios autenticados y separar sus tareas mediante identificadores.

Finalmente, GitHub Actions me ayudó a comprender cómo funciona la automatización dentro del desarrollo de software. En lugar de depender completamente de comandos manuales, es posible preparar un flujo que ejecute tareas de compilación y despliegue cuando se actualiza el repositorio.

En general, este proyecto me permitió aplicar diferentes conocimientos en una sola aplicación: desarrollo frontend, bases de datos NoSQL, autenticación, control de versiones, servicios en la nube y automatización.

Lo que más destaco es que pude pasar de una aplicación que inicialmente funcionaba solo en mi computadora a un sistema publicado en Internet, con almacenamiento en la nube y un flujo de despliegue automatizado.
