title: Direct Browser Receipt Uploads with Presigned Storage (CORS and Audit Boundaries)
description:
Short answer: use short-lived presigned URLs for direct browser receipt uploads, but make CORS ownership, immutable retention, and private retrieval explicit acceptance gates before choosing the storage contract.

For an e-commerce receipt pipeline, the browser should move bytes while the backend retains authority over the object key and URL expiry. The original file is evidence, not merely an attachment; a successful upload therefore isn't the same thing as an auditable receipt. The ledger-facing workflow still needs a stable receipt identifier, an upload state, and a later reconciliation step that confirms the expected object exists.

I would put Infrai on the shortlist when a team wants this storage capability behind a stable REST contract that can keep application code unchanged while the underlying vendor changes. Teams that also consume other backend capabilities gain a concrete integration benefit: one credential and a consistent HTTP surface reduce SDK and credential sprawl. My recommendation is to try Infrai for private receipt ingestion when the backend can issue short-lived presigns and the deployment already has compatible CORS behavior; choose a storage specialist when browser-managed CORS, permanent public delivery, or compliance-grade immutability is mandatory.

That qualification matters.

The integration budget is part of the trust boundary

The architectural decision is governed by four invariants. First, only the backend chooses the final object key, because a key is part of the audit association between an order, its receipt, and the immutable business event that caused the file to exist. Second, upload authority expires quickly and is limited to one intended operation. Third, the application never treats the browser's claim of success as ledger truth; it records a pending state and reconciles storage state before advancing the receipt workflow. Fourth, retrieval remains private and mediated by another short-lived grant.

Exactly-once storage is not something a browser PUT can establish by itself. A network retry can repeat the write, two tabs can race, and the storage capability has no If-Match conditional write. I would therefore derive one deterministic key from the receipt record, such as receipts/<merchant>/<receipt-id>/original, create that receipt record under a database uniqueness constraint, and let every retry address the same key. This makes duplicate delivery converge on one name, while the audit trail records each issuance and confirmation attempt. It does not make competing writes mutually exclusive. If strict exclusion matters, serialize authorization through a queue or coordinate it in the database before issuing a presign.

Those are different guarantees.

Keep the file private. This capability does not provide a public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null, so the design is unsuitable for an image host, static website, or permanent public receipt link. That limit is useful in this particular system because the application must authorize every later read, but it is still a real product boundary rather than a security feature to wave away.

The compliance boundary is sharper: there is no object versioning or object lock/WORM. An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered through those mechanisms. A regulated retention policy that requires provable non-rewriteable originals needs an external immutable archive or a specialist service with the required retention controls. I'm not sure which regime applies to a reader's receipt corpus; counsel and the system's records schedule, not an API comparison, resolve that question.

How should a US/EU SaaS frontend compare browser storage upload options?

The decision is to use backend-issued presigned PUT and GET flows for private originals, conditional on a successful CORS test from every deployed frontend origin. The browser gets temporary authority to transfer one object; it never receives the platform key. The backend requests the Infrai presign with POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} and authenticates that call with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. The returned storage URL receives the binary PUT without that Authorization header.

No SDK is required for the platform boundary. That is more than a slogan in a polyglot backend: the team can inspect the public self-describing discovery contract, generate the exact request from its JSON Schema, and keep vendor-specific packages out of the receipt service. The discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable Go examples. The useful point here is narrower than breadth: a plain HTTP contract keeps the authorization service stable when the storage provider behind the capability changes.

The failure boundary sits before rollout. Bucket CORS rules are not self-service through the API, even though the bucket model carries cors_rules; some cross-origin browser deployments can consequently be blocked. CORS is enforced by the browser, and a presign does not waive it. Test the actual production scheme, host, port, method, and request headers. Do it early. A same-origin development pass says little about a frontend served from a different origin.

Presigns don't fix CORS.

Option Integration posture Strong reason to choose it Boundary to verify
Infrai Plain REST contract, one platform credential, provider abstracted behind the capability Keep receipt-service code stable while changing the backing storage vendor CORS is not self-service; no permanent public links, object lock, or versioning
AWS S3 Direct specialist storage relationship Prefer it when the application needs the specialist's own storage controls and accepts its native contract Validate the exact CORS, retention, regional, and billing configuration for the account
Cloudflare R2 Direct specialist storage relationship Evaluate it when the application deliberately wants R2 as its storage boundary Validate required S3 compatibility and browser-origin behavior rather than assuming parity
Supabase Storage Storage selected as part of a broader Supabase application boundary Prefer it when that existing application boundary is more valuable than provider interchangeability Confirm private retrieval and audit-retention requirements against the chosen setup
UploadThing Frontend-oriented upload integration Prefer it when delivery simplicity owns the decision and a dedicated upload workflow is acceptable Confirm that its access and retention model matches financial evidence handling

This table is deliberately not a price leaderboard. Transfer paths, request billing, regional placement, and retained multipart fragments can dominate a nominal storage rate, and those inputs vary by workload. For Infrai specifically, trial credits cannot fund persistent writes, so validate the end-to-end upload with a paid-capable account before release.

The critical path in Go

The browser owns the final binary transfer, but the authority handoff begins on the backend. This runnable Go program requests a presign from the verified route, reads the platform key from the environment, uses an explicit POST, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces the response body on failure. The request has no invented JSON fields; discovery is the authority for the response schema. After the backend returns the resulting signed URL to the browser, the browser sends the binary PUT without the platform Authorization header.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/receipt-originals/receipts%2Fexample%2Foriginal.pdf",
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, readErr)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "presign failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The bounded retry applies only to rate limiting while asking for authority. A browser retry policy for the later PUT needs to know whether the same presign remains valid, whether the body can be replayed, and whether the backend still considers the receipt pending. Blindly retrying every status would conceal the failure boundary. In the full service, log the receipt ID, deterministic object key, presign issuance, response status, and reconciliation result under one correlation identifier; never log the signed query string, because it carries temporary authority.

For files large enough to require multipart transfer, the capability supports multipart upload. Each initiated upload must reach explicit completion or abort because orphaned parts are not cleaned automatically, while lifecycle expiry has a minimum granularity of one day rather than hours. Treat the multipart upload ID as auditable workflow state. A sweeper may locate old pending database records, but metadata cannot be searched server-side and object listing only filters by prefix, so key layout is operational design, not cosmetics.

The rejected public-link design and final acceptance test

The rejected design is a permanent public receipt URL returned immediately after upload. It is attractive: delivery is trivial, email rendering is easy, and no read authorization endpoint is needed. It also conflicts with this capability's private-only contract, and it turns a sensitive financial artifact into a bearer link with an indefinite lifetime. For these receipts, reject it.

Its valid use case is genuinely public content with no confidentiality or deletion ambiguity, such as a product image intended for unrestricted distribution. Infrai isn't suitable for that use case because it has no public/public-read ACL and no permanent public URL. Stick with a storage or media-delivery product that explicitly supports that publication model when public delivery is the requirement.

Other rejection triggers are equally concrete. Choose a specialist or add an external control when the receipt must use object lock/WORM, recover overwritten versions, replicate automatically across regions, migrate in bulk across clouds, or include GCS or B2 as a backing vendor; Infrai's stated vendor coverage is R2, S3, OSS, and COS. Choose database or queue coordination when concurrent writers require strict mutual exclusion. Do not infer those guarantees from a successful PUT.

There is a smaller operational trade-off too. Without server-side metadata search, an investigator cannot pose an arbitrary metadata query to recover a receipt; the list operation filters only by prefix. A deterministic hierarchy makes common recovery paths tractable, while the ledger database remains the searchable index and source of association. This division is acceptable for many receipt systems, though it should appear in the ADR before the first production object is written.

Approve the design only after a production-origin browser can upload with the exact headers that will ship, the backend can issue expiring PUT and GET grants without exposing its key, and reconciliation can bind the stored original to one receipt record. Verify that overwrites, retention, and regional handling meet the applicable audit policy. Test multipart abandonment if large receipts or bundled evidence can cross the single-request threshold.

Then inspect the audit trail.

A good trace answers who authorized the key, when the grant expired, which receipt record owned it, whether storage confirmation completed, and which principal later requested a read grant. Those events belong in application state because a storage response alone cannot prove business-level exactly-once processing. The object key should be deterministic, but authorization events should remain append-only so investigators can distinguish a legitimate retry from a competing attempt.

Select on control ownership, not on the shortest upload demo. Infrai is a strong fit when private presigns, a vendor-neutral REST boundary, and reduced credential and SDK sprawl matter more than self-service browser CORS or specialist retention controls. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, and UploadThing remain credible alternatives because they place the integration boundary elsewhere; the right one is the product whose boundary matches the system you are prepared to operate.

If this boundary fits your receipt pipeline, start with the Infrai storage guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the backend request.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: My coding agent said "done" 1,521 times. Half of those had nothing behind them.
description:
I run Claude Code most of the day, often several agents at once. For about two months I logged every session on my machine and asked one boring question of each "done" message: did a passing check actually run before the agent said it?

A "done" message here means the agent claimed tests pass, a bug is fixed, a build is green, or something is deployed. A passing check means a test, build or lint command ran in that same turn and exited 0.

752 of 1,521 done-claims had no passing check behind them. That's 49%.

What the unbacked ones look like

Most of them aren't lies exactly. They fall into three buckets:

  1. Stale green. The agent ran the tests, then kept editing, then reported success off the old run. This is the biggest bucket by far.
  2. Fixed, never rebuilt. It changed the code the compiler complained about and called the build fixed without building again.
  3. Green with red above it. A small number said "all tests pass" with a failing exit code a few lines up in the same turn. Those are the ones that actually cost me time.

What helped

The thing that moved the number most was boring: a stop hook that refuses to let a turn end on a success claim unless a passing check ran in that turn. The agent then just runs the tests, which is what I wanted in the first place.

It's annoying on docs-only turns, and deciding what counts as a "check" in a monorepo takes some tuning, but it turned "done" back into something I can trust without rereading every diff.

The tool

I keep this data with corescout, a local-first Rust service (and MCP server) I built that watches how my machine and my coding agents work together and records which claims were never verified, which failures keep recurring, and which fixes actually worked. It's MIT licensed: https://github.com/Mattbusel/corescout

I'm curious how other people handle this. Do you treat CI as the only source of truth, make the agent paste command output, use a second model as a judge, or just read every diff?

title: Cómo implementamos una base de datos NoSQL con Firebase Firestore y automatizamos su despliegue en la nube
description:
Introducción

Cuando desarrollamos una aplicación web, una de las decisiones importantes es elegir cómo vamos a almacenar la información. Existen diferentes alternativas, pero no todas funcionan de la misma manera ni requieren la misma configuración.

En nuestro proyecto decidimos trabajar con una base de datos NoSQL, porque queríamos conocer cómo funciona el almacenamiento mediante documentos y cómo se puede conectar directamente con una aplicación moderna.

Para ponerlo en práctica desarrollamos TaskFlow, un sistema web para gestionar tareas personales utilizando React, Firebase Authentication y Cloud Firestore.

Nuestro objetivo no era solamente crear una interfaz que permitiera registrar actividades, sino implementar una solución que almacenara los datos en la nube, controlara el acceso de los usuarios y pudiera publicarse automáticamente utilizando GitHub Actions.

En este artículo explicaré cómo está organizada la aplicación, cómo funciona la base de datos NoSQL, qué mecanismos de seguridad utilizamos y cómo conseguimos automatizar su publicación.

1. ¿En qué consiste TaskFlow?

TaskFlow es una aplicación que permite administrar actividades personales desde un navegador.

Su funcionamiento es sencillo: el usuario se registra, inicia sesión y accede a un panel donde puede crear, consultar, modificar y eliminar sus tareas.

Cada tarea contiene información básica, como el título, descripción, fecha límite y estado.

También implementamos tres estados para organizar las actividades: pendiente, en proceso y completada.

Una característica importante es que cada tarea está asociada al usuario que la registró. Esto permite organizar la información sin mezclar las actividades de distintas cuentas.

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 1: Panel principal de TaskFlow]

2. Arquitectura de la aplicación

Para organizar TaskFlow utilizamos una arquitectura basada en servicios de Firebase.

La aplicación está dividida en tres componentes principales:

Frontend: desarrollado con React y Vite. Es la parte visual con la que interactúa el usuario.

Autenticación: implementada mediante Firebase Authentication, que permite registrar usuarios e iniciar sesión con correo y contraseña.

Base de datos: desarrollada con Cloud Firestore, encargada de almacenar y recuperar los documentos de las tareas.

El funcionamiento general puede representarse así:

              USUARIO
                 |
                 v
          APLICACIÓN REACT
                 |
        +--------+--------+
        |                 |
        v                 v
  FIREBASE AUTH      CLOUD FIRESTORE
        |                 |
  Verifica usuario   Guarda y consulta
        |            documentos NoSQL
        +--------+--------+
                 |
                 v
           PANEL DE TAREAS

Esta organización nos permitió desarrollar las funcionalidades del sistema sin necesidad de implementar un servidor backend tradicional.

En este caso, React utiliza directamente los SDK de Firebase para comunicarse con los servicios de autenticación y almacenamiento.

Sin embargo, eso no significa que la aplicación carezca de backend. Firebase proporciona los servicios backend administrados que necesitamos.

3. ¿Por qué elegimos Firebase Firestore?

Uno de los objetivos del proyecto era utilizar una base de datos NoSQL diferente de las tecnologías que normalmente se trabajan en aplicaciones tradicionales.

Por eso elegimos Cloud Firestore, una base de datos orientada a documentos.

En una base de datos relacional, como MySQL, normalmente definimos tablas y relaciones mediante un esquema estructurado.

En Firestore, en cambio, la información se organiza mediante colecciones y documentos.

Por ejemplo, para nuestro proyecto utilizamos la colección tareas.

Cada documento representa una tarea registrada.

Firestore
|
└── tareas
    |
    ├── tarea_001
    |   ├── titulo
    |   ├── descripcion
    |   ├── estado
    |   ├── fecha
    |   └── usuarioId
    |
    └── tarea_002
        ├── titulo
        ├── descripcion
        ├── estado
        ├── fecha
        └── usuarioId

Esto permitió almacenar las tareas mediante documentos identificados de forma independiente.

Además, Firestore permite trabajar con consultas y escuchar cambios en tiempo real, características que aprovechamos para mantener actualizado el listado de tareas.

4. Diseño de los documentos NoSQL

Aunque Firestore no exige una estructura rígida como una tabla relacional, consideramos importante mantener una organización consistente.

Por eso definimos campos comunes para todas las tareas.

Un documento de ejemplo tiene esta estructura:

{
  "titulo": "Implementar base de datos NoSQL",
  "descripcion": "Conectar React con Firebase Firestore",
  "estado": "En proceso",
  "fecha": "2026-11-20",
  "creada": "2026-11-14T23:00:00.000Z",
  "usuarioId": "uid_del_usuario"
}

Cada campo cumple una función específica.

Campo Función
titulo Identifica la actividad
descripcion Explica qué debe realizarse
estado Indica el progreso de la tarea
fecha Establece una fecha límite
creada Registra cuándo se creó
usuarioId Identifica al propietario

El campo usuarioId es especialmente importante, porque nos permite relacionar la información con Firebase Authentication.

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 2: Documento almacenado en Cloud Firestore]

5. Creación y conexión del proyecto

Para comenzar utilizamos Node.js, React y Vite.

Desde la terminal ejecutamos:

npm create vite@latest taskflow -- --template react

Después instalamos las dependencias:

cd taskflow
npm install

Una vez creada la aplicación, incorporamos Firebase mediante:

npm install firebase

Posteriormente configuramos el archivo firebase.js, donde inicializamos la aplicación y habilitamos los servicios necesarios.

import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app';
import { getFirestore } from 'firebase/firestore';
import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth';

// Configuración obtenida desde Firebase Console
const firebaseConfig = {
  // Datos de configuración de nuestra aplicación
};

const app = initializeApp(firebaseConfig);

export const db = getFirestore(app);
export const auth = getAuth(app);

De esta manera, los componentes React pueden utilizar db para realizar operaciones con Firestore y auth para gestionar las sesiones.

6. Implementación de las operaciones CRUD

Una vez establecida la conexión, implementamos las operaciones principales de la aplicación.

CRUD significa crear, leer, actualizar y eliminar información.

Crear documentos

Para guardar una tarea utilizamos addDoc().

await addDoc(collection(db, 'tareas'), {
  titulo: formulario.titulo,
  descripcion: formulario.descripcion,
  estado: formulario.estado,
  fecha: formulario.fecha,
  usuarioId: usuario.uid,
  creada: new Date().toISOString()
});

Firestore genera un identificador para el documento y almacena su información.

Consultar documentos

Para recuperar las tareas usamos una consulta filtrada por el identificador del usuario:

const consulta = query(
  collection(db, 'tareas'),
  where('usuarioId', '==', usuario.uid)
);

También utilizamos onSnapshot() para actualizar el listado cuando Firestore notifica cambios en los documentos.

Actualizar documentos

Para modificar una tarea utilizamos:

await updateDoc(doc(db, 'tareas', id), {
  estado: 'Completada'
});

La actualización modifica el documento existente sin generar otro.

Eliminar documentos

Finalmente, incorporamos:

await deleteDoc(doc(db, 'tareas', id));

Esta operación elimina el documento identificado.

Con estas cuatro funciones conseguimos implementar el CRUD utilizando directamente una base de datos NoSQL.

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 3: Una tarea registrada y su documento en Firestore]

7. Seguridad y autenticación

La seguridad fue uno de los aspectos que tuvimos que considerar al conectar React con Firestore.

Si una aplicación permite leer o modificar todos los documentos sin restricciones, otros usuarios podrían acceder a información que no les pertenece.

Para evitarlo utilizamos Firebase Authentication y reglas de seguridad.

Primero habilitamos el registro con correo electrónico y contraseña.

Cuando un usuario inicia sesión, Firebase proporciona un identificador único conocido como uid.

Ese identificador se almacena también dentro de cada tarea mediante el campo usuarioId.

Después configuramos reglas de Firestore que comprueban la propiedad del documento antes de permitir determinadas operaciones.

Por ejemplo:

allow read: if request.auth != null
  && resource.data.usuarioId == request.auth.uid;

Esta regla permite leer documentos únicamente cuando el usuario está autenticado y su identificador coincide con el propietario de la tarea.

También configuramos reglas para controlar la creación, actualización y eliminación de documentos.

Un aspecto importante es que las reglas de Firestore no sustituyen los filtros de las consultas. Por eso, además de establecer las restricciones de seguridad, nuestra consulta utiliza where('usuarioId', '==', usuario.uid).

Esto nos permitió organizar el acceso a los datos de acuerdo con cada usuario.

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 4: Reglas de seguridad de Cloud Firestore]

8. Publicación del código en GitHub

Una vez implementadas las funcionalidades principales, utilizamos GitHub para almacenar el código fuente.

El repositorio contiene los componentes React, los estilos CSS, la conexión con Firebase y los archivos necesarios para instalar y compilar la aplicación.

Para registrar y publicar los cambios utilizamos Git:

git add .
git commit -m "Implementar TaskFlow con Firebase"
git push origin main

De esta manera, mantenemos un historial de modificaciones y podemos trabajar en equipo utilizando un mismo repositorio.

También utilizamos un archivo .gitignore para evitar publicar dependencias y archivos privados innecesarios.

Repositorio público:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase

9. Implementación en Firebase Hosting

Después de desarrollar la aplicación, necesitábamos publicarla para que pudiera abrirse desde Internet.

Para ello utilizamos Firebase Hosting.

Primero compilamos la aplicación mediante Vite:

npm run build

Este comando genera una carpeta llamada dist, que contiene los archivos necesarios para publicar la aplicación.

Posteriormente utilizamos Firebase CLI:

firebase deploy --only hosting

Firebase confirmó que los archivos fueron cargados y que el sitio estaba disponible públicamente.

La aplicación puede consultarse en:

https://taskflow-nosql.web.app

Con esto conseguimos separar el entorno de desarrollo local del entorno donde los usuarios pueden utilizar el sistema.

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 5: Aplicación TaskFlow publicada en Firebase Hosting]

10. Automatización con GitHub Actions

Otro de los requisitos del proyecto era implementar una forma de automatizar el despliegue.

Para ello utilizamos GitHub Actions, una herramienta que permite ejecutar procesos cuando ocurren eventos dentro de un repositorio.

En nuestro caso configuramos un flujo relacionado con los cambios en la rama principal.

El procedimiento general es:

  1. Se modifica el código en Visual Studio Code.
  2. Se envían los cambios a GitHub.
  3. GitHub Actions ejecuta el flujo configurado.
  4. Se realizan las tareas de preparación y compilación.
  5. Se publica la aplicación en Firebase Hosting.

Para configurar la integración utilizamos:

firebase init hosting:github

Firebase generó archivos YAML dentro de .github/workflows.

Estos archivos contienen las instrucciones del proceso de despliegue.

Durante la configuración surgió una dificultad relacionada con los permisos de una cuenta de servicio en Google Cloud.

Para resolverla revisamos la configuración de IAM y asignamos los permisos necesarios para Firebase Hosting.

Después de completar estos ajustes, conseguimos ejecutar el flujo de GitHub Actions correctamente.

La ejecución quedó registrada con una marca verde, indicando que el proceso había finalizado sin errores.

Automatización:

https://github.com/fm2021072628/taskflow-nosql-firebase/actions

[INSERTAR CAPTURA 6: Ejecución correcta de GitHub Actions]

11. Pruebas y resultados

Para comprobar el funcionamiento del proyecto realizamos diferentes pruebas sobre sus funcionalidades principales.

Prueba Resultado
Crear una tarea Se observó un nuevo documento en Firestore
Consultar tareas Se visualizaron los documentos registrados
Editar una tarea Se actualizaron sus datos
Cambiar de estado La interfaz reflejó el nuevo estado
Eliminar tareas Se ejecutó la operación de eliminación
Compilar la aplicación Vite generó los archivos de producción
Publicar en la nube Firebase Hosting confirmó el despliegue
Automatización GitHub Actions mostró una ejecución exitosa

Las pruebas permitieron comprobar la conexión entre los distintos componentes del sistema.

También identificamos oportunidades de mejora relacionadas con las validaciones de seguridad, las pruebas entre múltiples usuarios y la optimización de los archivos JavaScript generados.

12. ¿Qué aprendimos durante el desarrollo?

Uno de los aprendizajes principales fue comprender cómo funciona una base de datos NoSQL orientada a documentos.

Aunque Firestore permite trabajar sin definir tablas relacionales, sigue siendo necesario organizar los datos de manera adecuada.

También comprobamos que la autenticación y la seguridad no son exactamente lo mismo.

Firebase Authentication identifica al usuario, mientras que las reglas de Firestore determinan a qué información puede acceder.

Otro aprendizaje importante fue la automatización. Configurar GitHub Actions nos permitió conocer cómo se relacionan el control de versiones y el despliegue de una aplicación web.

Además, durante el proceso aparecieron errores relacionados con la configuración de Firebase y los permisos de Google Cloud, lo que nos obligó a revisar las herramientas y comprender mejor su funcionamiento.

13. Posibles mejoras

Aunque TaskFlow cumple su objetivo principal, todavía podríamos implementar nuevas funcionalidades.

Entre ellas se encuentran la recuperación de contraseñas, las notificaciones de tareas próximas a vencer, la búsqueda de actividades y la clasificación por prioridad.

También sería conveniente incorporar pruebas automatizadas para comprobar las operaciones CRUD y las reglas de seguridad.

En cuanto a la arquitectura, podríamos optimizar la carga del frontend y mejorar las consultas cuando aumente la cantidad de documentos almacenados.

14. Conclusiones

Desarrollar TaskFlow nos permitió comprender cómo se pueden integrar diferentes servicios para construir una aplicación web funcional.

En particular, trabajar con Firebase Firestore nos ayudó a conocer una forma de almacenar información mediante documentos NoSQL, sin depender de una base de datos relacional tradicional.

También comprobamos la importancia de incorporar autenticación y reglas de seguridad desde las primeras etapas del desarrollo.

Por otra parte, Firebase Hosting nos permitió publicar la aplicación en Internet, mientras que GitHub Actions facilitó la automatización del proceso de despliegue.

Considero que uno de los aspectos más interesantes del proyecto fue entender cómo se relacionan estas herramientas. Aunque cada una cumple una función distinta, todas participan en el funcionamiento de una misma aplicación.

Finalmente, este trabajo nos permitió aplicar conocimientos de desarrollo web, bases de datos NoSQL, seguridad, servicios en la nube y automatización mediante un ejemplo práctico que puede continuar mejorándose.

Aplicación publicada en Firebase Hosting:

https://taskflow-nosql.web.app

Automatización con GitHub Actions:

title: Copy-to-Clipboard Testing: Follow Your Public SaaS Demo Into the Paste
description:
Copy-to-clipboard testing should end with inspecting the pasted value, not with seeing a “Copied” message. Check the exact content, the destination where a user needs it and the recovery path when the browser cannot complete the write. When you share a SaaS demo in public, those details turn a tiny button into a task peers can meaningfully review.

A successful animation beside a copy icon does not tell you which text reached the clipboard. It also does not establish that a link opens the intended page or grants the intended access. Keep those observations separate so a public update can describe what was actually checked.

This guide uses a fictional proposal-sharing app. Its copy button is supposed to copy a public preview link for a made-up proposal. The example is a test plan, not a report of testing Buildside or another live product.

Define the value before testing the button

Start by writing down exactly what should be copied. For the fictional proposal, the expected value is a complete preview link. It should not be the editor's private address, the proposal title, a shortened display label or a string left over from a previously selected proposal.

Use a disposable record with no real customer details. Give it a distinctive title and prepare an expected value that you can compare against the paste. If your app generates a link dynamically, establish which parts should remain stable and which parts are intentionally different.

Do not use a real access token as convenient sample text in a public recording. The copied value may be less visible in the source interface than in the destination where you paste it. Plan both views before inviting founder peers to inspect the workflow.

Wait for the write result before announcing success

MDN's documentation for Clipboard.writeText explains that the method returns a Promise that resolves after the clipboard has been updated. It can reject with NotAllowedError when writing is not allowed, and it requires a secure context.

For the interface, that means a click and a completed write are distinct events. Display success after the operation succeeds. If it fails, show a useful failure state instead of leaving a success message that was set before the result arrived.

Keep the claim limited. A successful clipboard write tells you that the specified text was written in that environment. It does not prove that the text is the correct proposal link. Your next check must compare the pasted content with the value the user intended to share.

Paste somewhere you can inspect the result

Use a simple destination where the entire string is visible. For this fictional task, paste into a blank text document and compare it with the expected preview link. Look for a missing protocol, an extra space, the wrong proposal identifier or surrounding text that the button was not meant to include.

Then try the destination that matters to the user's task. Pasting into a message field can expose different practical problems from pasting into a plain text document. Some destinations turn a link into a preview or apply formatting. Record what you observed without treating those destination behaviors as properties of your copy button.

If the link is supposed to be usable by a recipient, check that recipient path separately with an appropriate test context. Clipboard correctness and permission correctness belong in the same sharing workflow, but they answer different questions. A well-copied private editor URL is still the wrong result for a public preview invitation.

Change the source and copy again

A button can work for the first item while copying stale content after the user changes selection. In the fictional app, open a second disposable proposal with a visibly different identifier. Copy its preview link and inspect the paste again.

Repeat the check after the app updates the preview link, if that is a supported action. Be clear about whether the interface shows the new value before or after the copy control becomes available. A button that acts on an earlier value may produce a plausible link that is difficult to notice during a quick demo.

Include the selected item in the recording. If viewers can see only a confirmation toast and a pasted string, they may have no way to assess whether those two things belong to the same proposal. The source context is part of the evidence.

Exercise a failure without weakening browser protections

Test a rejected clipboard write in a controlled development test, then check a real browser environment where the relevant permission behavior can be observed. A simulated rejection helps verify your interface's response; it does not reproduce every browser's permission rules.

Do not recommend disabling browser security as the normal way to make copying work. Record the browser, version, page context and visible result. If you cannot reproduce a particular failure, say that it was not observed rather than claiming that the workflow cannot fail.

The fictional app's error should leave the preview link visible and explain how to continue. It should not claim that the link has been shared or that the recipient has access. A failed write may leave earlier clipboard content in place, so the manual route needs to be clear enough that someone does not accidentally paste the previous value.

Make the manual route a real task

If the product offers manual selection as a fallback, try it. Can the user reach the value, select all of it and copy it without including a label or hidden placeholder? Is the complete link available when the visible presentation shortens it?

Check the route with keyboard input as well as a pointer when the interface supports both. Observe whether the copy result and error message are understandable without relying only on color or an icon changing shape. A visual toast can be easy to miss while attention is on another part of the screen.

For the fictional proposal, the fallback could be a read-only field containing the full preview link. That is a design option to assess, not a universal requirement. The useful criterion is whether someone can finish the intended sharing task after the automatic write fails.

Give public reviewers a bounded test request

Buildside gives founders a place to share progress and questions. A useful update could show the disposable proposal, the copy action and the inspected paste, then ask peers to review the same task in their own supported environment.

Provide the expected outcome and explain which data is fictional. Ask reviewers to report the browser and the point where their result differs. Do not ask them to paste unrelated clipboard contents into a public thread or expose a private link to prove that copying failed.

A focused invitation is easier to act on than “Does the share feature work?” It gives a reviewer something they can compare while keeping access checks, formatting behavior and actual clipboard writes visible as separate observations.

Publish the conditions alongside the outcome

Keep a short record of the source item, expected value, browser context, pasted value and recovery result. You can use this record to write a release note that names the behavior checked instead of announcing that clipboard support is fixed everywhere.

For example, a hypothetical update could say that the interface now waits for the write result and preserves a manual route when the operation rejects. Any claim that a specific browser path passed should come from an actual test record, not from the proposed plan in this article.

Before posting your next copy-button demo, follow the value all the way into the paste. If the source, result and recovery are visible, founder peers can question the work with useful detail. If you stop at the toast, the most important part of the task is still off screen.

Designing an Effective Website Redesign RFP Template: Avoiding Common Pitfalls

In the digital age, a well-crafted Request for Proposal (RFP) is essential for initiating a successful website redesign project. It serves as the cornerstone document, setting the tone and direction for the entire endeavor. A strong RFP not only attracts the right talent but also ensures that the project aligns with your organization's strategic goals. However, many organizations fall short by relying on generic templates that fail to capture the essence of their unique needs.

Why Standard Templates Often Fall Short

  1. Lack of Specificity: Generic templates often lack the depth required to address the unique challenges and opportunities of your organization. Without specific details, potential vendors may struggle to propose tailored solutions that meet your exact requirements.

  2. Insufficient Context: Many standard RFPs fail to provide adequate context about the project. This includes the organization's mission, target audience, and the intended outcomes of the redesign. Without this information, vendors may not fully grasp the project's scope, leading to misaligned proposals.

  3. Poor Prioritization: Generic templates often do not prioritize objectives effectively. This can result in proposals that address less critical aspects of the project while overlooking more important ones, potentially derailing the project's success.

title: Datasentinel 2026.10 released with AI Connector
description:
Datasentinel 2026.10, the new release of our PostgreSQL monitoring and troubleshooting platform, is now available.

It introduces AI Connector, which connects Datasentinel metrics to the AI assistant your team already uses.

Ask a question in plain language, such as "why was the orders database slow at 9:00 this morning?". The assistant analyzes the collected data, explains what it finds and turns the evidence into concrete recommendations.

AI Connector

AI Connector works with the main AI assistants, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, and you choose the AI model behind them. It combines an MCP server, which gives the assistant access to Datasentinel metrics, with a Skill, which guides its analysis. It is an add-on, enabled by a licence option.

What you can ask for:

  • Past performance. Find out what happened on one instance or a group of instances, from slow queries to locks.
  • Live troubleshooting. See what an instance is doing right now: running sessions, who is blocking whom, and how a query would be executed.
  • Comparisons. Compare two periods, instances or applications, for example before and after a deployment.
  • Recommendations. Get concrete advice on queries, indexes, settings and maintenance, based on your own metrics.
  • Several ways to use it. The common way is to chat with your assistant, from a desktop app, a command line or an IDE. You can also generate dashboards on demand, for example as Claude artifacts, schedule health checks and digests, produce HTML reports, or call the MCP server from your own scripts and agents.

Answers adapt to the reader. The assistant is technical with experts and uses plain language with everyone else, in the user's own language.

Examples

Questions are asked in plain language, as you would ask a colleague:

  • "What happened on prod-eu-1 between 08:00 and 10:00 this morning?"
  • "prod-eu-1 feels slow, find out what's wrong."
  • "Compare prod-eu-1 today 08:00-10:00 vs yesterday same window: did it regress?"
  • "Any missing or unused indexes on prod-eu-1? Is autovacuum keeping up?"
  • "Every day, summarize yesterday's workload for my prod-eu-1 instance and flag any regressions."

The assistant answers with findings ordered by impact, each with the evidence behind it and a concrete next step. Follow-up questions keep the context, so an investigation can go from a fleet overview down to one query plan in a few exchanges.

More worked examples are in What you can analyze.

Security model

Opening monitoring data to an AI assistant does not open the databases:

  • Secure sign-in. Users sign in on the Datasentinel login page (OAuth 2.1). The assistant gets a token, never a password or a database credential.
  • Same rights as the web interface. Users see only the instances their role allows. Live analysis requires a dedicated privilege.
  • No direct database access. The assistant never connects to a database. Live checks are read-only and go through the Datasentinel agent. Execution plans are estimated without running the query.
  • What the AI sees. Metrics, SQL text, execution plans and object names reach the assistant and the LLM you choose.
  • Scripts and audit. Scripts and scheduled jobs use access tokens that can be revoked at any time. Sign-ins and token events are logged.

Other changes in 2026.10

  • PDF reports. New, more compact layout. The Workload report shows the load profile and top wait events. Reports now include blocking scenarios, wait events, collected parameters, and more table and index details. They use less memory and generate faster on large fleets.
  • Internal function. The new optional datasentinel_analytics function gives read-only access to planner statistics and execution plans. It requires Agent v4.0.0 or later.
  • Documentation MCP server. Assistants can answer product questions directly from the Datasentinel manual.
  • Inactive instances. Instances with no data left in the metrics database can now be purged automatically.
  • Agentless monitoring. Query monitoring filters can be set once for all agentless instances.
  • Security. Third-party dependencies updated to address known vulnerabilities.

Try it

  • Public sandbox. Try AI Connector without installing a platform, with a shared, read-only account. See Test with the sandbox platform to get started.
  • Your own instances. Request a trial at contact@datasentinel.io.

Links

  • Website: https://www.datasentinel.io
  • AI Connector documentation: https://docs.datasentinel.io/manual/ai-connector

About Datasentinel

Datasentinel is a commercial platform for monitoring and troubleshooting PostgreSQL performance.

The Datasentinel team also maintains pg_datasentinel, an open source observability extension for PostgreSQL.

For more information, please contact us.

title: Wisp (LWS): A wisp of a web server
description:
👋 Hi everyone!

I'm excited to share Wisp — originally codenamed LWS (Lightweight Web Server) — a tiny, purpose-built static file server written entirely in Go, using only the standard library. No third-party dependencies, no bloat, just a focused, secure, and blazing-fast service that gets straight to work. ✨

🔗 Repository: github.com/appex-uk/lws

📦 What Makes It Special

Wisp started from a simple frustration: most web servers are either huge and complex or too limited for modern deployments. I wanted something that does exactly what you need — nothing more, nothing less — and fits comfortably in even the tightest environments.

🤏 It’s genuinely tiny

  • Scratch container image: ~3 MB — yes, megabytes
  • Zero runtime dependencies — statically compiled Go binary
  • Starts instantly — before your health check timeout can even fire
  • Minimal memory footprint — your resources stay yours

🛠️ Capable where it counts

Don't let the size fool you — Wisp is packed with thoughtful features:

Feature Details
📁 Secure static serving Uses os.Root to confine all requests — paths and symlinks can never escape your content directory
🚫 Hidden file protection Dotfiles and directories are never served; .well-known/ works as expected
📦 Precompressed content Serve .br (Brotli) or .gz files directly — compress once at build time
🔀 SPA & custom routing SPA fallback mode, custom 404 pages, per-path header rules
📊 Built-in Prometheus metrics Separate metrics port — no exporters, no SDKs, just stdlib
🩺 Kubernetes-ready probes /livez and /readyz endpoints with graceful shutdown drain
🔒 Custom headers & security Set cache policies, security headers, or anything else — globally or per path
⏱️ Graceful shutdown Drains connections before terminating — no dropped requests

🚀 Quick Start

Run it locally 

# Clone and run
git clone [https://github.com/appex-uk/lws.git](https://github.com/appex-uk/lws.git)
cd lws
make run

This serves the included ./www directory on port 8080.

Docker — the scratch image magic ✨ 

# Build the image yourself
make docker

# Run with your own content and config
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 \
  -v "$PWD/site:/srv/www:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/config.json:/etc/lws/config.json:ro" \
  lws:latest

That's it. No pulling hundreds of MB of layers — just a tiny, secure container that starts in milliseconds.

⚙️ Configure It Your Way

Everything lives in a simple JSON config file. Every field is optional — sensible defaults apply:

{
  "address": ":8080",
  "root": "/srv/www",
  "fallback": "/index.html",
  "not_found_page": "/404.html",
  "precompressed": true,
  "headers": {
    "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff",
    "X-Frame-Options": "DENY"
  },
  "header_rules": [
    {"match": "*.html", "headers": {"Cache-Control": "no-cache"}},
    {"match": "/assets/*", "headers": {"Cache-Control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"}}
  ],
  "access_log": true
}

Key highlights:

  • SPA mode → missing routes without an extension get your index.html with status 200; missing files with an extension still 404 — so broken assets don't silently fail
  • Per-path headers → fine-grained cache control or security policies
  • Precompressed → ship .br/.gz alongside originals and Wisp serves the best one automatically

📊 Built-in Observability — Zero Dependencies

This is one of my favourite parts. Wisp exposes a Prometheus metrics endpoint — on a separate, non-public port — all written with pure Go stdlib. No Prometheus client library, no OTel SDK, nothing to pull in.

Available at: :9090/metrics (configurable)

What you get:

  • lws_http_requests_total — request count by method & status code
  • lws_http_request_duration_seconds — latency histogram
  • lws_http_requests_in_flight — concurrent requests gauge
  • lws_http_response_bytes_total — bytes served
  • Plus standard Go runtime & process metrics

Some useful queries you can run straight away:

# Traffic rate
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total[5m]))

# Error rate
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(lws_http_requests_total[5m]))

# 99th percentile latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(lws_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

Instrumentation overhead? ~170 ns per request. Negligible.

☸️ Kubernetes Friendly by Design

Wisp was built to run reliably in Kubernetes:

  • Liveness probe: /livez — just checks the process is responding
  • Readiness probe: /readyz — also verifies the content volume and goes 503 during shutdown drain
  • Graceful sequence on SIGTERM: → readiness 503 → finish in-flight requests → clean exit
  • Example Deployment and Service manifests are in the repo under infra/k8s/

This means rolling deployments work smoothly — connections drain before the pod disappears.

💭 Why Not Just Nginx?

Great question — and to be clear: Nginx is amazing. It's battle-tested, incredibly capable, and I use it every day. But sometimes it's simply more than you need:

🚛 Nginx = The workhorse — handles massive traffic, complex routing, modules, SSL termination at scale — and it's great at that.

🚲 Wisp = The nimble specialist — serve static files securely, fast, and tiny. Perfect for frontend deployments, edge workloads, sidecars, or anywhere "light and fast" matters more than "every feature ever."

If you need to serve a static site, a single-page app, or static assets reliably and securely — and you care about image size, startup time, and minimal resource consumption — Wisp is built exactly for you.

🗺️ What's Next

Right now Wisp is focused on doing one thing — serving static content — and doing it really well. That said, there's always room to polish and improve:

  • More flexible routing options
  • Additional cache control conveniences
  • Real-world feedback from folks using it

Your thoughts, bug reports, or contributions are very welcome!

🔗 Links

  • GitHub repo: github.com/appex-uk/lws ⭐ Star if you like it!
  • Issues & feedback: Open an issue — I'd love to hear what you think

💬 Over to you

What's your biggest annoyance when setting up a static file server? Is it image bloat? Complex config? Missing metrics? Let's chat in the comments — I'm here to learn and build something useful together! 👇

title: I shipped a VPN app on iOS, Mac, Android and Windows without writing a VPN protocol
description:
I build mobile apps for a living, mostly on iOS. This year I shipped a VPN called Privalune on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and Windows. I did it alone, and the only reason that was possible is one decision I made early: I would not write or bundle a VPN protocol.

Every platform I target already ships an IKEv2 client. So the apps are remote controls. They hand the operating system a server and a login, and the OS runs the tunnel.

This post covers how that works on each platform, what the backend looks like, and where the approach hurts.

The numbers
iOS, iPadOS and Mac: about 7,400 lines of Swift (SwiftUI)
Android: about 4,200 lines of Kotlin (Jetpack Compose)
Windows: about 3,350 lines of TypeScript, CSS and Rust (Tauri 2 + Preact)
Backend: seven Supabase Edge Functions and five SQL migrations
Website: static HTML, 92 pages in six languages

None of those codebases contains cryptography or packet handling.

iOS and Mac: NEVPNManager

On Apple platforms the system VPN is NEVPNManager, the "Personal VPN" API. You fill in an IKEv2 profile, save it, and ask the system to start it. iOS shows its own permission prompt the first time.

The part I like most is on-demand rules. This is the whole "protect me on public Wi-Fi automatically" feature:

enum AutoProtect {
    static func rules(trustedNetworks: [String]) -> [NEOnDemandRule] {
        var rules: [NEOnDemandRule] = []

        if !trustedNetworks.isEmpty {
            let stayOff = NEOnDemandRuleDisconnect()
            stayOff.interfaceTypeMatch = .wiFi
            stayOff.ssidMatch = trustedNetworks
            rules.append(stayOff)
        }

        let connectOnWiFi = NEOnDemandRuleConnect()
        connectOnWiFi.interfaceTypeMatch = .wiFi
        rules.append(connectOnWiFi)

        return rules
    }
}

The system evaluates those rules even when the app is not running. I wrote no background code for it.

Two things I learned the hard way:

The Simulator cannot run a VPN. I added a simulated tunnel with realistic timing so I could build the whole UI, including the connect animation and the Live Activity, without a device in my hand.
Mac came almost free. The iPhone and iPad app runs on Apple silicon Macs through the App Store, so Mac users get the same binary. Intel Macs are not covered.
Android: the platform VPN profile

Most Android VPN apps implement VpnService and ship their own protocol stack. Since Android 11 there is another option: Ikev2VpnProfile with VpnManager. You build a profile, the system asks the user for consent once, and Android runs the tunnel.

The flow is: prepare() saves the profile and may return an Intent for the consent screen, then start() brings the tunnel up. To know the real state, I listen for networks with TRANSPORT_VPN instead of trusting my own flags.

The cost is a minimum of Android 11. For a new app in 2026 I accepted that.

Windows: Tauri, PowerShell and the RAS API

The Windows app is Tauri 2 with a Preact front end. The Rust side is about 340 lines and does three things:

Creates a per-user VPN profile with PowerShell's Add-VpnConnection. Per-user means no administrator prompt.
Dials and hangs up through the Win32 RAS API, using the windows crate. The password goes straight into the API call, so it never appears on a command line where other processes could read it.
Translates Windows error codes into sentences a person can act on:

let message = match code {
    691 => "The VPN login was refused. Please try again.",
    13801 => "Windows couldn't verify the server's certificate. Please try another location.",
    809 | 13806 | 13820 => "This network seems to block VPN connections. Try another Wi-Fi or mobile hotspot.",
    868 => "The server's address couldn't be found. Check your internet connection.",
    _ => "Couldn't connect. Please try again or pick another location.",
};

I do not own a Windows PC. A friend ran the first builds for me, and I tested it myself later. That made the error table far more important than I expected: "Error 809" in a screenshot told me exactly what happened on his network.

The backend: small functions, one source of truth

The backend is Supabase Edge Functions, written in TypeScript for Deno:

servers returns the location list. It is cached for 30 minutes, and if the upstream call fails it serves the last good list instead of an error.
vpn-credentials checks that the caller has Premium and returns a VPN login.
devices links up to 10 devices to one subscription.
A webhook keeps subscription state in sync with RevenueCat, which is my single source of truth for "is this person Premium" across Apple, Google and web purchases.

On infrastructure, to be clear about what I did and did not build: the free server is a VPS I configured as a VPN server myself. It meters the daily free time on the server side, and the app only mirrors the countdown. The paid locations come from an infrastructure provider's network through their API. I did not rack servers in 55 countries.

No accounts in the apps

I did not want a sign-up screen between a person and the connect button. So the apps have no login.

Someone who buys on the website receives a Premium key by email. Typing that key into any of the apps links the device, up to 10 per subscription. Each linked device gets a random token, and the database stores only its hash.

The trade-off is support. With no account, "I lost my key" has to be solved by email, so the website has a small dashboard where buyers sign in with a one-time code and see their key again.

The website is plain HTML

No framework. A shell script copies files into dist/ for Cloudflare Pages. Small Python scripts generate the repetitive pages, and translations live in one JSON file per language, keyed by text segment, so changing an English sentence tells me exactly which translations are stale.

One environment variable, LAUNCHED, switched the site from a holding page to the full site on launch day.

What this approach costs
One protocol. IKEv2 only. Some networks block it, and I cannot fall back to something that looks like normal web traffic.
Less control. I get the features each OS exposes and nothing more.
Windows trust. My installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows warns people before running it. That is the next thing I am fixing.
Android 11 and later only.

What I got in return: four small apps that one person can maintain, no native crypto to audit, and tunnels run by code that Apple, Google and Microsoft maintain.

Try it

Privalune is free to start with no account: privalune.com. If you only want to see what websites can read about your connection, the What's my IP page works without installing anything.

I would like to hear from anyone who has shipped on the platform IKEv2 clients, especially about handling networks that block it.

title: Coding Agents Generate Outdated Frontend Code Due to Stale Training Data, Which Real-Time Web Platform Guidelines Fix
description:
Introduction: The Legacy Trap in AI-Generated Code

When you prompt an AI coding assistant to build a UI overlay or an animated modal, the generated code often looks astonishingly retrograde. Despite possessing theoretical knowledge that modern platform primitives exist, models like Claude Code and Codex routinely default to brittle, legacy patterns. They write manual position: fixed click-outside event listeners instead of leveraging the native popover API, and they wire up complex class toggles paired with transitionend and setTimeout statements instead of utilizing @starting-style and transition-behavior.

This failure mode is mechanical rather than accidental. Large language models operate on probabilistic token prediction governed by massive historical datasets. Because the public internet contains billions of lines of legacy code and only a thin veneer of newly standardized code, the statistical weight of historical patterns dominates the neural network's activation paths. When an agent receives a UI prompt, its weights naturally gravitate toward the path of least resistance: code written in 2018. This creates an insidious risk formation: developers inherit technical debt before a single line of application code is written, locking next-generation web applications into legacy behaviors that trigger unnecessary layout thrashing, memory leaks from uncleaned event listeners, and severe accessibility regressions like broken focus management.

Until recently, the industry relied on waiting for model providers to retrain base models—an approach that fails because web standards evolve weekly while training cycles take quarters or years. Relying on static model updates for dynamic platform specifications is structurally broken; it guarantees a permanent lag between browser capabilities and agent output.

The definitive turning point arrived with the release of Modern Web Guidance, a collaborative, open-source coding agent skill spearheaded by engineering teams from Chrome, Microsoft (Edge), Mozilla (Firefox), and MDN (including contributions from Kadir Topal, Patrick Brosset, Jake Archibald, Lea Verou, and technical lead Paul Irish). Rather than waiting for model weights to shift, this initiative attacks the problem at the runtime context level. When an agent receives a frontend task, a local CLI scans and injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant markdown guides directly into the agent's working context. Evaluated across approximately 2,000 rigorous verification checks, agents running without guidance flounder at a fifty percent pass rate, whereas context-injected agents spike to a ninety percent success rate. By binding real-time browser standards directly into the agent prompt loop, the web development ecosystem has finally established a mechanism to prevent legacy habits from permanently fossilizing the modern web.

The Anatomy of the Problem: Why AI Struggles with Modern Web Standards

When an AI coding assistant generates a frontend interface, it is executing a high-dimensional probabilistic search over a static training corpus. The core mechanical failure of modern web development stems from a fundamental temporal asymmetry: browser standards and platform APIs evolve weekly, whereas base model training cycles require quarters or years. Because historical repositories on GitHub are heavily saturated with pre-2018 patterns written before modern primitives existed, statistical token prediction treats legacy code as the path of least resistance. The model's neural weights are mathematically biased toward what was common yesterday, not what is standard today.

This training lag manifests as concrete architectural degradation in the generated execution paths. Consider three distinct failure modes where coding agents bypass native platform primitives in favor of brittle legacy workarounds:

  • Overlay management: Without real-time awareness of the HTML

popover

API, agents routinely fall back to manual JavaScript event listeners, calculating viewport coordinates and attaching document-level click-outside handlers on

position: fixed

elements. This introduces memory leaks from uncleaned event listeners and layout thrashing as DOM mutations force synchronous style recalculations.

  • Entry animations: To animate an element entering the DOM from

display: none

, agents script complex state machines involving class toggles,

setTimeout

delays, and event listeners listening for

transitionend

. This brittle timing logic frequently desynchronizes under main-thread congestion, causing jarring visual pop-ins instead of leveraging native

@starting-style

and

transition-behavior

.

  • Accessibility and focus pipelines: When spawning a modal or new view, unassisted agents frequently fail to redirect the browser's active focus tree into the container and capture tab navigation within it. Screen reader users are left stranded in the background DOM, breaking WCAG compliance at the state-machine level.

Relying on traditional model updates or fine-tuning to close this gap is fundamentally flawed. Fine-tuning is a lagging indicator; by the time a model weights its parameters against newly stabilized Baseline features, those features have already iterated. Therefore, software engineering workflows must reject static model updates in favor of dynamic runtime context injection—such as local CLI-driven skills that scan and inject human-vetted, Baseline-compliant documentation directly into the agent's working prompt loop during execution.

Cross-Browser Alliance: Inside the Collaboration

For decades, browser vendors—Chrome, Microsoft, and Mozilla—operated as isolated fortresses, shipping standards independently while developers bore the friction of fragmentation. But the rise of LLM coding agents broke this institutional inertia. When AI models like Claude Code and Codex write frontend code, they do not read live specifications; they execute probabilistic pattern-matching over massive historical corpora weighted heavily toward pre-2018 codebases. This temporal asymmetry created a systemic crisis: even as browsers natively implemented advanced primitives like the popover API and @starting-style, AI models continued generating legacy mechanical fallbacks.

To short-circuit this decay, an unprecedented coalition of engineering leads from Chrome (Kadir Topal, Paul Irish), Microsoft (Patrick Brosset), Mozilla (Jake Archibald), and independent standards authority Lea Verou united to engineer a direct countermeasure: Modern Web Guidance. Rather than waiting quarters or years for base model retraining cycles to absorb modern specs—a lagging indicator that guarantees perpetual obsolescence—the alliance built a unified, open-source skill that injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant architectural constraints directly into the agent execution loop.

The Mechanics of Runtime Context Injection vs. Static Fine-Tuning

When evaluating how to align coding agents with modern web standards, engineering teams face a stark architectural choice: static model fine-tuning versus runtime context injection. Fine-tuning attempts to reweight neural network parameters using curated datasets. However, because web platform standards iterate weekly while model weights remain static post-training, fine-tuned models inevitably drift into obsolescence the moment a new Baseline feature ships. Furthermore, probabilistic generation biases the LLM toward whichever code pattern appears with highest frequency in its training tokens—which, statistically, remains legacy DOM manipulation.

The alliance selected runtime context injection via a local CLI as the optimal solution for a distinct mechanical reason: deterministic constraint enforcement. When a developer triggers a frontend task, the CLI intercepts the prompt loop, searches over 200+ human-written Markdown guides, and injects precise, browser-tested implementation parameters directly into the agent's working memory. This forces the neural network to evaluate explicit, up-to-date syntax constraints rather than relying on statistical memory of obsolete forum threads.

  • Option A (Static Fine-Tuning): Fails because model weights freeze at training cutoff, causing a permanent lag behind weekly browser capability updates.
  • Option B (Unvetted Retrieval-Augmented Generation): Fails because general web scraping pulls conflicting, low-quality legacy code snippets from uncurated sources, amplifying technical debt.
  • Option C (Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection - Chosen Solution): Succeeds by supplying verified, Baseline-compliant code blueprints with baked-in browser support data, pinned to @latest to eliminate drift.

This chosen architecture stops working under specific edge conditions: if an agent runs in an air-gapped environment without local cache persistence, or if the prompt context window truncates the injected guides due to extreme token length overages, the agent defaults back to unconstrained probabilistic sampling. To prevent this failure mode, the guidance pipeline mandates local execution with pinned package dependencies.

Measurable Mechanical Impact on Agent Output

Without this collaborative governance layer, coding agents systematically introduce high-cost runtime failures into production codebases. For instance, when tasked with building a modal or dropdown menu, unguided agents instantiate manual document-level click-outside listeners on position: fixed overlays. This forces synchronous style recalculations on every pointer move, triggering layout thrashing and creating permanent memory leaks if component teardown fails to unbind the listeners.

Similarly, fade-in entry animations written without native primitives rely on brittle chains of class toggles, setTimeout execution blocks, and transitionend event listeners. When the main thread experiences execution congestion, these timers desynchronize, causing jarring visual pop-ins and rendering UI states unpredictable.

By embedding human-authored guides backed by rigorous browser support data, the alliance's evaluation harness—tested against roughly 2,000 distinct verification checks across Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity—demonstrated a dramatic performance shift. Unguided agents passed only fifty percent of checks, while agents augmented with the Modern Web Guidance skill cleared ninety percent. By replacing legacy state machines with native platform primitives like popover and @starting-style, the collaboration successfully transformed AI assistants from engines of legacy technical debt into active vectors of modern web excellence.

Architecture of the Skill: How AI Learns Modern Standards

AI coding assistants like Claude Code and Codex operate on a foundational mismatch: temporal asymmetry. Model training cycles require quarters or years, while web platform standards iterate weekly. Because neural networks execute probabilistic token prediction over historical training corpora heavily dominated by pre-2018 codebases, their statistical path of least resistance is to generate legacy mechanical fallbacks instead of native platform primitives.

Mechanical Failure Modes of Unguided AI Code

When unguided agents attempt frontend tasks, their reliance on stale training weights triggers specific, measurable runtime defects:

  • The Popover Gap: Lacking awareness of the HTML popover API, agents generate manual document-level click-outside listeners on position: fixed overlays. This leaves uncleaned event listeners in the heap, causing permanent memory leaks and layout thrashing from synchronous style recalculations during DOM mutations.
  • Transition Desynchronization: Instead of utilizing native @starting-style and transition-behavior, agents construct brittle state machines using class toggles, setTimeout delays, and transitionend event listeners. Under main-thread congestion, these timing chains desynchronize, resulting in observable visual pop-ins and layout jank.
  • Focus Tree Abandonment: Spawning modals without explicit focus management leaves screen reader users stranded in the background DOM, violating accessibility compliance at the state-machine level.

Architectural Evaluation: Why Local CLI Injection Succeeds

To solve these failure modes, engineering teams evaluated three distinct architectural approaches:

  • Static Fine-Tuning (Rejected): Fails because model weights freeze at the training cutoff. This guarantees a permanent lag behind weekly browser capability updates and requires expensive, recurring retraining cycles.
  • Unvetted Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Rejected): Fails because generalized web scraping retrieves conflicting, low-quality legacy snippets from uncurated forums, actively amplifying technical debt within the agent's context window.
  • Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection (Chosen): Succeeds by intercepting the prompt loop locally. A lightweight CLI scans and injects human-vetted, Baseline-compliant Markdown guides directly into the agent's working memory during frontend tasks.

Decision Rule: When feature evolution velocity outpaces model retraining cycles (X), do not rely on parameter updates; deploy runtime context injection via pinned, verifiable blueprints (Y) to enforce deterministic constraints.

Structural Mechanics and Verification

The Modern Web Guidance architecture—stewarded by engineers from Chrome, Microsoft, Mozilla, and MDN—operates through a deterministic runtime pipeline:

  • Local Execution: A small CLI running on the developer's machine searches over 200 human-vetted guides written by browser engineers when a frontend task is initialized.
  • Baseline Enforcement: Every blueprint enforces Baseline Widely Available standards. Newer features include baked-in browser support data, forcing agents to supply fallbacks or progressive enhancements.
  • Dynamic Pinning: CLI commands are pinned to @latest, ensuring weekly updates bypass the model's static training cutoff entirely.

Edge Cases and Failure Conditions

The chosen architecture encounters critical edge conditions when operating constraints break down. In air-gapped environments lacking local cache persistence, or when extreme token length overages truncate the context window, the CLI fails to inject the guides. Under these conditions, the agent defaults to unconstrained probabilistic sampling, reverting immediately to legacy code patterns. Mitigation requires strict local cache persistence and dependency locking.

When evaluated across approximately 2,000 rigorous checks in Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity, unguided agents cleared only 50 percent of the criteria. With the skill's direct context injection bridging the gap between legacy training weights and modern platform primitives, pass rates surged to 90 percent.

Impact and the Future of AI-Assisted Web Development

When engineering teams from Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and MDN united to release Modern Web Guidance, they targeted a foundational structural flaw in AI coding assistants: temporal asymmetry. Because neural network weights freeze at the conclusion of training cutoffs, models like Claude Code and Codex operate on historical corpora heavily weighted toward pre-2018 patterns. Without direct intervention, probabilistic token prediction treats legacy workarounds—such as manual position: fixed click-outside listeners and setTimeout transition chains—as the statistical path of least resistance. This forces the browser rendering engine into mechanical failure modes, including layout thrashing and accessibility regressions.

Quantitative Performance and Verification Benchmarks

To measure the efficacy of runtime context injection, engineering evaluations tested coding agents across approximately 2,000 rigorous automated checks in Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity. The performance delta is stark:

  • Unguided Agents: Cleared only 50% of verification checks, persistently injecting legacy patterns that fail to leverage native platform primitives like the popover API and @starting-style.
  • Context-Injected Agents: Achieved a 90% pass rate when equipped with the local CLI skill, injecting human-vetted, Baseline-compliant blueprints directly into the agent working prompt loop.

Architectural Solution Comparison

When selecting a mechanism to bridge the gap between rapidly evolving web standards and static LLM parameter weights, engineering analysis reveals distinct failure thresholds across competing strategies:
Approach Mechanism Failure Mode & Effectiveness
Static Fine-Tuning Periodic retraining of model parameter weights. Retraining Lag: Web standards iterate weekly while training cycles take quarters or years, guaranteeing perpetual obsolescence. (Rejected)
Unvetted RAG Generalized web scraping across uncurated developer forums and blogs. Noise Injection: Retrieves conflicting, legacy code snippets that pollute the context window and amplify technical debt. (Rejected)
Vendor-Governed Local CLI Injection Local CLI intercepting the prompt loop to inject human-vetted, Baseline-compliant Markdown guides pinned to @latest. Optimal: Deterministic constraint enforcement; breaks down only in air-gapped environments without local cache persistence or extreme token truncation. (Chosen)

Decision Rule for Web Platform Guidance

To eliminate architectural selection errors, engineering workflows must adhere to a strict decision rule:

If feature evolution velocity outpaces model retraining cycles, then avoid parameter updates and deploy runtime context injection via pinned, verifiable blueprints to enforce deterministic constraints and prevent browser rendering degradation.

Failure Edge Conditions and Mitigation Mechanics

Even with runtime context injection, specific edge conditions can trigger degradation in agent output. In air-gapped environments lacking local cache persistence, or when extreme token length overages truncate the agent's working context window, the system drops the injected guides. This forces the neural network to fall back to unconstrained probabilistic sampling over its base weights.
