title: 🧱 A Java Architecture Stack, Layer by Layer: From APIs to Availability and Recovery
description:
A Java Architecture Stack, Layer by Layer: From APIs to Availability and Recovery

A production system is rarely one application. It is a stack of concerns that must work together: an API that accepts requests, a database that stores state, identity that decides who may do what, infrastructure that runs the code, pipelines that ship it, and mechanisms that keep it standing when traffic spikes or something breaks. Each concern has a layer, and a weakness in any layer shows up as an outage somewhere else.

This article walks through twelve layers of a typical Java architecture, from APIs and backend logic down to availability and recovery. For each layer we look at the purpose, the Java and Spring Boot tooling that usually fills it, and the decisions that matter most. The goal is a shared checklist you can use in design reviews.

1. APIs and Backend Logic

This is where requests enter the system and business rules run. In Java, the common choice is Spring Boot with Spring Web MVC for blocking workloads or WebFlux for reactive ones. Keep controllers thin, put business rules in services, and return stable DTOs rather than persistence entities.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final PlaceOrderUseCase placeOrder;

    public OrderController(PlaceOrderUseCase placeOrder) {
        this.placeOrder = placeOrder;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = placeOrder.execute(request.toCommand());
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(OrderResponse.from(order));
    }
}

Decisions here include versioning, idempotency for writes, and explicit validation at the boundary.

2. Database and Storage

Choose storage by access pattern, not habit. Relational databases such as PostgreSQL suit transactional data with integrity rules. Spring Data JPA or jOOQ provide the Java access layer. Use migrations with Flyway or Liquibase so schema changes are versioned and repeatable.

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderEntity, UUID> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("select o from OrderEntity o where o.id = :id")
    Optional<OrderEntity> findForUpdate(@Param("id") UUID id);
}

Plan for connection pooling with HikariCP, indexes that match real queries, and backups you have actually restored at least once.

3. Auth and Permissions

Authentication answers who the caller is. Authorization answers what they may do. In Spring, Spring Security with OAuth2 and JWT is the usual combination. Validate tokens at the edge and enforce fine-grained permissions close to the business operation, not only at the URL level.

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('ORDER_CANCEL') and #order.ownerId == authentication.name")
public void cancel(Order order) {
    order.cancel();
}

Keep roles and scopes minimal, and rotate signing keys through a JWKS endpoint.

4. Hosting and Deployment

Decide how the artifact reaches production. A typical path packages the service as a container image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, then deploys it to a runtime such as Kubernetes, a managed container service, or a virtual machine managed with systemd. Configuration belongs in the environment, not in the image. Use readiness and liveness probes so the platform knows when an instance can take traffic.

5. Cloud and Compute

Compute decisions shape cost and resilience. Right-size JVM heaps against container memory limits. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed heap so the JVM adapts to its environment. Choose between instance types, serverless functions, and managed containers according to workload shape, and prefer horizontal scaling for stateless services.

6. CI/CD and Version Control

Every change should flow through the same automated path: commit, build, test, scan, package, deploy, verify. Git provides history and review. Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or GitLab CI runs the pipeline. Gate merges on unit and integration tests, and gate releases on contract tests and a smoke test against the deployed environment.

Keep pipelines reproducible by pinning JDK and dependency versions, and treat the pipeline definition itself as code under review.

7. Security and Row-Level Security

Defense in depth means no single control is trusted alone. Validate inputs, encode outputs, keep secrets out of source control, and enforce data access at the database when the platform supports it. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) lets the database filter rows by tenant or owner, so a missed where clause in application code does not expose another customer's data.

ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

In Spring, set the session variable per request so the policy applies to every query.

8. Rate Limiting

Rate limits protect shared resources from abuse and accidental overload. Apply them at the edge with nginx, an API gateway, or a managed firewall, and add per-user or per-key limits inside the application when business rules require them. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off.

Libraries such as Bucket4j implement token-bucket limits in Java when you need them inside the service.

9. Caching and CDN

Caching removes repeated work. A CDN serves static assets and cacheable responses close to users. Inside the service, Spring Cache with Caffeine or Redis reduces database load for hot reads. Every cache needs an explicit invalidation strategy and a time to live. A cache without invalidation is a bug waiting for a customer to find it.

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
public Product findProduct(String id) {
    return productRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
}

10. Load Balancing and Scaling

Distribute traffic across instances with a load balancer or an nginx upstream block. Choose a strategy such as least connections when request durations vary. Scale stateless services horizontally, and keep session state in a shared store or in signed tokens. Scale stateful components, such as databases, with replicas, partitioning, or managed services, not by adding application instances.

11. Error Tracking and Logs

When something fails, you need to know quickly and understand why. Log structured JSON with a correlation ID on every request, and send exceptions to an error tracker such as Sentry or a centralized logging stack. Avoid logging secrets or personal data. Alert on symptoms customers feel, such as error rate and latency at the percentile level, rather than on every exception.

12. Availability and Recovery

Availability is a design target, not a feature. Define service level objectives for each customer-facing path, then design failure behavior to meet them. Use timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers through Resilience4j so one slow dependency does not exhaust threads. Run regular backups and restore drills, and document a recovery runbook with a measured recovery time objective.

@CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "queuePayment")
public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
    return paymentClient.charge(request);
}

Using the Stack as a Checklist

You do not need every layer on day one. A small internal service might need only layers one through four, plus logs. A customer-facing platform needs all twelve, with the most attention on security, rate limits, and recovery. Walk through the stack in every architecture review and ask, for each layer: what is the decision, who owns it, and how would we know if it failed?

Common Mistakes

  • Skipping the layers you find boring. Backups, logs, and rollbacks decide how bad an incident becomes.
  • Enforcing security in one place only. Edge checks, application checks, and database policies each catch different mistakes.
  • Caching without invalidation. Stale data is harder to debug than slow data.
  • Retrying without limits. Unbounded retries turn a partial outage into a full one.
  • Treating the pipeline as an afterthought. A deployment you cannot repeat is a deployment you cannot trust.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Keep controllers thin and DTOs stable.
  • Version the schema and test restores of backups.
  • Separate authentication from authorization, and enforce both.
  • Build once, configure per environment, and probe health.
  • Size the JVM for its container and scale stateless services out.
  • Gate every change through the same automated pipeline.
  • Use defense in depth, including database-level isolation where possible.
  • Limit request rates and cache only with explicit invalidation.
  • Log structured events with correlation IDs and alert on customer symptoms.
  • Define service level objectives and practice recovery.

Conclusion

Architecture is the sum of its layers. Each one answers a question the business will eventually ask: can it handle requests, keep data safe, let the right people in, run reliably, grow under load, ship changes safely, and recover when things break. Java and Spring Boot provide mature tools for every layer. The discipline is in deciding what each layer must guarantee, and in checking that the guarantees hold before the next incident checks for you.

Key takeaways

  • Treat the stack as twelve concerns that must all be designed, not as twelve tools to install.
  • Enforce security and limits at more than one layer.
  • Cache, retry, and scale only with explicit limits and invalidation.
  • Practice recovery as often as you practice deployment.

title: 🤝 How Cross-Functional Experience Makes Engineers Better at Building Software
description:
How Cross-Functional Experience Makes Engineers Better at Building Software

Some of the most useful engineering lessons do not come from a code review or a design document. They come from sitting with a support agent who hears the same complaint every day, from a product manager who has to explain a delay to a customer, or from a finance analyst who needs an invoice to match a database row. Working across functions gives engineers context that no tutorial provides, and that context changes the software they build.

This article explains what cross-functional experience looks like in practice, why it improves technical decisions, and how to build it deliberately, especially for backend and Java engineers.

What Cross-Functional Experience Means

Cross-functional experience is time spent working with people whose roles differ from your own: product, design, support, sales, operations, finance, legal, or security. It does not require changing careers. It requires regular, real collaboration on a shared outcome.

A few examples make the idea concrete:

  • An engineer joins a weekly support review and hears how customers describe a failure in their own words.
  • A backend developer sits in on a pricing discussion and learns why a rounding rule matters to accounting.
  • A tech lead works with a compliance team and discovers that an audit trail requirement shapes the data model.

Each interaction exposes a constraint, a vocabulary, or a priority that the engineering team could not have inferred alone.

Why It Improves Technical Decisions

Software is an answer to a question someone else asked. The better you understand the question, the better your answer. Cross-functional experience helps in three specific ways.

First, it sharpens requirements. A product request like "make the export faster" becomes clearer when you learn that finance runs the export at month end and needs a specific file format for the auditors. The faster solution might be a streaming endpoint, or it might be a scheduled job that prepares the file before anyone asks for it.

Second, it improves prioritization. Engineers often optimize what is easiest to measure. Support colleagues know which failures generate the most calls, which ones quietly lose customers, and which ones nobody notices. That knowledge redirects effort toward problems with real impact.

Third, it reduces rework. When a designer explains why a form field must accept spaces in a national identifier, or a legal reviewer explains retention rules before the schema is final, the team avoids a migration that would otherwise happen six months later.

A Java Example: Designing Around a Business Rule You Learned Elsewhere

Imagine you learned from the finance team that partial refunds must be reversible for ninety days, because the accounting close depends on it. A naive implementation might overwrite the payment amount. A design informed by that conversation keeps an append-only ledger:

public record RefundEntry(
        String refundId,
        String paymentId,
        BigDecimal amount,
        Instant createdAt,
        RefundStatus status,
        String reason) {

    public RefundEntry {
        Objects.requireNonNull(refundId, "refundId is required");
        Objects.requireNonNull(paymentId, "paymentId is required");
        if (amount.signum() <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Refund amount must be positive");
        }
    }
}

The class is simple, but the decision behind it came from a conversation with finance, not from a coding pattern. The entry is immutable, so reversals are new rows rather than edits. Anyone reviewing the code can trace the business reason to the design choice.

Translating Vocabulary Between Teams

Each function has its own language. Support speaks in symptoms, product speaks in outcomes, finance speaks in periods and balances, and engineering speaks in services and latency. Cross-functional experience teaches you to translate.

A useful habit is to restate every request in three sentences: what the person wants to achieve, what would make it fail, and how they would know it worked. This practice turns vague asks into testable acceptance criteria. It also builds trust, because the other team sees that their concern was understood before any code was written.

Building the Habit Deliberately

Experience does not accumulate by accident. Engineers who grow this skill usually do a few things consistently.

They attend a customer or support review once a month, even briefly. They read the tickets that reach their service, not only the summaries. They ask product managers what a feature is supposed to change for the user, not only what it should do. They invite a finance or operations partner to design reviews when money, data retention, or regulated processes are involved.

For managers, the lever is rotation and shared goals. Pairing an engineer with a sales engineer for a customer onboarding project, or assigning a developer to a cross-team incident review, creates exposure that a backlog cannot.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating other teams as blockers. Their constraints are usually requirements you have not heard yet.
  • Listening only for solutions. Ask about the problem first. The requested solution is often one of several options.
  • Confusing visibility with understanding. Attending a meeting is not the same as learning why a decision was made.
  • Skipping the follow-up. Tell the other team what you built and how it addresses their concern. Trust grows from closed loops.
  • Assuming your context transfers. A rule that is obvious to finance may be invisible to a developer who has never closed a month.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Attend at least one customer-facing or support review each month.
  • Restate each request as an outcome, a failure condition, and a success signal.
  • Invite non-engineering partners to design reviews for regulated or money-related features.
  • Document business rules next to the code that enforces them.
  • Share what you shipped with the teams that asked for it.
  • Rotate engineers through cross-functional projects when possible.

Conclusion

Cross-functional experience turns an engineer from someone who builds what is specified into someone who understands why it matters. The benefits show up in clearer requirements, better priorities, fewer rewrites, and software that fits the way people actually work. The investment is modest: a few conversations, a few reviews, and a willingness to learn vocabulary that is not your own.

Start with one conversation this week. Ask a colleague in another function what problem they are trying to solve, and listen for the constraint they have never had time to explain.

Key takeaways

  • Cross-functional experience supplies context that tutorials and code reviews cannot.
  • It sharpens requirements, improves prioritization, and reduces rework.
  • Business rules belong close to the code that enforces them.
  • Build the habit with regular, real collaboration rather than occasional meetings.

title: 🤝 Why "Customer-Facing" Matters: Building Software That Meets People Where They Are
description:
Why "Customer-Facing" Matters: Building Software That Meets People Where They Are

Engineers love internal details: the database schema, the retry policy, the service mesh. Customers never see any of it. They see one thing: whether the screen loads, whether the payment goes through, whether the error message tells them what to do next. The phrase customer-facing describes exactly that boundary, and understanding it changes how we design, test, and talk about our work.

This article explains what customer-facing means, why it deserves deliberate attention in Java and backend teams, and how to make customer-facing decisions concrete in code, APIs, and team practices.

What "Customer-Facing" Really Means

A customer-facing system or behavior is anything a customer can directly perceive or act on. That includes obvious surfaces like a mobile app or a web checkout, but it also includes:

  • The API contract that a partner integrates against
  • The error messages a user reads when something fails
  • The latency of a response that a person is waiting for
  • The notifications, invoices, and emails that arrive in their inbox
  • The support process a customer follows when they need help

The opposite term, internal, describes systems that customers never touch: batch jobs, data pipelines, internal dashboards. Both matter, but they deserve different trade-offs. A nightly reconciliation job can tolerate a retry that takes an hour. A checkout cannot.

Why the Distinction Changes Decisions

When a team forgets which parts of a system are customer-facing, priorities drift. Engineers optimize what they can measure internally, such as CPU usage or service count, while the customer experiences something else entirely: a spinner that never stops, or a confusing failure message after a successful charge.

Explicitly labeling customer-facing work helps in three ways.

First, it sets service level objectives where they matter. A customer-facing endpoint might target a p99 latency under 300 milliseconds and 99.9 percent availability, while an internal report might accept a much slower, less available path.

Second, it sets the bar for failure behavior. A customer-facing failure should degrade gracefully: show cached data, queue a request for later, or explain what happened in plain language. An internal failure can simply fail loudly and page someone.

Third, it shapes who is in the room during design. Customer-facing decisions benefit from product, support, and design input early, not after the API is already published.

Designing Customer-Facing APIs in Java

For Java backends, customer-facing usually means a REST or GraphQL API that other teams and partners depend on. Treat the contract as a product. Breaking changes hurt people you may never meet.

A few practices make that concrete. Version your endpoints and never remove a field without a deprecation period:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> getOrder(@PathVariable String id) {
        return orderService.findById(id)
                .map(order -> ResponseEntity.ok(OrderResponse.from(order)))
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}

Notice that the controller returns a dedicated OrderResponse rather than the internal entity. That separation lets you change the persistence model without breaking the customer contract.

Error handling is just as visible. A global handler can translate internal exceptions into stable, customer-readable responses:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PaymentDeclinedException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handlePaymentDeclined(PaymentDeclinedException ex) {
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
            "PAYMENT_DECLINED",
            "Your payment could not be processed. Please check your card details or try another method.",
            ex.getCorrelationId()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED).body(error);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleUnexpected(Exception ex) {
        // Log the full stack trace internally; never leak it to the customer.
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
            "SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE",
            "Something went wrong on our side. Please try again in a few minutes.",
            UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).body(error);
    }

    public record ApiError(String code, String message, String correlationId) {}
}

The correlation ID does double duty. The customer can quote it to support, and your team can find the matching log entries in seconds. That single field often turns a frustrating support ticket into a fast fix.

Latency Is a Customer Feature

Customers do not experience averages. They experience the slowest moment of their session. For customer-facing paths, track percentiles, not means, and set explicit budgets.

Timeouts belong in the design, not as an afterthought. If a downstream fraud check usually takes 80 milliseconds, decide in advance what happens when it takes two seconds. Fail open with a review queue, fail closed with a clear message, or serve a cached decision. Each option is a product decision wearing an engineering costume.

CompletableFuture<FraudDecision> fraudCheck = fraudClient.evaluateAsync(order)
        .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> FraudDecision.REVIEW_LATER);

Here the customer is not blocked by a slow dependency. The trade-off is explicit, documented, and easy to revisit.

Communicating Failure Honestly

Customer-facing communication includes what happens when things go wrong. Silence is worse than a clear, honest message. Customers tolerate delays when they know what is happening and when to expect an update.

Good practices include status pages that match reality, emails that confirm what was done and what remains pending, and idempotency keys so retries never charge a card twice. That last point deserves emphasis. A customer who clicks "pay" twice because the page froze should never be billed twice. Idempotent endpoints protect both the customer and the business.

Testing From the Customer's Point of View

Unit tests verify code. Customer-facing tests verify journeys. Build a small set of end-to-end scenarios that mirror real user actions: sign up, place an order, receive a confirmation, request a refund. Run them against a production-like environment on every release.

Contract tests matter just as much for partners. Tools such as Spring Cloud Contract or Pact let you publish the expectations partners depend on and fail the build before a breaking change ships. The customer never sees the failed build, which is the point.

Making "Customer-Facing" a Team Habit

Start by listing your customer-facing surfaces in a single document. For each one, record the owner, the target latency, the expected availability, the failure message, and the support path. Review this list in planning meetings, the same way you review security or cost.

Invite support engineers and account managers into incident reviews. They hear the customer's words directly, and their stories often reveal problems that dashboards miss. A ticket that says "the app keeps logging me out" points to a session issue no metric flagged.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating every endpoint the same. A checkout and an admin report do not need identical reliability budgets.
  • Leaking internals. Stack traces, database errors, and service names in responses confuse customers and expose your architecture.
  • Breaking contracts silently. Renaming a field can cost a partner a weekend.
  • Measuring only averages. A healthy mean can hide a painful p99.
  • Forgetting the message. A technically correct error that tells the customer nothing useful is still a bad experience.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Label every customer-facing surface and assign an owner.
  • Set latency and availability targets per surface, measured at percentiles.
  • Return stable, human-readable error codes with a correlation ID.
  • Version APIs and deprecate before removing anything.
  • Make write operations idempotent.
  • Decide timeout behavior with product input, not just engineering defaults.
  • Keep end-to-end journey tests and partner contract tests in the pipeline.
  • Include support and account teams in incident reviews.

Conclusion

Customer-facing is not a marketing label. It is a reminder that every design decision eventually reaches a person who is trying to get something done. The clearer we are about which parts of our systems customers touch, the better we can choose our trade-offs, our error messages, and our priorities.

Start small. Pick one customer-facing journey this week, map every system it touches, and ask what the customer would see if each one failed. The answers will tell you where to invest next.

Key takeaways

  • Customer-facing means anything a customer can perceive or act on, including APIs and error messages.
  • Explicit labels change priorities for latency, failure behavior, and design input.
  • Stable contracts, honest errors, and idempotent writes protect customers and the business.
  • Measure percentiles and test complete journeys, not only components.

title: Creating 3D-printable business cards with React Three Fiber
description:
Recently, I've been looking into ways in which we can connect both the web and the physical world. As a web engineer who sometimes does IoT-related projects, such as a lamp that changes colours when you send a message to a Bluesky account, I know that using microcontrollers is a common approach for this. And, of course, this can be great fun, both to develop and use! But, what about creating new things instead of just connecting to existing ones?

In this guide, we'll explore how to create an app that can make business cards which can be customised and 3d printed. We go from scratch: starting with a design and setting up the project, creating its UI using DaisyUI, adding all the interactive elements, and then creating the body and elements of the business card with React Three Fiber. Finally, we connect everything through a Zustand store to let us download the model.

Let's get started!

Notes:

  • This guide assumes that you already know how to use React and have a notion of how Tailwind works.
  • Some code blocks include comments to make it easier to understand and follow what's going on in them.
  • The code of the UI was partially created using Claude. The design and React Three Fiber sections of the code were done by hand.

What we will create

Throughout this guide we will be making the following app, which you can also try here:

It will consist of two parts:

  • The left part will contain a form that controls all the different properties that will make up our model: positions, widths, heights, contents of text and QR code, etc.
  • The right part will contain a 3d preview of the business card model and a download button for the result. Using the button, we'll be able to download the model as a .stl file, one of the standards for 3d printing.

As for the technologies we'll be using, we'll control the shared state of our application through Zustand, use DaisyUI for the User Interface, generate QR codes with node-qrcode, and React Three Fiber to create our models. For this guide, we will be packing everything into a Next.js application, but this can be done with any other React-based framework as we won't be using any Next.js-specific features. Additionally, you can use the final repository for guidance if you need some support.

Project setup

Let's start the development of this project by setting up our dev environment. For this first step you have two options: you can download the starting repo, which is part of the full repository, or follow the manual setup steps described below. If you decide to go for the first option, make sure you are using it in its initial status, the one labelled with the initial-commit tag.

Manual Setup

Packages installation

To prepare our files for the project we will need to create the Next.js app we will be using, install our dependencies, and set up some files. We can do the first two steps by using the following commands:

# Create a Next.js app
npx create-next-app@latest rtf-cards --empty --use-npm --ts --tailwind --react-compiler --eslint --app --src-dir --yes
cd rtf-cards

# Install our dependencies. This is all one single line.
npm i @react-three/csg @react-three/drei @react-three/fiber qrcode daisyui  zustand three @tailwindcss/postcss

# Install qrcode types
npm i -D @types/qrcode

Adding DaisyUI's config

Now, let's configure our project so DaisyUI's styles are added properly. Add a postcss.config.mjs file into the root of your project and paste the following content in it:

/** @type {import('postcss-load-config').Config} */
const config = {
  plugins: {
    '@tailwindcss/postcss': {},
  },
};
export default config;

Next, make sure your app/global.css looks like this:

@import "tailwindcss";

/* Add this line */
@plugin "daisyui";

Note: If you would like to add any custom theming using DaisyUI so your app looks just how you want it, you can do so in this file! Check out DaisyUI's Theme Generator to personalise the look and feel of your app.

Now we're ready to start creating our UI! You can start the app by using npm run dev in the root folder of your project.

Creating the UI for the form

The form will be the source of truth for our application. It will control the model, its texts, dimensions, and every other part of it. On its side, the 3d scene will only have to read the form's values to generate and render the final model.

Let's start by creating our types and configuring the default values of the application. For this, we'll create a src/types/cardFormTypes.ts in our project, where we will add the following:

export interface CardDimensions {
  width: number;
  height: number;
  thickness: number;
}

export interface TextBlockState {
  enabled: boolean;
  xPosition: number;
  yPosition: number;
  thickness: number;
  fontSize: number;
  content: string;
}

export interface QrCodeState {
  enabled: boolean;
  xPosition: number;
  yPosition: number;
  thickness: number;
  moduleSize: number;
  qrContent: string;
}

/** Shape of the whole card form. */
export interface CardFormState {
  card: CardDimensions;
  textBlock: TextBlockState;
  qrCode: QrCodeState;
}

export const initialCardFormState: CardFormState = {
  card: { width: 84, height: 53, thickness: 1 },
  textBlock: {
    enabled: true,
    xPosition: -40,
    yPosition: 14,
    thickness: 1,
    fontSize: 14,
    content: "Name Lastname\n\nSoftware Engineer\n\nMaker",
  },
  qrCode: {
    enabled: true,
    xPosition: 20,
    yPosition: -5,
    thickness: 1,
    moduleSize: 1.2,
    qrContent: "https://example.com/",
  },
};

The 84 by 53 represent something close to the standard size of a card in mm. Although the standard size is closer to 85.6 x 53.98 mm, making it a bit smaller will give us a bit of leeway for the card to fit in a wallet without issues due to its thickness. In addition, the application will always start with something realistic whenever a new user tries it out.

We'll save these as initial values in a Zustand store. This store will include not only these values, but also several functions that will help us manage them to make our life easier later. In the code below, note how we're creating this store and wrapping it in persist, which will save the values to localStorage so they are constantly saved after any changes happen. Additionally, the merge function fills in all the values that a returning visitor's saved data doesn't have.

Add the following content in src/stores/formStore.ts:

import { create } from "zustand";
import { persist } from "zustand/middleware";
import type { CardFormState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";
import { initialCardFormState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";

interface FormStateStore {
  form: CardFormState;
  setForm: (form: CardFormState) => void;
}

export const FORM_STATE_STORAGE_KEY = "formState";

/**
 * Merges a persisted form over the defaults, group by group, so fields added
 * in later versions still get their default value for returning users.
 */
export function mergePersistedForm(persisted: unknown): CardFormState {
  const saved = (persisted as { form?: Partial<CardFormState> } | null)?.form;
  if (!saved || typeof saved !== "object") return initialCardFormState;
  const d = initialCardFormState;
  return {
    card: { ...d.card, ...saved.card },
    textBlock: { ...d.textBlock, ...saved.textBlock },
    qrCode: { ...d.qrCode, ...saved.qrCode },
  };
}

const useFormStateStore = create<FormStateStore>()(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      form: initialCardFormState,
      setForm: (form) => set({ form }),
    }),
    {
      name: FORM_STATE_STORAGE_KEY,
      partialize: (s) => ({ form: s.form }),
      merge: (persisted, current) => ({
        ...current,
        form: mergePersistedForm(persisted),
      }),
      skipHydration: true,
    },
  ),
);

export default useFormStateStore;

If you, like me, are using Next.js, we need to ensure that the first render is done without access to localStorage. This is to avoid any mismatches that could happen between the server and the client. For this, we're using the following component on src/components/FormStateHydrator.tsx:

"use client";

import { useEffect } from "react";
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";

/** Restores the saved form from localStorage once mounted in the browser. */
export function FormStateHydrator() {
  useEffect(() => {
    void useFormStateStore.persist.rehydrate();
  }, []);
  return null;
}

Next up is the form. For this, we'll create a series of small, reusable components that will make up our inputs. We'll be using some custom implementations to make them look exactly how we want while keeping their standard HTML behaviour. Add the following under src/components/FormInputs.tsx:

"use client";

import { useId, useState } from "react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

interface FieldShellProps {
  label: string;
  htmlFor: string;
  className?: string;
  children: ReactNode;
}

function FieldShell({ label, htmlFor, className, children }: FieldShellProps) {
  return (
    <div className={`fieldset min-w-0 ${className ?? ""}`}>
      <label htmlFor={htmlFor} className="label">
        {label}
      </label>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

export interface NumberFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: number;
  onValueChange: (value: number) => void;
  unit?: string;
  className?: string;
}

const STEP = 1;
const SHIFT_STEP = 10;

/** What the field accepts while typing: optional minus sign, digits, one point. */
const NUMERIC_DRAFT = /^-?\d*\.?\d*$/;

function parseDraft(draft: string): number {
  return /^-?\.?$/.test(draft) ? 0 : Number(draft);
}

/**
 * Controlled number input with a trailing unit.
 *
 * Keeps the text being typed in a local draft: a controlled `type="number"`
 * input would re-render "1." as "1" and drop the decimal point before the
 * user can type the fractional digits. Both "." and "," work as the decimal
 * separator; the parsed number is reported through `onValueChange`.
 *
 * Being a text input, it restores the number-input behavior by hand
 * (WAI-ARIA spinbutton pattern): `role="spinbutton"` with `aria-valuenow`,
 * and ArrowUp / ArrowDown step by 1 (10 with Shift).
 */
export function NumberField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  unit = "mm",
  className,
}: NumberFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState(String(value));

  // The value changed from outside (e.g. restored form state): show it.
  if (parseDraft(draft) !== value) {
    setDraft(String(value));
  }

  function commit(nextDraft: string) {
    setDraft(nextDraft);
    onValueChange(parseDraft(nextDraft));
  }

  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <label className="input w-full">
        <input
          id={id}
          type="text"
          role="spinbutton"
          aria-valuenow={value}
          inputMode="decimal"
          value={draft}
          onKeyDown={(e) => {
            if (e.key !== "ArrowUp" && e.key !== "ArrowDown") return;
            e.preventDefault();

            const step = e.shiftKey ? SHIFT_STEP : STEP;
            const delta = e.key === "ArrowUp" ? step : -step;
            // Round away float noise
            commit(String(Math.round((value + delta) * 1e10) / 1e10));
          }}
          onChange={(e) => {
            const next = e.target.value.replace(",", ".");
            if (!NUMERIC_DRAFT.test(next)) return;

            commit(next);
          }}
        />
        {unit && <span className="label">{unit}</span>}
      </label>
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

export interface TextFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  onValueChange: (value: string) => void;
  placeholder?: string;
  className?: string;
}

export function TextField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  placeholder,
  className,
}: TextFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <input
        id={id}
        type="text"
        className="input w-full"
        value={value}
        placeholder={placeholder}
        onChange={(e) => onValueChange(e.target.value)}
      />
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

export interface TextAreaFieldProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  onValueChange: (value: string) => void;
  className?: string;
}

export function TextAreaField({
  label,
  value,
  onValueChange,
  className,
}: TextAreaFieldProps) {
  const id = useId();
  return (
    <FieldShell label={label} htmlFor={id} className={className}>
      <textarea
        id={id}
        className="textarea h-24 w-full"
        value={value}
        onChange={(e) => onValueChange(e.target.value)}
      />
    </FieldShell>
  );
}

For the sections that can be hidden, we use a small wrapper around a fieldset. When the switch that controls these sections is off, the fieldset gets disabled and hidden, so the corresponding section disappears. Create the following component on src/components/PropertyGroup.tsx:

"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";

export interface PropertyGroupProps {
  label: string;
  legend: string;
  children?: ReactNode;
  checked: boolean;
  onToggleChange: (checked: boolean) => void;
  className?: string;
}

/**
 * A DaisyUI toggle with a label, controlling a fieldset of input fields.
 * While the toggle is off the fieldset is disabled and hidden.
 */
export function PropertyGroup({
  label,
  legend,
  children,
  checked,
  onToggleChange,
  className,
}: PropertyGroupProps) {
  return (
    <div className={`flex flex-col gap-3 ${className ?? ""}`}>
      <label className="flex cursor-pointer items-center gap-2 text-sm">
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          role="switch"
          className="toggle"
          checked={checked}
          onChange={(event) => onToggleChange(event.target.checked)}
        />
        <span>{label}</span>
      </label>
      <fieldset
        disabled={!checked}
        hidden={!checked}
        className="fieldset bg-base-300 border-base-300 rounded-box border p-4"
      >
        <legend className="fieldset-legend">{legend}</legend>
        {children}
      </fieldset>
    </div>
  );
}

And, finally, the form that ties it all together. To make sure that all the fields read only from a single group, we create and use a helper with all the different inputs of the form. Add this onto a new src/components/CardForm.tsx file:

"use client";

import { NumberField, TextAreaField, TextField } from "./FormInputs";
import { PropertyGroup } from "./PropertyGroup";
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";

export interface CardFormProps {
  className?: string;
}

const GRID = "grid grid-cols-1 gap-x-2 gap-y-2 md:grid-cols-2";

export function CardForm({ className }: CardFormProps) {
  const state = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);
  const onChange = useFormStateStore((s) => s.setForm);
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = state;

  const setCard = (patch: Partial<typeof card>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, card: { ...card, ...patch } });
  const setText = (patch: Partial<typeof textBlock>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, textBlock: { ...textBlock, ...patch } });
  const setQr = (patch: Partial<typeof qrCode>) =>
    onChange({ ...state, qrCode: { ...qrCode, ...patch } });

  return (
    <form
      className={`bg-base-200 border-base-300 rounded-box flex flex-col gap-6 border p-6 ${className ?? ""}`}
      onSubmit={(e) => e.preventDefault()}
    >
      <fieldset className={GRID}>
        <legend className="sr-only">Card</legend>
        <NumberField
          label="Width"
          value={card.width}
          onValueChange={(width) => setCard({ width })}
        />
        <NumberField
          label="Height"
          value={card.height}
          onValueChange={(height) => setCard({ height })}
        />
        <NumberField
          label="Thickness"
          value={card.thickness}
          onValueChange={(thickness) => setCard({ thickness })}
        />
      </fieldset>

      <PropertyGroup
        label="Include text block?"
        legend="Text Properties"
        checked={textBlock.enabled}
        onToggleChange={(enabled) => setText({ enabled })}
      >
        <div className={GRID}>
          <NumberField
            label="X Position"
            value={textBlock.xPosition}
            onValueChange={(xPosition) => setText({ xPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Y Position"
            value={textBlock.yPosition}
            onValueChange={(yPosition) => setText({ yPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Font size"
            unit=""
            value={textBlock.fontSize}
            onValueChange={(fontSize) => setText({ fontSize })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Thickness"
            value={textBlock.thickness}
            onValueChange={(thickness) => setText({ thickness })}
          />
          <TextAreaField
            className="md:col-span-2"
            label="Text content"
            value={textBlock.content}
            onValueChange={(content) => setText({ content })}
          />
        </div>
      </PropertyGroup>

      <PropertyGroup
        label="Include QR Code?"
        legend="QR Code Properties"
        checked={qrCode.enabled}
        onToggleChange={(enabled) => setQr({ enabled })}
      >
        <div className={GRID}>
          <NumberField
            label="X Position"
            value={qrCode.xPosition}
            onValueChange={(xPosition) => setQr({ xPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Y Position"
            value={qrCode.yPosition}
            onValueChange={(yPosition) => setQr({ yPosition })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Thickness"
            value={qrCode.thickness}
            onValueChange={(thickness) => setQr({ thickness })}
          />
          <NumberField
            label="Module Size"
            value={qrCode.moduleSize}
            onValueChange={(moduleSize) => setQr({ moduleSize })}
          />
          <TextField
            className="md:col-span-2"
            label="QR code text (can be a link)"
            placeholder="https://example.com/"
            value={qrCode.qrContent}
            onValueChange={(qrContent) => setQr({ qrContent })}
          />
        </div>
      </PropertyGroup>
    </form>
  );
}

Let's add all of these elements into our page by modifying our homepage on src/app/page.tsx. We can add a layout, and prepare the rest of the app for all the components we'll be creating:

"use client";

import RTFContainer from "@/components/3d/RTFContainer";
import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { Visualizer } from "@/components/Visualizer";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/stores/FormStateHydrator";

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />
          <div>Our 3d visualizer will go here!</div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

Once you have added this content, your application should look like this:

Setting up the 3d space

Let's now get to the most fun part of the project: the 3d space and its objects. For this part, we can use React Three Fiber, as it lets us create 3d objects using React's jsx syntax.

We'll start by both creating a Canvas object for our 3d space and adding Drei's OrbitControls to handle camera movement, panning, and zoom. In a new file called src/components/RTFContainer.tsx add the following:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full bg-white/10">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />
        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

Here, we're doing three things:

  1. We're adding a camera and positioning it 100 units away from the centre of our 3d scene
  2. We're adding a set of controls to move the camera around the scene and setting them as the default using makeDefault
  3. And we're adding illumination to the scene, so we can actually see the objects in it once we have them

Next, let's add this scene into our page. For this, we can modify page.tsx like we did previously and replace our placeholder div with the following:

"use client";

import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/components/FormStateHydrator";
// Add this import:
import RTFContainer from "@/components/RTFContainer";

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />
          {/* We add the following elements: */}
          <div className="bg-base-300 rounded-box flex min-h-96 flex-1 overflow-hidden border border-base-content/10 p-6">
            <RTFContainer />
          </div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

You might have noticed that we are missing the download button that was part of our initial layout. Don't worry! We haven't forgotten about it yet, we'll just add it later :)

At this point our app is ready to show all of its 3d contents. However, with no objects to show, we just see an empty canvas!

Let's now focus on creating and adding our first object: the body of the card.

Rendering the card body

To render the body of our card we'll go for the simplest 3d shape: a box! For this, we can use a box geometry that's part of the standard tools that Three.js gives us. Its center will lie at 0, 0, 0, and it will take in the height, width, and thickness props of our form. Afterwards, we'll apply a white material, so the box will be visible on screen. Do the following in src/components/CardMesh.tsx:

import type { CardDimensions } from "../cardFormTypes";

const CardMesh = ({ cardProps }: { cardProps: CardDimensions }) => {
  return (
    <mesh>
      <boxGeometry
        args={[cardProps.width, cardProps.height, cardProps.thickness]}
      />
      <meshBasicMaterial color="white" />
    </mesh>
  );
};

export default CardMesh;

And add this new component into our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

// We add these two new imports
import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";


const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We add this line to extract the card props from the form state
  const { card } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />

        {/** And finally add this group with the card mesh */}
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />
        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

With this added, you should be able to see the first object on the canvas: a simple, white box. Because this card is connected to our Zustand store, you can even change the values present in the form to alter the size of the card in real time. And, thanks to the OrbitControls we added, we can move the camera around, even on mobile. Pretty neat, huh?

But, of course, this gives us no information whatsoever about the person that owns the card. So let's proceed by adding another element to the mix: the owner's text.

Rendering text content

We'll be drawing the text using Drei's Text3D component, which takes a typeface JSON file and manages its geometry automatically for us. For this project, I've prepared a file for Roboto Extra Bold, which you can download here from the GitHub repo. Once you have downloaded it, make sure to store it under your public assets, /public for Next.js, and call it Roboto_ExtraBold.json.

I created this file by downloading the font files from Google Fonts, picking the boldest one available, and then converting it using Facetype.js, a free, online converter you can use for these cases. You can follow this same process to customise your card even further, choosing whichever font you like.

To render the text object, let's now create a src/components/TextBlockMesh.tsx file and add the following content into it:

import { CardDimensions, TextBlockState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";
import { Text3D } from "@react-three/drei";

// The name of the font file you added
const TEXT_FONT = "Roboto_ExtraBold.json";

const TextBlockMesh = ({
  textBlockProps,
  cardProps,
}: {
  textBlockProps: TextBlockState;
  cardProps: CardDimensions;
}) => {
  return (
    <Text3D
      font={`/${TEXT_FONT}`}
      size={textBlockProps.fontSize / 4}
      position={[
        textBlockProps.xPosition,
        textBlockProps.yPosition,
        cardProps.thickness / 2,
      ]}
      height={textBlockProps.thickness}
    >
      {textBlockProps.content}
      <meshBasicMaterial color="black" />
    </Text3D>
  );
};

export default TextBlockMesh;

If you read the code, you might have noticed a few interesting things. First, we're scaling down the size of the text by doing fontSize / 4 so it doesn't change as drastically when altering this value. This way, if you go from font size 14 to 15, its size will just slightly change, making it so you don't have to play around with decimals that much. Second, the text sits at thickness / 2 on the Z axis. While this might seem confusing, this is due to us wanting to position our text directly on the face of our card. By making it so the text is raised by half the card's thickness, we make sure it's always resting on top of the frontal face of our card.

Now, let's add it to our scene by modifying our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";

// We add Suspense, as Text3D suspends while the font data is loading.
// You can read more about it here: https://drei.docs.pmnd.rs/abstractions/text3d
import { Suspense } from "react";
import TextBlockMesh from "./TextBlockMesh";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We destructure the textBlock values from the form state
  const { card, textBlock } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />

          {/** And we add the text block with Suspense without a fallback 
           * and control its visibility based on form props */}
          <Suspense fallback={null}>
            {textBlock.enabled && textBlock.content.length > 0 && (
              <TextBlockMesh textBlockProps={textBlock} cardProps={card} />
            )}
          </Suspense>

        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

As mentioned in the code, we're controlling the visibility of our text block using the enabled prop we created for the form. If you play around with the values of the form, they should automatically be reflected into our application.

The current app should look like this:

Rendering the QR code

The QR code will be the most complex but fun mesh we'll create here. We'll need to start by making a matrix of 1s and 0s, representing the final result. We can use qrcode to generate this matrix, which we'll then utilise to make every individual module — the squares that make up our QR code.

Similar to the text, the QR is placed at (thickness of card + thickness of QR) / 2 on the Z axis, so it's positioned on top of the card's front face. Add the following into a new src/components/QRCodeMesh.tsx file:

import { useMemo } from "react";
import QRCode from "qrcode";
import * as THREE from "three";
import { CardDimensions, QrCodeState } from "@/types/cardFormTypes";

/**
 * We use a low level of error correction. As defined in the type, possible
 * values are L for Low, M for Medium, Q for Quartile, and H for High. A bigger
 * level of error correction will make it easier for your QR code to be scanned
 * if it gets damaged, but it will also take more space.
 */
type ErrorCorrectionType = "L" | "M" | "Q" | "H";
const ERROR_CORRECTION: ErrorCorrectionType = "L";

const makeModuleSquare = (col: number, row: number, moduleSize: number) => {
  const x = col * moduleSize;
  const y = -row * moduleSize; // flip y: matrix rows go down, 3D y goes up

  // We form the square shape for each QR code module using simple lines.
  const shape = new THREE.Shape();
  shape.moveTo(x, y);
  shape.lineTo(x + moduleSize, y);
  shape.lineTo(x + moduleSize, y + moduleSize);
  shape.lineTo(x, y + moduleSize);
  shape.closePath();
  return shape;
};

const QRCodeMesh = ({
  qrCodeProps,
  cardProps,
}: {
  qrCodeProps: QrCodeState;
  cardProps: CardDimensions;
}) => {
  // This process is quite complex, so we memoize it.
  const qrCode = useMemo(
    () =>
      QRCode.create(qrCodeProps.qrContent, {
        errorCorrectionLevel: ERROR_CORRECTION,
      }),
    [qrCodeProps.qrContent],
  );

  const geometry = useMemo(() => {
    const { size, data } = qrCode.modules;

    const shapes: THREE.Shape[] = [];
    data.forEach((value, index) => {
      if (value) {
        const yCoord = Math.floor(index / size);
        const xCoord = Math.floor(index % size);
        // Shift the grid so the QR code is centred on the origin.
        shapes.push(
          makeModuleSquare(
            xCoord - size / 2,
            yCoord + 1 - size / 2,
            qrCodeProps.moduleSize,
          ),
        );
      }
    });

    const geometry = new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry(shapes, {
      depth: qrCodeProps.thickness,
      bevelEnabled: false,
      curveSegments: 24,
    });

    geometry.center();

    return geometry;
  }, [qrCode, qrCodeProps.moduleSize, qrCodeProps.thickness]);

  return (
    <mesh
      position={[
        qrCodeProps.xPosition,
        qrCodeProps.yPosition,
        (cardProps.thickness + qrCodeProps.thickness) / 2,
      ]}
      geometry={geometry}
    >
      <meshPhongMaterial color="black" />
    </mesh>
  );
};

export default QRCodeMesh;

And, similar to our other meshes, we add the object to our RTFContainer:

"use client";

import { OrbitControls } from "@react-three/drei";
import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";

import useFormStateStore from "@/stores/formStore";
import CardMesh from "./CardMesh";
import { Suspense } from "react";
import TextBlockMesh from "./TextBlockMesh";

// We import the mesh
import QRCodeMesh from "./QRCodeMesh";

const RTFContainer = () => {
  // We destructure the form values
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />
        <group>
          <CardMesh cardProps={card} />

          <Suspense fallback={null}>
            {textBlock.enabled && textBlock.content.length > 0 && (
              <TextBlockMesh textBlockProps={textBlock} cardProps={card} />
            )}
          </Suspense>

          {/** And add the QR Code mesh into our group similar to how we 
           * did with the text block
           */}
          {qrCode.enabled && qrCode.qrContent.length > 0 && (
            <QRCodeMesh qrCodeProps={qrCode} cardProps={card} />
          )}
        </group>
      </Canvas>
    </div>
  );
};

export default RTFContainer;

With this, our app should look like this:

This now has almost all the elements of our original design. The only thing we're missing is a way to export the model. So, let's add that button!

Exporting our model as an STL

Now that our model is created and customisable, our last step will be to find a way to download it from the browser. Luckily, Three.js includes an STLExporter that can help us do exactly that. It exports any object that contains meshes, but it needs a way to reach the group that wraps all the models of our scene. So, to make our lives easier, we'll create a small Zustand store that will help us hold a reference to this group so we can handle the download.

To make this store, create meshStore.ts in our stores folder and add the following code:

import { create } from "zustand";
import * as THREE from "three";
import { STLExporter } from "three/examples/jsm/exporters/STLExporter.js";

interface MeshStoreState {
  jointMesh: THREE.Object3D | null;
  setJointMesh: (jointMesh: THREE.Object3D | null) => void;
  downloadModel: () => void;
}

function downloadBlobAsFile(blob: Blob, filename: string) {
  const blobUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  const link = document.createElement("a");
  link.href = blobUrl;
  link.download = filename;
  link.click();

  URL.revokeObjectURL(blobUrl);
}

const useMeshStore = create<MeshStoreState>()((set, get) => ({
  jointMesh: null,
  setJointMesh: (jointMesh) => set({ jointMesh }),

  downloadModel: () => {
    const { jointMesh } = get();
    if (!jointMesh) {
      console.error("The model is not ready yet. Try again in a moment.");
      return;
    }

    // Make sure every child's world transform is updated before exporting.
    jointMesh.updateMatrixWorld(true);

    // We convert the model to STL
    const exporter = new STLExporter();
    const data = exporter.parse(jointMesh, { binary: true });
    const blob = new Blob([data], { type: "model/stl" });

    // And we download it
    downloadBlobAsFile(blob, "joint-model.stl");
  },
}));

export default useMeshStore;

Now we just need to pass our group to the store, which we'll do by using a React ref. For this, we'll change our RTFContainer like so:

const RTFContainer = () => {
  const { card, textBlock, qrCode } = useFormStateStore((s) => s.form);
  // Add this line. Don't forget to import the store!
  const setJointMesh = useMeshStore((s) => s.setJointMesh);

  return (
    <div className="h-full w-full">
      <Canvas camera={{ position: [0, 0, 100], fov: 70 }}>
        <OrbitControls makeDefault />

        <directionalLight color="white" position={[0, 0, 5]} />

        // And make sure to connect the group with the store, here
        <group ref={setJointMesh}>

        // Rest of the code

And, finally, we'll add the download button to our page. To do this, we'll modify the layout of our page.tsx a bit and add a few elements to it:

"use client";

import { CardForm } from "@/components/CardForm";
import { FormStateHydrator } from "@/components/FormStateHydrator";
import RTFContainer from "@/components/RTFContainer";

// First, we import our mesh store
import useMeshStore from "@/stores/meshStore";

export default function Home() {
  // We then get the helper function from the mesh store
  const downloadModel = useMeshStore((s) => s.downloadModel);

  return (
    <div>
      <FormStateHydrator />
      <main className="bg-base-100 mx-auto flex min-h-screen w-full max-w-[1600px] flex-col gap-6 px-4 py-6 lg:px-6">
        <div className="grid min-h-0 flex-1 grid-cols-1 gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
          <CardForm />

          {/* And we change this bit, adding the download model function to our button: */}
          <div className="border-base-content/10 bg-base-300 flex flex-col overflow-hidden rounded-box border">
            <div className="bg-base-200 flex items-center justify-center p-6">
              <button
                type="button"
                onClick={downloadModel}
                className="btn btn-primary"
              >
                Download .stl
              </button>
            </div>
            <div className="flex min-h-96 flex-1 items-center justify-center p-6">
              <RTFContainer />
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

And, with that, the application is done! The final result should look like this:

In our application, the form controls the store, which in turn controls the card 3d model. We can modify the model in real time, move it around in its 3d space, and even download the result! If you have a 3d printer, you can then print this model as a real business card and show it around. Isn't that neat?

Conclusion

As mentioned in the description, this project started as a way for me to explore ways in which we can connect the web with the physical world using 3d prints. For this, we first set up a form to control the properties of our 3d objects and then created a Zustand store to save its values. We then learned how to create a 3d space with React Three Fiber and move it around with Drei's helpers. Afterwards, we learned how to create 3d objects, give them simple textures, and position them in our 3d space. We added these objects using three different methods: standard geometries, Drei's Text3D components, and our own custom geometry. Finally, we created another Zustand store to let us download our model, and we added a download button to let our users export the final result.

While this project started as something similar to what we created here, I then decided to further expand it into a full application with some more complexity, which I decided to call g3co. Although it's still in early test versions, it allows for more customisation than what we created in this guide, and I plan to include some updates in the future to add more features and interesting parts. Moreover, it's open source! And you can find its repository on GitHub.

Apart from the exploration I wanted to do in this project and post, I wanted to use this app to learn something. See, I'm constantly looking to improve my design and development skills. For this, I figured out that creating an app about a topic that I'm already passionate about, 3d printing, was a great path to follow. And I hope you also learned some new things from it, and that you had fun while doing so.

So, if you learned something, please take what you've learned and made, and make it better!

title: Next.js 15 Custom Cache Handler: Self-Host ISR with L1 RAM + L2 Redis & Stop Cache Stampedes
description:
If you self-host Next.js 15 on Docker, Kubernetes, Railway, Coolify, or Fly.io, you quickly run into two production caching challenges:

  1. Multi-Instance Cache Desync: By default, Next.js stores ISR and App Router fetch caches on the local container filesystem/memory, meaning Pod A and Pod B serve inconsistent data after revalidateTag().
  2. The ISR Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a high-traffic cached route or query expires under 1,000 req/sec, dozens of concurrent requests trigger expensive regeneration queries against your database at the exact same millisecond.

To solve both problems with zero runtime dependencies in the core engine, we built KVDock — featuring a drop-in Next.js 15 Incremental Cache Handler, multi-tier L1/L2 caching, and single-flight stampede coalescing.

🎮 Launch the Live Browser Stampede Simulator — Simulate 5,000 concurrent cache misses in your browser!

⭐ Support open-source: Give KVDock a ★ Star on GitHub (We are just 13 stars away from our first 16-star community milestone!)

⚡ What Happens During a Cache Stampede?

Imagine a popular product page cache expires while 1,000 concurrent users load it simultaneously:

Metric Standard Uncoalesced Cache kvdock.getOrSet() (Single-Flight) Impact
Concurrent Requests 1,000 1,000 Identical load
Database Queries Executed 1,000 queries (Thundering Herd) 1 query (Single-Flight) 99.9% DB load reduction
Coalesced Callers 0 999 Zero lock contention

🛠️ 3-Line Next.js 15 Setup (next.config.mjs)

First, install kvdock:

npm install kvdock

Wire up the custom cache handler in next.config.mjs:

/** @type {import("next").NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  cacheHandler: import.meta.resolve("kvdock/next"),
  cacheMaxMemorySize: 0, // Let KVDock TieredDock manage L1 RAM + L2 Redis/SQLite
};

export default nextConfig;

🚀 Multi-Tier L1 (In-Memory) + L2 (Redis / SQLite) Architecture

Why pay a 2–5ms Redis network round-trip on every single read when 95% of reads can be served in 0.04ms from L1 RAM?

With TieredDock, you get sub-millisecond local reads backed by shared L2 persistence:

import { TieredDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";
import { RedisAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/redis";

export const cache = new TieredDock({
  l1: new MemoryAdapter({ maxEntries: 5_000 }),
  l2: new RedisAdapter({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }),
  l1Ttl: 60_000,      // 1 minute hot in-process L1 cache
  l2Ttl: 3_600_000,   // 1 hour shared Redis L2 cache
});

// Single-flight coalesced read-through:
const catalog = await cache.getOrSet("catalog:featured", async () => {
  return await db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE featured = true");
});

When an L1 miss occurs:

  1. TieredDock checks L2 (Redis, SQLite, Upstash, Postgres, or S3).
  2. If found in L2, it automatically promotes the value back into L1 RAM.
  3. If missing in both, Single-Flight Coalescing ensures only 1 caller queries your database while all other concurrent requests await the same in-flight promise.

🧪 Try the Interactive Playground & Star on GitHub!

We built an interactive browser simulator where you can test L1/L2 cache promotion and trigger a 5,000-request stampede live:
