title: Design accessible form success states: status, navigation, Undo, and confirmation
description:
Successful submission is a distinct UI state

A completed form needs to answer two questions: did the action finish, and can the user recover if it was accidental? Treating success as an error-summary variant or relying on a visual toast makes those answers harder to discover.

Start by choosing the announcement channel from the page transition.

If submission navigates to a new page or a clearly different view, put the result in the new document context: update the page title and expose a clear main heading such as “Task submitted.” This makes the destination state explicit rather than leaving the user to infer success from a changed screen.

If submission remains on the same page, keep the user in context and return a concise status message. The message should say what completed, not repeat a long explanation. The inserted example models this as a dedicated status result, separate from validation output.

Keep recovery and validation honest

Validation failures need a correction path: field errors identify what must change before submission can continue. They are not success feedback, and a successful result should not be inferred merely because an error summary is absent. Model these as separate states so the rendering layer cannot accidentally present success through an error pattern.

Next, choose the safeguard based on reversibility. For reversible work, return an Undo control after success and restore the prior item when the user activates it. Once restoration has happened, Undo should no longer be available. For permanent or otherwise critical work, do not offer a recovery promise that the system cannot keep. Require confirmation before committing the action instead.

Expected behavior is straightforward: a valid reversible submission produces a completion announcement and Undo; a page-style completion produces a title and heading instead of an in-place status; invalid input produces validation feedback; irreversible work pauses for confirmation and exposes no Undo control.

One important limitation remains: this flow can model the semantic contract, but it cannot prove the exact announcement order or behavior of every browser and assistive-technology combination. Verify the rendered markup and interaction in the environments you support.

Working example 

export const proofBoundary =
  'This model verifies the flow’s presentation contract. It does not prove how a particular browser or assistive technology announces a live region, title, or heading.';

function successPresentation(presentation, task) {
  const message = `Task “${task}” submitted successfully.`;

  if (presentation === 'page') {
    return {
      title: `Task submitted – Task manager`,
      heading: 'Task submitted',
      status: null,
      message,
    };
  }

  return {
    title: null,
    heading: null,
    status: { role: 'status', text: message },
    message,
  };
}

/**
 * Models a form submission UI. A real page can render `title` and `heading`
 * after navigation, or render the `status` live region after an in-page submit.
 */
export function createTaskFormFlow({ presentation = 'status', reversible = true } = {}) {
  if (!['status', 'page'].includes(presentation)) {
    throw new RangeError('presentation must be "status" or "page"');
  }

  let pendingSubmission = null;

  return {
    submit({ task, confirmed = false } = {}) {
      const normalizedTask = typeof task === 'string' ? task.trim() : '';

      if (!normalizedTask) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'validation',
          fieldErrors: { task: 'Enter a task.' },
          // Success is not represented as a server-style error summary.
          errorSummary: null,
        };
      }

      if (!reversible && !confirmed) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'confirmation-required',
          message: 'Confirm this permanent submission before continuing.',
        };
      }

      pendingSubmission = { task: normalizedTask };
      const feedback = successPresentation(presentation, normalizedTask);

      return {
        ok: true,
        kind: 'submitted',
        ...feedback,
        undoControl: reversible
          ? { action: 'undo', label: 'Undo submission', accessibleName: 'Undo submission' }
          : null,
      };
    },

    undo() {
      if (!reversible || pendingSubmission === null) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          kind: 'undo-unavailable',
          status: null,
        };
      }

      const { task } = pendingSubmission;
      pendingSubmission = null;
      return {
        ok: true,
        kind: 'undone',
        restoredTask: task,
        status: { role: 'status', text: `Submission of “${task}” was undone.` },
      };
    },
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/successful-form-submission-undo-accessibly

title: Wanted a Dictation App, Got Three Libraries
description:
I swapped my M2 MacBook with the old design for a new fanless M5 Air. A new computer feels like a clean start. So instead of dragging all my old apps and settings along, I went looking for lighter and more native alternatives. For example, I replaced VS Code with Zed and Chrome with Helium.

To talk to agents, I used a dictation app called Handy. But I really didn't like that it's built on Tauri, and I wanted something native. I asked an agent to find an alternative, but nothing it found worked for me. So I decided to write my own.

People on X are rewriting everything in GPUI Kit right now, so I decided to try it too. The author of Handy had also moved the speech recognition engine into a separate project called transcribe.cpp. So the task looked easy, especially with agents.

Week 1. Picking a GUI and prototypes

So I took GPUI Kit, the one everyone on X was hyping, and quickly built the first version of the UI with agents. It came out pretty well: the app with an open window used about 80 MB of RAM. But compiling was painfully slow. Part of it was GPUI Kit itself, and part was linking transcribe.cpp, which took about a minute on every rebuild.

I also didn't like that GPUI Kit pulls in over 400 dependencies, just like Node.js. Who knows what malware might be hiding in there? Besides, GPUI from Zed isn't a finished library with stable releases. So GPUI Kit depends on a dev version from the Zed repo, and the API can change at any moment. Another problem is integration with the system, like a tray icon or a native context menu. GPUI Kit doesn't have it, so all of that has to be written by hand.

I decided to look at other options in the Rust ecosystem. Back in the pre-agent era, I played with egui for UIs, and it left a good impression. It really was faster and lighter on memory, and it pulled in fewer crates. But all the native integrations still have to be written by hand, and the components need a lot of customizing to look nice.

I also tried native controls: Rust bindings to the system UI libraries (AppKit on macOS, Win32 on Windows and GTK on Linux). The idea came from another project I saw on X, mygo, which builds native desktop UIs in Go. But in practice I had to write a huge pile of integration code and repeat it at least three times. The app looked native on each platform, but so different that some features couldn't be done properly. And that's for a dictation app, which is literally a settings menu, a list of models and a history.

The most annoying thing the whole time was rebuilding: every launch meant waiting almost a minute for transcribe.cpp to link. And I didn't really get why there should be C++ in my Rust toolchain at all. So I decided to look at what's going on inside.

Week 2. My own speech recognition engine

Inside transcribe.cpp there was ggml, which has separate code for each GPU backend (Metal, Vulkan and CUDA). Each one needs its own tools to build. Rust has wgpu, where shaders are written once in WGSL and run on any GPU. And everything builds with a plain cargo build.

I got curious whether I could run at least one model on WGSL, though I had no plans to rewrite anything yet. I took GigaAM v3, which I use most often, and made a small demo with it. To my surprise, the agent wrote the shader code easily, and the results were close to the original library.

That's when it became a challenge for me. I remembered optimizing math on the secp256k1 curve in ecloop and optimizing RIPEMD-160, and kept digging. The first model was GigaAM v3 e2e RNN-T, which outputs punctuation and capital letters. I also decided to add other models from the same family to see how hard it would be. They differ in the decoder. CTC recognizes each piece of audio on its own, while RNN-T also looks at the text it has already written, so it's more accurate but slower. Each of them also has a version with punctuation (e2e) and one without.

I dictate in two languages, Russian and English. Since adding Russian was easy, I thought English wouldn't be a problem either. NVIDIA's Parakeet v2 is a good fit for English because it's accurate and fast. But when I started adding it, I found out that models come in different architectures, and each one needs its own compute code.

I took the models already packed into GGUF by the author of transcribe.cpp. It turned out that GGUF stores only the weights and some metadata about the model: the architecture name, layer sizes and vocabulary. The computations aren't in the file, so they have to be written by hand. That's the difference from TensorFlow or Apple's Core ML, where the model file describes a graph of operations and the runtime just executes it.

So I had to sit down and figure it out by reading and watching YouTube videos about how speech recognition models work. In short, long audio is cut into chunks (Whisper, for example, uses 30-second windows). Each chunk goes through a fast Fourier transform (FFT) and becomes a spectrogram (which frequencies sound at each moment). The encoder (a stack of neural network layers that mostly multiply matrices) takes the spectrogram and turns it into a sequence of vectors. The decoder reads them and outputs tokens (pieces of words) one step at a time, and these tokens make up the text. Most of the work is matrix multiplication in the encoder layers, and that's what the GPU computes.

Once I understood how it works, I added support for Parakeet v2. Codex wrote the first version overnight, but the code was messy, so I threw it away and rewrote it cleanly with Claude Code. In the end I got a pretty fast speech-to-text program that beat transcribe.cpp in my tests. Since I was on a roll, I right away added Parakeet v3, a multilingual model from the same family (I barely had to write anything new). Right after it came Whisper, as a reference model to compare the others against.

Parakeet differs from GigaAM in plenty of ways. The model is bigger (24 layers vs 16, and each one is wider). It compresses audio twice as much (one vector per 80 ms instead of 40). It also has a different way to mark when each word was said. But the main difference is the decoder (TDT): along with each token, it predicts how many of the next audio frames it can skip.

The program was turning out so well that I decided to release it as a separate project in the style of ollama. I named it wavo, kind of from WAV, and the name was free. Besides, I had needed local audio transcription before, and there was nothing good for it in the terminal. I tried whisper.cpp, but it's slow and inconvenient (it has to be compiled from source, and the audio has to be cut into chunks by hand).

Before publishing, I decided to clean up the code. The rustfft crate was still slowing down the build. People can use wavo as a library, so everyone who builds it would get that delay too. Once I found the cause, I wrote my own FFT just for this task. It came out at 176 lines of code vs 55,000 in rustfft, and rebuilds went from 11.9 down to 2.1 seconds. The crate itself is good, it's just built for every case, and I needed only one.

The last step before publishing was testing. Luckily, I have a few Macs at hand, an N100 box with Linux and an x86 machine with a GeForce card and a good CPU. I had the agent run the final tests and compare the speed with other libraries. On Macs my library crushed everyone on speed, no question (I'm still shocked it was that easy). But on Windows with an NVIDIA card it was a big failure. Again I had to dig in, and it turned out there's a thing called flash attention.

Attention is the part of the model where each vector is compared with all the others in the same audio chunk. For Whisper that's 1,500 vectors per 30 seconds, so more than two million comparisons in each layer. Regular code writes this whole table to GPU memory and then reads it back. Flash attention computes the same thing in small pieces in fast memory next to the GPU cores and never stores the whole table.

On Macs, the agent had already made such shaders earlier, but for Apple's matrix units (hardware acceleration). NVIDIA's units have a different size, so on NVIDIA wavo computed everything with generic code. After I added shaders for NVIDIA's matrix units, wavo on Windows caught up with transcribe.cpp and in some cases beat it. A short Whisper turbo recording now takes 201 ms vs 226 ms for transcribe.cpp, down from 637.

I made all the measurements on an RTX 4060 and didn't test on AMD Radeon at all. So I'd be glad to see results from other GPUs in issues.

During testing I also found that on M5, wgpu uses only the old matrix units. The M5 got a neural accelerator in each GPU core, which multiplies matrices three times faster (0.60 ms vs 1.89 ms). But it's only available through Metal 4, and wgpu doesn't support it yet. I worked around this with a separate Metal shader just for M5 and opened an issue in wgpu.

I also taught wavo to run on the Neural Engine (a separate part of Apple chips for neural networks), but that's another story. At the end, I ran a final comparison of Parakeet v3 in English against other engines, and the numbers looked impressive.

Engine Runs on 5 s phrase 1 h recording
wavo Neural Engine 0.12 s 200×
FluidAudio Neural Engine 0.13 s 175×
wavo GPU 0.14 s 160×
transcribe.cpp GPU 0.12 s 107×
parakeet.cpp GPU 0.77 s 90×
parakeet-mlx GPU 0.63 s 61×
sherpa-onnx CPU 0.83 s 39×

The table shows the time for a 5-second phrase and how many times faster than real time a one-hour recording gets transcribed (MacBook Pro on M5). In Russian with GigaAM v3 the gap is similar: wavo is 330 times faster than real time, and transcribe.cpp is 262 times faster.

Week 3. My own renderer

While I worked on wavo, another agent was experimenting with a UI library in the background. Every approach still needed a lot of hand-written wrappers to talk to the OS, so I decided I could write the renderer myself too. I also had some experience with UIs in video games, so the task seemed simple.

I've long been a fan of Sublime Text, and especially Sublime Merge, and their approach to UI. I thought that if the authors of these apps and of the Zed editor could write their own UI framework, then I, armed with an agent, could too. Armed with strings and nm, we looked at which system functions Sublime Merge uses and figured out the idea behind it. It was an interesting one ;)

The text there is drawn by the system itself (CoreText on macOS, DirectWrite on Windows, Pango on Linux), so it looks native everywhere. That's unlike egui, for example, which draws glyphs on its own. The system draws each glyph once and it goes into a cache, and after that the screen gets ready glyphs from the cache. Context menus work the same way and come from the system (GPUI Kit draws them itself by default).

So it turned into a kind of Frankenstein. The edges are system stuff, and in the middle, like the filling in a sandwich, is my library, which lays out elements in the window and builds components from them.

Rendering uses immediate mode (the frame is built from scratch every time, without a complex event system). Regular apps don't have that much interactivity, and a settings window doesn't need to be redrawn 60 or 120 times per second. Besides, the frame is rebuilt only when something changes, and an idle window draws nothing.

I decided to draw the frame itself on the CPU. It's the simplest code, and it works the same everywhere, without shaders, drivers and other junk that has to be integrated and then tested too. The finished frame goes to the system's regular 2D window output. For an app without complex animations, that's more than fast enough.

3D acceleration pulls in extra libraries, and the program starts eating more memory (on Windows a simple window with D3D11 takes 27 MB instead of 5.1). But if it's ever needed, I can always add it later.

The renderer itself came out at about 3,000 lines of Rust, and the agent quickly put together the basic components on top of it (around 6,000 more lines). Everything worked, and it seemed like the job was almost done.

Next I needed a context menu and a small popup that shows the text being dictated. That's where the pain and suffering began, especially when I ran everything on real computers with Linux and Windows instead of VMs.

Now I understand why there were so few GUI frameworks in the pre-agent era. The hard part isn't writing a renderer and a component system at all. The hard part is wiring all of it together on different platforms so that it works. Each cross-platform feature can easily take several thousand lines for three systems:

  • windows (open them, drag them and draw in them): 5,000 lines;
  • text fields and IME: 4,000;
  • tray, hotkeys and autostart: 7,000;
  • accessibility on macOS: 3,000;
  • native context menu: 2,000.

Of course the agent writes the code, but someone still has to read it, check it and test it on each system, and that's a lot of work.

For example, a context menu can be drawn by the app's own renderer, and that's how GPUI in Zed does it. But it looks janky, and more importantly, such a menu can't go outside the window. I had never thought about this before, but once I started writing, I realized it matters. Sublime Merge can do it, and I give it credit for that.

As expected, Linux was the biggest pain. On macOS and Windows everything goes through one system API, but Linux is a damn zoo. At first I tried to draw separately on X11 and Wayland to make the program as optimized as possible, but the amount of code grew exponentially. So I made a compromise and took GTK 3, which is on almost every distro. Sublime Merge does the same.

I named the library nimbo. A simple counter window built with it pulls in 14 crates on macOS, 5 on Windows and 3 on Linux. Almost all of them are system bindings, like objc2 on macOS and windows-sys on Windows. It builds from scratch in 11 seconds, and the binary is 1.3 MB. For comparison, here is the same counter on other frameworks (the number of crates on each system, a clean release build on M2 and the binary size):

macOS Windows Linux Build Binary
nimbo 14 5 3 11 s 1.3 MB
iced 152 159 237 59 s 10.9 MB
Tauri¹ 217 223 265 64 s 9.9 MB
Xilem 157 177 257 65 s 12.2 MB
egui 177 178 279 74 s 14.3 MB
Slint 248 244 345 84 s 12.5 MB
GPUI 300 270 322 86 s 8.6 MB
GPUI Kit 411 395 518 144 s 19.4 MB

¹ Plus the system WebView, which isn't part of the binary.

In the era of personal software and endless hacks, I want my own foundation for this kind of program, without depending on other people's frameworks. So I decided to finish nimbo properly. There's no first release yet because I'm still working on the API, so I have no time to make cool videos for X. But if you need something minimal in Rust, you're welcome to try it.

The library is built in three layers. At the bottom is a common API for system stuff (windows, tray, context menu and so on), so the app code never has to touch it at all. Above it are headless components (behavior without styling), and any design can be built on top of them. On top is a base design in the style of system controls. The model for the library's API is SwiftUI.

Week 4. Release: signing, packaging, updates

The program is ready and tested, and all that's left is to ship a release. But that turned out to be not so simple either. There were three problems: signing, packaging and auto-update, and they took the last week.

Signing

In recent versions of macOS and Windows, unsigned apps just don't run. Windows is easier: SmartScreen shows a warning on the first launch, and once the user accepts it, the app starts. On macOS, though, the quarantine has to be removed from an unsigned app by hand with /usr/bin/xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Wavo.app, and a regular user is unlikely to do that.

I had to pay Apple $99 a year. And their payment form is straight from the early 2000s: I had to type in my card details by hand, and Apple charged the card on its own sometime later. In the end the charge failed on 3-D Secure. I had to temporarily lower the protection on my card and ask support to retry the payment, and the whole thing dragged on for several days. I can't remember the last time I saw something like that.

Packaging

A program for three systems needs installers for all three. On macOS the standard is a DMG. On Windows it's a setup.exe that installs the program, usually made with NSIS. On Linux it's an AppImage and a .deb package. Linux actually has more formats, but for now I picked these two.

At first it seemed easy to do with a Python script, so I gave that to the agent. There was one requirement: build and signing are separate. The build step downloads and compiles other people's code, so it must not have access to the signing keys. The second step only signs the finished files.

The script quickly grew to almost 2,000 lines. That surprised me, and I went looking for ready solutions, since after so many years someone must have solved this. I found a few (Velopack, cargo-packager and the Tauri bundler), but each has its own problems. Some can't separate build from signing. The worst part is that almost none of them can do everything on one machine (DMG and signing for macOS only on a Mac, deb and AppImage only on Linux, and Windows also needs NSIS). Velopack can build everything at once, but only on a Mac. In my opinion this is crazy. Packaging and signing should work on one computer, and ideally on any computer.

I looked through other people's repos, and from what I saw, only Mozilla does it properly. They package Firefox on Linux, even the DMG for macOS, but with wild hacks. For DMG they have their own fork of the C library libdmg-hfsplus, which has no prebuilt releases, and their CI builds it straight from the repo at a specific commit. To use it myself, I would have to pull an artifact out of someone else's unversioned build, and I didn't want that. Well, I had an agent, so I gave this job to it too.

At first I wanted to make it part of nimbo. Then I realized it's a completely separate program and moved it to its own crate, shipo.

The main idea of shipo is that all installers can be built on any machine, even on Linux. Everything that exists on only one system (hdiutil on macOS, makensis for Windows, apt packages on Linux) is replaced with its own code. The other tools are downloaded at a pinned version and hash.

For macOS, shipo writes the DMG itself, together with the HFS+ file system per Apple's spec. It even includes the Unicode tables HFS+ uses to normalize file names. It also writes the .DS_Store that places the app icon and the /Applications shortcut in the window. It builds the .icns icon itself too, without sips and iconutil. Signing and notarization outside a Mac go through rcodesign and Apple's notarization service.

For Windows, the installer is custom too. It's a small prebuilt setup.exe in Rust with an empty marker inside. The packager replaces the icon, version and manifest in the app's exe and compresses the files into one archive. Then it appends the archive to the end of setup.exe and writes into the marker where that archive is. The uninstaller is the same setup.exe, just without the files.

For Linux, AppImage (a prebuilt runtime with a squashfs image of the app appended to it) and deb are built right in memory.

Auto-update

The third thing actually has nothing to do with packaging, but I had to do it too. On macOS many apps update with Sparkle, but it works only on macOS. For Windows there's WinSparkle, which has a similar idea but is a different library. I wanted one thing for all systems, but didn't find anything here either. I decided that building and updating are close things and can live in one crate, so I made them together.

The idea of auto-update is simple. Each release also includes a small file that describes the latest version. The app reads it from time to time, and if the version is newer, it downloads and installs the update by itself.

In shipo it's one text file, update.txt, in the latest release on GitHub:

version 1.2.0
notes https://github.com/me/hello/releases/tag/v1.2.0
macos-aarch64 394788 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-macos-aarch64.dmg
windows-x86_64 285930 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-windows-x64-setup.exe
linux-x86_64 412204 <sha512> https://github.com/me/hello/releases/download/v1.2.0/Hello-v1.2.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
sig <signature>

It has the version, a link to the release notes, and a line for each platform (size, SHA-512 hash and file URL). At the end is an Ed25519 signature of everything above. No separate update server is needed. The app just downloads the file from the latest GitHub release by a permanent link (releases/latest/download/update.txt).

The app checks the downloaded file by size and hash. It has two signing keys, a main one and a backup. If the main one leaks, the next release is signed with the backup.

The update uses the same installer as the first install. On macOS the library mounts the DMG, copies the app from it and replaces the old one. On Windows it runs setup.exe without a window. On Linux it replaces the AppImage file.

shipo has no separate HTTP library. Instead it has three short wrappers over the system ones (NSURLSession on macOS, WinHTTP on Windows, libcurl on Linux). So the updater has few dependencies: signature checking, errors and system bindings.

So in a week I got shipo, about 12,000 lines of code. Roughly 10,000 of them are the packager (with the setup.exe stub), and 2,400 are the library that goes into the app. Its packager builds installers for all three systems on one machine. The updater adds only 8–15 crates to the app depending on the system (Velopack and cargo-packager have over a hundred). In the end, releasing an app properly and setting up CI turned out to be harder than writing a UI renderer.

Wrap up

A program for a couple of days turned into a month of work. In that time there were about 850 commits and 167,000 changed lines (including prototypes and code I later threw away). Working with agents took about 90 active hours and 3.7 billion tokens, which is roughly $2,700 at API prices. The numbers are approximate because some agent logs got lost.

Most of the code was written by Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra did the reviews. Copilot on GitHub did about 390 more reviews until I hit its limit. Codex drew the graphics and images.

The work didn't end there. For anyone besides family and friends to hear about the program, I have to write about it on Reddit, X and other places, and that's a big separate job too. While doing it, I found a lot of similar programs. If I had seen them at the start, I probably wouldn't have built mine at all. But what's done is done. In the end I got my own cross-platform stack, and I hope to reuse it for other things.

All the programs from the post once more:

  • Wavo: local dictation for macOS, Windows and Linux;
  • wavo: CLI and Rust crate for speech recognition in the style of ollama;
  • nimbo: native UI library with almost no dependencies;
  • shipo: installers and auto-update for three systems from one machine.

I wanted to make one small dictation app, and got an app and three libraries for it.

title: wtfi3: Who Is Talking to Whom on My WiFi
description:
A router's admin page lists the devices on the network and stops there. I wanted the other half: who each one is talking to. Wireshark answers that, but I wanted something I could leave open in a tab.

wtfi3 is one Go binary. Point it at an interface, open http://localhost:8080, and it draws which device talks to which service, which of those are trackers, and how many bytes are moving right now.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi3
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/wtfi3 or go build -o wtfi3 ./cmd/wtfi3 (needs libpcap)

All screenshots here come from make demo, which serves the dashboard on synthetic household traffic. None of it is my network.

Metadata, not payloads

Nothing is decrypted. What wtfi3 reads is what is already in the clear:

  • IP and MAC addresses, with the vendor looked up in an embedded copy of the IEEE OUI list
  • bytes and packets per flow (source, destination, protocol, port)
  • DNS responses: which client asked for which name, and the answer
  • the SNI hostname in a TLS ClientHello on port 443 or 8443

The SNI parser is about a hundred lines in internal/tlsmeta/sni.go: walk the record header, skip the random, session id, cipher suites and compression methods, then look for extension 0x00. That is enough to know a device is on www.youtube.com, not which video.

Trying it without root

-r replays a pcap and needs no root. The repo has a generator for a six-packet capture: a phone and a TV doing a TLS ClientHello and a DNS lookup each.

go run hack/gensample.go sample.pcap
./wtfi3 -i nosuch0 -r sample.pcap -listen 127.0.0.1:18080
curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/api/state

I gave it a nonexistent interface on purpose so it would not read my real one. The log says so:

WARN offline mode: interface unavailable, LAN attribution limited iface=nosuch0
INFO dashboard serving addr=127.0.0.1:18080 spoof=false
INFO finished replay; dashboard still serving (Ctrl-C to quit) addr=127.0.0.1:18080

/api/state, trimmed to the interesting fields:

"flows": [
  {"src": "192.168.0.20", "dst": "93.184.216.34", "proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443,
   "bytes": 1584, "packets": 2, "sni": "www.youtube.com"},
  {"src": "192.168.0.31", "dst": "140.82.121.4", "proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443,
   "bytes": 984, "packets": 2, "sni": "api.netflix.com"},
  ...
],
"dns": [
  {"client": "192.168.0.31", "name": "api.netflix.com", "type": "A", "answer": "44.242.61.10"},
  {"client": "192.168.0.20", "name": "www.youtube.com", "type": "A", "answer": "142.250.196.142"}
],
"devices": null

devices is empty because a device is a host inside one of the capture interface's on-link prefixes, and with no interface there are none. Flows and DNS do not depend on that. On a live interface the same packets fill in the device rows.

The browser gets the same JSON over Server-Sent Events, once a second, from /api/stream.

Naming the trackers

Raw flow tables tell you app-measurement.com. The Simple view tells you Google Analytics. The dictionary is 26 regexes in internal/web/index.html, covering ad networks, analytics, attribution SDKs, crash reporters, and IoT and smart TV telemetry (tuyaus.com is Tuya cloud, samsungacr.com is Samsung TV telemetry). Every pattern is anchored at a label boundary, and there is deliberately no catch-all for telemetry or metrics, because that cannot tell a third party from the device vendor's own servers.

Each device card gets a tracker badge: green for 0, amber for 1 to 4, red for 5 or more. A device that joins more than 20 seconds after startup is flagged NEW for 90 seconds. Everything already there at startup is the baseline.

The Detailed view drops the interpretation and shows the tables:

Seeing other devices

On a switched network your machine only receives its own unicast plus broadcast and multicast. Passive mode shows exactly that. To see the TV's flows you have to sit between it and the gateway, so wtfi3 has an ARP-spoof mode:

sudo ./wtfi3 -i en0 -spoof -i-own-this-network

-spoof alone refuses to run. With both flags it ARP-scans the subnet every 30 seconds, poisons each target and the gateway every 2 seconds, turns on IP forwarding, and on exit sends the real MACs back three times to restore the caches. Forwarding goes through net.inet.ip.forwarding on macOS and /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward on Linux, and goes back to whatever it was before. The gateway is the default route on the interface you capture on, not just the first default route the host has.

A relayed packet crosses the capture interface twice (target to me, me to gateway), so in spoof mode only the leg addressed to my MAC is counted. Otherwise every byte would show up double.

This is an active man-in-the-middle. Run it on a network you own.

The dashboard leaks too

The dashboard shows every device's DNS names and destinations with no password, so it binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Loopback alone is not enough: a web page in the same browser can reach it through DNS rebinding. So while it is bound to loopback, any request whose Host is not localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1 gets a 403:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: evil.example' 127.0.0.1:18080/api/state
403

-listen 0.0.0.0:8080 still works and logs a warning. An SSH tunnel is the better way to open it from another machine.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi3

title: wtfi2: Find the Hop Where Your Wi-Fi Connection Actually Dies
description:
The Wi-Fi icon shows full bars. The browser says "Offline". Then I am in a terminal running ping and traceroute, trying to line the answers up in my head.

My first attempt at fixing that was wtfi, a Go CLI for macOS that printed every check as a flat list. It was still ten lines I had to correlate myself. So I rewrote it in Rust as wtfi2: it draws the connection as a chain, probes every hop at once, and answers in one line.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi2
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/wtfi2 or cargo install wtfi2 (the command is wtfi)
  • Runs on macOS and Linux, no sudo

One line, then the evidence

wtfi sweeps Host, Wi-Fi, Gateway, Internet, DNS and captive portal concurrently, then walks the finished chain for the first hop that failed. Everything after that hop is collateral and does not get a verdict of its own.

A DNS-only outage, from the hidden --demo flag (a --features demo build that replays scripted sweeps on RFC 5737 addresses, so nothing here is my network). These are the first lines of the report:

  ✓ You ─── ✓ Wi-Fi ─── ✓ Gateway ─── ✓ Internet ─✗─ ✗ DNS ─── – Portal

  BROKEN   ✗ DNS resolution is failing

A cause line follows, then the fix and how it was measured:

            → Switch resolvers to 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8, or flush the DNS cache.
            evidence: cloudflare.com. asked of 3 resolvers under a 3s deadline (2 answered), plus one nonexistent-name check
             (likely cause)

Every verdict carries that evidence line and a confidence. One dropped packet and a five-probe burst should not read the same. wtfi -v shows the metrics behind each hop:

"Your ISP is down" needs a hop number

When the gateway answers and nothing past it does, wtfi adds an Uplink node and runs a bounded ICMP TTL sweep. A healthy run never pays for it. Where the replies stop decides the verdict: at the first step outside the house it blames the modem, ONU or WAN cable; deeper in, it blames the provider and names the last address that answered so you have something to quote on the support call.

If a full-tunnel VPN owns the default route, the same trace went through the tunnel, and the verdict says so instead of sending you to your ISP.

Not measured is not broken

A lot of the fixes in the git log restore one rule: a probe that could not run is unknown, not a failure. One example is #72. On corporate Wi-Fi and client-isolated APs, the gateway drops every ICMP echo and TCP probe. wtfi used to say "Your router isn't responding" while the WAN probe was going out through that same router. Now a silent gateway with a reachable WAN is graded ok and marked Probes: ignored (filtered).

The exit code follows the same rule. 0 is fine, 1 degraded, 2 broken, 3 unsupported OS, and 4 means the OS tools wtfi reads the network through would not run at all. A script should retry on 4, not page someone.

$ wtfi --demo=dns --json | jq '{status, first_break, verdict: (.verdict | {headline, confidence, source, fix})}'
{
  "status": "fail",
  "first_break": "dns",
  "verdict": {
    "headline": "DNS resolution is failing",
    "confidence": "likely",
    "source": "dns",
    "fix": "Switch resolvers to 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8, or flush the DNS cache."
  }
}
$ echo $?
2

Each probe is capped at 8 seconds and the whole sweep at 20 (--timeout changes that), so a hung resolver cannot hang the CLI.

The outage you only notice afterwards

Wi-Fi tends to break while I am in the middle of something, and by the time I sit down to look at it, it works again. So wtfi can record:

wtfi --record --every 30s   # headless, and faster while the network is broken
wtfi --history              # the last 20 sweeps, one line each
wtfi --bundle 2h | pbcopy   # Markdown for an AI agent

contrib/ has a launchd plist and a systemd user unit to keep the recorder running at login.

--bundle groups the sweeps into episodes and adds latency percentiles, a timeline that marks Wi-Fi channel changes (roams, band steering), the full JSON sweeps around each change, and the OS's own network log around each episode (log show on macOS, journalctl on Linux). It ends with a request for a root-cause analysis. SSIDs, MACs, public IPv4 addresses and this machine's IPv6 addresses are masked by default. The episode table from five recorded demo sweeps:

## Episodes

| Start | Duration | Sweeps | Worst | First break | Headline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-11-14 21:31:25Z | 11s | 3 | fail | dns | DNS resolution is failing |

If you would rather let the agent pull only what it needs, wtfi --mcp serves the same history over stdio:

claude mcp add wtfi -- wtfi --mcp

["list_episodes","get_timeline","get_sweeps","get_os_log","get_bundle","diagnose_now"]

That is the tools/list reply from the server.

Platforms

On macOS, link telemetry comes from CoreWLAN, so RSSI, noise, channel and PHY arrive instantly without system_profiler. Since macOS 14 the SSID and BSSID are redacted for apps without Location permission, so an unsigned build shows them as hidden. Nothing that matters for the diagnosis is lost. A signed .app with Location access is on the roadmap.

On Linux it reads the same facts without root through ip -j, iw and resolv.conf, falling back to /proc when those tools are missing. There is also a Nix flake: nix run github:kanywst/wtfi2 -- -w.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/wtfi2

title: whosent: A TUI That Shows Who Sent the Agent
description:
A request shows up from research-agent. The token says Alice. Between Alice and that agent there was a chat UI and a planner, three token exchanges, and the scope should have shrunk at each one. Decoding the JWT and squinting at nested act claims does not tell me whether it did.

I wrote y509 for X.509 chains. whosent is the same idea for delegation chains.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/whosent
  • Install: brew install --cask kanywst/tap/whosent or go install github.com/kanywst/whosent/cmd/whosent@latest

Scope from nowhere

whosent demo ships 41 scenarios across the four formats, and demo --emit writes any of them out as real files. This one is three exchanged JWTs where the last exchange gained a scope:

$ whosent demo --emit fixture jwt-bundle-widened && cd fixture
$ whosent check tokens.json --trust trust.json --audience https://api.acme.example --at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z
=== tokens.json · 3 links · JWT · issuer https://acme.okta.example, access token (RFC 9068)
    at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z, skew 30s, audience https://api.acme.example

❌ INVALID: the chain breaks at link 2, and no authority reaches below it

  #  issuer → subject                   J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 J7 J8 J9 J10 J11 J12
  0  alice@acme.example → chat-ui        ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·
  1  chat-ui → planner-agent             ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓   ✓   ·   ·
  2  planner-agent → research-agent      ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✗  ✓   ✓   ·   ·
     ✓ pass  ✗ fail  ! could not evaluate  ? not checked  - skipped  · does not apply

Findings
  ✗ J8 link 2: adds files:write, which token 1 did not hold [whosent bundle rule, derived from RFC 8693; not a procedure any specification defines (section 4.2, scope)]

How authority narrows
  0 → 1  chat-ui → planner-agent
      + exchanged: planner-agent now acts for alice@acme.example
      = scope files:read
      - scope files:write dropped
      = scope calendar:read
      ~ expires 20m sooner
  1 → 2  planner-agent → research-agent
      + exchanged: research-agent now acts for alice@acme.example
      = scope files:read
      - scope calendar:read dropped
      ✗ scope files:write was not in the token exchanged
      ~ expires 20m sooner
      i https://acme.okta.example → https://api.acme.example
          audience
      = kept  ~ narrowed  - dropped  + added  ✗ widened (violation)

Every signature is fine. The planner dropped files:write, and the research agent's token has it back. check evaluates every rule on every link instead of stopping at the first failure, so a chain with three faults shows all three.

Note the bracket on that finding. RFC 8693 does not define how to check a bundle of exchanged tokens against each other, so J7 to J10 are my rules, and the output says so.

The same question from the command line:

$ whosent ask tokens.json --trust trust.json --audience https://api.acme.example --at 2026-09-12T08:01:00Z --scope files:write
DENIED (HYPOTHETICAL): the chain does not verify, so it permits nothing. Hypothetically, if it verified, the token would hold this

! the first token held files:write, token 1 dropped it, and re-adding it later does not bring it back

  link by link
  0  chat-ui                      holds
  1  planner-agent                lacks  token 1 does not hold files:write
  2  research-agent               holds

The research agent's token does hold files:write. whosent still says no, and says which link lost it. On a chain that verifies with every key, the answer is AUTHORITATIVE instead.

The issuer's word is not a verified hop

One access token with nested act claims looks like a chain, but the prior actors are just what the issuer wrote (RFC 8693 section 4.1). whosent draws them that way:

✅ VALID: every checkable rule holds, but 2 prior actors are the issuer's word, not verified hop by hop

  #  issuer → subject                   J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 J7 J8 J9 J10 J11 J12
  0  alice@acme.example → chat-ui        ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·   (asserted by the issuer, not verified)
  1  chat-ui → planner-agent             ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·   (asserted by the issuer, not verified)
  2  planner-agent → research-agent      ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·   ·   ·   ·

If the token carries actor proofs (draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-proofs) or an Actor Chain profile (draft-mw-oauth-actor-chain-03), and the actors' own keys are in the trust file, each hop becomes the actor's own signed word. A forged one fails:

  ✗ J11 link 1: proof 1 (planner-agent): the signature does not verify against actor-planner-agent.json kid planner-agent-2026 [draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-proofs-01 section 7; whosent fails the token on a rejected chain, where the draft only drops the evidence]

Drop the keys and nothing turns green. The same okta-style token without --trust:

⚠️  INCOMPLETE: nothing failed, but some rules were not checked, so nothing is vouched for
...
  ? J2 link 2: no keys for issuer "https://acme.okta.example"; pass --jwks https://acme.okta.example=PATH [RFC 7515 section 5.2]

That exits 2. VALID is 0, INVALID is 1, and --strict turns INCOMPLETE into 1 for CI. Keys only come from what you pass; a JWT's jku, x5u, x5c and jwk are ignored.

Four formats, one view

Format One link is Checked against
JWT (act, ID-JAG, Txn-Tokens, Entra agent tokens) a token or an act level RFC 8693, the two actor drafts, whosent's bundle rules
Biscuit a block the spec's 38 sample tokens; Datalog evaluator is whosent's own
UCAN 1.0 a delegation or the invocation the spec's 1.0.0 fixtures
Macaroons (libmacaroons, Fly.io FlyV1) a caveat go-macaroon or superfly/macaroon, on every run

The macaroon cross-check is live: if whosent and the reference library disagree on a token, it exits 70 and asks you to report it.

A UCAN that widens its command looks like this:

❌ INVALID: the chain breaks at link 1, and no authority reaches below it
...
Findings
  ✗ U6 link 1: /msg is not under /msg/send, which the delegation above granted [https://github.com/ucan-wg/spec#command]

In the TUI, t opens a timeline of every link and ← → move the clock, so you can watch a block or a delegation expire, x simulates revoking a link (Biscuit and UCAN, labelled as simulated and never fed to check), and a asks the same question as whosent ask, prefilled from the row you selected.

Where it came from

whosent started as a viewer for mandatum, my own delegation format. Two days in, I dropped that format and kept the four that agents actually carry. mandatum is archived now. The viewer turned out to be the useful part.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/whosent

title: prpr, a Terminal List of Every Open GitHub Pull Request I Can See
description:
My open pull requests are spread out: my own repositories, the 0-draft org, and upstream projects I send patches to. Review requests come from all three. GitHub's pulls page shows what I opened or was asked to review, but not everything open in the orgs I belong to, so checking meant a handful of tabs.

prpr is one terminal screen with all of it. Enter opens the pull request in the browser. When it merges, it leaves the list with a 🎉.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/prpr
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/prpr, scoop install prpr (bucket kanywst/scoop-bucket), or go install github.com/kanywst/prpr@latest

The recording runs prpr --demo, which serves a fixed fixture list instead of GitHub, so nobody's real account ends up in a GIF.

No config

prpr reuses gh auth login, so there is no token to set up. At start it asks GitHub for your login and every org you are in, then runs one search per owner plus two more:

is:pr is:open archived:false user:<owner>
is:pr is:open archived:false author:<you>
is:pr is:open archived:false user-review-requested:<you>

The last two catch your patches to other people's projects and review requests from orgs you are not in. Anything outside the watched owners goes in the elsewhere tab, next to all, mine, to review, drafts and bots. Dependabot and Renovate stay in bots unless one asks you for a review by name.

The searches run separately, four at a time, instead of OR-ed into one query. An org that enforces SAML SSO your token is not authorized for then costs only its own pull requests: it is named in the header and the rest of the list stays up.

A config file exists for when you want something else (owners, exclude_owners, interval, issues). Unknown keys are an error, so a typo does not silently do nothing:

$ prpr --config config.yaml
prpr: config.yaml: yaml: unmarshal errors:
  line 2: field intervall not found in type config.Config

Saying goodbye without lying

A pull request missing from a refresh is not necessarily merged, and several of the fix commits in the log are about that. The search that covers it may have failed, hit the 60-result cap, or come back partial because GitHub withheld nodes the token cannot read. Or it only dropped out of user-review-requested because I submitted my review.

prpr handles each case differently:

  • a covering search failed: the pull request is carried over from the last refresh, no lookup
  • a covering search was partial: carried over, and its state is looked up anyway, since a partial answer can repeat on every refresh and would otherwise pin a merged pull request to the list for good
  • a covering search hit the cap: its state is looked up, and nothing is shown if it is still open
  • only the review request held it: it leaves quietly
  • otherwise: one GraphQL lookup asks how it ended, and the banner says so 
┃ 🌸 prpr  kanywst · 0-draft                                                             ⟳ 61s ┃
┃ ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ┃
┃ ▸ all 3  │  mine 2  │  to review 1  │  elsewhere 0  │  drafts 1  │  bots 0                   ┃
┃                                                                                              ┃
┃ ✨ 🎉 0-draft/api#127 fix: nil deref on empty body merged! nice one 🎊                       ┃

That is the repository's render test (go test ./internal/ui -run TestDumpRender -v) against its fixtures. A closed one gets 🌙, and one that only stopped matching the search gets 👋.

The last list is cached on disk, so prpr shows it instantly on start while the first refresh runs. Anything that merged while it was closed still gets its banner then.

What else changes on the row

Icon Meaning
🟢 / 🟡 / 🔴 / ⚪ Checks passing / running / failing / none
✅ / 🔁 / 👀 Approved / changes requested / review requested
💥 Conflicts with its base branch
🆕 Joined the list since you last looked
🔔 Its checks, review or conflict state changed since you last looked

🆕 and 🔔 clear once the cursor lands on the row, and both count what changed while prpr was closed. 🔔 compares the icon, not the raw state, so a change the row cannot show does not ring.

/ filters by title, repository, author, #number and labels. d opens a detail pane with branch, diff stat, reviewers and body. --issues mixes open issues in as 🎫, and polling pauses while the terminal is not focused.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/prpr

title: Disk Viewers Show Sizes. I Wanted One That Says Who Put the Bytes There.
description:
My Mac was out of space, and the biggest single file was ~/Library/Application Support/rancher-desktop/lima/0/diffdisk: 81G. That is Rancher Desktop's VM disk. Inside the VM, Docker used 3.4G and the filesystem 3.6G. The other 77G was space the guest had already freed and never handed back to macOS.

docker system prune does not touch that. fstrim inside the guest does. No disk viewer I had would tell me either fact; they list directories and sizes. Cleaners delete a fixed list of caches, and a VM disk is not on it.

Same machine: a 54G podman-machine-default-arm64.raw that took 16G on disk because it is sparse. Tools that add up file lengths reported 54.

So I wrote chonk. It groups every byte by who put it there, says why it exists, and gets it back with that owner's own command.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/chonk
  • Install: brew install --cask kanywst/tap/chonk or go install github.com/kanywst/chonk/cmd/chonk@latest

The recording runs on a canned machine (CHONK_DEMO=1), so none of it is a real disk.

Walk first, attribute second

Before chonk I had a Caches tab in another tool, sweep. It knew eight caches: Go, npm, pnpm, yarn, uv, pip, Homebrew. The things actually eating my disk were a VM disk, a Podman machine, a Rust target/, a project .cache and the Nix store. A fixed list will always miss the big ones.

chonk walks everything first and attributes second. Rules claim subtrees (Rancher Desktop's lima dir, ~/.rustup, ~/Library/Caches/go-build, a git working tree and the target/ or node_modules/ inside it). Whatever no rule claims is still listed as "unclaimed", at the directory where its size concentrates, so nothing big hides behind an unknown name.

Sizes are allocated blocks (st_blocks * 512), not file lengths, and a hard-linked file counts once. That is what fixes the 54G-vs-16G Podman image, and it keeps the Nix store from being counted several times over.

Asking why one path exists

chonk why PATH does not scan the disk. It asks the rules about each directory from the top down to PATH and measures only what the owner claims.

To get output without putting my own home in an article, I pointed HOME at a throwaway directory: a Rust project tally with 437M in target/, a 20G sparse Podman image with 512M written into it, and three rustup toolchains.

$ chonk why ~/src/tally/target | sed "s#$HOME#~#g"
~/src/tally/target
  Cargo target/, 437M on disk
  build output of the project ~/src/tally

why:     Compiled Rust: every profile, every dependency, incremental caches.
regen:   Rebuilt by the next `cargo build`.
safety:  safe
written: 1m ago

biggest inside:
     437M  debug

reclaim:
  [safe] cargo clean
      cargo clean --manifest-path ~/src/tally/Cargo.toml --target-dir ~/src/tally/target
  [safe] Move to the Trash
      move to the Trash

The project around it is a different answer. chonk asks git what the tree holds that no remote has. tally has one commit that was never pushed:

$ chonk why ~/src/tally
~/src/tally
  ~/src/tally, 437M on disk

why:     A git working tree with work that only this disk has.
regen:   Only here: 1 commit on main that no remote has.
safety:  danger
written: 0s ago

biggest inside:
     437M  target

A tree that is clean and fully pushed says so and names the remote it would come back from. Uncommitted work, a stash, or a commit no remote has (on a branch, a detached HEAD or a tag) makes it danger. A remote on the same disk does not count as a backup.

The sparse image:

$ chonk why ~/.local/share/containers/podman/machine/applehv/podman-machine-default-arm64.raw
~/.local/share/containers/podman/machine/applehv/podman-machine-default-arm64.raw
  Podman machine, 512M on disk
  claimed at ~/.local/share/containers/podman/machine
...
inside:
  Disk image: 512M on disk (20.0G maximum), podman-machine-default-arm64.raw
  Sparse: 20.0G of file lengths take 512M on disk; tools that add up lengths overstate this
  Podman has no machine any more. What is left here is leftover files; moving them to the Trash is safe.

The last line is real too: podman is installed here, but with HOME swapped it has no machine registered, so chonk calls the image leftovers.

For toolchains it reads the pins in your projects (.nvmrc, rust-toolchain.toml, .tool-versions and a few more) plus each manager's default. My fake home has stable as rustup's default, 1.79.0 pinned by tally, and a nightly nobody asks for:

$ chonk why --json ~/.rustup | jq '.parts[] | {path, command: .actions[0].command}' | sed "s#$HOME#~#g"
{
  "path": "~/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-2025-06-01-aarch64-apple-darwin",
  "command": "RUSTUP_HOME=~/.rustup rustup toolchain uninstall nightly-2025-06-01-aarch64-apple-darwin"
}

That one is marked careful, not safe. A shell script chonk never read could still want that nightly.

Getting it back

Every action is the owner's own command: cargo clean, go clean -cache, brew cleanup --prune=all, rdctl shell -- sudo fstrim -v /mnt/data for Rancher Desktop, podman machine rm. Or a move to the Trash, which chonk tells you frees nothing until you empty it. chonk itself never deletes a file, and the commands come from rules compiled into the binary, never from anything it finds on disk.

Nothing runs without y on a confirmation that shows the exact command and its risk. enter does not confirm. If a process is running from what the action removes (the VM's host agent, a dev server in a project), the dialog says so.

After a run, chonk compares the volume's free space before and after, and appends what was expected and what actually came back to a ledger. When a VM prune frees blocks inside the guest, it runs the trim too, because otherwise the Mac sees nothing.

Things no directory shows

The header compares what the walk counted with what statfs says the volume uses, so the gap (swap, logs, other users, /Library) is not mistaken for nothing. Time Machine local snapshots, which keep deleted files' blocks alive, are listed as their own item. A running app's code-sign clone in /var/folders shows up as the second copy of the bundle that it is.

chonk schedule on installs a launchd agent that runs chonk snapshot once a day at low I/O priority, so chonk diff always has a baseline to say what grew since last week.

Speed

On macOS chonk reads directories with getattrlistbulk(2): one call returns names and allocated sizes for a batch of entries. On a home with three million files that took a full scan from 38 seconds (ReadDir plus lstat) to about 30. The rest is APFS metadata I/O, and more workers only contend on it.

Not yet

Purgeable space, which needs Foundation's volume capacity keys, and per-snapshot sizes, which APFS does not expose.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/chonk

title: I Log Every Movie I Watch as a Markdown File, Filed Through GitHub Issues
description:
I keep a diary of every film I watch: score, where it streams, a one-line impression. It lives in a git repo as markdown, and a small React site reads it.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/i-watched-movies
  • Live: https://kanywst.github.io/i-watched-movies/

One file per film

Every entry is movies/<slug>.md. This is the current top of the diary, trimmed (the cover URL and EN/JA summaries are cut):

---
title: 'Kingsman: The Secret Service'
title_ja: 'キングスマン'
published: true
tags:
  - 'Action'
  - 'Comedy'
national: 'UK'
streaming:
  - 'Disney+'
  - 'Prime Video'
checked: '2026-09'
release_date: '2015-01-29'
watch_date: '2026-09-23'
point: 8.9
---

Titles are stored in the original language (기생충, 無間道), with title_en and title_ja underneath when they differ. A build script walks movies/, writes one JSON file for the React app, plus an RSS feed, a sitemap and a static page per film so a shared link unfurls as that film.

Four flags split the files into five lists, and the precedence is fixed in src/partition.ts: dropped beats watching beats seen beats rated. Right now the 245 files break down like this (computed from the repo with that same function):

watched (rated)  76
seen (unrated)   60
dropped          76
watchlist        32
in progress       1

Yes, I have given up on as many films as I have rated. Dropped gets its own tab and stays out of the stats, so it does not drag anything down.

Adding a film is an issue

I almost never edit the files by hand. The repo has an "Add a movie" issue form. Submitting it starts movie-from-issue.yml, which parses the form, writes the file, runs lint, tests and build, opens a PR, squash-merges it and dispatches the Pages deploy. Progress shows up as labels on the issue: status: queued, processing, pr-opened, merged, or failed with a link to the run.

Filing an issue for a slug that already exists updates that entry, which is how a film moves from Watchlist to Watched. An empty field keeps the old value. Issue #1498 only bumped a watchlist rank, so its body is two fields:

### Title

九龍城寨之圍城

### List

Watchlist

### Recommend rank

32

Running the same parser locally against that body:

$ ISSUE_BODY="$(gh issue view 1498 --json body --jq .body)" ISSUE_NUMBER=1498 \
    node scripts/build-movie-from-issue.js
slug=twilight-of-the-warriors-walled-in
path=movies/twilight-of-the-warriors-walled-in.md
title=九龍城寨之圍城
list=Watchlist
watchlist=true
action=update

It found the existing file by title, merged, and wrote nothing new because the rank was already 32. The repo has 672 issues now. When I file a batch, they run in parallel, and a merge that loses the race to main retries up to five times with backoff.

The Stats page argues with me

The Stats tab compares genre, country and era averages against my personal average. From the current data:

baseline 7.65  median 7.85  spread 1.09
Crime     28 films  7.96  +0.31
Mystery   19 films  7.98  +0.33
Comedy    11 films  7.52  -0.13
Japan     23 films  7.35  -0.30
On release 29 films 7.38  -0.27
Catch-up   47 films 7.82  +0.17

Films I see within 90 days of release score lower than ones I catch up on later. A catch-up is usually something I already heard was good, so that gap measures picking as much as taste.

It also ranks the watchlist by the score the profile predicts. One rating broke that early. 新解釈・幕末伝 got a 1.0, and on its own it pulled Period to -3.04, which put Kingsman: The Golden Circle 42nd of 44 on the watchlist while the first Kingsman sat at the top. Now any score more than two standard deviations from the mean is capped before predicting. The averages on the page stay raw.

The page also backtests itself: predict every rated film from the other 75 and compare the miss against just guessing the average.

model error     0.71
baseline error  0.71

That is 0.705 against 0.711, and the page prints "That is 1% closer." Genre and country explain almost nothing about how I score a film. The page prints both numbers live, so the ranking never claims more than it has.

"Top of the diary" replays the #1 spot in watch order. 28 Years Later held it for 313 days, until The Devil Wears Prada 2 took it for nine.

Running it 

npm install
npm run dev

I ran npm test on a fresh clone: 21 files, 316 tests, all pure logic, no component tests. The README has a short list of what to change if you want to fork it for your own log.

title: howbad: What a Prompt-Injected Coding Agent Could Do With the Credentials on Your Machine
description:
Claude Code, Codex and Cursor run as me. A prompt injection in a README or an issue comment doesn't need a sandbox escape. It gets whatever my shell gets: the gh token, the npm token that publishes packages, the AWS profile from this morning, the Slack token pasted into an MCP config.

I knew roughly what was on my laptop. I didn't know what any of it could do. "There is a GitHub token" and "this token can push to 49 repos and rewrite their CI" are different answers, so I wrote a tool that gives the second one.

  • Source: https://github.com/kanywst/howbad
  • Install: brew install kanywst/tap/howbad or go install github.com/kanywst/howbad@latest

The report

This is the repo's demo harness (go run ./internal/demo): a throwaway home directory with fake tokens, and an httptest server standing in for GitHub, npm and Slack. Same binary, same report code.

  howbad · if a coding agent on this machine got hijacked right now, it could:

  CRITICAL  push code to 49 GitHub repos and rewrite their CI workflows
            e.g. acme/sdk-js (1830★), you/dotfiles (240★), acme/payments (12★)
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  CRITICAL  publish new versions of 3 npm packages (234k downloads/week) unless npm demands 2FA (inferred)
            e.g. @acme/sdk (184k/week), @acme/cli (41k/week), @acme/ui (9.8k/week)
            ↳ npm · you on npm · ~/.npmrc · #f54f870e
  HIGH      change settings on 2 repos (branch protection, deploy keys, webhooks)
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  HIGH      read message history in Acme: public channels, private channels, DMs
  HIGH      search every message you can see in Acme
  HIGH      post messages as you in Acme (trusted-sender phishing)
            ↳ MCP server "slack" (Cursor) · you in Slack workspace Acme · ~/.cursor/mcp.json · #dadd4c65
  MEDIUM    spend money on your OpenAI API account (not verified)
            ↳ $OPENAI_API_KEY · environment variable $OPENAI_API_KEY · #85bd6af8
  MEDIUM    create secret gists, a ready-made exfiltration channel
            ↳ gh CLI · you on github.com · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1

  one login away:
    AWS profile prod: likely do anything (role AdministratorAccess) once logged in again

  agents running as you: Claude Code (bypassPermissions), Cursor, Codex
  pasted straight into agent configs: 1 credential
  5 credentials · 3 verified read-only with the issuer · nothing sent anywhere else

Each line is a capability, not a token. The #e9e4a9d1 is the first 8 hex of the token's SHA-256, so you can tell two tokens apart without the secret ever being printed. The AWS profile is an SSO profile whose session expired, so it lands under "one login away" with the role name instead of being dropped. The footer lists which agents are installed and flags Claude Code because its settings set defaultMode to bypassPermissions.

Where it looks and who it asks

It reads env vars, the gh CLI (hosts.yml or keychain), .npmrc, ~/.aws, kubeconfig, gcloud and Application Default Credentials, and the MCP configs of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, VS Code, Zed, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Continue, Windsurf, Devin Desktop and Claude Desktop.

Each credential goes only to the provider that issued it, and only to read-only endpoints:

Credential Asked with Comes back as
GitHub GET /user, /user/repos, the X-OAuth-Scopes header repos you can push to, CI workflow access, admin repos, gists
npm whoami, token list, package search packages you maintain and their weekly downloads
Slack auth.test scopes history, search, posting as you
AWS sts:GetCallerIdentity, attached policies identity, account, policy or SSO permission set
Kubernetes SelfSubjectAccessReview per context cluster-admin, Secrets, exec, pod creation
GitLab GET /personal_access_tokens/self push, CI/CD, registries, runners, admin
Google Cloud testIamPermissions per project (up to 25) IAM admin, impersonation, Secret Manager, GKE

Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google API keys, Hugging Face tokens and database URLs are recognized by format and never called. That's why the OpenAI line says "not verified".

Where it can't read permissions

Fine-grained GitHub tokens, GitHub App tokens and npm tokens can't report their own permissions. For those, howbad reports the account's access as an upper bound and marks it inferred. The repo's own rule for this is "under-reporting is the dangerous direction", and it shows up in the code: a GitHub token with no X-OAuth-Scopes gets every repo the user can push to, prefixed with "up to".

--offline shows the same thing without any network calls. Everything becomes an upper bound:

  CRITICAL  likely do anything (role AdministratorAccess) (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ AWS profile prod · ~/.aws/config
  HIGH      use a GitHub token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ gh CLI · ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml · #e9e4a9d1
  HIGH      use an npm token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ npm · ~/.npmrc · #f54f870e

Being boring with live credentials

A tool that reads every token on the machine is itself a good injection target, so:

  • The secret is an unexported field on cred.Credential, and the type implements fmt.Formatter, so %v, %+v and %#v can't print it either. Tests assert no secret appears in any output.
  • --no-exec skips everything that runs a helper: gh auth token, gcloud auth print-access-token, AWS credential_process, kubeconfig exec plugins.
  • Configs in the current directory are read, but a cloned repo can't steer where a token goes. ${VAR} in a repo's .npmrc isn't expanded, and if both the token and its host come from a repo-local config, nothing is sent: 
case c.RepoLocal && h != "" && h != "github.com":
    // A cloned repo names this host; don't let it make howbad dial out.
    f.Status, f.Detail = finding.Unverified, "token and host both come from a repo-local config; not sent"

In CI

--fail-on high exits 2 if anything at or above that severity is reachable. It also exits 2 when a credential couldn't be checked, because "couldn't check" isn't "safe":

$ howbad --offline --no-exec --fail-on high
  howbad · if a coding agent on this machine got hijacked right now, it could:

  HIGH      use an npm token as its owner (inferred, not checked)
            ↳ npm · ~/.npmrc, ./.npmrc · #f54f870e

  1 credential · 0 verified read-only with the issuer · nothing sent anywhere else
$ echo $?
2

--json gives the same findings with severity, inferred and status per credential. Those fields and the exit code are treated as an API.

Not covered

Custom AWS policies aren't evaluated, only attached policy names. Remote MCP servers using OAuth keep their tokens in the agent's own store, often the keychain, which howbad doesn't read. Claude Code policies pushed through macOS configuration profiles aren't read either.

Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/howbad

title: The most humane invention in computing
description:
Originally published at https://ketushah.com/writing/the-most-humane-invention-in-computing/

The most humane invention in computing

To err is human. Pope wrote that in 1711, and three centuries later it is still the most important sentence in software design. People are going to make mistakes. Not occasionally, not the careless ones among us. Everyone, constantly. It is the starting condition, and any system that takes input from a user has to be designed from it.

Which is probably why undo was never invented once. It kept getting invented. A system at Brown had it in 1968. A Lisp programming tool had it by 1971. Xerox PARC put it in a text editor in 1974. These people were not copying each other. They were all watching the same thing happen: a person at a keyboard, doing something they did not mean to do, with no way back. When the Macintosh shipped, Undo sat at the top of the Edit menu. It still does.

So the rule I design by: wherever there is user input, there has to be a way to correct it. Self-serve wherever possible, a button, an edit, a window of time to change your mind. And where self-serve genuinely cannot work, an easy path to something that can correct it, another system or an actual human. Amendment or undo, in one form or another, everywhere input exists. It is not a feature to add when there is time. It is part of what accepting the input means.

Where it gets hard is the guardrails, and I will be honest: there is no formula for those. It is circumstance based. What decides it is the consequences of the undo itself. Before I let a user reverse something on their own, I want the action mapped, upstream and downstream. What consumed this input? What already acted on it? If the damage from reversing is contained, hand the user the button and get out of the way. If the reversal ripples into other systems and other people, self-serve is the wrong tool. That correction needs a process, checks, maybe a human reviewing it. The mistake gets corrected either way. The route is what changes.

The map has a clock on it too. Ask whether the mistake’s ramifications are permanent, and whether they have already landed. Order something online and you can cancel it, but the window depends on the vendor: zero minutes from one, fifteen from another. Then the order ships and the window does not narrow. It ends. Anyone who has tried to get UPS or FedEx to intercept a package or reroute it midstream has felt the far side of that line. The act left the database and entered the physical world, and only the database part was ever reversible.

Some of that is just physics, and physics is not a design flaw. Some of it is complexity that got baked in for reasons nobody remembers. Either way, once the act itself cannot be undone, the question changes to whether its consequences can be amended. You cannot un-ship a box. You can return it, refund it, send the right one. And the amendment has a simple test. It worked when whatever the user intended to achieve is achieved. Not when the ticket closed. When the person ends up where they were trying to go.

Gmail’s Undo Send is the famous version of this. Launched in 2009, and it has never recalled a single email. It delays the send, five seconds at first, up to thirty now, so the undo is really a grace period with good marketing. I mean that as praise. Where reversal is impossible, time is the substitute. A window before the act becomes real, and where that fails, an amendment after.

Given all that, why do so many systems give you no way back at all? Collect the reasons and they are mostly unglamorous. Complexity. Oversight. Cost. A dependency on some external party whose system will not cooperate. A product team that never foresaw the need. A mistake so rare that building the correction never survived prioritization. Those are engineering economics, and some of them are even true. But there is one more reason on the list, and it is not like the others. Sometimes there is no undo because no undo is the business model. A flow that takes ten seconds to enter and ten days to leave is not an accident. It is somebody’s decision, taken for gains.

Here is the part that should bother us. From the user’s chair, there is no way to tell those reasons apart. The screen does not say whether the correction path is missing because it could not be built, or because somebody chose not to build it. It is just not clear, not until the user makes the mistake and goes looking for the undo that may or may not be there. That is when a system shows you what it thinks of you. Ideally before you need to know.

Originally published at https://ketushah.com/writing/the-most-humane-invention-in-computing/
