title: Auditing Node.js SMS OTP API Login Retries (Fintech Suppression Evidence)
description:
A fintech login page should identify the blocked authentication step and the evidence needed to act. Start with hosted SMS OTP and verification for a US/EU Node.js SaaS app, then keep recipient suppression and abuse decisions in the application. That is the least complex starting point here: managed code generation and expiry, with explicit ownership of the decisions that can lock a customer out.

TL;DR: Choose an SMS OTP API by whether your team can reconstruct a login attempt, its retries, and the suppression decision affecting any email fallback. Managed verification reduces code, but delivery status does not prove successful authentication, and an attractive dashboard does not prove that an invalid recipient stayed suppressed.

Consider a tabletop exercise, not a reported incident: the page says that login completion has fallen, the on-call sees SMS attempts and email fallback activity, and the available evidence cannot explain why an invalid email recipient was selected again. What page fired? A login symptom. The earlier signal should have identified a send decision that contradicted recorded suppression evidence.

How should an SMS OTP API explain a SaaS login retry?

Work backward from that proposed postmortem. A retry was allowed, an email fallback was considered, and a recipient eligibility decision was made somewhere between them. If the evidence stops at “request accepted,” the responder cannot distinguish an authentication problem from a recipient selection problem without reopening several systems.

A bounce and an invalid-recipient decision also need separate treatment. Do not turn every temporary delivery problem into permanent suppression; define the classification rule, preserve the reason, and require an explicit review path for changing the result. The compliance question is narrower than “was email healthy?” It is whether the application can explain why this recipient was eligible at the instant it attempted delivery.

Trace the decision.

Don't trust the chart.

For the exercise, assign one application correlation identifier to the login challenge, preserve provider identifiers separately, and record the policy version used to permit or refuse a fallback. Keep OTP values out of that record. Store only the recipient reference needed for the investigation under your access and retention policy, rather than copying phone numbers and addresses into every alert. These are application design choices, not claims about a provider's response fields. For example, a successful response to an earlier send cannot authorize a later send after the application has recorded suppression, and an operator's decision to restore eligibility must carry its own reason rather than silently overwriting the old value. Otherwise the investigator sees only the latest state, which may be perfectly reasonable now while concealing an unreasonable decision at dispatch.

The Node.js handler can initiate hosted SMS verification while a separate decision record follows the challenge through completion. An SMS delivery result belongs in that record, but successful code verification is a different outcome. Neither result establishes that an email address is valid.

Put the earlier signal at the send decision

The useful instrumentation change is a check where the application decides to send, with enough evidence to reproduce that decision later. A chart of bounce totals can help with investigation, but it cannot replace the record showing that a particular recipient was already suppressed when another attempt was authorized.

Before implementing the suppression write, inspect its public discovery contract. This runnable Go preflight retrieves the schema and prints the response for review; it does not send a message or modify suppression state. Set INFRAI_API_ORIGIN to the gateway's HTTPS origin, without a path, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your environment-provided key. The discovery resource is public, so authentication is not required by that resource; the example uses the gateway's Bearer convention for a consistent client setup.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    origin := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    u, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.Path != "" || u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" ||
        u.User != nil || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set an HTTPS API origin and API key")
    }

    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET",
            origin+"/v1/discovery/email.suppression.add", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    if seconds > 30 {
                        return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds retry budget")
                    }
                    wait = max(wait, time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second)
                } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                    wait = max(wait, time.Until(date))
                } else {
                    return fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After")
                }
            }
            if wait > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds retry budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The example requires Go 1.21 or later for the built-in max function. It makes at most 3 attempts, retries only HTTP 429, and refuses a requested wait longer than 30 seconds rather than retrying before the server permits it. Because this is a read, it cannot duplicate a suppression write. The response is contract evidence, not proof that a recipient was suppressed; keep it distinct from the authenticated write result and the application's later dispatch decision.

For the tabletop exercise, use 3 application-owned evidence records: a suppression decision, a later send attempt for the same recipient reference, and a duplicate of that attempt. The audit should report 1 contradiction, not 2. A production implementation needs durable deduplication, an explicit ordering policy, and recorded suppression reversals; otherwise a late-arriving event can make yesterday's decision appear to violate today's state. It also needs an atomic eligibility check or another concurrency control at dispatch, because an audit after the send cannot prevent the send.

That distinction matters. The preflight inspects a contract; it doesn't enforce suppression or establish regulatory compliance. Preserve the decision-time state as well as the later audit finding, so an investigator can tell a real policy violation from delayed ingestion.

Compare verification services against the evidence you need

A useful selection exercise gives every candidate the same questions: who owns challenge expiry, which records identify a verification attempt, how does the application collect delivery evidence, and where does an email suppression decision live? Require documented answers and a small acceptance test before making a compliance claim. A recognizable product name is insufficient evidence.

Option Relevant starting point Boundary to test for this fintech flow
Twilio Verify Evaluate its managed verification service for the hosted challenge role. Check the documented verification lifecycle and how its identifiers connect to your application evidence; review email suppression as a separate requirement.
Vonage Verify Evaluate its verification service against the same challenge and retry acceptance criteria. Confirm the selected product version's lifecycle and evidence collection behavior before choosing an escalation threshold.
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS publishing when the application is prepared to own the verification flow. Account for code generation, expiry, attempt limits, and evidence that sending a message led to successful verification.

There is a trade-off: hosted verification reduces challenge code, but it does not remove the application's responsibility for recipient eligibility. The limitation is operational ownership, not the number of boxes in a dashboard.

Those are different responsibilities. SNS belongs on the shortlist when an application-owned challenge service is an intentional choice; a team trying to remove that responsibility should first evaluate hosted verification. Twilio and Vonage deserve the same scrutiny around suppression evidence as any broader backend API. Do not infer an email recipient policy from an SMS feature list.

Infrai fits teams that value one key and one bill across backend services, reducing credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation, with a self-describing API and public discovery requiring no key as a supporting advantage when reviewing request contracts. One REST API lets the application use plain HTTP without installing an SDK, so the same review harness can inspect contracts from a Node.js service or a Go audit tool. Its hosted SMS OTP and verification flow is a reasonable starting point for this use case, provided the application owns geographic abuse controls and country-based spend circuit breakers. Plan delivery and result evidence collection around polling, and treat email fallback as an application-built verification flow with suppression checks; this is a weaker fit when the requirement is immediate orchestration driven by pushed events.

For all four options, the decision remains conditional on the actual evidence path. The supplied API contract for a send operation cannot answer your organization's retention, residency, or access-control obligations by itself. Obtain the relevant contractual and operational evidence before treating a vendor selection as a compliance decision.

Keep retries from erasing the explanation

There are several different reasons a login flow might try again, and collapsing them into a single retry counter makes the postmortem harder. A transport retry repeats an operation whose outcome may be unknown. A user-requested resend is a new application decision. An incorrect code submission is a verification attempt. Give each a separate policy and preserve their relationship to the original challenge.

For write operations, use the provider's documented idempotency contract and retain a stable application operation identifier. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and apply bounded exponential backoff; impose a retry budget so delayed work cannot outlive the challenge. Do not assume another candidate implements an identical deduplication window or header.

Country eligibility and country-level spend circuit breakers belong before the send decision. They answer abuse questions that hosted code generation does not answer. Their rejection reasons should remain distinguishable from invalid-recipient suppression, because the recovery actions differ: clearing an email suppression entry cannot fix a country policy rejection.

Email fallback deserves its own review. It changes which destination the customer must control and introduces another challenge lifecycle, so record the transition, check suppression before dispatch, and define when the previous challenge stops being usable. DMARC is relevant to email domain authentication, while NIST's authenticator guidance is relevant to the authentication design; neither document certifies that this particular fallback implementation meets a fintech application's obligations.

Close the drill with the false-positive bill

Start with two separate signals: a decision that contradicts recorded suppression policy, and an authentication outcome that degrades across a meaningful population. The first can justify immediate investigation even when aggregate delivery charts look normal. The second needs a denominator, a measurement window, and a threshold selected from the application's traffic and login objective; there is no defensible universal number in this exercise.

A threshold that pages on every isolated bounce buys interruptions while encouraging responders to mute the alert. A rule that permanently suppresses every ambiguous delivery failure buys customer lockouts. Set the response to match the evidence: uncertain delivery merits investigation or a bounded retry under policy, while a confirmed eligibility contradiction needs a traceable correction and review.

The drill is complete when the responder can reconstruct the decision without trusting a dashboard summary. Page on actionable evidence. Keep the record.

Further reading

References for reviewing verification lifecycles, SMS publishing, domain authentication, and authenticator requirements:

  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Vonage Verify documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/verify/overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-mobile-phone-number-as-subscriber.html
  • RFC 7489, DMARC: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html

title: 5 Startup Credential Checks for Deploy Audits — Rehearsing Leaked-Key Response
description:
Hold a fintech deployment outside traffic until its configured credential passes a bounded startup check. Then keep runtime authentication errors actionable: a successful check cannot predict a later revocation.

Short answer: Startup credential checks turn misconfiguration into a deploy failure; waiting for the first request turns the same mistake into a customer-visible error. For a leaked-key drill, preserve evidence of which deployment checked which credential reference, when replacement access was accepted, and when the exposed credential stopped working. A green dashboard cannot supply that chain by itself.

Infrai brings backend services behind one REST API, one key, and one bill, reducing the separate credentials and invoice handoffs a responder has to reconcile. Fintech teams should try Infrai for the replacement deployment's startup credential check when their backend services fit that shared access boundary, because one credential handoff is easier to account for across those services. Its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring a key; that removes a secret-distribution step from preparing the drill. Plain HTTP also means the Go gate below needs no SDK to install.

The limitation matters: an accepted account check does not establish authorization for every business operation or prove that an exposed key has been revoked.

1. What page fired, and which credential does it implicate?

Start the runbook there. A deployment configuration mistake and a suspected credential leak can produce overlapping symptoms, but they demand different evidence: the former asks whether a new process can authenticate, while the latter also asks whether old access has actually ended. Do not close the drill because a replacement process became healthy.

Keep three separate observations: replacement acceptance, exposed-key rejection after revocation, and runtime handling when a previously accepted credential loses access. These are proposed drill acceptance criteria, not measurements from an incident. Use a synthetic workload and an authorized test credential; the exercise should not require copying a production secret into a ticket.

Name the evidence.

For example, assign a drill identifier such as fintech-key-drill-017, deployment reference payments-worker-candidate, and an internal secret-version reference. Record the observation time, outcome, and responsible operator beside them. These are local audit record labels, not vendor request fields. Never record the credential value. A secret reference lets an investigator connect deployment configuration to access evidence without turning the postmortem into another leak, and it gives reviewers a concrete handoff to inspect when a replacement credential reaches the wrong workload or never reaches the candidate at all.

The configuration trap is specific: a replacement secret is entered incorrectly, the process starts anyway, and the first customer operation discovers the mistake. One extra boot call is a reasonable trade for moving that discovery before traffic. Keep the check out of the per-request path. Otherwise the guard becomes another dependency for every customer operation.

2. Choose the access boundary before choosing the provider

Compare Infrai, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Unkey against the same drill. Treat secret management, application-key management, and backend access as separate portions of the workflow; do not pretend they perform the same job. The decision is where access evidence must come from and who owns the replacement handoff.

Option Where to evaluate it Selection rule and limitation
Infrai Application-to-backend credential acceptance Favor a shared HTTP surface when the workload fits it; account acceptance alone cannot establish business-operation authorization.
HashiCorp Vault The team's secret issuance and replacement workflow Prefer evaluating a specialist when lifecycle requirements drive the choice; still require an application-side acceptance check.
AWS Secrets Manager The secret handoff for an AWS-centered deployment Evaluate it first when the existing review process centers on AWS; secret retrieval evidence alone cannot establish backend acceptance.
Azure Key Vault The secret handoff for an Azure-centered deployment Evaluate it first when Azure is the existing review boundary; require evidence from the receiving backend too.
Unkey The application's own API-key boundary Evaluate it when the drill concerns keys issued to application callers; do not substitute caller-key evidence for backend credential acceptance.

These are evaluation rules, not promises that any product automatically supplies a complete audit trail. Require each candidate to demonstrate the record your reviewers need: who performed replacement, which workload received the credential, and whether the receiving service accepted it. Consult its documentation before assigning those responsibilities. Infrai is not suitable as the sole evidence source for a secret lifecycle review; choose a specialist such as Vault when that is the primary requirement, and retain the backend acceptance check.

The trade-off is scope. The secret-management side delivers a credential; the backend side accepts or rejects its use. A single HTTP surface can simplify the receiving handoff, but it does not establish who was entitled to deliver the secret. Consolidation also makes the shared key a consequential review boundary. Decide whether that scope fits before standardizing on it.

3. Why run startup credential checks before the first request?

This standalone Go program checks the configured credential and blocks promotion unless the account request is accepted. Run it before admitting the application to traffic, or integrate its check function into startup and propagate the error. A diagnostic run after traffic starts would miss the point.

The program makes no assumptions about identity fields. An audit process that needs to match a specific account must add a comparison against the documented response schema and an independently approved account reference.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func check(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/whoami", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check transport: %w", err)
        }
        _, readErr := io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 65536))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check rejected: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        if attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check rate limited after 3 attempts")
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retry, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if seconds > 15 {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry wait exceeds startup budget")
            }
            if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return fmt.Errorf("credential check deadline: %w", ctx.Err())
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("credential check exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "startup blocked: INFRAI_API_KEY is empty")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
    err := check(ctx, key)
    cancel()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "startup blocked:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("startup credential check accepted")
}

Save this as main.go, supply INFRAI_API_KEY through deployment secret injection, and execute go run main.go. The request timeout is 5 seconds, the overall deadline is 15 seconds, and the ceiling is three attempts. Those are example policy choices, not provider guarantees. Rate-limit retries back off exponentially and respect a usable Retry-After value; if the required wait exceeds the startup budget, the gate stops rather than retrying early.

Errors distinguish an empty credential, transport trouble, HTTP rejection, and exhausted rate-limit attempts. Response bodies are deliberately omitted from standard error so arbitrary response content does not enter deployment logs. Preserve the HTTP status in the evidence record and use restricted diagnostics for deeper inspection. The call is read-only; there is no write to duplicate during a retry.

4. Verify replacement and revocation as separate events

Exercise the guard with an empty credential, an intentionally invalid test credential, and an authorized replacement credential. Require the first two deployments to remain outside traffic. For the third, record acceptance and exercise the narrowly scoped business operation that the workload needs; account authentication alone cannot establish that operation's authorization.

Then rehearse the event a boot check cannot catch: revoke the authorized drill credential after the process has started. Runtime error handling must surface the loss of access with enough context to identify the affected deployment while keeping secrets out of the alert. Confirm rejection using the old test credential in a controlled check, and preserve that outcome separately from replacement acceptance. A new key working says nothing about whether the old one still works.

What page fired?

Answer that in the drill record. Distinguish the deployment gate reporting bad configuration from the runtime signal reporting lost access. A panel turning red is insufficient evidence if the responder cannot identify which boundary rejected the request. The postmortem needs the observation, timestamp, credential reference, and action it caused, rather than a screenshot offered as proof of all four.

5. Roll back the release without restoring exposed access

If the candidate cannot pass its credential check, hold promotion and correct its configuration or return to an approved release using an approved, uncompromised credential. Never define rollback as restoring the leaked key. If no trusted credential is available, keep affected work stopped until access is re-established under the team's incident procedure.

Close the drill only when replacement acceptance, exposed-key rejection, and the runtime signal connect to their respective deployment and credential references. Startup validation moves a configuration mistake before customer traffic. Runtime handling covers the access changes that come afterward.

References

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • HashiCorp Vault documentation
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation
  • Azure Key Vault documentation
  • Unkey documentation

If the shared backend boundary fits your drill, start with the account and discovery material in the Infrai documentation.

title: Your static site probably doesn’t need React
description:
About a year ago, when I was a fledgling frontend developer, I created a website with React. This website was a single page app built with Vite and React, and it used all the cutting edge bells and whistles but had only one problem: it wasn’t performant. On mobile, the main content took 11.3 seconds to show up; after I rebuilt it in Astro, it took 2.1.

Evaluating this site a year ago, it was simple to see the pitfalls I fell into: a lot of images were uncompressed, and I was shipping way more than necessary to the client. It got me thinking however, though a lot of these mistakes were my fault, wouldn’t it be nice if there was a framework that blocked a lot of these mistakes by default? Something like… Astro?

For those that may not be familiar, Astro is a frontend framework that by default, ships no JavaScript to the client. It’s based on default web technologies i.e HTML and CSS. Because of this, it’s extremely performant. You opt in to complexity, unlike most frameworks where you opt out.

The claim of this article, is that for your static, content driven site, no matter what experience in development you have, you probably don’t need React. I’ll start by walking through a few pitfalls I made in my earlier project and show how Astro, by default, would have prevented this.

Fault 1: The site wasn’t rendered until it received all the JavaScript required for the page to render. In React, the fix is a framework that renders the HTML ahead of time, like Next.js. In Astro however, each component by default is an island. This is a static wrapped server rendered piece of html with zero JavaScript by default. When you need interactivity, you isolate that piece (said island) and you tell Astro when and how to load that island. These islands are framework agnostic, so you can have islands of React, Svelte, Vue, no problem.

Fault 2: Embarrassing mistake upcoming😂, but I was shipping the admin page with the blog editor — and that includes the login, image upload, you get the picture — to the client. So all visitors of the site were receiving a huge amount of JavaScript that wasn’t even being used: one 752 KB bundle, with about 60% of it unused on the homepage. React.lazy could have split the admin out, but I didn’t know to reach for it. If I was using Astro, each page would only ship the JavaScript for its own islands, so the admin code would have stayed on the admin page unless I deliberately made the mistake.

React is an extremely powerful tool, and one of the best we have in our toolbelts as developers — this article is not meant to dunk on it. In fact, the Astro version of the site still uses React islands for things like the slideshow and the blog list. For web apps generally, sites or apps managing complex state, React proves invaluable. This article is mainly meant to point out that for static content sites however, or for developers early on in their career, Astro is well, like a gas lighter — off by default. You light the stove and it’s automatically off even if you forget. React however, is like a naked match flame. Very powerful and versatile, but easier to burn the house down with😂

title: What "accurate" means for a geocoder, and how I decide a change is safe
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

“How accurate is it?” sounds like one question, but a geocoder answers several at once. Did it find anything? Is the answer in the right country? Is the point close enough to be useful? Is it as precise as the address you sent, a house for a house and a town for a town? And when it returns a house number or a postcode, does that agree with yours?

This post explains how I score those questions for OpenGeocoding, how close I count as close enough, which losses I accept when I change the engine, and how I keep the test set from grading the index on its own data. The first post has the pass rates; this one is about what stands behind them.

A pass has several conditions

The scorer looks only at the first result. A best-of-several answer would flatter every service, and an application usually takes the first one. It ignores the confidence each service reports, because those numbers don’t mean the same thing from one provider to the next. A case then passes when the answer meets all of these, taken from the case’s expectation (what a pass means):

  • the country is one of the allowed countries;
  • the point is within the case’s distance tolerance;
  • the precision is within the allowed range, so a house case can’t pass on a street;
  • a house number or postcode it returns agrees with the request.

Failures are not one bucket either. The evaluation guide separates too_coarse (right country or region, but not the precision the address asked for), abstain, near_miss, far_miss (more than 100 km away), wrong_country and a few others. They matter because they aren’t equally bad. A country answer to a street address is a different failure from a point in another country, and the second is the more serious one.

How close is close enough

The tolerance depends on what the case asks for, and the corpus records it per case instead of using one global number:

  • Registry houses: the tolerance is recorded on each case. The US sample uses 150 m, or 300 m where the register places the point at a parcel centroid, and a separate sample of US addresses with loosely placed points is scored at 500 m and reported apart (US sample).
  • Landmarks: 1 km. Those cases measure coarse coverage, not the position of an entrance.
  • Company-address town cases: 5 km, rising to 10 km from 50,000 people and 20 km from a million (GLEIF cases).
  • Indonesian villages: twice the radius of a circle with the village’s area, between 2 and 25 km.

None of this tells you whether a point is the front door. The scorecard says so directly: the pass rates don’t measure postal deliverability, entrance accuracy or unit correctness. Whether 150 m is good enough depends on your workload. For enriching company records with a town and a region it is more than you need. For routing a courier to a flat it is not enough.

Which losses I accept when I change the engine

A pass rate says how good the engine is. A change needs a different question: what did it break? Every pull request that touches the service, its data or the test corpus is evaluated against the commit it branched from, on the same index, and the two runs are compared case by case (gates).

The rule has one exception:

  • A case that passed before and fails now fails the change, as does a case that moves to a worse failure class and a new critical result.
  • The exception is the panel built from OpenStreetMap addresses, which measures agreement with data the index itself reads. There I accept at most 5 locations that newly fail, and only when at least 5 times as many newly pass and nothing else fails.
  • Losses on registries, Wikidata, GLEIF and constructed cases are never traded for gains elsewhere, because those measure accuracy against sources outside the index.
  • Speed is a separate gate: the change fails if SearchAddress, SuggestAddress or ReverseGeocode gets more than 15% slower in total, at p50, p90 or p99.

So the acceptable loss is zero where the evidence is independent, and a small, explicit trade where it is not. Two experiments in the engine’s notes show why I keep it strict. A change to town matching reached 2,360 passing towns, but introduced 52 regressions where a coarse answer or an abstention became a point more than 5 km from the expected one. I dropped it. The version I kept finds 1,880 and, in the local comparison, adds no newly failing check. Another prototype gained 17 passes by trusting a place-type word alone, and it selected the wrong Samoa namesake, so I rejected that too.

A gate like this measures change, not accuracy. It tells me a commit didn’t make the cases I know about worse. It says nothing about the addresses nobody wrote a case for.

Not grading the index on its own data

A geocoder tested on the data it was built from will look good. The corpus has several defences against that, and each has a limit.

Expected answers come from outside the engine. Wikidata, national address registries, the US Census geocoder and similar sources provide them, never Nominatim, another geocoder or this service. GeoNames and Overture, which the index also reads, only chose which places to ask about.

Registry samples start from the registry. Cases first drawn from the index’s own Overture data and then checked against a register can’t show an address the index lacks, so recall stays invisible. The registry samples are drawn from the register first, and the index is asked about whatever was drawn (registry-first samples).

Overlap is reported, not hidden. Several registries used as expectations are also inputs to the index, so in those countries a pass measures fidelity to the register. The OpenStreetMap panel measures agreement with the index’s own source. Wikidata towns partly come from GeoNames, so some town gains reflect a shared origin. The reports group results by kind of evidence so the independent sources are not blended with the self-referential ones.

Balance, and how much a number can carry

Counts per country are not equal, and the headline rate depends on that. Town cases take up to 100 settlements per country, company-address cases up to 50 and the landmark house-coverage cases 20, so no country dominates those groups. The registry samples differ in size: from 120 cases for French Polynesia to 2,794 for South Korea, and they make up most of the 29,013-query selection that the published pass rate is computed on. That is why the scorecard also breaks results down by cohort and by registry, and why the cohorts differ in level and difficulty.

Variants of one location (a typo, a missing country) share a key, so they don’t count as independent places. About one location in five is held out from development and reported separately. With around 250 cases in a slice, the evaluation guide notes, an aggregate rate carries several points of uncertainty, and a single country’s row is one piece of evidence rather than a rate. I read the per-country tables that way, and I’d ask you to as well.

One more limit applies to all of it: this is a vendor-run evaluation on my own corpus, as the scorecard states at the top, and human review of the cases is still pending.

What to do with this

Use the same method on a sample of your own addresses. Decide first what close enough means for your workload: a town for enriching profiles, a house within 150 m for deliveries. Then geocode a few hundred addresses from each country you care about and look at the failures, not only the rate. The free plan has 50,000 requests a month with no card, and the bulk geocoding guide has a script that geocodes a CSV. The methodology is in the evaluation guide, and if a country of yours behaves worse than these tables suggest, I’d like to hear about it.

title: A coding agent is only as good as its harness
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

A coding agent can write a fix for a geocoding bug in minutes. The hard part is knowing whether the fix is right, and whether it quietly broke something in another country. That is a question for the harness the agent works in, not for the agent. This post describes the harness around the OpenGeocoding engine: what checks every change, why the world index had to rebuild quickly for any of it to work, and the part that still isn’t stable, which is the speed gate.

The engine’s public repository merged 281 pull requests between 12 and 27 October 2026, and many of them were written by a coding agent. At that pace, I can’t judge every change by reading it. I need the checks to tell me what the change did to the whole world.

Why a geocoder needs this more than most code

Address matching is a long list of rules that interact. The engine has rules for Japanese block addresses, Korean road names, Dutch postcodes, Czech house numbers and many others (the first post has a few examples). A rule that helps one country can change the answer for an address somewhere else, and nothing in the code tells you where. Unit tests catch the cases you thought of. What I needed was a check that runs every case I have, in every country, on every change.

A world index that rebuilds in minutes

That check is only meaningful on a full world index. A synthetic test world is useful for logic, but the regressions that matter come from real data: a street in Australia that happens to share its name with a town, a Japanese address whose block number sits in a different field than expected.

So the gate needs the real index, and the base and head of a pull request have to be compared on the same one. Changes to the index format are frequent: 28 commits between 13 and 27 October set a new builder hash, and each of them names a new world index. With an import that takes days, as a Nominatim planet import does, testing each of those changes against the world wouldn’t be practical.

The engine’s builder produces the world index in about 7 min on one machine (build record). That number is the foundation of everything below. When a change alters the index, the agent’s instructions say to rebuild it locally and run the comparison there before pushing, rather than wait for CI. On the cluster that runs the CI gate, a first build for a new builder is slower and can take hours, so the local build is what keeps the loop short.

Expected answers from registries, never from a geocoder

The gold suite takes its expected answers from official and public reference sources: national address registries, Wikidata, the US Census geocoder and others. They are never taken from Nominatim, another geocoder or this engine’s own output. The cases are generated by a command, evaluate build-gold, from a list of seeds, and the generated file is never edited by hand. The suite also includes a panel of addresses drawn from OpenStreetMap; since the index reads much of the same data, that panel measures agreement rather than accuracy, and it catches regressions all the same. Today the whole suite has 36,920 cases (evaluation guide).

The rules in the engine’s AGENTS.md matter here as much as the data. An agent with a failing check has an easy way out: loosen the expectation. The instructions close that door explicitly. Expectations are never weakened, cases are never dropped, and a failure is never relabelled to make a gate pass. Known failures carry a known_failure label with their cause, stay visible in every report, and the label comes off only after a fix is verified. About one location in five is held out by a stable hash and kept out of tuning.

Base against head, on every pull request

Every pull request that touches the service, its data or the corpus gets a staging image, and its merge base already has one from main. A private cluster evaluates both images on one full world index and compares the two runs. The result comes back as two comments on the pull request (how the gate works):

  • gold-full, the quality check: passing checks per RPC on both sides, pass rates for each country where anything changed, and the cases that changed. It fails on any case that newly fails, fails in a worse way, or gives a new critical result.
  • gold-speed, the latency check: SearchAddress, SuggestAddress and ReverseGeocode timings on both sides. It fails when the total, p50, p90 or p99 of any of them is more than 10% slower.

The comparison is relative on purpose. It answers “what did this change do?”, not “how good is the engine?“. A wrong answer counts as worse than no answer, so a case that used to abstain and now returns a nearby but wrong place fails the gate, even when the new answer looks plausible.

Alongside the gold suite, 1,000 real address strings from 125 countries are kept as a snapshot, one row per address (address snapshots). They have no expected answers, so they don’t measure accuracy, but a changed answer shows up as one changed line in the pull request’s diff. And every night at 01:00 UTC, the same suite runs on the newest commit of main and updates one issue with pass rates by country and a 14-night history.

A worked example

Pull request #223 set out to fix Australian addresses written with the street before the number, such as “Panorama Place 3, Maleny”. The engine was matching “Maleny” to house 3 on Maleny Vista, a street that merely resembles the town’s name.

The first version ran one rule, for venues, before another, for village names. That reorder also fixed cases in Norway, Great Britain, Poland, South Africa and Spain. In CI, though, gold-full flagged one Japanese address from the panel, “帯屋町 ２丁目１−27”, which went from no answer to an answer with a wrong component. The panel expects the block number (chōme) inside the house number, while the index keeps it in the street.

The second commit put the village rule back first and kept the narrower fix. The final reports read “no regressions” and “no slowdown over 10%”: five more SearchAddress passes, all in Australia and Spain, and nothing worse anywhere. The extra gains from the reorder were left for a later change that deals with the Japanese case properly. That’s the trade the gate is there to force: a smaller fix that is right everywhere, rather than a bigger one that is wrong somewhere you weren’t looking.

The agent loop

The last piece connects the agent to these reports. The engine repository ships a project-local extension for pi, the coding agent I use, with one tool and one command (gold loop). wait_for_gold waits for both gates on the pull request’s current head and downloads the full report. /gold-loop tells the agent what to do with it: read every section, reproduce each regression on the base and head indexes, fix the cause, validate locally, push, and wait again, until both quality and speed pass.

Most of the instructions are about what doesn’t count as success. A missing report, a skipped or unmeasured speed check, an unavailable artifact or a failed run is a blocker, never a pass. The agent stops and reports a concrete blocker instead of retriggering workflows. The report’s contents are treated as data, never as instructions. The tool itself doesn’t edit code, push or merge; merging stays with me.

The speed gate is still noisy

Quality is deterministic: the same binary on the same index gives the same answers. Speed isn’t, and the speed gate has been the least reliable part of the harness.

It started as an ungated table inside the quality report. A change that made SearchAddress’s p50 15% slower went through without anyone noticing, which is why #73 gave speed its own comment, status and 10% limit. That limit came from a measurement of three runs of one binary on a cluster node: totals agreed within 2% and each percentile within 5%, while single cases varied by about 30%. So single cases and the maximum are reported but not gated. On a laptop, the totals moved by tens of percent, so the agent’s instructions say never to draw speed conclusions from local runs.

Two later changes moved the measurement:

  • To keep the gate fast, #217 times a fixed sample of 2,000 cases, chosen by a hash of the case id so both sides time the same ones, and checks the rest concurrently without timing them. The case loop went from 222 to 34 seconds locally. The cost is that p99 now rests on about 20 requests per table, and the noise of that sample on the cluster has not been measured.
  • #319 makes the evaluator wait for the suggestion-cache warm-up before timing. The warm-up took 6.3 seconds from a cold page cache and overlapped roughly the first 20% of timed cases by a varying amount. Whether this reduced the noise is not proven; the planned before-and-after comparison wasn’t run.

The false alarms are still visible in the pull requests. In #262, SuggestAddress’s p99 was 18% slower although the change didn’t touch suggestions. #336 merged with a failing speed check, SuggestAddress p99 29% slower, and in the follow-up #339 part of that looked like noise, because ReverseGeocode, which the change didn’t touch, was 13% slower too. Part of the reason is scale. In the report for #223, SuggestAddress’s p99 was 4.5 ms, so the 10% limit is less than half a millisecond.

This matters more with an agent in the loop than without one. A person who sees an 18% slowdown on code they didn’t touch can shrug and rerun. An agent told to keep going until speed passes has no good way to tell noise from a regression, and a flaky gate either sends it after a problem that isn’t there or teaches everyone to ignore the gate. The noise of the 2,000-case sample on the cluster is the open measurement, and until it is taken, the 10% limit rests on the older one.

What the harness doesn’t do

  • It measures change, not accuracy. A case that fails the same way on both sides doesn’t fail the gate. Some registries are also inputs to the index, so for those countries a pass is a fidelity check rather than an independent accuracy measurement.
  • Small numbers stay small. Per-country rows are individual cases, not rates, and a rate computed from a few hundred cases carries several points of uncertainty.
  • The report has no per-case responses. The cluster returns only the report, so debugging a listed case means rerunning it locally on an index from the same builder.
  • Outside contributions need approval. Pull requests from people outside the project wait for a reviewer, because approving one runs that author’s code in the cluster.

None of this makes the agent smarter. It makes the agent’s work checkable, quickly and against the whole world, and that is what lets me merge it.

The engine, its evaluation tools and the gold loop are on GitHub: Mokto/opengeocoding. The evaluation guide and AGENTS.md are the best places to start if you want to build something similar for your own project.

title: Building a geocoder whose world index rebuilds in minutes
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

I build and run OpenGeocoding on my own: a geocoding engine written in Rust, and a hosted API in front of it. This post covers why I built it, how it works, how I measure it and where it is still weak.

Updated 5 November 2026: the benchmark and coverage figures now measure release 1.7.0.

The problem: an index you can’t rebuild

Geocoding at scale means turning a lot of messy text into coordinates. Take a team that receives a few million company addresses, job locations and profile locations a month, in dozens of languages and formats, and needs a country, a region and, where the data allows, a house for each one. The engine’s unscored test sample is 1,000 real strings of that kind.

I first tried to build on Nominatim, the geocoder behind openstreetmap.org. It is good software, but its build time was the problem. Its installation guide strongly recommends 128 GB of RAM or more for a planet import, requires at least 1 TB of disk, and describes the import as taking around 2.5 days on a well-configured machine.

When a rebuild takes days, you don’t rebuild often. Data updates wait. It also means you can’t test a change to parsing or ranking against the whole world, because the thing you would test against takes days to produce. I wanted an index I could rebuild whenever the code or the data changed.

What I built

OpenGeocoding is one Rust process. It parses an address with libpostal, looks it up in a read-only index and answers. There is no database, and nothing is downloaded at runtime: the index and the libpostal models are mounted read-only.

The index is built from Overture Maps, with OpenStreetMap, OpenAddresses and GeoNames as additional inputs. Places, streets and postcodes go into Tantivy, the Rust equivalent of Lucene; house numbers go into finite-state transducers beside it. Dropping the Nominatim base for a search-engine index was the most important decision in the project.

The last recorded world build, on 17 October 2026, took 409 seconds on an 18-core Apple M5 Max with 64 GB of RAM, with a 32.2 GB peak memory footprint and a result of about 16 GB on disk. Source downloads are not included (build record and methodology). This is not a like-for-like comparison with a Nominatim import: the inputs, the indexing work and the hardware all differ. What it changed is how I work. I rebuild the index whenever the builder or one of its source datasets changes.

Rules per country, not exceptions per address

Every country writes addresses differently, and libpostal, a statistical parser, gets some of them wrong. The tempting fix is to patch the address that failed. I try never to do that, and to write the rule for the country instead.

Postcodes are the simplest example. The engine knows the postcode shape of 21 countries:

("gb", r"^[A-Z]{1,2}\d[A-Z\d]?(\d[A-Z]{2})?$"),
("nl", r"^\d{4}([A-Z]{2})?$"),
("ca", r"^[A-Z]\d[A-Z](\d[A-Z]\d)?$"),
("pt", r"^\d{4}(\d{3})?$"),
("us", r"^\d{5}(\d{4})?$"),
("de", r"^\d{5}$"),

The table is used to recover a postcode the parser labelled as something else, and to decide whether a postcode belongs to the country the query names. Other rules work the same way: German, Austrian and Swiss street names with a misspelt “strasse”, Portuguese streets under the national register’s abbreviated names, Japanese block addresses the engine reads itself because libpostal splits them, and Korean road-name addresses resolved through their province, city and district hierarchy.

What keeps this honest is a gate. Every pull request that touches the engine runs the full test suite on a full world index, base against head. A case that newly fails, or fails in a worse way, fails the change, and expectations are never loosened to make it pass (evaluation guide). A one-off patch for one address usually breaks another one somewhere else, and the gate shows it.

One process, in Rust

An early version ran the index as a separate process and called it over HTTP. Merging the two into one process took one connection from about 220 to about 360 requests per second, and memory from 6.0 GB to 3.5 GB. Later work on how lookups use Tantivy cut CPU time per request from 8.2 ms to 1.4 ms, mostly by merging index segments at build time and by filtering document kinds in the collector instead of walking a term with 40 million postings. These were single measurements on a busy laptop, recorded in the lookup history, and they are not comparable with the benchmark below.

The hosted API is a separate service

The geocoder stays stateless: no authentication, no database, no writes. Everything commercial lives in a separate service. A Rust edge in front of the geocoder holds API keys, per-second limits and credit balances in memory, so no request waits on Postgres. Every 5 seconds it flushes usage counts and reloads keys and balances. Each flush writes its batch number and the usage counts in one transaction, so a retried batch is never billed twice. If Postgres goes down, the edge keeps serving from its last snapshot. Only successful replies are billed.

How accuracy is measured

The test corpus takes its expected answers from official registries and public reference sources: Wikidata, France’s Base Adresse Nationale, the Dutch BAG, the US Census geocoder, postcodes.io, Kartverket, swisstopo, CartoCiudad and other national address registries. Never from Nominatim, from another geocoder, or from this engine. A case passes when the first result is in the right country, within the case’s distance tolerance and at the right precision (house, street or town), and any house number or postcode it returns agrees with the request.

I sent every provider the same queries, with no country or proximity hints, between 17 October and 5 November 2026, and scored release 1.7.0 against their answers (scorecard and methodology):

Service Full corpus (29,013 queries) US/Canada subset (1,947)
OpenGeocoding 85.6% 97.7%
Geoapify 70.5% 81.0%
OpenCage 51.3% 50.8%
geocode.maps.co 42.8% 38.7%
Geocodio not measured 89.3%

I ran this evaluation myself, on my own corpus, so read it with the caveats in the scorecard. Several national registries used as expectations (the US, the Netherlands, France, Norway, Switzerland, Spain, Czechia) are also inputs to the index, so in those countries a pass measures fidelity to the register, not independent accuracy. The corpus is not a random sample, and most of its cases were available while I developed the engine; on the fifth of locations held out from development, OpenGeocoding passed 86.4%. The OpenGeocoding row ran locally on an index from the release’s builder, close to but not identical to production. These are pass rates on a test corpus, not a production accuracy estimate.

Performance

On the hosted API, the geocoder’s average processing time was 5 ms over about 87,864 completed requests in the 24 hours to 19 October 2026, 11:55 CEST. That excludes the edge, the network and response delivery (measurement details).

For throughput, I benchmarked release 0.14.0 on 19 October 2026: one Kubernetes pod, 16 concurrent connections, three runs of 20,000 requests each. The runs reached 2,675, 2,656 and 1,774 queries per second, with p95 latency between 18.4 and 29.9 ms, and all 60,000 requests completed without errors. The pod requested one CPU with no limit and used 4.1 to 5.0 cores of a shared Intel Core i5-13500. The client cycled through 1,000 repeating queries with the parse cache warm, and called the pod directly, bypassing the ingress, TLS and the edge. It is a short warm-cache run, not a sustained capacity figure. The third run was slower than the first two; the methodology and raw record has all three.

Where it is weak

House-level coverage across most of Asia and Africa is still poor. In the coverage measurement of the release 1.7.0 world index, India has 85,266 house numbers for 1.46 billion people, China 44,614, Indonesia 68,068, Pakistan 96,337, Nigeria 7,245 and Ethiopia 424. The United States has about 113 million, France 27 million, Japan 22 million and Taiwan 5.7 million. In the weak countries, expect a town or a street, not a house. The benchmark shows the same thing: of 151 street and house cases in Asian countries such as Malaysia, the Philippines, India, Vietnam and Thailand, OpenGeocoding passed 43, against 61 for Geoapify, and of 2,794 Korean school addresses, 795.

The engine is strongest where open address data is dense: North America, most of Europe, Australia and New Zealand, and a few others such as Japan and Taiwan. Outside those, treat it as a town and region geocoder until you have checked your own addresses, and check your towns too: in the 78 countries and territories the corpus has no registry for, OpenGeocoding found 58.4% of 3,240 towns, behind Geoapify (68.4%) and OpenCage (66.4%), mostly because small settlements are missing from the index. The index has streets in 240+ countries and territories, but streets everywhere is not houses everywhere. Asia and Africa are what I’m working on next.

The licence

The engine is source-available under PolyForm Shield 1.0.0, not open source. You can read it, run it, modify it and redistribute it, including commercially, and you can self-host it inside your own product. What you can’t do is offer a product that competes with it, for example by taking the engine and selling it as a geocoding API. A free competing service counts too. I picked it so the project can’t simply be taken and resold as someone else’s API.

The data keeps its own licences: OpenStreetMap and parts of Overture are under the ODbL, and the attributions page lists every source.

Pricing

The free plan has 50,000 requests a month at 2 requests per second, with no card. Paid plans start at $29 a month for 300,000 requests. Autocomplete is free, and when credits run out billable calls stop instead of creating an overage charge (pricing).

Try it

The fastest way to judge it is the demo on the homepage: type an address from your own data, no account needed. The API docs cover search, autocomplete, reverse geocoding and regions, and the engine is on GitHub. If it gets your country wrong, I want to hear about it.

title: Billing every API request exactly once, without a database on the request path
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. This article originally appeared on the OpenGeocoding blog on 20 October 2026. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

The first post was about the geocoding engine. This one is about the smaller service in front of it: the edge that checks API keys, applies rate limits, spends credits and counts usage for billing. It is written in Rust like the engine, runs on Kubernetes as several identical replicas, and one rule shaped all of it: nothing on the request path waits for a database.

The edge lives in a private repository, so I’ll describe it rather than link to it. The one code sample below is a simplified version of the real query.

Why not write to the database on every request

The obvious design is to look up the key and write a usage row in Postgres for every request. It’s simple and exact, and it’s what I considered first. The problem is throughput. In the engine’s benchmark, a single geocoder pod served 1,700+ searches a second (methodology). If every one of those requests also writes to Postgres, the database has to sustain the same rate, for all customers at once, and keep sustaining it as the geocoder scales out. The engine would only be as fast as the billing database behind it.

Latency points the same way. The geocoder’s average processing time is 5 ms (how it’s measured). A database round trip on every call would add its own latency on top, and a slow or unavailable database would become a slow or unavailable API.

How backend processing time was measured

The request-weighted mean was 4.71 ms across approximately 87,864 completed RPC observations, from 18 October 2026, 11:55 CEST to 19 October 2026, 11:55 CEST, rounded to the nearest millisecond on the homepage. The mean divides the increase in summed gRPC handling time by the increase in completed RPC observations over that window.

Over 99.9% were address searches, so this is not an all-endpoint benchmark. The timer excludes the public API edge, network time and response serialization/delivery. Public and internal callers are not distinguished. Rollouts and missed scrapes limit completeness; this is a dated observation, not a latency guarantee.

So keys, limits and balances live in memory, and Postgres is updated in the background.

Kubernetes first

Everything runs on Kubernetes, and I designed it that way from the start rather than moving it there later. Each part is a Deployment with several identical replicas spread across nodes, and none of them assumes it is the only copy:

  • The geocoder is stateless and read-only. Each pod pulls a complete, immutable index from an S3-compatible store in an init container and serves it from a read-only volume. A small leader, one of two pods sharing a Kubernetes Lease, starts a build Job when the index named by the chart’s settings isn’t in the store yet, and rolls out the serving pods once it is. New pods load their index before old ones stop, so a rebuild never interrupts serving (engine Helm chart).
  • The edge, the subject of this post, runs three replicas by default. Each has its own in-memory snapshot, its own counts and its own random ID. The replicas never talk to each other; they only meet in Postgres, every few seconds.
  • The web app (marketing site, dashboard and signup) also runs three replicas.

In front of the edge, an L7 ingress balances each HTTP request and gRPC call across pods, not each connection. Rollouts start a new pod before removing an old one, and disruption budgets keep node drains to one pod at a time.

Most of what follows is about how the edge replicas agree on keys, limits and money without asking each other.

What a request does

For each request, the edge:

  1. hashes the API key with SHA-256 and looks it up in an in-memory snapshot of active keys;
  2. takes a token from the account’s per-second bucket;
  3. for billable operations, checks the account’s remaining credits;
  4. calls the geocoder;
  5. counts the request if it succeeded.

“Succeeded” is narrow on purpose. Only a JSON 2xx reply or a gRPC reply whose final grpc-status is 0 is billed. Over gRPC, an HTTP 200 can still end with an error status in the trailers, so the edge buffers unary gRPC replies through their trailers before it counts anything. Backend failures return a generic error and aren’t billed. Autocomplete and region lookups need a key and share the rate limit, but they don’t spend credits.

The remaining credits are worked out locally: the balance from the last Postgres load, minus the requests this replica has counted that the balance doesn’t include yet. When that reaches zero, billable calls get a 429. There is no metered overage.

Each replica subtracts only its own counts. Requests served by the other replicas reach its balance through Postgres, after their next sync and its next reload. That gap of a few seconds is where the small overshoot described at the end comes from.

The 5-second sync

Every 5 seconds, each edge replica runs one sync. It takes its pending counts as a batch, gives the batch the next sequence number and writes it in a single transaction:

BEGIN;
-- Adds nothing if this batch was already written.
INSERT INTO edge_flush (edge_id, seq)
VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

-- Only when that insert added a row:
INSERT INTO usage (key_id, day, count)
SELECT * FROM UNNEST($3::uuid[], $4::date[], $5::bigint[])
ON CONFLICT (key_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET count = usage.count + EXCLUDED.count;

-- Lock the accounts' credit grants, then spend the batch
-- from the grant that expires soonest.
SELECT 1 FROM credit_grant
WHERE user_id = ANY($6) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE credit_grant SET used = used + ...;
COMMIT;

The edge_flush row is what makes it exactly once. edge_id is a random ID each edge process picks when it starts, and seq numbers its batches, so replicas flush independently and their batches never collide. If the transaction fails, or commits but the reply never arrives, the batch stays in memory with the same sequence number and is sent again on the next sync. A retry of a batch that already committed hits the existing row and adds nothing; a retry of one that didn’t commit writes it for the first time. Either way, it lands once. A test against a real Postgres database flushes the same batch twice and checks the count. The row is written even when the batch is empty, so it also serves as the replica’s heartbeat.

Credits are spent in the same transaction. Each paid period and each free month is a separate grant with its own expiry, and a batch is spent from the grant that expires soonest. Locking the account’s grant rows first means two replicas flushing at the same moment take turns instead of spending the same credits twice.

After the commit, the sync reloads active keys, each account’s per-second limit and balance, and the number of edge replicas that flushed in the last 15 seconds. A batch stays counted against the local balance until a reload that includes it succeeds, so there is no moment where requests are neither in Postgres nor in memory.

For Postgres, this means one write transaction per replica every 5 seconds, with rows per key and day rather than per request.

Rate limits without shared state

Rate limits are the part I simplified most. A strict per-account limit across several replicas needs a shared counter, usually Redis, consulted on every request. Instead, each replica takes its share. With N replicas that sent a heartbeat in the last 15 seconds, an account’s bucket on each replica refills at limit / N tokens a second and holds at most the larger of limit / N and 2 tokens.

As an example, take the free plan’s 2 requests a second across 5 replicas. Each replica refills at 0.4 a second and holds 2 tokens. Starting from full buckets, a client can make up to 10 requests, and then the refill settles at 2 a second overall. The two-token minimum absorbs short bursts when the load balancer happens to send a few requests to the same replica. Retry-After is rounded up to the next local token, so an empty bucket in that example answers with 3 seconds rather than a fixed 1.

Scaling needs no configuration. A new replica’s first sync is also its first heartbeat, so the others count it at their next reload, within 5 seconds, and lower their share. When a replica stops, its last heartbeat ages out after 15 seconds and the others raise their share at their next reload. While that happens, the shares are briefly off, which is one of the inaccuracies listed below.

When Postgres is down

If Postgres is unreachable, the edge keeps serving from its last snapshot and keeps counting in memory, and the counts are written once the database is back. I chose to use a snapshot of any age rather than turn away paying customers. Signup, dashboard changes and the website demo do stop, because they need the database. The edge’s liveness check doesn’t depend on Postgres, so an outage never makes Kubernetes restart pods that are holding cached keys and unflushed usage.

A new edge pod can’t load keys without Postgres, so it stays not ready while the existing pods carry the traffic. A rollout during an outage stalls instead of replacing working pods with ones that can’t serve.

Shutting down without losing usage

Rollouts are the other moment where counts could go missing. Kubernetes replaces edge pods one at a time, starting the new one before the old one stops. On SIGTERM, the edge drains in-flight requests for up to 30 seconds, stops its background sync, then freezes billing and flushes everything still pending, retrying for up to 15 seconds. A request that finishes after billing is frozen gets an “unavailable” error instead of a successful reply that would never be billed. If the final flush still fails, the edge logs the lost usage and exits with a nonzero status. These budgets, a 10-second preStop delay and the error reporter’s 2-second close timeout all fit in Kubernetes’ 60-second grace period.

What this costs

The design accepts a few known inaccuracies. I’d rather list them here than have someone find them later:

  • A replica that crashes loses up to one sync interval, 5 seconds, of counts. Those requests are never billed.
  • A balance can be overspent by roughly one sync of traffic plus bucket bursts. At the Growth plan’s 25 requests a second, that is about 125 requests plus bursts.
  • Rate limits are approximate. Burst capacity grows with the number of replicas, restarts and changes in the replica count can briefly allow extra bursts or throttle early, and uneven routing can return a 429 below the account’s nominal rate.
  • A persistent connection pinned to one pod only gets that pod’s share of the limit, so the load balancer has to balance each HTTP request and gRPC call, not each connection.
  • Successful replies are charged when they are prepared, before delivery. A client that disconnects while the reply is on its way is still billed for the work.

Most of these fall in the customer’s favour. Lost counts are never billed, and an overspent balance means a few free requests rather than an unexpected invoice, because there is no overage to bill.

The improvement I’d like to make later is sticky routing per account. If the ingress sent every request from one account to the same edge replica, that replica would hold the account’s whole rate limit and see all of its unflushed usage. Limits and balance checks would then be exact, without Redis and without a network call on the request path. It isn’t built yet, and it brings its own trade-offs. The ingress only sees the API key, not the account, so an account with several keys needs a way to land on the same replica. A very busy account would load a single replica. And when replicas are added or removed, some accounts move to another replica and start there with a fresh bucket.

Shared counters in Redis would also make the limits exact, but at the cost of a round trip on every request, and I’d rather not pay that. Keeping Postgres in the background also keeps another option open: because the edge only talks to Postgres in the background, a second region with its own edge and geocoder could use a distant database without slowing anyone down.

Try it

The free plan includes 50,000 requests a month at 2 requests a second, with no card. Create a free account, make a few calls, and you’ll see them in the dashboard’s usage, written by the sync described above.

title: Mintu v0.2.3: Building Desktop Automation, Apple-Style Spring Physics, and Safe Evaluators with Tauri & Rust
description:
Introduction

With the release of Mintu v0.2.3, our open-source Dynamic Island desktop companion advances from a passive interface into an active, automated desktop assistant.

Built with Tauri v2, Rust, and TypeScript, Mintu runs locally with offline models (via llama.cpp) or connects to modern cloud providers. This release tackles core user experience pain points, desktop automation, and runtime security.

What We Built in v0.2.3

1. Real Desktop Automation

Users can now delegate OS-level tasks directly to the model:

  • VS Code Code Generation (create_code_file): Instruct the pet to write scripts in Python, TypeScript, Rust, or HTML and immediately launch them in VS Code.
  • Media Integration (play_spotify & search_youtube): Direct playback commands for songs, albums, and video tutorials.
  • Desktop Guidance (desktop_guide): Screen guidance and cursor positioning via native Win32 APIs (SetCursorPos).

2. Solving the Streaming Auto-Scroll Problem

In real-time token streaming interfaces, unconditionally setting scrollTop = scrollHeight traps the user at the bottom of the viewport.

In v0.2.3, we introduced user scroll intent detection:

  • The scroll area tracks upward displacement (distanceFromBottom > 50).
  • If the user scrolls up to inspect previous code snippets or responses, token streaming updates the DOM without dragging the viewport down.
  • When the user scrolls back to the bottom or submits a new message, automatic following resumes.

3. Apple-Inspired Spring Morph on Music Events

Whenever media playback starts or a track changes, the island applies spring physics velocity impulses:

  • springWidth and springHeight expand fluidly before settling into equilibrium.
  • A radial background glow samples the dominant tones of the active track's album cover art.

4. Expanded Model Catalog

  • Local: Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B for local code authoring and DeepSeek-R1 Distill Qwen 1.5B for step-by-step reasoning.
  • Cloud: Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek-R1 Reasoner, and OpenAI o3-mini.
  • Every catalog entry now indicates tool-calling compatibility so users know which models can execute desktop actions.

5. Comprehensive Security Hardening

  • Replaced all legacy new Function math execution with a pure, recursive-descent math parser supporting operators (+, -, *, /, %, ^, **), unary signs, and division-by-zero protection.
  • Hardened file sandboxing to strictly use Rust internal directories.
  • Enabled production Content Security Policy (CSP) blocking external eval.

Open Source & Community

Mintu is free and open-source under the MIT license.

  • GitHub: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu
  • v0.2.3 Release: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu/releases/tag/v0.2.3

title: Before You Ship an AI-Built Web Feature, Test the Browser Fallback
description:
Imagine you're building a workshop registration page. An AI coding tool adds a polished session picker. You open the page, pick the afternoon slot, and register. Good enough to send to the client?

Not yet. You know the picker worked in the browser you opened. You don't know what a visitor sees when their browser can't apply the styling or positioning the picker relies on.

This article was prepared with AI assistance. The workshop example is hypothetical.

On November 10, Chrome for Developers announced Modern Web Guidance 1.0, with Firefox and Edge joining the effort. The project gives coding agents web platform guidance that includes browser compatibility data. Its fallback guide makes a distinction worth keeping even if you never install it: sometimes an unsupported feature can disappear harmlessly, and sometimes you need a second way to complete the task.

Here's the release checklist I'd use for that session picker.

1. Name the browsers before you name the solution

Write down the browser and device combinations the feature needs to support. Use the client's known requirements or product traffic when you have it. If you're starting from scratch, pick a reasonable initial support target and label it as an assumption. Don't let the coding tool infer the target from whichever browser happens to be on your laptop.

Baseline is a useful starting point. Newly available means a feature works across its core browsers; widely available means 30 months have passed since that point. Neither tells you which versions your particular visitors run. Ask the assistant to name the exact feature it wants to use and explain how it fits your targets. Check that answer before you approve the approach.

2. Define what must work without the enhancement

For the workshop page, I'd start with a labeled native select and a submit button. If the decorative layout doesn't apply, a user should still be able to see the available sessions, select one, submit, and read which session they booked. The native control doesn't have to look like the enhanced control. It has to finish the same job.

Make that difference explicit in the ticket: "If the enhanced picker isn't supported, show the regular session field. Submitting either version must use the same session identifier and show the same confirmation." Keep the enhancement separate from the submission logic so both paths don't drift into maintaining their own rules for a sold-out slot.

3. Run the same task through both paths

Try a registration in a supported browser, then repeat it where the feature isn't supported. Use test data and check the confirmation, not just whether the button was clickable. On both paths, try submitting without a selection and make sure the error tells you what to fix. Check that you can choose and submit with the keyboard without losing track of focus.

If you can't get the target browser right away, exercising the fallback in a test build can catch a logic error. Record that as fallback-path evidence, not proof that the target browser works. A smaller viewport is useful for layout testing, but it doesn't change which features the browser implements.

My handoff would be two short rows: browser and version, picker path, session chosen, confirmation observed, and any failure. If only one row has results, that's the honest state of the release.

The question isn't whether the enhanced picker looks good. It's whether someone can still register when that enhancement isn't there.

The $3 AI App Builder Starter Prompts help turn a feature request into checks you can actually run. The $9 AI App Builder From Zero e-book covers the path from planning to testing and release. The $10 learning bundle includes both.
